I'll probably keep this simple and sweet, because I want this to be mainly about if you, the reader should buy this game and play it - regardless of my political or religious stance, for or against it.
Simply put, That Dragon, Cancer is about a family's ordeal with their son's cancer, and eventual death. It deals with both the happy moments that are brought about from that small time of interaction, to both the internal turmoil it no doubt brings. It also strives to encapsulate how many of us deal with death, be it an accepting fate, or looking to God for advice.
Does it handle it well? I'd say in 70% of the game, it does. That 30% also isn't bad by any means, but it's done in a prose that gives it an air of presumptiveness that I highly doubt it means to give, but I couldn't help but wanted to move on to the next scene from. That said, That Dragon, Cancer's high moments EASILY overpower these failings, and a few select chapters are exceptionally strong on their own.
To avoid the longwinded discussion of "what is a game" and abuse of funds this title gets tied into, I think this experience is well worth the price. As usual, it's a more whole-hearted reccomendation at a sale price, but I feel it's something that everyone will get something from, be it personally or in a larger sense.

A number of people have been buying this on sale just for the trading cards, but it's actually a great little game.
The block graphics are really well done. The waterfalls in particular are nice, and I get a smile on my face after killing every normal-size bad guy: the legs left standing for a few seconds are pretty funny.
The first two levels are extremely easy, but then it gets much harder quickly. The controls are a little clunky (I've had half a dozen deaths already from poor jumps, and timing melee weapon swings can sometimes be tricky), and there's no tutorial, but it does't take long to get the hang of it.
For the few of you out there with Nvidia 3D Vision, the game even mostly works with that, although the crosshairs are in the wrong place and there's a bit of shadowing at high convergence and depth settings. That said, it works a lot better with 3D Vision than a lot of AAA games do out of the box.
There's no story and sound effects are pretty lacking. The music has even grown on me over the last hour of playing.
Overall, Dead Bits is a fun little game, especially for the price, even without the trading cards. I'll be keeping an eye on anything else this developer produces.

The multiplayer was broken, and still is limited.  Features that existed and functioned well in beta disapeared.  SInce release it seems like a 2 steps forward 1 step back approach is being implemented on the updates.  For every 2 advances in stability or gameplay features we get an update that fundamentally changes the game.  The most recent example of this is the 1.4.2 beta patch.  It promises us more advanced AI and easier management of your empire.  And I suppose it achieves this by eliminating the player ability to micromanage their planets.  Having your planetary governing skills labotomized would make the AI appear to be harder and also simplfies the managing of your empire, but it is done so by taking away a very powerful resource held by every human player, the ability to use ones intelect and planning to stregnthen ones own position.  Now I have every hope that the developers of this game would see the angst bestowed upon the paid customers of this game and remedy this situation.  But until things are fixed and updates stop attempting to take away from the player, I cannot say I am glad that I bought this game and therefor cannot recconmend it.  I hope one day to be able to change my review to positive, but for now it just remains my hope.

As a police officer not too many things can make me cry these days.  I heard the movie UP was supposed to be a tear jerker but it really didn't phase me.  That Dragon, Cancer... well, this game is a different story.  Simply put, this is the most emotional game I've ever played.  I knew the game was only around 2 hours long, and I originally had plans to play another game I recently got immediately after finishing this one, but by the time I finished this game the only thing I wanted to do was pick up my baby boy and hold him tight.
I imagine this game will be more powerful for those who have kids, and I imagine it may even be TOO powerful for those who have had kids with terminal illness or have otherwise lost their children at a young age.
In this game you essentially get a glimpse of what a real family went through with their son, from finding a tumor to hearing the news that chemotherapy had failed and that their son would die within months.  You feel for the parents as they experience a wide range of emotions from sadness, anger, despair, doubt, hope, peace and faith.
Yes, the game has strong religious messages within, but I don't feel this should detract from the game even if you aren't a believer, because this is the real life story of a real family and what they went through, and that includes their faith, their doubts, etc.  Regardless of whether you believe in God or not, you can still relate to these parents' grief and come away with something.
As a cessationistic Christian, I appreciated the fact that this wasn't some implausible story of a boy being miraculously healed or even raised from the dead.  It showed that the parents desperately wished for those things to occur and prayed for them to occur and hoped that they would occur, but ultimately rested in God's wisdom and that He does all things for His glory with the joyful reminder that one day they will see their child again in Heaven.

I was afraid to go ahead with my purchase of this game when I saw the many negative reviews I saw, but in the end I'm so happy I didn't listen!
I love The Neverhood, as well as Skullmonkeys, so much.  I was so happy to see that this team decided to make another game after all these years.
In a lot of the comments I saw that people were not pleased with Armikrog; that it wasn't like The Neverhood. I can't tell if these people are just bitter, or what.  Now I haven't actually beaten the game yet, but from what I've played, it DEFINITELY feels like The Neverhood.  Of course it's not going to be exactly the same, but it's got that spirit.
I haven't encountered any game-breaking bugs (perhaps because of the patches?) but I do see some slip ups here and there programming-wise I suppose (for example, when climbing the tentacles or riding in the little buggy) but nothing that's made me want to stop playing.  The puzzles are a bit challenging, but you do end up going back and forth a lot and clicking a lot of stuff, but isn't that the point?
The only thing that really bothers me is the fact that sometimes when the characters are speaking in-game outside of cutscenes, their mouths don't move.  It's not a big deal, just a little off-putting to me I guess?
Please, if you're a fan, give this game a chance.  It definitely gave me the feels.

This game very effectively captures the 'old school' vibe of the M&M games of the days of yore, but also effectively moves the gameplay into a modern context.  The Xeen series is clearly the main inspiration for this title and the various RPG systems in the game interact effectively to create a compelling and addictive experience.
Exploring the world and discovering new locales is really enjoyable although the graphics are relatively cut-rate compared to similar titles.  Some locations look more impressive than others.  The dungeons in particular are quite well-designed, but the overworld and towns lack visual cohesion and suffer from occasional performance hiccups.
The combat is the meat of the game and  is purely tactical.  Enemies have a variety of abilities to keep you on your toes.  Don't settle into any one tactic or rely on key-spamming, you constantly have to adapt your abilities to the foes at hand.
The lore and world building gets the job done, although exposition is occasionally heavy-handed and long-winded.
The grid movement system may feel constrained at first, but if you think of the game more like a series of large chess-like game boards, it makes more sense.  Simplifying the spacialization of enemies and move options to a grid forces you to make specific choices over what you can do spatially in combat - a good thing for a game of relatively modest scope.
The main point I want to get about this game is that, as much as the game wants you to, you don't have to look at it through a nostalgia lens.  The RPG systems and tactical combat that hold this game together transcend both the weight of history that hangs over the series and expectations from fans of the genre.
Come in with the right amount of expectations and you'll find that the developers acheived what they set out to do: bring the essense of what made the old Might games such a joy to play and put it in a modern context.  Given the modest resources they had at their disposal and the weight of history they had to stare down, I believe Limbic Entertainment succeeded admirably.

That Dragon, Cancer Review
I knew from my first moment laying eyes on the trailer for this game that I would have to approach this game differently. I knew I would need to approach slowly and methodically, understanding what this game really was. That Dragon Cancer is a memoir to the passing of a real life child named Joel Green who was afflicted with cancer. He died at 5 years old, too young and too short a life by any imaginable standard. His parents Ryan and Amy Green created this game as a tribute, a diary, and a message of who Joel was and as a reflection of what he had to endure at such a young age. While I knew what to expect from the game from the moment of its inception, I never truly knew how affecting it would be until the credits rolled. I truly have not played or experienced a work of art quite like this because it his almost wholly unique. This game lies on a plane beyond gruff action protagonists, high score chasing and the pursuit of dominance or “bad-assery” that the majority of the game industry covets and chases at all costs. It is personal at the highest level, a bittersweet invitation into the hardship and inevitability of a real life struggle that the Green family and numerous others around the world have and continue to face every single day. It’s an in-depth look at the role of faith and God in the lives of everyday people, and how it brings reflection and comfort in the most difficult of times. And while this remains a review of the game you’ll be receiving, it’s also a hesitant, judgment-free and meticulously gentle word to compliment the immense payoff you’ll receive from playing the game.
Presentation:
The game has a simplistic and geometric visual style grounded in abstract expression. Many of the textures and details are purposely omitted in favor of primary colors to express concepts and ideas. The visuals evoke many of the games deeply human concepts effortlessly, whether it be mentally in the minds of Ryan, Amy or Joel, or through the depiction of a story accompanied through dialogue and more. Even the digital forms on screen are simple in design but effective enough to know exactly what you are looking at. The music is non-intrusive, harmonious and decisively melancholic, allowing you to get lost in the flowing of emotion on-screen and within ourselves. Even the dialogue spoken by characters is distinctly soft, but poignant due to the subject matter. It’s clear the aesthetics were designed solely so you could get lost in the spirally roller coaster of Joel’s battle with cancer, from his initial diagnosis and all events proceeding it. The games presentation is so hard hitting and vividly affecting because it is all real. These are digital recreations of real events and the thoughts within the Green family’s minds. This is not a video game with a fictional premise or epic narrative. It’s a family surviving the most difficult moment life can bear: the inevitable and helpless loss of a child. Every narrative moment and dialogue delivery held my attention with utmost respect and complicity because I knew these events actually happened. Every moment felt like I had payed to get a personal glimpse into the most haunting and excruciating moment in the Green family’s life, which gave me pause every time the thought crossed my mind.
Gameplay:
The gameplay, outside of a few sections, continues the trend of non-intrusive interaction. Relying almost entirely of pointing on objects and directions to proceed for the next piece of narrative. The game will often let you interact with its world and writings, but almost always in limited fashion to advance the story. It is purposely minimal in scope and practice, which suits it because it’s difficult to imagine a single genre that could adequately encapsulate and push forward this tale by mere gameplay alone. The game has some diversity in various sections that work beautifully as game-driven storytelling. It has a driving section in the Green’s home where you briefly take a third person driving view within Joel’s wonderful imagination. There is a simple side-scrolling section with a few enemies and the head of a dragon which match a somber story being told to Joel with cancer as this powerful dragon that many of tried to conquer, to no avail. These are mostly solid, but there are times where it feels like the game was grasping at straws trying to find something interactive to do to fill its gameplay sections, even though I would have been fine simply existing in this space as a bystander and not sticking to normal game conventions in this case. Everything fits well in the context of Joel’s imagination though and these sequences often gave us a breath of air in a deeply reflective and contemplative experience, showing how at the darkest of times humans must sometimes retreat and engage our imaginations to escape a terrifying reality. That Dragon Cancer nails this feeling at almost every turn.
Overall Value:
Once again, I’m floored at how I feel I must construct this section of the review differently. Value is a very strange metric to measure, since its objective nature leaves it on a person-by-person basis. The game retails for $15 for about 2 hours of game, which is a price/length ratio that has been criticized heavily in the past. However, I believe the subject matter, personal nature of the family’s struggle and general unique atmosphere and drama of the title lends it weight that few other games have ever matched. The price feels like a mere inconvenience in all honesty, a simple step you engage in to gain access to the work and I paid without a second thought merely due to my desire to view their experience close up. You could easily do research on the Internet to find out Joel’s ultimate fate or watch a Let’s Play and save the money, however there is something about supporting the family and viewing it in my own way that was extremely important to me. Objectively though, the game admittedly offers minimal gameplay and interaction, with only a few sections to speak of on that front, with the rest offering a viewing experience or clicking on papers to read with voiceovers. Gamers who focus heavily on gameplay will likely not be satisfied with what’s on offer, however lovers of narrative driven experiences with gameplay as a simple tool to experience the world will love this title. This title will be poignant in the highest regard to players whose friends or own families have been affected by the wide reaching effects of cancer in real life and to those people, it will likely be a quicker decision.
Verdict:
That Dragon Cancer is a very special and personal game. No other video game I’ve ever played has ever given such a blunt and harrowing view into the lives of real people. Often times it feels like the player is opening the diary of the family and peering into the darkest recesses of their hopes and fears, all as they fight and eventually accept the ultimate fate of their child. While terribly sad, it also shows the incredible power of hope and how faith can give us strength in impossible circumstances. Engaging with that sense of inevitability and powerlessness is ultimately this game’s most superb yet surreal achievement. The visuals are simple but effective enough to serve the purpose the game is trying to fulfill. Gameplay purists may leave the title with buyer’s remorse, but that may likely be overridden with the other gifts the game can provide. This game will truly offer very different things to different audiences, something powerful that cannot be fully valued. For me, I also leave the experience with a sense of pride in the game industry I haven’t felt in years, learning the lengths that games continue to strive towards to provide artistic experiences. If art is meant to touch the soul of a person and make them reflect on their life, That Dragon Cancer may be one of the finest examples of art our medium has.

The graphics and the music were gorgeous, really great, but it felt like 80% of the resources for the game were spent on them. The important part about this game was suposed to be the puzzles. I expected that feeling, when you have collected so many clues you have no idea where  to use, and as you progress in the game you find some riddles you have the answer, and find some more clues, and in the end it all FITS it all makes sense. When you are being told a story but there is some fulcral detail you discover in the end that makes you suddenly understand the hole game. I am really sad I didn't have that, the game felt so empty. Most of the clues you knew what they were for not that much later into the game. You never really had to turn back to solve a puzzle that has the answer further ahead.
It was really linear and really short.The puzzles were not that hard, and I was expecting something much more complicated, more conected, more complex. The game was short, the story had so much potential to be developed and it wasn't. But it wasn't, because to have a satisfactory story the game would have to be SO much longer than it was. They probably didn't have the funds or the time, and that is verry sad indeed, because this game was full of potential.

I thought it was bizarre at first how your items, spells, and special abilities all had to be used with simultainious button presses (up + left for example). In most roguelike games, you have to navigate confusing menus to do most things more advanced than moving or attacking. Crypt of the Necrodancer does away with the slow, plodding, ways of other roguelikes in favor of a quick and easy to use system.
A note though, and this goes for ALL games I have with this. It is a problem I have not with the game itself, but with the genre tags. Since when was "female protagonist" a genre? Man or woman, the hero is going to save the day and rake in the loot right? It isn't a genre. It isn't worthy of being mentioned as a feature. It isn't going to make people buy the games more. It. Does. Not. Matter. What does matter? This games great soundtrack. Thats what matters.

EDIT: NEW REVIEW AFTER 25 HOURS OF PLAYING FULL RELEASE...
LOVED IT, even better than I thought it would be. I never meant to compare this title to the old series coz I didnt care to do so to begin with!
For me it's old school rpg coz its a 4 party, turn-based, 1st-person game.
Totally different from what EA gave us and REALLY fun to play...for me its the opposite of Skyrim and I think the devs did excellent job to bring something that goes the opposite direction from today's mainstream rpgs.
In my opinion: Well-balanced, tough fights on warrior-mode, open world-meaning that there are some enemies that you have to comeback even in Act 1 in order to fight 'em after you beefed up in levels, better AI and monster behavior, better skill/magic/buff system, smooth heroes/enemy movement and so on.
Yes, they could have added some extras to make it really great game, but I think it's an awesome start. I understand that there are ppl who are disappointed coz they expected something else along the lines of an exact copy of an older MM game with modern engine/graphics...BUT I'M EXTREMELLY HAPPY the way this game is AS IT IS!!!
Hope next one in line is a monster...good battles to all the brothers who are enjoying MMX.
OLD REVIEW: Loved it even with its early access faults...when they balance enough aspects of the game, it will be really great fun to play.
Not for people who expect a game like Skyrim, its for old school rpg fans with the benefit of auto-mapping...just wish they'd put more riddles along the way and maybe more quests affecting the outcome of the main story or the characters.
Sure the devs wont follow on all the great suggestions from the community but still it will be worth playing and enjoy yourself if the content of the final release is big enough.
To expect the perfect game on all aspects/parts of a game and on top of that to have the devs please all different kind of rpg fans is useless...READ the reviews and then DECIDE if that's the game you want to play or not...the game is a tile-based/turn-based and they should improve the parts of the game based on that idea...dont mind if they had the option for free movement but it shouldnt be a pre-requirement to play an rpg-game like this...there are tons of other rpg games for that.

Summary:
I would only recommend this game if playing with friends. This game needs a ton of content, or a price drop (which wouldn't be a good idea). The game is no where near "diabolically hardcore." I beat this game on my second character, and the first one died only because I wasn't familiar with the controls yet. Enemies are boring and predictable, crafting system is not engaging and incredibly small.
Pros:
- I personally think the graphics/art style is great, but of course you may think otherwise.
- The combat, after playing a level or two, is easy to pick up and feels good. Not too simple, not too complex.
- The humor that is sprinkled around in dialogs and written in text on walls is usually pretty funny.
- Randomly generated levels.
- Neat weapons and skills (charge attacks, jump attacks, etc).
- Crafting system.
Cons:
- Neither the combat nor the dungeons themselves are difficult.
- When you get hit, it's barely a scratch. At higher tier armors you can take on a horde of enemies and it takes way too long for them to chip away at your health.
- You will likely complete your first playthrough (9 levels) in a few hours.
- Enemies are boring and predictable. You can just side step every enemy, hit them, and win.
- Enemies will sometimes get stuck on rocks or ledges, and do not have any kind of AI pathing to correct that.
- The "Elite" enemies are way too easy.
- The crafting system, while a great idea, is too lacking for any real use. Bombs that I don't need to use, potions that I don't use or don't know what they do, you get way too many ingredients to make rations (which restore health and stamina). For example, on level 2-3 I have enough to make 60+ "Iron Rations" which restore a big chunk of health and stamina.
- The tomes you can buy that carry on to the next playthrough are extremely underwhelming. You won't know that they do anything until you look them up. Only one or two are useful in any way.
I could honestly go on with the problems with this game, but I'll stop there. The worst part about this game BY FAR is the difficulty. This game would only be "diabolically hardcore" to young children. If they had a difficulty setting with a much harder difficulty, I'd be all about it. I mainly play this game at work, because it feels like such a casual game that I can play it while not paying much attention to it.
The only real enjoyment I get out of this game is just exploring the dungeons over and over. The combat can be fun at times, but is mostly repetitive. The only fun moments are when a ton of enemies randomly spawn and come after you, but even then it's just too easy.

Magical Diary isn't for everyone. It's an indie visual novel and sometimes dating sim (romance routes are optional and the game can be finished without dating anyone) that apes Harry Potter in an anime-influenced art style. At face value, this can seem like an amateur game, filled with predictably trope-laden characters. You are a teenage girl and a wild seed (a magical person born to a non-magical family), starting their first year at a magical school for witches and wizards. You're automatically assigned Horse Hall, which is roughly analogous to Gryffindor (although the traits valued are a little different, given that there's only three houses), and your roomates, Virginia and Ellen, are your equivalents of Ron and Hermione. That's really where the similarities end, although Professor Grabiner clearly refers back to those fanfiction versions of Professor Snape.
Your basic goal is to learn enough magical spells (across five different categories, each associated with a colour, and learnt by attending classes on your weekly schedule) to pass your exams and advanced to your second year. Gameplay takes place across a year, with events being triggered on certain days of the week, if you've met the criteria necessary to trigger them. This is where the game's replay value comes in: as with most visual novels, you won't be able to run every path in one playthrough, particularly if you're going for the achievements. This can get a little tedious after a while--most of the romantic routes don't really trigger properly until after Christmas, so you'll spend the first four months of the game going through similar motions on each playthrough. On the other hand, you can prioritise different magic skills on each runthrough, and the exams have various solutions to them that you can have fun figuring out different ways of tackling the puzzle.
My only real complaint about Magical Diary is that it's never gotten the sequel it needs, which is to say that no matter what path you take, you'll always be a little frustrated about the game's lore and the rules the school enforces. As a wild seed, you're understandably a stranger to the magical world; while other characters, especially Virginia, will flesh out some of that knowledge, there's a lot that invariably never gets discussed. This may also just be my interpretation, but there's routes where I would frequently get the impression that the school raises its students in an almost cult-like manner, telling them not to do certain things (such as mixing science with magic) but without giving them a good explanation of why, and then forcefully wiping their memory when they disobey. I would love to know more about that, but without a sequel--and I'd love to see one even if it's just following your character through the rest of their time at the school--we'll never get that information.
Despite that, I do think the game is a lot of fun, and the characters are fleshed out. While they may seem generic at first, pursuing their routes reveals hidden depths that really brings them to life. Your character customation options are a little limited, but I do appreciate the ability to choose from a range of skin colours and between two different body types. No matter what it looks like, I think the developers put a lot of thought and effort into the game, and it really shines through in the characters.

I don't usually review games, you can look at my history to prove that. But after reading the reviews, I knew I had to say something. Never have I felt that reviewers were being ignorant or decietful. I'm not saying that people were lying, but when my playthrough of the game is different than what everyone else is saying, then I know someone isn't doing something right. Many of the bad reviews that I've seen talk about it being "Copy-and-paste," and I even remember one reviewer saying that if you played through a minute of the game, you would have seen it all. From what I have experienced, nothing can be further from the truth.
I had read somewhere that in order to unlock new biomes and enemies, you had to interact with these broken crystals. You would rebuild them and regain some health in doing so. The Brazen Head, the main antagonist in the game that mocks you, would then say something like "Ah, I see the mountains of 'so-and-so' have been rebuilt. Thank you." So I made sure that as I would play, I'd go out of my way to find these crystals. I went through three lives in this game as of writing this. In the first life, I stumbled through the halls and died at around level 2. I was still getting used to everything.
The second life was my longest, and I made it all the way to the boss fight at level 9 before dying because I ran out of food and healing potions. In that life, it was pretty easy. Enemies could do a bit of damage, but nothing I couldn't handle by keeping track of everything. Enemies did seem to hit harder as I went down to each level, and there were a few "oh crap" moments where I watched enemies eat my health down to almost nothing. But other than that, it was rather easy.
Then I started my third life, and enemies had changed. They may be varients of old ones, but they had new attacks and abilites that almost killed me on level 1! That's when I smiled and knew that I had made the right choice in picking up this game. Enemies started using different ranged varients who would hit me from afar while their melee counterparts advanced. They have started dodging and blocking more freaquently, requiring me to fall back and use ranged attacks of my own. I no longer have the supplies to make tons of rations to keep using my power attacks, as I can't replenish my stamina as often. Each level has gotten bigger and more complex, consiting of multiple paths that can take me to different level endings, meaning I have the choice to either advance down to the next level or go back to another path that I might not have tried yet. The broken crystals were still appearing, and I was making sure to rebuild all that I came across in all of playthroughs.
Considering everything, I can say with full honesty that a lot of the reviews I have read were not fully correct, in fact, most of them seem more copy-and-paste than the game they ironically claim to be copy-and-paste. That being said, I can't attribute all of the negative reviews to ignorrance or deception. Necropolis, by its very nature and design, is rather vague in all of its descriptions. When you unlock a new biome, the game doesn't plainly tell you this, it hints at it through phrases like the one I mentioned at the start of this review. Potions don't tell you whether something heals you or makes you stronger, but instead uses descriptions that hint at what they do. The same can be said for codexes. I can see where people could get confused or discouraged, especially after the spending $30 for the game. I do think it would benefit Harebrained Schemes to clean up some of the descriptions so that some people could interpret their properties. However, mystery seems to be a large part of the game, and it makes sense that the Brazen Head wouldn't tell you what everything does, as he is your enemy after all. I don't want to think that people are purposely lying, but I do think a lot of reviews were made in ignorance. I feel like some people just rushed through some of the levels and ignored exploring for the game's many secrets. I'm sorry, but someone who gives a game a negative review and has less than an hour or two of playtime obviously hasn't seen everything there is in the game. In fact, I'm still finding new things at hour 8, and I can tell there are tons of things I have yet to see.
TL:DR, I recommend playing the game for yourself. The reviews I've read don't draw an accurate picture of the game as a whole. The game is rather pricey, but it is a great and fun game that I've gotten much enjoyment out of in the short time I've gotten to play it. More content is always welcome, but I think the price is rather fair for the game you get. If you're looking for a game that gets harder as you play and rewards players for exploration, than this is a great buy.

I am going to cut to the chase. This game is good. It's not "the quintessential steam game", but it's good. However, I'm gonna say, this game is also very difficult and at some points frustrating. Now I don't mind that because I like a challenge, but I know this type of game won't suit everyone. That being said here's some pros and cons.
PROS
+ Great electronic, pumping soundtrack.
+ Combat that is intense and in some ways a bit strategic.
+ Challenging gameplay. You''re given unlimited trys and it's unlikely you'll ever get a level the first try.
+ Plot moments that really are trippy.
+ Story telling through gameplay.
EHS
/ Plot is a bit confusing due to the amount of twists and being in an almost prepetual state of "Is this real?", which both works to the advantage and disadvantage of the game. I enjoyed it, but I know some others won't
/ Sometimes inconsistant AI. One turn they'll pick up on you straight away, others they won't see much at all.
/ I don't know about anyone else but I experienced some crashes after playing for an hour which made me restart the level I was on. Added the challenge of a time limit, but wasn't apriciated.
/ Not much replay value, but a decent amount of content despite.
CONS
- Might repeat a point, but the plot is ultimately unresolved unless you find these secrets in every level. I had found none after my first playthrough. This turned me off as I was left with so many questions, but I couldn't go through all of the levels to do that.
- I mentioned that this game was challenging, but that paired with the inconsistent AI and a few levels do go into unfair territory. Some levels are fun to go through, some become a chore and the game feels almost taunting at soe points. You could argue that the payoff is more satisfying that way, which isn't a bad argument, but unles you do good you're not really rewarded that much and that turned me off, and undoubtedly some other players.
All in, I do reccomend this game. It's pretty damn good as far as this goes. However, do take the cons into consideration when buying this. Unless you're willing to die again and again, be frustrated at points and even ceated out of at others, do not buy this game. This is for those like me who enjoy the challenge and overcoming the seemingly impossable.

Alright. This will be my first review. I have played the game for almost 6 hours, and as of now steam has refunded the game for me. I have beat the game, and this review will contain spoilers. I would like to add that I predicted this game to be my 2016 goty, oh boy was I wrong.
Necropolis was to be a souls like game with meaningful combat and was supposed to be difficult. The issue with Necropolis is that the enemies themselves were not difficult due to a lackluster AI which controlled them, not to mention that your character could fight any enemy in the game by attacking and backstepping until they die. The animations with the majority of weapons are just very slow and some are very choppy, attacking with weapons just feels pretty clunky due to it. There are very little weapon choices in this game, infact anything in this game you can use has very little variety to it.
The game follows a very minimalistic art style and the world can feel very empty, and that would be a cue to add some mechanics to add puzzles, minibosses in optional areas, neutral npcs, and bosses at the end of each floor. By puzzles I mean anything which challenges the player. Jump puzzles would have been fine, some areas where jumping through is possible but hard, give a reward at the end which the player feels is fair, and then have them not go through the puzzle again to leave, have a small drop off somewhere so they don't risk dying to continue. Which brings up another point, falling off the edge does not kill you (it teleports you to where you fell) , I find that really bad game design, and I find fall damage is way too little also. Falling 25 feet should not do 1/12th of your health bar, that should kill you. Back to puzzles though, you could have simple things around levels which reward the player, in either gems, tokens, weapons, potions, scrolls, or ingredients. A riddle on the wall would even beat nothing, having players interact with objects, or having small events happen. NPCs could just ask for money and hopefully give you something good in return. Mini bosses and end of level bosses should not be the same boss each time, there should be a good pool of them and they should be fair to fight. Difficulty can be hard while still having the boss be fair, thats why everybody loves the soulsborne games.
If you compare The Binding of Isaac to Necropolis and only look at game mechanics which make the game hard but enjoyable, you will see that BoI has lots of variety in all playstyles and difficult but fair gameplay, Necopolis doesn't have that variety and you kill normal monsters all the way to the end of the game, the difficulty in Necropolis is them swarming you with trash mobs.
The only boss in Necropolis is the final enemy you fight, which is a very tall mechanical giant, having 4 arms and a broken blade in his hand which is very big. He has a very boring moveset (Fires a spirit bomb at you [ranged], spins his sword around like a blender, and swings his sword at you.) and has a ton of health for no reason. He will go invincible for periods of time when you damage him, in a group of 3 players we had him hunched over more than he was even attacking and the fight still took over 15 minutes. This is the worst boss design I have ever seen, his attacks either oneshot you if you don't have many blessings of the gods and T4 armor, or twoshot you if you do. This enemy was by far the worst thing in the game, and is the gate to beating the game.
There are things I haven't went over, on how there are under 20 weapons (I do not count the recolored weapons who have the same attacks but a different color) for people to use in the game, and there are 2 different types of weapons overall, being the swords / staves (which the magical staves are only melee...) and the crossbow / wands which take a shield slot but are ranged weapons which do very little damage.
The codexes are a different thing all together, and most of them are decent.
The last thing that bothers the heck out of me is that there are no stats anywhere on anything. You get a greatsword and you hope to see some type of damage and you either have a one sentence story on the weapon or a pun / joke about something mindless. HBS please.

NB: I bought ABZU at 70% off and had a vague idea what I was getting for my money.
An underwater sight-seeing simulator with more sea-life than Billingsgate Market
As the silent, unnamed protagonist of ABZU, you'll traverse an array of (mostly) underwater landscapes, from the familiar to the alien, and from natural to technological, in your quest to restore/reclaim the ocean.
While there are some very basic puzzles to solve, ABZU is less of a game and more of an exercise in immersion (pun not intended).
The central character is incredibly well-animated, as she (?) swoops, twirls and dives around with nary a hitch, and the rest of the cast are not far behind.  The environments range from vibrant coral reefs to murky, algae-ridden caverns to sunken temples to a whales' graveyard, and a lot more besides; each one beautifullly detailed, and the vast majority teeming with life. You'll encounter fish and other denizens of the ocean of all sizes; wrasse, lionfish, deep sea anglers, giant squid, sharks and whales; even the occasional thing that you thought extinct. You'll frolic with dolphins, dive to deeper waters with whales, hurtle through jetstreams with shoals of smaller fish.
But it's not all frolic in the waters of ABZU. Dangers lay in wait for the unwary diver. There's not much else I can say here without giving away spoilers.
The lore of the world of ABZU is largely told through mosaics on the walls of buildings you find, which seem to be telling an origin story, or creation myth, for the ocean, with a few surprises.
The sound is crisp and clear, and fills the available space without being overbearing, while the orchestral and choral soundtrack hits all the right emotional notes.
There are items to find for the collectors and points of interest for explorers to come across, but ABZU can be completed without any of them, barring plot-critical ones which are never all that far off the beaten path.
All in all, I found ABZU an absolute joy to play but, if you like more gaminess in your games, it may not be for you. If I had to compare it to anything, it would be Journey, and I'd be hard-pressed to choose which one is the better.

Battling cancer is a story that has been told through other media, but That Dragon, Cancer is the first I can think of that has elected to use an interactive game as the medium of choice.
First off, for those who are still wondering whether they should still buy the game: if the kinds of games you're used to are games heavy on  mechanics like MOBAs, RPGs, FPSs, and RTSs, this isn't really that kind of game. The closest experience I've had in a game was probably the Stanley Parable, but unlike the Stanley Parable, this game is pretty much a linear narrative. It's probably more correct to call it an 'interactive story' than a game as games are usually known for. This is important to know, because if you approach this game as a gamer expecting well-designed mini-games to tell this story, you're probably going to be disappointed.
If you approach this as an interactive story, it's a lot better. The experience reminds me of the interactive experiences you can have on VR headsets like the Google Goggles. It's scripted, but you get some enjoyment from the autonomy of perspective that you choose by looking around.
Onto the story itself: this is the probably the best part of this game. It's based on real life, and the interactivity provides an immersion and intimacy to the struggle of the Greens as they battle cancer together with their son. Like many other players, I was in tears for much of the game. The strength of the interactivity helps you get into the shoes of the Greens, and it's this second-person perspective that makes the game such a powerful experience.
Regarding the Christian parts mentioned in the game: yes, if you do not come from a Christian background, you might find the Christian content offputting. But for many people of any creed, their religion will be a part of their philosophical struggle when they have to confront the death of loved ones. One can find empathy in the pain and difficulty of accepting the death of loved ones, no matter whether you believe in a god or not. Approaching it this way, perhaps a non-Christian can identify with the basic human desire to see their loved ones alive and well.
I'm divided about the graphics. I didn't really like the faceless human models, but I loved the use of light and colour for the scenery. I think I generally found the visuals and imagery beautiful and striking, and combined with the moving soundtrack, this game was generally a positive experience.
However, I wish that the controls were less finicky and didn't depend on point-and-click. I would have preferred a WASD free movement, similar to FPSs, with E to interact with surroundings. The best references I can think of for fluid environmental interaction and being guided on a rail while providing the illusion of free movement are Half-Life 2 and The Stanley Parable, both based on the Source Engine.
My overall conclusion:
Pros: Powerful story, striking visuals, moving music.
Cons: Did not like point-and-click controls, polygon models a bit too rough for me.
Caveats: Must be aware of Christian content and  nature of gameplay before buying so you know what to expect.
Thank you for reading. Overall it's still a Yes for me.

I have always been a M&M loyal friend.  Even though I considered IX one of the worst of the main series, once I saw X:Legacy, I jumped on it like a kid on cake.  When I found out they went back to the original mechanics of grid-based movement, I was intrigued.  I grew up with I-V, and although I really enjoyed VI-VIII, there's something special about keeping true to the game that started it all.
Now that I've covered my background story, here's my main review points for X:Legacy.
First, it's raw... as in "Early Access Beta  Test" raw.  I discovered early on that if a conversation with an NPC is a bit long in narration, it's cut off early.  I really wanted to hear more of what the Guard Captain of Sorpigal-by-the-Sea after his Quest was completed.
Second, when I toured the city and found the "Training Grounds"... I expected that to be the place I would level my characters.  This has been the case for 9 games, but when I found out I can level... for FREE... on the SPOT!  I was shocked...   I really don't know if that's a good or bad thing.
Third, I don't know if I am missing something, but there are certain things that seem lacking right off the bat.  The ability to ID or Repair via Skill or Spell was something I found necessary.  Yes, I do remember having to rely on a shopkeeper early on.  However, in the past, there was ONE shop. It did everything.  X:Legacy seems to bring together the worst of VI and the worst of I-V by having THREE different shops, each with their own repair and only one with the ability to ID my loot.  You mean to tell me that a Armorsmith can't ID "Armor"?  I also remember there were Robbers/Theives who ID'd traps/treasures/etc. and Sorcerers who could manage the same via spells.  Having to walk 500 blocks just for an ID isn't friendly.  Yes, this was probably my harshest of the criticisms... but as I stated before, this game is 'raw'.
Next, Character Manual Creation... I liked its implementation in VI, but this new skill tree led to some ... odd circumstances.  I wound up with a 'Healer' without the ability to fight... even with his/her fists.  There used to be a standard set of things that came with a character.  Light armor/Small Weapons... A sling! of all things.  But to be completely unarmed and unable to fight except through spells? Unheard of, at least as far back as I can remember.  To top it off, for early weapons, I was not pleased to see that a simple staff REQUIRED EXPERT skill.  Since when?  No weapon in all of Cron or Terra or wherever required a minimum skill...  Class/Alignment restricted sure, but not skill.  Skills improved the basic ability of a weapon, that's how it should be.  This is my other harsh criticism thus far.
Finally, everything else.  Graphically, it's ok... M&M has never been known to have particularly 'state of the art' scenery.  But what it lacked visually, it made up for in huge worlds labyrinthine worlds.  Now here's X:Legacy!  Nine sequels since the original. I'm going to use Sorpigal-by-the-Sea as my example.  It's not even a tenth of what Middlegate was (MM2) It's barely the size of Sorpigal (MM6). And it's grid based with borders that load a whole other area.  I'd almost expect the place to be Crap-My-Pants BEAUTIFUL!  Especially with the very minimal interactions with the enviroment, minimal movement options, and extraneous people/obstacles that are only there for visual goodies and serve NO purpose but to be in my way.  I haven't made it far into the so-called "Open World" but so far, it's a bit lackluster for what I'm able to see in such limited space.  Take a look at even older games as EQII or WoW or even new games like FFXIV.  Those worlds were free-roam with powerful imagery.  I'm in a grid-based static world and the imagery is just above mediocre.
The Combat system is ok... a bit clunky feeling but for a turn-based set up, it's ok.  Again, graphically, it lacks quite a bit, in my opinion.  Ambushes are fun, that's for sure.  Do like them ambushes. LOL.  The auto-loot mechanic is ok.  Too subtle for my opinion though.  I miss the searching and the booby traps (MM1-2) or just the searching (MM 1-9).
Sadly, I haven't fully explored the game so far... and finally earned enough gold to buy some new spells... that find traps and hidden areas.  I'm hoping those are useful.  However, since I haven't found a way to respawn monsters yet... there's a bit of a limitation in gold and thus... food/rest/mana potion options.
Overall, I'd rate the game RAW out of 10!   I'll come back when the Full Game is launched and patched a few times and give an honest score. :)

TL;DR: Game not worth the full price by far. The OST might be nice by itself, though you have to decide for yourself how much you want to pay for 17 songs/51 minutes.
Let me start with the good stuff:
+ Visual style (Claymation) is nice, though bland animations and static lighting ruin the effect.
+ Music is great, though it occasionally just stops in between.
Now for the disillusioning rest:
- This is not a game, it's barely a trailer! My steam library says 4h, though that's because I was cooking something in between! Actual gameplay is more around 1.5h, and that even only due to unskippable videos, forcedly slow waiting-puzzles, no possibility to run and the requirement to re-walk through every location just as you’re about to finish.
- Gameplay missed every piece of usability learned during the last 10-20 years… There are no indications for what is clickable, what is not, or if you just missed the seemingly random click areas. Obvious interactive elements, which are just not yet active, are simply not clickable without any indication why this might be the case. Things that are interactive have terrible click zones, which sometimes leaves no option as to leave and reenter a room in hopes to make the clicking work again. And occasionally buttons have to be pressed by your companion dog, because they’re 3cm too low for the main character (who can’t be bothered with bending down that much).
- Even the level design occasionally doesn’t make sense. Complete sections could have been simply skipped or severely shortened without losing any part of gameplay, story or mechanic. On the other hand there is one part with critical information for the finale, which is impossible to revisit as soon as you actually need this information (spoiler-less hint: as soon as you get the “translations”, take a screenshot and learn the spoken sequence by heart!).
- Finally even the story does not make sense (It doesn’t affect the gameplay at all, but be warned: spoilers ahead): Three brothers are sent out into space to collect a critical energy source for their home planet. The protagonist randomly crashes somewhere, flees into a castle full of convenient riddles, has to safe a baby in between, and suddenly one of the brothers turns up being evil, having caused havoc apparent minutes before the game started, and threatening you for no reason. All of a sudden the “ancient” texts turn into a live commentary, and the whole setup was only to give you the power source you needed anyway after testing your honor? The third brother is only ever mentioned in the end without any other context other than to try and tie in a forced sequel?
I backed this game on Kickstarter, only because I was so interested in the Claymation style. Good thing, the game was already delayed so often, so I already wrote off that money, otherwise I’d be (more) annoyed by this waste of money.

Before reading any further, please note! The game has been reported "dead" by the publisher. No more DLCs or bugfixes will be provided.
While the game runs okay for most players, it unfortunately has been left with some serious unfixed problems on some system configurations that range from overheating on laptops, freezes on Macs, and annoying stuttering on some NVIDIA cards that may render the game almost unplayable, to (in rare cases) crashes to desktop. Be warned that customer service will probably not provide you with much more than "have you tried turning it off and on again" in case you are affected by any of the above mentioned bugs. Purchase at your own risk!
If you loved the M&M 1-5 games (and have a graphic card that can handle it), you may actually enjoy the game just for the fan-factor. It may not be the expected "big sequel" but it is solid and entertaining.
If you are new to M&M however, or you have just played "Heroes of Might and Magic" so far, this game may disappoint you.
Also if you are looking for a "Legend of Grimrock"-like RPG, be warned that this game has a very different feel to it. While the game-mechanics are similar, the gameplay actually feels a lot more static and not as action-oriented.
1. The game itself
M&M 10 is playing after the story of Heroes of Might and Magic 6. The gameplay and "feel" of the game however is mostly based on Might and Magic 3-5.
The game is grid-based with turn-based combat. This means you move through the world 1 step at a time and there is no free movement. If you encounter an opponent the game stops and switches to a turn-based combat mode. You then give your party members commands to attack, defend or use magical powers. Once you have done that the round switches to your enemies who will do the same until either you or your opponent drops dead, whatever comes first.
Since the gameplay is based on M&M 3-5 fans of the series will find some nostalgic elements, like barrels containing liquid that buffs your attributes, riddle chests and the like.
The story is solid but unfortunately also pretty generic. (I won't spoil it here though, so that you can still experience the fun yourself)
The map is unfortunately -again- rather generic. Where M&M 1-5 featured treetop houses, cities in the sky and even space-ships, all you got in M&M10 is pretty standard villages. Not even your run-off-the-mill castle. A little more fantasy wouldn't have hurt the game here.
The size of the map is not large but "medium". So where the description says "3 towns, 1 city, 20 dungeons" it literally means just that. Except that they don't mention that some of the "dungeons" literally have just 1 room.
Graphics quality is ... not good. The game looks like it was more or less pieced together by using whatever texture or model was laying around at that time. Thus some objects are very nice and detailed, but the majority unfortunately looks blurry and washed out even on "ultra" settings.
The sound quality is acceptable. However the soundtrack is quite generic and not very memorable.
In total the game is fun with enough solid gameplay to keep you occupied for like a week.
2. The downsides
The game was produced on a tight budget by Limbic Entertainment. A small studio that has no experience whatsoever with AAA-class games. They clearly state on their website that their field of expertise are "social and flash games". The name as their greatest success so far: "Mein Ponyhof 2", a horse-barn simulation for little girls.
They also stated in their blog that M&M10 was a "test" for Ubisoft to see wether or not people would still spend money on the series.
I'm actually very sorry to say that but all of the above and especially the tight budget actually shines through. And unfortunately not just in the fact that all horses in the game have beautiful textures.
Also it has to be mentioned that the game requires a UPlay account and installation of the UPlay client on top of Steam. If having to create yet another account with yet another company just to play the game is a big "no-no" to you: I recommend you stay away.
3. Not included in the game:
Despite what the store page tells you this game does NOT include a free modding editor.
The "modding kit" is/was actually just a resource pack for a long gone version of Unity Pro, that is no longer sold, and had an original price tag of 1500 USD when the game came out.
4. For "digital deluxe" purchase
This version contains an additional dungeon and a mini-campaign. The dungeon is just standard.
The reactions on the DLC have been mixed. Most people rate it "solid" at best. I would suggest you expect to get some "solid" extra hours of "acceptable" gameplay that may be quite enjoyable but will be nothing to tell you grandchildren about.
Note however, that the DLC has been reported to break the option to run the UPlay client in offline mode, so that you need to be always online in order to play it. If you can't be "always on" for whatever reason, I recommend to stay away from the "digital deluxe" version.
The "digital soundtrack" is 30 minutes of unmodified in-game music encoded as 128KBit joint-stereo MP3. Despite what the store-page tells you, you are NOT getting the "official soundtrack on audio CD".
The files don't show up in your Steam library. You find them in your installation folder. The music quality is okay, but nothing really memorable.
Note that there is another dungeon and some minor extras as well, that can be unlocked by earning virtual currency through getting achievements. However, I experienced that the achievements don't unlock properly and thus I have been unable to access any of that.
4. Limitations
- The 32-Bit version of the game is limited to medium texture quality and voice-over is deactivated.

A very profound and impactful narratological experience/experiment about the nature of loss and pain. I feel a deep sense of compassion for the Greens and the team behind this labour of love. It may be one of the deepest attempts at expression of the emotions we feel when we lose someone so close to us.
Ryan's narration at the beginning of the game captured something I've often felt about my relation to the ones I love, and it opened up something inside of me that I've felt before, but never encountered in such a personal and moving way.
The experience of the game is like being carried by the words and images that swirl around you. You float and observe things in an almost whispy, ghost-like way. It has a way of disconnecting you from your existence and life outside of the game.
It's beautiful, tragic, towering, intimate, playful, distressing, but ultimately it's human. Potentially the most human 'game' I've ever experienced. It's a beautiful monument to a brave boy and his family.

This is one of the only Early Access games that I have purchased very early on. It also happens to be the first early access that I have absolutely loved from the beginning and it's probably one of the only early access games that I purchased that actually came out as a complete game.
Crypt of the Necrodancer immediately caught my eye because of its unique gameplay (or was it just an impulse buy because of the pun?). It's essentially a Rythm Roguelike game. It has most of the elements of a Rogue-like, except you have to stay on beat!
The soundtrack is absolutely amazing (and now offered in 3 different variations!) and the game is deceivingly difficult. It's very easy to pick up, very hard to master and highly addictive.
Even having played through the first 3 zones countless time while I waited for the fourth one to come out, then all four a bunch of times when it did, I still enjoy playing this game from time to time (I have played a lot more than Steam indicates.)
I often despise randomly generated levels but in this game it works very well and follow a set of logical rules. Each level will always be similar while always offering something new. There are tons of different items that will help you on your runs and different characters that provide different challenges when you get bored of Cadence, the main character.
Quak!Quak!Quak!--and more--Quak!

The Island:
-- There are numerous locations on the map to explore and discover, each with its own set of challenges, creatures, and resources to tackle. In fact, if you're going to build out everything in the game, you're going to have to do some exploring.
Survival:
-- To me, survival isn't vastly different than most games in this genre. There is hunger and thirst. Hunt for food (at least five different types discovered so far) and collect water. Yes, the game advertises other survival metrics, but they don't seem to play a huge role. Stamina is really only about how fast you can cut things down or throw a spear. You're able to sprint indefinitely. Hot vs Cold (at least in story mode) only seems to apply when walking in fire or in a couple of "cold" locations that you can quickly dip into, get what you need and get out.
Audio:
-- Aside from the voice acting (which could use some work) the audio is really solid. The island makes so many different noises from regular ambient noise to the various creatures on the island. In fact, early on, until you've learned the noises each critter makes, the audio can really keep you on the seat of your pants.
Weapons:
-- So far, I've found six weapons, I believe, which really helps in survival. So far, I haven't felt the need to build many traps.
Story:
-- The story is pretty basic, so far, but it has provided a really nice motivation to the game. Everytime I think I'm about to escape the island, I find I need to solve one more "puzzle". How do i get in here? How do I get one of those? Etc. Its given me reason to explore the island without making things seem easy.
Overall:
-- If they keep developing the game it will really shine but, as it is, its a good spend for $15ish. I think I'm about 10 hours in and can see myself spending a few more (I really want to figure out how to get off the island). Multiplayer would be a nice touch, but maybe just for survival mode, not the story.

I was scratching my head when I was playing this. First of all, I know it is grid-based. It says it in the description and it's what the devs keep saying. But let's take a small look at the title. Might & Magic X. This is supposed to be a SEQUEL to VI, VII, VIII and IX. In other words, I expect something better that keeps innovating the genre. Why the *#$&* they went back to IV, V is beyond me. As if VI (1998) is not retro enough to duplicate.
Me? I started playing the series because of VI. I loved it. I could never get myself to play I - V because it's not what I was used to. VI - IX had open worlds to explore and do quests at your own pace. Going from one side of town to the other did not take take 10 freaking minutes like it does with this game.
So, the game is grid-based and I started to accept that. But even if I did, the system here is done horribly. Everything, from the controls to the animations is very ackward. You can only cast damaging spells or shoot arrows when you're enemies are in a straight line! My D&D board game allows me to shoot monsters diagonally, and that game does not even have a game engine! It's a board with some plastic figures on it and it functions better than the almighty M&MX.
Graphics are terrible. Every single human being and monsters look like plastic. I can make better animations shooting Stop Motion with my Lego-sets using a iPhone 1. The levels, towns and dungeons are poorly designed. And to add insult to injury, the graphics suggest that there are things to click on. Which is impossible, because most of the objects that seem clickable are out of range. Grid-based. Great Idea.
I can write an entire book about why I am disappointed with this game. It's pretty ironic that if you purchase this, you get the best Might & Magic game; Might & Magic VI: The Mandate of Heaven. I would recommend buying the older games on
and leave this game alone.

- You can use your own music for the rhythm game.
- The difficulty curve is agreeable.

- You get to kill dragons. And there's as chess battle fight.
- Local multiplayer mode.
Cons:
- You can buy powerups with diamonds you find in the game, but you run out of powerups pretty early on, and the currency feels hollow.
- The game gets pretty repetitive after awhile.
- Nothing about the game is exactly riveting, mostly just something to do.

The best RPG series I have ever played, and one of the greatest games of all time.
It has a very extensive and deep lore based off the Polish novals.
Characters are diverse and all very well written.
The basic story is built around the "I was framed for a murder I did not commit, so it is up to me to clear my name". However, it builds up to a much greater plot which is incredibly non-linear and very interesting. It is probably the best game to make use of player choices where they actually affect the world and the story. There is no illusion of choice like in Telltale games, and they are not so black and white like most Bioware games. Your choices really matter here.
It deals with many mature themes which grey the lines between good and evil. A web of politics, murder, racism, sex and♥♥♥♥♥♥ are just some of the points this game covers quite well.
Gameplay is very fun and responsive, but can be very punishing at the same time. It is closer to Dark Souls as opposed to hack-'n-slash Skyrim. You will rely on preparing posions before battle while ensuring you are leveled enough and sufficiently equipped to face an opponent. Even so, during battle you can't take many hits. You have to rely on dodging, parry and riposte, signs (magic) etc. Even a basic creature can kill you if you do not watch your back. However, once you are past the first chapter, it is not much of an issue - it becomes second nature and you are quite well equiped to face just about anything. I loved it; some people don't. It depends on you.
Graphics are really good, especially for a game that came out in 2012 and runs on DX9. It looks as good, if not better, than any game out in 2015. Turning on Uber-sampling and bring many modern machines to their limit.
If you like The Lord of the Rings, Game of Thrones or games like Dragon Age but with a darker, more mature story, I think you would love this game.

I can't say enough good about this game. When I first saw the trailer, I had high hopes. I knew it was going to be good. And when I did finally buy it, my expectations were more than exceeded - and that's an understatement. It is incredibly fun to play, and offers a decent amount of challenge even on the easiest difficulty setting; at least, it did for me. I'll do my best to keep this review spoiler-free.
I'll start with the obvious protagonist, Dust. A living mystery, he's a little bit of a rogue; even though he's on the side of good and has a strong sense of valor and justice, he's not afraid to cut down any who oppose him or threaten the innocent. He's a bit generic at first glance, but some people (me) find a really cool character under that equally cool hat.
The hack-and-slash combat can be either really fun or really boring, depending on the person. A rather small variety of techniques are available to use from the beginning. You can uppercut your target to the skies to perform aerial strikes, parry and counterattack from the ground, or just button-mash to cleave your way through the crowd. You can also launch projectiles that are weak at first, but then amplify their power to wreak mass destruction upon the battleground. Projectiles can range from magic missiles to fireballs, which can be powered up to missile storms or flame pillars.
The music is probably the best part about this game. I can't get enough of it. Sometimes it's calm, and sometimes it's tense. But it's always encouraging, thrilling, and outright epic. There's nothing like dashing through a rainstorm and slashing down monsters with that loud, exhilarating violin and piano in the background.
The story is linear and straightfoward, but is really quite touching at some points. Dust travels through the land of Falana after waking up without memory. A magic sword arrives as his generic sage-guide, and leads him to specific areas because reasons. Throughout the story, Dust helps out whoever he can and takes down villains, all the while trying to find clues as to who he really is. Though not much is explained, a big reveal near the end clears up a lot of potential confusion and can be traced back to the beginning of the game. While the story is linear, it's still pretty well thought out.
The characters are a little flat. While most people in the game have distinct personalities, they usually just have one character trait and can be described in about two sentences. However, that does not mean that they can't be charming. You'll meet a lot of people throughout the game, and while each one has his or her own unique role, whether you love or hate them is entirely up to you.
One of the biggest elements of this game is the treasure hunting. There is a limited number of keys hidden throughout the world, and each one is expended after opening a treasure chest. Some treasure is very easy to find, especially in the early levels, but some is really cleverly hidden. Sometimes you might actually have to read a note that you picked up to be able to find a secret! The horror!
There are, of course, a few cons to this game. However, they are rather minor.
There's not much replayability. More or less, it feels like the same game over and over again. Although it's great to experience the story again, and the higher difficulties add much more challenge, it's not a game that will last forever.
Combat is precise but strange. Sometimes, if you fall from a large height, one or two enemies will be waiting for you on a lower platform and will attack as soon as you land. It takes either great reflexes or a bit of luck to avoid damage from these "ambushes."
The boss fights are basic and potentially unmemorable. They have little to no strategy and can be beaten by simply spamming The Undoing, which strikes your target helpless and throws them to the ground for massive damage.
I still love them, though.
It is definitely not the longest game in the world, and once you've done everything story-related, completed all of the sidequests, and collected all of the treasure, there's not much else. In fact, it's the exploration and treasure hunting that stretches the game out. The story itself is rather short and linear, and the game has quite a closed end.
I love this game and usually like to defend it. However, it does have its minor problems. All in all, though, the game is a masterpiece, especially when you consider that most of it was done by one guy alone. I'd like present to Dust: An Elysian Tail a score of 9/10.

This game (call it a "walking simulator", not a bad thing by any stretch) is amazing in what it is trying to do: to convey a story about a four year old boy, Joel, who lost his battle with cancer after it was found at an early age. The story is done in a typographic font way, with the voice acting carrying the narrative really well, conveying each emotion extremely well.
And emotion you will have, because the game's story ends up getting more and more heart breaking the more you get into it. Later on in the game, you end up seeing the sheer pain of what Joel's parents had to go through (there is one particular scene later in the game that can be rather hard on the psyche to have to listen to, I won't say any more than that). The family seems to try to be strong and not let Joel's sickness get in the way of a livelyhood, but the narrative shows just how tough things were for the family, and how tightly knit things were when dealing with the realization of the inevitable. It's carried by a very riviting soundtrack (and yes, the game's recommendation of using headphones to listen IS one you should heed).
This is not to say the game is perfect, though. Does have a few flaws. There are a few spots in which the game's controls seem somewhat off in a few scenes, and when you get to those sections, you will know what I'm talking about. It also, in a few sections, fails to give the player enough feedback of what they are supposed to do to advance the story. These are few and far between this 3 hour experience, but you'll know them immediately when you get to them.
But don't let these small flaws hinder you from picking this one up. If you want a truly emotional, heart breaking experience that won't take you a ton of time to finish, then this will be your title. A word of warning: the game does lay on several religious aspects hard, so keep an open mind about those. But even if you aren't religious in the slightest, the emotion, immersion, and the symbolic scenes are more than enough to warrant a recommendation.

Armikrog is finally here and does the game live up to the hype? Well, yes and no.
In a nutshell, Armikrog is a beautiful game from beginning to end. The claymation aesthestic is gorgeous and makes it stand out than other games on the market. Both the characters and backgrounds are delightful to look at and you can tell a lot of work was put into it. Unfortunately, if only the same thing can be said about the gameplay.
Armikrog is your standard point 'n' click game that requires no input on the keyboard (except for saving which will get to later), just the mouse. The problem is is that the game doesn't do a good job of explaining that to you as there is no tutorial or guideline to tell you the basics. The game assumes that you know how to change characters, that there's no inventory menu, and that the save/load screen is in the option menu, which is weird.
Overall, Armikrog feels very outdated as the UI design is lacking and the puzzle solving requires you to memorize icons and patterns. I believe this is what the developers are going for but as much as I enjoy nostalgia, it just doesn't feel right. I don't want to be writing down stuff and halt my progress - I just want to keep playing. Throughout the game, there are these green conveyor belts that you use to move from one area to the next. I find personally find them a bore because there's nothing much going on in the background. It's a filler more or less. In addition, I had trouble of knowing how to stop the conveyer belt and exit the vehicle. Again, the game assumes you know how to do it.
Soundwise, it's great. The soundtrack is most definitely the highlight of Armikrog and I find myself listening to it on my iPhone. Unfortunately, the music tends to cut off or starts off out of the blue which can break the gameplay experience. Same goes with the voice over, which is of low quality as if the voice actors recorded them in their bedroom and not in a real professional studio.
The biggest disappointment for me is how short the game is. It took me about 3 hours to complete it and when I first saw the credits, I thought it was joke. It's strange how to story got resolved very quickly just as things were about to get more interesting. I was hoping to see more claymation cutscenes but it didn't happen. I also wanted to explore more of the environment but there's only so much you can see or do, which is a letdown.
Again, I was disappointed when the game ended but the next day, I played it again and ended up enjoying it than before. I guess I began to appreciate what the game has to offer the second time around. Plus, I have a soft spot for claymation. Despite its technical flaws, Armikrog is pretty enjoyable. It's by no means a masterpiece but you have to give it credit for the amount of effort the developers put into making Armikrog a reality. There is no way this game can ever be made by a AAA publisher in this day and age so be thankful that this game isn't just another mindless shooter.
If you are into claymation like me and are looking for a one-of-a-kind game with catchy music and interesting world to explore, I'd say give Armikrog a try but if you're in no hurry, just wait until it goes on sale.

That Dragon, Cancer will likely be cited in the future of interactive media, not for being amazing, but for being one of the first to tackle more mainstream issues that we see more in film and novels.This is an experimental game / experience that presents the emotions and journey of the Green family through their son Joel's battle with cancer. It has zero replayability except to show it to others and lasts 2-3 hours. A scene in the middle, dehydration, is one I never want to experience again. Joel is screaming and crying in pain for several minutes on end.
I don't have kids, but I'd imagine this game to heartbreaking or near impossible to play for parents. People I've mentioned the project to have been blown away it's even being tackled as a "game," whatever that means or might mean in the future, if we begin calling such experiences as some other name.
The game is very approachable in terms of its controls. It plays like a Qaunatic Dream production like Heavy Rain or Beyond Two Souls, where your cursor's actions change based on context, but much less complex than those games. People have complained about clunky controls or not knowing "what to do" to complete each scene, but this is trying to convey feelings and is less of a game with levels. The game provides clear cues as to what is happening and I never got stuck. Some parts in the middle of the game present what is I'm assuming to be artwork and letters to and from other sick kids ot members of their families. So this isn't just Joel's story, but a collection for many families and future kids with cancer and other terminal illnesses.
I can see people getting a bit angry at the comparison between the temple of man and the temple of God. The implication is that the Green family or perhaps mostly Ryan sort of scoffs at people deciding to use medicene to heal people, since in his world view this seems to be a kind of arrogance because God is who heals, not man with his weak collection of machines. But that is common among religious people to sort of dislike science and scientists, although of course that doesn't apply to everyone.
I grew up in the Christian faith for 18 years and was confirmed, as were many people but I'm no longer religious. So I understand where they're coming from. Amy and Ryan conflict about how to handle grief and what to expect will happen to Joel and how God should answer their prayers. Obviously non religious people will see this as delusional. Replace God with Aliens and flying saucers and we can start a comparison. But people of faith will likely keep believing no matter what happens or what new evidence they see. It's very deep for them and there is a lot hanging on religious ideas, like keeping alive the place where deceased relatives live. The thought of friends and family possibly dying forever, as Ryan fears insignificance, is too terrifying for most to even acknowledge as a possibility, so heaven and all its implications of god such teachings MUST be true and fought for being proven true forever.
This game is not jamming beliefs at anyone, it contains a family's experience of a terrible situation and I think everyone can relate to it. There are terribly sad moments, but also joyful ones. Near the end, a pheonix is presented on the floor of a grand cathedral, which I think is a unifying message. One that we all can rise up from bad events. It doesn't matter what we believe.
