5/10: Surreal style and nostalgia can be fun, but with nearly two decades having passed since The Neverhood, the limited content, obtuse logic, and backtracking undermine the impact of this point-and-click game.
Admittedly I backed this due to the nostalgic memory of enjoying Earthworm Jim, and to a lesser extent the Neverhood. Armikrog is unfortunately similar to Neverhood though, with odd puzzles, mechanical annoyances, and limited content detracting from a unique style and a lighthearted story.
As with most point-and-click games, the key frustration (not challenge) of this game is context confusion. Despite the absence of the genres "combine inventory items" logic problems, the surreal style of Armikrog and utter absence of contextual dialogue exacerbates the issue of figuring out whether something is not working because you don't have the right thing or because the wrong character is interacting with it. For a specific example, low buttons can ONLY be opened by Beak-beak, rather than by Tommynaut bending over slightly. Combined with the long delays incurred by repeated backtracking and revisiting rooms as you look for potential pickups and clues that may have been overlooked, Armikrog is a perfect storm of point-and-click mechanics problems.
Stylistically, the game is innovative. There's no doubt that a lot of attention was paid to claymation and music, although the music often went silent for an oddly long time before starting again later. Still, I can't help but feel all the effort put into the claymation is undercut by the 2d point-and-click interactions, especially since it seems that is what most of the money was probably spent on.
The story is solid but not especially dramatic. I won't go into specifics, but here's how to make sense of the story for those who are playing (potential SPOILERS):
- What you see at the start is just the setup to explain why Tommynaut and Beak-beak are there.
- In the second building, in the room with the statues, is a literal wall of text. That's the deep backstory.
- The gibberish the Octovators are saying when Beaky interacts with them throughout the game is the recent backstory, and becomes understandable to Tommynaut at the end of the game. You will have to visit each one again to finish the game anyway.
Upon its conclusion, Armikrog left me feeling underwhelmed. Despite a decent story and creative visual style that borders on Seussian, the game is mechanically dull with few real challenges but several frustrations. Maybe if it had released within a few years of The Neverhood, it might have retained some of the same impact. After nearly two decades though, the disjointed logic and backtracking shared by Armikrog and the Neverhood have been largely abandoned by even point-and-click games in favor of deeper stories and relevant puzzles.
Bottom line: avoid it unless you REALLY love Doug TenNapel's work and/or point-and-click games.

Gorgeous to look at, fun to poke at and explore, more leisurely than The Neverhood but arguably grander in terms of the mythology it hints at. Puzzles are repeated in a way that builds on past experiences, resulting in a gradual increase in difficulty I found to be an improvement on The Neverhood. Its most egregious bugs have been patched (transparently so by the folks at Pencil Test), and while it retains a few UI quirks (the lack of feedback for interactive elements can be frustrating), neither of these prevented me from completing the game a few days after its debut.
Like Broken Age, Armikrog may be a victim of the challenges game developers face when updating point-and-click adventures for a modern audience: Many of the conventions most coveted by hardcore fans directly contradict contemporary tenets of game design and usability. My impression from Armikrog is that the team chose to favor the qualities of The Neverhood that aged best and set it apart (the clay visuals, the soundtrack, the mythology) over those that wouldn't be as charming to modern players.
Also like Broken Age: Armikrog is imperfect, but I love it anyway.

This kind of game, it isn't really a game. It's a story, and it's a personal one, or at least similar to many other stories children and their families can tell or are living right now. As someone who fought the battle, this is all too familiar. The first time I booted up the game, I felt sick and I couldn't continue on, because it was hard to watch the story progress. It was my experience, my friends' experiences, and the Green family's experience all melded together. Even if you're not interested in the gameplay, or the way this story is told, you should buy it. I think it makes cancer something real to people. Through the experiences of the Green family, cancer stops being that thing you only hear about through fundraisers, the media, fictional books, or potential charities to donate to. Make no mistake, you will cry. You will smile. You will despair, but you will also hope just as these people did. There's no point in rating this game, because you can't rate something so personal. I would say that you should buy the story, and let yourself be changed for the better because of it.

Ok, now i will give some general info to familiarize you with some aspects of this project, i find rather questionable and controversial. Starting with:
1) Size of the game world.
M&MX is told to be consisted of 4 Acts, with Act 1 available during the Early Access. Act 1 location (including both Sorpigal by the sea and Peninsula maps) feels to be half the size of, for ex., Castle Ironfist location (from M&MVI). Act 1 offers us five dungeons, those being: Spider cave in Sorpigal; Lighthouse, Bandit Hideout, Catle Portmeyor and Cursed Ruins (which is not available in the Early Access phase) scattered all over peninsula map. Also we have two caves, each holding a single Cyclop monster inside and an empty puzzle cave. The size of these dungeons are medium, and it won't be much of an exaggeration to say that Castle Darkmoor (MMVI) would be able to contain all of them within itself.
Now, to make an approximate estimation of the overall world size, you can take a look at the "World Map" picture, where i marked the borders of the area Act 1 occupies.
2) Character creation and development
2.1 Races.
M&MX creators offer us 4 races to depict our party members from. Those being: human, elf, dwarf and orc. The difference between them lies in starting stats, certain level of mastery they can advance to in different skills, names of the classes for each race to choose from, appearences, and minor starting race-dependant bonus, like elf having +5 evade, +10 earth resistance from the beggining.
2.2 Classes.
Only three classes are at our disposal to choose from for each race. Basically we are given three same classes for each race, being: warrior, archer, mage (so it goes like: Human Warrior, Human Mage, Human Archer/Elf Warrior, Elf Mage, Elf Archer, etc.). The difference between them is: how they are named, ex: Mercenary (HW) against Barbarian (OW); their promotions; level of mastery they can achieve in a certain skill and appearences.
2.3 Class promotions.
Each class has a promotion to be achieved through the game. There will be only one, against two in the later M&M games. It will give one additional ability to the character, no other bonuses are know about at the current moment.
2.4 Character customization.
After choosing a race and class it is time to customize character appearences. You have a wide variety of two drawn pictures for each gender (one male body/one female body), each in turn having two faces you can switch between (giving us four different portraits to sum it up).
2.5 Skills.
Developers have cropped all non-combat related skills like: trap find/disarm, repair, trade, identify (there will be a spell), diplomacy, perception...any other player-world interraction skill you can think of. Leaving three groups: weapon mastery skills, magic mastery skills and misc combat related skills like dual-wielding, dodge, evade, skill adding crit chance to a spell based attack, etc.
2.6 Magic.
Developers decided not to implement magic system from the later M&M games, where you were able to learn every spell at basic level, and advancing in magic mastery upgraded effects of each spell differently, based on the spell itself. Now it is more standard "magic mastery of certain level requirement for each spell". You can learn certain spells at basic level, certain at expert and so on. Spell effect doesn't change while you advance in magic mastery.
The following picture will show you all Air magic school spells (basic to GM), that will be available in the game.
Spell description:
There will be no Item Enchant spell, in case anybody is wondering.
2.7 Inventory.
We will have combined inventory now, each item occupying one slot. Also no paper-dolls (items won't be shown on player's picture being dressed) Equiping this or that item won't alter character picture in any way.
3) Character/world interaction.
Due to absence of non-combat related skills, player gaming experience is limited mostly to combat, opening objects (chests, barrels), getting buffs (one buff statue in Sorpigal, one in Peninsula). There is one quest in the first act, which implies on giving the freedom of choice to a player (you can kill or let go bandit leader), other than this, there are no player-choise driven situations.
4) Combat.
This is what it is all about. Judging from absence of non-combat related skills, lack of player-world interaction besides engaging your enemies, and answers from developers themselves, LE are trying to create combat oriented game (tile- and turnbased gameplay fits this concept idealy). Unfortunately they are not succeeding here either. Combat is rather standard and despite the looks of it, doesn't provide you with enough tactical depth you would anticipate. Poor variety of character classes, lack of significant race dependant perks/abilities, standard skill set, absence of really valuable effects of tactical (not damage dealing) spells, ect. make the game unable to offer reach and thrilling combat experience. Not to go deep: you cann't aim anything in case it is not standing in the adjacent tile.
This meaning: if you have two or more opponents approaching you, apart in two or three tiles, you won't be able to target specific one to use a spell on or attack from distance (with an arrow, for ex.). This game should not have been released.
I'm a UI Engineer with a classical animation background and I proudly backed this game on kickstarter. I knew it was a medium that most studios would never take on. Not only is stop motion animation incredibly time consuming and therefore expensive, but this project also entered a level of unkown in compositing the work into actual gameplay that could have ended it years ago.
I did not play Neverhood, so even after reading the first reviews I still went into this with an open mind. I'm a big enough fan of point and clicks that I could accept a clunky UI for a beautiful game, well thought out puzzle-plots or outstanding artwork alone. However, after playing the game to the point that I could not finish it because of the bugs, I will say that this game has absolutely no polish and should not have bene released.
There are more inconsistencies than are worth listing. The number of game-breaking bugs is simply unacceptable. 'Let's just put a negative filter on the image' was a terrible choice in art direction.
I'm hopefull that the team will clean up the project, but I'm afraid that the game's framework is too broken to save.

Admit it: you like to burn things.  No no, don't deny it, we can all tell it's true.  Fortunately, Little Inferno has your pyromaniac needs covered.
The concept is simple: order things from a catalog with money.  Put those things in a fireplace.  Burn those things.  The act of burning those things earns you more money than you paid for them.  Repeat.  No time limits, no points system, no one telling you OMG DO THIS NOW.  Burn, burn, and burn some more.
That's not to say there's nothing else to the game.  There's combos to create to unlock achievements, along with stamps that help your ordered items arrive faster. Money also lets you purchase access to more items, as well as expand the number of items you can hold at once.  And believe it or not, there IS a plot, given mostly through letters you receive in the mail, along with an epilogue that is a surprising gameplay shift, but still fits in just fine.
You don't have to do any of that though: you're welcome to just burn things without purpose for as long as you like. Doing so is surprisingly entertaining, and really, there are worse reasons to play a game.

12 hours of gameplay.
12 hours of utter joy.
I2 hours of building what I thought to be a decent empire only to be crushed to pieces by my neighbors when our borders crossed.
Short Review:
If you like DW and the immersion factor of your galaxy and exploring and finding new races, artifacts - its a must buy. Especially as this is the first release. Not a single bug or crash encountered.
If you like MOO type games where you spam colonize, race the tech tree, and have a quicker gaming experience - not for you.
Long Review:
For an initial stage 1 release - a work of art - which will only get better with DLC, enhancements etc.
The galaxy is IMMENSE and there is so much to explore and find.
The random alien races are my favorite feature. It truly feels like you are exploring space.
Is this up to par with EUIV yet? Of course not. Thats been out for years and has several DLC and enhancements.
Is this capabale of standing on its own as first release and an enjoyable "consuming" gaming experience?
Yes. 100% without a doubt.
You can see the work that went into this game with all the events, details, artifiacts.
You can see the balance at work with your resources.
Do I spend that energy credit for an extra mining base? Its a balancing act.
I truly enjoy the random research. I like the idea of not following a static tech tree and "racing" to get a nuclear warhead etc. You really need to plan and build how you want your empire to act.
On my 1st playthrough I created a desolate angry desert race. As I met more and more races they all despised me - hence my race being eliminated. I should have focused on military techs etc but I did not play the race properly and ended up crushed.
I honestly cannot say enough kind words for the Paradox team on this release.
Thank you for the immersive enterainment value.

First off, I wish there was a star system on top of a thumbs up/down, because I don't dislike this game, per se, I just definitely wouldn't recommend it.
The character is a very definite, set character without any influence of the player's. This isn't so much a problem, but she isn't fleshed out for you in the beginning, so you will continue to learn things about her that you probably should have known from the start all the way through.
Customization is pretty good, has a fair amount of choices and the inclusion of two different body types was great!
The music was absolutely perfect for the game, each song fit the mood of the scene it was in, and I could usually guess which characters were going to appear depending on the song.
The choices can be a little odd. If, for example, you have choices A and B, and in B you would meet a new person/group of people, but you choose A and don't meet them, the game still continues on slinging their names around as if you know who they are, despite never having met them before. It makes it all feel very one demensional.
The art is charming, very bright and cute, but (and this is admittedly nitpicky) the character's facial expressions don't always fit the mood they're trying to portray, and that's not always a bit deal, until you're unsure as to why they look perfectly calm, despite the music and text telling you they're really angry.
All in all, this game is okay. I had an alright time with it, it's certainly not a bad game. Just not one I would recommend.

*Disclaimer A: This is an ongoing review, I'll update it once I progress further into the game*
*Disclaimer B: This review was originally a negative one, it now has been edited*
Thank you, killJoy12345! My initial review was very negative. It was based on me trying the game with a controller. Here is recommendation no.1: Do not try to play this with a controller. Who knows, I am sure some will succeed playing the game with one... I didn't. At all. The tutorial alone, attempted with an Xbox-controller, frustrated me so much that I had to quit right in the middle of the arena. It just felt so incredibly imprecise, confusing, clunky and weird. I compared it to being drunk out of your mind while trying to control an overloaded 40 ton-truck with a wobbly old joystick from the early 80s or something. I quit and uninstalled, not bothering to try again as I had bought this for like 3 bucks during a sale.
I have changed my mind very much, and am falling more in love with the game the longer I play it, and I think I start to understand just why the game is so revered. I am now playing this with a mouse and a keyboard. The mouse to look around and using my attacks, the keyboard for moving.
I use a Razer Naga, and with the number keys on its side, it's quite easy to control using the standard/default key settings
With these numbers (with the Naga or keyboard), WASD, Q and R plus the Alt key to target-lock, the controls get much better.
I'd also recommend to adjust the mouse settings, and lower the sensitivity. With the naga, it's set to the lowest possible value. This works well for looking around without being too slow, plus it is precise enough to handle the arm-wrestling minigame (which you need for a quest, where you do that instead of paying with money). Said arm-wrestling takes a tiny bit of practice, but I was then able to beat most opponents.
Now for the game itself.
Graphics/Setting/story
I said that the graphics are merely ok. I kinda stick to that, even considering the game isn't brand-new. They're quite pretty, but they're not exactly total state of the art even for the time it came out IMO. They ARE quite atmospheric though, and help to suck you into the game.
And gee, there is a lot to be sucked into, as the game REALLY is quite addictive and enticing IMO. The story is quite interesting... a bit of cliché sometimes, but mainly a well-written and multi-layered story.
Depending on how you want to play Geralt, you can be either a nice goodie-two-shoes, sticking to a moral high-road, or you can be a rather intimidating, threatening and sinister figure, doing whatever it takes to achieve his goal.
The dialogues are nice, sometimes you have to pick your answers quickly. I am not that far into the game yet... I mentioned this will be an ongoing review, I will add updates once I progress more.
So far, I am VERY into it, want to see how the story plays out, want to learn more about the world it is set in.
Handling/Controls/Fighting
I mentioned above that the combination of KB plus Naga works quite well. I still need to practice a bit, as some of the controls are a bit...wobbly. It sometimes takes a tiny bit longer to target a lootbag, ladder, climbing/point.
Fighting feels pretty dynamic, and you can succeed even if you don't target-lock enemies. So far, it was pretty much up to me how I wanted to fight mobs... using mostly swords, signs or quickslots (traps/bombs/daggers). I am sure that later on, you need to decide on some of these for specific mobs, acting with a bit more tactic, while right now, I am slashing my way through the mobs rather easily while throwing in an occasional Aard or Ignis for tougher mobs or those that shield themselves.
Regarding controls and handling, this game gets a 7 or 8 out of 10 so far. I wish it'd feel a bit more precise especially out of combat, when you pick up stuff or loot. Not as good as some AC or Arkham-titles in my opinion.
Update: Just did the first boss fight, and it was tough. I did have to do some research on YT. An NPC gives you SOME hints during the fight, but Im not sure how much they'd help to figure out the correct tactic without help. However, I eventually beat it, and it was quite satisfying.
Soundtrack/Voice acting
Very very nicely done. The music isn't annoying you, it rather adds to the atmosphere, and even with quite a few repetitions, it doesnt get boring.
Pros:
- Graphics are decent to very nice. Not mind-blowing, but pretty dang good.
- Music and voice-acting are very well done and work nicely for the vibe.
- FIghting feels dynamic... even if sometimes it's buggy (fighting my way out of a prison often had me light or extinguish torches on the wall while trying to actually slash away at a guard. Didn't die, but the combination of "use torch with left-click, slash at opponent with... left click" wasnt helpful.
I hear Witcher III will be even better when it comes to controls.
- Interesting and deep story, very nice to follow and read, even though there are a LOT of plotlines and chars, so maybe some extra research at a wiki would be helpful to understand it better.
Cons
- Controls often are a bit too wobbly, not quite precise enough. If they weren't, the game would be close to absolutely perfect. This doesn't apply much to the fight, but more to everything in between.
- 2 crashes so far, hope this doesn't happen more often. The game does autosave, but I recommend to manually save from time to time. 2nd crash was on exiting an instance, and not even CTL AlT DEL would help to close the crashed game (funny: the "loading icon" was still moving, but the game had crashed)
- One big immersion-killer: You can't jump. Yes, you can jumproll in certain directions while fighting to dodge attacks (direction key plus space, took me a bit of practice). So this powerful demon hunter walks through the area, and there is a 10 inch rise in the landscape... you can't raise a foot or jump up, you have to walk all around it. This kinda kills the immersion and feels weird. I guess they wanted to do this to guide you with paths in between rises, but that adds a "on rails" feeling while also feeling very unnatural.
- Some of the QTEs are very fast and you might fail a few times, especially since the first ones happen quite surprisingly. DOn't worry, they won't kill you quickly, you just need to adjust quickly in order to succeed.
YMMV:
- Your questlog fills up rather quickly. A lot of the quests have a tracker to help you find the right spot and person, but some require you to think or search a bit. Also, read the questlog (which is well-written!). If you are used to WOW-type questing, with handholding to the extreme, TLDR-summaries at the bottom and trackers for every single quest, you might have to readjust.
- Some might dislike the minigames like the wrestling. It does take practice for sure.
- The menus can be quite overwhelming at first. Alchemy, talent trees, meditation etc... take your time.
And that leads me to one big piece of advice: I think (at least so far) this game is MUCH more enjoyable if you take your time and savor each step. Watch the cutscenes. Read the questlogs and information provided. Enjoy the quests and solving them instead of trying to rush through them as much as possible. Try some different approaches to fights, don't ignore the quickslot items or potions or signs. If you prefer swordplay, then go ahead, but I recommend to try different styles, or mix them up a bit.
I haven't fought a boss-yet... so far, the game hints that it will be a bit of work to kill the first one, and requires tactics. I hope it does, and I hope I will figure it out.
So, for now: A solid 9/10, very fascinating and immersive, with a cool story, cool main-character, a very nice and sinister vibe to it (the 18-rating is pretty appropriate as far as I can tell), and it's obvious that a LOT of work went into this. WILL UPDATE!

Final Fantasy VI is considered by many to be Squaresoft's Magnum Opus.  Final Fantasy IX was loved by many as a return to form in a big way for the company in it's twilight years before merging with Enix.  Final Fantasy VII, however, will always hold a special place for me.
I was a Genesis kid growing up, until one day in 1997 while visiting family I got to spend time playing with some cousin's Sony PlayStation.  And my first introduction to the PS1 was the iconic deep bass sound of the system BIOS, and the opening and early gameplay of Final Fantasy VII.
Before then, I'd often seen the epic sounding commercials.  The advertising for VII was nearly impossible to avoid, in fact.  Everything had characters from FF7 emblazoned onto it, even Pepsi was running a huge promotion with character art and backgrounds of Midgar plastered all over just about everything sold by the company.  But this was the first time I actually had my hands on it.
I stunk the place up at the first boss I'll admit.  This was mostly due to an unfortunate translation error in which Cloud encourages the player to attack at a point where doing so will result in a powerful attack severely harming the party.
The Steam version of FF7 is a way to finally play this gem without having to spend a ridiculous amount at a classic games store or on Amazon.  Note however it does have it's problems.
For one, it requires you to log into a Square-Enix account to launch, which is always a pain in the rear.  Second, little to no configuration options are available.  The original game ran in 640x480 native PSX resolution, but the Steam version will run in a screen-filling window size no matter what.  Worse, it becomes immediately clear the menu screen and the field screen where most gameplay takes place are running in different resolutions.
This lack of polish is annoying to say the least, especially when you find yourself fighting in the woods around Junon or Gongaga to recruit a certain once secret party member that's not so much a secret nowadays.  Or while attempting to get some character's final limit breaks on Disk 1 just because you can.  It's times like those I like to fire up Netflix or YouTube, and that's hard to do when I can't even run the game in a native resolution window.
The game is also a bit long in the tooth, particularly for those who celebrate the downfall of random battles in RPGs, but still well worth the asking price.  You may not agree with some on it being the best in the franchise, but starting up the game and putting yourself in the shoes of kids or even adults firing it up for the first time in 1997 should give you insight into whay it's still so incredibly hyped.
And you don't have to set your PC upside down before it melts the system, so there's that too.

I see a lot of reviews comparing this to Darksouls, but this isn't a Darksouls game. This is a Rogue Lite. While combat may be similar to DS this isn't that type of game.
This is a Rogue Lite, procedurally generated levels with tons of secret areas  and hidden things to find. Interesting traps that will make you yell for not seeing that it was a trap and a ton of surprise enemies. The game feels a lot more to be about exploration. Looking through every section of the level to discover everything before moving on to the next one.
The art style plays very well with the theme and is visually pleasing, and I really enjoyed the soundtrack.
One of the other nifty things is the way that the story is delivered. It's not a linear story that is handed to you, instead you have to discover it as you go along. Yes, Brazen Head will give you quips here and there, but finding the writing on the wall or the various land marks is fun. I do enjoy the humor of the game as well, it's very dad joke heavy which has made me laugh and sigh in equal measure.
The exhaustion system is also interesting. The more you do, the more you burn through your stamina, which is pretty par for the course. However the introduction of fatigue or diminishing returns on that stamina adds a nice flavor, and keeps the game from being a complete hack and slash. It encourages you to use the crafting system, find recipes and may influence the decision in what codex to have active, in order to recover from your exhaustion.
I think the game is at its strongest as a multiplayer game. The first thing to note is that it is incredibly easy to dive into the game with 3 of your friends, there's no complicated glyphs to drop or local co-op only mode, and having 4 people going to town is crazy fun. Friendly Fire is a thing, and you will kill your friends often, but then there is the revive mechanic which allows you and your friends to revive eachother after you've been knocked out. While you're dead, there is no timer until your body releases, but instead there is a creeping darkness from the edges of your screen that circles in around you. If you die, you lose all the gear you've gathered and respawn with your basic weapons.
overall, the game is fun, but probably the most fun with friends. I look forward to seeing what the game holds in the future and hope we see more items added over time, more enemies or more combinations. I think currently it's worth the price tag, so much so that I've bought it for a friend, but that's only as long as you don't expect it to be Darksouls. Something more akin to Castle Crashers meets Rogue Legacy.
If dungeon exploration in a procedurally generated environment with comedic overtones and fun multiplayer sounds like something you would enjoy, than this is the game for you. If you're looking for another Darksouls, this won't be what you're looking for.

Have you ever wanted to attend a magic school? Did you grow up hoping you'd one day recieve a letter in the mail informing you that you are a witch? Magical Diary is the game for you.
Magical Diary is a very well done school life simulator set in a magic school, and one that gives you more freedom to choose your patch without a game over screen than most visual novels. You can make friends (or enemies), engage in a wide variety of romance paths, become a star pupil or flunk out, run for student office, become embroiled in magical disasters, uncover conspiracies, etc. All the main characters are very well developed and the stories fun and well written.
There are things the game could improve upon. The exam mechanic where you use your magic explore a small dungeon to practically demonstrate your powers is extremely well done, but not used much; I wish there'd been more use of this mechanic. The story also feels incomplete, like it is the first school year of a series - which it is, and so the game could really use a sequel.
But overall, this game is an amazing magical school life simulator.
Also an obligatory warning: This is a visual novel, with very little actual gameplay. If you do not like visual novels, this is not the game for you.

ABZU has the potential to be an incredible experience: if you're prepared for just what this game is.  If you're looking for a story-rich game that provides you with a clear picture of what is going on, or if you're looking for an adventure game with a great deal of action and puzzle-solving; ABZU would probably disappoint.
If you're looking for a beautiful game with fantastic environments that beckon for you to explore them and a linear story that pulls you from area to area with ease - then you will love what ABZU has to offer.  ABZU is a game that sparks the imagination while also allowing the player to relax knowing that a game over is not lurking around the corner for them.  It teases at the player's curiousity with hints of story, well-articulated environments, and an awe-inspiring amount of species to discover.
The fun in ABZU lies within the relaxation and beauty it brings to the table.  I would highly recommend to pick this game up (especially during a sale for those who are unsure) simply to experience the wonder it had to offer.

Je m'approche de la fin du jeu (mieux vaut tard que jamais...), que je n'avais jamais terminé à l'époque de la 360.
L'arrivée du 3 étant imminente j'ai décidé de lui donner une seconde chance.
Ma conclusion reste à peu près la même, je ne parviens pas à comprendre pourquoi ce jeu est autant encensé par les joueurs : la narration est certes correcte (même si là encore j'ai vu largement mieux ailleurs), les personnages sont plutôt charismatiques dans l'ensemble (mais là encore même remarque) et graphiquement c'est vrai que c'est joli, malgré une direction artistique qui ne me plait qu'à moitié.
Mais alors côté gameplay, c'est vraiment abyssal. Les maps semblent hyper vastes mais sont découpées en routes/couloirs hyper exigus qui ne laissent que très peu de possibilité d'exploration, la map est complètement inutile (bonne chance si vous vous perdez et que vous n'avez pas le sens de l'orientation comme moi)...
Les quêtes additionnelles sont automatiquement 'ratées' si on progresse trop loin dans la trame principale, mais le jeu ne nous en avertit à aucun moment (ça peut être à la dernière phase de la trame principale, mais aussi avant... on ne peut jamais savoir), c'est totalement arbitraire.
Mais mon pire cauchemar dans ce jeu, ce sont les combats. Je crois que je n'ai jamais vu un système aussi bancal. Dans Witcher 1 on pouvait faire plein d'esquives différentes, roulade, vault etc. Là on n'a étrangement plus que la roulade. Si contre les mobs de base, il n'y a pas énormément de préparation à faire à part pour le stuff, pour les boss, il vaut mieux avoir pris quelques potions avant. Le problème... c'est qu'on ne sait jamais trop si on va se battre contre un boss, ou du moins quand exactement, et il n'est pas possible de prendre des potions pendant un combat. Du coup, il nous reste deux choix... présumer qu'on va tomber contre un boss et prendre les potions avant, au risque que le boss n'arrive que 5 minutes après (les potions n'en durent que 10 dans le meilleur des cas), ou arriver contre le boss à poil et recharger la partie pour prendre les potions juste avant.
La plupart des boss sont d'ailleurs à moitié invincibles, surtout dans la première partie du jeu (passé la deuxième moitié du chapitre 2 ça va un peu mieux).
Il y a un boss dans le chapitre 1 qui peut flinguer Geralt en deux ou trois coups voire moins, et pour qui il doit falloir genre... 1 milliard de coups avant d'en venir à bout ? Dans une arène hyper exigüe ou les problèmes de caméra sont nombreux. Il faut un timing parfait pour le battre. La moindre erreur et c'est la boule de feu qui te vide la moitié de ta vie, ou la bombe de poison qui fait pareil (et ce n'est pas comme si à se stade du jeu on avait beaucoup d'unité de vigueur pour la magie).
Un bug étrange survient aussi également, la barre de vie en combat disparait. Si on combine ça avec le fait qu'on ne sent pas du tout les coups que l'ennemi nous porte (l'animation de Geralt n'est par exemple pas interrompue lors d'une roulade durant laquelle il s'est fait attaquer) on perd rapidement la trace de la santé restante et on crève avec un étonnement certain après s'être pris un coup totalement lambda.
Autre petit truc rigolo : je parle à un marchand près d'un feu de camp dans le premier village. Après la fin de la conversation, mon personnage s'est étrangement déplacé sur le feu, et est donc en train de cramer. Ma barre de vie baisse dangereusement.
Je réagis rapidement en lançant le signe QUEN (qui est une sorte de bouclier) pour annuler les effets du feu.
Le problème c'est qu'il n'est possible de lancer des signes qu'en combat. Geralt sort donc son épée, et lance le signe, je suis protégé. Mais les gardes du village ont pris ça comme un signe d'agression (le fait de sortir l'épée) et sont venus me mettre sur la tronche.
Le poids des objets dans l'inventaire est également infernal (heureusement qu'il y a des mods pour virer cette notion) et n'a aucun intérêt à part faire perdre du temps au joueur.
Après, il y a aussi du bon. Comme je le disais, la narration est de qualité, et se laisse vraiment suivre. Par contre, j'attends encore de vraiment m'attacher à des personnages, pour le moment je dois dire que ce n'est pas le cas, même si j'en aime bien certains.
Les choix sont pour certains difficiles, et semblent donner de véritables embranchements différents dans l'histoire (pas comme dans Mass Effect quoi).
En clair, j'espère franchement de très grosses améliorations de gameplay dans le 3. Je sais que le côté Open World va améliorer pas mal de choses dans la façon de naviguer les maps, on sera surement moins 'concés', mais apparemment les combats sont pas encore formidables d'après les premiers retours, et sont toujours aussi difficiles (et par difficiles je veux dire injustes).
Je recommande tout de même... mais avec quelques réserves.

First off, I know I don't have much time spent on here to have a review of it. Though that actually just reinforces the point I'm about to make even further. Basically, my point is to not pay attention to the negitive reviews too much at the moment.
So many reviews I've seen have had less time spent on the game than I have, and yet leave a negitive one and say its cause there is no content, or it's bad that it's only sword and board, or that the repeating areas are boring. But even with my limited experience with the game, I can tell that's not entirely true.
Also first and foremost, if you come to a ROGUELIKE game that advertises and explains what that is, and then complain about how there is perma-death and leave a negitive review because of it, I... I dont really know what to say to that. That's a special kind of idiocy, and also just flat-out rude.
It's almost impossible to say that you've run out of content in a game like this in less than 2 hours. People have 'beaten' it. yes, but from what I can tell they have beaten it as much as, say, defeating Mom for the first time in Binding of Issac. Which brings me to the repeated areas. As you progress further, the maps do stay the same for that run. But what I've seen is that based on actions on earlier runs, that opens so much stuff on future ones. My first run was a generic one, and only got to the 4th floor, and all those floors were the same. The next time, I found out that touching crystals in areas, that made the Eye comment that I was rebuilding the realm or something along those lines, added biomes to the game that I hadn't seen before. New enemies with new weapons and maps to explore in. Finding new recipies and such, and other types of offhand weapons. All sorts of new stuff. After just my first time playing, in less than a few hours.
Now I will admit that there are gripes with the game that I have. There are what I would consider 'queued commands' that go through if you press too many buttons (for instance, if you spam the dodge button before the first one has finished it's animation, it'll cause another to go through, or if you hit accack twice and are staggered after the first, even though you've stopped inputting attack commands now you'll get flinched and then attack again up to a full second after the command), and though there are other offhand items such as wands, you always start with a sword and shield, which I never use cause I prefer dodging. A mixed opinion is that I've seen many people complain about how the Codicies do not explain exactly what they are, and that the potions and scrolls are unknown until you use them. First, I get it, but those still give a good general idea of what they are beforehand. Second, those are a staple of roguelikes so again, you're just playing the wrong genre to be complaining about that.
But all in all, I've found this game to be quite enjoyable, and it's extremely sad to see everyone downvoting it immediately just cause the vast majority of the reviews I've seen seem to have not read anything about the game or watched the trailers.

Title: That Dragon, Cancer
Platform: Windows, Mac
Rating: Not Rated
Developer: Numinous Games
Publisher: Numinous Games
Price: $15
Release Date: 12/1/16
That Dragon, Cancer is a purely narrative game made for Ryan Green, whose son; Joel Green passed away from cancer back in 2014.
The game was announced back in PAX 2013 and is about Joel and the struggles of him and everyone around him, especially his parents and how they deal with his cancer.
Now normally, the gameplay would be the main element of this game, but this is a narrative. The story comes first, meaning the gameplay itself is simple, which is okay because this game isn’t meant to be a gameplay heavy game.
It’s a narrative that completely works on so many levels to show the happy, sad and frustrating times about this little boy who has cancer, as seen from the eyes of his family, but mainly from the eyes of his father. And this is when the game shines. When the father would monologue, I was moved by what he says and truly felt an emotional attachment to Joel and everyone else.
The wife’s speeches were also done well. And her belief that god would save the baby and the utter realization of there not being anyone to help them, made me feel very emotional and even tear up a little. The graphics while pretty bland are actually done well because it didn’t take me away from the narrative but still helped me paint a picture.
The soundtrack makes the game amazing too. While you won’t find things that really stand out it accompanies the narration and story, and that’s enough. The acting, as I said before are done very well and this is what mainly made the narrative so moving and really let me see how the parents were in their own shoes.
The gameplay itself is simply clicking and looking around rooms usually being narrated by either the mother or father and the soundtrack in the background.
The start does this very well even though the boring clicking is there, it’s only there to show the narrative, which makes it wonderful.
But nearing the end of the game I felt that it started to become too gameplay heavy and while the narration was there, which was done great as it was the whole way through; it still didn’t drown out the boring clicking enough as it became more focussed on gameplay.
But like I said, the narration is there and other than a small bug forcing me to skip a little part, that there’s nothing really wrong with this game.
So this game, I’m guessing; was made to show people the story of Joel, and how the up’s and down’s of his story affected the parents; to make us feel what they felt.
And this game completely does that, no doubt. With its great soundtrack, graphics which may be dull but good enough to paint the picture, and a moving dialogue, makes this game a must play to all gamers who can enjoy a narrative even though this game has some issues such as a couple bugs and some boring sections nearing the end of the game.

TL:DR
The first thing I would like to mention is that I only played the first half of this game while connected to Steam. That is why it only registers as me having 1 hour. I have finished the game, however.
Also, mild spoilers.
"That Dragon, Cancer" is intended to be a heart-wrenching, tragic depiction of a young boy named Joel's struggle and eventual death at the hands of the most hated disease known to man: cancer. It's based on a true story, and chronicles the parents' emotions, feelings, and spiritual musings as their son's state gradually deteriorates.
Here are my pros and cons:
PROS:
-Beautiful soundtrack.
-Competent voice acting, considering the voice actors are the parents of the actual boy himself, and are amateurs.
-Unique and intriguing art style.
-The emotion in the game is real; if embellished, it's very subtly done.
CONS:
-Ridiculous $14.99 price tag.
-Textures clip and animation falters several times.
-Controls are laggy, counterintuitive, and annoying, even for a sort of point-and-click.
-Mini games accomplish nothing and often serve to disconnect from the overall theme. They don't convey much emotion and feel out of place.
-The game has to be finished in one sitting, or you're completely emotionally disconnected and just kinda annoyed.
-It's often hard to tell what the game wants from you. I spent ten minutes with Dolphin Dad doing underwater flips with no idea what I was supposed to be doing.
-I completely broke the "Jesus loves me" song and ended up with it playing over itself out of sync half a dozen times. Honestly, that was pretty funny. That should be in the pros.
Now, to the actual review.
"That Dragon, Cancer" is a good story in the form of a terrible game. The artwork, while initially charming, eventually loses its beauty, becoming a confusing miasma of fractured textures and unimpressive design. The controls are laggy, buggy, and sluggish. The minigames feel forced and pointless. I would have enjoyed this a lot more left as a pure walking simulator.
Now to the story.
You feel the pain of Joel's parents as their child struggles to grow, his disease evident to even his siblings. The beginning of the game is promising, even a bit tear jerking, although I did not cry. (Not to say I'm incapable of crying. Games such as "Undertale", "To The Moon", "Among the Sleep" and "I am Bread" made the tears flow liberally.) The parents are struggling as they attempt to find peace through a completely tragic experience, putting their faith and trust in God to save their son. This is a recurring theme, and perhaps even the main theme of the game, more so than Joel's cancer. The father feels angry that God is allowing this. The mother is angry that the father is angry. Where is God? Will Jesus take their son to heaven? Will he live?
The emotion is often times well conveyed. The hospital scene near the end was one of the painful scenes I've ever played. The utter helplessness you feel annoyed me at first, until I realised that is exactly what I was supposed to feel. At which point, I appreciated it. That I was trying so hard to find a way to escape the room, to escape the crying, was a testament to good storytelling. Either that, or i have 7 youngest siblings, and I hate to hear babies cry. One of the two. On the other hand, sometimes the emotion is horribly portrayed. Like dolphin dad. That was just stupid.
So this game is a bit up and down. One moment, you'll feel the pain, the emotion, and the beauty that this game is conveying, and the next, you'll be utterly lost. Like that "Throne of God" scene. What was I supposed to do with that piano? I just spammed lmb at that point. Which is too bad, because I think that was a really important moment in the game?
Also, the portrayal of heaven is strange. I mean, that is a lot of pancakes.
So, in conclusion:
I'm a Christian. I wanted to be touched by this game. I wanted to cry. I wanted to come away with that same feeling of awe that I felt upon finishing "The Beginner's Guide:" that feeling that my perspective on something had been integrally changed forever.
But I couldn't. I just couldn't get into it. Every time I would, I would immediately be pushed out of it by something strange and unwieldy the game threw at me. I sat there, staring at the credits, feeling guilty that I hadn't like the game.
Don't bother with this one unless it goes on a big sale, folks. Until then, it's just not worth it.

I don't typically write reviews about games, but I saw this on the Store and I was drawn to it. As someone, whose mother, and grandfather died from Cancer, I was hesitant about purchasing a game that was making its money from such a taboo subject.
However, the game developers have truly done the game justice. The beautifully innovated scenery, music, and characterisation of the family was breathtaking. I did read a view of the reviews whilst hte game was downloading, and saw the mention of religion. Now, I am personally, a self-proclaimed atheist, but the use of religion merely is a personal attribute that was a coping mechanism for this family. As it is based on the game creators/writers' family, I can understand why religion was used and why it was an important aspect of the game.
I truly cried, and laughed (at times) and this game was an emotional rollercoaster. The subject of Cancer was handled well, and it does not appear to be a game made purely for the money-making aspect as many other members of the Steam community wish to point out. It truly is an inspiring and beautiful game.
The only flaw I would give it, is that the control system was a little odd, and the price tag is a little high.

The biggest Pro for me?  It was easy to get into even though I have played only "casual" strategy games such as Civ 5 and more RTS style games such as starcraft.  I felt overwhelmed only for a few moments when things began happening, but as long as you read / listen to the helpful robot you will get the hang of it quickly.
It is worth noting there is a LOT to do in this game but the majority of it is entertaining and none of it felt completely like a chore.  If you do not take interest in building each little planet hand-by-hand you can even set it inside of a zone that takes care of it for you (at least after the first few hours when the tutorial takes you there).
Replay-ability will of course be massive as there is so much random generation each game will always be different.
Looking forward to dying of the space plague sometime in the near future of my first play through.

Combat is enaging and there's no shortage of random aliens to dust it up with. Going up against other empires can be costly unless you have a clear technological and naval advantage. The diplomacy is very similar to Civ 4 or 5, but I've noticed a couple of glitches on the trade screen that I hope gets cleaned up in the coming weeks.
Based on my early game impressions, if you're into space exploration and empire building games, you should definitely give Stellaris a shot.

This really had much more to it than I initially thought!
So, you play the part of a girl who discovers she can be a wizard, and goes to Hogwarts... (well not Hogwarts, but I don't remember the actual name).  You choose what classes you want to take, go through the events, and get to the end of the year (or get kicked out).  The story is usually goofy and lighthearted, if a bit simplistic.  The music is pretty standard, not too memorable.
What makes this more than one would think?  Each playthrough really seems to have the potential to be totally different.  I've tried three different runs now, and although each run is fairly quick, each run was also quite different.  There are a LOT of different events that pop up depending on your choices, be it deciding which magic you want to train, or which people you are friendly with, or how you deal with that persistent demon... Also, the dungeons seem quite carefully planned out so there are many different ways you can come up with for escaping (though I did get stuck a few times).  The characters have more depth than I gave them credit for at first also (oh, so they AREN'T just a troubled child...)
I had (and am still having) quite a bit of fun with this... $15 may be a bit expensive to suggest as a price, perhaps wait for a sale.

Magical Diary: Horse Hall is a game that lives and breathes the phrase "looks can be decieving".
From its premise to its presentation, it almost seems like it goes out of its way to make you underestimate it. You play as a sixteen-year-old girl of your own design (with the default name Mary Sue. Heh.) who goes to a school for wizards and witches. The game is very aware that this sounds a lot like Harry Potter, and not only makes few attempts to keep the player from making comparisons, it even takes a few playful jabs at itself with that punchline (for example; there is a student who inexplicably looks exactly like Harry Potter himself. He acts nothing like him and isn't important to the story at all.).
The actual gameplay is pretty simple. It's mostly a visual novel, with some light RPG elements (you take classes to raise your stats in various schools of magic, sorted by color, to learn new spells) and occasional puzzle dungeon gameplay (you r tests consist of being teleported into a literal dungeon and using the spells you've learned to solve puzzles until you find a way to escape), and a bit of dating sim is in there, too. Each class you take, you randomly gain 1-3 points in the color of magic you're studying, and an equal amount of stress (bit of advice, your stress isn't worth worrying about until it's at least at 30, and resting just once drops it by no less than 20), and you usually learn a new spell every 5 points. There are a lot of spells, too many to learn them all in one playthrough, and not all of them are useful. The good news in that every dungeon has multiple ways to solve its puzzles, usually one for each school of magic, so as long as you know how to use what spells you have, you can probably escape the dungeon. Finding different ways to solve each puzzle is a good, viable way to prevent each playthrough from getting stale if you're trying to go for all the endings.
The writing is arguably the best part of the game. As I've said above, the game is heavily based around the idea that looks can be decieving. So, naturally, the game starts out trying to look very cliche'd and unoriginal. Every character's first impression is incredibly tropey and shows a clear archetype that, while not entirely false, is definitely just what each character is on the surface.
The list goes on. Most named characters you meet have their own route, and you aren't likely to get much information on them if you don't pursue that route, which also adds to the replay value.
The game's weakest point is probably its presentation, mainly the art and music. The music isn't bad, but there aren't very many tracks, so you're going to get used to hearing a lot of the same songs. The star wipe screen transition is incredibly overused, even being used for characters appearing in a scene in place of them simply fading in. Hope you like stars a lot, this game sure does. And lastly, the art isn't impressive. I'm reluctant to call it bad, but it looks like it was done by a talented young artist; it shows potential, but looks immature. A lot of characters are also clearly made using the same character creator you use to make your Mary Sue, which is pretty noticeable. On the other hand, it's a good way to tell if someone is actually important or not; important characters have unique art.
Ultimately, Magical Diary is all about faking you out, making you expect one thing, then doing something else, without it feeling forced or un-foreshadowed. If you're looking for a visual novel where you can get through a route in under 10 hours, with a better-than-average amount of replay value compared to most of its kind, that likes to keep you guessing, Magical Diary: Horse Hall may be for you.

Final Fantasy VI is considered by many to be Squaresoft's Magnum Opus.  Final Fantasy IX was loved by many as a return to form in a big way for the company in it's twilight years before merging with Enix.  Final Fantasy VII, however, will always hold a special place for me.
I was a Genesis kid growing up, until one day in 1997 while visiting family I got to spend time playing with some cousin's Sony PlayStation.  And my first introduction to the PS1 was the iconic deep bass sound of the system BIOS, and the opening and early gameplay of Final Fantasy VII.
Before then, I'd often seen the epic sounding commercials.  The advertising for VII was nearly impossible to avoid, in fact.  Everything had characters from FF7 emblazoned onto it, even Pepsi was running a huge promotion with character art and backgrounds of Midgar plastered all over just about everything sold by the company.  But this was the first time I actually had my hands on it.
I stunk the place up at the first boss I'll admit.  This was mostly due to an unfortunate translation error in which Cloud encourages the player to attack at a point where doing so will result in a powerful attack severely harming the party.
The Steam version of FF7 is a way to finally play this gem without having to spend a ridiculous amount at a classic games store or on Amazon.  Note however it does have it's problems.
For one, it requires you to log into a Square-Enix account to launch, which is always a pain in the rear.  Second, little to no configuration options are available.  The original game ran in 640x480 native PSX resolution, but the Steam version will run in a screen-filling window size no matter what.  Worse, it becomes immediately clear the menu screen and the field screen where most gameplay takes place are running in different resolutions.
This lack of polish is annoying to say the least, especially when you find yourself fighting in the woods around Junon or Gongaga to recruit a certain once secret party member that's not so much a secret nowadays.  Or while attempting to get some character's final limit breaks on Disk 1 just because you can.  It's times like those I like to fire up Netflix or YouTube, and that's hard to do when I can't even run the game in a native resolution window.
The game is also a bit long in the tooth, particularly for those who celebrate the downfall of random battles in RPGs, but still well worth the asking price.  You may not agree with some on it being the best in the franchise, but starting up the game and putting yourself in the shoes of kids or even adults firing it up for the first time in 1997 should give you insight into whay it's still so incredibly hyped.
And you don't have to set your PC upside down before it melts the system, so there's that too.

This is the ONLY game I have EVER played where I actually read the credits at the end. Why you ask? You probably havent but I am going to tell you anyway... This game is so beautifully done that I felt by the end of it it deserved the time to read the names behind it. I really can't find anything to fault with this game. It is, simply put, charming in its delivery.
The characters are great, the story is very well delivered and keeps you invested in the what is going on while giving adequete spaces between story for action and mini puzzles.
The combat, while simple, also has a degree of complexity that does take some time to master but when mastered makes you feel like such a bad*ss while also punishing your mistakes (keep in mind I only played this on the hardest difficulty setting and quite frankly, at times, it was a f*cking nightmare. It may well be quite easy on the easiest setting).
Level design is very well thought out with a great mix of miniture puzzles (to find loot and 'friends'), hazards and a great assortment of enemies to go through.
There is even a simple crafting system and an RPG style levelling system that is also VERY well done as it is simple yet effective in what it does. What does it do? Gives you what I would call 'Freedom Control'. Your free to choose the way you are controlled. 'This armour is the best you can get at the moment (controlled)... now would you like to buy that, craft it by hunting enemies for materials by grinding or buy the materials needed?... Your call chuckles.". It works very brilliantly. Even with the leveling system for Dust. While you can be a powerhouse hitter and kill everything in a few hits, you cant be SUCH a heavy hitter that you die in one hit yourself.
I would recommend this game to everyone. Not that I think everyone will enjoy it on the level I did but because it is so well done that it deserves to be played by lovers of games. It is masterfully done.

1: Genre (2/5)
This game doesn't really know what it wants to be, its part RPG, part dating-sim, part puzzle-solving but this indecisiveness leads to the game not being a complete version of any of those things. Its usually not a bad thing to mix genres, but then they have to be interlocked better and they cant just be done half way.
2: Gameplay (3/5)
I liked the mechanics of the game. Your options were plenty and it felt like, what you chose really made a difference.
Sadly, what I liked most also lacked the most  - the dungeons. They were always really short, and you either figured out how they worked really fast or you fail. This caused you to get demerits which ultimately lead to expulsion. The final dungeon which is your exam gives you almost no options which is particularly sad.
3: Story (3/5)
Its an okay story with some more or less predictable plot twists. The problem is that some story lines you chose are way shorter than others.
4: Playtime (2/5)
The demo felt like a third of the whole game for me, maybe if you played it a couple times through it would be worth it, but not for me. You only get one year of playtime, with the end of your first semester, the game ends. Many storylines still open and many things you couldn't do.
5: Graphics & sound (3/5)
Fit okay to the style of the game, nothing memorable, nothing new, nothing exciting.
Overall (2.6/5) - All in all it felt incomplete and too expensive.

If you can look past the down-right goofy looking characters and art style, Magical Diary is a solid game. Like many similar dating simulations, what Magical Diary lacks in artistic substance it makes up for (for the most part) in character and story.
The game takes place in a setting quite similar to Hogwarts of the Harry Potter universe. You attend a school for the magically gifted where you make friends, learn spells, go to classes, and so on. Stat raising is crucial in this game, just as in many other dating sims, but here it's far less repetitive in comparison to others of this genre. Various events happen on a regular basis within the game, so instead of just doing class after class of monotonous repetition, the game gives you opportunities to interact with characters and make important choices.
The "puzzles" of this game are less than stellar. They tend to be either painfully simple or just plain frustrating, very rarely does the game find a middleground. As well it's easy to "get stuck" during the game, which is why I recommend using multiple save files. This is important becaue if you don't study the right magic to the right extent early on in the game, it's possible to be faced with puzzles that you simply lack the ability to solve. Again, this is very frustrating, but at the same time a necessary evil for a game of this variety.
Finally, there's the characters. For anyone who wants an idea of what the different romanceable character routes are like, you can choose between romancing your professor (who as many people have pointed out, has striking similarities to a certain Harry Potter character), the generic mysterious bad boy, the school prankster, or either of your two best friends. The characters certainly aren't unlikeable for the most part, but I'd still definetelty recommend considering their personalities before deciding if this game is for you. The characters are one of the things that made this game enjoyable to me despite it's flaws, but if you don't find them as appealing it likely won't have the same effect.
Overall Magic Diary is a decent game. Just be sure to carefully consider the characters and the art style before you decide whether or not it's something you want to try.

If I had to describe Necropolis in a few words, I would say it's like a Randomized Dark Souls Nuzlocke.  The combat and difficulty is akin to Dark Souls, but every run will be different and if you die, you have to start all over, just like a Randomized Pokemon Nuzlocke.
That being said, I think that this game is fantastic.
- The combat feels great.  Not as polished as Dark Souls mind you, but I still love it.  I always have enough control over my character so I don't die from stupid mistakes or lack of control.
- The difficulty of this game is just enough so it doesn't feel hopeless, but is still a good challenge (for solo play at least, I can't speak for multiplayer yet).
- The game itself has funny humor to it.  Think along the lines of Deadpool humor.  I've caught myself chuckling while playing more times than I can count.
- The look of the game is absolutely beautiful.  If you think the graphics look good in the trailer, wait til you experience it in game.
One of the biggest complaints I've seen about the game is that it isn't worth the $30 price tag.  And that is debatable, and is really up to each person individually.  I could see why people say that, but for me personally, I feel like the game is $30 well spent.  Ultimately, I feel like it depends on what you want out of this game.  If you plan on just beating it once, solo or with friends, and calling it good, you may or may not feel like the $30 is justified, depending on how long it takes you to beat it.  But if you want to 100% the game, I would say the time you'll spend in Necropolis would make the price worth it.  But again, I can't speak for everyone.
Another complaint I've seen, which is somewhat tied to the topic above, is the lack of variety in the game.  And honestly, I'm not sure where this idea is coming from.  With 11 hours in the game at the time of writing this review, I'm still finding new things in every run, be it a new weapon or a new enemy.
TL;DR: I don't regret buying this game in the slightest, and if a Randomized Dark Souls Nuzlocke sounds like fun to you, then you should consider giving this game a go.
The developers put a lot of effort into this game and it shows in spades. It shouldn't be about the length, you're getting an experience that can't be had elsewhere.

The Witcher 2 is one of the best action-RPGs around.  Well-written and mature story, plot, and dialogue.  The characters are well-developed. And, the decisions that you make throughout your journey changes the game dynamically.
The controls are fluid, intuitive, and mapped in a style that is conducive to gameplay.  For those that are curious, I played all 60 hours of gameplay with a mouse and keyboard.
Visuals are excellent for its time, and it has aged well.  Also, it is well-optimized.  My graphics and video options were set to ultra, 1200p, all maxed except for uber-sampling.  When I played The Witcher 2, I was using a GTX 670, i5-2500k.
However, The Witcher 2 focuses less on monster hunting lore, and more on the political aspect of The Witcher universe.  Even then, there is some monster hunting and ghouls to fight during your downtime before you return to the game's political intrigue.
If you are a fan of The Witcher books, The Witcher 1 videogame, and its universe, you owe it to yourself to play this game.  Maybe, even twice.

The Witcher 2: Assassins of Kings is a intense, mature, and politically intriguing RPG that received rave praises and reviews alike from critics and fans. You play as Geralt of Rivia, a monster slayer with "superhuman" capabilities, must pursue an unknown assassin throughout the Northern Kingdoms. After the events in the first Witcher game, Geralt of Rivia seeks answers and personal ambitions in a world where war and politics blend together in a destructive force. It is obvious that every RPG gamer has to get the Witcher 2, but why?
One of the greatest features in the Witcher 2 is player choice(s). Sure, player choices is literally in modern RPG, but what is so special about this feature in the Witcher 2? You see, player choices can actually change the course of the story, depending on which "sides" to choose. This alters various story dynamics and able to meet  "never-before-seen" characters that you (probably) would never meet if you select one particular side.  This strongly encourages replay value, and each side has many interesting story plots. Another great feature in the Witcher 2 is how player choices are not classified in a "black-versus-white" scenarios; it's mainly in the shades of gray, the selection of picking the "lesser evil". The world in the Witcher (and in reality) cannot be based upon pure morality, but based upon your critical thinking and your personal ("moral") compass to decides on what choices are the lesser evil. Lastly, the game has an intense politically intriguing storyline that will get you hook in an instant (if you like to have such stories). Basically, Temeria (the main setting in the first Witcher game) is in the brink of societal and political collapse and other Northern Kingdoms are debating on who should take over. Meanwhile, the Southern Kingdom (mainly Nilfgaardian Empire)  are at war with all of the Northern Kingdoms. I won't tell too much details in the story, but compare the Witcher to Game of Thrones, and you will probably get it.
The Witcher 2 is not perfect since it has a few issues. One negative aspect in the Witcher 2 is game crashing to desktop. It happens here and there, but this is caused by high numbers of automatic saves. Another negative attribute has to do with the highly frequent autosaves and no override a saved game. The story can be a little too complex and too many characters to memorized. While the game respects each character to have its own development, the player would probably lose interests on caring about "minor" characters. There's a lot of them. The inventory system is a bit of a mess and disorganized in some areas. Some textures in the Witcher 2 are bland, and certain objects look like blobs or grayed-out.
Overall, the graphics and environment are stunningly gorgeous and visually indulging. The sounds quality are top notch and Triss Merigold is such a beautiful woman; I'll tell you that. The Witcher 2 is frequently on sale at Steam or GOG so take this opportunity to get it now and enjoy it. Oh, did I tell you how much I love red-haired women? *Wink* *Wink*

The description says "From the art director of Journey", which in itself is a masterpiece- if you own a PlayStation 3 or 4 and haven't already, then buy and play it.
The beautiful art of Abzû isn't the only thing that's similar to Journey, the music, the gameplay, the cutcenes, the color variety, the camera, the derelict ruins of civilization, the art pieces left in the world, the second level (like the fourth level in Journey - the slide), the ending level, the achievment system with hidden things to find, and the reward for collecting everything, it all calls Journey.
Not all is similar though, Abzû is underwater which makes it more difficult to control three dimensions (a controler helps a lot), it doesn't have the loose Coop-Mode of Journey, and it doesn't have enemies that make you loose something when hit (which helps to eliminate the fear you might have in this alien environment, sharks and other predators don't bite you).
But it has other things, most of all: animals, a lot of underwater creatures, including bigger ones that you can ride, like sharks, whales, tortoise and dolphins, some birds, a polar bear and even penguins. By finding hidden objects you are unlocking additional marine animals in the current area, that you can ride or watch how they live by using meditation shrines. You aren't always underwater, there are some (rare) passages where you leave the cold water and walk on your feet.
Finishing the game took me 3.5 hours, but I'm a slow player and I took my time to investigate everything, enjoy the athmosphere, or to have some fun with the engine beside progress. Rushing through should take between 1.5 and 2 hours, but I'd strongly advise against doing so.
I'm a bit ashamed for having it bought in a sale for € 6. It's worth more, and the developers deserve every cent of the regular price of € 20. I hope they will release a boxed collector's edition with soundtrack sooner or later to spend my money on.

This game is a piece of interactive art that explores the emotions and experiences of the Green family, and their struggle with their son Joel's battle with cancer. With every sound and visual cue, we're given tiny pieces of a story that is carefully crafted to ensure that the weight of the situation is conveyed to the audience.
I very rarely play games that have me so emotionally invested that I cry actual tears. There was a specific moment, that I'm sure you'll all experience, that made my heart ache so much that I had to take a break from playing.
I'm no longer a believer in any kind of deity, but the I feel the the inclusion of religion was important to the story. Many people who deal with these tragedies seek out spritual guidance. While not everyone does, the Greens did and its inclusion in the story is better for it. It portrays the struggle of keeping hope and faith alive in times of strife, which is very relateable.
I'm very happy to have backed this game on KickStarter, and I recommend it to anyone who's looking for an answer to whether or not video games are an art form.

I'm usually not one to write a review for a game that I don't recommend, but I think I need to for this.
Being a big fan of The Neverhood, I was obviously very excited when the Kickstarter for Armikrog launched almost two and a half years ago. However, after finally having gotten to play it, I can't help but getting a sour taste in my mouth.
While the art design and animation is superb, the aspect that it truly falls flat on is the puzzles, and that's pretty bad for an adventure game. There are truly only a handful of variations of puzzles throughout the whole thing, only ramping up in complexity each time, and the only way I can easily explain them is: Tedious. It felt like a chore to work through these puzzles, and I was actively looking forward to the whole thing being over after a while. I can only describe it as being boring.
It's sad, but this turned out to be a prime example of why Kickstarter is such a gamble. You can see the love and dedication that the team put into this, but it is also painfully obvious that they ran out of time and money a lot sooner than they thought they would, leaving an end product that is neither satisfying or ultimately worth your time.
The game is very fun with a great amount of replay value and customization. If you enjoy 4x games or grand strategy games, Stellaris is a must-own.

12 hours of gameplay.
12 hours of utter joy.
I2 hours of building what I thought to be a decent empire only to be crushed to pieces by my neighbors when our borders crossed.
Short Review:
If you like DW and the immersion factor of your galaxy and exploring and finding new races, artifacts - its a must buy. Especially as this is the first release. Not a single bug or crash encountered.
If you like MOO type games where you spam colonize, race the tech tree, and have a quicker gaming experience - not for you.
Long Review:
For an initial stage 1 release - a work of art - which will only get better with DLC, enhancements etc.
The galaxy is IMMENSE and there is so much to explore and find.
The random alien races are my favorite feature. It truly feels like you are exploring space.
Is this up to par with EUIV yet? Of course not. Thats been out for years and has several DLC and enhancements.
Is this capabale of standing on its own as first release and an enjoyable "consuming" gaming experience?
Yes. 100% without a doubt.
You can see the work that went into this game with all the events, details, artifiacts.
You can see the balance at work with your resources.
Do I spend that energy credit for an extra mining base? Its a balancing act.
I truly enjoy the random research. I like the idea of not following a static tech tree and "racing" to get a nuclear warhead etc. You really need to plan and build how you want your empire to act.
On my 1st playthrough I created a desolate angry desert race. As I met more and more races they all despised me - hence my race being eliminated. I should have focused on military techs etc but I did not play the race properly and ended up crushed.
I honestly cannot say enough kind words for the Paradox team on this release.
Thank you for the immersive enterainment value.

This does not mean I did not enjoy the game- I greatly enjoyed it. But I cannot recommend this game to anyone I do not know: It is a very specific taste of game.
This will not appeal to the average gamer. If you are looking for depth, you may enjoy it. If you are looking for a great gameplay experience, you likely won't. If you just want to burn everything, you'll love it. The gameplay is built around repetition and waiting, as a satire of AVGM and the pay-to-win formula used in Facebook games. But this means that the game is designed to be repetitive: Not a great trait in most games. And if you don't like waiting five minutes to burn a single thing, it'll cost you stamps, which are an in-game currency you slowly accumulate.
The entire game takes place in front of a fireplace, with the exception of the end, which serves to teach a preachy lesson about wasted time. But there is more to it than that, if you're willing to look into it. The depth is a decent hook for game analysts, and the meaning of the ending is vague enough to be interpreted as a good number of things, all positive and optimistic. Most people won't look into this, though, and I don't blame them.
The atmosphere is just as fantastic and eerie as World of Goo was (Same creator), with that silver lining lingering in the distance. The dialogue is kooky and fun, yet reveals a dark and sinister motive. But I expect most gamers' reactions to this would be "so what?" Atmosphere does not make the game. It cannot serve as the initial hook, and only becomes tangible when the player is immersed.
So no, I don't recommend it. It has fantastic atmosphere. It has a dark theme. It has a sweet-but-simple ending. It has great idle gameplay. But you would need to be an "artistic" gamer to acknowledge most of this. If you don't look for atmosphere in games, you won't care about it in this one. If you play games to play games, this falls short of the criteria.
However, my negative rating of this will likely draw people that are honestly researching into if they should get this game. And, as you read through my review, you may notice that I am not describing you. You may think "I'm not an average gamer. These assumptions don't apply to me." If that's the case, then enjoy Little Inferno, as I have.
