So, now that the game is in full, lets get down to the♥♥♥♥♥♥and grits of the game.  What is wrong with it? And what is right with it?  Well.. currently, I am engaging in a full playthrough.  In my first 30 minutes, I discovered that the game seems to require MUCH more system resources than it should for the type of game you are playing.  The game also seems to take several steps BACKWARDS!! in regards to the progress that has been made in the dungeon Crawler genre of games.  It makes a sort of Dated, modern take on a familiar genre that has had leaps and bounds of progress made, 10 years ago.
It may get better later... but currently, it clearely shows dated mechanics that I would have expected a company like Ubisoft to invest in improving (IE full voice overs, a fully explorable world) if they actually believed in the project.
Currently, SOME of the main quest givers actually speak, and the game moves in a old school (and I mean super old school) grid method which is dated even for the 90s.  The game runs poorly which is honestly unforgiveable.  And last but not least, it just seems limiting in regards to the way you make your party.  That last one is a minor gripe, but I am in a nit picky mood at the time of this review.
So what does the game do right?  Well, currently it seems very balanced, and the game is full of lore if you do not mind reading.  The story ties in with a familiar world (thus far) if you have been paying attention to the previous games in the series, and even comes with several nods to those games.  It isn't a terrible game, it could have been much worse, and the game is most certainly playable.  It seems balanced (at the time of the review) and I have yet to encounter a real problem space that I simply could not finish.  I will complain though, that I have yet to discover a way to flee a combat.  Which I find to be in poor taste... there is simply no way I have found to disengage from a fight once something closes the distance etoo you.  So I would suggest to be VERY careful.  Makes you think actually, which is a good thing in a manner of speaking.  Unfortunately, some fights you will not know you can't deal with until you start the fight, so save often.
is the game worth getting?  Currently, I am totally torn.  The super fan of this genre is willing to accept even a mediocre title, and invest.  The game itself is not above 30 dollars in charge, but at the same time I am torn to say that you should wait till it goes on sale before picking it up.  Why get a game from a big company, when you can get a great game from a smaller indie company... (go get legend of Grimmrock)  If you are a true blue fan of might and magic, and you want another dungeon crawl to add to your list, then by all means, the game is not unplayably bad.  But just understand, that you are supporting what seems to me, like a cash cow attempt to milk the might and magic license from your friends at Ubi-soft.
If the late game is terrible, then I will add to the review, if it is good, I will also add to the review later.  Till then, I will, sort of recommend this game to folks.  Just watch my vids and see if you like what you get.

IT'S MIGHT AND MAGIC ♥♥♥♥♥EEEEESS!
Post-completion review:
Ok so, I've been playing Might and Magic games since 1997 and finished every campaign for any and all games with M&M title that came out since then. I've completed M&M6 about 10 times and rest of the games in the series at least 3 times each.
Keeping that in mind, I didn't hesitate to buy a game from the franchise, which was though to be dead, and frankly is not appealing to the younger generation of players. It is a great gamble to publish a game like this and I thank Limbic and Ubisoft (which I actually don't like very much).
However, accepting the reality of this game's probability of success for modern player base and the monetary resources devoted to the game are no doubt limited, the game feels very "incomplete" in every way.
As much as i can see on the internet, people ♥♥♥♥♥ about the grid based/turn based mechanics of the game. My personal problem however is not about it's mechanics but about it's setup. Game is considerably short (finished in 45 hours or so. In M&M 6 you can't even clear 3 cities and related regions/quests in that time) and game world is extremely small. Entirety of M&M X sums up to 2-3 regions in M&M 6, 7 or 8. Considering that M&M 6 had 12 regions and MASSIVE dungeons, M&M X is a huge disappointment in that regard.
My second problem with the game is the linearity story. M&M games always had that freedom feeling (not like the sandbox games like TES series of course) which allowed the player to go to Dragonsand at level 1 and instantly♥♥♥♥♥♥♥by 200 dragons in range.
The story itself in previous games also had a classic purpose of gathering up different factions against a common enemy, then going in solo to crash it. M&M X lacks this quest line too, as we are getting railroaded into a single minded purpose. In M&M 7 the light vs dark choice had a game changing effect, and less so in 8. M&M X doesn't have this story feature as it lacks any type of choice over the story.
There are also issues with the game mechanics themselves. The class promotions are almost useless to get (which were CRITICAL to have in previous games), and the lack of honorary promotion quests breaks some of the dungeons (like if you don't have a paladin in your party, you can't complete the quest about shantiri disc). Skills are restructured and the removal of most miscelenaous skills (like lockpick, merchant, armsmaster, disarm, repair, identify item, etc.) makes the game more combat oriented than before.
On the positive side of things, the setting of the game was done quite well with the "new" world of Ashan. After the failure of M&M 9 and it's poorly thought setting, M&M X used the story began with Heroes 6 quite well. Race specific classes were also a great idea and made the game replayable (for me at least)
My evaluation of the game in general comes down to these:
- Very short story
- VERY small game world
- Too linear storyline and the lack of choice
- Bugs (less than I expected actually)
- Poor game engine performance
+ Franchise connected backstory
+ Large number of classes for replayability
+ 4 player party system and turn based combat
+ BEING A MIGHT AND MAGIC GAME
7/10
PS: If the game gets a few DLCs to make it longer (like twice longer or something) and add regions like a city from Irollan, a single location from Seven Cities and a city from neighbouring Unicorn Duchy my rating would go up to 7,5-8/10

Fairly mediocre adventure game. Unfortunate to see Earthworm Jim's creator continue to make a game that suffers the same mistakes two decades later, which is to say that Armikrog feels like a game designed by visual artists instead of actual game designers. I will give it credit for being very aesthetically pleasing, but under the surface I found it to be a very sloppy, toothless gameplay experience.
I found very few of the puzzles to be particularly well-designed. Many are simply designed to be time-consuming rather than require actual problem solving (the most egregious examples of which are repeated multiple times over the course of the game). The game utilizes a very minimalist interface that sounds fine on paper, but in practice is hampered by a complete lack of feedback and some appallingly broken hotspots. On more than one occasion I tried to perform an action to no avail and was stumped until it randomly decided to accept my inputs for no discernible reason. The player isn't even allowed to make the protagonists press buttons if pressing it won't do anything; they have to solve the corresponding puzzle first. This is compounded by the game's lack of any kind of feedback, leaving the player to wonder if they're not solving it correctly or if the game is outright broken. Maybe it would have been too costly to get Tommynaut's voice actor to say "Hmm... nope. That didn't do anything.", or animate some kind of shrug, but the game ought to AT LEAST trust the player enough to press a button!
Storywise, Armikrog is merely passable. The cutscene animations are very well done, and it seems like a lot of effort was spent on the game's lore, but beyond the game's opening cinematic Tommynaut and Beak-Beak have almost no character. Outside of a couple cutscenes they're almost totally mute. The opening cinematic would have you believe the game is a fun, character driven, buddy adventure in the vein of Sam & Max or Grim Fandango, but in actuality their dynamic can be boiled down to "one of them is small enough to fit in small spaces, the other is not as small".
Armikrog is not a very long game. This is not a problem in itself, but it's so lacking in charm and fun gameplay and it feels so stretched-thin as it is, for a game of such brevity. In the interest of full disclosure, I have never played The Neverhood at the time of this writing, but I backed Armikrog on Kickstarter based on its strong pitch that painted it as The Neverhood's spiritual successor. Instead, I received what feels like a half-finished cautionary tale about crowdfunding. I wouldn't say Armikrog is an outright terrible game, but it's so half-baked that your money would probably be better spent on just one of the myriad superior adventure games that have come out in the last twenty years. You'd be better versed in adventure games than any of Armikrog's developers, to be sure.

Crypt of the Necrodancer is a beautifully crafted mix between a rhythm game and a tile-based roguelike. You play as one of several characters who are forced to move to the beat of a catchy soundtrack, each with their own quirk to make the game frustrating, painful, and gloriously addictive. Everything can be done using a single set of four context-sensitive buttons. Just press a direction to move, attack, or dig in that direction, and the game will pick the action most conducive to progress. That, of course, doesn't mean you're not going to die. Through the pressure of moving to the beat, you're going to make stupid decisions, and they will be entirely your fault. Every enemy telegraphs their moves and attacks in a predictable pattern, and if you end up cornered by three enemies and your back to a wall, you only have yourself to blame.
Every zone has three floors and a boss. The stairs to the next floor are only opened by defeating the miniboss, but you can fall through a trapdoor at the song's end to get to the next floor, if you don't mind the miniboss and several other monsters following you down, forcing you to kill it before you can actually explore the floor.
Each boss has their own quirks. King Conga skips the eigth beat, and if you miss a step he'll get off his throne and charge at you. Deep Blues is a literal chessboard, swarming you with pieces that you must clear out before the King stops running away. Coral Riff floods the area, creating water tiles that stop you from moving if you step in them. Death Metal works through several phases at the pace of the fastest song in the game.
And, of course, there are the story bosses in the last zone if you're playing as Cadence, Melody, or Aria. Fight the Necrodancer and reclaim your freedom!
You can choose to start at any zone after the furthest you've finished, at the cost of not being able to complete more than one zone at a time, or take a top-to-bottom all zones run that starts you with no character upgrades. Completing and exploring individual zones rewards you with diamonds, which allow you to upgrade your character, unlock equipment, spells, and weapons, or buy items to start with in your next zone run.
Of course, unlocking items just means you can find them in your next runs! This is a roguelike after all, and every sword, armor, ring, and spell has to be found in the Crypt itself for you to use them.
Play as Melody and only attack when moving! Don't get cornered!
Play as Eli and blast your enemies to bits... if you don't blow yourself up first!
Play as Dove and friendship the monsters away... for a while before they mob you!
Play as Monk and find even more ways to die, since you can't touch money!
Play as Dorian and realize that moving two spaces at once is more frustrating than helpful!
Play as Bolt and learn that double speed is somehow both faster and slower than you expect!
Play as Aria and discover that perfect rhythm is even harder when you gotta stay alive too!
Play as Bard and move to your own beat... coward.
And, once you've done all that, play as Coda, the Monk-Bolt-Aria hybrid. That's all the description you need. Good luck!
Overall rating: 4/4 time.

Necropolis is a third person dungeon crawling adventure, with permadeath that can be played as single player or online co-op.
Combat is what makes up most of the game. At first, I didn’t like it very much, especially with weird keybindings, and certain weapons having crazy slow swing animations, but it felt a bit better once I got the hang of the controls.
The constant threat of death does make combat more interesting, but the combat itself doesn’t feel all that exciting. I spent practically every encounter doing the same thing though: quick hit, dodge path, and kite enemies around the room, repeating this every time I got my stamina back. There are more powerful attacks, but when fighting groups of enemies, I found using them would often result in me taking additional damage while stuck in the combat animation, but they were effective in 1v1 encounters.
Different weapons have different ranges and speeds. It seems like they all have their advantages and disadvantages, but it definitely feels like some weapons just aren’t as effective as others, like maces for example have a fairly short range with a very slow attack speed, and you’ll often take damage while trying to attack. Also, drinking potions and eating food takes time, and you have no way to cancel once you start, so you need to be very careful about where and when you eat or drink.
There is a story in Necropolis, but you learn about it by reading random texts on walls. I really don’t have any idea what exactly is going on in the story, since I spend most of my time too busy running from monsters to stop and read the story text.
The minimalist environments look decent enough, but there are some areas that are pretty dull looking, especially in the earlier levels of the game. Exploring just often seems like I’m finding more of the same areas though.
With the game being procedurally generated, and death being permanent, there is always the potential for replay value, but it does start to feel repetitive seeing similar areas, and fighting the same mobs over, and over again. I’ve played the game over 11 hours so far, and it’s not a bad game, but I feel that the price is too high for its current state. Although, I’m mostly enjoying the game, it’s not quite as much as I had hoped. It’s a good concept, and it has potential, but there are definitely some issues that need to be addressed.

First off, Yes this is a Early Access Review and yes I totally understand that it's in development.  I applied for a refund, didn't get it so i'm writing a review for others instead.
What really really drove me to give a negative review is the lack of actual content.  Now yes early development means not much content but believe me, 80% of it is absolutely useless.  This game is literally a game of a guy, who is lost using the same spear, eating same food and drinking the same water, There's no point in building anything other than the tent to save the damn game.
First off, weapons.  Your given multiple weapons, Bows, arrows, matchete, club, bombs, spears.  Sounds like alot of weapons right?
There's only 1 you will need and ti's the spears and it's the first thing you make with a stick...
The bow does not function properly, no draw back, can't aim down either and arrows are extremely expensive to make.
Bombs are impossible as the item needed is so far away and your bag space is so limited, spears are better.
Everything else is the same, pretty pointless cause the amoutn of attack you need to 1 spear is 3:1.
Second, Buildings - Traps/Fences/Towers/Storage/Totems.
Now survival games you got, the small simple one, some travel one and it gets bigger and bigger and bigger.... This game doesn't provide that aspect, sure the building IS bigger, but the size difference... it's like... going from a tent to a Dumpster (BIGGeST SIZE) and the material you need from 1 to the other... will take 1-2 days of farming the mats.  Not even worth it.  No extra functions either, purely cosmetics (Barely).
Traps are great, except the mats you need to make them require way too many and I mean... WAY too many.  Also SOME traps require very unique mats which is just way too far to get, take a full day to run there and back + food + water + weapons.  Your not really protecting anything as nothing hostile ever enters your base... and even if there was there are totems! (explain later.)
Fences... they're way too short and really again provides nothing as nothing ever attacks your base...
Towers... yea nothing attacks your base... again... and mats is way too many, takes a full day to farm that stuff for no reason... you might as well run around throwing spears instead, better aim.
Storage... There's so many individual item storages... that it's absolutely frustrating.  I mean it's cute but there are items I had in my inventory that I couldn't store.  So.. I had to throw them away.
Totems...  Since I said i'll explain later, it's basicly an item to ward off monsters... every monster I killed I got a totem.  So... my base had around 30 totems just around... but nothing attacked me so I don't even know if they worked TBH.  They were my only line of defense lol.  My whole base was open.
So thats why 80% of the buildings are useless.  I had a ton of storage... but I never actually took anything off the storage as I didn't need like... 80% of the items I found.  All I ever needed was Stick/Spear, Meat and water (First thing your taught when you enter the game basicly...)
Third Combat, Combat is just run back throw spear once spear hits once, stunned throw the rest and they're dead.  They just run at u and attack, no abilties not even different run speeds.
To the Devs,
I believe that adding content or improving current content to have some value.  Reworking current content is probably the better idea.
Adding abilities or benifits to towers... or actually making towers taller (but your AI already has massive issues vs players on different height levels)
Walls need to be taller too.  Kinda weird it's so low.  Evolving the walls to have spikes or even holding the heads as totems would be nice as well.  Or adding enemy carapace to the walls too.
The Homes could actually be bigger as well, the fancier homes you have aside from the tent is actually really small and would take forever to build them.  I mean I can barely put anything inside those homes.
Food could use a huge huge upgrade.  At least add a different value for every item... doesn't make sense an EGG feeds as much as a whole rack of ribs.  Adding different benifits would be nice, like making u feel full for a while.
Weapons could get a few upgrades too.  Spear is the ezest and only thign worth having for a weapon.  Arrows are so weak, same distance as spear.  Melee weapon is so hard to obtain and not worth the farm again.
I truely believe that 80% of your content actually does nothing and it really really needs a rework to add a significance to the game so that it makes me feel like I NEED or WANT to make it.

the crime scene. Technically, it's not timed, you just need to find all of the evidence. Which gets inserted into your e-Handbook as
You'll use Truth Bullets later, for now, just collect all of them. You may be asking, "Well, how DO you find these 'Truth Bullet' things?" Easy. You have a cursor. You control it by either your mouse or your right analog stick. Hover the cursor over an object and press the A button or the right mouse button. And depending on what it is, it may be a piece of evidence or just something you can inspect. Once you've collected all of the Truth Bullets, the investigation will end and you'll enter the Class Trial.
"What the hell is this 'Class Trial' you're suddenly talking about?!" This is where everyone debates about the case, much like actual murder trials. You debate about anything from how the murder played out to the cause of death. There are multiple components to the class trial. First is the Nonstop Debate, where all of your classmates will debate. Your job is to find contradictions in what they say and refute it. BUT. This time, you're able to agree with them. Be careful, make sure to figure out whether you're supposed to refute or agree with them. Next is the Advanced Hangman's Gambit. Like before, you need to spell out the answer. But this time, it's way harder. The letters will fly across the screen left, right, up, and down. And you need to pair them up before you can fire them into the spelling space. Alright, let's get to the new stuff, such as the Dive Drive. In this, you have to, um...slide across what is pretty much an obstacle course (in your mind) and answer up to four questions about something everyone got stuck on. You might have to think about it for a while though. Hopefully none of your classmates become impatient and rush the trial while you're lost in thought... Randomly, you'll get objected to and will enter the Cross Swords. You will have to cut through your classmate's words and stab some sense into them. Lastly, I present the best for last to you: the Panic Talk Action, aka P.T.A. Okay, so this isn't exactly totally new, as it's very similar to the B.T.B., but it's controlled diferently and has new music. It's also slightly harder. In the P.T.A., you face off against a classmate that you have backed into a corner. You have to destroy their insults, excuses, and whatnot to completely break them and have all of your other classmates agree with you. It's not as bad as it sounds. It's rhythm-based gameplay that is really fun! In this game, you have to hold down the button and let go of it. It doesn't sound too bad, right? Wrong. You have to time it with the beat counter that is indefinitely scrolling across your screen. When you hold it down and let go of it, it has to be on the beat. You have a separate button to shoot down their statement thing and a button to reload your bullet counter. When you get a high enough combo, the tempo changes and BPM gets bigger, meaning the music gets faster...which means the beat counter scrolls faster. Once you've weakened them enough, you'll enter the final blow mode where you have to spell out the word(s) that will refute their final statement. When you successfully refute that last statement, you completely screw them over (usually) and win. Puhuhu~. Happy arguing, you ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s!
Overall, the game is a pretty fun and interesting experience with happy times, sad times, hope, despair, and tough choices. This one is way, way, WAY longer than the first game. The Class Trials have recesses in the middle of them, spliting it into two halves. If you thought you experienced despair in the first game, oh boy, are you totally wrong. This game presents to you the true meaning of despair. I won't spoil the game anymore, puhuhu~. After all, Monokuma has a distaste for spoilers, so I don't want to get executed. He only allowed me to spoil only the prologue, since it's not very important and it's when he makes his appearance in the game, and half of Chapter 1, since he wants me to talk about the class trial, the best part of the whole game. Have fun playing~!

I'm usually not a GIANT fan of Civilizations games... but I've enjoyed Galactic Civilizations 3 thus far.  Here's a breakdown of high points, and low points
The Good:
-Well Paced game... Definitely feels like exploring a universe.
-Lots of potential build paths to take, each of which grants seeming benefits
-Integration of Culture, governance styles, adjusting production, trading, lots of different mechanics to play with.
-Ship builder allows a lot of customization options.
-Active development... Many negative reviews state that Stardock released an unfinished product... and I'd argue that it's not unfinished, but it is a little rough around the edges at times.
The Bad:
-Incredibly RAM heavy... My CPU was built back in 2010 or so, and only has 6g of RAM.  I can't run on a map size anymore than a medium map, otherwise my RAM and SWAP usage max out and crash.
-Ship Builder allows for some incredibly exploitive options... Build a SUPER TINY, FAST builder ship that costs nothing rather than the default starbase builders.  Or build a ship with a Beam weapons and stacked missle defense when fighting an enemy that uses a fleet of all missle attackers and kinetic defended ships.
-Sometimes CPU are SUPER POWERFUL for no apparent reason.  It's not uncommon that I've found myself in a game, finally reach a neighbor, and his power is like, 10x mine.  Just 'cause.
Overall though, I do recommend this game... Maybe not at the full list price, but definitely one to watch to see if it ever goes on sale to grab it.  I've definitely gotten my money's worth out of the game thus far, and look forward to building a sick rig to be able to handle massive maps in the near future.

When you look at this.. Think The Forest** without crazed, mutant tree jumping cannibals.
Think instead.. somewhat crazed, strange aliens, some who live here anyway.. and some sucked here like you and your companions via a vortex.
Dont get used to the companions.. they dont hang around long.. as in just long enough to get you started.. then.. well things happen.
Unless your playing in Survival Mode, which is you tending to a wounded comrade and trying to survive.. the only difference between the two is that instead of looking out for yourself.. your looking out for him also.  I advise you dont start in that mode. I did and it does not include the helpful advice that Story Mode does.
Graphics wise.. Not bad at all.. I have seen better.. but I ve seen worse.. and its not system taxing.
It is a survival game. You save via your base house ( like a lot of them do these days )
Crafting is easy, minus the part that you have no idea where or how to get a few things you need.. but that makes it better. You are on an alien planet, you have no idea what is what. Of course you can just look it up via the information on forum etc.. But my advice.. Dont. Enjoy the not knowing at first. It is not hard to figure any of it out. Normally in the form of pick something up and then you know.
The control setup seemed confusing at first.. as the listed controls are for controler and PC both.. and I could not get them to change. But it didnt really matter because they are all standard setup anyway for KB / M
One thing I have not made up my mind about yet.. you cant sleep time. IE.. I built my house. Trust me.. night is scary right now.. like the Forest when your getting started.. but no way to fast time it. So I spent my first two nights hunkering in fear at the sounds around me, hiding behind my fire.. which thankfully seems to scare off a few critters that came running full tilt at me.. keeping my back to my hut wall.
Its not a bad play at all so far. I am even scared that my next day will be my last.. again.
BTW. Happy Birthday.
** I refer to the Forest, which could be considered a competitor to this game, or vice versa simply to get the idea accross.  When I say its like the Forest.. I mean it. If you recall the Forest about midway of it's EA life.. This is that, only the things that want to eat you are different.  It is also a bit slower paced here, yes.. easy to die early if you have no clue.. but the enemies are not so unforgiving.
Consider this a bit more low stress. My daughter is scared to death of the cannibals. Aliens she enjoys.

Greetings fellow gamers! This is Gamer Guy (In a Suit) from the Echo Army YouTube channel! Today I am bringing you a review of the new point & click adventure, Armikrog!
(NOTE: This game was reviewed using a key provided by the Developer)
Video Review:
The "Too Long, Didn't Watch" Review:
A beautiful game, visually. However, I cannot justify the $24.99 price tag. Poor gameplay, uninspired puzzles. 2 out of 5. Pick up at 75-80% off during a Steam sale. Perhaps diehard fans of the original Neverhood may enjoy this sequel.
The "Meat & Potatoes" Review:
The game play is your very basic point and click adventure. You click a spot,  you move to that spot. You click an item, you interact with that item.  Unfortunately you appear to have been cursed with seeing the basic, standard Windows cursor as your clicker thing. Nothing fancy should have been expected, but a little creativity in these spots would go over much better. Any cartoony cursor would have been better. Also, while you do pick up and acquire items,there is no inventory at all. None. Pick up everything and then when you arrive at the applicable puzzle, the item will automatically work for you upon simply clicking the object. The puzzles, otherwise, are fairly standard and none are truly noteworthy or overwhelming.
The noteworthy and overwhelming things to be enjoyed here are the graphics and sounds. You can certainly tell that a massive amount of the budget went into the art. The art itself is simply magnificent.  The claymation style must have taken nearly every single moment available for production. It truly is breathtaking at points, the flowing art style and claymation are beautiful. Almost equally solid is the music. The sounds are awful...squishy at times, but the game has a soundtrack of music that would be worth every penny if sold separately (It is). If you enjoyed the opening intro to the game, you'll love the music. The voice acting is also top quality.  Featuring none other than Mike Nelson as Terrynaut. Mike you may know from a funny little thing known as Mystery Science Theater 3000 and/or Rifftrax. Armikrog also features Rob Paulsen as Beak-Beak (Raph and Donatello on tmnt and Pinky and Animaniacs). Surely you'll recognize a few other voices as well!
All in all,  even the awesomeness of the voice actors and the very, very beautiful art cannot justify the $24.99 price tag. Out of 5 stars i couldn't rate this game much higher than a 2. It is, at best, worth a look if/when it drops to a nice 80% off during a Steam sale. Perhaps diehard fans of the original Neverhood may enjoy this sequel. I cant really say i do.
Happy Gaming!!!

Got the game on a whim, having never played many "Grand strategy" or "4X" games.  To be honest I wasn't sure what those tags even defined prior to playing this.  This game is sweet.  If you like in-depth strategy games this is a fine one.
The biggest Pro for me?  It was easy to get into even though I have played only "casual" strategy games such as Civ 5 and more RTS style games such as starcraft.  I felt overwhelmed only for a few moments when things began happening, but as long as you read / listen to the helpful robot you will get the hang of it quickly.
It is worth noting there is a LOT to do in this game but the majority of it is entertaining and none of it felt completely like a chore.  If you do not take interest in building each little planet hand-by-hand you can even set it inside of a zone that takes care of it for you (at least after the first few hours when the tutorial takes you there).
Replay-ability will of course be massive as there is so much random generation each game will always be different.
Looking forward to dying of the space plague sometime in the near future of my first play through.

I'm 6 hours into my first play through as a Human military dictatorship and I'm very impressed! If you're a fan of the Masters of Orion series, you'll find a lot to like here. The spirit of those games lives here, but there are also a lot of parellels with modern 4x games. Stellaris feels like the rightful successor to Masters of Orion 2. The traditional "Paradox" learning curve in games like Europa Universalis or Crusader Kings doesn't apply to Stellaris. The game's UI is seemless but I highly recommend playing through the tutorial.
Combat is enaging and there's no shortage of random aliens to dust it up with. Going up against other empires can be costly unless you have a clear technological and naval advantage. The diplomacy is very similar to Civ 4 or 5, but I've noticed a couple of glitches on the trade screen that I hope gets cleaned up in the coming weeks.
Based on my early game impressions, if you're into space exploration and empire building games, you should definitely give Stellaris a shot.

Dust is artistically beautiful throughout, cartoonish in a way that belies some of the deeper, potentially heartwrenching, storyline aspects.  There are a few decision points that might affect the story, but don't seem to; even those are rare enough to be surprising when they  come up.
Combat is simple, even repetitive, once you get the hang of it, and the world is small enough to explore fully, after gaining a few movement abilities.  Mashing buttons works well enough to entertain a child, and the story progresses quickly enough to entertain adults.  Save points are frequent, and most supplies are plentiful with the shopkeeper's help, so there's little danger of actually losing.
The nods to other games can feel a bit out of place at times, but all work within the framework of Dust's skill set, and are amusing when you understand the reference.  They're also out of the way, though you'll probably run across most of them while looking for something else.
So, is this game for kids, or for adults?  For novice gamers, or for the indie in-crowd?  Perhaps both, for each question.  I wouldn't recommend it for hard-core gamers who value gameplay far beyond storyline, but for the rest of us, it's a fun way to spend a few evenings.

A beautiful addictive game. Beautiful, as in the first 30 seconds of gameplay made my jaw drop with the gorgeous graphics and smooth animations. Addictive, as in the core combat is exceptionally fun. While I had to kick up the difficulty to Hardcore to make the enemies a challenge, the combat never grew boring after that; I was a one-man army, but if I let my guard down for even a moment, things will get ugly and I have only myself to blame. I love that balance.
The main characters were very likeable too. I expected to be annoyed by Fidget, a whiny-voiced flying character, but she made me laugh so much I couldn't help but love her too. Dust is interesting from the start.
The story is acceptable. The game spends so much time building up to a conclusion... with mystery, epic battles, raw emotion... this journey was great!, but for a barely passable conclusion. It didn't make any sense. Dust has a radical change in character that left me baffled. And there wasn't nearly enough exploration of the villain's character. And that last 60 seconds... *shivers*
While the final 10 minute battle was a joy to play (due to the aforementioned excellent combat), the story conclusion left a foul taste in my mouth. It wasn't terrible, but I'd rather forget it ever happened. Yet I will never forget the amazing 30-hour journey through a beautiful world with epic battles. Definitely recommended.

I'll be honest: this is the first visual novel / dating sim game I play, so I cannot compare it to others, and see how well (or not) it fares. No matter what, this game I bought only because it was at an interesting discount during the Christmas sale... well, this game was a pretty good surprise, and I've enjoyed it tons.
First: it doesn't take itself too seriously, which in my book tends to be a good thing. Of course it's inspired by stories like Harry Potter (one of the teachers is clearly reminiscent of Prof. Snape). Your character's default name is 'Mary Sue'. The other students you meet are often cliché in their own ways: the funny troublemaker, the sporty girl, the somewhat shy roommate, the playboy with a dark past, and so on. But this is fun. If you enjoy toying with such tropes, it's fun. Also, some of the romance/friendship paths you can explore may turn in unexpected ways, darker than what the pastel colours and cute character let you think at first.
The game also embraces diversity without feeling compelled to point at it, which is good. Some students are not fully human (Pastel is half-fairy) and nobody cares (granted, some do about Damien, however it's often more about his behaviour than about his demon wings). Not only do the romance options offer same-sex paths, but these are also fairly balanced: 3 main het vs. 2 main same-sex possibilities—no 10 vs. 1 imbalance here—and, again, nobody will give your character sh*t because she wants to date another girl (one student even has two dads). You may even end up with a teacher, although to be fair, I'd have loved a Potsdam-path possibility (she's so cute and over the top at times ^^).
The exams are held in small dungeons, and you can solve their puzzles/challenges with more than just one spell, depending on the paths of magic you decided to follow. They were fun to tackle, even though I thought the magic wasn't exploited enough—for instance, apart from these dungeons, I would've liked to be able to cast more spells during daily/romance/life situations in general.
Conclusion: Good replayability factor, enjoyable characters with their own little side stories to discover, and if you like boarding school settings, magic schools, and customising your character, this game is likely to be an appropriate choice.

This game actually made me physically sick. I stopped at stage 8/9 because I felt like I was going to vomit. I'm not even the kind of guy to get motion sickness, and I also play a lot of video games.
Short review: This game is awful and you should only buy it if you could sell the trading cards for more than you payed for it. It's a walk backwards and click on things simulator. I know it's made by one man, but I've seen roblox games that are better than this. This should be an alpha at best, which makes sense when you realize that each level is a "test". I feel like the creator just said "screw it, I'm bored of making this game. I'll just sell it as is for five dollars without a sale.". EA wishes they had guys like this scheming for them.
Long review:
Menus:
Options Menu: Only options are to change lighting engine quality, fullscreen mode, and mouse sensitivity. Mouse Sensitivity is only available for change when you're ingame, so you probably won't figure that out until you decide you want to play this windowed.
Main Menu: Has Options Menu, a Question mark (which doesn't tell you how to play the game, it's the credits), a New Game button, and the exit button.
Stage Select: Barebones flash-game-style level select, a 3x3 grid of levels. The thumbnails show extremely insignificant previews of the levels, but they're better than nothing.
Graphics: They're bad. Graphics exist to serve the aesthetic, but there's no consistent aesthetic so graphics is all it really has going for it. The land is mostly square, caves and underpasses are partly square and partly curvy. enemies are trapezoids. There are no textures. Just different colors. The guns do not fit the rest of the game at all, they're cool-looking when the game should be going for whimsical or at least completely bad. There is graphics options. All it does is change the lighting engine.
Plot: A bad excuse as to why you're doing what you're doing. Summarized:
"You get abducted by aliens or something, now you have to fight zombies in what are probably simulations. whatever. I already got your money, just go play this game to make back as much as you can from trading cards."
Gameplay:
Controls: Barebones, and you can't even configure them. You move with WASD, shoot with left click, zoom with right click hold. There is no sprint. This can make the game seem boring when you repeat, as you are forced to move at what feels very slow when you inevitably die to poor design. In TF2 and other games like it, you can air-strafe by holding A or D and moving your mouse. Not in this game, the jump is totally uncontrollable and you are commited to wherever it leads. scroll wheel does not change weapons, you HAVE TO use 1 2 3 for that.
Weapons: They all suck.
1: an SMG. It's accurate, fast and does very little damage. The most common weapon and the most practical
2: a shotgun. It does more damage, actually only fires one shot (so you can only hit one enemy) and is slow. you will likely rarely use it, and even then you shouldn't use it exclusively.
3: a bat. IT does less than the shotgun, fires faster, and has a range that never seems to be consistent.
Other Stuff:
When you die in a level that's it. It's back to level select. No "retry?", no checkpoints, no extra lives. you have to do it all over again.
Stages:
Stage 1: you have a gun and there are 2 enemies. Very short and dissapointing level
Stage 2: Stage 1, except there's some pipes to go through tacked on with smaller enemies.
Stage 3: You only have a Baseball Bat. You fight a boss. You fall into a cave filled with zombie conga lines.
Stage 4: you go through pipes with a baseball bat. The floor is broken into pieces and looks horrible because of it. You fight more conga lines, get a gun, shoot big guys that hide little guys behind them, and then are forced to fight huge guys, then do awkward platforming to finish the level
Stage 5: you fight a really big guy by walking backwards and clicking on him. You then get a shotgun and have to fight off crowds of weak enemies, which the shotgun is ironically useless against, considering that is the purpose of a real life shotgun. After that you run along a walkway with guys who throw snowballs at you. promising level, but still bad.
Stage 6: Hell. You run a gauntlet with reskinned snowball guys who throw fireballs at you. The water that is present in other levels is replaced by lava, which kills you instantly. This coupled with the lack of air control means you will likely die a lot to stupid jumps. There is no music. Once you get to the end of the stage, you get a gun and music starts to play. Then a huge guy with like a million health who flies around randomly and throws fireballs at you appears. It is nearly impossible to beat him, as he can go straight above you and shoot at you, while you can not look straight up and shoot the fireballs down. You have very limited space to avoid his attacks. The level is long and arduous so it wears on you after all the time you have to spend getting back to the boss, not even taking into account the times you die to lava. I was tempted ot quit on this level, but I wanted to see if the game got any better after this.
Stage 7: Timed Level. Long tube with instakill things that look like they should be powerups. periodic MANDATORY battles with enemies you've NEVER MET YET and are not used to. At least you're fast and jump good though.
Stage 8: waves. health pickups that you can pickup at full health and waste. boring. repetitive. Kitefest. I quit here because it isn't worth it.

I’ve heard many exceptional and peculiar things about Hotline Miami, but the foremost would have to be its speed, as it kicks in from the very moment the game begins. I’ll be honest; it takes some getting used to. But then again, that’s what truly makes the game iconic; it’s ability to make you simultaneously scream at your computer and contemplate your existence, while at the same time restarting the level for one “final” go. This intensity never ceases, and it’s one reason thousands of players regularly decide to revisit the game and its successor.
   
One of those reasons, besides the addiction-inducing return, lends itself to the restrictive story that bridges the sheer brutality of Hotline Miami to something more human-esque. In between the piles of bodies you’ve decapitated and slaughtered, phone calls and conversations continually grasp at your curiosity, giving the once unknown indie game it’s capacity to keep the players on the edge of their seats as the masks reveal their mysterious tendencies over the five hour story. You’ll walk away confused and emotional, with bloodstained hands and weapons galore, and that’s precisely the point.
That’s not to say the difficulty is for everyone, many have walked away from Hotline Miami, never to open the game again due to its head-battering frustration. Indie games have pushed the genre to new heights, and part of that is due to Miami’s leaps and bounds toward an inherently more challenging video game space.
The next progressive step would be the next sense: hearing, in this case, the fantastic soundtrack. Beyond the original overwhelming fast pace, the groovy and electronic beats & melodies flow from your ears to your hands, heightening your adrenaline. Tracks like Miami Disco transport you back to the late 80’s underground sound, raising your heartbeat with every downbeat. It’s gotta be said, at the end of the day, the soundtrack of Hotline Miami bumps it over the edge from great to amazing.
From a bedroom in Gothenburg, Sweden, to millions of copies sold, Hotline Miami has redefined the indie space, has fascinated players for years on end, and has properly secured its place as one of the greatest independently created video games of the decade.

I never experienced loss from cancer or ever faced the tragedy that is death. But to be in that position, to experience something like that, that's something any form of art and medium can show. To have the player exploring those hardships, and the internal thoughts within them.
That's this game.
This is
The game's scenes take you through a story about Joel Green, a young boy diagnosed with AT/RT cancer. The story faces a lot of ups and downs, with moments of hope and many of despair. What I feel like is sort of important to note is that despite cancer being a major subject in the game, it's not what the overall message really is about. It's a story about coping with death. The inevitability of it.
I really like just how beautiful it is. It's polygon-bsaed artstyle is unique, it's set-pieces and locations are bizarre, and the way dialogue appears as if it was a typography is really cool. There's really nothing that's like this game in terms of presentation, and that's what makes it shine.
The game has a lot of themes regarding Christianity, and believing in faith. While I'm not really one to believe in a religion, I do think that it's part of what makes this game so interesting. I'm not a believer of Christ, I don't understand how saying something among the lines of "God will save me" or "God will heal me" will do anything in a situation like dying. But here, I understand, and that's something I really didn't expect from this game.
Sometimes the dialogue is obscured due to certain cases (Such as in one chapter where it is being blocked by water)
What I love a lot about this game is how personal it is. The developers of the game are actually Joel's parents, Amy and Ryan Green. It's really their commitment to make such a honorary tribute to their son that made this experience so memorable.
I'm having so much fun just exploring and tempting the safety net of my own galaxy!

Let’s start with what Dust gets right: the game is downright gorgeous. The backdrops of each level are beautiful and rich with color and detail. Each environment has a distinct look and feel to it, and every detail makes it look spectacular. The character sprites are very well done as well with crisp colors and animations. You can tell that a lot of time and energy was put into the artwork, I wish some of that time and effort were put into the story and gameplay.
The story starts out with the main character Dust waking up in the middle of the woods with amnesia. He is approached by the Blade of Ahrah, a sentient floating sword, and Fidget, the guardian of said sword. Fidget wants to bring the sword back to where it belongs (which is never established), however Ahrah wants to assist Dust with recovering his memories. So the trio run off to a local village to do just that.
Here is the first stumbling block of the story. Main characters with amnesia at the start of the story are boring and uninteresting. By default they have no personality, they have no likeable  or unlikeable qualities about them. They are a blank slate void of character until the plot decides to paint some onto them. They have no motivation for any of their actions because their personality hasn’t been constructed yet. Any action they do is simply because the plot had to move forward somehow.
While the gameplay is a bit more competent than the story, it is still lackluster. The core of the gameplay is solid. Typical button combinations activate different moves, you gain XP per kill and bonus XP according to how many hits you inflict within a certain amount of time, and you can upgrade your equipment via drops or a crafting system. The execution of the system is a bit sloppy.
After the first boss fight you get a ridiculous upgrade to the Whirlwind attack in which when Fidgets projectiles are thrown into the Whirlwind, three huge columns of fire erupt dealing damage to anything within it, above and below the screen. These also stun enemies caught within it and rack up the combo meter like crazy. There is no other reason to use any other combo moves that Dust may have, this is your “I Win” button combination. After upgrading Whirlwind you don’t gain any other new combat moves, which makes combat incredibly boring after the first hour or so of the game.

Final Fantasy VII is an experience that everyone should try at least once.
I have played through it a few times and I can say that this game truly deserves a medal.
I honestly believe that it is the best game that has ever been made based on several factors.
For me, Storyline is a big factor. FF7 is a game that actively progresses through the story.
There are no long breaks where nothing seems to happen.
The actual battling is turn based, rapid, and thrilling.
Containing an almost never ending assortment of difficult and amusing enemies and bosses that will keep you entertained throughout all three parts.
The plot is immense, with surprises, twists, and excitement up until the stunning climax. Graphics wise,
the game is not lacking. Although the characters may be somewhat blocky, the battles and cut scenes are magnificent.
The soundtrack is one of my favorite parts of the game. The soundtrack fits well with the gameplay and the battle themes are just amazing. Overall, I give it a perfect 10.

The Island:
-- The island really is very well done.  I'm running a 780Ti and have absolutely no problem pulling 60 frames per second.  Its well designed and gives a lot of attention to lighting.  There are numerous locations on the map to explore and discover, each with its own set of challenges, creatures, and resources to tackle.  In fact, if you're going to build out everything in the game, you're going to have to do some exploring.
Survival:
-- To me, survival isn't vastly different than most games in this genre.  There is hunger and thirst.  Hunt for food (at least five different types discovered so far)  and collect water.  Yes, the game advertises other survival metrics, but they don't seem to play a huge role.  Stamina is really only about how fast you can cut things down or throw a spear.  You're able to sprint indefinitely.  Hot vs Cold (at least in story mode) only seems to apply when walking in fire or in a couple of "cold" locations that you can quickly dip into, get what you need and get out.
Audio:
-- Aside from the voice acting (which could use some work) the audio is really solid.  The island makes so many different noises from regular ambient noise to the various creatures on the island.  In fact, early on, until you've learned the noises each critter makes, the audio can really keep you on the seat of your pants.
Weapons:
-- So far, I've found six weapons, I believe, which really helps in  survival.  So far, I haven't felt the need to build many traps.
Story:
-- The story is pretty basic, so far, but it has provided a really nice motivation to the game.  Everytime I think I'm about to escape the island, I find I need to solve one more "puzzle".  How do i get in here?  How do I get one of those?  Etc.  Its given me reason to explore the island without making things seem easy.
Overall:
-- If they keep developing the game it will really shine but, as it is, its a good spend for $15ish.  I think I'm about 10 hours in and can see myself spending a few more (I really want to figure out how to get off the island).  Multiplayer would be a nice touch, but maybe just for survival mode, not the story.

~TL;DR~
As far as roguelikes go, Necropolis is fun. It is a great game to play with friends, but not so much alone. The information and stats for items could use some work, and the game needs more content to justify its price, but I don't regret buying the game. $30 is a bit steep for the content available, but it isn't a bad game by any stretch of the imagination. - 7/10 -
Necropolis is a fun and challenging game that tasks you with escaping the labyrinthine necropolis that you have woken up in. To do so you begin with some fairly barebones equipment and two floors with controls and items meant to teach you how to play and craft items before sending you onto the depths of the actual game. Combat changes with each weapon you have. A dagger is quick, but less powerful, while a two-handed sword (you wield it one-handed) is slow but powerful. Alongside your weapon you can also wield a shield, a wand, or crossbows to aid or defend yourself. Armor gives boosts to health, and consumables range from crafted food, mystery potions, and mystery bombs. Later in the game you can also buy recipes for better crafting. However, one of my main complaints about the game is there just isn't enough information to go with the items. Items have a tier and a description of the weapon, but aside from that there isn't any real indication on whether it does more or less damage than what you currently have. As annoying as this was, it didn't really negatively impact my time with the game. The game is definitely at its best when playing with friends. It helps to ease up the number of enemies mobbing you, but also requires communication as you can hurt your allies. Which I did a lot. Hitting an ally usually does more damage than a regular enemy's attack, to compensate allies can revive each other or if the screen fades to black you revive at the entrance of the area with your base gear. Throughout exploring the dungeons you can acomplish certain tasks, such as breaking pots, to earn coins. Alongside that any currency not used before you die is added up at the end and earns more coins. These coins can be used to unlock skill books, golden chests with rare weapons, or different colors for your armor. The skill books and colors are carried over to your next life. Unlike most roguelikes, Necropolis doesn't have randomized dungeons. The content is pretty much the same each time through, and I definitely wouldn't mind additions to it. As far as roguelikes go, Necropolis is fun. It is a great game to play with friends, but not so much alone. The information and stats for items could use some work, and the game needs more content to justify its price, but I don't regret buying the game. $30 is a bit steep for the content available, but it isn't a bad game by any stretch of the imagination. - 7/10 -

Vortex: The Gateway is a disappointing game in the open-world survival genre. It's light on content, buggy, and poorly optimized. It never ran above 30 frames per second, even with a GTX 970.
It's hard to see the point of most of the game's crafting features. Spears, made in seconds, kill most enemies in a few hits, I experienced one bug where all of the material needed to create buildings vanished from the game world.
There is a story mode, but it is undeveloped and does nothing to explore the cool concept. I was hoping for something like the game Miasmata, but instead, exploring and surviving are pretty trivial, and beating the story mode was a pretty anti-climactic fade to black.
You can safely skip this.

I pledged for this game back when they did their kickstarter. A big fan of Dougs work on Earth Worm Jim and calling this the spiritual successor of the Neverhood I couldn't say no to this.
I will get the pros out of the way first. Animation and voice acting is stunning. The visuals pop and you can see that charm we have grown to love.
The backstory is amazing. If you read the hall of records and learn the tale of Armikrog its an amazing story.
It made me feel like I was back in the computer shop playing my childhood all over again.
But as for the negatives. The main characters do feel like they are out of place in a story that is so much grander. Its almost as if they dont connect too well. The back story is well versed but when trying to play the game you feel its overshaddowed by characters that dont belong.
I love the writing dont get me wrong its amazing. But when Klayman was a part of the Neverhood he was a part of the story. Here it just feels like a side note to a grand story.
The game even though Ive heard is the same length in screens seems way shorter. I beat it in two days over an hour a day. And the ending is clear they want to continue with the story but Im not invested in Tommynaught as a character.
The puzzles are repeated alot. The Neverhood mixes them up. Having not just button pushing or slide puzzles but puzzles that have a different look and feel to them. Some may operate the same but they physical appearance changes which keeps it fresh. Here it just felt filled in.
Some of the assets seem repeated besides the puzzles. In particular stretching a character to make him seem taller instead of making a new one seemed cheap. Same with mixing cartoon eggs with animated ones. The styles clashed alot.
The soundtrack was something I was looking forward to the most but the game decided that instead of theming rooms with songs that it would just pick and choose what to play. Id like to think this is a glitch. Because I dont know what the hell they are going to put on the soundtrack. Honestly each rooms music made it. Here it doesnt even function.
There was a lot less cutscenes. Even quirky ones that made the Neverhood fun to play. The ones that just stick out and dont mean anything but are just plain funny to watch. Even in SkullMonkeys they had that down easy!
And last. The glitches are so high! From my save file being erased. Passing through doors I shouldnt. Clicking something that doesnt work only to leave or move slighty to the right and clicking it again until it does. Crashing the game and seeing the hotspots not even mash with the mouse. The Unity engine almost seems like a last thought in making this work.
To delay the game an extra month makes me wonder what they did. Not in a rude way but Id like to know what went wrong. The bug testing team didnt do a damn thing. And the other night someone from the team said there wasnt too many issues and they were happy with it.
I can accept everything else. If it wasnt for the glitches. A month is enough time to fine tune it. There should be no issue.

Losing a child is the lived experience of many, many people who are a part of our lives. We just don't know it. Whether through miscarriage or illness, the death of a child is an issue that we too often sweep under the rug in social interactions. We don't ask people how they're coping. We don't ask people what they're feeling. It's a scary topic and we ignore it. We think they don't want to talk about what they've gone through, and while in some cases this may be true I also believe that's an excuse we use to avoid the conversation.
This videogame brings the issue of child loss to light in a profound and inspiring way. As the father of very young children, this game filled me with both overwhelming gratitude and overwhelming saddness. Yet in playing it I bore wittness to an experience that has been a silent part of the lives of so many people I know: family members, friends, colleagues, etc.
Thank you for designing this incredible experience. It is a beautiful memorial to your son and it has changed me for the better.

Never before have I played a game that so captured my imagination, my intellect, my emotions, and my faith for a journey through despair, hope, and purpose. That Dragon, Cancer is a work of art that asks and answers, “Death, where is your sting? Grave, where is your victory?” in no less than the two to three hours that it takes to complete its fourteen scenes/chapters. Play it for the experience. Play it for the insight. Play it for the inspiration. Play it for Joel.

- The visuals are amazing. I really love the claymation and how they mixed that up with other materials like cardboard or fabric to make the surroundings visually attractive.
- The story is well-rounded and clear, you learn more about the background and purpose while playing and the end-scene wraps it all up nicely so you end the game with a feelgood experience.
- The puzzles. If you're an experienced puzzle-game type you might feel different about this but as I generally suck at puzzles I really enjoyed these. Some were easy, others a bit more challenging but never frustrating. Having played the Neverhood ages ago, I knew I had to keep a notebook nearby to keep track of symbols and hints. Who knows, you might need them later on.
- The humor. Sometimes a bit goofy but I had a smile on my face while playing and laughed at certain scenes when I expected something huge to happen and it actually turned out to be completely different.
- The music. I'm going to be humming the name song for days.
- Some of the graphic details have an unfinished feel, but there was only one room where I really felt annoyed by it. They 'stretched' an item in a really obvious and ugly way and the interaction with that item was sloppy as well (it got kinda seethrough when moving it). That might have been a time or budget-related thing but I hope they'll fix it.
- The gameplay is mostly smooth but I got stuck during my first attempt of finishing the game and there was no other option but to start a new game. Also: I get the feeling some doors that are supposed to be closed, only to open after solving a puzzle can now be walked through without solving. (ofc. I still solved the puzzles...you never know what you might need it for later)
- As much as I understand claymation takes ages to make, the game is on the short side. Right now, I don't know if there are enough easter-eggs and little details to make me want to explore the game again, especially since the puzzles don't change and once you discover how they all work it takes away some of the fun.
I really loved playing Armikrog even though there are still things they need to work on. It is a feelgood game, and I really enjoyed exploring, solving puzzles, discovering new things. The 'world' is limited but funny and quirky and leaves me wanting to see more. Right now, I wouldn't play the game again but finishing the game was a fun journey. I really hope Pencil Test fixes the issues reported (especially the gamebreaking ones but it couldn't hurt finishing some of the graphic/stretching issues) and when they do, I'll play the game again to see how it was intended to be. If you're willing to 'forgive' Pencil Test for releasing a game that still could use some work: go ahead and buy.

I played two campaigns so far, one with the United Nations to get used to the game, and one with a custom empire. So let me tell you a short story how that went for me.
I started on a large ringshaped galaxy, my empire consists of collectivist militaristic space slugs with several heads, so naturally i try to expand as far and fast as possible and prepare for war. My neighbour didn't like that very much so he insulted me. Bad move buddy, that's it, WAR!
Damn what's that? Oh god how did his fleet pop up right next to my capital world? Wormholes? Oh well... There goes my star port, good thing i have two more, and a bigger fleet. So cleanup time, crush the fleet, and destroy everything he has. He capitulates and grants me all his planets except his capital.
Great, 3 worlds full of slaves!
And that's when everything took a sinister turn... i just couldn't stop the slaves from rebelling, and i didn't want to grant them independence, so there was only one option. Start the purge!
And this is how this game made me into a genocidal space menace within 10 hours.

If you'd rather not read the entire review, and would like a simple awnser at the beggning, here it is: Buy this game. It can't get simpler than that. This game is well deserving of its price, and I would've payed five dollars more for it. Let me walk you through reasons why you should buy this:
1. Storyline
You play as Dust, a quite and charming protagnist weilding a speaking blade of Elysium. Oh, and not to mention Fidget, whom is the most cuddly and possibly the best compainion to ever exsist. The game is littered with cute dialoge, and any moment the player has a thought the character comments on whatever just happened almost the same way the player thought, like if a character seemed dickish or just plain insane, Dust and Fidget immediatley have a small talk afterwards about just that, giving insane immersion. The characters are loveable, and there are almost no characters I wouldn't want to speak to. It has a perfect little twist of comedy in all the seriousness, with Fidget being adorable as ♥♥♥♥ and small little refrences to other games that'll just make you sit in your chair smiling at the computer going "Ahhhhh, I see what chu did there", and it is overall just an amazing experience.
2. Gameplay.
The gameplay is insanley fluent and is amazing to say the least. From the get go, there's not too much challenge, so the game isn't very frustrating allowing for a very casual expereince. With many combos using really only left-click, right-click, and W. You will hardly have a moment where you don't just go "How the ♥♥♥♥ did I do that!?!?" like throwing an enemy into another before throwing them into the air again or shooting off into the sky for no reason killing several enemies in the process. It's just fluent, balanced, and overall an enjoyable expereinece. As far as quests go, you unlock new abilities at a nice pace, and you'll always find yourself learning new tricks. The side quests, though few in number, are very well thought out and innovative for each and every one. Try saving Corbin or finding Reed's Box. These are both sidequests that are done astonishingly well. You have a sense of a new experience, plus you get to just straight up see characters happy. It actually immerses you as a character.
3.  ♥♥♥♥ THREE. BUY THIS GAME.

The visual novel part of the game is that you are a girl named Mary Sue (That's literally her name! Though you can change it. This was hands-down absolutely stunning to play. It's essentially the game Flower, under the ocean, with added mechanics and exponentially more detail. So relaxing to just swim around or drift in the currents, explore the varied sea life and even grab on to some to take a ride. The sharks were especially entertaining to grab on to, tossing you around as they scramble to feed on the passing fish. A tip here is to let the less-than-cooperative predators feed on fish first, you'll then be able to influence where they swim.
These developers did a fantastic job nailing the transitions to each environment and the transitioning musical score to accompany it. It gives you as much freedom as possible while still providing a focus on the goal. In fact I don't think the game has a way to punish players (that I saw) which helps re-iterate the focus on exploration. The controls were sometimes a bit off, but only rarely and it didn't really mess anything up.
Also, if you have a >60hz monitor, and the video card to push it past 60fps, it really makes the densely cluttered scenes come to life.
Side note:
There are some reviewers complaining of the short play-through time for the base cost of the game. I can see that, just remember the amount of time you spend enjoying this is up to you. Some may just rush point A to point B, in which case they've missed the point entirely regardless of cost. Explore, look around, even just stop entirely and let the environment sink in for a moment. Just wait for a sale if anything.

I have only played this game in single player and I'll give an honest opinion. IT needs work but it's a great game regardless. The combat mechanic is a throwback to Darksouls, it's a roguelike dungeon delver with many different enemies items. Let's go over it's pro's and Cons:
Pro:
Mechanics are sound
Combat is engaging and does require some level of skill (though not a high level)
Enemies work off five or six different bases but have a diversified look and combat style.
Weapons have a decent variety  light swords, med swords, heavy swords, heavy hammers, shields, crossbows, and wands (note: staves fall under hammers and all have slow attack speed.)
Light swords have a fast attack speed. period.
Medium swords have a medium or fast attack speed.
Heavy swords have a medium attack speed.
Heavy hammers have a slow attack speed.
Crossbows, wands and shields are all off hand and have offhand weapons have different effects such as elemental damage.
The levels are proceidurally generated making this a true rogue like  No dungeon is the same.
Final death is a thing but there are ways around it. (Two to my knowledge)  Save for certain exponentially difficult enemies (will not spoil) you can get through with minimal damage if you can gauge when to block or dodge. Do not flurry attacks or you'll leave yourself open due to the fact both blocking and dodging take stamina just like attacking. The other way around is there are certain potions (I don't know the actual name of it) that will give the text "you feel IMMORTAL" that allows you to die and get back up.
Cons:
Difficulty jumps happen a lot in the later levels, one room you're just struggling not to die, next room you're fine then you're dead.
Spawns... Well they're a thing, and certain ones make sense, like seeing a pile of corpses on the floor or skeletons and they spawn holowmen or skeletons accordingly when you get close. But when you clear a room and are forced back by a strong enemy spawning random enemies in a room you already cleared is nothing but annoying. Especially when most of the enemies that spawn you can one hit so they're just mosquitos.
Final level is hard. REALLY HARD. It is beatable on single player mode but only if you're REALLY GOOD and have a really good equipment set. Speaking of...
Equipment! Make more variation and stop dropping tier 1 and 0 weapons at level 8. Just a suggestion.
Final qualm? Mutliplayer mode. This game is made around Multiplayer (to the point where you can't pause even in single player...) It's like Dark Souls 1 with permanent co-op, is this a bad thing? NO I would love to say the co-op in this game is a good thing, but one problem with it persists. HOW DO I CO-OP? I have my world set to open and not invite only. Meaning people can join, buuuuuuut... one problem. THERE IS NO JOIN FUNCTION. There is no match making there is no online co-op. You have to be friends with the person playing the game and either have them invite you or join through steam. Persisting problem being? I'm the only person I know with this game.
Summary:
This game is amazing, the artstyle and gameplay are pleasing, everything everyone complains about is not an actual problem to me. If they make a matchmaking system where you can join people who aren't on your friendslist this game would be top notch. I do reccomend this game, but only if you have friends willing to play (and don't need to buy it for all of them...)

I really enjoy playing this game, there's a lot in there that's a lot of fun to play with... The research, the production, the ship designing and creating your own factions... There's a LOT in this game that's a lot of fun.
The problem is though, there's a lot of issues as well. Everytime I try to set up a multiplayer game, me and my brother end up having to set up games over and over usually around 3 - 4 times because one of us will be randomly disconnected before the start of the game.
Sometimes it works, sometimes it doesn't.
We love playing with mods, and for a game like this, having mods gives an endless supply of changes and tweaks that can make the game more fun, the only problem is.... They can't be used multiplayer.
It's disheartening when new 'content' is released for 5 dollars that seems to only break the game further, where many comments point out that yeah, it's fine that new stuff is released, but when the system is already buggy, these new systems add only more bugs and problems.
Please just fix the game first, get multiplayer running smoothly, get mod support for multiplayer, right now if you look online, you barely see any games being hosted and those that do (I've been in a few and just asked about it) are from people who already know eachother... Noone is hosting games to find random players because the system is so unbelievably bad for setting something like that up.
If you join a room, you know nothing about the game, about the selected win conditions, about the planet and universe settings, you just have to jump in blind... Who wants to jump in blind in the hopes of getting into a good game... The amount of times I've hosted a game and a random player joined only to leave when they found out what the game speed was set on, or the galaxy map, or any other part.
It needs a better interface for multiplayer, more information that is given to joining players so they know (maybe even beforehand) what they are joining, instead of just hoping for a good game somehow.
The game is fun, a lot of fun even, but the systems, the interface all make sure that multiplayer is a gruelling experience you only want to step into if you have people you know very well to play with.
I plan on playing this game a lot more, especially multiplayer, but untill mod support is given, I cannot buy any expansion and add more content when the content that is there sometimes barely works as is.

This game has promise, which is why I'm not returning it at this time. The basic premise is solid, the opening cut scene is solid, though it looks about as impressive as a 2007 game, and the rest of the graphics would be fine if they ran on my computer.
Let's get into the dirty stuff though. The game runs at 5-10 fps on low settings on my alienware, this would be regularly unplayable for me, but I thought I'd try for the sake of a review. Turns out it's barely playable and I was able to make a small bamboo house with a fire. Then night came and my frames dropped under 5 and I died immediately. I understand that this is still an Alpha, but please at least make it playable if you're making people pay 20$ for it, or 14$ in my case, because of the winter sale.
The crafting system is interesting. If you've played The Forest, a game I absolutely love, you know exactly what you're in for, down to picking up and moving 3 logs at a time. I actually thought that the same devs that made The Forest were working on this game, until I looked it up. There's nothing wrong with ripping of the crafting system of another game, as long as it works and you make it your own, but when you break it with a clunky interface and restricted recipes based on inventory items, you've just made it worse.
Gameplay is almost identical to The Forest from what I can tell. Start at a location with a small selection of vital supplies, gather up what you can, build a base, and hold down the fort until you die. When I say almost identical, I mean go play an hour of the forest and reskin it to look like an alien planet, now make the mutants spawn only at night. Now release that game for 20$ on steam.
What it feels like to me is that the devs took The Forest and said, "I want to make a similar game on an alien planet with a different story but mostly the same vein of gameplay." Then they took The Forest and made a crude copy of it as a foundation to work off of until they are able to develop it into a more individual and unique experience. At least, that's what I hope happened. It could be that they're just greedy ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s out to make a quick buck, but I like to assume innocence.
I would advise any potential buyers to watch this game for a while, maybe a month or two, and look out for how the devs respond to feedback and whether or not they try to improve the game. If you're willing to take a change with that extra Christmas money and get this game, go ahead and give the devs some meaningful feedback, instead of just destructive criticism.
I'll try and update along with the game, but as of now, I would not recommend.
UPDATE: Wow, the devs on this really managed to pull it out of Day One: Garry's Incident territory. Since this review, they've fixed most of my major complaints about the game. The framerate was fixed and the weird crafting system was improved upon, though it still takes a bit of getting used too. At this point, the only things I could really say about it is that it lacks polish. Movement is a bit weird, swinging with a weapon is a bit weird, throwing spears is a bit weird, but nothing realy breaks the game or detracts significantly from teh experience.
The writing is a bit clunky, but in a loveable B-movie way. Mike is a likeable dude, for all the introduction we get to him, and his imediate exit had me chuckling in my seat. The character's lines during gameplay don't add deep characterization, but they're enjoyable enough, especially the line of "That's a strange being." whenever you see a new animal. Just adds a bit of charm to the whole thing.
It's an enjoyable experience, and somewhat relaxing.
