It's not a horrible game, but finding it on Steam and it's retail price, that's asking for too much.
This game would have been a good few minute time killer to avoid finger tapping, but it wasn't much more than that. I'd expect to see a game such as this on Newgrounds or any other flash game site, maybe even facebook. I'll begin with a general pro/con list then detail the good and bad to each test.
Pros:
+I bought it for $0.14 while it was on the Steam sale
+It did manage to create at least two "startling" scenarios, simply because of enemies appearing in close range with no prior warning, jump-scare if you will
+Some levels kept a focus between platforming and shooting
+The weapons each have unique functions: machine gun, shotgun, melee, explosive
+Weapons are introduced individually to give you a feel for their function
+The levels are generated exactly the same every time, so you'll know exactly where everything is/spawns if you should die or replay the level.
Cons:
-Retail price is 5 dollars
-At any point if there is a possible advantage of terrain or shortcut, the game finds a way of nullifying that with either flying AI or invisible walls that you may see too late
-There is a "bloom" in the crosshair, but any movement, continuous fire, or jumping does nothing to affect your accuracy. Your accuracy is always 100% no matter the condition.
-Crouching does nothing to help you, with 100% accuracy, fast moving enemies, and projectiles mostly in hip range, crouching doesn't provide any advantage.
-Enemies shatter into blocks. Anything too large of a block of that enemy will usually physically impede your movements when you collide with it. This becomes irritating when strafing suddenly comes to a stop because the block is on the ground nearby.
-Any moving platform does not physically move you. This would be fine if all the rotating platforms were all either irregular shaped or squares. This leads to the point where if you're too close to the edge, the second the blocks under your feet become space, you fall, typically to your death.
-Death starts the entire level over, and in most cases having prior knowledge of what's upcoming does nothing to help you progress faster simply because of the grind to kill enemies.
-The enemy AI pathing is both good and bad. It can follow the blocks presented to make a path to you, but sometimes it ignores "space" and walks over the air to reach you. They also may find themselves hung up on walls. And I mean literally as well, sideways on the wall stuck.
-Jumping has a commited jump arc. If anyone remembers the NES games of Castlevania, it's like that. It is exactly like that, buy a wedding ring for that jump because you're stuck with your jump direction til death do you part.
-The game does a terrible job of explaining your environment and how it interacts with you. Several instances will lead to your death. You'll find yourself doing a trail and error with the game's environment if you see something you haven't seen before.
-The levels are exactly the same down to enemy generation, it provides no replayability.
-The game fails to follow a flow, each level is drastically different in what you just played. The only thing that follows, if it does, is just reskinned enemies.
-The slow-motion does not follow your mouse movement and just interferes with your game. If you spin the mouse to fast, your character will turn back and forth between opposite directions because the mouse speed forced in slow-mo can't follow your mouse position. Red Dead Redemption and Max Payne had a function for using slow-mo as an advantage. One Finger Death Punch added slow-mo for flair, but it gave you a break and prevented interfering with the game by not allowing enemies to be within reach during tha time. Dead Bits scripted slow-mo on certain enemies or cues, whether you like it or not.
-Dubstep. It would be fine if the creator of the dubstep didn't also thin himself out to make everything else in the game.
-Music is not consistent throughout the game. You'll play in complete silence sometimes then the music kicks on "cues". Then at other points the music just leaves entirely if playing for too long on one segment.
-There is no pausing the game, you just open the menu and the game continues.
Sadly due to character limit, I cannot go into detail on each level, but I'll leave the first two here as example.
Test 1
+Introduces machine gun, shoots bullets
+Introduces you can't shoot outside of starting box
+Shows basic enemy
+Shows how they interact when near you
+Cool slow-mo show at the end of the level
+Lets you determine how to find the exit to a level based on the only change in the level
-Doesn't let you fall off the level, you die if you fall off any other level
-An entire test is given with no instruction but you just instinctively shoot at zombie looking things because you've played a zombie game before
-You can shoot the trees, but it does nothing
-That shrilling sound at the start of the level will be the sound you hear at the start of every level from now on
-That number on the bottom is your health, but it's only a number with no indication unless you see that the enemies attacking you and seeing that number decrease are relatable
Test 2
+Introduces shotgun
+First test of weapon switching
+First test to introduce platforming
+First test to show you the destruction of trees as well as how destructable environments can also prevent enemy advancement
+Enemies can come in different sizes shown in this level
+Further proves killing all enemies is needed to progress
-You can die immediately after starting the test by simply missing the jump down
-First instance of enemies walking over space to pursue you
-The tree hitboxes are giant prisms, they do not possess a detailed hitbox
-You begin to understand that the enemies' death blocks can block your way
-That spinning platform at the end, it is possible to die just before exiting if you fall between the small gap of the block and the end of the tunnel
-Music leaves mid-level because you've left the starting 5 zombie rush
Again, it's not a bad game, it's just asking for too much and I felt the developer spread himself too thin on a pretty nice idea. There are some bad concepts to it but also some good ones. I'm mixed, but the only way I could recommend this game is for the 14 cent sale price. At least then you could get your money back selling the cards.

My recommendation for this game is qualified. Read on:
What does it mean to vote up or down? Voting up does NOT mean I enjoyed playing this game. I DID NOT ENJOY IT...
This is the most emotionally challenging game I've played. But I expected that. The developer walked a tightrope between genuine creative expression and potential sensationalism. I'm certain they struggled with this.
At its heart, "That Dragon, Cancer" gives us a very intimate perspective of a family's struggle with cancer, diagnosed in their youngest and most vulnerable member, baby Joel. Throughout the game, baby Joel becomes our baby. Your baby. And that's where it hits you hardest. That's where it does something no other game has... AND that's where it does something ONLY games can do!
The art style is simple but effective. Player interaction is also simple, relying mainly on you looking around for cursor prompts to click on. I often felt as though I was waiting on the game to catch up on my intentions. But the game surprised me often enough to keep me interested. And of course, I was busy looking after baby Joel.
For all its flaws, the game is only successful to me because it forced me to care. And that's something few games do.
Are games the proper medium for this type of content? Maybe. There are a million ways to do this WRONG. But the developer did a lot of things right, and I want to recognize that. This is dangerous territory... And though I'm not a Christian myself, I recognize grace. I'm proud of them and I want to support games like this.
This is not a fun game and it defies most of the criteria we use to judge games. That is also precisely why it is worth playing.

Such a disappointment. I didn't back this on Kickstarter because I didn't have the money at that time, otherwise I would have, just because I'm a big fan of Doug TenNapel works, like the Earthworm Jim franchise and The Neverhood. I did however pre-buy the digital copy via Steam 2 or maybe 3 months before release. I remember seeing the game pushed back over and over and thinking "Oh, this is getting so much work done, it's going to be amazing!". These are a few of my first thoughts while playing the game (I'll try not to spoil anything):
- The game starts with a cinematic with it's own soundtrack piece, telling us a little introduction to the story, keeping it brief and entertaining. Next, the first clay motion pictures start rolling. We see the main character and his sidekick, great animation, the voice acting is amazing, some jokes here and there, even the non-clay materials from the ship and wandering monsters look awesome. Great start! ...and sadly it all goes downhill from here.
- You are presented with the first room where you can actually interact with stuff. The first thing that caught my eye was the cursor, Windows default cursor. I mean, really? I know a fair amount of designing and programming, and I can tell you, making a custom cursor for a POINT AND CLICK GAME is a must and easy as f***! Do a friggin clay arrow and throw it in there! But at that time I was still hyped and didn't care.
- You can actually look out the window, which triggers a series of events going on outside that don't affect you at all, but are quite interesting and funny. You get to see multiple cutscenes of the outside situation. And that's it! Never again in the whole game you encounter such thing again. Come on! A point and click game feeds on these kind of "events" throughout the entire game!
- Moving on, you go through the next couple rooms, encounter some characters and your first couple puzzles. Now, I haven't played many games like this, but my first reaction when you pick up the first lever was "Ok lets open the inventory and see what I just grabbed". Hit I(nventory), clicked Tommy's body, hit Esc (more on that later)... nothing. Huh... You go up to the door and it's closed, so you click on the thingy next to it and he pulls out the lever and does all the action automatically. Would've been more exciting to at least do the thinking of "What do I use here?" right?
- Esc brings up the Menu, if you wanna call it that. You got the Resume and Quit button, of course, and Options. Go into Options to find some resolutions, subtitles and... Save?? WTH? Since when is Save inside the options of a game? I don't wanna sound like I'm ♥♥♥♥♥ing about everything here, but in my opinion these things make the game look unfinished and unprofessional.
- Next, lets talk about the puzzles. I've read people saying the game is super hard and that the puzzles are near impossible to figure out without a walkthrough. I don't think they are that bad. Personally I like getting handed a puzzle and figuring it out on my own. But here's the next thing that went wrong: the interactivity is terrible. You are not sure what is an object and what is just clutter. I am not saying "Make it obvious", but at least the objects could get highlighted when you hover above them. 15 minutes into the game, I was already stuck. I clicked everything, went back and forth, there was a point I even thought I had glitched something out. Apparently, when you control Beaky, he is blind or whatever, so he sees things differently. Once you go through a tunnel you come out on one of the previous rooms, where I had clicked everything a thousand times. Here you are supposed to "speak" to an octopus-like creature that is hanging from the ceiling and serves as the elevator. Tell me, how the hell are you supposed to know that, having clicked on it countless times as Tommy and Beaky, but only going back through the hole and doing it, works!?? AARGGHH!!! I don't think that is a hard puzzle, I think that is poor design.
- Last, but not least, game length. Finishing the game takes you from 2 to 4 hours, unless you get super stuck and decided to invest a whole afternoon just trying to get through the game without help. I even figured it out while I was halfway through it, since you are collecting some items and you already have half of them. This is the thing that hurt me the most. So much waiting for a couple lousy hours of entertainment. Even if they didn't add more content to the main story, they could've added more random stuff like the window event from the first room I mentioned earlier. And with these, you can add a lot more stuff. Doing certain random stuff unlocks Concept Art pieces, Interviews with the creators, Videos showing the creative process of the whole game which is AMAZING. The worst thing is all this already exists!! I've seen it countless times! And this also gives the game replayability. For f*** sake if I can think of this stuff how didn't they!!!???
Anyway... rant aside, I think the only positive side of this game is the art that makes it come to life (except for some areas where they decided to go with Photoshop, for whatever reason...). Did they dump all the money on the creative process and were left with very poor programming? It makes me wonder how bad it was before they decided to push it back. I'm not mad, I don't think this was done neither on purpose or due to lack of interest, you can clearly see the creators working on the game with passion for what they do, but somewhere between that and the release, something went terribly wrong. Again, I'm not mad. I'm just terribly disappointed :(

I really wanted to enjoy Necropolis. The idea of a Roguelite with Dark Souls-like combat sounded really enticing. Unfortunately the game does not live up to that hope. At it's core it has the possibility to be a great game. Maybe even one of the best Roguelikes out there.  At the moment though, the game is horribly unfinished and not worthy of the $30 price tag. There is only one type of class; a sword n' board playstyle that can get dull quickly. It doesn't help that there are only like four different weapon types, all of which don't have much significant differences in playstyle. The combat  and animations also feel floaty and unsatisfying. Along with that the weapons feel like foam swords because higher level enemies absorb a ridiculous amount of damage before dying. Speaking of enemies, there are only a handful of types with higher level ones just having more health. Just like the enemies, the nine levels that the game offers all horribly dull too. I understand that the levels will not be as complex as similar games due to it's procedural generation, but the rooms themselves are all horrendously bland and uninteresting. I personally love the style of this game, but it definetly does not help the rooms look any less dull. Admitedly I have not played the Co-op. I assume that the multiplayer aspect of the game would make it more enjoyable, but that is the same with any game.
Although I am no developer, as someone who has played the game I have some suggestions on how to "fix" the game.
-Qualty of life features: Goes without saying, but this game needs simple things like keybindings, gameplay options, and little stuff like being able to craft multiple items at once. These are things that are just expected of any game.
-Tweak and tighten up the combat: As the core gameplay loop the combat has to be perfect if they want to make sure players don't get sick of it after a couple hours of playing.  Right now the game feels too slow which is odd because the player moves fast, but when he attacks he looks like he is wading through mollasses. Along with the inability to cancel attacks, this makes the combat slow and frustrating. The animations have a lot to do with it. Through winding up the attack to actually hitting something your swing speeds remains the same. Along with that, don't make later enemies as bullet-spongy. Of course, them being tougher is a neccesity, and you should make them have more hp than the weaker enemies, but the basis of their difficulty should be based of their ai and attacks. Make their attacks more difficult to dodge, more interesting. Also make them more competent fighters to be more of a challenge. As would be expected, look at the souls series as a good example of these suggestions.
-Loot is boring and the thousands of weapons that drop are annoying. Sure, it is kinda interesting that all enemies drop their weapons, but they are so annoying when you are trying to pick something up from the floor when it is littered with a bunch of rusty swords. Just give the option of a loot menu for a radius of enemies. A simple quality of life improvment like this would improve the game a lot. When it comes to the loot itself, it is bland. All weapons types share an almost identicle moveset and tiers of weapons usually just mean a bit more damage. Like any proper dungeon crawler, their should be variations, rarity, and unique weapons that can be found or even made. I would remove tiers entirely from the game. Make all weapons equally viable, personal choice and your character build determine what weapon you use. Again, similar to Dark Souls. A nice touch would also give more types of attacks to different weapons like running attacks, rolling attacks, two handed/alt form, etc.
-Either enhance crafting or remove it entirely: Right now crafting feels more like a hindrance to this game more than anything. It is so underdeveloped and makes the game too easy. I almost always have an overabundance of crafting items and can easily create more healing items than I would ever need. Most of the bombs and other items you can create are useless too. If you don't feel like taking the time needed to fix the system just modify drop rates of other items and remove crafting entirely. If you want to fix it you need to expand it and balance it. Firstly I feel like you shouldn't be able to craft everythign wherever you want. It removes inventory managment entirely when you have infinite storage space for crafting reagents. Between levels or randomly placed throughout the level there should be different types of crafting stations for different types of items. Cooking station for food, enchanting table for crafting scrolls and potions, and a smith for creating and modifying weapons. As I stated earlier, make all weapons equal and let the player imrpove them how they see fit. Let them take apart weapons and upgrade their own with different features, like special properties or simple changes like faster attack speed for weaker damage. Since I already have written a huge wall of text I will leave this part here.
-Multiple playstyles and character choices. Goes without saying, give starting classes. Knight, rogue, wizard, healer, summoner, etc. It adds replayability to the game. Along with that give internal and external run progression. As it is right now, there is almost no reason to spend tokens within a run besides opening a little chest. Make it a balancing act for the player between saving up tokens for long term rewards or upgrading your character now to ensure that they can actually beat the run and get the rewards for doing so. Essentially the tokens are the souls of the game. Between levels you use them to upgrade your character. More health, better with certain weapons, more stamina, etc. Of course, you can just not level up but you risk losing the run and like in a souls game you lose the tokens on death. If you make it to the level you died on you get them back. Another option is for you to play it safe and store your tokens at a 2 for 1 rate. The tokens will be stored at the start of the game and you can pull them out when you wish to. Your incentive for not spending them is that you can use them for permanent upgrades to all your runs. You know, the typical roguelite stuff. New classes, new levels, new loot, etc. Just because it could be hard for certain players to consistently beat runs to upgrade their game. This can be done at the  triangle god at the beginning of the dungeon.
I have already gone on long enough so I will abbreviate a couple more suggestions.
-Level bosses + legendary enemies that drop special loot.
-More interesting levels
-"Soapstone" co-op. At the beginning of each level option to join up with random players for a short time.
-Invasions and Arena mode. Invade other players for tokens. Arena mode is alternate game mode (like Greed Mode in Issac). Go into duels, if you win get stuff to upgrade character. Keep duelling with other players until you retire or lose a fight.
Sorry for the rant. I was just really looking forward to this game and was dissapointed by it's mediocrity.

OK so this is a first impression as you will see I don't have that many hours in gameplay. However I have got to say that this game keeps you on your toes. There is no time to chill out and have a picnic. Provided you have the right strategy you should be able to survive. People say they die too quickly, that is just because their strategy sucks. Keep getting thirsty? Then build your base where you know there is a water fruit node nearby! Keep getting hungry? Pull your finger out and do some hunting! Keep getting killed by dragon? Stop prancing around like julie andrews all over the hills and be a bit more stealthy! Everything else killing you? Stop swinging your machete like it's the only weapon you can get and make yourself some spears which are sooooo easy to make! It takes some getting used to I am not going to lie but how boring it would be if there wasn't a challenge!
Something I will say is that while there are a few hours gameplay here and some nice areas to explore it would be so much more fun with a friend, but watch this space because 2 player co-op is planned! Well done devs! Make it happen!
There are downsides too but they seem to be far out-weighed by the positives. This game has the potential to make you jump with some heart-pounding sounds and an atmosphere that a lot of people will feel on edge in. Again this is where people get stressed...it's like trying to teach a kid to sit on the toilet. They flip out because they have to stop have everything done for them and do it themselves.
All in all not a bad game AT ALL. Performance could be better get around 25-30 fps but there are no lags and although the creatures can look a bit strange and not as attractive as some games the atmosphere combined with these is spot on.

Im writing this as to make it clear this is not a bad game despite the current 'mixed' status it has.
Pro's
1. It is a at times hard and rewarding experience even more so when played with friends.
2. There are lots to unlock and fun and interesting books and weapons.
3. Every single play through is different, no matter how you start it will go differently even to give you more than one way to descend tot he next level on the same go.
4. There are tons of funny moments and dialog throughout your experience only adding to the fun factor.
5. in co op the reply value is nice because its always funny hearing your friends cries of anguish from being insta killed by the vikings.
Con's
1. weapons could be a little more varied but it is only a minor thing given the stats they have.
2. if played alone it can grow thin and tiring, this is more a co op game if anything,
3. Not to much in the way of monsters, has a decent range but appear to commonly in different colours.
What i feel they need to change/lose/add
1. Sub-bosses for each level / random end game boss
2. more unique stats for weapons.
3. more effects on the weapons or ones with bigger AOE effects that damage.
4. key binding, having to use V instead of shift to run is a little annoying and having 2 different keys to pick up and drop would be nice instead of fiddling about on the ground trying to pick a certain thing up.
5. a difficulty setting, what it is now should be classed as easy imo, having more difficult enemies early game would be pretty intense.
Additional note
If you intend to play this solo, think twice because like i said, this is a very co op orientated game, solo is only fun if your looking to do a more hardcore run through and put it on youtube or something, unless of course you like playing solo games.
Overall i feel this is a really promising game and it does need a few tweaks here and there but it is bar far not a bad game despite many of its bad reviews, the only thing i can agree on is the price, as it is maybe not worth the price tag of £23 but with the changes suggested by myself and other reviewers i would be inclined to agree with the cost because this is a fun game and i can 100% recommend playing it.

Danganronpa 2 builds on the first entry in many ways. Most of them for the better. I felt the characters were better storied and more interesting. The plot itself was more in line with what I expected of the first game, with a better story to help keep interest from waning. The trials are expanded in a few ways. Most of the changes to the trials work well enough, but I wasn't a fan of some of the 'improved' minigames. And, thanks to playing the first game, I knew not to stress maxing every relationship before beating the campaign.
Overall I'd recommend it if you're into visual novels or Ace Attorney-style cases. But if you are interested in Danganronpa 2 I would highly recommend playing the original first. While I would say 2 was better, it feels like a continuation of the first from a gameplay aspect. The gameplay feels more like a 'hard mode' of the first game, and might seem more unforgiving to those new to the series. Plus you would miss out on the references and parodies of the first game.
And now to wait for 3 and hope it comes out for PC as well.

This was hands-down absolutely stunning to play. It's essentially the game Flower, under the ocean, with added mechanics and exponentially more detail. So relaxing to just swim around or drift in the currents, explore the varied sea life and even grab on to some to take a ride. The sharks were especially entertaining to grab on to, tossing you around as they scramble to feed on the passing fish. A tip here is to let the less-than-cooperative predators feed on fish first, you'll then be able to influence where they swim.
These developers did a fantastic job nailing the transitions to each environment and the transitioning musical score to accompany it. It gives you as much freedom as possible while still providing a focus on the goal. In fact I don't think the game has a way to punish players (that I saw) which helps re-iterate the focus on exploration. The controls were sometimes a bit off, but only rarely and it didn't really mess anything up.
Also, if you have a >60hz monitor, and the video card to push it past 60fps, it really makes the densely cluttered scenes come to life.
Side note:
There are some reviewers complaining of the short play-through time for the base cost of the game. I can see that, just remember the amount of time you spend enjoying this is up to you. Some may just rush point A to point B, in which case they've missed the point entirely regardless of cost. Explore, look around, even just stop entirely and let the environment sink in for a moment. Just wait for a sale if anything.

Thumbs up although it feels like the game is not yet completed.
There is something with the DNA of the game that makes all Galciv series addictive, but never the less this release has some issues yet to be resolved and definitely there is a lot of room for improvement. Just a few cons that come randomly in my mind:
1. The game consumes a lot of a system's resources making it “unpleasant” to run for your computer, especially if it is a couple of generations behind (Even with quad core SPU, 8Gig of memory and an GTX 550 GPU). Personal experience in first boot of the game started with a crash on desktop, not the best way for a “first contact”...
2. You just cant get some info at a simple glimpse like you did with its precursor. For example you have to hover the cursor over a selected unit to see it's movement info which is not displayed in the left bottom corner of the unit dialog box.
3. Ship types in the designer and the shipyard are sorted by default in a way that it is not helpful. An ability to sort theme out via attributes (especially by hull size) and keep things organized is not possible.
4. One should expect to see some features of previous galsiv releases be improved and new ones added. But the ones added do not make such a great impact in the game and unfortunately others have been removed or simplified (e.g politics).
5. Research, well for the standard of a game at such a level, is surprisingly poor(!) especially for one that inevitably makes comparisons with Galsiv II. It is shallow and generalized and even though the science screen in a first glimpse looks nice and developed with new features, some things are poorly designed (e.g the tech tree where you can't zoom in and out).
6. Surely the game is well polished especially with it's graphics, sound, artwork, etc... but maybe over polished on how it is presented and missing the essence.
In the other hand the AI of the game seems to be smart and quiet challenging even in normal difficulty mode. Ship designer is great and really exciting. But most of all the game has character and personality which is the timeless quality that distinguishes all galsiv series from the competition.
Summing it up; Is it worth buying it? Well, if you are a newbie in space 4X games then go for Galsiv II which even though is older, still is way ahead in the competition (and guess it will stay for a long time). However get it if you find it in a special price. If you have experience in this genre of games and you have devoted some gameplay hours in the galsiv franchise but you are sort of a hypochondriac person then don't. Just wait some time until the devs do what they have to do and improve things with future updates (which thankfully are frequent). And finally, if you are a strategy game addict and space 4X junkie (like me) than it is a must!

Armikrog is a beautiful point-and-click puzzle/adventure game. It starts off with a wonderful animated intro sequence and good music, followed by an exciting and enjoyable claymation cinematic that kicks off the game. You are pumped to get started, and for the first few minutes, it's very promising.
After that, though, the game starts to fall apart (gameplay wise).
Ignoring the missing menu text that was fixed in a timely fashion, the game seems unpolished, and far from ready to release. I had to restart the game from nealy the beginning after discovering that you could not overwrite saved games. The game did not tell you this, because you get no feedback when you press save to know that you have actually saved it.
Bugs and frustrating moments leave you with the question "Is this supposed to be like this, or is this just another bug".
Some buttons you can press, some buttons you can only press if all the conditions are met, and some buttons you can press, but the game won't let you unless you hit a sweet-spot with your mouse cursor, and so you might think that you have not met the conditions to press this button yet, so you move on to the next puzzle, and so the confusion begins.
It feels untested, even though it has gone through a beta. After almost year of delay, you'd think that it would be well tested. As of now, one puzzle can be skipped entirely by walking straight through a locked door. Everyone seem to have this problem. I can't imagine this would go by any sort of QA.
Armikrog, again, is a beautiful game, and I want to recommend it. But I can't. Not now.
It's not about the price. That is something I'm willing to pay for this kind of beautiful claymation adventure. But the game is simply not DONE.
The voice quality of the dialogue is varying from bad to okay at best. The main characters start off the game talking to each other as you progress, but apart from cinematics, they barely speak past a few rooms, which enforce the 'not done' feeling permeate this game.
I want to like you, Armikrog, but you got to take the few extra steps.
Buy/play this game once the bugs have been fixed, and it might be enjoyable enough.

It's good, but ...
This is really a game that can only recommend to fans of point and click adventure games, or those who like to solve headscratching puzzles. Before you start this game I highly recommend having a notepad ready at your desk to draw symbols, as you'll be doing a lot of that in this game.
First the good stuff about this game
The Stop Motion Animation is fantastic and is a artform that rarely gets any love in any media these day, the voice acting is also suburb with the likes of Michael J. Nelson and Rob Paulson as the two lead characters providing excellent banter with some humorous dialogue.
Make no mistake though these puzzles are tough, like so tough you think the game's broken cause its not holding your hand tough, its really not for the type player that is just going through the motions.
However on the subject of broken, there are indeed a few technical issues with this game as of the 1.01 patch, sometimes sound effects would stop playing, animations would sometimes freakout and there's a weird design choice towards the end of the game where a puzzle wouldn't open up until the jingle stopped playing.
The world of Armikrog is also a bit of a letdown, rather than a sprawling organic world to explore, the game is instead divided into different segments where you solve a few puzzles there, and then move on to the next area, while it is possible to backtrack at any point, having the world split like this really feels a tad disappointing. Though perhaps the most disappointing part is that some of the puzzles would often repeat, and its at this stage where all your doing is going through the motions.
I've heard other people complain about the length of this game, however considering this game was made in stop motion animation (which is a VERY time consuming process) I don't really see that as a deterrent, especially considering that this game was an indie title with a small production team. However I will say that at the current price its a bit too much, while I would recommend this game, at the current price its asking it's not quite worth it.
FINAL VERDICT: 6.5/10
Admittedly this would be a 7 if it weren't for the technical issues, as it stands now I'd say wait for a Steam Sale or price drop.

When i was 18, My mom died of cancer. it was not an easy experience. since then i've grown distant from my family, hardly talking to my siblings or stepdad at all. I can't remember the last time i actually took the time to pick up the phone and just say "hey, i love you" to them. I Have three younger siblings that i've seen once since her death, and my grandparents (her parents) call me every major holiday and every birthday, and even send me gifts all the way from Tennesee to Texas.
And I always let it go to voicemail, because the thought of reminding myself of her scares me.
I'm 23 now, and i've been avoiding this demon for far too long. i've been living in a town hours away from my family, working dead-end jobs and generally not going anywhere with my life. I have a girlfriend that nobody in my family has met in person, despite her being with me for two years.
I suppose what i'm trying to say is this:
Dont take the people you love for granted, because they won't always be there.
Take five minutes out of your day, call your mom, dad, sister, boyfriend, whoever. Just call them and say "hey, i thought about you today." because tomorrow, a thought is all they might be.
I'm going to recomend this game because it serves as a reminder of how fragile our lives truly are.
When i feel like i'm starting to forget about my family again, or if i think it's okay to not talk to them anymore, i'm going to play this game. I'm not going to run away from this anymore. i'm going to call my stepdad, siblings, grandparents, and i'm going to tell them i love them, because in five years i might not get the chance to say it again, and i've already got five years of time to make up.
dunno if the devs looks at steam reviews, but if they see this, then thanks. you've helped me rediscover the love that only a family can give.

Don't go into this game expecting it to be entertaining or 'fun'. If you want that, play the LEGO games or GTA or something like that. That isn't the point of this game. It's a tribute to a lost son and the times he had with his family, but told in a way no movie or book could. When you see or hear a story like this, you empathise and are sad about the pain. But this game makes you feel it. For example [IF YOU WANT TO EXPERIENCE THIS COMPLETELY AUTHENTICALLY, SKIP THE REST OF THIS PARAGRAPH]: in a scene where the doctors tell the family that the cancer is now inoperable, and that Joel -the son in question -is living on borrowed time, you have the option to rewind the scene and experience it from the persepective of each different person in the room. But it starts to rain. No matter how much you rewind, the rain will not stop. It gets worse, until the room is flooded. You find yourself in a rowboat, and Joel is in front. You row around the room, navigating the storm. You try to sail towards Ryan and Amy -Joel's parents -but everything fades to darkness. And soon, Joel and the boat disappear, and you are left floating in a flood, desperately searching for Joel, desperate for hope.
All the pain, all the joy, all the hopelessness, and all the hopefulness. You don't see it. You feel it. There are moments in the game where you don't know what you have to do to progress, and it's frustrating, but that's the point. It's their frustration, conveyed in a way that we can understand -not in a distant, detached, intellectual way, but in a way that you feel it and know their pain deep within your soul. Some may find the Christian undertones off-putting, and one person seems to have criticised the use of religion as a 'crutch'. But faith was obviously a major part of their struggle, so of course they would include it; this was made from their worldview, not anyone else's. And is it really so bad that, in such a horrific struggle, they found hope and leaned on that hope?
This may just be the most important video game ever made, not because it is innovative from a technological perspective, but because it uses the medium to let a grieving family to share their pain but also their hope. If you play this game from this perspective, I doubt you will come out of it the same person.
And all the proceeds from the sales go to the hospices that helped the family with Joel, so your money won't be wasted regardless of how you feel about the game :)

Armikrog is a smaller indie version of The Neverhood. It had a much smaller budget to start with, and no game studio to keep the development funded twice as long as originally intended, which unfortunately happened. When you come to terms with that, it is actually a fun little game worth playing.
$25 is too expensive, though, because the playing time will probably not exceed 5 hours and the content is not that dense. Fine for Kickstarter purposes, but after release, the price should (and probably will have to, eventually) reflect that.
PRAISE
+ I mostly appreciate the visuals, which are expertly animated, beautifully crafted and Mike Dietz with Ed Schofield really showed us that they still got it.
+ The same goes for the music by Terry Taylor, which could be a little more prominent in the game.
+ There are some original, pretty and fun puzzles.
RANT
- The scripting and the story are the weakest point. The plot is explained in 4 pencil-animated sequences, including the intro, and the ending is just a plain deus-ex-machina. The villain wants to get the child, eliminates its mother and father, who then help you to save the child. Unfortunately, that's not a dumbed-down version, but pretty close to how the story is actually presented.
- All of the characters are very superficially treated and undeveloped. The authors threw away the main advantage of having two protagonists, who only act in the few cutscenes there are.
- Bugs that are annoying, but at least in my experience, they were not game-breaking.
It seems to me that the developers, facing the fixed budget, must have focused on the most expensive and essential thing to do: the hand-crafted, hand-animated visuals. You cannot have such a game without that. The biggest problem is that this part comes last, after all the story and all the pencil-testing are finished. Rolling this big boulder before them must have been pretty daunting, and the game looks like they needed to plan much less than what they hoped for, out of fear that there would not be enough money to finish.
I think that this game is cursed with both "not appealing to the mainstream enough" for any game studio to fund it, and "too budget-tricky" for Kickstarter, which is a shame. This one is sad and hopeful, poetic, honest and brave.
A very personal and intimate reflection on grief, faith, joy and the love of a child. It is also a vessel for carrying messages and artwork from many other people, who backed the project on Kickstarter and decided to share their own losses and stories.
Whether this is a game or not is not very relevant. Let's just say it's an interactive experience in the form (or format) of a video game... Know this: instead of walking freely, you click on clearly indicated hotspots and navigate between fixed waypoints where you can freely look around. There are no puzzles and it takes roughly 2 hrs to play through. There is replay value if you go back and read all the messages, study the artwork etc.
If you think you can't handle the emotional content in this game - it's actually not as sad or depressing as you may think. There is playfulness and laughter here too, surrealistic dreamlike sequences and a few bittersweet minigames. If you feel any of the vignettes is too heavy to handle, you can quickly press Esc and switch to another chapter.
The Green family are Christians and that is mirrored in how they are coping with hardship and tragedy, but they are not trying to preach or convert you. Rather, this is their very personal struggle with faith and doubt, hope and despair. In the game, the couple are even quarreling over how to handle their emotions and beliefs.
Ryan & Amy Green, their kids and their small dev team deserve all the love of the gaming community for daring to share their life and loss in this way. This is not everyone's cup of tea, but its existence is making our broken world a slightly richer place.

By far one of THE best RPGs I've ever played.  The storyline focuses on making tough decisions (some tougher than others) that have far-reaching consequences for the game's world, grey-and-gray morality in abundance, and it does two things very few games have done.
1) It allows importing saves from "The Witcher", though the impact such imports have is negligible
2) It features an extremely divergent storyline, as the final decision made in Act 1 will split the game for Act 2, and directly impact the available decisions and knowledge the player has in Act 3.
It also accomplishes something that a lot of media largely ignores, and that's giving the villains (largely) reasonable motivations for what they're doing.  The Scoi'atel raid human settlements, but that's in reaction to humans marginalizing and persecuting elves and dwarves.  The humans, in response to said raids, then become even more suspicious of the elves and dwarves living among them, underscoring how useless such tactics are in a practical sense.

Stellaris met my expectations and then some. Complete with the same kind of modder support, Stellaris delivers the grueling grand strategy experience that made me such a huge fan of the Crusader Kings & Europa Universalis series, and brings it to the grand stage of a space opera.
I particularly appreciated the race creation system, whereas in Crusader Kings II, the 'Ruler Designer' came as DLC, the race creation system is embedded in-game, allowing you to create (almost) any fictional race you could think of. While there are still limitations on the races you can create as of release (such as the inability to design hivemind intelligences, such as Star Trek's Borg), I imagine, staying true to Paradox's releasing detailed DLC for other games built within the Clausewitz Engine, this shall be rectified in the near future.
The early game is basically a race to start colonizing and gathering minerals. Mid-game, so far is a little bit of a drag, but I'm told as it nears endgame, Paradox has some unique events in mind for players who stick it through.
Regardless, I highly suggest this game for anyone who enjoys the grand strategy genre that Paradox has seemingly mastered, and for anyone who enjoys a good space opera.

This was yet another roguelike i was awaiting eagerly to get my hands on. I am a huge fan of the dark souls games and this game plays very much like the souls series. The controls may not be as fluid as you would see in a souls game but the similarities are uncanny.
Now i'll go over the good the game has to offer then the bad:
Gameplay: As stated before the game plays very similar to the souls games. RB/R1 are light attacks, LT/R2 are heavy attacks, the LB/L1 and LT/L2 controls your shield. Dodging is Circle or B, item use on X or square. The game has a unique mechanic in that using special attacks will cause a drain on your maximum stamina, making them cautionary to use in certain situations. As with most roguelikes you have certain traits you can unlock as you meet certain criteria on your playthroughs. This gives the game it's only replayability though.
The problems start to arise when it comes to weapons. There's only a handful of weapon types split into 5 tiers 0-4 and outside of their special attacks, all behave the same way.  Light daggers, medium swords, heavy maces/greatswords, staves, and crossbows make up the types of weapons you will find. If you have friends, you will find the game to be quite easy especially if you and your friends are souls veterans. If you go down your friends can pick you up. Playing solo isn't as hard either. The game throws materials at you with which you can make way too many meats and potions to recover with. This leads to the point of using stamina attacks sparingly as the threat of stamina loss is negated by the sheer number of recovery items you can make.
Sound wise the game is at an ok level. Nothing to write home about, yet not entirely drown it out with your own music either.
Graphics to me aren't everything, and the game has an ok asthetic when it comes to models, but the levels themselves are very bland. Each level has one color palette and not much else.
Lastly and probably the one reason the game lands on my not recommended list is that the game is only 9 levels deep, and even on a solo run will take you about 60 minutes to complete. If it were more varied in level and enemy design, it would barely slip in, however i cannot recommend a game such as this for 30$. I unfortunately refunded the game as i had 84 minutes in it and had no desire to push through the 9 levels for only 1 boss over and over.

A beautiful survival game with some interesting mysterious elements
Vortex: The gateway has a lot of potential if it continues to improve.
This game, just like many other survival games, have a hunger, thirst, temperature and stamina meter. They're self explanatory so I won't go into detail.
Where the interesting stuff lies, is the backstory and world. During the day, you're gathering resources, and crafting stuff (with a easy to use system) as you normally would expect. However, when the first night hits is where your world is rocked.
A giant vortex opens up, and a Ship beams something down. Without spoiling some of the cool stuff, there are small things like this that keep this from being 'just another survival game". Where most of those have boring worlds, this has an interesting story to uncover, as well as some beautiful scenery. Glowing mushrooms, winding trees, the game looks beautiful. Although, at the moment, the game still needs a good bit of optimization, but it's not awful.
So far, I haven't really found a way to progress much in the game, so I'm assuming there isn't really much of a goal at the moment. If that's a problem for you, keep that in mind before purchasing the game. It's a fun world to explore, and there's a decent amount of interesting stuff to craft.
Overall, it's a pretty cool game, and I'm excited to see it grow. It needs a bit of polish, and more content, but I'm hoping we'll see the game go somewhere!

I purchased Vortex because it had an interesting premise and I really enjoy similar games like "The Forest" and "Subnautica". And while it does have some decent visuals, that seems to be about all it has going for it for now.
The overall performance of the game on my system was not great. Movement and action were a bit sluggish. I'm not sure if this was due to my computer performance or if that is just how the game is currently functioning. I currently use an AMD 6300 FX 6-core processor, 12 gigs of ram, and an AMD Radeon R7 with 2 gigs of memory. Not a top of the line setup but it has no problem running "Subnautica" or "The Forest" or any other game, now that I think about it.
The build mode and user interface leave something to be desired. To build something, you have to first gather a type of resource. A stick, a piece of bamboo, some leaves. THEN you get to see what you could possibly build from these. This is something that "The Forest" does way better. Everything you could build is already there for you to see with a list of what you would need to collect.
Build mode in Vortex is all through the ugly inventory screen. You select what you want to build, hit the little hammer icon, place the item and start throwing resources at it. But there isn't much to build just yet.
Collecting resources isn't the best. You start with a machete and use it to cut plants. So far, you can cut down a piece of bamboo and get 3 bamboo logs. But when you hack at a tree, you get nothing. Hack at a leafy bush, get a seemingly infinite supply of leaves. Hack at a shrub, get a seemingly infinite supply of sticks. This is another thing that "The Forest" has done very well. In that game, you can hack down just about everything and basically clear cut a huge area while collecting resources. In Vortex, it's nothing like that.
One major problem I found is that falling from any height, no matter how minor, seems to damage the player. It's very unrealistic and kind of annoying when you are trying to climb down a rock outcropping.
The other thing is that food and water are pretty difficult to collect. Water appears to be almost non-existant. So far, the only water I could find came from a water plant. Hunting for food comes down to crafting some throwable spears and chucking them at these pig-like creatures. As far as I can figure, that is it.
So to sum it up, this game has potential to be something good. It's just not there yet. I would recommend holding off for a while until it has been further developed.

I've been playing Galactic Civilizations from the start of the series.  Fans of the earlier titles are likely to enjoy this iteration.  Most of the core ideas are well-implemented, and the look of the game is appropriately updated.  Particular highlights include a more diverse body of random events (even before obtaining the Mega Events DLC), an ideological system, race-specific tech trees, and an incredibly nuanced ship designer.  Of course, there is robust support for custom-designed content, which should proliferate as the playerbase grows.
For people unfamiliar with the series, Galactic Civilizations is about competitive empire-building.  In the standard game, a player begins with a spacefaring race still limited to its homeworld.  Simultaneously managing exploration, settlement, economic development, technological growth, and security concerns; the aim is to colonize distant worlds and thrive.  Victory conditions often include peaceful options like diplomacy or even transcending physical existence itself, though violent conquest is also on the list.  Managing large happy colonies provides the resources to attempt the loftiest goals.
Having played many games in this 4X genre, I feel Galactic Civilizations III strikes a nice balance between accessibility and complexity.  It is possible to control every detail right down to the placement of decorative fins on warships, but delegating to the AI to focus on high-level questions and strategic command is also a viable approach.  I don't yet have enough experience to have a strong opinion about the AI, but I find the normal difficulty setting suitable for learning the ropes.  Ideology is a particular treat, giving significant consequence to the morality of crucial choices.  For players willing to put in the time a serious strategy game demands, Galactic Civilizations III should provide many hours of pleasant satisfaction.

So I beat the game, read everything on that giant wall of text, rewatched every tentacle-elevator story cut scene, you know - really got into all the nooks and crannys.
And my general impression is - eh, it's alright.
There are tons and tons of "escape the room" puzzle games out there with much harder to figure out puzzles that you can play for free. There are tons and tons of games out there that are more immersive in the world they create that you can play for the same price as this. And there are games out there that put those two elements together better than this does.
The reason I still recommend it is because it's creators trying to do something that most game makers don't do anymore - take chances. I'm honestly not upset in the slightest that this game isn't as good as was hyped, because at least they weren't just giving us the same old, same old here.
Most of the reviews you'll see compare this to one other game - the Neverhood. The thing is, if there were more companies willing to take this kind of a risk, or just risks in general, there'd be more than one game for this to be compared to.
People need to realize that not every game will be a home run - and that it's okay that that happens as long as it's happening because they were trying to do something unique. I'll take 50 games trying and failing to be their own thing over any number of games trying and succeeding at following the leader (looking at you, first person shooter genre).
From all accounts I've seen, Neverhood is better - but honestly, this game still has plenty of good that you can get out of it - especially if you're playing *this* game instead of trying to play the Neverhood by starting up Armikrog.
It's worth buying, though waiting for a sale might not be a bad idea, but I still don't regret backing this on Kickstarter.

Before I get into this properly, I need to say this game is over-priced. That Dragon, Cancer is a deeply emotional experience that I think everyone should experience, but it has no reply value. You cannot play this game again and expect the same emotional punch to the gut. It's a tight narrative that emerses you briefly in the world of a dying child and his grieving parents, and then you leave, and move on, and you never play it again.
$15 for a one-time, 2 hour experience is simply unfair. While I recommend you play this game, you should buy it only on sale.
Anyway, the game itself is good. The graphic style is very artist, with high-saturation colours and blurred out faces. It's the sort of look that only works if you like that aesthetic; I thought the game was beautiful, but others might find it lazy and ugly. The gameplay is mostly walking around clicking on objects to start cut scenes, but there are some puzzles. The puzzles are extremely simple and require no real thought; you click until something happens, and if you do get stuck like I did, click harder and angrier, until something finally happens. The controls aren't the best and can exacerbrate little frustrations with puzzles.
The voice-acting is wonderful. The dialogue feels very authentic , which only adds to the pain of the situation. It jumps between conversations to poetic waxing, but I feel it does this skillfully. There's enough family dialogue to give the characters life, but not so much its boring, and enough poems to allow for introspection, but not so much it feels pretentious.
This game is very religious. This is neither a good nor a bad thing; much like the artstyle, how someone reacts to this particular aspect depends on their own opinions. I'm not religious at all, and I'd be lying if I said I didn't find the talk of "God's glory" somewhat grating, but I understood why they looked towards their god for guidence. It didn't effect how emotional I got or how much the game hurt me.
Overall, That Dragon, Cancer is an extremely emotional and upsetting game with wonky controls, no reply value, and a higher price then it needs. It's a one off experience that leaves you drained, in need of a hug or a nap. It'll make you cry, and curse how unfair life.

As user Puggsoy put, "Little Inferno is not a game of skill. It's a game of discovery." That is exactly what the game is. I've read that some people were disappointed, claiming that the game felt like it was missing something or lacking, but it's all in the eye of the beholder. I was perfectly pleased and fell in love with it. There's not a lot of challenge to it, if any, but there is a lot of beauty and discovery and fun for the curious who like to experiment. This is not a game for the people who crave constant action or stimulation. If anything, Little Inferno will soothe and calm you. There's something very relaxing about watching the objects burn, and the atmosphere has a very ambient feel despite wondering about the sinister intentions behind your Little Inferno Fireplace that was given to you by a big company, Tomorrow Corporation, that you know very little about. But the premise is that the world around you is freezing, and you have to keep burning things to stay warm and farther more, although it's unspoken, most likely to stay alive.
This game is often described as a "Fireplace simulator," but there's a little more to it than that. It has a plot with a few surprises with a twist that left me surprised and emotional. On top of that, watching things burn never grow tiring. In fact, they often burn with pizzazz. There are a lot of unexpected outcomes, from sounds, to special effects, to beautifully colored flames. You'll be excited to burn the next thing to see how it reacts.

Alright, I heard about this game while it was still being developed and Joel was still fighting his battle against cancer. This game has a couple frustrating things mentioned in some other reviews, but overall the story telling is worth the price in my mind. Here are some pros and cons [Spoilers].
Pros:
-The atmoshpere and lighting throughout most of the game really enhances the story telling
-Most of the voice acting throughout the game is good quality, and holds with the above
-This game made me actually feel genuine sorrow for Joel and his family, not many games do that anymore
-The art in many levels is amazing for the polygonal style that was chosen (more in cons)
-Towards the end when they give the bad news about Joels cancer, it talks about how the doctors and people who helped feel genuine sadness about not being able to help Joel, and gives you insight into what they thought
-Pancake parties... need I say more?
Cons:
-The art in other sections of the game did feel like there could be more detail, but it did not impede the gameplay
-The game sometimes made me do an option or two twice and played the same dialog before furthering the story, maybe just a bug, but was slightly imersion breaking
-Towards the ending it gets REALLY religious on the parents part, which in a smaller dose would have been fine, since many people turn to religion in grief, but by the end I found myself wishing to just get through the references already
Honestly, through out the story, it holds true to what the story is about, a family trying their hardest to help their young son fight his battle with cancer. You will probably get the feels.

A really great game and a very satisfying Metroidvania, once you get past the immediate differences (combat and art style, most of all).  The combat makes a very strange first impression, I thought, but after it becomes familiar, it quickly seems both solid and smart.  By the end of the game, the fighting is truly fun and you begin to feel as powerful as your character becomes.
I can't say the cartoon characters or the art style were any particular draw for me at first (and were actually a bit hard to take at times), but the strangeness of that wears off over the course of playing the game as well, and leaves off with a generally satisfying story.  Even so, I'd recommend this for its gameplay far more than for its story.  The soundtrack is also very good, and even great on a few of the tracks.
As a huge Metroidvania fan, I pretty much immediately started this game over again after I beat it, using the second time through to try its hard mode.  I liked that mode a lot more by the end of the game, but it has a huge difficulty curve at the front of the game, which is sort of a shame.  It's much easier to cope with once the combat flow and mechanics are familiar -- but I can't imagine it would be any fun for a brand new player.  There are a few weaker platforming sections of the game (which were frustrating enough in normal mode) that didn't scale well with the huge damage increases of the hard mode.  Still, even the normal mode felt satisfying and challenging in places, which would make it plenty satisfying on its own.
Well worth the money, and it delivered a solid 30 hours between the two playthroughs.  Enough to make me hunt down all of the achievements.  I'd call it very replayable, although maybe with a long break between playthroughs.
Lastly, and almost the most important to me -- this game was almost entirely made by one extremely talented developer, and I hope other people find that as inspiring as I did.  However people feel about the art and the story, this is an extremely solid vision executed with a great deal of clarity, from the artwork all the way down to the game mechanics.  A really rare level of vision, creativity, and talent.
Highly recommended, particularly for fans of the genre.

As a kickstarter project, it's a charming throw-back to the stop motion Claymation that made games like The Neverhood so unique. I will probably reference The Neverhood quite a lot in this review. It's perhaps a bit unfair to compare Armikrog and The Neverhood, truth be told. But it's rather difficult not to when describing some of the nuances of Armikrog; as both games draw from the same creative water source.
Armikrog has a wonderful introduction sequence, with great music from Terry Taylor, and oozing with fun clay-sculpted, stop-motion imagination. Hitting planet side has a real feeling of wonder of what's in store for us! I wonder what catchy ditty the first room will have!?
Until the gameplay starts.
One of the things that made The Neverhood so immersive, was the amount of interactive things in the world. The mushroom tree, the scorpion booger monster clipping Klayman's head off if he strayed too close to the door. The freaking drain, that is clearly signposted as being 'deadly', and can end your game if you jump down it anyway. To name but a few instances where the world can be interacted with, and interact with you. The areas are all distinct, yet skillfully connected.
Armikrog offers nothing to really 'pull' players into the world around them. And what little there is, it's just another vehicle to advance the story. The ants were kind of cool, but are random with no actual context or reason for being in Armikrog. Abraham Lincoln ant with a puzzle clue, right next to a completely unrelated puzzle? It's not immediately clear whether the two are somehow connected (
), so I spent a frustrated half an hour on that alone.
The overarching story is communicated predominantly through the ceiling barnacles, and I find it a bit neat that the developers used a very particular language for them. There's no real incentive for the player to bother learning it themselves however: the story isn't deep enough to warrant that level of commitment.
The cassettes that contained the Neverhood story were brilliant for one simple reason: they made learning the story, a puzzle in itself. You explored this colourful world and catchy soundtrack, Klayman's rythmic plodding your only companion, but the world fed you bits of information here and there. And each thread organically flowed into the next, weaving the whole story together by the end.
You can get the gist of what happened at Armikrog very, very quickly. And the only drive forward after that, is to find some power source that you have no idea what it looks like, and
at pre-determined points in the progression.
The puzzles aren't particularly rewarding to solve, and the process of figuring them out is monotonous. There's really no other way to describe them.
Beak Beak is a nice physical design (but I was always a sucker for Barking birds), but the buddy system feels very tacked on, and it's nothing groundbreaking in this day and age.
The music ost is worth getting hold of, and has just the right amount of nostalgic style, while still doing it's own thing; a treat to listen to in-game. When it plays anyway.
Which leads me onto another thing that bothers me: through experimentation, it appears the music play as a nod of "yeah you're doing it right" as you progress. But if you hang around too much, or take a wrong turn, it abruptly ends, and you will be back to silence. It's never enough time to really appreciate it, to the point it might as well not even be in the game itself.
It's less memorable than the Neverhood OST, but it's still worth a listen.

I personally enjoyed the gameplay very much, but be warned. The gameplay can be pretty easy, at least on regular difficulty. The bosses are quite easy, and I only died a few times during the game to a couple of mini bosses early on. Even those deaths were more my learning the game than the game being challenging. If you're looking for a challenge you should crank up the difficulty.
The Art is fantastic. It gives me a nostalgic feeling for old cartoons I watched when I grew up like An American Tail. The art is consistant and the backgrounds are lovely.
For the most part, the voice acting is really good. All of the main characters are voiced well and with charm. A few quest givers had noteworthily good voice acting. A few voices could do to be improved, but they won't be speaking much.
The main story is short and predictable. Once you learn the situation the world is in, it's pretty easy to know exactly how the rest of the main story will progress. While the main story is predictable, the way the story is told is well done. The story telling isn't innovative, but has many interactions between characters. Between the well written character interactions and the good voice acting, these interactions save the story from being boring.
The music is nice, but not anything that I would buy separately, if that were an option. It's nice background music, but I wouldn't be opposed to listening to another soundtrack while playing this game.
Ultimately, this game is fun. I would happily pay full price for this game. I enjoyed my experience with it, and it has volted itself up to one of my favorite games. I highly recommend it.

Now, I was a huge fan of World of Goo which was created by the same team as Little Inferno, it has a charming characterization of goo and a Tim Burton-esque art style (I hate to always compare anything with a dark cartoon like style to Tim Burton but whatever). Not to go off on a tangent, but World of Goo was a great puzzle/engineering game, it was stylish, polished, sympathetic, and magical, I was totally enraptured by the whole experience.
When I heard that they were making a new game I immediately became elated, I watched the teaser trailer for Little Inferno and was hooked. Constantly I wondered what the gameplay was going to be like. And then I heard the news… Little Inferno was little more than a simple app; a time waster, an “I have 5 minutes to kill so I’ll play this silly game” game. I felt defeated. I tossed away my hopes and moved on towards other titles.
Then it just so happened that Little Inferno was in fact, in one of the Humble Indie Bundles, of course I bought it for Hotline Miami but hey, I might as well check out Little Inferno and form my own opinions. Well, I cannot say that it was not what I was expecting. It is a game where you burn stuff, yeah that is it. A game for pyromaniacs. Now there are quite a lot of things to burn, mind you, but the entire game is buy things from a catalog and toss them into your “Little Inferno” and burn, burn away.
If you were ever a kid (and I am sure most of you were), then you may remember a point in your childhood wherein you took to the matches and lit stuff on fire, either army men, toys, sticks, etc… That is what this game is, it taps into your inner pyromaniac; watching the warm orange glow of a smoldering grandma; it all feels very comforting.
Now, as you play, you will constantly unlock new things to burn, some things burn nicely, like stuffed animals or wood, and others not so much, like fragile china. It all feels very rewarding, in that, you purchase stuff to burn, and when you burn it you get more money for burning for which you can spend to purchase more stuff to burn; it is a vicious cycle. A very simple concept, yet it somehow is extremely hypnotic.
I have not quite explained everything though, there is a slight puzzle element, where you need to burn a combination of items based off some keywords, for example: CORNFLAKES – you need to burn corn and a box of cereal. Some of the word puzzles are fairly simple, and others can be quite a stretch. These puzzles leave a bit of room for thinking while you wait for your products to arrive. Yeah, I don’t quite know why they incorporated a time period for items to be delivered to you other than to pad gameplay, but it becomes especially obnoxious once you have done everything in the game and must wait around a minute to get your items. You can use coupons to speed up the delivery but come on, I have ‘beaten’ the game, just let me burn stuff.
And that about covers the entire game; Oh, I almost forgot, the story. Now, I will admit, that I did not quite understand the ending or even what the whole story was really about. This is what I gathered – global warming. Yeah, I really hope I am wrong about this, but the entire concept is that the world is getting colder and nobody knows why, so stay inside and burn all your toys. It is not that hard to see the correlation; but it is not like it really matters, they do not even expand upon this idea, it feels like there is about as much depth in the narrative as there is in the gameplay.
Well, I think I have said all that there is to say about this one. Is worth your time? Not really. Is it cheap? No, in the same manner as Proteus, it is offered for an outrageous price of $10, two dollars seems more appropriate. I won’t complain since I got it in the bundle, but you should avoid paying full price. Overall, it is a cozy and entrancing little game yet too shallow to really offer an experience.
So no I cannot recommend it.

Stellaris met my expectations and then some. Complete with the same kind of modder support, Stellaris delivers the grueling grand strategy experience that made me such a huge fan of the Crusader Kings & Europa Universalis series, and brings it to the grand stage of a space opera.
I particularly appreciated the race creation system, whereas in Crusader Kings II, the 'Ruler Designer' came as DLC, the race creation system is embedded in-game, allowing you to create (almost) any fictional race you could think of. While there are still limitations on the races you can create as of release (such as the inability to design hivemind intelligences, such as Star Trek's Borg), I imagine, staying true to Paradox's releasing detailed DLC for other games built within the Clausewitz Engine, this shall be rectified in the near future.
The early game is basically a race to start colonizing and gathering minerals. Mid-game, so far is a little bit of a drag, but I'm told as it nears endgame, Paradox has some unique events in mind for players who stick it through.
Regardless, I highly suggest this game for anyone who enjoys the grand strategy genre that Paradox has seemingly mastered, and for anyone who enjoys a good space opera.

When I first started playing this game, I was extremely excited. I had heard it described as a Dark Souls/Binding of Isaac/Dungeon Crawler with co-op. I hyped it up to all my friends, promising what I thought would be a great game to play together while coming down from the day.
The issue is that while it bears similarities to other smash-hit games, it doesn't bear these similarities where it counts.
It doesn't have the exciting combat of Dark Souls. In fact, after you've tried the 3 weapons (hidden under many different skins), you begin to feel bored fighting enemies.
It doesn't have the exciting loot from Binding of Isaac, Enter the Gungeon, or other such games. Each weapon or shield you pick up is not only not a game changer, but doesn't give any sort of feeling whatsoever.
Roguelikes are popular for their intense difficulty, but also in providing you with ways to beat the game. The big issue with Necropolis is that difficulty has not been created through complexity, but rather through sheer numbers of enemies. The most difficult challenge I experienced was a massive room filled with skeletons and viking(fain). I didn't enjoy having to constantly run away while periodically swinging my sword once. I doubt you will either.
Loot is also another important part of the genre. Sometimes the loot is terrible, and you die immediately. Other times you feel like a god, and chasing that feeling is a big part of the genre. I haven't felt that with Necropolis, nor do I expect anyone could. Every weapon and shield felt exactly the same, and I never once felt "powerful". Most of the money earned in game is spent on cosmetics or on tiny buffs. There needs to be an ability to purchase meaningful weapons or shields.
Wonderful idea, with very subpar execution. Save your money.

I prepurchased this. You should only buy it when it's cheaper.
Short description of the gameplay:
You start with a "zero" character.
You collect weapons, shields, armor and gems to upgrade yourself.
No stats. The only upgrade you get is to your health and you buy that from gems.
Weapons have different animation, reach and speed. Try each.
Kill monsters to get items, materials and gems. Open chest, duh.
From the materials you can craft food, potions and other usefull items. For most of them you need the recipe though.
If you die you lose all this♥♥♥♥♥♥
The main objective is to reach the end of level9. I know of no further levels though this is the kind of game that would typically surprise you with 20 more levels ... and then with 99 more levels... and so on.
You get sub-objectives (maximum 3 per level) which you can fullfill to earn tokens that remain even if the character dies.
Any if of the completed objectives get replaced with new ones once you enter a new level.
From these tokens you can buy codexes, dyes, and at each entrance of each level (after level1) a chest with random loot.
Codexes are passive gameplay modifiers from which you can equip 1 at any given time (jump higher, get all potion recipies, never vomit from bad food, ...).
Dyes are color schemes for your character.
You only need to buy the Codexes and Dyes once. They remain even after you die.
Once you die or reach the end your accomplishments will be summarized and you get even more "perma-tokens".
So next time you can buy a new codex or a color scheme.
This would be all well.
GRAPHICS:
Love the style of the main characters armor sets. Love the weapon design. Also this game has the best dungeon merchant design that I have seen in about 6 years.
Hate the design of most mobs. Really. Maybe it's because there aren't many. Maybe because clockwork pyramidhead soldier #701 was 651 too many. The bonespiders look nice.
The dungeons look nice BUT many areas are more confusing because of the art style than the actual layout. I got lost in the swamps twice and high-bridges once. Everything looks the same => there are no landmarks to look for while navigating.
Like the small touches, like the scribbles on the walls. Would prefer it even more if there would be (more interactive) statues and other "sights" too.
The camera can AND WILL go epileptic in wall vicinity.
SOUND:
Mobs are recognizable by sound. The mobs are repititive but the sounds even more so. weak nordish undead guy has the same scream as slightly less weak nordish undead and really strong nordish undead guy. The gibberish of the evil floating pyramid head is also not helping there.
MUSIC:
turned it off. I think it's not my style. Can't comment on it.
GAMEPLAY:
Controls can't be remapped right now. They should patch it.
Inventory is a clunky.
The recipes don't really make sense on display ("meat, meat, ichor" instead of "2 meats, 1 ichor").
Item descriptions are almost completely useless (though there is a potion that revives you once, and it's craftable).
The combat works.
Monsters are dumb ("walk into attack range" then "use random attack"). Difficulty lies in the numbers (both monster stats and count). Also you can cheese the from a distance.
OVERALL:
The game is good but it doesn't feel like 28euros ... more like 12-15.
Map design wise the corridors feel empty and big (a smaller more claustrophobic one would have worked better, I think then again the camera spaz there... oh well).
I'm hoping for content patches because in my 8 hours most mobs felt repetitive.
It would be worth the 28euros with an AI upgrade.
Without deaths the game can be completed quite fast. I'm guessing with proper evasive tactics within an hour (for speedrunners that's a good starttime). In 8 hours I died twice and completed the game while I cleared everything, tried to complete each objective and wanted to gear up.
Still, this is a good game.
BUY IT WHEN IT'S CHEAPER.
