If you enjoyed The Forest from early development days, can expect a similar experience.
Game starts off with an office party,  news is being broadcast on tv about worm holes appearing around the planet. As the warning about the latest location is announced one happens to appear locally. Moments later you blackout, followed by waking in what seems to be another dimension, dreamworld or perhaps limbo. Might sound a little same old but it's quite well presented some of what separates Vortex from other survival sims imo.
After waking you find belongings scattered about, collecting these helps to guide you further. Each item picked up automatically shows available blueprints, giving ideas for crafting and your next objective. Like most survival sims, the objective is to survive. Surprise! In daylight most animals encountered were seemingly passive, setting up the initial camp wasn't too challenging. When things get dark however, the game changes, things go bump in the night. While minding your own business and harvesting resources, don't be too surprised when a giant vortex appears over head dropping headhunting aliens into the world. Other then watching enemies, will need to satify your hunger, thirst along with keeping warm. Nothing too complex, personally I like that. Saving could be done using a tent or house once it was setup, did not run into any problems with loading or corruption.
Performance could be improved but quite respectable given the amount of detail on screen. If using a low-end system the game should still be playable. Runs on unity, screen resolutions of 4k+ were supported along with the standard quality settings, no options available in-game at this time. Another pretty solid survival sim, which makes two in a week, almost gives me some faith in steam again (almost!). Copy was provided by developer, doesn't change my thoughts. Cheers.

I REALLY want to enjoy NECROPOLIS. It had a lot of potential, the trailers made it look great, and I love the art style. The first 30 minutes to about an hour of gameplay was pretty fun, but the issue comes in after that hour.
After you've played this game for about an hour, you'll start to realize there's no real difference in any of the weapons, shields, or armors. Some of them may block more damage, but all in all, most of the weapons are the same, just reskinned versions of other weapons. Some of the armors look cool, but have no real functionality it felt like. The areas all look about the same, and you end up going through the swamp area about 6 times in a playthrough. Seeing a new area was pretty cool, but when you find it theres nothing that new there to explore. There might be a few chests with potions and crafting supplies, but besides that it's just mostly the same enemies that were in the areas previous to that one.
For a game that calls itself a roguelike, I feel like I can't come back to play this like I can with other roguelikes, because theres no real end goal besides reaching a portal. The end "boss" was a joke, and was just a big enemy with a lot of health, and once you kill him you can go into the final area, which is just a portal which fades away, and starts the credits. The only reason to come back and play this game would be if you wanted all the codex's (?), or if you wanted to unlock more colors, but for the price of $30 dollars, I can't really reccomend this to anyone. It feels like an early-access game, and if I were thinking of buying it, I would wait for the price to go down.

It's a pretty fun game if you treat it as an online brawler and not an online cooperative Dark Souls clone. Which is funny since it burrows so much from Dark Souls, like its cumbersome attack animations or its similar control scheme. It's true that you only fight mooks and not face anyone who appears to be the boss of a level, and I wish that there were boss fights but unfortunately there are none. Your primary opponents will be the environment, the usual dungeon dwellers, and your buddy who FREQUENTLY accidentally hits you when he is trying to kill steal from you, yes there is friendly-fire.
I hate how the game only gives you a riddle of a description of what an object, like an equip-able perk (named Codexes) or a consumable item, may do to you, and I wish that there were visible statistics on what an equip-able item may offer you. This isn't a typical RPG where you level up your stats from gaining XP after slaying a monster numerous times, so you're left with drop-able loot to be your only means of character progression. So it's important to know whether that tier one broadsword that you're currently wielding does more damage than this tier two stave that was found after opening a chest.
After playing for a while, I had a feeling that the game lacked content. You're always starting from square one again after dying, so it's a rare treat to be able to go deep into the necropolis because of its perma-death. You will always repeat the same boring closed corridors of the top floor and hardly venture the mysterious and open environments of the bottom floors. Which is a shame since it feels like most of the good stuff is down there, especially the loot that's found in the deep floors.
The game is boring when you're playing on your own. And its also completely unfair for a solo player compared to a team of players. If you're playing with others, your death won't mean the end of the game since your teammates do have the opportunity to revive you. However, once you die by your lonesome, the game instantly ends in game over. There is a bit of resource management when playing with a full team, since there can only be so much odds and ends for everyone to use to craft healing or buffing consumables, but I feel that this doesn't do enough to justifying playing on your own, where your able to use all the crafting items by yourself. Being able to be revived is a much better proposition than being selfish.
Now, do I recommend the game? The game has plenty of flaws, but I did had fun playing it and exploring its dark and murky environments. In its current state, I wouldn't recommend the game, and I wish the game was released as an early access game because that's what basically it feels to me. It needs more content all around, and the AI needs to be a bit more smarter because the AI that's found in an MMORPG is a lot more smarter than the AI that's found in this game. I was thinking about getting a refund, but since I found a group of buddies to play the game with, I've decided to cancel that refund request and to continue to play the game with them. So, if you're thinking of playing on your own, don't purchase this game unless you feel like the developers will give you freebies for sticking it out with them, which I am doing and hoping since its release is really botched. But if you have a group of friends that like the sound of the game and is bugging you to buy the game so that you can play with them, go for it. It is a really fun ONLINE BRAWLING game.

Alright at first thought this may be just another survival game with lizards but this one totally caught me by suprise.   Here is what I am loving about this game so far:
Performance-  Running maxed out and getting about an average of 40 fps (gtx780, 16 gigs ram, i7, etc.).  No crashes or bugs as of this posting.  While good probably will continue to need optimization as it develops.
Visuals- Game looks fantastic and very atmospheric (great work on the skybox as well).
Sound- This is where the game is a 10/10 already!  The sounds in this game will have you on the seat of your pants especially at night.  Not to much and not too little just enough to get your imagination running wild.
Environment-  Plenty of area to explore, great foliage, various animals to hunt, creatures that hunt you (very scary at night),   Resources are available but you do have to venture out and explore.   Hope to see island/landmass increase over time as indicated.
Crafting-  Works well but UI could use some fine tuning and current carrying capacity should/could be either increased or allow for additional containers to be crafted.  You can craft a storage container out of bamboo but doesn't seem to currently offer option to store extra items (bug?).
Resource (water/food)-  Food seems to be plentiful but the water is currently hard to find and limited.  I do think the water consumption rate needs to be looked at as it depleates too fast in my opinion.  Will be nice to see more animals added that you can hunt (really fun).
Story- Yes there is actually a story/plot!  While limited now I hope to see this expanded upon...where are we? Why are we here?  Can we escape back to Earth? etc. etc.

Vortex: The Gateway is yet another Unity Early Access release. It seems that there is a new one released every day. I was skeptical at first but I was drawn in by the game trailer video and screenshots. It looked interesting so I thought I'd give it a shot.
One thing that sets this game apart from the other EA Unity releases is the story. The game begins at a party with you having a good ol' time dancing, drinking and socializing. Faintly, you can hear a TV news report in the background spewing some information about a black hole or Einstein-Rosen bridge....wait, what? Then the sky turns purple and it begins to get interesting. Next thing you know, you're on some alien island with stuff thrown about.
Game play is similar to other games of this genre where you run around exploring a large land mass or in this case, an alien island, gathering supplies and crafting tools, weapons and other useful items. You start out with a few basic supplies to get you going but they will not last long. You will need to get to work gathering nourishment quickly. There are a few animals running around, screaming loudly, that you can hunt for food. I did not encounter a water source but I really didn't look for one either. The enemy or monsters or aliens are lacking a bit as they don't pose a real threat since you can easily outrun them. I actually jumped on top of something and was fairly safe from one for a while.
The graphics are well done and the island does indeed look alien. The animals that I saw were unique, interesting and had decent AI. They ran away from me but also attacked me trying to protect themselves as I was trying to attack them. During my game play I only saw one alien whose entrance to the game was spectacular! However, the excitement that his entrance created was short lived as his AI needs tweaking. He was able to track me but he was slow and caused little damage to me as he was hitting me. I was unable to cause much damage to him as I was having issues with dehydration and low stamina.
The game performed well on my mid-range system with the graphics set to "high". I didn't notice any lag issues or other performance problems. The sounds and music in the game were very loud and do not yet have a volume control that functions. You save your game progress by pressing the 'V' key.
All in all, even for its initial release, the game is pretty stable and very playable. I did not encounter any game breaking bugs or issues. Of course there are minor bugs and other issues that I'm sure the developer will be working on. I enjoyed my game play and am actually looking forward to playing more.
I do recommend this game and if you buy it while it's on sale I believe it's worth the price. You may, however, may want to wait a few days to see if the developer releases any patches, just to see how determined he is to continue the game's development.

Matchmaking feels like a chore, especially as it's supposedly one of the most played games on Steam. Even then, every player must be "ready" before selection which furthers the searching process more if everyone is not "ready".
Once selection starts, if not everyone selects by the end of the time limit then you will dragged back into the search. I find this to be the worst when there's a new Champion, where a player will refuse to choose as they don't get the champion that they wanted.
This game is team based, but the lack of communication between teams is present. The VGS I find useful at times but very difficult to use while in combat. Also, memorising the commands can be a pain if you wish to know all of them.
For Ranked, this isn't so much of an issue but for Casual it is. Casual allows you to pick any champion you want so long as it isn't selected and I'm fine with the variety except when there are 3 or perhaps 4 damage Champions on one team.This makes the game less fun as there is a much higher chance of me losing as opposed to a balanced team.
If someone disconnects or leaves, they will be automatically placed back into the match that they left/disconnected on. I would rather for me to have a choice to play upon returning, and waiting for a ban to be lifted than to AFK an entire game. If I rejoin, I would rather have default stats and no current upgrades than to have the bots stats and upgrades. I'm unsure if the game still runs on EAC, and I don't have any problems with EAC but I know a lot of people who do have problems with it so keep that in mind.
Graphics are okay, the cartoonish style of it is pretty cool, but nothing too lavish. Personally some of the models (such as Viktor) don't feel like a nice balance between realistic and cartoonish that the game itself has set up. Also FPS is fine, and will run nicely even on slow computers.
Maps are also okay (again nothing too lavish), but some (such as Fishing Market) don't feel as used as other maps (like Stone Keep). Perhaps this was intention but personally I don't like part of the map being empty of engagements.
Cards are more of an annoyance to me. It brings about a slight disadvantage to more casual gamers, and personally I rarely ever touch them. With the introduction of a third currency (essence) coins have become far less useful to me, and getting this third currency takes too long and is unfairly distributed. For duplicate common cards especially, the essence rate is severely low. You'd hope that by playing this game everyday you'd stand in for a chance at getting all legendary cards for all champions: no.
Levelling Champions is also far too slow in my opinion. For the hours I've put into this game my highest Champion is only 11. I feel as though the levelling rate should be a bit higher to entice players to get to Mastery 25
Crystals, the premium currency. You may think that playing everyday and doing 2 friend referrals would give you enough Crystals to buy a fair amount of item cosmetics. No, and this makes me want to play the game less.
PvE feels very unfair, and usually requires a certain type of team whenever it's up. I don't want to be constricted to Champions that I will never want to play.
The lack of modes and the lack of decent skins for most Champions is present. There are less than 5 modes to choose from and I find that disappointing considering how long that this game has been out (on Early Access). Hopefully the amount of skins and modes will improve over time.
Quests only reward coins, which I can get from matches. I don't have a desire to complete them. Even if I was rewarded with just 5 Crystals per Quest I would be more willing to complete them. Also, it would be nice to see Daily/Monthly Quests rather than just Weekly. As well as this, I think character specific quests would be a nice thing to implement into the game.
Lag has been an issue for me in the past and some others but not anymore. Though matches are usually unstable with one every so often disconnecting me, or forcing me to.
My main issue for this game (aside from the current false advertising) is it's just not fun for me anymore. My favourite Champions feel a lot more weak, and I feel pressured into choosing certain Champions just because they're stronger even though they're in the same class. I also feel like Hi-Rez gets balancing wrong, especially when new Champions come out. These new Champions have mostly all been overpowered and overused during the first few weeks of its release, and I hate that.

I don't usually go in for reviewing games here, but having seen the Kotaku article about some of the things being written here about this game, I'll bite. I became a father eleven months ago. My partner, the mother of our daughter, saw me reading about 'That Dragon, Cancer' last month and asked what it was about. When I told her, she looked stunned and asked: 'Why would anyone want to play that?' I had no answer for her, but just knew that I did want to play it. Now that I have, I think I know why, and why I recommend it.
The death of a loved one is painful and traumatic. We cope with it as best we can; which is to say we utterly fail to cope with it, but try to go on living. I hope never to experience what the Greens went through, watching their son Joel dying, but admire their strength and courage in facing that experience and trying to make something positive of it. For me, the revulsion people feel about the notion of 'playing' this 'game' (I'll admit the words really don't fit) is a shamefully cowardly response - at the end of the day, we can hit Quit, and nothing has changed in our livess. The Greens lived this and did their best to process and communicate it. That's what art is all about, and shying away from it just because it makes us uncomfortable is symptomatic only of our own weakness, our insistence on an artificial safe-zone.
As a card-carrying atheist, I'm on a polar extreme away from the faith the Greens have, but I still found every moment of this episodic narrative driven audio-visual experience utterly relatable and overwhelmingly human. That's no mean feat, and speaks volumes of the honesty, the sheer soul-bearing earnestness that's gone into this harrowing project. I'll grant that the visuals may not be to everyone's tastes, the thematic examination of faith may be too cerebral for some, and the fundamentally morbid subject matter (but no - this is a celebration of a life, along with all the agony of its too-soon death) will put many off; but accusations of profiteering from their son's death can only sit somewhere on a spectrum between flat-out trolling and plain ignorance. If you sit somewhere toward the latter end, I urge you to play the game and experience it. It won't be much fun, but it will be worthwhile. As for the trolls, I hope they find some happiness on their own.

I laughed. I cried.
I sometimes got frustrated with the controls.
But overall, I really admired what this game is grappling with, sometimes very successfully, sometimes less so. If you're interested in experimental narrative games like Thirty Flights of Loving or The Beginner's Guide, you won't regret picking this game up. Just make sure you approach it in a receptive mood with some extra patience for awkward controls. I would also try not to look too much into the reporting around the game and just play it for what it is first.
As a non-religious person, not yet a parent, and lucky enough never to have lost anyone close to me to cancer, I could seem like the worst possible audience for this game. However, I actually feel like this game taught me a lot, and that it has helped prepare me for a part of life that we will all have to deal with one day. I can picture myself sitting in a hospital room years or decades from now and thinking back to the raw--but beautiful--imagery of this game and the deep questions that it asks. This is a gift that I will carry with me always. This is what experiential narrative games can be.
After reading more about the family and the making of the game itself, I wished that TD,C had gone into more detail about Amy and Ryan as a couple. Amy originally seemed convinced that Joel's miraculous recovery would inspire others in their Christianity, and as that dream slowly fades, I wanted to know more about the impact that had on their faith and their relationship.
But I can understand why the developers shifted gears to making the game more of a memorial to Joel, when it started out as a game more focused on the impact Joel's cancer had on his parents. Joel only recently passed away. Amy and Ryan agree in-game that "we ended up in the same place," in terms of their faith, but as a player things felt more fragile. This is a game very much written "from the trenches" of loss and pain, rather than from the typical distance that developers are able to take from these issues. I think that is what makes this game so unique. Its immediacy and lack of distance can be jarring, and as a player, even one who typically plays narrative games, it can be hard to know how to react.
At the beginning of this review, when I said I laughed while playing this game, I meant it. I laughed hard at Joe's giggle, at the antics of Joel's siblings and at his parents' witty frustration with "cancer culture." I also mourned, brutally, for the loss at the center of this game. As the game says at one point--and I'm not sure about the exact quote--living through cancer, just like living through life, is "all the things"--happiness, joy, sadness, skepticism, sarcasm, irritation, love, and again, so much joy.
Thank you to Ryan and Amy Green for sharing your experience with us. I miss Joel, too.

When I'm looking for a good racing game, I'm looking for something with breathtakingly immersive and realistic physics. Something that just feels right, responsive - like everything that happens is a direct outcome to my inputs.
Rfactor 2 has exactly that.
Yes, the graphics may not be the best on the market, and the range of content is no where near as comprehensive as its competitors, but the sheer quality of the engine is outstanding.
If you want a racing game, it should be noted that this isn't a game. This is a simulator, on par with F1 simulations, and Rfactor's ability to set up game-like scenarios is limited.
However, if you're looking for the most realistic racing simulator on the market, this is by far the best choice. The depth of detailing in the physical simulation, tyre wear, setup management, and damage models is so far ahead any other game that this purchase is well worth the sheer joy of feeling like you're in control of a real car, not one of those artificial, watered-down engines like Codemasters' F1 games.

I don't recommend people buy this game, but I'm still glad it was made. Interactive experiences like this are a new art form that deserve support, but not all experiments bear fruit.
Here's what I liked in no particular order:
1) Nice music, although it got a bit repetitive at times.
2) When viewed from a distance, the abstract human figures looked quite nice.
3) Some of the fanatasy imagry was beautiful. I particualrly liked to see balloons carry Joel ride on constellations come to  life.
4) The cancer ward filled with cards was simple but devastatingly effective. It conveyed how many people had fought to live in those halls.
5) A lot of Ryan's narration was quite moving. I wish we had been "in his head" the whole game. I thought the episode where he's trying to get Joel to settle down was well done. It wasn't a bug that Joel was invisible -right? I was able to empathize with Joel much more in that scene than I could at most other times...
Here is what I disliked:
1) The abstact character models were a big, big, turn-off for me when viewed close-up. Whenever I was forced to get physically close to Joel, I was repulsed. I was acutely aware that this thing in front of me was just a collection of polygons, and it just felt "wrong" to pretend I was playing with a real toddler. The fact that this was all based on a little kid that had really died made things even worse. I would be as if someone made a doll that looked like Joel and expected me to pretend that lifeless, inert doll was a a living, breathing child.
2) The controls were frustrating. I get that the creators wanted to limit interactivity to help maintain the tone they wanted and to focus the narrative. However, there are better ways to do that which don't have me constantly wondering where I'm allowed to click or what I have to click before I can procede. This might have been less of an issue if there weren't parts of the game that I disliked and wanted to get through ASAP. Still, any time that I'm thinking of how to get through the game as a GAME means I'm stepping back from being immersed in the experience you're trying to create.
3) On that note, the driving and platforming mini-games were clumsy and un-fun.  I enjoyed break from the monotony of click-hunting, but you have a problem when you need mini-games to distract from the tedium of your core gameplay.
4) The one place the clicking around really grated on me was when you're fluttering around the ocean filled with bottles. I didn't know where I had to go and got frustrated.
5) This might seem cruel, but I didn't like Amy's voicework or what she had to say. Because of that, it was a real chore to have to listen to all of those bottles filled with her letters. Her stuff seemed very one-note to me while Ryan had more of an arc. It also seemed like we didn't see her worry, suffer, and grieve as intimately as we saw Ryan do all of those things. I recogize that she doesn't have to do so the same way or as visibly as he does, but it seemed like everything we saw of her was through the lens of her religion while Ryan was more human and nuanced.
This whole review probably comes off as cruel, but I feel like a public work of art deserves public critcism. If Ryan or Amy ever read this, wish you all the best and commend you for your courage in making this game.

After some banter between the Dust and Fidget, the small, yet tempermental guardian of the sword, the adventure is on its way. Now I won't go any further in spoiling the fun, as I would hate to take anymore of the suprise away from the game. The gameplay is phenomonal, user-friendly and quick to be memorized, and are much easier on the fingers than most games played on a keyboard, and a great graphic style to boot, the artistic visions of the lands that Dust must go on his quest mapped out with by expert eye and hand. Even the detail put into it is great, from the fluid movments of Dust, to the movement of the cloth of his pants flapping as he dances in his battle-ready pose. Storywise, it was a fantastic, as the story kept me drawn in, and I quickly picked up on the lore of the world, and it wasn't nothing to see time pass buy quickly as I was drawn into the tale of Dust. To add to the visual spectacle of this game, the soundtract was beautiful, and the voice-acting superb.
All in all, I would definitely reccomend this to anyone who enjoys a great game. Thank you for your time.

So, I love the Neverhood. Love its quirky world, its oddities, blah blah, so call me nostalgic if you want. Maybe I am blinded by that, if you want to accuse me of not being fair. I think I am being fair though, and Armikrog did a lot of things that rubbed me the wrong way that weren't technical, just bad decisions. This contains spoilers, so please do not proceed if you mind that.
The cursor thing. Everyone has talked about this. No need to elaborate, although the complete lack of feedback as to what is interactive/where you can go would have helped immensely (how many of you got stuck before you realized you could keep going up on the first octovater? Or that beak beak needed to talk to the octovater? Why not put a similar sonar effect on the octopuses while you are beak beak?) For that matter, Tommynaut has a "hnnnn" idle animation. Use that to show a puzzle/object that cannot be solved yet rather than giving the players... no feedback whatsoever. Heck, even the blue creatures puzzle has a "negative" sound effect when you can't move them, use that as well.
The graphical shortcuts like the stretched out orange creature (seriously, just put two ontop of each other if you need one to be twice as tall, that's way better looking and less jarring than the photoshop mess that it is), or the shrinking tommynaught when quickly re-entering a room in the background have been talked about.
The fact that there are multiple rooms you cannot re-enter really bugs me. One has the hall of records in it, so, if you were halfway through reading it or figured you could come back and check it out later, well, no. Start over.
And here is the big sin: The clue to the one of the final puzzles in the game. The room with the 4 words. Didn't write them down? Figured you could come back and write them down when you understand what they are? NO. TOO BAD.
Put the roller-parts of the path on a separate, lower path than the path to get to that area. Leave it solved when solved. That way you don't have to reset that path to allow the player to move between areas, and they can still access that room later in the game when they are undoubtedly making their rounds to listen to all the octopuses again.
I'm sorry, I don't think the neverhood had ANYTHING like that. No crucial clues or absolutely necessary bits of information that were 1 time access. The worst was that place where you had to put in all the symbols with the weird sound, and only because the clue and the puzzle were a good long walk away from each other, but it's not like one just locked itself away forever after you had visited it.
Other things that really bothered me were the "beak beak" or "tommynaut only" buttons, especially because there isn't even a sound effect to tell you the button isn't working before. So not only is it cryptically doing nothing earlier, but when it can do something, you need to assume only beak beak can use it? That's bad. There are animation files for both characters pushing buttons. Just have both of them be able to push it. Seriously, let them push it before the power machine is on, even, and just give an empty clicking sound. This also applies to the blue button and the creature wall puzzle. I clicked the button, nothing happened, so I wandered around for about 10 minutes until I accidentally clicked the symbol and the puzzle started. The puzzle should include the blue button in its initialization hotspot.
The repeating mobile puzzles were not great, and especially made worse by how they just appear with no context and then force the player to try and decipher fragmented measures of music that don't feel like a unified recording over the constant screams of an infant.
The final sliding block puzzle: there is no indication that it should be solved on the "top" slot, as every other one encourages you to solve via the "bottom" slot. Also these are tedious. The "H" block puzzle was the worst in the neverhood, these are just that... 3 times.
One of my favourite neverhood puzzles was the final one, which took the first puzzle of the game and remixed it in a clever, creative way. Nothing like that exists in this game. There are almost no puzzles that feel environmentally contextual.
The final puzzle of the game: was there a clue as to which "notch" you needed to be on to solve it? That would have helped immensely, because otherwise it felt like a brute force "try every combo, try another notch, try every combo" type affair.
I'm not even going to touch the plot or the fact that the characters had... very little character at all. Or the fact that the world itself was pretty bereft of any of the kinds of stuff that made the neverhood memorable. The fact that the opening section of the game contains a lot of commenting and dialogue that quickly gets phased out tells me that more was probably recorded, but became irrelevant as the game went through redesigns.
The art and animation are gorgeous, but that's not nearly enough to save the mess the game actually is.
The music is great, when it decides it wants to be heard which is infrequently.
The voices sound like they've been recorded in a tin can at the bottom of the ocean, but mercifully disappear almost entirely after the first segment.
I want to like Armikrog, I was so excited... but I feel like there was a lot of wasted potential with really obvious design problems. I appreciate the obvious love that went into it, but I feel like there were just some real problems I have a hard time overlooking.

What a wonderful game. The acting, art, engine fluidity, and soundtrack are cohesive; Dust succeeds at living up to it's own expectations. Backdrops are varied and lush; a rainbow floureshed forest leads to an endangered town. Do they know how beautiful it is beneath them? Animations are butter smooth and the combat doesn't get tiresome at all.
I'm the last person to care for 100% completion or Achievements; still, I find myself wanting to find every area on the map. Still I plunder every enclave Fidget senses there is treasure. Ha, Fidget.
The chraracters are easily memorable. From Box-obsessed Reed to snobby Gianni to gadget-girl Hailey.
Dust wears it's furry aesthetic on its sleeve. And with it, carries the best in being cute, charming, gritty... the humor is peppered in perfectly. The dynamic between FIdget and Dust is a pleasure to watch unfold. Much like Metal Gear Solid and Earthbound that enjoy pokeing you through the fourth wall, Dust revels in its absurdities and trope commonalities.
"Dust... please tell me you saved."
The art will make you want to masturbate. Rivaling the likes of Vanillaware's best, [Odin Sphere, Dragon's Crown] Dust is beautiful and detailed. Effects flurry the screen in numerous layers; a little something at the corner of your eye will lead to a new exit or a ton of treasure.
I... just really like this game. It's deep without being overbearing. Sidequests feel purposeful becuase the dialog is mint and the crafting system doesn't require grinding thanks to the common sense vendor system. Sell something they've never seen before? Well now we can catalog it and keep stock of it for you.
Negatives? Well, to be honest, once you're done Dust, there's not much to do. I recommend getting as much as you can before the end of the game. FIll out your maps, get all the treasure you can; it's worth finding blueprints for the crafting system. And while you lovingly explore, your level magically goes up! Just kidding; it almost feels that way. You never have to grind in this game; but you want to, becuase the combat is gravy on fluffy mashed potatoes.
Mmm.
I suggest playing with a controller and on the "Tough" difficulty setting; Normal is too easy and Hardcore is too punishing. Dust deserves to have it's story earned and combat is more satifying when a strategy is required, rather than mindless button mashing.
Play this game. Love this game. But love it while you can. Cause when you're done, you'll have to wait with uncertainty as to whether there will be another game like this that hits you in all the nice places Dust does.

Necropolis isn't like every other game out there- you know, thrash the level till you know every nook and cranny, and then blow up the boss at the end. I feel like this is the game I've always dreamed about. Think about Civilization, made by the creators of Crusader Kings II and Europa Universalis IV, with a slice of Distant Worlds and Galactic Civilizations. It pretty much sums up this game for me.
Pros
+ Each race is unique. I don't think I've ever met two of the same species on my three playthroughs. Some aren't even advanced and live in, for example, Medieval or Industrial age.
+ Research is fun and a bit random. I heard the perfect description for the research system of this game: You have a deck of cards and when you select your research, you pick three cards from that deck. You aren't guaranteed to get those thrusters next time since you picked improved mines now, so you might have to improvise if you needed those thrusters.
+ Traits. You aren't bound by them for the rest of the game. So you can be really weak but fear not, you can modify your species after a specific tech.
+ Events aren't always the same. Depending on your policital traits and/or biological traits, the events can be different, the lore can be seen in different perspectives and you may get additional choices on some events.
+ Design your own ships. This isn't anything new to space games but this one just seems like it was done so incredibly right. You can pick which front, back and middle section you want for your ship, creating some very good looking ships that can blast your rivals back to stone age.
+ Game looks beautiful. The stars, the aliens, the event pictures, they all looks so gorgeous.
Neutrals
+/- Victory conditions. I've never made it that far in the game yet but the two victories is either destroy everyone or take their planets. Seems a bit dull but personally, I tend to play this game like a game of EUIV, it just goes on until it doesn't, there's no actual victory.
+/- Alien wars. I don't know if it's just on my playthroughs but none of the aliens seem to fight against one another. There are a bunch of wars going on on the other side of the galaxy but my neighbourhood is just races insulting everyone else living near them or forming alliances with each other.
Cons
- War goals are a bit lacking in my opinion. I haven't had much experience in declaring wars but I've only seen three war goals: Vassalize, take a planet or release a planet. I don't want to release a planet nor do I want it, I'm an ocean type, you guys are arid type. And I really don't want to keep a fleet around your worlds just to pacify you if you decide to rebel.
- Depending on your start, you might not have any minerals or energy for you to work with, only option is to expand early on which might crush your economy. But this isn't really the games fault, you just had a really bad start. So not an actual con.
I'd say this game is easily 9/10, I highly recommend this game to anyone who even thinks they might enjoy this.

I'll preface by saying that I fell in love with this game a long time before it was released.
It had the capacity to be so, so good, but it just doesn't quite make it.
There are a number of problems that are probably more personal than objective, but here goes:
-1: There are no stats. For those of you coming here looking for a Souls-Style game, this is not that game.
-2: The combat is floaty. See above: this feels nothing like Dark Souls or its ilk. I was really hoping this was the soulslike that I could play with my friends hours on end that I'd been waiting for, but its combat just does not cut it. It is difficult to find a rhythm with which to utilize dodging, and power attacks, arguably the best way to kill enemies, drain your hunger so fast it's not even funny.
-3: as many others have said: Once you've seen the first enemy, you've basically seen all the enemies. Same goes for loot. I encountered a variety of different swords that I was reasonably confident were all reskins, and that's no fun.
-4 The enemies are incredibly easy. See the points about how this game isn't Soulslike above. Turtling behind a shield is sufficient to defeat many enemies in the game.
I'm really sad that this game turned out like this. I bought it at the earliest possible time and refunded it 33 minutes later. It has the capacity, it really does, to be one of the most fun games of the year with a little developer support. Or: an even better idea: Simply release the source code and let modders go wild.
TL;DR: Don't buy it yet. Wait for a price drop, developer support, or Steam workshop.

I'm not huge on the visual novel games, but I figured if I'm going to play one I should go all-out and get a pricier one, right? I had already seen the first series of Danganronpa, so I picked this up 'cause I wanted more. I was initially turned off by the price tag, for an extremely linear game with little in the way of replay value. Safe to say, though, I got my money's worth.
PROS:
- Story-driven, and it delivers. There were many times I caught myself exclaiming something out loud at certain parts of the story. I seriously didn't think I'd enjoy it as much as I did.
- If you're not cheating, the class trials actually do manage to pull out some difficulty, although there are times when the correct truth bullet-to-response doesn't QUITE make sense. Surprisingly (and fittingly) this game doesn't hold your hand. But you'll find class trials to be the real meat of the game, and they actually take a while to complete.
- Interesting characters.
CONS:
- Linear, weak replay value, the game modes that aren't the main storyline are just kinda boring.
- I didn't play on the hard difficulty, but in regular difficulty you practically don't need any of the skills you get from farming hope crystals or w/e they're called through building relationships between trials.
NEUTRAL:
- Pacing is slow at times, but this is probably intentional. The anticipation of the next exciting thing to happen will just build and build. Kind of standard anime fare.
- The voice acting is good, but there's not a whole lot of it. Only during the cutscenes do we hear full dialogue rather than a canned phrase. Still, at least it's there.
On the whole I recommend this to anyone looking to try something with fresh gameplay that's an emotional rollercoaster.

Watch My Second Game Video Here:
First off, this game is EPIC AWESOME so far people!  For anyone who played and loved "The Forest".. this game is a MUST-BUY for YOU!
For being in early access and on alpha right now at such an early state of development, this game is AMAZING!  The graphics and sounds are great, the controls work fluidly, and the game can straight up scare the heck out of you at night when you get the wrong creatures chasing you!
You start off the game watching yourself at an office birthday party and the news going off about how mysterious worm holes are taking people to some far off place.  Well, for you this is a great thing because it turns out that earth is being invaded by aliens.  The bad thing is now you will be all alone on a mysterious jungle like planet and will need to find a way to stay alive as you find clues and reports of what is happening back at home on the planet earth.
Now is where you get to actually control your character from the familiar first person perspective in these sandbox survival games.  You see around you a few broken pieces of your landing pod and a few items including a bag of chips, a instant food package, a box of grape juice, a lighter and most importantly a machete.  You'll need to pick all of these items up and hope for the best because you'll need it on this alien planet.
Using the machete will help you acquire recources you'll need to discover all of your craftable goods.  You'll need to find and collect resources to learn how to make items that use those resources in the recipe.  For example, all you need to make a spear is a stick and your machete, but you won't know how to make a spear until you'd cut down and collected a stick.  To make a house, you'll need to find and collect bamboo logs and large leaves and so forth.  To craft an item such as a tent or a house, once you know how to make it, simply click the craft icon even though you will not have all the needed components and place the framework or "plan".  It will stay where you have placed it and be glowing blue until you bring all the components to it and placed them onto it, at which point it will be a completed structure.  Use houses or tents either one to save your game progress with the V key when you are near it.
At this point, you cannot "sleep" and will usually spend the hours at night looking for items and resources needed to survive.  As with the usual survival game, water and food are critical to survive.
At night, you'll notice the beautiful fauna that grows in this world as well as a huge earth-like planet that rises over the horizon.  You may also here and see an alien space craft arive in one of the warmholes much like how you got here and this spacecraft will drop a green alien round pod that you may later find as you travel about.  Beware however that aliens will start populating this world and the longer you survive, the more challenging and populated your world could be with this very aggressive alien zombie-like creature!
Also threatening you are little ostrich like creatures that will definitely take the opportunity to peck you in your back if you aren't looking (I've had this happen a couple of times) ...and a huge very powerful orange wolf type creature.  Add to this the non stop threats of hunger, thirst, getting lost, and more and you have a very fun and addictive survival game that beckons you to come back long after you log out with its gorgeous graphics and glow-in-the-dark atmosphere.
This game may only be in early alpha, but it looks already to be a survival crafting sandbox game that any fan of such games shouldn't dare miss!

This game has most of the trappings of what would make a good game, but its overall incompetency, childish humor and EXTREME lack of content utterly kill any and all potential this had.
In essence it's a souls-esque roguelite, which sounds great on paper and an adequately executed game of that genre would probably be loads of fun, but this is not that.  It is CLEARLY trying to piggyback on the dark souls bandwagon with the tagline "SPOILERS: You'll probably die trying".  Unfortunately, this game is nowhere near as hard as dark souls and this tagline is nothing more than an attempt at baiting a desperate souls fan wanting more.
CONTENT
So theres permadeath, you wander aimlessly through a procedurally generated dungon that has FAR too few seeds and base layouts (I came across the same exact room AND enemy layout , in the same level, 4 times in roughly 5 minutes) and try and make it as far as possible (each playthrough consists of 8 levels).  There is a scant few number of "biomes" generated for each level, but you will mostly be dungeon crawling through a boring looking dungeon.  There are others like a swamp or a kind of scorched, rocky environment but you mostly get a blue tinted dungeon as your biome.  Based on what mind numbing tasks the game randomly throws at you (like drinking 5 potions, casting 5 spells, breaking 45 pots) you get a token.  These tokens are the "roguelike" element of the game, they are persist with you through death and different characters and you spend them to buy either game modifiers (of which you can only have 1 active) or different colored robes.  Yes, that is the entire motivation of the game, different colored robes.  You also get tokens based on the amount of gems (money) you accumulated over the course of your run once you die.  My first playthrough I made it to level 4 and got enough tokens to purchase the best and most expensive modifier in the game.  This took about an hour to accomplish, alone, on my first blind run through the game.
COMBAT
So we've tackled the lack of content and motivation to play the game, but at least the combat is good right?  No.  It's terrible.  Controls are EXACTLY like dark souls, but the mechanics are not.  You have a stamina meter that is used for attacks, like in the souls series, but using a special attack permanently lowers your stamina until you heal it back.  Again, a roguelike element, but one that is pointless.  It's not even a hindrance as you can easily find ways to replenish it, its just tedious.  Your dodge is anything but, it is simply an animation canceller.  But since it is a dodge, it consumes stamina, and the movement animations and mechanics in this game are so bare bones that it is FAR more efficient to just turn around and run away from an enemy's attack for a second than it is wasting stamina for an ineffectual dodge.  There is a small selection of weapon types, but it doesn't matter because they all swing exactly the same way, side to side (even the spear), all of their specials is just some twirly spin that ends up producing a shockwave around your character.  It COMPLETELY kills any and all motivation to find better loot.  In short, the combat in this game is a joke.
ETCETERA
So all that aside, how is the atmosphere/story of the game?  The story, too, is seeded from a very small selection of dialogue lines that the goofy, floating pyramind will ramble about.  Of course, there aren't any actual "characters" in the game, its more just a bedtime story that the pyramind is telling you, nebulous names and events that have literally 0 meaning.  Since it is randomly generated, there is no actual lore or over-arcing story to follow between playthroughs.  Throughout the dungeon you'll find randomy gibberish on the wall that the pyramid translates for you, quotes and clippings from the supposed story that is going on.  So again, they are trying to rip off the souls trope of telling the story through progression and discovery, but this is not what is actually going on.  These random quotes have a humor injected into them, a humor that seems as if it was written by the people who wrote that book about minecraft jokes, unironically.  Things like how one of the story characters power sources is cheese.  Give me a second, I have to wipe the tears from my eyes from that one, what a knee-slapper!
Considering the lack of content, terribly under-implemented combat system and lack of story with forced, childish humor at every turn, I would NEVER recommend this game.  Maybe if it was less than $10, go for it.  Until then, this is only fit for a <10 year old child who wants a souls game but can't handle one.

Nation Red is a good example of a simple gaming trope (top down arena shooter) well executed is all that’s really necessary to make a game fun and worth playing.
Basically if the idea of wading through waves and waves of 2 legged creatures of various sizes and shapes with different offensive capabilities while you take down as many as you can in the process sounds enticing... well it is quite enticing.
Lots of weapons and powerups to keep the action interesting and make you consider variables such as stopping power, depth of effect, range and reloading time to pick what suits your particular character class best. The perks system is very extensive and the variety of the combinations you can manage just serve to enhance the gameplay even further.
The game excels both in single player and multiplayer and you can even play local co-op with up to 4 players as long as you got enough gamepads to accommodate them. I have to say if you are a fan of classic arcade shooter action this game is one of the best values in gaming in my view. For those with competitive juices the varied leaderboards and achievements will serve as an impulse to replay the game to see just how much further you can survive and better your personal best in the different game categories.
If you like what you read so far just get it as soon as you can and enjoy it by yourself and with friends... repeatedly.

Essentially "Civilization" in space, but with more features. Highly recommended for anyone who enjoys turn based strategy.
Pros:
Takes many existing features from the Civilization series and improves upon them, then inserts into a space scify setting. No longer shall your units "bump" into each other only to have numbers subtracted from their health. The ability customize your fleet both in aesthetics and equipment is fantastic. This allows you to come up with a unique strategy or preference on how you wish to do battle. Although you can not control the ships during combat, being able to set the AI beforehand (during ship construction) adds a dynamic which makes observing your handiwork during the battle all the more rewarding (or dissapointing).
The planetary construction is fun and very strategic as well. In order to achieve a maximum result buildings must be placed in certain locations as each building provides a bonus to buildings on surrounding tiles. This, coupled with natural reources on the planet (which also provide bonus to surrounding tiles) makes designing your planet a fun experience rather than a chore.
The game is acually quite beautiful. The maps are not just static "space" there are nebulae and other such obstruction which add both a tactical and aesthetic value. Additionally, the actual space battles are quite fun to watch, with missiles, lasers and railgun fire I never get tired of viewing them.
Cons:
I wish planetary defense buildings had more of an effect. While invading a planet the attackers seem to have a huge upper hand.
The tutorial does not give a lot of information which I think is essential. After probably about 30 hours of gameplay I still can not figure out how the base production or research value of my planet is derived. Hovering over them gives no information other than what modifiers are effecting the base value. I should not have to go searching around the internet in order to determine how such an important value is determined. It is possible a missed something back in the tutorial but it is not overty apparent in game how this value is set.
Game still has some glitches. Although these usually do not interfere with the gameplay, it can be annoying. Most of them seem to be in the UI, but I have had a couple crashes to desktop. I am not sure yet if that is from the game or from my RAM issue (see below).
More "base" model ships to pick from would be great. When designing a ship there are only about 5 for each size category and some of them look very similar.
Notes:
This game requires more RAM than I had expected. I am currrently using 4gb of RAM on windows 8 and I have constant problems with freezing especially the longer the game goes on. Also important to note you CAN NOT play on the largest size maps without at least 6gb of RAM. It simply will not let you start the game. I highly recommend at least 8gb of RAM to take full advantage of the game.
Overall great game with lots of replayability! Also I have not tried mutiplayer yet so am unable to comment.

It's the second game of The Witcher Franchise.  The whole game mechanics and graphics have improve greatly compared to the first game. It's beautiful looking game with a strategic combat mechanics. Yes, as an RPG game, more of the Action RPG side, it have a quality storytelling campaign with a challenging combat. You have to learn how to time your combat rather than just go with a 'typical' mob mentality. It's hard at first but rewarding along the journey. Once you get the rhythm, it will be Dark Souls like kind of enjoyment out of fighting, especially if you ramp up the difficulty. But for people who just want to play it for the stories, just choose the lower difficulty. It's no shame on choosing it, cause you do have to strategise before you enter combat with potions etc.
Campaign wise, it's way wayy better that Witcher 1 for sure, and it's even have two seperate campaign after 1st chapter and its totally different set of environments/quests and you might want to replay the other side of the game later on (keep extra save games for that part). Both set line of quests offer a different agenda rather than just same old RPG style quest that make no different in the end. In Witcher 2, both side have their own agenda and it's up to you which one you like to explore. The sidequest also interesting and most of the time it's not requires too much time to be completed as it is near etc. So pick it up and enjoy the quest.
Along the way, you will be presented with a lot of choices in term of how your choices affect the game storylines. The result of some choices might appear straight away or only near the end of your journey.
You choose what you like, there's no definitive right or wrong. Most of the time, it's just a lesser of two evils ..... it's your choice.

Billed as the spiritual successor to 1996's The Neverhood, Armikrog for the most part follows through on that promise.
Despite being a point and click adventure game in the classic style, Armikrog makes a number of streamlines to the genre design. For starters, your movement is much faster than the plodding steps of the Neverhood, which makes backtracking relatively painless in this game. Inventory management is automatic, and you'll only be carrying three items at most at any time. The puzzles are pretty standard fare though, sticking to an approachable increasing difficulty structure, and they don't reach the esoteric variety that was present in Neverhood.
Playing with pen and paper is recommended. It's how Neverhood worked, and it adds a lot of fun to a playthrough to jot stuff down and reference your notes when doing puzzles. There are a number of pictographs scattered around the titular Armikrog so it's best to write them down.
Like Neverhood Armikrog's story is fairy slim, the most exposition you'll get is in the cheesy opening song. Unfortunately the lack of a proper finale event left me a little wanting for one last puzzle. Thankfully there's voice acting to flesh out the wider cast, and Tommynaut and Beak Beak make a very charming duo.
Armikrog works with a much wider range of materials than Neverhood's clay to shape it's enviornments, but unfortunately the difference in production value shows. There's no first person view segments, and the budget doesn't allow for a 6 minute long cutscene. This game was crowdfunded for just under a million dollars, but the cost of stop motion adds up, and the game cuts corners in a number of ways. That said finding an enviornmental detail that catches your eye or seeing one of the protagonist's numerous idle animations can bring a smile.
Terry Scott Taylor return to do the soundtrack, and while the ingame audio isn't as in-your-face as the iconic tunes from the Neverhood, some like the aforementioned intro theme of the game have a lot of charm.
Unfortunately this game had a troubled development. A number of delays and a not-great game design philosophy (hey, Earthworm Jim was panned for being a game developed by artists) hamper the initial release of the game. While my four hour playthrough was absent of any major issues, there were a number of minor visual flaws I noticed during my experience.
If you can justify paying the price tag for the stop motion visuals, Armikrog is a nice experience that stands in contrast to That Other Point and Click Revival Game.

It's a fun little game set in a dystopian future where the world is growing ever colder and so a company is selling fireplaces and a variety of items for you to buy and burn. It's a simple puzzle game where you place objects in the fireplace and lit them up and try to create combo's from the different reactions the toys have to fire and destruction.
You start with some coins which always gradually increase as you burn more and more and as you burn newer things and complete combo's you unlock more pages of items you can order and burn.
Along with this is an eerie storyline told through mail from your neighbour and others along with other little details about the world. The futility of the world growing colder and you and everyone's desperate attempts at trying to heat yourselves up is chilling.
So yeah, atmosphere is great. Gameplay is simplistic but fun and unique. The storyline is light but through its storytelling it doesn't need a heavy narrative.
Only problem I have with the game is that some of the combo's don't make a whole lot of a sense and forced me to use a wiki to cheat. Other than that I love this gem.

Little Inferno is a game about fire and friendship. Capitalism and closure. It is a game that talks about topics it has seemingly little knowing about. The gist is you play as a person. Like every person in the ever-snowy city this game is set in, you use your Little Inferno Entertainment Fireplace to keep yourself warm and happy. Of course, there's more than that in the plot, including a surprisingly emotional gut punch, but I'm not going to spoil it for you.
The gameplay consists of you buying items from a catalog, and then burning the items so you can get money to buy more items to burn. It can be surprisingly addictive, thanks to the beautiful and humorous animations that accompany the burning items. The game looks very good, with an art style akin to World of Goo that feels friendly and sinister at the same time. The game also runs well even on a potato computer such as my own, though there was some slowdown when I burned too many things at once.
The game is easy to reccomend, and although there is not a lot of replay value the game is a very well designed, 4-7 hour experience that is worth the money.

It took me quite some time to get into RF2.  As a matter of fact, it took me walking away and trying Assetto Corsa and Project Cars in order to come back to RF2 and appreciate it for what it was.  I watched a bunch of Youtube reviews and I think that Empty Box has it right.  For some of us, the eye candy only goes so far.  Once you're in the thick of it none of that matters.  What matters is how the car feels.  Can you connect with it via your steering wheel?  For me, that's a YES!  HELL YES!  I'm not fast, I'm no alien.  But within my skill level, I like to think I drive cars to or close to their limits (even if that ends up being slow).
This is a simulation that forces you to do some work.  Some that do not take this into consideration become frustrated.  I love it.  I've done a bit of real life racing and I've been involved as a helper on a few amateur teams.  It takes a lot of work by all involved.  So, I don't mind it.  I like it.  I like that car setup is greatly influenced by driving style.  If you run this sim like a sim you'll soon realize that, if you suck at driving like me, you'll need to fine tune the balance of the car to make up for it.  You have to warm up your tires.  You'll want to adjust your gearing.  The preload can be important.  On cars like the Celica GTO you'll have to adjust the front and rear downforce devices.  Brake bias is for real...
Force feedback, to me, is phenomenal.  The FF transmits enough information for you to know what the tires are doing front and rear.  It's weird... in a good way.  You can sense when a car's rearend is breaking loose and coming around.  The tire model is sick.  Seriously, deformation, damage, deflection, They are truly dynamic.  Temperature and pressure are a huge deal.  Nothing, NOTHING is better, to me, than the dynamic weather and track system.  The racing line gets stickier as cars deposit more and more rubber as the race progresses, the marbles gather off the line.  In the rain, the racing line becomes dryer and off line you're in standing water.  Track temperatures change similarly.  Weather changes dynamically and it affects everything.  Your perfect setup isn't so perfect when the temp drops/rises, when the rain drops and stops, etc.
There's so much to this game... if you're into simulation.  If not, there are other great titles out there.  Personally, I spend most of my time in RF2.  Assetto Corsa is another one of the titles I own and like.  It has its merits, for sure.  The eye candy is top notch.  The damage simulation, especially to mechanical systems is great.  But there's something canned (scripted) about the handling of the cars.  I can't put my finger on it.
Addendum: I race offline a lot because of time restrictions... the AI is pretty good on most tracks.  Compared to Project Cars it is great.  Second to RF2 is Assetto Corsa.  The AI is decent at overtaking, defending, etc.  I don't usually get crashed out by the AI.

I feel like this is the game I've always dreamed about. Think about Civilization, made by the creators of Crusader Kings II and Europa Universalis IV, with a slice of Distant Worlds and Galactic Civilizations. It pretty much sums up this game for me.
Pros
+ Each race is unique. I don't think I've ever met two of the same species on my three playthroughs. Some aren't even advanced and live in, for example, Medieval or Industrial age.
+ Research is fun and a bit random. I heard the perfect description for the research system of this game: You have a deck of cards and when you select your research, you pick three cards from that deck. You aren't guaranteed to get those thrusters next time since you picked improved mines now, so you might have to improvise if you needed those thrusters.
+ Traits. You aren't bound by them for the rest of the game. So you can be really weak but fear not, you can modify your species after a specific tech.
+ Events aren't always the same. Depending on your policital traits and/or biological traits, the events can be different, the lore can be seen in different perspectives and you may get additional choices on some events.
+ Design your own ships. This isn't anything new to space games but this one just seems like it was done so incredibly right. You can pick which front, back and middle section you want for your ship, creating some very good looking ships that can blast your rivals back to stone age.
+ Game looks beautiful. The stars, the aliens, the event pictures, they all looks so gorgeous.
Neutrals
+/- Victory conditions. I've never made it that far in the game yet but the two victories is either destroy everyone or take their planets. Seems a bit dull but personally, I tend to play this game like a game of EUIV, it just goes on until it doesn't, there's no actual victory.
+/- Alien wars. I don't know if it's just on my playthroughs but none of the aliens seem to fight against one another. There are a bunch of wars going on on the other side of the galaxy but my neighbourhood is just races insulting everyone else living near them or forming alliances with each other.
Cons
- War goals are a bit lacking in my opinion. I haven't had much experience in declaring wars but I've only seen three war goals: Vassalize, take a planet or release a planet. I don't want to release a planet nor do I want it, I'm an ocean type, you guys are arid type. And I really don't want to keep a fleet around your worlds just to pacify you if you decide to rebel.
- Depending on your start, you might not have any minerals or energy for you to work with, only option is to expand early on which might crush your economy. But this isn't really the games fault, you just had a really bad start. So not an actual con.
I'd say this game is easily 9/10, I highly recommend this game to anyone who even thinks they might enjoy this.

ABZU at its best is a breathtaking visual experience. At its worst, it is a visual accompaniment to Austin Wintory's swelling and wondrous score, which isn't at all a bad thing. At times I wished the game's underwater world was a bit more interactive, but ultimately the game doesn't seem interested in this so I can't really fault it for that. Where ABZU feels shallow is in its story. The game's environmental storytelling is great, but the apparent story presented explicitly to the player feels a bit formless early on. I felt like I was simply moving from one environment to the next. Of course, I was in awe of the game and one can draw their own conclusions about this section, but it's the only weak spot I can think of. The second half of the game resolves this issue with a few firmer emotional beats and an exhilarating conclusion that left me stunned. Ultimately I was really pleased with the game.

Game Title : Final Fantasy 7

Genre: RPG / Turn Based / Not turn based you can turn if off.
I first started playing Final Fantasy 7 when I was 8 years old. I loved everything about it the world, people and music amazing. This game was my first RPG and really set the bar for others. If you ever read about why Square has not made a remake they state it is because and I quote here. "CEO Yoichi Wada said that a remake of Final Fantasy VII will happen once the company makes a new Final Fantasy title that succeeds the seventh game in terms of quality and sales, something the company has to date failed to do". Think about that for a mintue this game was made in 1997 almost 20 years later no other game they made has yet to top it...
Story: This game is set on earth in another place and time. A place where the planets very blood "The lifestream" discovered by a company called Shinra, INC. Shinra found a way to turn lifestream into a power source and built reactors all around the world sucking up the lifesteam and killing the planet. You are Cloud Strife "mercerany" hired by your old childhood friend Tifa to help her and AVALANCHE put a stop to it... this story unfolds into an epic tale of love that puts the very life of the planet in your hands.
Game play: The gameplay is smooth and seemless you always know what you need to do next. If you ever get stuck there are many guides that will help you figure it all out.  Battling enemies is fun you can make it turn based, or set it to active (no turns) for a greater challenge. There are many very fun and challanging mini game series in this game. A motorcycle challenge, submarine battles, snowboarding, and a few others. This game supports controllers I played the whole game with a Xbox 360 controller.
Graphics: For the time period 1997 the graphics were soild the few in game movies have really nice graphics. Otherwise it's mostly blocky textures. There are graphics mods out that give the game a more updated feel. They are hard to install but, pay off if you get them to work.
Audio: The music now updated is very nice! One of the only games where I used to play it just to listen to it.
Overall: It has everything a rpg fan loves. A great story with wonderful music, the people all have backgrounds your can really get into. There are many side quests and challenges. You can't forget the Chocobos everyone loves those for dinner... I mean to race them.

Necropolis wears its Dark Souls inspiration on its sleeve and tries to pull from a few different rogue-like games that are popular for inspiration while keeping its main inspiration Dark Souls.
Descriptions for weapons and items are extremely vague. While the weapons actually have stats, they are never explicitly said to you and can only be implied from the description and comparison against other weapons, which really leaves you guessing as to what weapon you have is actually worth keeping. Generally speaking, the bigger one so you can knock down enemies.
You wouldn't guess it from the style, but the game actually has a sense of humor. A giant illuminati pyramid constantly heckles and makes snide remarks while you explore the game, which aren't so frequent that they truly become grating, but do happen a few times per floor. There are also writings all over the walls where random names and deeds are described often ending with some sort of unexpected twist at the end, again, not really grating since you can ignore the writings, but the joke wears itself thin quickly. I can say that the main thing I actually like about the comedy is just that it means the game doesn't take itself too seriously, even though its art definitely implies it would.
Crafting also is included in the game, you can pick up ingredients from slain enemies and make potions or meat rations from them. The feature doesn't feel bad, but it really doesn't feel necessary, since enemies constantly drop potions and rations anyway, and it just sort of feels like its there just to be there where the items you gain from it could honestly just be added into the pool of drops more than they already are without it really taking anything away from the game. It's not a pain and during the early game it does have moments where you need to stop and make some rations which changes the pace for just a bit and is not entirely unwelcome, but it just doesn't really add anything.
Combat in the game can be tense like in Dark Souls, but it really doesn't happen all that often, especially if you're playing with friends. At its core, it feels vaguely familiar and is fun, early game struggles can be real intense, but as soon as you get ahold of a weapon that can knock enemies down or stun-lock them, it really stops being a challenge. I hate to say it as someone who loves playing as rogues and hit-and-run type fighters, but heavier weapons are just objectively better in this game. If you have a sword or hammer that can knock down an enemy in the first swing, as long you have a vague sense of timing, you can just make enemies trivial more than threatening.
Multiplayer feels polished, I am an American and was primarily playing with a friend in Finland and we had very little lag betwen us, even with my internet generally being pretty sub-par. The game becomes drastically easier than it already was with someone to help you, though; one friend kites enemies around while the other uses the knock-down method I explained earlier. If one of you gets downed, the other can revive you within a certain amount of time, otherwise you die and lose all of your items, levels and armor. That doesn't sound like a big deal since you did come here to play a rogue-like, after all, but since it respawns you so you can continue playing with your friend, really it just turns you into dead weight until you can feed off his scraps for long enough to actually be in fighting condition. A huge point that I am just now getting to is that you deal damage to your friends, your wide swings can easily kill your friend if fighting in close quarters and it's certainly an odd choice, you end up trying to divide your battles into two small skirmishes where you can and rarely engage the same enemy at once. I'm not saying it's a bad choice, I'm sure the developers could give me a pretty good reason, but it was just obnoxious at times.
Honestly speaking, this game isn't great, and I can't actually recommend it in its current state. It certainly feels done, and it has all the atmosphere and polish it could really hope to achieve, truly. The problem with the game simply comes from a lack of really refining what it wants to be, in my opinion. I honestly believe a few big updates could turn it into an amazing game, it's got so much lined up correctly that it could be saved from mediocrity and I believe Harebrained Schemes could probably figure it out, given time. Do I like the game? Yes, I'm actually going to continue playing even though it has its flaws, but I won't be trying to talk any of my other friends into picking it up anytime soon.

Galactic Civilizations 3 feels like its in beta, because it haves so many game changing glitches. They introduced some new mechanics, removed others and held others from Galactic Civilizations 2.
Here is some problems I found that makes the gameplay loses its immersion:
- A.I. in war with each other just stand next to each other making some attacks 50 by 50 turns.
I had Drengin and Marauders fighting each other in my territory for over 100 turns and each one of them had 4 fleets staring at each other but they just don't attacked each other.
- Alliances doesn't matter anymore. That's right! One of the funniest things in GalCiv 2 doesn't work anymore. If you are allied with someone and other faction declares war with you, too bad, your allies don't care at all. In GalCiv 2 when someone declares war at one of your allies you have only 2 options: Declare war on the attacker or break alliance.
- Battle view is broken, if you choose to watch a battle of your fleet, you watch it with 1 result then it justs do a quick battle after and with a completely different result and that counts, the previous one don't.
- The A.I. declares a war or ends a war randomly. The events dont have any connection at all when its between A.I and A.I.
- The United Planets... God its annoying. They propose the same thing over and over and over again. With 20 united planets meetings in my playthrough 11 of them was to propose the same festival (10% morale bonus all races), 6 to elect the chair race (and my race was not mentioned ever), 1 to end all wars, and 2 to other random events.
Here is some new mechanics in GalCiv 3:
- You now have a territory, not just that old influence territory, now other races haves to negotiate an Open Borders treat with you to legally stay in your territory. And if you refuse? They just stay anyway and you receive a spam message in your notifications inbox EVERY SINGLE TURN, and you don't have a way to disable it. And if you enter another race territory without permission they starts to dislike you.
- Your planets now have a "standby" mode. You can choose to increase economic, research or influence by 5%. If you don't know this the game just don't let you pass the turn, you have to google it to learn and continue your playthrough.
- Now when you have an Idle colony, ship, shipyard or just finished a research, your "pass turn" button turno into idle
colony, ship etc. The weird part is that you have to set the ship to explore, survey or guard to ignore it.
Here is some improvements from GalCiv 2:
- Graphics.
- Sounds.
- The grid(map). It's the most beautiful grid I've ever seen in a turn based game, and you can rotate, zoom, move however you like. Awesome!
- Instead of building ships in a planet now you have to build shipyards that stands in space. You have the option to unanchor it and move it 1 square each turn but the farthest from the sponsors planet the slowest you build. And you can have more than one planet sponsoring each shipyard, which is very nice.
- Custom races: You can now choose more details of your custom race, it helps when you decide to play against them. You can even change the images of the race.
- The ideology tree and ideology points are much better now. There are powerful ideology skills to choose from.
I don't recommend the game. I bought it with 50% discount and I regret it. Just buy Galactic Civilizations 2 Complete instead, you will have much more fun. Maybe I will play this game next year to see if some glitches have been patched.
