I bought Dust on impulse when I first saw it on the main store page. It was on sale, and I didn't know a single thing about it, but after looking at a few videos I was convinced. And I don't regret getting this game, not for a single minute.
Dust follows the tale of an anthropomorphic (rabbit, wolf, something?) named Dust who wakes up without his memory in a beautiful field (emphasis on beautiful, but I'll get to the graphics later). He is approached by a sword called Ahrah, one of the Blades of Elysium, who tells him that he has summoned the magic sword for unknown reasons. Ahrah is closely followed by a little nimbat named Fidget, who is guardian to the sword and has chased it down to where it followed Dust. The blade does not have many answers for the confused Dust, but promises to accompany him as he attempts to recover his memory, along with the irritated Fidget. Now, the story is rather generic. Main character wakes up with amnesia. Check. Magic Sword. Check. Quest for oneself. Check. But the story is far from dull. No spoilers, but there are a surprising amount of emotional moments in this game. The morals behind these are simple but effective when paired with the main and side characters. The game is split into 5 chapters, each with its own story to experience, and all filled with sorrow and hatred.
Dust himself is a functional protagonist. His past is a important yet at the same time unimportant part of him. I would think that Fidget would just be an annoying complaining partner, but she always made me smile and laugh at her terrible jokes. She's not just comedic relief, though; Dust would not have gotten anywhere if it weren't for Fidget's advice. I won't say anything about the other characters for now, but they're certainly not to be forgotten.
Now for the graphics. First of all, the environments are
! To think that they were designed by one man is an amazing feat. Every detail seems purposeful and neat. Dust and his enemies' animations look fluid and clean, and combat flows very easily. The one downside I can think of is in the character design. I really like the idea of anthro characters, but I wish that they weren't designed in such a cartoony style with large eyes and anime hair.
The voice acting is solid by most of the performers, especially in the case of Dust. I can't imagine him (or Fidget) with another voice. Fidget's voice was especially effective during the sad moments. Well, everything about Fidget is great.
The background music is good at creating an atmosphere, from the deep echoing of Cirromon Caverns to the hectic Boss themes. The sound effects, especially during combat, give a nice solid feel to your movement and sword swinging combos.
As an action platformer, Dust sure satisfied. The combat is fast and often takes to the air with a whirl of blades, slicing the enemy and slamming them into the ground. The combos that you can perform are good, but my main complaint with combat is that there is not a huge variety in moves. Fidget is able to assist you with a projectile, but there are only 3 different ones to obtain. In combat, Dust is a glass cannon. He deals out death in the blink of an eye, but cannot take many hits himself. This was especially evident on the harder difficulties, and I felt that Hardcore presented a very nice challenge. Experience is gained by killing enemies and, more importantly, racking up large combos. Getting a high hit count without taking damage will give you a nice experience bonus, eventually leading to a level up. Upon leveling up you get a skill gem, which you can use to raise either Health, Attack, Defense, or Fidget (Her projectile strength). I felt that the leveling curve throughout was well planned, and I only had to do a bit of grinding on Hardcore in order to continue through. Aside from the occasional item, enemies will also drop money that you can use to buy healing items, equipment, and other tools from the mysterious reptilian merchants that have set up tent throughout the land. Another way to get equipment is by crafting it using materials dropped by enemies and following a set of blueprints. This is a helpful way to create armor, but I feel like it was rather limited. The only other complaint I have about the combat is that the bosses were surprisingly easy, and this was a bit of a disappointment. As for the puzzles and platforming, neither were particularly difficult, but they were a nice break from the action. Dust's movement is a little slippery, which sometimes led the platforming to be just as tense as a difficult fight, but his traction is far from Luigi levels of slipperiness.
All in all, there's no reason I can think of to not get this game. On the first time that I played through it, Dust was almost magical to me; I had a dumb smile on my face whenever the story wasn't taking a tragic turn and I can't think of many times when I've enjoyed a game as much. I can never get that first experience back, but I will continue to play this game and enjoy it for as long as I can. And if there is a sequel, you can bet I'll be getting it on day one.

Listen Necropolis, I'm not mad at you, I'm just disappointed.
Necropolis is a good game, don't get me wrong, I enjoyed every last minute of the very few minutes it actually provides you. This game has two beaming problems, and thats difficulty and play time.
Difficulty: Now, this game advertised itself based on it's difficulty, claiming you would die regardless of you abilities, as death is unavoidable. They lied. This game feels like it's fixed on easy difficulty, but like Dark Souls, the franchise it used as the main game it compared itself to, there is no difficulty setting. I breezed through the game, I only ever died once and that was within the first room of my first run because my controller gave out. I have to say, I feel a bit ripped off. If they made this game as hard as they advertised, they could have easily passed off the immense lack of content as death would extend how long it would take you to succeed.
Game length: To short. Under most circumstances, I won't base a game on it's longevity because really it's not about that. If a game is more symbolic and story driven, I could give less of a crap how long it is. But this game isn't about the story, the most you ever get story wise are some ancient lore scrawling on the walls. No, this game is about the gameplay and the combat, two things you need to delve into over time. The devs, in my opinion, did great with the gameplay and combat. Controls were smooth, hit boxes were accurate, and dodging was perfect. Problem is, you barely get to play with the amazing combat because the game ends you off with a disappointing clunky boss fight at the end of 10, short, repetitive floors. Rougelikes are intended to be completed over multiple runs, you're supposed to learn and unlock new things as you go so you can get further the next run. This game, paired with it's easy difficulty, is just way to short.
I mean for gods sake, I beat this game on my first try. Thats really unacceptable in any game, let alone a rougelike that prides itself on difficulty.
The devs will likely be updating the game, fleshing it out with more content over time, but as it stands right now the game earns itself a negative review from me.

NECROPOLIS is a Souls-like rogue-lite where you fight knights that strike with spite and dogs that bite with might.
NECROPOLIS is a game that I
want to like, but a lack of consistency and polish holds me back from giving it a positive review. It does feel like the game was designed for co-op in mind, with the single-player coming second - as a result, the solo experience feels rough and lacks any unique rogue-lite elements. It is by no means a terrible game, but it isn't a very good one.
There are several aspects of NECROPOLIS that really bring the title down as a whole. Fighting enemies in the game can feel very finicky sometimes, with odd inconsistencies with hitboxes and framerates. This is especially apparent in later floors where hostiles get tougher and spawns become more sporadic. In addition, the enemy AI is dubious at best; sometimes hostiles will get caught on different assets in a room pathing towards a player, or completely lose aggro mid-combat. In addition, a mediocre sound design makes the combat feel weaker than it should be. Specifically in solo play, permadeath is extremely punishing in NECROPOLIS; a player dying in later floors can make each run feel like a big waste of time, and collected items don't carry over in any way between runs.
Some of NECROPOLIS' ideas sound great in theory, but are a mixed bag in practice. There is not enough variety in the items that can be purchased with tokens (currency that carries over across all runs); items that you
buy don't feel worth the tokens due to ambiguity with lore. Speaking of which, the lore in the game does add a nice touch of humour, but there are times where it feels there's too much of it; all of the items in the game exchange stats for story, giving the player no practical information about an item whatsoever. In terms of aesthetics, some of the rooms are surprisingly breath-taking and intricate in design, while others are needlessly wide and very bland. Several enemies can backspawn a player mid-combat, a feature which works in co-op, but is extremely punishing in solo play.
With all that being said, there are things to like about NECROPOLIS. Co-op is easily the best aspect of the game. A surprising amount of communication and tactics are required when fighting hostiles, thanks to the addition of friendly fire. Diplomacy over new items and sharing needed resources is exciting and engaging. To touch on some of the other pluses, the combat does a fair job of emulating Souls-style combat, and it's fairly easy to get into. In addition, the overall aesthetic of the game is very different and appealing, with some of the environments and enemy design pleasantly fantastical and bizarre.
Overall, while NECROPOLIS ambitious, it is not worthy of a $30 price tag - especially if you are planning on playing it solo. Players will get the most value out of it with a group of friends. While it does a fair job of emulating Souls-style combat, as a rogue-lite, it doesn't feel very complete for a game classifying itself in that genre.

If I had to sum up Stellaris in one word, it would be "Epic". This is Paradox grand strategy mixed with traditional 4X, mixed again with the story elements of Alpha Centauri, with a little randomness thrown in for good measure. If you found Gal Civ 3 to be lacking in some way, or maybe just a little too shallow, you should definitely give Stellaris a shot. If you're hesitating because you've tried Crusader Kings or EU in the past and found the learning curve to be too steep to get into things, you should know that Paradox has done a much better job crafting tutorials and "special project" missions to help guide you in. All in all, I strongly recommend giving Stellaris a try if you're a fan of the genre.

I wish there was a "I kinda recommend this game" button, because I am about to go on a mega rant about what a masterpiece this game could be, and what a disappointment it is. This game goes at the top of my "Games with the Most Potential That Fell Short Ever" list. This game combines the art style I love, primarily feeling like Journey, the fighting style I like, with my multiple play throughs of Dark Souls 3, and the entire idea of Rogue-likes, with my love of Binding of Isaac. Like every other review out there, though, I will agree, this game NEEDS work INSANELY bad, and here's why.
1. It gets repetitive. And I'm not going to whine like everyone else about the floor lay outs, because in other Roguelikes I see the same rooms 20+ times in one run, and in this, even if it is the same room lay out, somethings are moved and enemies are MAYBE different. I'm, not going to make that a primary complaint. The enemies,though,  simply get more health per floor, and a few more new ones are introduced on each floor. This is the same with armor and weapons. But the variety is truly not there. The enemies are recolored and given a slightly different weapons. The weapons are reskinned clones of another weapon with different particle effects and the same exact move set and it doesn't need to be that way. And oh my god the off-hand weapons are absolutely awful. The ONE OFF HAND WAND IN GAME, takes like 62 attacks to kill the most basic enemy. The off-hand weapons need to change. Maybe add dual wielding or buff the off-hand weapons or something. It is so awful only using a shield all game. Also, THERE ARE NO BOSSES. Sure, at first I was optimistic after reading that. "Maybe the enemy variety and the fact that some of them may be like mini bosses will make up for that". No. It doesn't. Bosses would seriously add, and this isn't an exaggeration, %100 more content in my opinion. Bosses are what make rogue likes like Binding of Issac and RPGs like Dark Souls flavorful and worth pushing through. They're fun and interesting, and I really feel like Harebrained Schemes can very easily find a way to add bosses in this game.
2. The tone. For some ridiculous reason, this game has WAY to much out of place and painfully bad "humor" to it. I love the mysterious vibe, I love the confusion and discovery vibe. When I see this art style, I think artistic and mysterious, seeing as it clicks to me to match Journey. But, Harebrained Schemes did NOT need to bring humor into this. The giant all knowing being feeling like an awful knock off of Handsome Jack from Borderlands, with about 1/1000th of the likeableness absolutely hurts. The mysterious "codexes" and the items and food and weapons and shields and and wall notes and floor notes and just EVERYTHING. They tried adding humor to ALL of it, and it entirely does not fit this style of game they were going for and it is almost uncomfortable how much it doesn't sync with the feel I get from this art style and gameplay style. I don't know how, but it's got to go. Completely.
3. The difficulty is ENTIRELY non-existent. The enemies aren't scary unless they're in a massive blob, and even then, just block and they'll kill each other. No time in this game have I truly felt that something was difficult, unless I was presented with 15+ enemies. That's not Rogue-like esque, that's more dungeon crawler-y. Honestly, the first time I played this game was with a friend, and we COMPLETED it on our very first try. And the "Final Boss" (spoiler alert) is a kind-of bigish slow moving guy that is literally so easy to kill in co-op, it's unbelievable. My first run of this game ever. Beat it. That's not rogue-like at all. I've died seriously 1000s of times in Binding of Isaac, so why not in this. Buff everything, I want to die and get frustrated and get SO PUMPED FOR MY NEXT RUN I can't handle it and I skip work and class to do it.
3.5. A side note to add on to that difficulty, is the fact that the crafting system is GARBAGE, healing is slow and clunky, your stamina is drained INSANELY FAST, but still doens't make this game hard, and the constant need to make and eat and make and eat is the only reason this game can take longer than an hour to eat. I want to record a play through and see how many times I have to; Stop. Make food. Eat food. Make food. Make food. Make food. Then move on. It's insane and awful and needs to change. If you've ever played Journey on PS3/PS4, you'll know what to expect going into this game. It's short, it's stunningly beautiful, and the gameplay is simple and meditative.
Exploring these underwater seascapes never becomes frustrating or boring thanks to subtle environmental cues, which highlight points of interest and various objectives in creative ways; like using contrasting color pallettes to guide you in the right direction, or showing schools of fish travelling towards a mysterious cave, or swarming around a magical pool that leads you to your next destination. It's a natural and organic feeling of progression, and I wouldn't be surprised if ABZU was used to demonstrate these videogame design methods in an actual classroom.
Did I mention how ♥♥♥♥ing beautiful this game looks?
Playing this game becomes a near-religious experience thanks to gorgeous, fantastic, stunning, not-enough-synonyms-to-describe visuals, and you'll be tempted to screencap everything in sight. It's eye candy on a massive scale, and I won't soon forget how awe-struck I felt while taking it all in. You'll definitely want to show this game to friends and family who can appreciate just how jaw-droppingly beautiful it is, not only as a videogame, but as a true work of art.
The game's length is probably its weakest asset, clocking in at just under a couple of hours for your standard playthrough.
Twenty dollars might be somewhat steep, but I would argue that this game's value shouldn't be judged on length or replay incentives, but on the solid foundation of it's stellar art design, setpieces, environmental design, and pacing. It's not often that a game manages to nail every one of these aspects, and further padding the game with meaningless objectives would've only lessened it's overall impact.
ABZU won't satisfy players who are looking for more involved or detail-oriented gameplay, but almost anyone will be able appreciate the game for what it delivers artistically (in spades) through it's focused, direct approach to creating an unforgettable journey with a minimal degree of interaction. This is an absolute must-play for PC gamers, and I can't recommend it highly enough.

A decent update to Galactic Civilizations 2, but could have been more. Wait for a few more patches for Stardock to bring in some of the more recent features to the 4X genre and it would be a lot better.
GalCiv 3 is basically a prettier GalCiv 2 with some new stuff added in and some old stuff taken out. The mainstay races (Terran, Drengin, Iconian) are still here, and some are out (Arceans). The system for building planets is improved, with adjacency bonuses on planet improvements further encouraging specialization. The shipbuilding process is for the most part better, since ships are now built in a shipyard (basically a non-improvable starbase that builds ships) that is fed by production from up to 5 worlds. The combat system and the tech tree are more or less the same from GalCiv 2. Minor races are out (at least for now). The diplomatic system is still as good as GalCiv 2. The map now uses hexes instead of squares. And the ship designer is still as good as it was.
If GalCiv 3 is to be judged on its own, I'd say it was a competent sequel. Some of the changes I like (planet improvements, shipyards), some I dont (lack of minor races). The game doesn't crash and its enjoyable to play.
The problem is that Endless Space and Distant Worlds: Universe exist. These games have added features to the 4X genre that I just can't imagine being left out anymore. Though Endless Space stole A LOT of ideas from GalCiv 2, it added several good ones of its own (adding player input during starship combat, planet and ship leaders that gain XP and have skill trees). Distant Worlds: Universe is the master of selective automation. You can choose to control only the aspects of your empire you want to control, and the AI will competently take care of the rest (at least most of the time). There are also race-specific branches in the tech tree, which really do change how to select techs when you play those races.
GalCiv 3 could have benefited a lot by taking some of these features.  Selecting strategies during combat would make it worth watching the space battles, and ship leaders make your fleets more than just a collection of ships. Automation becomes almost essential in the late stages on even a moderate sized map. No, I don't want to manually select the upgrades for all of my 30 starbases. Yes I would like to be able to say "Build me 10 battleships, 5 carriers and 10 escorts in the fastest possible time and move them here" instead of manually selecting the shipyards and setting up their build queue. I would like to be able to say, "Here, take control of these boring garrison fleets and patrol the homefront while I take the Kickass Fleet of Awesomeness to pound the Drengin to dust."
GalCiv 3 is still a good game and I would recommend it, but it could be so much better with the addition of several features from more recent 4X games.

Little Inferno is a game that cannot be played seriously. Most games with this attribute are like this because they are some combination of light and silly and are a good for bringing a smile to one's face. Little Inferno is that, but it also turns anyone who tries to play it seriously into the butt of a joke. This game has no qualms making fun of anyone who tries to finish it, whether because the player is a perfectionist or intrigued by the vague, ultimately unrewarding story (non-specific spoiler: the plot's big punchline is gamers should go outside more often).
The problem with this game's approach is that this is actually one of the better implementations of this type of casual game - the "object combination" genre, for lack of a better term. The art style and sound design make the game's quirky sensibility aesthetically appealing. The game gives just enough hints that most of the combinations should be solvable (at least enough to reach the ending). One of the game's biggest satirical points - requiring a special currency (stamps) to speed up the delivery of packages containing items to combine - actually forces players to think about the object combinations rather than turning the game into a click-fest.
Mechanically, the only complaint is that there are still a few combinations that will require some trial-and-error to discover. I figured out about 90% of them on my own. I was glad I looked up the solutions to the final 10% as some of them I would have never figured out (and doubt anyone else would either).
Ultimately, I can't recommend this game because the experience is just too vapid. Instead of taking the genre and making the best game possible with it, the developers seized the opportunity to make a satirical point about how simple casual games can be turned into psychology manipulators. I appreciate the point of Ian Bogost's Cow Clicker Facebook game, but that doesn't mean that I ever had any desire to play it. By actually delivering a product somewhat resembling a quality game, the developers of Little Inferno ultimately delivered a game where both the message and experience is watered-down, if not extinguished.

I'll be completely honest, at first I was coming to the game thinking that I would have a good laugh at an Overwatch ripoff, then uninstall it (I know that since Paladins came out first, it's more complicated than that, but that's what I was expecting nonetheless). And though there are some uncanny similarities that force us to compare the two games, and though Paladins doesn't quite have the production value that a Blizzard game can have...I actually have more fun with Paladins than I do with Overwatch. And I kind of LOVE that game.
---
Presentation:
I think the art direction is bit all over the place. I'm happy to see that colorful shooters are not going away since TF2 and I think the maps look pretty neat. But as far as coherence goes, the cast of characters is kind of a mess. I find some of the characters to be plain ugly (like Willo), some pretty random/uninspired (like Skye, Viktor or Barik), while I really like some other designs (Evie, Cassie, Mal'Damba or Inara); in that regard it is subjective though. Still, the juxtaposition doesn't work as well as in Overwatch, or Battleborn. You have a dragon with a jetpack, a pixie, a gobelin in a modern robot suit, sort of a vodoo sorcerer etc. It's not plain and simple bad, far from that, but there is a lack of cohesion in terms of lore/universe. Plus, and this is where the nature of the game itself (a f2p competitor to Overwatch) starts to be a problem: a lot of characters are sort-of-Overwatch-characters. You have sort-of-Dva, sort-of-Torbjorn, sort-of-Reaper, sort-of-Soldier etc. Because of that the game can feel really derivative -unfairly admittedly since the game released prior to Overwatch. Which is too bad because, there still is a lot of little touches given to the animations, the voices (especially the voices) and the look of the heroes that bring personality to these archetypes that feel taken straight from Blizzard's FPS, if you played that one first. It's good, but it's just not always enough to make it a really polished art direction.
The music is equally in that sort-of-Overwatch vibe. It's good, it works ingame and in the menus, but it's nothing special. The sound design on the other hand is actually pretty good. I think the game telegraphs well most of the threats. The sound feedback is simple, functionnal, sometimes funny (when it comes to ultimate especially). The weapon noises are super satisfying. It's snappy and helps selling the weapon you are using. I think the only minute gripe that I have is with the noise when standing on objective or pushing a payload; there is a sound everytime you gain some points, and if you stay next to a payload, you are gaining points continuously and hearing the same noise on repeat. And it can be a bit annoying.
---
Gameplay:
What about the meat of the game then? Well, again, it can feel derivative, you can't really argue on that. Even if not all the OverwatchPaladins-characters lookalike have the exact same role, and play the exact same way, some can really feel like conterfeits if you played Overwatch first. Ruckus, Drogoz, Fernando (<3) and Barik are almost copy-paste in terms of gameplay, with similar habilities and roles. And if you've played tens (if not hundreds) of hours of Overwatch, this can either be a good thing (you're not lost) or a bad thing (it doesn't feel fresh). But thankfully a couple of characters are pretty unique in terms of gameplay and ultimate. And more importantly, the pacing, the level-design and overall game-design can set the game apart enough, in a good way. I'd say that from what I feel most characters have a really decent DPS. You can help a great deal in terms of dammage, even with a healer. Meaning, if you like a character's look or way of moving, chances are you are not going to be yelled at if you chose it at the beginning of the game.
To be clearer, it feels like you are supposed to have a balance in your team (it works best with at least 1 tank, and 1 heal/support as it should)  but that no matter who you pick in each categories, you can help with her/him/it. There are some combos and counters, but you can do a decent job with the character you like. This makes the game easier to pick up and play, without sacrificing the strategy. And it's less of a guilt trip when you are playing your main despite a composition that would benefit more from another character in the same category as your main.
The level-design also participate in making the game more of a quick fun (even more than Overwatch that is to say). The maps are smaller and work around a center (or lign) of symetry. Both camps are mostly mirrors of what the other team have, with a couple of little differences. The main mode, the one I played the most so far, starts with a king of the hill and segways into an escort the payload. So for each match, each team can be on attack or defense depending on how well it performs on the king of the hill part of the match. All this makes for mostly quick matches (15 mins) and sometimes really short (6-7 mins) and rarely really long (+20 mins).
So more DPS/bit-less disparities between characters (still all unique but more in movement and style than DPS), smaller maps, quicker movements overall too (with the use of ridiculous horses when you start for your base, seriously why are Willow or Drogoz on a horse?), and an emphasis on rush in the main mode, give the game a feeling of fast-Overwatch. It looks a lot like it, but feels a little less "complicated" or restrictive, more direct, as much as it feels less refined in most sector. And so far, I like this balance more. It feels like a concentrated version of the games I enjoyed playing in Overwatch, with amidetly a bit less depth to it (I'm waiting the moment I'll access the competitive modes to judge the meta).

---
Progression and monetization:
Overwatch works with this absolutely awful loot box system. I hate, profundly HATE that the only way to "evolve" in Overwatch is to loot boxes and hope that the RNG gives something related to your character. Especially when the game has tones of cool outfits and that you paid full price to play it. For someone like me that cares a lot about art direction, it's painful to play hundreds of hours to have ONE skin for Mercy and ONE skin for Dva, the only two characters I play.
Paladins still has that but it feels like a bit less of a grind thanks to the cards. In Paladins, each character can equip cards that serve as a buff on habilities; it lets you tweak the qualities of your characters. You can make your own loadout of cards (5) and then multiply there effect. So you can make a character who's designed to be about movement and stealth, stealthier or quicker, using the right cards. And so you loot cards too. And that is actually really enjoyable!
Of course it's still character related. You can still find yourself winning cards for characters you don't play. But you can, à-la-Heathstone change these cards into a currency that you use to craft the cards you want. Simple, but neat.
As for skins, it's a bit of a mix-bag. Since Beta51 most legendary skins can be bought or found in chests (loot boxes) that you buy with gems that win really slowly (or buy directly). The cost is pretty high imho. But the characters are all accessible really quickly if you play enough, without the Founder's Pack. And if you buy it, all previously bought characters are refounded. Good deal!
---
TL;DR
And that's Paladins. It's fast Overwatch. With a bit less depth, quicker matches and f2p. And I finally bought the founder's pack after 50 hours on the game, which is really a good sign especially since I was going in expecting a laughable attempt at copying Blizzard. It feels derivative at times depending on what game you played first. And admittedly it's not as polished as it could yet (it's in Beta though), but it's still very (very) enjoyable in its own way, with its own merits. I recommend wholeheartedly.

Absolutely do not recommend this game, especially at full price. If you're really curious, PLEASE buy the demo first, or else buy at a 90% sale, or just read Harry Potter. The story relies too heavily on the aforementioned novel series with none of the magic, and the characters who were based off of actual HP characters (e.g. Hermione, Snape, etc.) are very watered-down, very fanfic-y versions of those characters. There is even the concept of being Muggleborn ("Wildseed"), though so far (I've played till January of the school year) it hasn't really come into play except for one professor mentioning it.
The game is largely a visual novel: it involves a good amount of reading and some choice-making, which does impact your relationship with the characters. The only "gameplay" really is selecting your classes for the week and passing your midterm and final exams. There are 5 magic types (red, blue, green, black, white) but very little lore behind the magic, except for the occasional info-dumps which I had no patience for given the poor introduction to the magical background of the world. As you continue to take classes, you collect spells which you can use to pass your exams. As another reviewer said, it is NOT true that you don't have to study all of the magic types.
The player character's personality is pretty nice but given the "lack of magic" I feel from the general story, I'm finding it hard to even complete the game and get even /one/ of the endings.

The game is amazing in many ways. There are moments when the Greens did an amazing job of capturing the frustration, self doubt, and myriad of emotions that one goes through during an experience such as this.
It felt *real*. And up until about the halfway point in the game it felt like one of the *realest* experiences I've ever played through.
That was until the Greens, specifically Amy, began to use religion as a crutch. While this is obviously their story, and it would have not served them well to leave out the ways they coped, for me I could not relate to these parts. I found myself cringing at every piece of narrative that invoked God or Jesus, and there are times when the scenes are, nearly literally, drowning in these references.
At this point I realized the story was less about Joel and more about their struggle with their faith. Admittedly, I felt as though there was a bit of bait and switch and play here. And I found myself sad for what the game could have been versus what it actually is.
I'm not suggesting the game should be different. I'm simply disappointed that something that was so emotional suddenly took a sharp left into territory I could no longer relate to. Something that dealt with the fear and terror of loosing a child that doesn't begin to rationalize it all away by invoking heaven and God's plans, etc... would have been much more relate-able to me.
While the Green's faith is obviously real to them... to someone on the outside it really felt like more of a delusion. Their anger at God for taking their son quickly turns to the tried and true mantras of "just have faith" and "God know's best". Going so far as to have the player go through a story of Jesus and his disciples rowing a boat across a lake in a storm.
I don't fault Ryan and Amy Green for their faith, or even for implementing their faith into the game. This is their story and I'm glad they have decided to share it. But I do feel that people who don't share their faith should be aware of exactly where this story is heading. It can be quite a shock to go from a scene where I am crying due to how well they invoke the frustration of a child you can not heal to feeling uncomfortable as I listen to another conversation where Amy professes her blind faith that Joel will be OK.
That said, I don't regret my play through. I simply regret that a universal story of loss and grief becomes niche and is no longer relate-able to many non Christians by the second half. In many ways it was an amazing game.... it just wasn't a game for me.
The gameplay itself can be quite frustrating as well sometimes. There are no choices in the game, you simply move forward and let the story unfold. It is possible to get stuck if you don't go the right direction. Other times the player gets stuck on purpose, as Ryan designed certain sections to be frustrating to mirror his own frustrations. Unfortunately the lack of context clues can either be seen as clever or poor design. It all depends on how patient the player is. Anyone would be hard pressed to call the controls anything but clunky, however the controls don't necessarily need to be smooth in a narrative like this. Ultimately, if you choose to play this game, don't expect a challenge, don' expect smooth controls, do expect to move slowly through the game, and be prepared for a faith heavy last half.
edit:
A continual misinterpretation with my review was that I was offended by the faith in the game, when I feel that I was pretty clear that I simply could not relate to it. The assumption that faith is universal, and therefor all people should be able to play this game and relate to it is completely ignorant. Faith is no more universal than any other belief.
To be clear here, had the game ended with aliens abducting Joel, I would not have been able to relate to that either. Had the game ended with Joel suddenly gaining mutant super powers, destroying cancer, and then flying to the center of the earth to procure a cure for all cancer patients, then again, I would not have been able to relate to this either.
The best parts of the game were the REAL ones. The frustrating night(s), the memories, the moments of just Joel and his parents, the final prognosis.... These parts of the game were absolutely fantastic. They are universal because human suffering is universal. You don't have to have lost a child to sympathize with the pain the Green's describe in these sections.
Ryan actually has one of the best lines in the game. Near the end Amy is apologizing to him for being upset that they took different routes through grief to arrive at the same place. And she wraps up by saying, "But at least we both know Joel will be ok." Ryan responds, "I don't.". Amy asks, "You don't what?" And Ryan finishes by saying, "I don't know that he will be ok. I hope he will... but I don't know that he will."
That is the "delusion" I was speaking of. The delusion of believing he will be ok no matter what the doctor says, no matter how far Joel deteriorates, and no matter how harsh reality is. And Ryan has lucid moments during those times where he questions these things, but ultimately, Joel's death is too much for him and he rushes back to his faith for that final comfort. As I said originally, I do not fault the Green's for their faith. I would never ask them to change this game. It is their experience. But to say that I, or anyone/everyone else should be able to relate to this experience is absolutely ignorant. If I were to design a game that dealt with the loss of a loved one with zero with zero faith, or even overt denials of faith, then would it be realistic for me to blindly state that everyone should be able to relate to my point of view? Not at all.

As it is right now, it's so broken that you can easily lock yourself out of the ending.
Game is ridden with progression-breaking bugs, from items that appear in your inventory before you pick them up; the ending easily becoming unreachable if you accidentally miss a thing with no way of coming back to fix it; some broken sound playback (audio cues playing where they shouldn't or stopping halfway through); as well as iffy detection boxes that make you think some key items are just part of the background and can't be interacted with.
Not only that but the game itself is very poorly designed, a lot of puzzles require extensive pixel hunting to be solved, since there are absolutely no hints to what to do.
On top of all that, the soundtrack isn't even in high bitrate (only 256 kbps MP3), opposite to what would be expected of any official game soundtrack in the year 2015.
Even though my playtime is 5 hours, I must say that at least 40% of that time was spent mindlessly backtracking and clicking on things searching for solutions that weren't even there, and searching the steam community for said solutions.
As sad as it makes me (been a fan of The Neverhood since my childhood and been hyping up for this game since the kickstarter campaign was launched), I cannot recommend this game, since as it is right now, the game is not at all worth its cost, and regardless of the cost, it's highly unsatisfying to play, as well as very short and repetitive.

Armikrog is a strange vibrant adventure filled with style and plenty of personality. The games visuals are what sells it, from the claymation to the stop motion animation. Armikrog visually is top notch, with a comedic twist but it doesn't stop there. The soundtrack, voicework, of Armikrog is also a treat for the ears. The games intro immediately sets the tone for whats sure to be an entertaining adventure. Now where things begin to get hazy is gameplay and bugs. Armikrog was a game that was delayed a few times and I think it would've benefited from staying in the oven a bit longer. Mostly Armikrog lacks polish, areas like the options menu, interactions with the environment, and lack of inventory make the gameplay feel hollow at times. While I didn't run into many game breaking bugs I did notice some sound issues would occur after cut scenes. It's these types of things that need to be patched out, which I am sure the developer is working on. At the end of the day though I don't think these issues hold the game back from being enjoyed. If you read between the lines you can see that the game is a passion project and it shows. Everything is there as far audio/visuals, all the game needs is a little TLC and polish.

This is me Fuse, saying that this not my review of Dust: AET, but it's by Jon Morcom over at PCGamer. I couldn't find the words myself to describe this game, so I take great assurance that Jon's review will help me out, along with you. Enjoy the review!
Anthropomorphic animals can be a divisive fictional device. But if we can accept cities floating in the sky and assassins who can blink themselves across high rooftops, it shouldn’t be too big a stretch to invest some belief in the cat-like samurai and his talking sword in Dust: An Elysian Tail. This obvious labour of love was developed near single-handedly by Dean Dodrill, whose background as an accomplished illustrator is so enjoyably evident in this exquisite-looking action RPG.
Eponymous and amnesic hero, Dust is on a quest to discover his true identity and establish who is ethnically cleansing the mystical world of Falana. As Dust, you carry the sentient Blade of Ahrah, a swishy bringer-of-death given to dispensing pearls of wisdom at key points in the story. Fidget, a ‘nimbat’ (a flying cross between a fox and a ginger tabby) is the guardian of the sword and your diminutive companion. Disconcertingly curvaceous with an irritating voice, Fidget punctuates this otherwise solemnly-related tale with some knowing, flippant remarks that keep the cloying earnestness at bay.
This port has received a lot of love, and the keyboard commands work well. WASD and space are used to move and jump, while J and K let you chain light and heavy strikes into combo streaks. L orders Fidget to throw a cluster of tiny fireballs into melee which, when combined with Dust's blade-spinning Dust Storm attack, become a blazing swarm that can sweep the screen of enemies. Dust Storm can also be used to wrangle explosive fruits and break through fragile walls, revealing secret areas or opening up paths to quest objectives. Completing quest and creating huge combo chains generates XP that lets you level up and assign a booster gem to Dust's attack power, toughness, or Fidget's spark-flinging ability.
The multifarious enemy creatures infesting Falana queue-up to be dispatched through combat that feels smooth and intuitive but may be too easy for some on Normal difficulty. Bosses require a bit more finesse - parry and avoid combined with some health bar whittling from Fidget's ranged attack. Indigenous hordes of goblins and rock giants will scatter loot and crafting materials across the scenery when they die, and the drops are generous and varied enough to make crafting almost redundant. Dust can equip buff-giving items and regenerate his health with everything from apples to the fully cooked roast chickens that fall out of walls when you break them.
A host of varied side quests complement the main story objectives, all of which open up different parts of the world map and provide tantalising glimpses of hidden areas that present some tricky navigational challenges. However, the game does suffer from some overly-long cutscenes which aren't entirely skip-able and frequently disrupt the immersion and the tempo. Commendably, the save system has multiple slots but the in-game save monuments are spaced such that an unexpected death can occasionally lead to some laborious replay.
Although the dialogue could use some judicious excising and the combat a bit more variation, the game rewards bold exploration with some imaginative platforming and beautiful, widely-varied environments. Never mind that on first look, Falana and its doe-eyed denizens presents like the sort of mind-numbing fodder Channel 5 screens early on a Saturday morning, this is a game with abundant cross-generational appeal. Dust: An Elysian Tail - the acceptable and furry face of fantasy violence.

The Neverhood is one of my all time favorite games and holds a very dear place in my nostalgic gaming heart. I can understand the want for others to hold Armikrog to the standard of its spritual predecessor, but I'd like to steer clear of a direct comparison as I believe it's a tad unfair to do so. After all, The Neverhood was a big budget title published by Dreamworks Interactive, green lit by Spielberg himself, and released at full game price. For the lack of this financial support and a smaller team Armikrog is a bit shorter and a smaller scale.
Visuals:
Pros: Armikrog has creative character models and envoronments that made me feel in a sense that I was picking up right where The Neverhood left off. I can't enough of these claymation worlds. Armikrog is quite colorful and real treat to look at. If I had to give Armikrog anything over The Neverhood, it would be the be expanded color pallette and extra care that was put into the detail of the rooms overall. The animation and cutscenes (though few) were top notch. I played it on a 55inch tv at 1920x1080 and it looked great.
Cons:  I get this feeling though that more in the way of cutscenes (not to mention dialogue and immersive elements) but may have been cut for budget or time. I would like to have seen more easter eggs similar to the monster scene when you look through the window repeatedly. Another odd thing is that there is no lip movement from the characters outside of cutscenes.
Sound:
Pros: The music of Terry Scott Taylor is top notch as usuall, though I would like to have heard a couple more memorable tracks. The sound effects are acceptable.
Cons: I feel like not including more dialogue between our 2 heroes was a big missed opportunity. Even just a funny exchange about each room you enter would have been a huge improvement.
Gameplay:
Pros: Fairly straight forward and liked the addition of a second character (Beak Beak!). There were atleast 3 big puzzles that I found to be quite unique and creative.
Cons: I feel like the overall difficulty on some of the puzzles could have been kicked up a notch. Also thought it would be nice to include a bit more complexity to how you use BeakBeak. For instance maybe he could eat other things that give him other abilities you could add to the puzzles. Perhaps swimming or digging.
Story:
Pros: Overall I loved the story that was told here. Where The Neverhood had an entire biblical chronical written, Armikrog offers some of its lore in a different way. You couldtell that a lot of time was spent on the hieroglyphs and the alien language that you can for the most part transalte your self. When the games translates it later and the full back story is known, I couldn'thelp but be reminded of the Willy tapes.
Cons: I would like to have had a bit more back story on Tommy, Beak Beak, and the main villain. Again this could have been easily fixed by more dialogue exchange to deliver some exposition. The ending/wrap could have been a bit longer and tad more rewarding.
Bugs: I didn't experience any and really do believe some of the reports are people losing their patience or maybe (perhaps never had) their old school adventure gaming skin. If the lever you have doesn't work, than it is the wrong lever. If a button or control panel doesn't work, than you prob haven't activated it. Just Sayin...
Armikrog is not as good as The Neverhood. In someways it was problably incapable of being that, but there are flaws they could have without a doubt avoided. Overall though I enjoyed the experience and would buy another game if they made one.

Came home, sat down and installed the game - started it and the arrow keys weren't working - as a kid I knew how to use only arrow keys and i didn't even try to bother with other ones, so i tought the game was broken - and god bless my ignorance, i think that a couple of days have passed when i've figured out the controls - numpad.

Paradox continues to deliver top shelf Grand Strategy, this time a Space Opera.
Where to begin? It looks fantastic, and sounds incredibly good with its spacey soundtrack ranging from feel-good to being simply majestic, Interstellar style.
Using the Clauswitz engine like Crusader Kings 2 & Europe Universalis 4, it plays much the same; realtime with speed slider and pause features. Unlike previous Grand Strategy titles however, the Tutorial is brilliant. This, combined with starting out small with a single star system and a handy 'quest log', it eases you into the game concepts and never gets overwhelming.
UI is very sleek like always with paradox, and it feels very cohesive having everything from technology to combat done directly on top of the beautiful map.
Races are varied and cool, and the palette for aesthetics and ideologies is rich.
I started my campaign as the good ol United Nations of Earth, being Democratic and starting out with Warp Travel tech and old-but-effective Nuke weaponry. After learning the ropes I soon managed to colonize the Alpha Centauri system, with felt great.
I havent had much time with the Diplomacy yet, part from getting to know and soon forming an alliance with a neighbouring species of Righteous Bird people. Then we went to war together and managed to liberate part of another nearby system, from their plutocratic and evil overlords. So far so good :)
What more to say at this point? Get it now!

To me in many ways, this is better than the first Danganronpa. I was surprised to know this year that both games went to Steam and personally, I feel like that was ultimately a good decision to expand these bizarre yet great games to other people who don't own a Vita or don't want to import or emulate the PSP versions.
Just like the first game, you and your classmates are forced into a killing game where you need to find the murderer and only they get to be executed but if you choose wrongly, everyone else instead of the killer gets executed. This time though, it's on an island instead of a school and the game is more off the walls than its predecessor.
To keep things fresh, Spike Chunsoft added and refined some of the segments during trials. Nonstop Debates are back but are refined so you can agree with classmates instead of just pointing out flaws in their arguments. There's also Hangmans Gambit which is retooled but in my opinion, is not as good as the first one because this time you need to grab the letters, match them, and select them to put them in and making sure they don't hit a different letter which sometimes feels impossible. MTBS are back in the form PTAS(Panic Talk Action) and are similar to the first games MTBS but this time you gotta form the word. Closing Arguments are back and are virtually the same.
New to the trials though are Rebuttal Showdowns and Logic Dives. Rebuttal Showdowns make you "slash" at peoples words and basically "cut" into their argument which is nice. Logic Dives however is basically like a snowboarding mini-game into your mind where you need to jump, dodge obstacles, and choose the correct pathway to figure out a part of a case and in my opinion, I don't like them since it gets annoying trying to jump all narrow spots.
In my personal opinion the new cast of characters is great and have some of my most favorites in the entire series. Like the first game you can interact with them through some Free Time Events so  you can get to know them better, gain some hope shards so you can buy some skills, and even gain said characters exclusive skill.
To people new to DanganRonpa, I heavily recommend going through the first game first before touching the 2nd game so you can understand everything better. To people who are into Visual novels, Mystery games, fans of the first game, or into something off the wall, I recommend this to you.

If you've ever played Journey on PS3/PS4, you'll know what to expect going into this game. It's short, it's stunningly beautiful, and the gameplay is simple and meditative.
Exploring these underwater seascapes never becomes frustrating or boring thanks to subtle environmental cues, which highlight points of interest and various objectives in creative ways; like using contrasting color pallettes to guide you in the right direction, or showing schools of fish travelling towards a mysterious cave, or swarming around a magical pool that leads you to your next destination. It's a natural and organic feeling of progression, and I wouldn't be surprised if ABZU was used to demonstrate these videogame design methods in an actual classroom.
Did I mention how ♥♥♥♥ing beautiful this game looks?
Playing this game becomes a near-religious experience thanks to gorgeous, fantastic, stunning, not-enough-synonyms-to-describe visuals, and you'll be tempted to screencap everything in sight. It's eye candy on a massive scale, and I won't soon forget how awe-struck I felt while taking it all in. You'll definitely want to show this game to friends and family who can appreciate just how jaw-droppingly beautiful it is, not only as a videogame, but as a true work of art.
The game's length is probably its weakest asset, clocking in at just under a couple of hours for your standard playthrough.
Twenty dollars might be somewhat steep, but I would argue that this game's value shouldn't be judged on length or replay incentives, but on the solid foundation of it's stellar art design, setpieces, environmental design, and pacing. It's not often that a game manages to nail every one of these aspects, and further padding the game with meaningless objectives would've only lessened it's overall impact.
ABZU won't satisfy players who are looking for more involved or detail-oriented gameplay, but almost anyone will be able appreciate the game for what it delivers artistically (in spades) through it's focused, direct approach to creating an unforgettable journey with a minimal degree of interaction. This is an absolute must-play for PC gamers, and I can't recommend it highly enough.

And that it is very much an art form in the truest sense of the word when done right. And That Dragon, Cancer gets it right. Through a minimalist art design, it retains focus on the narrative itself, which is not only based on but the sole focus of a true story of a family and their battle against the cancer ravaging a young boy.
The graphics and level design of the game overall magnificently accentuate the thoughts and emotions that the game is attempting to convey. The simplistic gameplay mechanics might seem droll to some at first glance, but this reviewer took it as a way for the game designers to accentuate the age of the child that was the focus of the game, his battle, his family’s titanic struggle, how inspirational the boy had become to so many people.

This is the story of Joel. This brave hero was a young kid that had to fight a very very big bad dragon going by the name of Cancer. And Cancer had also a huge impact on his parents and family. From trying to make him smile by playing with him to keep him company in a place where doctors are trying to cure and defeat Cancer, Joel will never be alone.

Playing that game is paying a tribute to everyone who lost againt Cancer, to everyone that pinned down Cancer so Cancer leaves them alone, to everyone that saw Cancer attacking their loved one and that were feeling so powerless that the only thing they could do was caring, holding an hand, crying and mainly giving so much love so that their loved one don't feel alone or unloved, to keep at bay the darkness, to try to find the light when the darkness is too much...

I'll be completely honest, at first I was coming to the game thinking that I would have a good laugh at an Overwatch ripoff, then uninstall it (I know that since Paladins came out first, it's more complicated than that, but that's what I was expecting nonetheless). And though there are some uncanny similarities that force us to compare the two games, and though Paladins doesn't quite have the production value that a Blizzard game can have...I actually have more fun with Paladins than I do with Overwatch. And I kind of LOVE that game.
---
Presentation:
I think the art direction is bit all over the place. I'm happy to see that colorful shooters are not going away since TF2 and I think the maps look pretty neat. But as far as coherence goes, the cast of characters is kind of a mess. I find some of the characters to be plain ugly (like Willo), some pretty random/uninspired (like Skye, Viktor or Barik), while I really like some other designs (Evie, Cassie, Mal'Damba or Inara); in that regard it is subjective though. Still, the juxtaposition doesn't work as well as in Overwatch, or Battleborn. You have a dragon with a jetpack, a pixie, a gobelin in a modern robot suit, sort of a vodoo sorcerer etc. It's not plain and simple bad, far from that, but there is a lack of cohesion in terms of lore/universe. Plus, and this is where the nature of the game itself (a f2p competitor to Overwatch) starts to be a problem: a lot of characters are sort-of-Overwatch-characters. You have sort-of-Dva, sort-of-Torbjorn, sort-of-Reaper, sort-of-Soldier etc. Because of that the game can feel really derivative -unfairly admittedly since the game released prior to Overwatch. Which is too bad because, there still is a lot of little touches given to the animations, the voices (especially the voices) and the look of the heroes that bring personality to these archetypes that feel taken straight from Blizzard's FPS, if you played that one first. It's good, but it's just not always enough to make it a really polished art direction.
The music is equally in that sort-of-Overwatch vibe. It's good, it works ingame and in the menus, but it's nothing special. The sound design on the other hand is actually pretty good. I think the game telegraphs well most of the threats. The sound feedback is simple, functionnal, sometimes funny (when it comes to ultimate especially). The weapon noises are super satisfying. It's snappy and helps selling the weapon you are using. I think the only minute gripe that I have is with the noise when standing on objective or pushing a payload; there is a sound everytime you gain some points, and if you stay next to a payload, you are gaining points continuously and hearing the same noise on repeat. And it can be a bit annoying.
---
Gameplay:
What about the meat of the game then? Well, again, it can feel derivative, you can't really argue on that. Even if not all the OverwatchPaladins-characters lookalike have the exact same role, and play the exact same way, some can really feel like conterfeits if you played Overwatch first. Ruckus, Drogoz, Fernando (<3) and Barik are almost copy-paste in terms of gameplay, with similar habilities and roles. And if you've played tens (if not hundreds) of hours of Overwatch, this can either be a good thing (you're not lost) or a bad thing (it doesn't feel fresh). But thankfully a couple of characters are pretty unique in terms of gameplay and ultimate. And more importantly, the pacing, the level-design and overall game-design can set the game apart enough, in a good way. I'd say that from what I feel most characters have a really decent DPS. You can help a great deal in terms of dammage, even with a healer. Meaning, if you like a character's look or way of moving, chances are you are not going to be yelled at if you chose it at the beginning of the game.
To be clearer, it feels like you are supposed to have a balance in your team (it works best with at least 1 tank, and 1 heal/support as it should)  but that no matter who you pick in each categories, you can help with her/him/it. There are some combos and counters, but you can do a decent job with the character you like. This makes the game easier to pick up and play, without sacrificing the strategy. And it's less of a guilt trip when you are playing your main despite a composition that would benefit more from another character in the same category as your main.
The level-design also participate in making the game more of a quick fun (even more than Overwatch that is to say). The maps are smaller and work around a center (or lign) of symetry. Both camps are mostly mirrors of what the other team have, with a couple of little differences. The main mode, the one I played the most so far, starts with a king of the hill and segways into an escort the payload. So for each match, each team can be on attack or defense depending on how well it performs on the king of the hill part of the match. All this makes for mostly quick matches (15 mins) and sometimes really short (6-7 mins) and rarely really long (+20 mins).
So more DPS/bit-less disparities between characters (still all unique but more in movement and style than DPS), smaller maps, quicker movements overall too (with the use of ridiculous horses when you start for your base, seriously why are Willow or Drogoz on a horse?), and an emphasis on rush in the main mode, give the game a feeling of fast-Overwatch. It looks a lot like it, but feels a little less "complicated" or restrictive, more direct, as much as it feels less refined in most sector. And so far, I like this balance more. It feels like a concentrated version of the games I enjoyed playing in Overwatch, with amidetly a bit less depth to it (I'm waiting the moment I'll access the competitive modes to judge the meta).

---
Progression and monetization:
Overwatch works with this absolutely awful loot box system. I hate, profundly HATE that the only way to "evolve" in Overwatch is to loot boxes and hope that the RNG gives something related to your character. Especially when the game has tones of cool outfits and that you paid full price to play it. For someone like me that cares a lot about art direction, it's painful to play hundreds of hours to have ONE skin for Mercy and ONE skin for Dva, the only two characters I play.
Paladins still has that but it feels like a bit less of a grind thanks to the cards. In Paladins, each character can equip cards that serve as a buff on habilities; it lets you tweak the qualities of your characters. You can make your own loadout of cards (5) and then multiply there effect. So you can make a character who's designed to be about movement and stealth, stealthier or quicker, using the right cards. And so you loot cards too. And that is actually really enjoyable!
Of course it's still character related. You can still find yourself winning cards for characters you don't play. But you can, à-la-Heathstone change these cards into a currency that you use to craft the cards you want. Simple, but neat.
As for skins, it's a bit of a mix-bag. Since Beta51 most legendary skins can be bought or found in chests (loot boxes) that you buy with gems that win really slowly (or buy directly). The cost is pretty high imho. But the characters are all accessible really quickly if you play enough, without the Founder's Pack. And if you buy it, all previously bought characters are refounded. Good deal!
---
TL;DR
And that's Paladins. It's fast Overwatch. With a bit less depth, quicker matches and f2p. And I finally bought the founder's pack after 50 hours on the game, which is really a good sign especially since I was going in expecting a laughable attempt at copying Blizzard. It feels derivative at times depending on what game you played first. And admittedly it's not as polished as it could yet (it's in Beta though), but it's still very (very) enjoyable in its own way, with its own merits. I recommend wholeheartedly.

Paradox continues to deliver top shelf Grand Strategy, this time a Space Opera.
Where to begin? It looks fantastic, and sounds incredibly good with its spacey soundtrack ranging from feel-good to being simply majestic, Interstellar style.
Using the Clauswitz engine like Crusader Kings 2 & Europe Universalis 4, it plays much the same; realtime with speed slider and pause features. Unlike previous Grand Strategy titles however, the Tutorial is brilliant. This, combined with starting out small with a single star system and a handy 'quest log', it eases you into the game concepts and never gets overwhelming.
UI is very sleek like always with paradox, and it feels very cohesive having everything from technology to combat done directly on top of the beautiful map.
Races are varied and cool, and the palette for aesthetics and ideologies is rich.
I started my campaign as the good ol United Nations of Earth, being Democratic and starting out with Warp Travel tech and old-but-effective Nuke weaponry. After learning the ropes I soon managed to colonize the Alpha Centauri system, with felt great.
I havent had much time with the Diplomacy yet, part from getting to know and soon forming an alliance with a neighbouring species of Righteous Bird people. Then we went to war together and managed to liberate part of another nearby system, from their plutocratic and evil overlords. So far so good :)
What more to say at this point? Get it now!

Summary: At worst, this is a competent racing platform with lots of customizable options and great racing.  At best, it is potentially the best racing sim to date.
Like others, I could describe the great feeling of driving any car in the sim or the plethora of options that set it apart from the competition.  Or the idea that it is lacking in graphics somewhat to prettier counterparts like Project Cars or Forza.  Or that the menus fall a little flat.
But despite the technical wrongs and rights, it just feels spectacular to drive - the most important aspect of all.  And more than that, there is a competent studio behind it, Studio 397, who is continuing to not just invest in the title with major overhauls in all areas but with constant communication with its user base as well.  And that communication goes both ways which is a huge win in this industry and for this genre.
There is some paid content being developed alongside free content but it is well worth it and helps them to continue improving the sim.  If they have the approach like Assetto Corsa (I wish I could merge the best aspects of both sims) which allows you to race against purchased content online without paying for it, I'm all for it.  Sometimes the groups I run with don't want to/can't afford to throw down for a new car mod.  And that's fine.  I hope it proves to be a profit center without upsetting the balance of the game (which it shouldn't based on their approach so far).  I know I plan on buying some cars here and there.  They do fantastic work.
And they are making the ability to mod the platform easier and ever better which means more quality, free content from community developers.  Should all their plans and intents come to fruition as far as improving graphics, UIs, plugins, online experience and content, I see rFactor 2 gaining as much success as its predecessor, if not more so as THE racing sim of choice.

This game's very existence is one of the reasons one should think twice before taking what the average simracer says for granted. The helpful-to-unhelpful ratio for any negative review for this game should be seen as a warning as to the nature of the community, something which is even better illustrated in places like RaceDepartment.
The force feedback with a wheel is dull, dead, constant and bland, giving almost no valuable information whatsoever. The car feeling is largely nonexistent, with the FFB seemingly mostly emulating only the track itself. In fact, the handling itself appears to be broken - even after looking up information on "good" FFB settings in multiple places, none of them made any of the car I tried handle like they are supposed to - when losing traction, for instance, the steering barely reacts at all, making death slides (already a common theme in games powered by ISI's engines, but taken to the extreme here) frustrating beyond belief.
Frankly, when even F1 2016 (hell, even F1 2013, and that's saying something) has better force feedback, I have no reason to consider this game, hence why I refunded. It goes without saying that the graphics, particularly the UI, are mediocre as well, and the heavy reliance on mods does the game no good either as it almost completely nullifies any of the few good elements of the feedback through the general low quality of most community-made works.
Get AMS instead. I don't like that one much either due to its questionable feeling, but it still completely trounces rFactor 2 in every regard. Even the graphics are barely any worse.
Also, keep in mind that the demo does not actually give an accurate representation of what the game feels like. The demo 100% uses an older build, with multiple cars feeling completely different from the way they feel in the full-priced title while still being unrealistic and offering terrible feedback.
And just in case you're doubting the realism factor, you need only check the lap times in the World's Fastest Gamer event: they're seconds faster than real life. And that's with an actual serious car and not a modded one.

No other game has recreated such a graceful underwater world. Especially fascinating are the detailed fish banks and their highly convincing swarm behaviour. The music is also very pleasantly fitting.
Yet for all its zen elegance, its storytelling is either absent or very abstract. At one point the game momentarily appears to attempt a statement on industrialism and the fragility of life over these destructive aspirations, but it is all too brief. The moment the plot seems to take form signals the beginning of the end.
My feelings towards the game are torn between obvious artistic merit and disappointing design direction. It is a very attractive zen experience, but also very repetitive. The lack of diversity is easily felt during the first half. I never played Journey for comparison but I expected more from this spiritual follow-up, both in terms of story line and meaningful interactions.
The second half of the game is definitely more satisfying, where it breaks free of its initial routine and goes into unexpected but welcome directions that include sci-fi elements and even brief walking sections. Without spoiling anything, there is one moment where you may develop a strong emotional connection but again the game does not fully capitalize on this opportunity.
Controls are smooth and give a persuasive impression of swimming, although some levels actually feel more like flying with the strange notion of a world within a world. There is no real danger or state of failure, nor is it really possible to get lost, making this game very accessible and straightforward.
It could have benefited from the inclusion of proper puzzles instead of a myriad of useless collectibles. The areas built by (presumably) an ancient civilization seen throughout the game remain completely underdeveloped and the game provides no answers to the brief mysteries it sets up. That said mysteries are not even that intriguing in the first place is a bigger problem.
ABZÛ is only recommended for players looking for a short and unchallenging experiential discovery, those with an indisputable love of marine life, and people unconventionally fascinated by triangles.

Danganronpa is a point-and-click adventure game/murder mystery visual novel starring Persona 4's Teddie, only evil. It's a bizarre combination of Battle Royale or Hunger Games and a Phoenix Wright game with an art style that says, "I couldn't give less of a♥♥♥♥♥♥" It's whacky, strange, funny, and most importantly, you get to helplessly watch everyone you've ever cared about tear eachother apart and die in increasingly over-the-top or brutal ways, until you wonder why you ever held hope in the first place and give in to absolute despair.
Then Danganronpa 2 took everything I loved about Danganronpa, and made it so much better*.
Danganronpa's puzzles had the occasionally iffy answer, but I never had that problem in DR2. DR2's puzzles were much harder, and this time you don't have Kyoko around to shove you into the answer. While some characters do nudge you in the right direction, the hints never feel like the game's treating you like a -complete- idiot. They gave you all the clues you need, so figure it out, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.
A lot of the soundtrack is repeats or remixes from DR1, but it's fine, because DR1's soundtrack is great. DR2's original songs, however, are absolutely fantastic. The characters are all nicely fleshed out and three-dimensional, well, you know, aside from the lack of literal depth. Get it. Because they're sprites...mymomtellsmeI'mfunny.
Now, DR1 isn't a bad game, and I would very, very highly recommend playing DR1 first. On top of still being a pretty good game, the stories are sort of linked here and there. And really, if you're playing a point-and-click adventure or a VN, it's for the plot, right? DR1&2 are about 50~60 hours long combined, so you'll probably get your money's worth for both of them. (I would also recommend setting both Puzzle and Action difficulty to Mean, personally.)
I would say Danganronpa is a must for people into murder mysteries, especially something like Phoenix Wright, and even if you aren't into all this anime, at least give it a shot and see if you warm up to the art style.

This all started with me with a friend buying a game for another friend for the first game. Now nearly a 100 hrs clocked in for the sequel, I can safely say it's very solid sequel.
Danganropa 2: Goodbye Despair is a light novel mystery game that similar to Phoenix Wright series but has it's own flavor to make it stand out for itself. Similar to the events of the previous game, sixteen students of Hope Peak's Academy are on a vacation trip within an isolated resort known as Jabberwock Island. Things went from a peaceful school trip to a killing school trip when a familiar saboteur known as Monokuma gains control of the island for his new playground of murders. Now playing as Hajime Hinata, you must solve the island's mysteries while surviving the horrors of your classmates killing each other.
Story:
The story is similar in ways with the previous game but has its own twists and turns that makes it a little different. The player plays as Hajime Hinata, an ordinary high schooler joining a high ranked school known as Hope Peak's Academy. Weirdly, he is awaken with fifteen other students on an tropical island with a magical bunny Usami. Unfortunately, the series mascot Monokuma showed up to make the peaceful school trip to a deadly school trip. Hajime and the other students must find secrets about the island's mysterious nature and solve cases of fallen school mates when a murder occurs.
Overall, if you played the first game, you pretty much know what's going to happen. If this your first time, it's going to be quite an emotional trip and adventure with fun and excitement in the mix. There will be a few chapters that are weird, but it tends to even out later in the game. But since this is a pretty decent light novel, the story is well done in this department.
Gameplay:
For the most part, this game is a standard point and click game with the usage of a controller or mouse (keyboard for some inputs). As the game goes to class trial mode, you'll play a series of mini-games to press on contradictions and lies of classmates' statements and find out who was the mastermind in the case. If you played the first game, most of the mini-games are reworked and some are added on. The Non-stop Debate even has a new feature of agreeing with a classmate statement. For me, additions of Rebuttal Showdown and Logic Dive were pretty good while reworks of Hangman Gambit and M.T.B. (now known as P.T.A.) are sub-par or poor constructed. The bigger culprit for that is the difficulty levels. They were changed to be harder than in the previous game. So Mean in the first game is pretty much Kind in this game.
Overall, the gameplay is a decent update to the previous game. The first game was fairly too easy but they beef up the difficulty to make it challenging. There are a few niche updates that I forgot to mention but the game came a long way.
Graphics:
Since it's a light novel, it'll pretty much display itself like one. At first I wasn't too crazy about it since the characters are literally 2D paper cutouts, but then it was pretty interesting how the areas they visit literally build itself to our view. It's an even more powerful theme to this particular game setting, but a nice touch. Some parts of the game will feature a manga style look, which has really nice art to it. The animations for Monokuma segments are really interesting and dark too. There are some 3D elements to this game as well, but it's still quite weird to me.
Overall, it's pretty much what you expect from a light novel look. Nothing outstanding, but something unique and rarely done well.
Sound:
If there's one thing that both the first game and this game did right is the music. Masafumi Tadaka (you probably know this person dealing with arrangements from Shining Soul series, killer7, No More Heroes, and even Smash Bros.) composes most of the music for this game series. There are returning tracks from the first game, but still have a lot of new tracks in the mix for this game. It fits well for most parts of the game. From calm and relaxing tropical music when the students are trying to enjoy themselves, to the intense rave-like music during class trials of finding the murderer. For the most part of this game, the music fits extremely well to the game and always gets you pumped or despairing at the right moments. Even to the point as you pass more chapters, some songs tend to get stronger along with the cast.
Overall, if you like variety of music, this game will greatly accomplished it for you. Tadaka's work was a total surprise for me and he does not disappoint.
Overall:
Danganropna 2: Goodbye Despair is that rare game that somehow gets me in the right places and I would've never realized it unless my friends influenced me. If there's any alternative mystery games like Phoenix Wright, this is totally it right here. Even the first one is ideal as well. It's even more interesting to say that the game somehow fulfilled a certain kink I loved for a long time. Never expected that at all with this game. But I must say, it's great for its money and I recommend this game very much. But it's best to play it after finishing Danganropa: Trigger Happy Havoc. This game is still good without playing it, but it makes more sense if you played it before this one. But still, totally recommend it.
