Created (designed and programmed) entirely by one person, Dust is a beautifully articulate love-letter to seminal games like Castlevania, Metroid, Ys and Devil May Cry. It’s full of secrets to uncover, areas to explore and enemies to kill in fantastically over-the-top ways. Getting a 1000-hit combo during a fight with dozens of badguys is not only immensely satisfying, it’s also almost effortless.
The story may not be that unique or special, but it’s charming enough. The graphics are lush, and wonderfully animated, betraying how it was all done by a single individual’s hard work over the last three years. But the real soul of Dust is the confident combat system, which struts up to you the moment you start playing, takes you by the hand and encourages you to have fun. It’s not Bayonetta levels of sophistication , but it doesn’t have to be. The combination attacks are simple but empowering, launchers take you into the air with ease, and the Dust Storm (a kind of magic attack with several spells to uncover) has you stun-locking herds of enemies, experience points exploding around you like New Years fireworks.
If games are a dialogue between the player and the game’s creator, then playing Dust is like sitting down with an old friend who’s back in town, full of fresh stories to tell and eager to reminisce with you about the good times.

A more mature successor to The Witcher, this was both a more enjoyable experience and a frustrating one. The story writing has improved and the flow is smoother than the first game, but it is still rife with immersion-busting inconsistencies. The difficulty curve of the fighting is still uneven despite patching, with early stages unreasonably difficult and late stages unreasonably easy. Odd bits of 'girl power' affirmation rest weirdly next to the continued shallow titillation the series is known for. It makes the male homophobia all the more pronounced (lesbianism is okay so long as it's sexual in this game) and really in the 21st century, story and plot aside, this just has no justification anymore.
I spent over 200 hours in the first game, but much of it was milling about trying to finish every side quest. The Witcher 2 needs nowhere near as much investment timewise to compete it. I loved little things cropping up that were a result of my choices in the first Witcher game. Those touches are delightful. I hope that continues into The Witcher 3 - and that we continue to see the studio mature in its quality of storytelling and gameplay both.

I first saw this at PAX two years ago, but I was too afraid to play it.
2.7 hours is what it took for me to finish this game, which isn't really a game--more like a memoir, and a very personal account of one family dealing with the unthinkable realities of terminal illness, and all of the conflicting, complicated, messy feelings that this can entail.
It also deals quite a bit with the faith of the Green family, and although I'm not in the least bit religious, I appreciated those very personal insights into their struggles, doubts, and hopes. If religious discussion bothers you, I suppose it might put you off, but it's not there to preach to anyone, it's just a powerful underpinning of the way in which this family tried to approach coping with something that most of us can't really imagine (and will hopefully never experience).
It is challenging to experience, even from the position of outsider looking in. It was a brave thing to commit these experiences to any medium and turn them loose in the world. I hope it was healing, too. By the end of it I couldn't keep the tears at bay, but it was so, so comforting to see the credits at the end, and the long--long, long--list of backers from the kickstarter campaign...all those people who rallied behind the story of one family (which is, in its way, the story of many families).

'That Dragon, Cancer' is one of those games that I don't think I could recommend easily, because it lacks in actual gameplay. If you're into games of this genre, then Yes. Definitely play this game. The little gameplay to be found is made up with enthralling moments, amazing story-telling, incredible art and sound, and probably one of the best stories I've read/experienced in some time.
You 'play' as Ryan Green, the father of a young baby named Joel that has cancer. You experience the lives of Ryan, Amy & Joel during this period in their lives, from their amazing highs (playing in the park, feeding ducks, 'leaving the hospital' party) to their dreaded lows (conversation with doctor, final moments with Joel). The experience is truly something worthwhile.
That being said, for me personally, I did not particularly enjoy the ocean/drowning section of the game, when Ryan seems to go on a lot about God & Jesus. I understand that this was Ryan's way of dealing/coping; I am fine with that, I have nothing against it. My problem is, it pulls you away slightly from the immersion of a father trying to enjoy the last moments he has with his son, and it becomes more about him justifying having faith when he didn't before.
Again, I'm not bashing it; if that's what he used to help him get through those last few days, I wholly understand why. I just think that it pulled away from what made the game great FOR ME. The ending, however, is probably one of the best endings I've experienced in some time; seeing Joel with the puppy and the pancakes made me grin from ear to ear.
All in all, I loved this game. It was worth every penny. The game has as much replayability as watching a movie, in my opinion. I hope we see more games like this is in the future, because they're incredible when done right.
And 'That Dragon, Cancer'? It was done incredibly right.

My 4th best game of 2015, and for good reason. One of the best mashups of genres that I've seen over the last several years, Crypt of the Necrodancer has that addictive quality that will keep you playing the game over and over again, and enjoying every moment of it.  Strong internal game design revolving around the movement, not the rhythm, and yet the rhythm enhances every moment of gameplay. Dancing in between enemies and getting in the first hit while protecting your precious little health does keep you super aware of your surroundings, and enemy pattern movements force you to think outside the box, digging into the environment to escape or just give yourself a breather. A great solid soundtrack that's designed with the gameplay in mind, and yet importing songs works rather nicely too in a majority of cases. Look, I could go on and on about Crypt of the Necrodancer's design, it's smart gameplay, it's hours of re-playability, but I'm just going to get down to the chase. Everyone who even remotely likes roguelike/roguelite elements will have a fantastic time with this game, and those looking for something out of the rhythm genre will find something fresh and new here. Well worth the full price of admission, no questions asked.

Paradox continues to deliver top shelf Grand Strategy, this time a Space Opera.
Where to begin? It looks fantastic, and sounds incredibly good with its spacey soundtrack ranging from feel-good to being simply majestic, Interstellar style.
Using the Clauswitz engine like Crusader Kings 2 & Europe Universalis 4, it plays much the same; realtime with speed slider and pause features. Unlike previous Grand Strategy titles however, the Tutorial is brilliant. This, combined with starting out small with a single star system and a handy 'quest log', it eases you into the game concepts and never gets overwhelming.
UI is very sleek like always with paradox, and it feels very cohesive having everything from technology to combat done directly on top of the beautiful map.
Races are varied and cool, and the palette for aesthetics and ideologies is rich.
I started my campaign as the good ol United Nations of Earth, being Democratic and starting out with Warp Travel tech and old-but-effective Nuke weaponry. After learning the ropes I soon managed to colonize the Alpha Centauri system, with felt great.
I havent had much time with the Diplomacy yet, part from getting to know and soon forming an alliance with a neighbouring species of Righteous Bird people. Then we went to war together and managed to liberate part of another nearby system, from their plutocratic and evil overlords. So far so good :)
What more to say at this point? Get it now!

This game is wholly flawed yet somehow very enjoyable. I'm a fan of the Souls series and this is a flawed yet enjoyable spin on that formula. People who are complaining that it's too hard are missing the point. It's both a rogue-lite and a souls style game so difficulty is the name of the game. At least until you have a few plays under your belt and then it'll be less of a challenge and more of a romp to see how far you can get.
So what's flawed? The animations are awkward, the enemies get repetitive, the environments are far too minimal and the overall core combat isn't as satisfying as any rogue-lite or souls game that it's trying to base itself off.
Lets also talk about technical difficulties. This game was made in Unity and it shows. Not only in aesthetics but also in how the game performs. On lower end hardware you may have problems with some physics effects and you'll probably need to turn off the resolution super-sampling. On launch there were also problems with the game running on my Multi-Display setup and while I eventually got video going to my Steamlink it cuts off the audio shortly after I start streaming.
This doesn't stop the game from ultimately being fun enough to keep playing it. This game could definitely get better with a few patches and a bit of aesthetic readjustment. If you enjoy souls games and rogue-lites this will be fun. For me I bought this because it scrathced a bit of an itch and for that was all I needed. Is it worth $30? Even in it's flawed state it was worth that to me. With a little work this could be a game I get horribly addicted to but not just yet.

There was even one case were they needed a taller version of an object, so they just STRETCHED the sprite! It looked horrible, like some kind of joke.
The voice acting hurts the game and you gain nothing. The story is told well through just the actions of the charters, there's no reason for the bad voice acting. The game is short. For the price, it's not bad, but I only got about 4 hours out of it.

Highly underrated, deserves an overwhelming rating if you ask me. It just requests a little patience with it's clunky UI and pathetic presentation and offers possibly the most engaging virtual driving experience in return.
A lot have talked about how this is a hardcore sim that can't be appreciated without a wheel. While it is true that it's been made with the hardcore and the wheel in mind, I can vouch for the fact it is highly enjoyable even with a gamepad (which is what I use). It may be a fine simulation, but strangely fulfills my simcade needs better than any of the simcades or other sims. Yeah, I pirated or used a demo to try 'em all out and this easily comes out on top as far as the driving experience goes, it's so much fun to even just fool around on an empty track.
My very point of this review was to highlight that the game can be enjoyed just as much by gamepad casuals (like me) as purists do. Just play around with those assists to find the right simcade balance for you. I personally use everything OFF except Auto-Clutch and Invulnerability ON, with the Transmission being Auto or Manual depending on the car. That's the settings I dig for my simcade, though this may vary for other non-purists. But do note that regardless of settings, a keyboard simply won't do, you'll atleast need a gamepad (or basically anything that allows partial throttle-n-brake at the very least).

This game is pretty much an ideal sequel to the original Danganronpa, and well worth your time if you played the original. I'll keep it short and sweet, and drw up some comparisions.
Over the original Danganronpa, it has:
Better characters - every member of the cast has something unique about them, and avoids the cookiecutter anime nerd/lolita/sport girl stereotypes of the previous cast.
More robust gameplay, with more things to do during trials.
More replay value with additional items and a new Hope Fragments system which rewards character interaction in Free Time.
A virtual pet to break up the visual novel aspect somewhat, as well as some other modes I haven't looked into yet.
A more varied set of locations - you're on an tropical archipelago, not some stuffy fortified school.
Better music - the score is a lot more lively and varied, though it does recycle some old tracks from DR1.
The places it falls short of the original;
Overarching plot exposition - I loved the ending of the original, but this one kind of falls flat when it comes to exposition at the end -though it does have some great 4th wall breaks.
Some of the trials at the midgame seemed a bit phoned-in.
Overall, a vastly superior sequel, definitely recommended if you played the first. Let it surprise you!

Created (designed and programmed) entirely by one person, Dust is a beautifully articulate love-letter to seminal games like Castlevania, Metroid, Ys and Devil May Cry. It’s full of secrets to uncover, areas to explore and enemies to kill in fantastically over-the-top ways. Getting a 1000-hit combo during a fight with dozens of badguys is not only immensely satisfying, it’s also almost effortless.
The story may not be that unique or special, but it’s charming enough. The graphics are lush, and wonderfully animated, betraying how it was all done by a single individual’s hard work over the last three years. But the real soul of Dust is the confident combat system, which struts up to you the moment you start playing, takes you by the hand and encourages you to have fun. It’s not Bayonetta levels of sophistication , but it doesn’t have to be. The combination attacks are simple but empowering, launchers take you into the air with ease, and the Dust Storm (a kind of magic attack with several spells to uncover) has you stun-locking herds of enemies, experience points exploding around you like New Years fireworks.
If games are a dialogue between the player and the game’s creator, then playing Dust is like sitting down with an old friend who’s back in town, full of fresh stories to tell and eager to reminisce with you about the good times.

ORION: Prelude has a lot of issues, but it's a lot of fun and it's really cheap, especially right now that it's on sale for 74 cents. Even the full price of 99 cents is probably less than the developers deserve for this game, even considering all of its flaws. The game plays like a budget mixture of Halo: CE, Borderlands, and Killing Floor: After selecting your class (One of three) you and your teammates get a short period of time to buy weapons, upgrades, and vehicles, after which a wave of various kinds of dinosaurs attack you and your power generator, which you must protect. If your whole team is killed or your generator is knocked offline for too long, you lose. Players respawn between waves, when you have the opportunity to buy more stuff with the money you earn from killing dinosaurs. Every so often, your team needs to travel to another area of the map and kill one or more large dinosaurs, which are often stupidly hard to beat, and cause smaller dinosaurs to spawn as long as they are alive. Once that wave is completed, various vehicles spawn, depending on the wave - many of which are quite reminiscent of those from Halo, including one very obvious Warthog shout-out.
ORION: Prelude isn't a pretty game by any means, but it's a lot of fun, and definitely worth the price. Pick it up.

text:
It's a real shame. This game is just a few steps from being good. A little more time spent on the story, or gameplay, and it would have been brilliant. As it stands though, I cannot recommend this game for the asking price.
Dust: An Elysian Tail is about Dust, a moody protagonist who most people probably won't give two ♥♥♥♥♥ about after awhile. He is assisted by a furry bat called Fidget, who the player will either be amused by, or will want to rip her ♥♥♥♥ing wings off and jam down her throat so she shuts up. I honestly found her the former. Sadly, she is the only character with any sort of depth. Most other characters are just there to give you quests.
The story itself is also pretty weak. You basically plod along doing quests and saving people, before getting involved with a race known as the Moonbloods, who are on the verge of extinction. You will only interact with one for most of the game, who is a shop keeper, and he isn't very interesting. You have no time to attach yourself to any characters in the game. It's also pretty dark, for what appears to be a game aimed at younger gamers (granted most of them are playing COD and GTA so who gives a♥♥♥♥♥♥ right?)
So what about the gameplay? To begin it feels sweet. Combat is fast, responsive, and powerful. You'll be slaughtering monsters for miles. Then you'll hit the point where you realise "This is pretty much it, just mash the attack button, or use wind blast with one of Fidget's abilities". It doesn't really through any curveballs at you, and you'll spend 90% of combat slaughtering weak enemies. Dying is rare until the last section of the game, which throws this 'epic' battle scene, with both allies and enemies. I lost my character in pretty much every battle, so it just turned down to luck to dodging any incoming attacks, I have yet to beat this section, but it was very disorientating, and it has well-passed its welcome.
There are also RPG stats and levelling, which serves no point. Items are boring and just at +whatever attribute. Yawn. There was no point to it and I feel the developers could have put their energy into something more meaningful. There's no point in crafting, unless you really want to breeze through the game.
To the developer’s credit, the art style is incredible. The environments are beatiful, and the characters are well designed. It's a shame the rest of the game is not on the same level.
The music itself does the job. Not outstanding, but nice enough. The voice acting is pretty solid, which is awesome considering this is an indie game. All the characters sound spot on for what they were going for, even if they weren't well developed.
If the gameplay or story had pulled its weight a bit more, I would easily give this game about a 6 or 7 out of 10, but as it stands, I can honestly only give it a 4/10.

It's a shame the characters in this game are animals, drawn in the particular style they are. People cried 'furry' before the game even had a chance, and it never got as much success as it deserves.
I'm not here to tell you that you have to look past the furry art. If that bothers you there's likely nothing I can say that will change your mind. If, on the other hand, you are indifferent to it like I am then you should really give this game a shot. It's a fanastic metroid-vania type game with some of the best animation I've ever seen in a 2D game. It's insane that this was created by one person. Killing stuff is just tons of fun. The combos flow together and feel great. While the actual powers you get are kind of few and far between for a game of this style, mostly being alternatives to the type of magic your constant companion can spit at enemies (you start out with a generic 'magic' attack and then get fire, electricty, etc.), it's enough to keep you entertained for the nine or so hours it should take to beat the game, and the core combat always feels fun.
The story is one of the better ones to appear in a game, and the voice actors are generally surprisingly good. Without going too much into it I'll say that the main themes are genocide, amnesia, and personal growth. I'm generally not a fan of the amnesia thing, as it's been done so much, but the payoff is actually well worth it here.
Definitely worth playing if you can look past the style of the characters.

What brought me to this game is the article that I read in Wired Magazine:
while waiting for an oil change, about two days before the release to Steam.
I haven't played the entire game. I've only made it through a few of the scenes, but I can tell that this is going to be a heart-breaking, painful story to follow- especially after reading the background of the couple who endured this story.
Many comments and reviews have questioned why someone would sell this game, not give the money to charity/research, etc. These questions can be answered by having empathy for the creator and his wife, the parents of the child displayed in this story. Not only do medical bills pile up, but also to continue making this game and deal with the grief of losing their son, this family lived off of savings for several months to finish this game, this masterpiece, to help not only themselves, but also (hopefully) others through the loss of a child in this manner.
The score of background music fits so well with the scenes of the game. The narration feels real and the script is on point. The mechanics of the game are easy to follow and smooth, not much thought process in the beginning (again, I haven't played through), as most is explore, point, and click. The colors, sounds, and overall feelings of each scene are truly cathartic and calming at some points.
I highly recommend "That Dragon, Cancer" to anyone who is looking for something with true meaning, something that is mechanically easy, and something that will allow them to go down a slide as many times as they want with no time constraint or urgent mission to accomplish.
This is a game that I cannot wait to finish, then play again throughout my life. This memoir is beautiful and reminiscent of "Death be not Proud", one of my favorite books.

I've never been moved by a game in this way, and I hope you'll experience the same. I've cried during games before, but it's always been inside a crafted narrative, played out by fictional characters, and that facet of "this is fake" was always in the back of my mind. In contrast, That Dragon, Cancer is less performance (I think that as a game, performance is a necessary part) and more conversation. Human to human. It felt like Ryan, Amy, and their family were not just telling but showing me their story, in the way that only visual media can. And I was there, crying and laughing along with them, like we were old friends.
It's small in scope as games go, but the striking, hyper-realistic audio coupled with the minimalist UI and low-poly visuals creates a quick sense of immersion. At once both vivid and dreamlike, mirroring the emotional state of Ryan and Amy. And in the first 20-30 minutes, I reached that place too. I felt like I was walking along with them all the way until The End, about 160 minutes in my playthrough.
I ran into a couple bugs that were annoying enough to warrant mention. I had to restart a chapter because the scripting broke, there was a voicemail I couldn't click, and a single letter played at 10% volume relative to the others. Annoying not in their own right but because I wanted so much for this story to play how it was intended. I will note though that I was immersed again within minutes, and the bugs ultimately didn't take anything away from the story.
If you're interested in That Dragon, Cancer, then you probably know at least a little bit about it, and I'm not going to spoil anything. Just buy it and play it, alone or with a loved one. It's a tragic and hopeful human story. It's not about the glorious triumph of faith, it's about the endurance of faith even when it's seemingly failed. It's gorgeous, moving, and well-told. There are scenes that will be with me for awhile, and I'm glad for that. Play it, and you'll find your own.

As someone who lost their mother to cancer a couple years back, I expected going into That Dragon, Cancer that things would strike a chord with me. While the game did exactly that, several times over, it was a relief to find just how much of a testament to life, hope, and joy the game was despite its grim subject matter. Regardless of your history or whether you've had to deal with tragedy regarding loved ones, there's a good chance this will resonate with your humanity.
I loved how That Dragon, Cancer balances interaction and gameplay with its story and presentation. Rather than limit things to one point of view, you essentially get a glimpse of events through every set of eyes involved, some of which I didn't even expect. The visual style is haunting even in its brightest moments, and music is interwoven as a perfect complement to your progress as you carry on. My favorite element, however, would have to be how the different Kickstarter backer submissions were included. I started getting choked up working through the hall full of art and photographs, and I nearly had to step away from the keyboard once there were cards to read. That's when the whole thing really hit home.
It was also nice to have the more gamified asides at certain points, like a kart race and a knight's adventure, to both lighten the mood and give you more of a sense of control. With the situation spiraling as it was for Joel's parents, there's a certain helplessness to only being able to stand by and listen to their retelling of it.
I'm sure I missed a thing or two on the first playthrough, so I'm glad there's a scene select option, but I'm gonna need some time before I dive back in. It's a lot to process, but I'm really glad this game exists, and I'm glad the Greens found the strength to share their story and the help they needed to make it shareable. It's not often I back crowdfunded projects, but I'm glad I helped make this one a reality.

I'll preface the following by saying that I'm a father of a 3-year old girl whom I love deeply. All parents I feel are haunted by the fear, irrational or not, that their child may die. And I wanted to know what Ryan Green, the creator of this game, had to say about his lost son Joel.
Was I touched by this game? Yes.
Did it drive me to tears? Yes.
Did I miss Joel by the end? Yes, and I think you will too.
But let's be honest here, this game is being published on Steam as a game. Is it a commercial release? No. Is it an art game? Yes. It has a message and a point it wants to drive home. But honestly, this game is almost utterly devoid of gameplay whatsoever. And the little existing gameplay is frustrating, hard to interpret, and repetitive. Is it a good game? No.
The game has essentially been constructed as a linear walkthrough of several mnemonic palaces or rooms. The player is herded from point to point, triggering memories, sound clips, letters, experiences with Joel. It is certainly touching, but also excruciatingly boring at times. The interface is so minimalist that it drives you to spam clicking, hoping an action will be triggered. Part of this is deliberate, since the game is communicating Ryan and Amy's frustration and lack of power, there is no question about that. However, it is also true that the game is asking to be treated like a game, and as such it should be judged on its own merits and demerits. The fact of the matter is that the clunky controls, linearity, and lack of clear direction distract the player and detract from the greater purpose.
I think Ryan and Amy deserve sympathy for suffering through Joel's death after a long, frustrating, and painful battle with terminal disease.  But they also deserve praise for the love they displayed by memorializing Joel's brief life. They also showed courage by bearing their own raw grief in a way that is unprecedented for games and may also be unprecedented in other media. People will remember this game for its originality of concept, its tenderness, and for the fact that it was a labor of love, a heartbreaking commemoration of a life barely lived. Because the game delivers such a powerful message of loss, Joel too will be remembered and missed by everyone who plays this.
I'd recommend this game, especially the scene where Joel will not stop crying late into the night, to young single people who haven't yet experienced the intense love a parent feels for a child. It will put you in that place mentally where all of us parents have been, and I would say that it is the game's strongest scene. I wish Ryan and Amy all the best.

My 4th best game of 2015, and for good reason. One of the best mashups of genres that I've seen over the last several years, Crypt of the Necrodancer has that addictive quality that will keep you playing the game over and over again, and enjoying every moment of it.  Strong internal game design revolving around the movement, not the rhythm, and yet the rhythm enhances every moment of gameplay. Dancing in between enemies and getting in the first hit while protecting your precious little health does keep you super aware of your surroundings, and enemy pattern movements force you to think outside the box, digging into the environment to escape or just give yourself a breather. A great solid soundtrack that's designed with the gameplay in mind, and yet importing songs works rather nicely too in a majority of cases. Look, I could go on and on about Crypt of the Necrodancer's design, it's smart gameplay, it's hours of re-playability, but I'm just going to get down to the chase. Everyone who even remotely likes roguelike/roguelite elements will have a fantastic time with this game, and those looking for something out of the rhythm genre will find something fresh and new here. Well worth the full price of admission, no questions asked.

I usually don't write reviews, but being an avid Neverhood fan and a Kickstarter backer of this project, I think I can give you a detailed review.
The main question hanging over the game: does it live up to be the true spiritual successsor to The Neverhood?
In short: no. Can't even say it comes close.
GAMEPLAY
Similar to The Neverhood, this is a 2D adventure/puzzle game (Unlike The Neverhood, no first-person segments.)
When it comes to the puzzles, it's a mixed bag of quality. Some puzzles are challenging and memorable, some others ridiculously easy, some are overly cryptic and not fun.
The Neverhood was famous/notorious for a particular overly long corridor where your ONLY objective was going right for 10 or so screens, only to wander back after reaching the end. In that game, it was original and charming. For some reason, they wanted to capitalize on and one-up this aspect of the original, creating tedious overly-long timekillers, and puzzles where you KNOW what you are supposed to be doing, but need to do a task several times in a cryptic way, going between the connected scenes over and over again to see if you are actually making progress.
Your loyal friend Beak-Beak, is great at being in the way when trying to interact with objects, and restricting SOME identical below and above-waist buttons to only be able to be pressed by a certain character is a great way to confuse your players. (Why can't Tommy bend down? Or Beak jump a bit to press a button? Or atleast be consistent with it?)
The game in it's current state, despite the year-long delay, is riddled with bugs, both graphical and gameplay-like, some even stopping you from completing the game.
STORY
Unlike The Neverhood, which created a clay-made world and sucked you in it, this game barely has anything going for it other than the clay scenery.
The big collection of cutscenes which you "properly unlock" at the end of the game creates a fine backstory, but your little journey (as in, 4 hours altogether if you don't know what you're doing) is still rather meaningless and bland. They added voice actors to our main characters, but forgot to add any lines for them, lol. Both Tommy and Beak Beak barely say anything despite being able to, leaving them completely characterless and uninspiring.
The rest of the cast is even less developed.
A fine little game for a couple of bucks, if you are new to the point and click genre and want to kill a couple of hours. Other than that just pass until a sale comes.

A lot of criticism on this one, so, to be clear:
This game is hard (not hardcore, but pretty hard for a modern audience) with amazing visuals (let's remind that Claymation is one of the hardest form of animation, and they did a brilliant job) and plagued with bugs. They need to fix audio, save states and crashes. All the reviewers made a point saying that is nothing compared to The Neverhood. Yeah.
But.
This game is made with 900.000$, for who doesn't know is a standard/low budget for a game made in Claymation by an indipendent studio, by a little team. An impressive load of work. trust me.
The Neverhood was financed by two major studios in 1996, when game selled so well that even Spielberg invested in the industry (Dreamworks Interactive was founded by him). Huge effort, and a bigger team, but low sales.
So, make another claymotion game is not only an act of courage, but an act of pure love for this forgotten form of art.
You can criticize the result, but pay respect for those who made Armikrog. Because is a visually stunning and good written game.
I hope for a bug fix soon, because Pencil Test Studio deserve better. And i hope for a sequel.

Without a doubt, rFactor 2 is an amazing game. It has a phenomenal and top of the line physics better than any track based racing game I've ever tried before. The driving physics beats out anything out of the market as the driving is overall satisfying and enjoyable.

All of this is backed by the thriving modding community behind the game that provide exciting and suprising content to the table. However, rFactor 2's reliance in mods isn't always good as some tracks or cars are proven to be somewhat clunky compared to the official tracks and cars made by the Studio397. But rFactor 2 still remains to have fantastic modding support.
rFactor 2 is seen as a left for dead sim racing games, overshadowed for Assetto Corsa and iRacing. however, one thing rFactor 2 has what these other popular racing sims has that rFactor 2's overall cost and efficient simulation remains one of the best bang for buck racing sims out there, even having superior physics than AC alongside with its physics able to compete with iRacing, a subscription based racing sim.
Ever since rFactor 2 was given development to Studio397, the game has a bright future ahead of itself. DX11 and VR support is coming, giving the game to address its previous criticisms and attain attention from the media and the public to show how rFactor 2 is a different racer compared to Assetto Corsa and iRacing. To show how underrated and overshadowed it has been, and how it has the guts to compete with these sim racers.
Overall this game is a sim racing masterpiece, despite its weaknesses and clunkiness.
(Now if you want to try out rFactor 2, I would suggest buying it instead of trying the demo. The demo is known to be an old previous build that is shown to be unfunctional on people's setups including mine when booting up the game. Sixteen students, one tropical island, one mascot, and the instruction to make such good friends with one another that, somehow, those bonds give you the Hope diamond in return sixteen times.  Only after doing all this can the class escape from the island.  This is what you, as Hinata Hajime, have found yourself dealing with after Hope's Peak Academy's environment got flushed down a toilet and replaced with an
.
For those of you who have played the first game, it's pretty apparent, immediately, that disaster and
are right around the corner.  In the form of Monokuma, no less, this is proved correct within just a scant hour of playtime.  Begin at the beginning, but, this actually is important for the story.
But let's talk about the story first, shall we?  It's not really the best, in my opinion.  Characters that seem written around their trope and the Rule of Cool, who have unnatural reactions to the occurrences around them.  The one good trade-off that we get from the former title is that you aren't always slamming through their points with your evidence and counter-points, but can sometimes agree with the few intelligent things they say.
Much like the previous title,
gives us a killing game in the style of Battle Royale.  Students must kill another student in order to escape the island, and all without anyone being able to pin the blame on the culprit.  Therefore, there is a class trial, where the game's main action occurs.  This is all parallel to a larger mystery that, as the game progresses, ends up intersecting right into the cast's circumstances...just like the first.
The whole game is littered with a lot of references to the first game, to the point where I would say: if you haven't played the first Danganronpa, don't bother until you have to play this one.  These can be clever little nods in the presents you roll for from the Monokuma tree, to blatant admissions by the writers that they are, in fact, practically mirroring the last story.  Here's the biggest failing, actually.
The whole story comes across as being written for the audience, rather than a series of circumstances being displayed to the audience and given credibility.  There are even points where Hinata's inner monologue and other characters' dialogues will lampshade this fact.  It might be held a clever bit of tongue-in-cheek by other viewers, but I didn't particularly enjoy it, myself.
The biggest problem, though, would have to be: the cases do not really make sense.  Even though the cases in the first were sometimes considered 'easy', this was probably because people were piecing them together based on the logical information provided to the player, since you're supposed to be investigating and coming to conclusions.  In this one, more often than not, motives, evidence, and circumstances will be entirely contrived to make the story fit the case, rather than fitting the story with the cases.
As mentioned before, the characters seem largely written around their tropes and Rule of Cool.  There are few of them to care about, and few of them to really surprise the player.  Much of the time, it seems their characterization is put out there for the writers to make a certain point, or to try to manipulate a response out of the player.  This doesn't really work, especially if you come into the game expecting more of the cleverness behind the first Danganronpa.
I'll explain further: in the first Danganronpa, not only were the situations given credence by how characters reacted to them and the circumstances surrounding them, but the characters themselves were given credence by how they reacted to situations, themselves, and each other.  In the second game, they all come across as either being there as plot tools or ways to
.  It's cheap, it seems to work, but it's not as clever as the first.
For all the failings that the story and characters have, the sound choices were still right up there with the first game.  The new tracks fit the locales and the situations, while the old ones from the first game are used in much the same way one would expect.  The only major error is that they overuse one such track, to the point where you might not be sure if you're about to witness comedy or tragedy.  Maybe there's a deeper point there, maybe not.
As for the basic SFX surrounding gameplay?  Pretty much the same as the first: it's there, you probably won't remember much besides the shattering sound that accompanies blowing through a contradiction, but this is good.
While Danganronpa can be best described as a visual novel with adventure game elements, with a little Ace Attorney mixed in, Danganronpa 2 seems to really want to push the
part of it pretty hard.  This, in and of itself, seems a really bad design decision, and in some cases it is: Hinata gains levels from walking from place to place, so there's no need for the jumping around options that they give you to eliminate that bloat.  Thankfully, though, during free time you can look at your map to see where your character-of-the-day is.  However, I mentioned that,
, but it's also a major clue - I can appreciate that much, at least - to the game's overarching mystery.
The class trials themselves have had a total revamp.  Nonstop Debates get hit the least with it, but you can also, as mentioned before, now agree with your peers when they come up with good points.  This really breaks down the problem of the last game, where characters' statements either only existed to guide Naegi's conclusions, or for Naegi to blow them away.
The Hangman's Gambit has been 'improved'.  You will hate it.  The letters fly across the screen, and you take damage when non-matching letters smack into each other.  You need to combine matching letters, and then add them to the hangman slots in order, otherwise you'll take damage, or dispose of them if they begin to get in the way.  There's too much waiting and luck involved in this though
Little duelist sections have been added, where the characters will rebut your latest point.  You then have to slice through their statements to get to the meat, and reach a point where you can slash in with your counter-point.  It's basically just an evolved Nonstop Debate in a 1v1 setting, and could have been explained better in terms of its pacing.  There's only one time where it's detrimental to use a keyboard with this control scheme, so it isn't too bad.
The Logic Leap is another new mini-game: you run through a TRON-esque interface to follow the logical path to your conclusion.  It replaces many of the situations where you would have to choose from a multiple-choice drop-down, but it's full of waiting and dodging easy obstacles.  It was unnecessary to add.
The rhythm minigame still exists, but, instead of just blasting through the noise, you also have to break down barriers that look suspiciously like the locks from Ace Attorney, to get to the final statement.  You then piece it together using the four cardinal directions, and that's your final statement.
The Climax Inferences have been reworked as well, to the point where you need to hover over the empty panels to look at what they're supposed to contain, and then hover over the options to see what they're supposed to depict.  Once you match up a series of them from the set you receive, you get a new set - it just drags out the ending portion, and also makes it impossible to fail, though that is better than going through only to see you made a mistake on Act 4.
Same as Danganronpa 1.  Nothing to really write home about, although the FMV portions are better executed.

No spoiler in this review. In a few words, Dust's strongest points are its gameplay, writing, and art design. The music and level design is also good. The story is the weakest part, not because it's bad, but because of lack of quality." There, now onto the longer review.
Ok, so like I said, the gameplay is great. Dust is smooth, responsive, and feels great. I used a Logitech PC controller and rarely had issues. I think he's a bit floaty when he's jumping off walls, but that only becomes a problem for some challenges. Combat is fast, chaotic, and feels great. The screen can fill up, and become hard to see Dust. This is very true in the final level. But in that case, just do the aerial attack and you'll find yourself falling at the ground real...fast...*SPLAT*....ew.
I might have confused you with the writing being strong but the story being the weak. What I mean is the way the character's dialog and delivery are very good, but the plot is lame. I'll talk more about it later. The character are strong, and very likeable, my favorites are Fidget, the Blade, and the shop keeper. I feel like he was a RE4 parody, and surprised he didn't say "What are you buying stranger?" Oh yeah, this game is filled with in jokes. There's even a "Castlevainia 2 Simon's quest" call back, even if it’s a bit cruel. The 12 friends you can find are basically an Indi game roll call, and a cute way to support the community. And I think that's the best word for the writing, it's cute. Innocent and nice, but can be darkish at times, while never leaving that family friendly feel. That's not to say it is all perfect (the villain is a bore, again I'll save it for Plot), but it's writing that anyone can enjoy.
I think all you need to do is just look at the art design to know what I mean. It's simply amazing. The colors, lighting, shading; man everything! It's just breath taking. I like the character designs, and love how everything is an anthro animal. You just don't see that anymore in triple A games. I don't really have a problem with it, but I'm not too picky when it comes to graphics and stuff like this. Environments, characters, animation...it's all very nice. I will say I think the anime scenes (which only show up at the end of the game) feel very out of place. I think there’s only 3 or 4. I would have put one at the start, then maybe one in the middle, and the last two at the end. They just come out of nowhere, and aren’t that impressive compared to the rest of the game. Save for the one before the final boss, that one is awesome. And I’m not going to lie; I think the villain isn’t intimidating at all. I mean, we hear him do a lot of bad things, but he’s no Darth Vader.
I'll just say the music was good to listen to while I was playing it, but a bit generic. Nothing really stood out, but it did its job well. It fit the mood, and wasn't annoying in the slightest. As for the level design, I have no real problem with it apart from back tracking. I know, it's a Metroid-vainia game, but I hate back tracking! I've heard people say it’s like "Castlevaina, Order of Ecclesia" but the difference is in that game, you didn't have to back track until you got to the final area, because it was huge. It's only hard if you don't know how to use the map, so read the key. Still, that's the main problem, so that's why it takes the hit.
Alright, we're here....the story. It's G E N E R I C! Oh god, it's bad. First: main character has amnesia. It's implied he did some bad things before, and works to rede- you know where this is going. The characters do their dance you know they’re going to do, and things will end the way you know they’re going to end. And the villain, oh god does he suck. I don't know his motivation, apart from racism. And it's never explained why he is the way he is. Even worst, we don’t see him >DO< anything! “The evil general cause nothing but death and destruction!” “Yeah? Mind if I see that? And no, the flash back at the start of the game doesn’t count!” And I know they talk about him and another character’s friendship, but we don’t see any scene between them. But I will give credit, the villain may suck, but our hero and his friends are great. Dust despite looking like the brooding anti-hero from most anime, doesn’t whine that much, and is generally a good guy with some funny lines. Has some corny lines as well unfortunately (“Fidget, I think things are about to get a whole lot worst” No kidding?). Fidget is adorable, and sassy. This is never a bad thing. The sword, while not given that many funny lines, is great when he does. But…even this can’t save the ending of the game….ugh. The ending is a huge let down, because you know what is going to happen. There is no suspense what so ever and comes across as just doing the motions. However, I think they might be sequel baiting in the end, and I would love to see another Dust game come out.
I can whole heartedly recommend Dust: an Elysian Tail! It's really great, even with the poor story. I would say buy it at full price, or at less at 10 bucks. Anything less would be a crime. I would say you've got a good 12 hours of gameplay, 20 if you go for the achievements. Have fun, and please for the love of god, don't open your eyes if you try to do a Dust Storm. Otherwise you're going to paint the room in vomit.

Recommended for people who've never played Journey, or aren't planning to. Not recommended for people who've already played Journey, and are expecting the same experience.
ABZU is a lacking imitation of the masterpiece that is Journey. No offense to anyone for calling it an imitation, however Giant Squid has marketed it as a successor of ThatGameCompany's Journey themselves.
It's common knowledge by now that Matt Nava (the art director) and Austin Wintory (composer), which were both part of creating the masterpiece that is Journey, created a new imitation game called ABZU. Unfortunately, those two talented and crucial people who contributed on making Journey a masterpiece, weren't enough to create a masterpiece on their own.
The underwater environments in ABZU are pretty impressive. It's clear that Matt Nava put a lot of effort into his 'baby', however the music was lacking. It seems like Austin Wintory just recycled some of his tracks from Journey, and didn't really put his soul into this game as he did when composing for Journey. That ending track of Journey.... What a beauty!
However, the main issue I have with this game is pacing. It's too chaotic and all over the place. You don't get the feel of accomplishment or that slow build up to something great. There are many design decisions that I don't understand. What's the point of collecting the snails? Did I miss something? In Journey you were able to collect lights to increase your cloak, and change your outfit to show off to your silent co-op partner. Also, it acted as a 'health bar'. Why was Journey's 'chirping' mechanic added to this game? Was it really necessary?
I think for your next game, make sure to hire a talented game director. Art and music alone isn't enough to make a compelling game.

ABZU has a legendary heritage to live up to in the form of its creator's previous masterpeice, Journey. As someone who considers Journey to be gaming's greatest artistic achievement to date, my hope for ABZU was an experience as breathtaking as Journey without being an underwater-themed copy of it, and I believe that it mostly delivers on that promise.
ABZU and Journey have comparable artistic design in the form of gorgeous, explorable environments with striking lighting that, through contrast between vibrant and dismal scenes, enhance one's sensory experience while they explore the equally  similar setting of the ruins of a fallen civilization. In this manner, ABZU dazzles the senses while piquing curiosity in same manner as Journey, but with an environment and plot that are easily different enough for you to not feel as though you're playing the same game again.
Like Journey, the soundtrack is by Austin Wintory, and it fluidly accompanies the character's progression thorugh the game while amplifying the emotions evoked by the art design. He's my favorite soundtrack-composer, having also done the Banner Saga I and II's soundtracks, and he was a critical choice for making the game come to life.
The gameplay mechanics, likewise, have a degree of fluidity and smoothness that helped make Journey such a unique experience and applies extremely well to motions underwater. Travel and interaction are accomplished with graceful movements in environments whose openess can be awe-inspiring yet not feeling tedious to explore in detail.
I have two primary critques of ABZU, which I might not have posted except in that, by mentioning its creator was Journey's art director, it is forcing itself to be comparable to the aforementioned title. First, Journey's method of preventing you from going off-course in open-ended levels is a creative wind-blowing effect that becomes gradually more powerful as you approach the boundary until it finally flings you back; it is preferable to the "invisible wall" technique of many games that lazily just stop you from moving beyond the gameplay area. While ABZU doesn't use an invisible wall, per se, their method is to very abruptly turn your character around and have it emit a light pointing in the right direction. I found this to be a little rough and tended to break my feeling of immersion.
My second critique is more serious and, in my opinion, is what really differentiates the two titles. Journey's beauty was, as the plot progressed, accompanied by feelings of ominous dread as you were made aware of the machines that destroyed the civilization, came into contact with them, and were forced to desperately struggle forward, inspired by feelings of wonder while being motivated by fear and tension. Part of this fear is accomplished by there being real and irrevocable consequences for being found by the enemies. ABZU does have conflict, but, without releasing any spoilers, I can say that it is far less pronounced and emotionally relevent than in Journey. There are awe-inspiring scenes were you are confronted by an enemy, and your means of defeating them in the late game is very entertaining, but they feel too tame in my opinion. I never felt fearful of the enemies, nor did I possess a sense of dread at what they had done to the underwater civilization; furthermore, there are no long-lasting consequences for encountering them, making them more of an annoyance than a threat. I feel this insufficient amount of danger makes completing the game feel less satisfying than Journey.
Overall, ABZU is a great artistic achievement that is as fun to play as it is marvelous to behold. It's experiences, borrowing from but not copying Journey, evoke an emotional and thrilling adventure through a breathtaking using mechanics whose fluidity live up to their predecessor's. As compared with Journey, it lacks the same sense of accomplishment upon completion and is, altogether, not quite as memorable an experience as Journey, but what game is? I highly recommend ABZU an enjoyable and beautful experience that lives up to expecations based on its predecessor even if it doesn't quite match it.

The following is my review of the actual game itself;
I went into this game expecting to cry a lot. My family is no stranger to cancer. My grandmother was diagnosed with Breast Cancer when I was around 15 years old. She beat it, or so we thought. It reappeared in her lymph nodes when i was 19. By the time I had turned 21, it was back full force. I was away for most of the year after I joined the military, and when I finally came back home, she was no longer the strong woman I once looked up to. She was one of the closest people in my life and the struggle of watching her deteriorate absolutely broke me. There is still a feeling of guilt and remorse to this day for personal reasons I don't wish to divulge. But now my Aunt is also struggling with terminal cancer, she's already living past when the doctors expected. My mother just underwent surgery on her lip for a cancerous group of cells. My grandfather had skin cancer on his nose. My other grandfather battled with prostate cancer. This game was going to hit very hard in a very tender spot for me.
All that being said, I was crying by the second scene. By the time I hit the scene with all of the cards (you'll see) I was an absolute mess. Tears, snot, shaking uncontrollably, all of it. I had to walk away from the computer for an entire hour to compose myself. It hit too close to home. I couldn't read any more of those god damned cards. By the time I had finished the game, I almost felt a shred of relief. But the credits even got me going again.
This game also deals with a struggle of faith in christianity, none of which I can personally relate to as I am agnostic. But it might reach out to some of you folks more than it did for me.
As for the actual game itself, the controls felt a little clunky, and even upping the look sensitivity felt a little too slow still.
There were quite a few completely unneeded mini-games strewn throughout as well, often not giving you any sort of instructions. I feel that these interrupted the flow of the story being told, and were too distracting. This would function better as an interactive experience instead of feeling like it was forced to have more game like qualities.
In short, I got more than I bargained for in the emotional department.
The game tries too hard to be a game sometimes instead of focusing on the storytelling experience.
Overall, if you enjoy extremely emotional (and true) stories, it's worth playing through. Just be prepared for the occasional mini-game that feels out of place.

This is the game that made me a fan of Hanako – not as polished in some ways as their later projects (Long Live the Queen, Black Closet) but a solid example of what they do: a unique mashup of visual novel and RPG that I don't think anyone else has really pulled off.
In Magical Diary the system is relatively lightweight; you can see all the attributes in the screenshots above. It is still deep and well-balanced enought to provide some challenge/interest on each playthrough.
But the real star here is the writing. The story, though short, has a surprising number of branches, each well-plotted and believable in the context of the story world, with some good reveals. Yes, it's genre writing, but the characters are well-drawn and the dialogue is solid – on par with or better than many popular comic series. Without spoiling anything, it also offers a pretty realistic portrayal of some kinds of problematic relationships teens can get into, in a way that is sensitive and not preachy (pretty hard to pull off, if you ask me).
The art style put me off a little, because I've come to associate it with ... well, bad writing, particularly for female characters. But once I got past that it really didn't bother me.
tl;dr: it's a unique take on interactive narrative, with an unusual protagonist and a well-thought-out world. If you like story games, give it a try.

It's really tough to downrate such a beautiful game that so much effort has clearly gone into but unfortunately (in my opinion) this game is unpolished and needs work.  It's probably worth me adding that I have never played the Neverhood,  so that hasn't factored into my review.
Pros
+ Fantastic aesthetics - the claymation is truly brilliant
+ Great music (although I hear that for some it doesn't always play)
+ Interesting puzzles
Cons
- Dreadful UI. I know this is a matter of preference, so you may well feel differently, but for me this just wasn't what I would expect from a modern point and click adventure. The cursor is the standard windows one - this may not sound like a big deal but I don't ever remember seeing this on a game I've paid for... I was so surprised in fact that I thought the game hadn't loaded correctly. Pixel hunting is rife in this game. While I can understand that some may not want the feeling of being handheld by having clear hotspots or a dynamic cursor, the game just doesn't give you feedback leading to a bit of frustration, clicking on everything repeatedly. Why? The hotspot sensitivity/radius is really odd (sometimes you have to click in a slightly odd place to get something to work); sometimes the clicks don't seem to register even though you're clicking on something that's definitely interactive; and sometimes when you're clicking on, for example, a button 'too early' (ie a puzzle somewhere needs to be solved first) you'd expect the character to press it (and it then does nothing). Actually the character does nothing at all, there's no feedback/sounds or anything, so you're left thinking perhaps it isn't something you can interact with (even though it is). I can't help but think that this is not where the puzzles are supposed to be. Clicking on a button for 10 minutes to get something to happen just isn't fun. I don't expect puzzle hints, I do expect some even vague clues on how to play the game. There's no inventory, for example - in fact it's purely pointing and clicking, there are no keyboard controls.
- Very little story or character development. Yes, there is a (text only) novella part way through the game but usually in a point and click I'd get a decent story propelling me throughout that compels me to keep playing. I didn't get that from this game at all. There's very little dialogue and not as much humour as I had expected.
- Lots of bugs, some of which are minor, others are more major - you can get yourself stuck in no-win situations, for example, and in some instances the save game function is not working properly (for instance when overwriting a previous save). I understand it only launched yesterday (at time of writing) so I'm really hoping these things will be fixed soon.
- Quality on the cinematics/sound seems poor, as though it had been over-compressed.
- Bit short for the price at (approximately) 3-5 hours playtime. Little replay value (as it is linear)
Ultimately although the devs doing the claymation did a stellar job, I really feel this game has been let down by gameplay mechanics, story and bugs. I would love to give this a recommendation but I just can't in its present state. Hopefully over time the game will evolve into a more polished version, and at that time I'll play it through again and amend my review.

My 4th best game of 2015, and for good reason. One of the best mashups of genres that I've seen over the last several years, Crypt of the Necrodancer has that addictive quality that will keep you playing the game over and over again, and enjoying every moment of it.  Strong internal game design revolving around the movement, not the rhythm, and yet the rhythm enhances every moment of gameplay. Dancing in between enemies and getting in the first hit while protecting your precious little health does keep you super aware of your surroundings, and enemy pattern movements force you to think outside the box, digging into the environment to escape or just give yourself a breather. A great solid soundtrack that's designed with the gameplay in mind, and yet importing songs works rather nicely too in a majority of cases. Look, I could go on and on about Crypt of the Necrodancer's design, it's smart gameplay, it's hours of re-playability, but I'm just going to get down to the chase. Everyone who even remotely likes roguelike/roguelite elements will have a fantastic time with this game, and those looking for something out of the rhythm genre will find something fresh and new here. Well worth the full price of admission, no questions asked.

I cannot help but compare this game to “The Neverhood”, since it was advertised as a spiritual successor to it and I don’t think it’s wrong in any way.
Pros:
• Some parts of the game are made of clay, which is a rare thing.
• Nice overall design, somehow rich visuals.
• Made me replay and realize the beauty of ”The Neverhood” for the third time.

Cons:
• Lots of technical issues revolving around:
1) localization (some of them fixed as of 1.01, but you still cannot choose the language via options menu or launch parameter / config), 2) subtitles, 3) cursor, 4) controls, 5) sound, 6) music, 7) transparency masks.
• Lacks polish and feels like an unfinished low-cost product, which is unacceptable for an adventure game which lacks branching plot and has almost none to zero replay value.
• Easy, boring, uninspired puzzles, some of them are recycled three times.
• Not heavy, but noticeable recycling of the assets.
• Inconsistent background resolution.
• Inconsistent use of clay, there is clay animated in PS.
• Not enough quality claymation sequences.
• “The Neverhood”s humor is not included.
• The story is dull, has no closure. Ending sequence is so ugly, it’s cringewothy.
• Generic music which hardly creates any mood. Truly disappointing work, Mr. Terry S Taylor. No lossless OST in the Deluxe package, low-bitrate MP3s only:
.
• The resolution of the assets could have been higher, last time I checked it was 2015.
• Protagonist’s sidekick exists purely for gameplay purposes, there is no smart or funny dialogues between him and the protagonist.
Even though the game has no game-breaking bugs and could be played through, the release version still feels like a deep beta, looks like the QA was either non-existent or made by deaf and blind people.

Expecting a Neverhood experience will leave you disappointed, but taking the game as a standalone experience will give you nostalgia of what it was like to game nearly two decades ago. Admittedly, the release is not without many glitches, some of which I can understand, some of which I cannot fathom how a programmer can miss; but if you're looking to scratch your head for a few hours, then Armikrog is worth the money.
I do have a few criticisms for the developers:
The puzzles are repetitive and many lack ingenuity. For example, to enter one of the first doors in the game, you must solve a simple slider puzzle. Eventually, you encounter two more doors where the slider puzzle is the key, each one having some additional tricks to confuse you, but it's still the same concept. Similar with the baby mobile game - the audio and sequences to match get a bit tricky, but it's still the same puzzle over and over. And then there's the sliding block monster puzzles...
The puzzles are intuitive, but the exploration is not. There was no outstanding visual clue that I needed to speak to the Octopi while playing BeakBeak in order for me to progress - this in turn made me struggle to power the generator to activate the lift to find the final glyph for one of the first puzzles. It also took me longer than I'd like to admit to even realize that the first Octopus lift was multi-leveled. Later on, when you feed BeakBeak a bug that allows him to fly, it's not clear that you have to click above him to get him to sprout wings first. In the same area, there's no visual clue showing that you have to click on the background etching in the wall (and not the button next to it) for you to move forward.
Glitches and frustrations galore - you can enter doors without solving the slider puzzles (again, a simple programming mistake). The railcars will always bounce on a switch, which makes traveling to another screen frustrating. Sometimes the audio will cut out after a cutscene. Sometimes you cannot pick up the octopus drop if you leave the screen and then come back for it.
Lastly, the character development could be improved immensely. When I played The Neverhood, I listened to snippets of Willy's story throughout the adventure and, although never interacting with him, I grew fond for the character. Klayman in the neverhood was a silent protagonist with childhood curiosity, which made him relatable when you're exploring a world you know nothing about. Tommynaut's and BeakBeak's personalities do not fit for an adventure-game, and their stoic behavior makes it difficult to feel a personal connection with the characters.
Regardless of the negativity of the above comments, Armikrog is a place I enjoyed exploring, and definitely hope to see more from this studio in the future!

This certainly was a journey for me. I really enjoyed all the characters. The characters were very expressive, silly and lovable just like previous games (Neverhood and Earthworm Jim). Now I'm more or less going to recommend and defend this game. Puzzle point-and-click adventure games in general are not too long. It's just their make up. Personally, some of the puzzles were fun, and some were confusing (just overlooking some things which made me not understand the puzzle) This game's design is not without flaws of course, but the sheer heart and soul that went into this game is breath-taking!
Now before people get all bent out of shape and start saying "Oh it's too short for how long we had to wait," feeling self-entitlted much? Do you have any idea how long stop-motion animation takes and with how small of a team Pencil Test Studios is? Some of those movie sequences could have taken MONTHS to make. The animation quality that Mike Dietz and Ed Schofield put into this game are incredible. Plus you guys are forgetting that like The Neverhood Chronicles, everything was hand-made with clay. Every room you stand in in the game was made with clay. In my opinion though, I'd say for the game's context, it wasn't too short, we had a good prologue, then a conflict, and then an ending. That's the basic principles for a good story, beginning, middle and end. Also you can read up on some of Armikrog's history on the wall if you don't understand the back-story for Armikrog, and thank God it isn't about 15 screens of writing this time!
In the game Armikrog, you play as two characters side-by-side; TommyNaut and Beak-Beak. TommyNaut is the main protagonist of the story that sort of has a hero-complex and wants to be like his older brothers. Beak-Beak is his best friend and is like a drinking buddy (if you guys have one of those, you'll understand his character). You're stuck in a fortress called Armikrog and have come to realize, a lot of events has happened in this place. I won't spoil the game, so you'll have to see for yourself.
I'm sure you all have come to a cross-road where you are really stuck and have no earthly idea what to do. You've clicked everywhere on the screen, you've visited the hint statue more than once, and still no results. This game does not want to hold your hand while you play it. It wants to make you think and explore. Just like The Neverhood, only Neverhood gave you no auditory hints. If you wanted hints, you'd have to visit your mail box and see what Willie wrote you (Which I might add is at the very beginning of the game, that's a lot of backtracking)! I noticed as well that Pencil Test Stuidos designed the game in mind so that you didn't have to backtrack as much as The Neverhood (thank you)! I will agree that some hints didn't really help me, but after looking around the environment, I eventually figured it out. My advice, every symbol you see, screenshot it, it could come in handy. Some times the hints are too cryptic/ambiguous to understand, just look around the environment  to understand. Some things you may have missed might be right under your nose. Look dilligently through the rooms and use process of elimination when you aren't sure what to do!
So I guess my verdict, the game is definitely worth checking out! But if you want to wait till all the minor and major bugs are fixed, I wouldn't hold it against you. Just remember guys, minor and major bugs are already being resolved by Pencil Test Studios.

I was rather hyped for this game, because I know people that worked on it. We even went to college together. But I have this to say about it: After my first death, second death, and third death, I was entirely bored. I understand Harebrained is going for a minimalist-vibe with Necropolisl, but that also makes me wonder what they spent so long developing (probably the level layout algorithm, monsters, and animations is my guess). I still plan on beating the game, but I will stop playing it after that.
I really like minimalist art, but something in Necropolis seems off to me. It probably has something to do with how tall the rooms actually are. I think this is probably the case because there is just too much left blank on screen.
I like the lock-on mechanic for combat, but the number of times I got backed into a corner without realizing it sucked. This made the camera do some uncomfortably sharp turns. I will have to try to not lock-on during group encounters. It is great for 1v1 fights, though.
The jump ability feels incredibly floaty as if the character and his/her weapons have no weight. I hate this very much in games.
The stamina bar actually depletes very quickly from the maximum amount available. This is very annoying and time consuming compared to how other games have trained players how stamina bars should work. Any time it gets too low, I have to spend time crafting food or potions to use which is annoying.
Levels are big in a bad way. My first death I was only on level 1, second and third deaths I made it to level 2. Each play through was over an hour, except for the first one, since I did not know what I was doing yet. When I died, it made me feel like my time was not well spent. I compare this to Rogue Legacy where when I die after over an hour, my time does feel well spent, because I would probably have cleared the first and/or second boss and their respective areas in that time. Oh yeah, did I mention there are no floor bosses in Necropolis? Having no floor boss feels rather lacking for when you make it to the end of a level.
EDIT: I forgot to mention the times after I clear an area and enemies are still spawning in it and/or from behind me. This is so silly and incredibly annoying.

The game is actually really fun.
Pros
-Challenging Combat
-Replayability (I find new weapons, biomes, etc every new playthrough)
-Nemesises (Some monsters fight other monster types, you can use this to your advantage)
-Crafting System (I find new potions every playthrough as well!)
-Small amounts of progression in the forms of books, normally there wouldn't be any progression at all, so they compensate by making the descriptions for them vague. you have to find out what they do!
-Ocarina of Time-style targeting system, I personally don't use it much but I'm sure some people find it useful
-You can cancel attacks by dodging
-invincibility-frames that you can time and use to your advantage in the later levels
Most people have only spent ~2 hours on this game and do not know the extent of what it has to offer. There's a thirty dollar price tag for a reason, guys.
Cons
-Not many enemy types, but about half of them are minibosses/tanks
-In place of new enemy types, there are hordes of tanks and instakill creatures
-Not much techno music like in the trailer :(
-Most secrets are just writing on the walls that pull back into a room with 2+ chests, the game is easy if you find them, however
-Not really balanced for multiplayer as far as I've seen, but I haven't been to the later levels in singleplayer so I wouldn't know
(Multiplayer kind of feels like an afterthought, as there isn't permadeath in multiplayer, you can respawn and ressurect unlimited times {you respawn with starting items if you aren't ressurected in time} as long as one person is still alive)
Conclusion: what the game has to offer is fun, but there is room for improvement. If they polished up on animation, added more rooms and biomes and weapons/potions, added classes, and more enemy types, this game would quite possibly be the best rougelike I've ever played. I kind of wish the company published it as early access and then added the content they plan to release as DLC as part of a free update, as they would compensate for the money they'd recieve from DLC with feedback from players. Most of the bad reviews you see are angry 12 year old/Dark souls fanboys who have never really played rougelikes, and are sick of the game because they're awful as it and have seen all the rooms the first few levels have to offer. I encourage you to give it a try and leave a positive review, as if the devs get positive feedback, they will release the rest of the game as dlc (and maybe even free dlc, at that) and the Mixed review status you see will shoot up to Very Positive
(Also keep in mind that the reviews are based off of ~700 people's answers)
P.S. Oh, I forgot about the humor. People are hating on this game for it's humor, and they're forgetting the dev studio's name (ha) and that the game's lore is based around an illuminati pyramid that can create worlds at will. Jeez guys, cut the devs some slack.
Call me the cringelord, but I actually find the humor takes the edge off of being instakilled 4 times in rapid succession. Maybe that's the real purpose of it.

I had seen it on sale a few times before and thought it looked cool but never took the plunge and actually bought it until about the third time I saw it for sale. I was glad I made that purchase. Not to say that the game was perfect in every way, but its pros DEFINITELY outweighed its cons to me.
The gameplay was easy to grasp (played on a 360 controller) and felt smooth the whole time. Although there weren't a lot of combos and attacks, there were definitely different ways to chain them together to pull out some impressive moves and finishers. There's a good amount of exploration and learning new abilities will see you backtracking and finding more and more areas to explore. I'm a huge fan of soundtracks and this game absolutely delivered! The music always fit with the scenario and I found myself listening to the soundtrack itself quite often. And the story, to me, was amazing! Do not want to spoil anything so I will leave it at that.
The only cons worth noting are the easy boss battles, which I've heard are a lot better when played on a higher difficulty and the occasional crashing. Concerning the crashing, and maybe this was just me, there is a way to fix it. When you run this game, Alt+Tab immediately and pull up your Processes tab in the Task Manager and Check Affinity and set it to just one core for the game. I don't know if this is a common problem, but it happened to me and it can get frustrating having your game constantly crash.
Other than that, the game is awesome!
