So, heads up?  Furries.  There are furries and while not overtly sexualized playing this game made me feel a little weird at times, because there are things that I would do to that bat girl, dark things that should never be spoken.
What?  Sorry.  Dust: An Elysian Tail.
The furries are a little weird but most of them are adorable in An American Tail sort of way.  You never really stop being aware of it, but you become kind of numb to them.
Past that, everything is fantastic.  Graphics are so pretty and the music/sound is fantastic.
Gameplay?  ♥♥♥♥ yes.  It's not super complex is the thing and usually involves just doing two or three different combinations of attacks (flying spin attack+magic worked the entire game, for example).  Beating on hordes of paper thin enemies is fun, though.  There are some that aren't as thin, sure, and the game kind of gets a little bogged around those points but whatever.  The game is almost entirely combat and I liked the combat.
However, the controls are only ok.  They feel a little slippery/slidey at times and for a game that demands some (slight) percision platforming at times, that's annoying.  Minor complaint?  Definitely.  I did die several times in certain areas because controlling the jumps is frustrating at times, but whatever.  I wasn't stuck at those spots long.  Elsewhere there are a few leaps of faith, though not a lot.  These spots are usually when you're diving from a high point to a low one, as you can't tell what's below you (and sometimes it's just spikey damage traps).
I enjoyed the challenges.  They were difficult without being overbearing.
Gear was not the most balanced in my opinion, nor was the leveling: magic and attack just trump everything else.  You do have to level your stats somewhat equally to advance further down the trees, and I might have dropped some points into defense/health if I wasn't forced to but I'm sure I would not have put as many in as I did.
End of story?  Good game, you should play it.
Oh, except for the one quip I have.  I keep hearing that this entire game was done by one guy, except for one or two parts?  If so, why are the credits so obscenely long?  Think I'm being misled a bit.

With how many negative reviews were posted yesterday with between 0.4 and 1 hours playtime, I felt I should pitch in on the side of experience. I started yesterday and finished the game tonight with a 7 hour overall run, no deaths and a lot of exploring and careful play.
The first couple floors did indeed feel somewhat easy, but then I'm coming from a background of previous roguelikes and Soulsborne games. Going deeper is definitely rewarding, however. Enemies do get somewhat tougher, particularly those infected by the grine (red crystalline variants), and become more varied. Unfortunately, I do feel that toning down the respawn system a little and increasing the difficulty on the remaining enemies would give it a better feel. At least once on level 5, I was stuck for a good while clearing the same area repeatedly until I could make headway through a Grine area. Other levels weren't nearly so problematic. Level 6 had the least respawns for me, but probably the toughest enemies I faced, mostly in single combat, and was easily what swayed me back to a positive feeling about the game after level 5.
The environments also become more varied the deeper you go, and without going into detail about them, I can't help but feel that some of the early reviewers may have seen the difficulty and relatively mundane environment of the first 2 floors and expected the rest of the game to be the same.
I found enough variation in the weapon movesets to be satisfied, although I mostly stuck to a rapier I found in the second half, with lunging light attacks that made evading and countering pretty easy. I do wish that staves did something other than a slow melee attack, however, considering how rare the offhand counterpart, the wand, is.
On the subject of combat, the animations do feel somewhat stiff initially, but once you get used to it, it works pretty well. There's no recovery time after attacks, so as long as you have stamina you can get in for a hit or two and either dodge out or block. Dodging also seems rather generous with its timing in my experience, as long as you're moving to a place outside of the attack hitbox.
Overall, it's a fun game, with a slightly prohibitive initial price tag, but I get a lot of enjoyment playing slower and checking everything, and had no problem paying for it. I've already started over, in co-op with 1 friend this time, and it seems just as fun solo or co-op. Just watch that friendly fire!

First off, I'd just like to say that I have never played the first game, and I have never read the books that create the basis for this game. If you are looking into buying this game, go onto t"The Witcher" youtube channel and watch the small little overview they offer about the first game. The graphics are absolutely stunning and run quite smoothly, the artwork and textures are brilliant and vibrant, yet bleak enough to preserve the game's "feel". Speaking of feel, this game has a dark, mature attitude full of corruption and disgust. The moral choices in the game require Geralt to make morally ambigious decisions. The plot has enough turns to keep things flowing, but it's not ridiculous. Plenty of sexual encounters. To conclude, I rate the game as a strong 9/10, and highly recommend it to anyone who is looking for a good game. I got 60 hours out of it and bought it for 2.50.

The Witcher 2, a superb game that has a fantastically balanced mix of fantasy, politics and themes. This game by far is in the top RPG's of this generation and should be played by anyone who is remotely into RPG's regardless of subgenre. With having to be careful of which skill points are placed where, creating the correct potions and playing each side of the story correctly, The Witcher 2 will keep you on your toes.
There ARE ways to make this game even better. I highly recommend playing the first game first, the porting your save over as there are points that will effect the story within The Witcher 2.
But over anything else, I highly suggest playing the Scoia'tael (the elves for people who haven't played the first) story line first, before playing the Order's, regardless with who you sided on in the first game if you completed it.
The Scoia'tael story line, in my own opinion, is only a third of the game. It brings up many questions without answering them, which are all answered in the Order's line. The Order's line also has many more plot changing choices which are available to the player, which may lead to you not enjoing the Scoia'tael if played secondly after the Order.
The Witcher 2 is an incredible RPG, and is deserving a place on your computer.

****ORIGINAL REVIEW FROM SEP 2015****
So here is  review from someone who has passionately played the gal civ series for a while. TLDR; I'd recommend if you are a serious fan of 4x space games or a gal civ fan, but not for most people (yet)
So what are the positives?
++The game has far finer control for making custom races
+The ship creator is much more detailed
+++The mechanic of ships having roles is actually pretty interesting (if a bit weird to figure out at first)
+++The addition of space resources to harvest for powerful buildings and ship weaponry and fleet boosting modules is pretty awesome and can really change the way the game plays out
++The wide number of tech trees makes custom races feel more unique, and each race feels more unique for the tech trees
+Space combat is pretty interesting both due to a large number of support modules and ship roles.
+The new space ports (which i hated at first) have grown on me. Now you can build big vessels by focusing five worlds together, which means that those massive vessels late game won't take 150 turns to build.
+More support buildings make it easier to specialize worlds and create more powerful empires earlier on.
+++The new morality system is much more rewarding than the old system, as it grants you bonuses in every alignment based on how many points you spend in each area. It really makes your empire feel like the sum of its choices instead of just paying money to change alignment.
Now for the negatives
---Planetary invasions are as dull as dishwater. There are no battle scenes, rather you just look at the planet to find out your odds. This needs MASSIVE support to fix.
---Still no customization of invasion forces. I would love to see it set up so you could choose how you want your invasion forces to look (even something simple like 30% infantry, 25% Heavy vehicles, 15% anti air, 30% air support would be a nice improvement in my opinion).
---Diplomacy is god awful in this game. No matter how close you are to a race, if they are stronger than you, they will attack you. It doesn't matter how many fleets you destroy with your super vessel, as long as their combined stats are higher than yours, then they don't care. I built, for example, a ship with over 400 stats in every offensive and defensive role, and could wipe out entire enemy fleets with every turn using that ship. I was destroying them as quickly as they could spam them, however, so the AI never let me sue for peace. Pretty broken mechanic imo.
--I wish you had the option that no player can build anything in another's ZOC. It really ticks me off that the AI keeps building starbases in my territory, then I have to either bribe them to give it to me, go to war with them, or accept that I can't have those resources, which really sucks.
--The campaign seems like a boring tutorial more than the in-depth fun storylines they used to be.
So overall do I recommend this game? Yes, I do. If you are a fan of stardock, gal civ, or are a huge fan of space 4x games. But unless you fall into one of those categories, I would recommend you try out Gal Civ 2 first, and wait for more support on this game. The good news is they plan on supporting Gal Civ 3 for a long time, so I am sure these issues will be addressed.
****UPDATE FEB 2016****
Now I left the original review up there for a reason. I want to show the known issues of the time versus the new ones. So it has been several months, and I have to say I am borderline upset at how little progress has been made with core components of the game that I would think would be high priority. But first, some new complaints altogether:
---They removed the better ability to control a planet's output. When I wrote my original review, they had a system where there was essentially a production wheel, almost like a color wheel in MS paint, and you could choose exactly where to put production. So maybe planet A was 26% production, 32% research, and 42% economy, while planet B could be 48% production, 48% research, 4% economy. They have since REMOVED that feature, and gone back to civ 2's mechanic of choosing where to focus, but with no fine control. This deserves a special mention since they actually removed a fantastic upgrade, all in the name of "simplifying" the game. There is, to my knowledge, no way to re-enable it.
--- You can not adjust the freaking sound sliders mid game without restarting the game. Seriously? It may have been there before, but I never noticed it until now. How can a game made by a reputable company have this kind of issue?
Now, the other reasons I am upset with stardock:
5+ months later, military invasions are still just "look at the odds and decide if you want  to attack or not". This is a massive DOWNGRADE from the previous entry in the series, and the fact that they have still not addressed it shows a lack of any interest to fix it anytime soon, despite how lack-luster it is.
Diplomacy is still identical. Any race you encounter will attack you if you are considered weaker than you, regardless of who they are. This means that relatively peaceful races in the game, including the religious ones, will just outright attack you for being weaker.This just seems so wrong. Other than that, there is no change from Gal Civ 2, so there is not much else to say, outside of it is disappointing.
The AI will still build bases in your territory, with not even a toggleable option to change their ability to do it. See my above review to get the general idea.
The AIs also still just build into massive debt. They just keep producing units, and go quickly bankrupt. Imagine if america suddenly multiplied their military budget by a 1000 fold, and you get the idea of what they do. But of course, these are usually weaker units, and your ships can ususally take them out by the fleet later on. This means that you get stuck in wars that go no-where, as they just spam to keep their numbers up, while you destroy as quickly as you can, making little progress. Since you can only dent their fleets temporarily, you will find it hard getting peace treaties if they get too large, just because tanking their military rating will be so hard.
And of course, we have to talk about the DLC. They have all these issues, but they keep releasing more DLC. in the five months between my original review and the current one, they released two new DLCs, but so many big issues that I have outlined multiple times (both in this review and in comments made to the devs in discussion boards) seem to go unnoticed/ unresolved. I did not expect this from Stardock, and I am thoroughly disgusted by it.
So overall, I am changing my review to no, not recommended, unless you are a massive stardock fan, and the issues above do not bother you. The game seems to be making no real progress, unless you want to buy DLC, and that seems to be their focus. The military is bland when it comes to ground forces, and the diplomacy is down-right attrocious. I was willing to overlook those issues in my old review because I had seen the game making positive gains, and I did make sure to note that there was still a lot of work to be done. But now that the game seems to have stalled on progress for DLCs and other cash grabs, I can not recommend this game. If they start making good changes and fix the bigger issues I have mentioned, then I will revisit my review and will give them credit. Until then, however, you have lost a customer here Stardock. Sorry.

That Dragon, Cancer is an experience I cannot recommend highly enough; not as a gamer, but as a human being.
I'll leave the story for you to explore for yourself. The trailer should give you the right amount of information to know what's going on. With that said, the vulnerability and honesty presented in this game is more abundant than any work, game or otherwise, that I've ever encountered. There are no pulled punches, and yet the end result (for me, at least) is a feeling of hope, not despair.
The sound carries most of the narrative weight, allowing those involved in the story to tell it from their hearts, with the abstract graphics removing any risk of distracting by the false facial expressions and out-of-place animations so common in games, and instead focusing on broad strokes of color and texture.
This game carries such a powerful story and presents it so well that I consider it a must-play. I believe that you will, too.
(EDIT: Since I've had to delete more than a few comments from readers that misread the opening line: I do not mean for you to infer that gamers are not human beings. Rather, the scope of this game encompasses broader themes than can be tackled solely from a gamer's perspective. I loved Gal Civ II and spent way more time creating races than I am willing to admit, and here-in lies the charm of Gal Civ III: the customisation. The game is a robust 4X space game but the real beauty comes from the fact that you can upload your own art to be the face of your race, or other peoples that you have got off the internet, so easily. Modding the game is as easy as dropping a jpeg into a folder! And the customisation of the ships, although a little fiddly sometimes, is really really varied, and gives you even more power to customise your race. You want a race of floating shafts in space led by your leader Bagpuss the Mighty? This game has you covered. The combat is still pretty simple (think civilization style), you watch but don't have much control. The building on planets is very similar still to older games such as Master of Orion, and works well enough. The map you do most the playing on is great, and works well up close, and automatically changes things to easy to see tactical icons when you zoom out further. The tech tree is varied enough to keep things interesting, and knowing the previous Gal Civ games this will get even more love down the line. The diplomacy is good (not great though), sometimes the aliens do make crazy decisions and go to war over the drop of a hat with a more powerful race, but it keeps things interesting. The sheer size of the galaxy is crazy when playing on the larger map settings and makes for a long game with a lot of scope.

If you've liked The Neverhood, this game is for you.
This is an old school point and click adventure game, with all the good and the bad, and although I really enjoyed it, it also reminded me of why the genre is dead today.
+ Amazing clay-graphics and beautiful not-clay animation (in some cutscenes).
+ Great Terry S. Taylor soundtrack and great voice acting.
+ Deep and immersing story, especially if you read the in-game huge text-wall.
+ Balanced not-too-hard puzzles that you can solve if you sit and think about them for a while.
+ For a Kickstarter game that funded 950,000$, It's pretty long. If you know what you're doing in both games, I believe it's as long as The Neverhood is, although in The Neverhood the puzzles were much harder, so that would make the game much longer on a first playthrough.
- Some pixel hunting and tricky hot-spots.
- Too much backtracking with no shortcuts.
- Puzzles are easier than The Neverhood, and sometimes not as original.
- Less animations compared to The Neverhood and smaller world. It FEELS like a Kickstarter game.
- You can't view your inventory, so it's hard to keep track on items you have on you or not. I solved two puzzles by mistake before using an item that should've given me a hint about one of them, and although I didn't need to use it later, it really confused me to hold an item that I couldn't use.
- Some repetitive puzzles that feel like an annoying mini-game you have to solve.
- A little expensive for what you get in my opinion.
And one last thing: you will need a paper and a pen when playing this, a LOT. I pressed the PrintScreen key and copied pictures to MSPaint every time there was some weird shape in the background, so I would remember small details for later puzzles. I enjoyed it, but you might not. It's that kind of puzzle game.
If you've enjoyed The Neverhood, it really is as close as you can get today, as long as the genre is dead. I felt at home.
I've bought The Neverhood when it was out, at the end of 1996, and played it for hours. I didn't have an internet connection back then, and finding out how to solve hard puzzles was freaking impossible. We had to ask gaming magazines for help, and I still remember how happy I was when I finally solved the BOBBY puzzle.
Kickstarter is a great platform that helps small companies "skip" big companies, but I was first disappointed with Broken Age - only 15 hours of gameplay (for both parts), for almost 3.5mil$. Leisure Suit Larry Reloaded, Dreamfall Chapters and who knows how many more games that I decided not to fund, and soon to be Mighty Number 9, were all the same. I knew they would be short, but not as bad as they were (Dreamfall Chapters is probably the worst of them all. Seriously, if you think Armikrog is a bad descendant to The Neverhood, you wouldn't BELIEVE how far The Longest Journey and Dreamfall Chapters are from one another).
When I invested in Armikrog, I already knew it would not be The Neverhood. It barely scratched the 900k$ it needed, and you have to remember that not every coin goes to game development. 10% goes to Kickstarter, and who knows how many more to rewards, sometimes up to 30% (!).
I knew that they would release a four hours game that would remind me of The Neverhood, and they did. Actually, Armikrog is FAR better than what I've expected. The Neverhood had so much more money, people, time and resources to work with, not to mention DreamWorks and Microsoft, who gave the development team everything they needed. you can't even imagine what great work they managed to pull off here with barely nothing.
Bugs are fixable, and they were fixed. Yes, it was wrong to release it like that. But would you rather them releasing it in 2-5 parts, like other Kickstarter project did? Broken Age was released, surprisingly, in two parts, because of money problems, and Dreamfall Chapters in FIVE! So yes, for the amount of money they had, I really am satisfied with what I got. I can only hope that a big company (like Daedalic Entertainment) would take these amazing people and fund a BIG project, like The Neverhood was at its time.
Armikrog is not The Neverhood and it was never meant to be. It's a good game on its own, and I had fun playing it. It's the only game since The Neverhood that made me use a pen and a paper. It has beautiful clay art, good enough music for the amount of money they had to pay for it, and fun puzzles. It's not perfect. It's not The Neverhood. But it's as freaking close as you can get.

NOTE: This game was given to me by the developer for review purposes. This did not influence my review in any way.
Blade Ballet is a multiplayer-only arena combat game featuring robots and a unique spinning-blade fighting mechanic.
Graphics - Title screen graphics are nice, with a cartoony-but-artistic feel to them. Interface graphics are nice and clean, and from what I've been able to see so far everything seems to move smoothly.
Sound - Title music is okay, reminding me of an old Saturday morning cartoon show. I can't comment on the in-game music or sound, as I haven't been able to get that far yet.
Gameplay - Blade Ballet allows you to select a robot from the lineup and enter an arena to deal spinning-blade death on other robots, or at least, that's what I can make out. However, as Blade Ballet is multiplayer only, includes no bots or ways of launching a single-player game, and currently seems to have no one playing on the official servers, I've not yet been able to play it.
I have noticed the following minor issues with the multiplayer lobby system:
. There's no way to select game servers manually. I've had 'AUTO', 'US-WEST', and 'JAPAN', but never yet found a game or had anyone join mine
. There's no way to get server or game stats in game, so you have no idea whether anyone else is even online looking for a game on the server that the game picks for you
. The online "Waiting for Players" state times out after one minute, making waiting for a game an exercise in frustration
. There's no way to go back to the main menu when you're sitting in a local game lobby all by yourself (ESC doesn't work after you've selected your robot)
Pros:
+ It looks nice
+ Trading cards
Cons:
- It's multiplayer only and there's no one playing it
I'd like to be able to recommend Blade Ballet. Well, I'd like to be able to actually play Blade Ballet first, and then recommend it. But in over two hours of frustratingly pressing "FIND MATCH", waiting for a minute, and then pressing it again, I haven't found one other person playing.
I hope the player base increases and I can actually play it, but for the moment I can't recommend it unless you want to buy a few copies for your friends. And given the asking price, I'm guessing that's not going to be very many people.

Half-Life 2: Lost Coast is a very short but enjoyable game. It was originally intended to be released with Half-Life 2 but was then later cut. It takes roughly twenty minutes to complete but is worth playing for sure.
Of coarse, we once again step into the shoes of Gordon Freeman as he hikes up the steep cliffs of the Lost Coast. On his way, he'll encounter several different combine soldiers. As he pushes on, you'll find Gordon inside of a monastery in which he needs to destroy a combine weapon. Short afterwards, he'll step out into the world only to get rained down upon by an combine helicopter. Upon completing his mission, Gordon makes his way back down the mountain to once again talk to the old man.
You'll have to play the game yourself to find out who this mysterious man and to see what he has in store for you...
All in all, Half-Life 2: Lost Coast was an enjoyable experience and I would recommend it to other players.

The Witcher 2 is one of the best RPG/Fantasy games you can buy. It has a very mature, political storyline, great characters and a unique but excellent combat system.
The story is extremely political and many times light on the fantasy, but that doesn't detract too much. One of the best aspects of the Witcher 2 is that there are many choices that you make throughout the game that truly change how story unfolds. The choices generally aren't obviously good vs. bad, so you can make your choices without feeling like you are fitting into the typical molds.
The combat is a tricky thing to judge as it's very unique. At different times I've disliked and loved it. It has a sort of a clumsy/awkward feel to it at the same time that it's concept is very good. You have one steel and one silver sword, for regular and monster use respectively. You also have offensive and defensive magical "signs" you can use throughout battle. You cannot generally heal once your in battle which means many times you'll end up loading more than you'd like if you aren't extra careful. The combat is excellent, but it could definitely use quite a bit of refinement.
The game took almost 40 hours to complete for me, doing a lot of the optional quests. I actually played the game 23 hours in, stopped playing just long enough to want to start from the beginning, and then played through it again. Since I played the first third of the game twice, let me say that the prologue is extremely long, drawn out and (relatively) boring. This along with the generally sluggish combat can turn people off early on, but the game is well worth sticking with, as the story and choices are where it's at.
One of my biggest problems with the game is that it is actually quite small/linear. Every chapter of the game you basically have a hub world where all of the main and optional quests take place. Once you finish the chapter, you're at a new hub world, completely separate from the old. It's not one seemless world, not even close. It wants you to feel like it is, but it becomes painfully apparent how closed off you are.
Although the Witcher 2 has it's share of problems, it does many things extremely right, and if you are a fan of Fantasy RPGs or adventure games in general, you should give it a shot.

TL;DR: While Steam reviewers seem to be giving negative reviews after only one playthrough and are missing content because of it, Necropolis still has a lot of core issues that need to be fixed for it to be a worthwhile game.
So I had a lot of hope for this game, and suffice it to say that I'm disappointed. However, I don't think that the Steam reviews for this game are attacking all of the right issues, and I want to express that most of the problems this game has can be fixed quickly.
The most common complaint in the highest rated reviews is that you will not see anything new in your second playthrough. I can confirm that this is false. I saw three new tilesets - all of which were vastly more interesting than those from my first playthrough - along with three or four new enemy types when I went through a second time. Most reviews that make this complaint have about a playthrough's worth of time on record, so I implore them to suck it up and play the game through again to give it a full review.
However, that's where the real problems start: there is not a lot of game here. There are only nine floors, one of which is a gauntlet that's the same every run. There is only one boss, and it is incredibly easy to defeat. The crafting system makes healing trivial since all required mats drop frequently, and it also makes it so the "horrible" maximum stamina penalty from using special attacks to clear packs of baddies is negligible at best.
Worst of all, the game is not hard. The first time I died was on level 6 in my third playthrough, and it was because I didn't find any armor the whole time and got mobbed. Single enemies have the same problem as those of Lords of the Fallen, another Souls-like, in that poise is basically meaningless; once you find a weapon that can stagger enemies in a hit or two, you'll never need anything else. Period. I wouldn't even need to use most of the substantial number of healing items I make if buggy enemy animations and unclear dodge frames didn't plague my progress, especially in lower floors.
All of this can be fixed if Hairbrained Schemes is watching the reviews. I'm going to hold out hope that they are listening to player feedback and will try to fix these errors. As it is, the game feels like a beta, which from my understanding HBS skipped in their release process.
Maybe with some constructive feedback that points out the real problems with the game, the devs can improve on the solid groundwork of this concept and make it a truly worthwhile experience. Until then, this game is not worth the price tag.

Gameplay: Pretty decent hack and slash side scrolling. A bit simple and about 1hr in you've seen everything that matters. And that includes jump attacking through the air and hitting the magic button now and then while you spin like a missile left and right. Decent if unspectacular. It will never pose a challenge if you play smart and keep your gear upgrades current. Bosses are in particular big let downs.
The RPG level up system is again very simple but gives a nice sense of progression and the illusion of customization. Which even an illusion is satisying. I liked it. But it really isn't deep enough to consider Dust AET any sort of RPG.
On a huge positive the game has the in menu option to turn “Auto Fire” on so you don't batter your gamepad to hell. I really appreciated this.
However a pure negative is the last level which an atrocious attempt to become something special but just becomes a chore. The game fills the screen with NPCs both friend and foe trying to become some "Epic" battle but really only becomes an eye boggling mess because of limited scale of what a 2D sidescroller can portray. Dust's magic attacks have a bad habit of blocking out too much of the player vision anyway but it truly gets painful in the finale trying to figure out what enemy is what and if they foes are even blocking.
Story: Awful melodrama to be honest. I was a bit surprised by the murder, genocide, and general cruelty in the themes contrasted to the disney bright colors and anthro characters. The voice acting and dialogue became so tedious I rushed to the "skip" option on the pause menu after a few words and still got the entire tone and intent of the story while cutting out about an hour of Furry fan fiction. If the story was supposed to be "GrimDarkSerious" don't use saturday morning cartoon bunnies to portray it with 4th wall jokes. Though I was amused by the jokes at times. The light humor moments were far more welcome.
Oh and those unskippable end credits. So much rage...
Overall I give it 6/10 (Furries should feel free to add 2 points from your bizarre vaguely pedo fetish) and to be fair a sequel or expansion could possibly alleviate all my problems by fleshing out the gameplay and settling on a more focused, interesting, and appropriate tone of story.

A hack and slash dungeon crawler more in the veign of Gauntlet than what so many have been comparing to Dark Souls. Co-op (which is instant drop in via steam friends list works like it should) is extremely fun and satisfying to play. Coop also adds another degree of strategy as you are able to whack your party members with your chosen weapon when you crowd enemies.
The controls are intuitive and responsive, and I didn't have to tweak anything to suite my liking.
The combat is simple in layout with both heavy and light attacks (the heavy being able to charge), and yet complex enough to not become mundane, with different move sets, different swing arcs, and different swing speeds for weapons. By the end of my first co-op run through with some of my friends we had all figured out which weapons works best for certian enemies and strategies for defeating them.
The randomly generated dungeons and levels all follow the same art style yet vary in genre, with the portalesque type humour coming from the giant pyramid and scribbles on the wall.
Through completing quest that the pyramid gives to you, you are alloted token which can be used to purchase different skills, abilities, and character colours. Gems are found as loot around dungeons, from chests, and defeated enemies and allows you to upgrade your health, buy recipies, potions and other items.
I have yet to complete a full solo play through however I can see myself running through this game a bunch more times.
Would reccomend.

Like many RPG games or even games with RPG elements, Dust can feel a little slow in the beginning, but after the investment of a few hours, the metroidvania style, combo worship and ambition kicks in.
The game has good pacing and an adequate duration, with my first playthrough easily exceeding 10+ hours. Optional sidequests and tasks add further incentive to invest in to the world of Dust and the experience overall is very enjoyable, although at times the combat can feel slightly repetitive.
Gaining new abilities is great but finding treasure chests may often feel disappointing as the yield from these is arguably underwhelming and never feels like a unique treasure but rather yet another chest full of currency and generic health items.
Other than those two mild irritances the game provides a solid reason to invest and fondly reminded me of my first experience with Metroid Fusion on the Gameboy Advance all those many years ago.
Anyone looking for something to keep them entertained while providing its own identity will most likely enjoy this title, although it is aimed at those with an interest in exploration and the RPG genre.

Comparison to The Witcher 1
PROS
- Combat more intuitive and engaging, with the combat controls more intuitive.
-  More loot and with greater diversity
- Added a new crafting element to the game.
- Skill trees/ semi-web, this time which allow you to get a few select skills without the need for the previous skill.
- Stunning Aesthetics and level design, the background scenery is truly stunning at times.
- Monster design, Enemy human design and setting design are comparable to the Dragonage franchise if not better (in my opinion).
- You have a scabbard for your swords instead of them floating on your back.
- The choices you do vastly change the progression through the story.
- Quick saving is very useful
- The journal entries for the fluff about people, places and quest write ups are cleverly done, written from the perspective of Dandelion the bard, it expresses exactly what you need to in a manner befitting him as well as giving insight into a lot of the Witcher 2's Lore and without reading the copious ammount of information in the Journal I would not of enjoyed the story anywhere nearly as much as I did.
- Unlike the standard affair of Elderscrolls games with the silent protagonist that you know nothing about (except that he is a prisoner of some kind) or the Dragonage protagonist, where is it practically all about that characters interactions with the infinitely more colourful party members, The Witcher has a main character unlike most other main characters. he has a personality, he has a history, when you walk down the street and a random pleb shouts "the White Wolf!" They have stayed true to the original game in one of Geralts main motivations into doing stuff is uncovering the mystery of his past and figuring out the events that transpired 5 years prior to the start of the game. because the character has a history that we learn in incriments it tantalises the players desire for more information and curiosity. I find the choice to do the game around the main character who has been in 6 or so books odd as it is usually a side character or unknown gets made so the player can imprint their own selves onto this avatar in game, but I am very, very satisfied in being able to play a character with a bit of character for once. I cared for Geralt and his actions had more weight to them than a dragonage game would.
- I am fairly certain that I could of played this game without any prior knowledge of any of the universes surrounding the Witcher as the whole motivation is geralt finding out himself which puts him in the same boat as the player.
CONS
- The original Witcher only allowed you to create potions at campfires out of combat and it took time, and effort to collect all the ingredients and you had to make use of those ingredients to first make an alchemical base with which to use in creating the actual potion. this point I feel stressed the difficulty and uniqueness of the playstyle of the Witcher as a race of mutant human. In the second game you can sit down anywhere and kick out a load of potions whenever so it never felt like you were without them.
- You can only drink potions outside of combat whilst meditating, they swapped round that you can brew a potion whenever you wanted but couldn't drink them unless sitting down ready to meditate. which defies logic as it requires much less time to drink a potion than brew one. it stops them being a main and integral part of the combat style and instead become an annoying 5 minute side distraction. One of the only difficult fights in the game I had no idea was about to happen so I did not drink any potions to prepare and that fight was so frustratingly difficult I had to reload before.
- Potion use is further undermined by the fact that you do not even need potions unless you are attempting the hardest difficulties. Where in the original game every time you had to delve into a dungeon you took a quick swig of cat and tawny owl and you could brave it, but you wouldn't know the enemies in there until you venture inside, then you could drink a potion that enhances the most useful trait against them and apply an oil to increase damage against them.
- The inventory has been dragonaged... before it was realistic, you could only carry the swords you had because you had space on your sword slots, only tiny things could be stacked numerously like ingredients, now I can hold 19 pairs of boots and still sprint down the road, the emcumberance mechanic they have used is broken aswell, it weighs 0.1 point for a single diagram of a potion, by the end of the game i was holding about 10-15 points of my 250 pound inventory in diagrams when i was carrying 40 odd weightless books.
- The Journal is completely pointless when it comes to being a bestiary for information on how to deal with the monsters you learn about. it was dissappointing as a few quests stress the importance of finding books on certain monsters to learn how to effectively deal with them. But all they ever explained was that they lived in nests or hung around corpses or some other rendition of the same thing (to deal with monster 'Y' you have to deal with the 'X's (where X means nest, eggs, corpses, tunnels etc)) the old journal gave you strengths, weaknesses, tactics of the monster, weaknesses and immunities which as you can imagine is incredibly helpful when they really matter. Unlike the Witcher 2 that you can fight any monster and it is just dodge the swipe and smack it a few times till it stops breathing even boss monster fights. In the original game if you wasn't fighting the right style for the monster you would do no damage at all, if you were using iron instead of silver on a monster that needs silver you would do a fraction of the damage.
- The Plot is, as you can discern from the title, very politically involved, far more so than originally. I prefered the relatively infamous Witcher Geralt going around dealing with issues that are personal to him and relatively contained, but in this game is so politically charged it goes against why i found geralt really cool which was his general indifference.
- The magic used by Geralt in this game is fun, but they have made it more of a force to be reckoned with. Which is odd for a con but to me the Witchers would use their martial prowess and alchemy skills with the signs as a last ditch ace up the sleeve for a desperate situation. However in order to have the signs cause any sort of damage you have to get pretty far along the sign skill tree which screws up any form of prowess in swordsmanship.
- The skill trees lack of skills is one of the main draw backs to the game, 102 skills, 51 skills total but 2 levels to each skill, and only 34 points to spend is painful, especially considering alchemy has been given one of its own trees, so if you want to be good at alchemy you can not be very good at magic or swordsmanship, they should capped the levelling at 50 instead so if you wanted to you could get the majority of skills or be really good at a few.
WARNING SLIGHT SPOILERS IN THE LAST PART! I will try to be as vague as possible!
Overall I understand I have more to say about the critical side of things but thats because I felt they were so close to doing it perfectly for me. I absolutely love this game, I was deeply involved in the main characters story, the combat was engaging and fun even if the uniqueness of the original games monster weakness exploiting has been lost somewhat, the story was deep and there are some really, really tough and painful choices to make. in particular the chapter 2 main choice (damn I spent so much time I almost didn't wanna Let Roache).
The way The Witcher has aged and/or The Witcher 2 has improved from the original game in a gameplay perspective I believe that if you are going to start this series of games, you should not play it retrospecitively. After playing the second one, the first one feels aged and clunky. But do play both!

First of all, this game is getting a LOT of hate that it doesn't deserve.
I played this game co-op with some friends 6 hours straight when it released and I had a TON of fun!
So it's a rogue-like game where you obviously lose your gear when you die.
You have quests you complete through playing levels and you earn points whenever you complete them.
You can spend said point to either buy tomes that give you a ton of recipes, attack power, defense and much more.
After every level there's a gold chest you can open with 1 point to get a higher tier weapon or armor set (they look cool).
When you complete a floor there's a small HUB area where you can buy upgrades for your characters (tomes, pots, etc).
This game has temples, swamps, ruins, engine rooms, etc.
So many negative reviewing people complained about levels being the same and uncreative...honestly...git gud and get the f*ck out of the tutorial area already.
Levels contain chests which contain potions and sometimes rare loot (armor sets, weapons) and sometimes a chicken who's a merchant.
This game has crafting, Minecraft copy spotted...get out.
You can craft meat, potions and other stuff to help you during your quest to slay the Illuminati.
Meat restores HP and Stamina that gets consumed by special attacks (see Weapons).
Potions can do: healing, buffs, summoning monsters, etc...
Items you buy from merchants are added to your crafting list so you don't have to keep running back to the merchants.
There's a few weapons to pick from such as hammers, spears, axes, swords/ greatswords, staffs, bows, etc...
Some weapons have special attributes like spawning a ring of green fire or just rapidly smashing the ground.
Special attacks use up stamina but this can be restored by eating some meat, so no worries.
Ok so, people also complain about getting the same enemies over and over, the only thing I can say is 'git gud and get to see all the other ones by getting further into the game.'
There are a few same enemies but they're edited a bit when you come across them and I personally don't really care if there's not as much variety in enemies (see Dark Souls bit).
Enemies drop weapons you can use/ swap with your weapons.
The only problem I really have is that there aren't any bosses on the end of floors which is really sad.
So people are comparing this to Dark Souls all over the place...It's nothing like dark souls.
When a game is 3D and uses swords and a rogue-like mechanic is suddenly becomes Dark Souls?
Back to the lack of enemies, people complain about it in Necropolis but seriously all of you Dark Souls fans...take of your pink glasses and look at all the goddam knights/hollow enemies Dark Souls series keep using over and over (Especially 2 and 3).
It's a great game and I recommend this to people who want to have a fun experience with a great Rogue-Like game.
I have to agree 28$ is a bit much at the moment, but I have high hopes for this game and you should support it.

Let me just start by saying, if you're very religious, I recommend not playing this game. The Binding of Isaac can have sensitive material that might be offensive to some people.
Aside from that, I enjoy this game very much. Isaac is a six-ish year old boy who changes over time during the game from a weak, naked boy to a full-on killing machine. Gathering items changes your gameplay that either helps or harms you. Items start to stack on and you soon find yourself in a position where you don't want the game to end.
It all feels like a minigame, almost. The game can be insanely short or completely too long, based on your gameplay.
I have heard that "gamers hate innovation" and "gamers are destroying the gaming industry", and it's true. Gamers are scared of what innovation might bring and wish to stay in an era with no innovation at all. But without innovation, popular gaming franchises wouldn't have hit the shelves and become the games we know and love today.
The Binding of Isaac is one of those games.
The game does have some pro's and con's about overall gameplay:
Pro's:
-The game is randomly generated and players never have the same gameplay twice
-Collecting items is basically the equivalent of "leveling up" and can help you tremendously throughout the rest of the game
-Coins are found scattered across the maps and can be used in the Shop to purchase more items
-Items are never found more than once in one game (with the exception of a few items, such as the Cube of Meat)
-You can unlock more items by completing challenges or achievements
Con's:
-Wrath of the Lamb can make your game either extremely easy or extremely hard, depending on the types of items the game generates
-Can have very sensitive material and might be offensive to religious players
-Can generate rooms with an overwhelming amount of enemies, and it is near impossible to avoid all of them
Overall, I would rate this game 9/10. It is incredibly fun and can help you take your mind off of more pressing matters. The choice now is... which tarot card do I take?

Final Fantasy VII is universally recognized as the best installment of the series, and maybe one of the best RPG ever. I played the original, on the PS1, all the way through at least four or five times. FF7 was the only game I liked enough to get me to shell out the extra 20 bucks for the guide, just so I could find and/or beat every little side quest or hidden area. It absorbed many countless hours of my youth.
Not to long ago, I found FF7 on Steam and quickly bought it for second time. Now I never did find my old guide (not that you need it with the internet), but I played Final Fantasy VII once again and loved every minute of it. I was reminded of it’s great story and characters, awesome weapons with unique leveling up, the way powers can be mixed together, and the great interface for both battle and world map. I enjoy that you can spend hours racing giant birds around for an awesome hidden item or fighting through a tough dungeon for a unique weapon. But the game doesn’t make you, very little of the required gameplay is grinding. This game does not require continuous, fast button mashing. So if you like to take frequent, short breaks from the game controller to enhance your video gaming experience, Final Fantasy VII is great for that.
After completing this game once again, even though it took a bit longer because of that pesky thing known as a job, I still find it to be my favorite game ever. It has everything that made it great on the PS1, but the PC version is much smoother because of the updated hardware. If are a fan of the original, have played others in the series, or just enjoy RPGs or good games, it will be more than worth it to buy FF7, a great game all around.

If you're at all a fan of visual novels then Magical Diary is one well worth picking up. If you're not a fan of the genre but feel like giving one a try it also is, if you're not the type of person who'd be put off by it being a romantic comedy. It can be cliched at times, but it's one of those things that prove cliches aren't necessarily bad, here they make a fun sweet game full of likable characters. And sometimes those cliches get turned on their ears when you aren't expecting them.
So far as dating games go, Magical Diary is head and shoulders above many of them. All of the love interests you can choose from have a wide variety of scenes to see with them, many long before you're ever locked into their path, so you don't get get that "We've met each other twice for two seconds, now let us date!" feeling that lesser games can leave you with; by the time the main character's thoughts seriously turn to romance you've seen enough of the person she's chosen to understand why she wants to be with them. I also really appreciate that in almost all the routes you can aim for a friendship ending instead of a romantic one, so if you decide none of the characters appeal romantically you can still aim for an ending besides being all alone.
More importantly, you can get a good variety of scenes with characters you AREN'T chasing too. This isn't one of those games where you must constantly stay focused on the love interest you choose from the moment you start to get a good ending. And there are characters you can't date with plotlines spread through the game too, giving the world of the school a more fleshed-out feeling.
The dungeon sections are also great little puzzles. Periodically in the game you're tested on how you're doing in your studies by being stuck in a small dungeon and having to find your way out. The thing that makes these sections great is that there are many many ways to beat the puzzles each time, depending on what types of magic you've focused on. There's no set path of classes which you MUST take to make it, so long as you don't spend almost every day resting or hanging out in the gym you're almost certain (I won't say guaranteed, but you should have options) to have something in your spellbook that will see you through even if it isn't immediately obvious.

Paladins: Champions of the Realm is a team-based shooter where players select between a variety of heroes and fight to capture objectives. Brawl it out in 5v5 matches as one of a colorful cast of characters, each imbued with their own abilities. Players can further customize their characters by enhancing some abilities over others through an extensive card system. *Contains spoilers for the very beginning of the game*
The spiritual successor to The Neverhood. A game that I love and cherished in my childhood for its creativeness, that dark, scarey tone, and bits of comedy. This game however feels lacking in just about all of that. You play as Tommynaut, 1 of 3 brother astronauts that are sent on a planet saving mission to find P-tonium, a source of fuel they rely on. Tommynaut ends up crash landing, and takes shelter in the fortress Armikrog where the game takes place.
Puzzles: The game did not feel as difficult as The Neverhood, but then that may have been because the younger me had trouble with the Neverhoods insane puzzles, but even when I played it recently, the puzzles were still difficult... Armikrog did not have that problem. I had trouble with one puzzle because I overlooked one teeny tiny detail so the answer was incorrect. Aside from that, some puzzles took no time at all, some took no more than 5 minutes, 10 minutes at the VERY most.
Stability: Being Day 1 Release, the game did have some bugs, despite being delayed for the past two months. Nothing game breaking, just annoying. Some sound issues, clipping issues, and a save issue that set me back a few minutes.
Length: Very short. Granted you can only put so much into a point and click adventure/puzzler that takes place in a fortress, I finished this game in about 5 hours. The neverhood took me 6-8 hours last I played it, and I played it straight through with no breaks. Plus the neverhood felt more full, having a much larger world to explore, a 3D point of view, and tons more puzzles. Armikrog recycled 2 seperate puzzles 3-4 times each, and the others were similar in concept.
Music: I couldnt tell you how much I loved the music from the Neverhood, but the music in Armikrog does not live up to that unfortunately. Armikrogs music was good when I could hear it, but the game's bugs often cut the music for me, leaving me with very little noise. The music in the Neverhood was a lot of fun, you even find yourself singing along to the gibberish sometimes, but Armikrogs music was a bit more serious, more mysterious, less entertaining.
Overall: I am honestly disappointed in this game. I DID have fun while playing it, but it just felt too short, too easy, and did not live up to the Neverhood's legacy. If you enjoyed the neverhood, you might still enjoy this game, but dont set your hopes too high.
** END OF GAME SPOILERS**

Warning: Minor spoilers ahead. You'll see why.
In my personal opinion, The Neverhood was a game whose charm arose primarily from the presentation and the unspoken intrigue. You have no idea who or what Klaymen, or for that matter, anything else is, and set out to find the story of the world and yourself by solving a series of often lackluster puzzles. The things that really string you along are the occasional zany claymation sequences, and the infodisks scattered around that contain segments of Willie telling the game's story in snippets. It has a hook that holds it through, and the puzzles, while cumbersome and uninspired, are not usually a major nuisance as long as you have pen and paper handy.
Armikrog dispels half of its intrigue out of the gate by endowing its protagonists with, star talent as they may be, some of the most boring (and poorly recorded) voices I've ever heard, and giving you a synopsis of the backstory in the damn title sequence. You want to know the story? Here it is: you need to find a rare energy source on another planet to help sustain your people, but end up crash-landing during your trip.
The game assassinates its own intrigue before you even get to play it. I don't have any questions about who these oddballs are, they're just some dumb shmucks on a delivery run. There is a Hall of Records equivalent a short ways into the game detailing the life of an enslaved miner from some point in history that is infinitely more interesting than whatever is going on here!
Once you do start playing, you'll probably get about 3 screens in before the utter purple monkey dishwasher leaps of logic required to progress start to sink in. Blocking a doorway with a large, fuzzy creature will cause a tentacle elevator to descend from a trapdoor in the ceiling. The thing those tentacles are attached to is actually a key item and massive plot-dump device (speaking in an alien language so as to blue-ball you as much as possible with regards to deciphering what lore is left to uncover), but only if interacted with while playing solo as Beak-Beak. There are no prompts or hints whatsoever towards this. The incidental characters so far have not been a bizarre face sticking out of a TV, a murderous green crablike creature, nor a giant robot with a teddy bear. Instead, they have been Abrahant Lincoln and Thomas Jeffersant. Get it? Like the historical figures, except ants. Ha. Ha. Ha.
And then I spent a solid hour working on the Planetarium puzzle, which is of the breed of puzzles that you know exactly what to do with from one quick prod at it, but takes an agonizing length of time to actually execute.
It is also at this point that I feel the need to mention that the game is, despite its delays, bugged out the butt. Clicking hotspots are extremely finicky sometimes, the wall-mounted rider will always get stuck on certain sections until you manage to dislodge it, and clicking on the wrong thing at the wrong time WILL break the game and render progress impossible. Of course, if you don't click on everything in every possible way then you're not going to find out how to progress either!
Neverhood was an interesting story told in a fantastical manner, with a series of dumb puzzles standing in your way as an excuse to call it a game. Armikrog may yet have a fascinating story to begin to unravel, but has been such an abjectly miserable gameplay experience that I can't bring myself to care enough to continue bashing my head against it.
It's still well animated, at least.

I had a number of things spoiled for me before I even bought this game, so I was a bit skeptical as to whether or not I would enjoy it to its full extent. My fear was severely misplaced. Even if you know the answers or the final outcome, the mysteries in this game are more than complex enough to be perplexed by them a second time around. What surprised me the most though, was the emotion this game had to offer. Dangan Ronpa 1 was fantastic in a lot of ways, but I feel like this one was more emotional overall. In the first game, there are 2 trials in particular that are execptionally emotional to me. In this game, there are 3. It may just be one more, but as this game's 2nd, 4th, and 5th trial all made me cry like a baby...well, I think that speaks for itself. In short, buy this game. Buy it right now, or wait for a sale. It doesn't matter. Just make sure you buy it. It provides more than enough hours of play just by going through the main story once. Beyond that, there's also extra game modes to be played (like island mode, which can sometimes take just as long as the actual main story to complete 100%), achievements to be aquired, in game items to get, etc. You'll get your money's worth no matter what you pay. It's an emotional rollercoaster with some incredibly tense moments and complex mysteries. I would reccommend playing Dangan Ronpa: Trigger Happy Havoc first, as multiple references are made to it in the story, but that's also not required if you really don't want to. The one problem I have with this game is that some of the characters can fade into the background if you don't spend your free time with them, and there's never enough free time in the main story. Then again, that's the whole reason they have island mode and let you replay chapters once you've beaten them. Great game from a great series, can't wait for Dangan Ronpa 3.

I have very mixed reviews about Danganronpa 2: Goodbye Despair. In all honesty, I think I would have preferred to just see this an anime. I loved the story but when it came down to the trials, the game honestly was incredibly boring. The story begins with you, as Hajime Hinata, preparing to enter Hope's Peak Academy. Suddenly, you find yourself drawn to a mysterious door. After entering the door, you find yourself in a classroom with 15 other students. A rabbit named Usami introduces herself and says that you've all been brought on a school field trip and that everyone is meant to get along. The classroom falls away and reveals a tropical paradise. Suspicion slowly fades and as everyone begins to enjoy themselves, Monokuma, the derranged half/half bear from Danganronpa 1 shows up and crashes the party. You're told that you need to kill someone and get away with it to get off of the island. Sound familiar?
The game gives the big reveal from Danganronpa 1 right away, that you're students from Hope's Peak Academy that have had your memories erased, the world destroyed, and you were brought to this island for an unknown purpose. The great twist in the story is finding out the true nature as to why you were brought to the island and this is where the game really shines. Unravelling that mystery is done really well. However, the main gameplay element of the game, the class trials, are the game's biggest weakness. The trials were unnecessarily extended out and minor details were given extreme importance just for the sake of placing in another minigame or extra feature. That brings me to a second issue I had with the trials. Since this game was originally for the PS Vita, the new features were more made for the Vita rather than the PC. The new slashing mini-game during the trials seems especially the case. The "Improved Hangman's Gambit" also seems to be the case. The best non-Vita specialized minigame were the rebuttals by various students, but that feature was also a problem since it caused a lot of unnecessary extension of the trials. You usually had to rebute someone's gut feeling who was rebuking your evidence-based theory. The trials seemed to get more and more frustrating as they went on, as the developers seems to really try hard to make each trial extend out into 3-hour long affairs (broken into 2 convenient parts).
Keeping all that in mind, I think I give a light recommendation to Danganronpa 2. If there is an anime coming out based on this game, I would definitely say wait for that to come out. It might also be better to just watch a playthrough and get through the first couple of trials to see if it's something you'd be interested in.

A metroidvania with solid combat that misses a few basics of the genre.
I've reached a point with Dust where I don't really care to complete the game. I've had fun with it for the ~10 hours I've played, but at this point I've kind of realized that the game doesn't have anything else to reveal, and so I'm not really compelled to keep playing.
The basic combat is fun, but the fact that your gear and upgrades don't actually affect how you fight enemies means that it gets stale after a while. You have the same weapon throughout, and gear upgrades for the most part are just that: straight upgrades, with little to make the player think, "would a little more of x or y be better for how I play." Unlike the game that I consider to be the gold standard of the genre, SotN, where finding a new weapon might make you more powerful, but also can change how you approach combat.
The controls seem good at first, but as you advance you find yourself needing to platform more and more, and the controls are too sloppy for really precise platforming controls. They animations and control are set up to create a flashy, exciting combat experience, with lots of extraneous movements by your character that look cool, however these extraneous movements create moments of real frustration when you're trying to precisely jump on platforms or navigate areas with other environmental hazards such as ground and wall spikes.
The story is bad, basically a crappy Western interpretation of crappy anime/JRPG tropes, but it's not too intrusive.
The art is a mixed bag: the environments are incredibly gorgeous, but the character and enemy sprites look like a high schooler who might be good with a lot more practice drew them. Again, there is a heavy influence from mediocre anime in all of the character designs.
So finally, I'm going to give this a tentative recommendation, but only if you can buy it on sale.

I have plenty of Steam games in my library but have never felt compelled to review one. Until now !
ABZÛ is not simply a game. It is a masterpiece delivering something so refreshing from the norm.
Once I'd started to play through this graphically stunning puzzle/adventure game I literally just couldn't drag myself away. I just had to play it through to completion.
2.8 hours that took me (or about 2 hours 50 mins). No that isn't a massive amount of time but given the work that has gone into this colourful, mystical creation I think it's fair.
Difficulty wise it isn't too hard. In fact I reckon young teenagers would be able to complete this without much difficulty.
But I don't think the level of difficulty matters as long as the game engrosses you and gives your brain just enough of a challenge to make you want more.
ABZÛ achieves that easily. The underwater environment is spectacular, as are the animations. Using a gamepad I found controlling the diver to be easy.
There is a rather touching storyline to this rich graphical adventure too. All told without a single word being spoken.
I must also mention the music which plays throughout your journey. Each piece has been composed beautifully to match the scene being experienced. Everything - graphics, gameplay, audio and storyline come together seamlessly to create a game you will remember.
You'll even remember the credits (don't stop playing as they roll).
"But 2.8 hours and it's all over !" I hear you say. Well not if you enjoy this as much as I did. I can't wait to play through this again and to experience the relaxing beauty of ABZÛ and it's extensive recreation of a marine life rich underwater world.
Besides, their are achievements to be gained (objects to be found etc) and I can pretty much guarantee you'll be left with a good few of these to attain after the first playthrough.
ABZÛ is the first game in a long, long time which kept me entertained into the early hours (4am!). So good I didn't want to sleep!
If you are into nature, especially aquatic life, you  will also find this an educational experience. I won't say why as that would be a spoiler.
Does ABZÛ lack anything? Yes - A sequel ! I would love to see what else this developer could come up with. Perhaps with a few slightly more demanding puzzles to keep you in a  scene longer and overall extending a game to at least 5 hours.
I'd recommend this wonderful undersea adventure to anybody. It's a work of art !

rF2 is an improvement over the most excellent rF1 (king of online racing of yesteryear) but it needs a lot of polish around the edges to compete with other current titles of the genre. The physics model, tyre & weather simulation and top notch FFB are what differentiates rF2 and makes it "just about" worth its current price-tag (p2p online).
On the other hand the dated graphics, interiors/cockpits, lacklustre tracks (laser scanned anyone?), no official licenses, minimalist steam workshop implementation and non-existent multiplayer lobby beg the question of choosing rF2 (pay to play online) over racing titles like iRacing (sub and fees) or Assetto Corsa (perhaps Project Cars too), which are seemingly more accomplished in much less development time. To put it in perspective, in a mere couple of years, Assetto Corsa has improved by leaps and bounds and currently established as the preferred choice of the modding community and online league racing sim enthusiasts.
In spite of the stiff competition, I would recommend rF2 to dedicated and serious racing enthusiasts for the sim experience. In addition, now that Studio 397 have taken over, the development road-map looks very promising (monthly updates, DX11 at long long last, UI revamp, VR, spotting, mp lobby etc) which at long last will bring rF2 a much wider recognition (not just for purists) and instead of a maybe vote it would be a definitely yes to buy vote.
-----
EDIT: A small correction, as mentioned in the comments, rFactor2 now includes online multiplayer in the price tag (no more online subscription or lifetime payment). Thanks.

So you are thinking of buying a Dinosaur FPS... for $1.  What does that mean?  What can you expect?
This game is heavily based on Unreal Tournaments invasion gameplay mode, you and a group of other people spawn and try to 'protect your base' from swarms of varying types of dinosaurs.  Some are simple to spray and smear, others require larger amounts of bullets, etc etc.
Does it even stand out from mods you can download for unreal?
Personally... I enjoyed the little bit of it I played.  While half of the features I was expecting to see didn't exsist or work, the game itself worked like you'd expect.  Aim gun, pull trigger, watch dinosaur get mad/die, rinse and repeat.  Some of the dinos had some entertaining bugs, but overall nothing too special.
What makes this game a bit interesting is the melee system they added in for PVP.  It almost feels like PVK (Pirates Knights and Vikings) with about as much hit detection issues.  It's laughable, and in some cases terrible.  But strangely I enjoyed the experience (probably because I realized I got the whole mess for less than the cost of a humble bundle minimum).
Would I recommend this game?  Not really no, as honestly your money should mean a bit more to you than to waste on a game that already exsists in another franchise.  But if you are bored, have a buck, and wanted to waste a bit of time trying to play a game that doesn't really have that much to offer, I guess you couldn't go too wrong.

Let me just start by saying, if you're very religious, I recommend not playing this game. The Binding of Isaac can have sensitive material that might be offensive to some people.
Aside from that, I enjoy this game very much. Isaac is a six-ish year old boy who changes over time during the game from a weak, naked boy to a full-on killing machine. Gathering items changes your gameplay that either helps or harms you. Items start to stack on and you soon find yourself in a position where you don't want the game to end.
It all feels like a minigame, almost. The game can be insanely short or completely too long, based on your gameplay.
I have heard that "gamers hate innovation" and "gamers are destroying the gaming industry", and it's true. Gamers are scared of what innovation might bring and wish to stay in an era with no innovation at all. But without innovation, popular gaming franchises wouldn't have hit the shelves and become the games we know and love today.
The Binding of Isaac is one of those games.
The game does have some pro's and con's about overall gameplay:
Pro's:
-The game is randomly generated and players never have the same gameplay twice
-Collecting items is basically the equivalent of "leveling up" and can help you tremendously throughout the rest of the game
-Coins are found scattered across the maps and can be used in the Shop to purchase more items
-Items are never found more than once in one game (with the exception of a few items, such as the Cube of Meat)
-You can unlock more items by completing challenges or achievements
Con's:
-Wrath of the Lamb can make your game either extremely easy or extremely hard, depending on the types of items the game generates
-Can have very sensitive material and might be offensive to religious players
-Can generate rooms with an overwhelming amount of enemies, and it is near impossible to avoid all of them
Overall, I would rate this game 9/10. It is incredibly fun and can help you take your mind off of more pressing matters. The choice now is... which tarot card do I take?

After seeing the game in the Microsoft Sale for just 2€, and watching a huge amount of reviews calling this game "close to perfection" and giving rates like 4/5, 9,5/10, and even a few perfect scores for both profesional reviews, and even players from Steam, I decided to give it a try, to see what's the hype all about. And if there's something I can't stand, are lies. This game was NOWHERE close to perfection, and it does feel unfinished at times. I still had fun, and I still think this game is worth the purchase in a good sale, but let me explain everything properly, and as usual, I will start with the stuff the game does NOT do well:
First of all, and for me, the biggest dissapointment I had with the game, is the difficulty. OR RATHER, THE LACK OF ANY. This game is HELL EASY. Want to know something else? I started my first playthrough of the game on the hardest difficulty, "Extreme", hoping to get an enthrilling experience, like when you play Dark Souls for the first time. And what did I found out? All the difficulty does, IS JUST MAKE ENEMIES HURT MORE. That's NOT difficulty, that's ARTIFICIAL DIFFICULTY. AND IT SUCKS. It doesn't matter if the enemies kill me in two hits, WHEN I CAN STILL KILL THEM IN ONE! Specially in this game, where the Devs put a lot of work into the Dodge moves. Yeah, enemies kill me in one hit, BUT THEY CAN'T EVEN HIT ME. THAT SURE IS EXTREME! IS IT ALSO POWERED BY MOUNTAIN DEW? This lack of difficulty reaches the highest settings of stupidity on the bossess. There are, literally, just 4 legit bosses on the game, and a handful of mini-bosses, that are nothing but enemies you'll find later in the game anyway. And are those bossess extreme? HELL NO, THEY'RE EVEN WEAKER THAN NORMAL ENEMIES, HOW IN THE ACTUAL F#CK IS THAT EVEN POSSIBLE, MICROSOFT!? And if that wasn't laughable enough, you can buy gems that will revive you to full-health whenever you're defeated. They're just expensive, but I had a good amount of them when I reached the last stage of the game, anyway, because I had WAY TOO MUCH GOLD (more on that later). The only thing this difficulty does achieve, is making the dangers of the dungeons and maps become ACTUALLY DANGEROUS. The Ice-caverns, for example, where ice-shards drop from the ceiling? I liked that part, because it required some skill, timing and luck to dodge them, but getting hit once was an insta-kill.
Another issue I have with the game, is that it's rather short. It took me 13 hours to complete it at 113% (I still don't know why the hell it says 113% and not 100%...), getting god-damn everything, rescuing every "friend", and all the side-quests done. If I didn't bother to do all of those things, I would have probably gone through the entire game in 6 or so. I did just spend 2€ on the game, so it's fine for me, but think about the people who paid full price. And no, it doesn't really have much replayability. Just a few achievements you can't get in the first run of the game (mainly because you have to choose one thing or another, but you can indeed get them on the first try by making two different saves).
The third big issue about the game, is the Item system. Don't get me wrong in this, it's an amazing idea. But sadly, it feels rushed and unfinished. Nearly all enemies on the game drop a huge amount of different items you can use to make items. What's the deal? Those items you can build with blueprints, can later be bought anyway, so I found myself ignoring completely the crafting aspect of the game, and sold every loot-item I got right away. And I still beated the game without much trouble... And what I said before, I ain't kidding: A Goblin, or a Soldier, drop the same items as a ugly giant spider, or EVEN A GOD-DAMN FIGHT-JET. Only a few of them drop unique items, and most of them are either expensive, or only good for crafting.
The last issue with the game, are the enemies. Like I said before, bosses are a complete joke (beated most of them without even taking damage, even the final boss, who has 4 fights in a row, that I beated on the first try, and didn't took damage on the first two), but the normal enemies are no different at times. Pretty much 80% of the enemies in the game will do nothing but to rush at you blindly, and if there's anything on the way, they might get stuck, or rather commit suicide by falling into a river of magma, or getting impared by spikes/ice-shards.  The rest of the enemies are okay, though...Except one. In the "Graveyard-like" dungeon, where you have to roam arround to find 4 items for a old-lady, you will mainly find 3 enemies: Zombies that share the same dumb IA as most enemies, Zombies with giant tumors on their heads that, for some reason, act as the Creepers from Minecraft and explode when you get near them, and Necromancers, who deal NO damage, and do nothing but spawn infinite amounts of Zombies, and Zombies with tumors. And can you kill them easily? NO. They only get damaged by magic, and magic is both not powerful, and not that useful. So, you will spend a few minutes trying to spam magic to kill him faster, while Zombies with tumors surround your♥♥♥♥♥ and you have to choice but to kill everything. And everytime one of those ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s appear, I end up farming enough XP to level up once. That's just being dumb. Maybe that's why I was so powerful at the end of the game, those guys kept appearing, and when I left the area, I had like 20 levels more...
Now, leaving all that crap behind, what does the game do good?
The story, even though short, and a bit obvious at times (I saw the mayor plot-twists from a mile ago), it does get the job done, and it can get you hooked up for more. It goes arround "Dust", a young boy who has forgot about who he was, and seems to have been chosen by a talking sword. He, the sword, and Fidget, some sort of "cat-bat", then go in a long (or rather short) journey to find out who is Dust, what happend to him, and since were at it, save the world.
The combat system has some problems, mainly a lack in melee combos, but it's quite cool while it lasts. Casual players could understand them easily, and experienced players would love them. During the game you also get some new attacks, like the Storm, or magic for Fidget...Even though magic is kinda useless. You see, it's only prupose is to get huge combos. And what do you get from combos? More XP. Spamming magic like a casual gives you huge amounts of XP, like I've said before, and it ends up making the game easier, especially when you notice the huge range it has.
The soundtrack and voices are probably the highlights of the game. Even though I found Fidget a bit annoying at times, breaking the 4th wall without reason, the characters are well voiced, and the music fit perfectly.
Something I also liked about the game, are the "Friends" I mentioned before. What are them? Exploring a bit arround might lead you to find some sort of box (that seriously reminds me of the ones you would see in the first Rayman games...You know, THE GOOD ONES), and by using 4 keys, you can rescue a character from another indie game (or even two ducks that are supposed to be the guys who made the soundtrack). And not only that, finding these easter eggs gives you a permanent HP buff. Maybe I was also unstoppable because I found most of them without any problem, but the ways you find some of them sure are original. For the Fez character, you go into a messed up 2D style. For the guy from Braid, you summon a god-damn tornado, making a sick parody of the Tornado-crap from Castlevania Simon's Quest (Does somebody actually remember that game? Good old times), and then end in a dungeon where the soundtrack only continues whenever you're moving.
The game is, despite the amount of issues that make it look infinished, or at least unpolished, quite fun. I would not buy it for full price, but I do recommend it in a good sale. But still, Bastion is way better. Buy that instead if you haven't yet.
