If you think you know the answer, you probably don't .
If you are certain you know the answer, you definitely don't.
Before playing Danganronpa 1, my experience of visual novels was non-existent. In fact if I were asked to play a visual novel, I probably would have replied 'no' or 'what's that suppposed to be some kind of picture book?' Luckily a friend of mine gave me a brief overview of the story and I figured I'd give it a shot; this was before I had any idea what life changing ridiculousness I was in for.
I purposely omitted reviewing the first Danganronpa after finishing it as I wanted to get a better sense of visual novels by continuing with the sequel; Danganronpa 2: Goodbye Despair. Although It would make sense to start by reviewing the story, it is too easy to accidentally give away plot points, so I will keep my comments about the story to a minimum and instead just give some generic comments.
**No spoilers**
Characters:
If you have played Danganronpa 1 its very easy to wonder how the 'unique' bordering on insane characters could be topped, but honestly the characters in Danganronpa 2 go leaps and bounds above the first game. The characters in the second game make the characters in first seem comparatively... ordinary. None of the characters come across as unoriginal or uninspired. In fact, I often wondered what kind of insane being would have come up with some of the characters. I'm tempted to reveal names, but it's worth finding out for yourself - I loved Chiaki and Hiyoko
Fortunately Monokuma returns and brings so much more humour to the game. He has definitely been improved upon and it was great to see a new character to complement Monokuma too!
The voice acting is incredible. The level of skill in the actors performances is insane. That includes every character (...Terteru).

Gameplay:
This is the only part of the review where I actually have some criticism (although it is minimal).
Gameplay can be split up into 3 main categories: exploration, class trials, and extras.
Exploring the island was incentivised by the amazing variety in scenary. It must have taken some extremely creative thinking to shift the games themes and mechanics from a school to an island. Nevertheless the island setting had so much promise and it certainly delivered. Controlling the main protoganist operates very similar to the first game, however the camera perspective and controls change depending on your location. Whilst the first person perspective from Danganronpa 1 is maintained, the second game introduces a new 2D perspective which was quite nice to see in terms of freshening up the gameplay. The choice of setting the game on an island certainly allowed the creators to play with different ideas from holiday resorts to an industrial environment.
The class trials were developed from the first game. I'm not sure if the developers intended to merely improve upon the trials from the first game, or bring in new ideas entirely  - probably a mix of both.
The majority of the class trials remained largely the same with new mechanics being added to every task within a class trial. Hangman's Gambit changed almost entirely which is my main criticism for this game (but lets face it, this is a petty criticism. I'm scraping the bottom of the barrel for something bad to say). No matter how quickly you have worked out what the missing words are, you have to be lucky enough for the required letters to appear in pairs on the screen whilst simulateneously trying to prevent other letters from crashing into each other... Its less about logic and more about how fast you can move your mouse across the screen.
Two new components have been added to the class trials. The first is the Rebuttal Showdown which, as the name suggests, is a pretty rapid and intense 1 v 1 debate against another character. The music alone gets you fired up!
The second is Logic Drive which is a snowboarding minigame with questions about the particular murder case within it. I really liked it, although it may not be for everyone. I thought it was a nice change in gameplay.
There are numerous other extra elements of gameplay which cannot be found in the Danganronpa 1 such as an arcade game. But again, it would be better not to divulge into the details in a review.
Story:
There's not a lot which can be said without revealing any sort of plot points implicitly, however what I can say is that not only is the story engaging throughout, but the ending is surprisingly satisfying (although there are a lot of questions left unanswered - or maybe I just have too many questions).
As expected, the story is filled with many twists and turns which naturally led me to write the first two sentences of this review with ease. Even if you think you know the answer, you never really know the answer. I took out a pen and paper just to draw diagrams and take notes to help me solve class trials. Although I didn't need to do this, the story was so engaging that I wanted to make sure I understood everything that was happening... NO GAME has made me do this before. Some of the class trials really help you learn creative ways of murdering people in real life too... Yeah the games great. Real inspiration.
Music:
As a self-declared video game music junkie, an amazng soundtrack instantly makes me fall in love with a game... I fell in love agan!
Firstly, I'm glad quite a number of music pieces in the first Danganronpa retrurned (or were modified slightly) for the sequel. The majority of the music in the class trials remained the same as the first game and a few other pieces (such as Monokuma's theme) remain unchanged. This was not a problem for me at all! It did not feel as though any piece of music was overused or underused. As for the new pieces, they were true masterpieces; they even had me dancing from time to time. I can't dance, but who cares.
Conclusion:
I didn't write this review in the hope of convicing people to buy the game, ironically. If you loved Danganronpa 1 then its more likely than not that you have already bought this game. In which case I'm preaching to the choir. If for some reason you hated Danganronpa 1, then the chances are you wouldn't even contemplate buying the second. I'm writing this review because this game damn well deserves reviews to be written for it. This is one of those rare games which needs to be talked about so much more than it already is. I never would have touched Danganronpa had it not been for ONE friend who just happened to have watched a Youtube lets play covering it. Both games in the series have opened up my eyes to a whole new genre... My friend must be the... Ultimate Hope!

Currently the best racing simulator on the market for physics, ffb, A.I and dynamic track/weather. Definitely not the best for graphics, multiplayer or usability. Hopefully the online component will improve when the U.I gets updated and is a bit more user friendly. The driving model has a pretty steep learning curve, but once you put in the hours you'll discover the depth of the physics engine comapred to other titles.
I've read the usual 'not enough grip' comments, and they are based on ignorance. It's been said before but I'll say it again - you REALLY need to wait for the tires to warm up, and then for the track surface to become 'rubbered in'. Once you do that there's plenty of grip, provided you don't just mindlessly crank the steering into the corner carrying way too much speed. You must be smooth with the steering and have the front tires pointed in the right direction (sounds obvious but takes practice), and be very gentle on the throttle mid corner. Look at the speedo and realize how fast you are traveling before you conclude that there isn't enough grip.
The ffb is the benchmark in the genre, though it takes quite a while to tweak it to your liking. I've read comments such as 'too much vibration' or 'too much rattling'. This is caused by two things, firstly a flat spotted tire from a lock up, secondly, rF2's ffb is extremely detailed and some consumer wheels (such as the G27) can't handle it - this isn't a problem, simply turn up the 'smoothing' and it's fine.
A.I is fantastic to race against, provided you know racing etiquette and are respectful of the A.I's track position. They will race you hard, overtake, and defend thier position. Not perfect by any stretch, but agian, the best in the business.
Leans heavily toward racing cars as far as content goes, though the road cars included are great.
Objectively the most advanced physics and tire model.
Ultimately it comes down to this - if you have time, patience, the ability to focus, and enough intelligence to understand the dynamics of car handling, this is the most harcore racing experience and is the sim for you. It will feel totally different from what you are used to, but give it time and you'll see why this is the sim of choice for the most serious racers. If you're just after quick fun, go buy another game, this will be an exercise in frustration.
Abso-posi-lutely amazing. Would recommend for those who enjoy thinking fast!

One of my favorite RPGS of all time.
I first got the opportunity to enjoy this amazing game on the xbox 360. Hearing good things about it but not in posession of a gaming pc at the time, I was astonished by the quality of the game after playing through it. It's not a particularly open or long RPG, nor is the gameplay perfect, but it's the story rich atmosphere that drove me finish the game. The Witcher games are based on polish author Andrzej Sapkowski's works, but take place after the novels. He has truly painted a unique fantasy world, where alliances and belief systems hang by a fragile thread, and each character has their own personal motivations that are as complex as any real life web of intrigue. The world is a dark, violent place, with more in common with real world medieval europe and Game of Thrones than Lord of the Rings. Compared to Dragon Age, for example, which in my opinion only has a thin veneer of a so called "dark fantasy" setting,♥♥♥♥♥♥goes down in this game that is truly ♥♥♥♥ed up. Towns get♥♥♥♥♥♥♥and pillaged, innocents get slaughtered, and the game does not spare your feelings at all when it comes to heavy♥♥♥♥♥♥
However, this expansive and interesting world lends itself to some really tough moral choices your character needs to make. Unlike Mass Effect's polar opposite choice system (Mother Theresa vs. Skeletor), most choices in this game don't have a truly "right" option. Everything is muddled in shades of grey, and the game benefits because of it. Sometimes I found myself regretting a choice I made only because of unforseen ramifications that don't reveal themselves until later on. It's definitley the most "choice driven" RPG I've ever played. No spoilers, but a choice made in the first act dramatically alters the second act so much that it's not even in the same location. That's right, the developers made two seperate areas complete with their own quests, characters, and scenery just so you will feel the weight of your decisions. Rather than avoid the risk of putting in the development time into a setting that a full 50% of your customers won't get to see, CD Project Red went all out with the second act. Amazing.
The world, for all of its expansive nature and setting feels a bit constrained. Character prattle on and on about wonderful locations, but for the most part, the Witcher 2 may end up feeling really linear for some players. You may feel the desire to run off into the woods and explore everywhere but unfortunately, there isn't much exploring to be done. This game is a tight, story driven narrative that ends a lot quicker than you'd expect. Hopefully, the Witcher 3, with its expansive open world will help scratch the itch to explore, but for the most part in the Witcher 2 the adventure is strictly linear. It's also a lot shorter than expected, taking about 20-30 hours to complete, even with most side quests. This is partially supported by the central plot, as your character is only a very specific personal mission, versus just milling about like in Skyrim, per say.
The combat in this game is serviceable but can also be frustrating. This game is hard, and will often put you against overwhelming odds, even at the very beginning. You'll be rolling all over the place in order to avoid getting one or two shotted. Later on it becomes easier, as you become more adept at fighting with multiple skills and "light" magic abilities, but the combat system certainly has it quirks.
Regardless, if you go into this game without expectations for a huge, open world, and can forgive the less than perfect combat, the Witcher 2 is an incredible experience. It's old enough that it regularly goes on sale for $5 at times! I only beat it on the PC so my save file (with all my choices) will transfer over to the upcoming Witcher 3, which as of now is my most anticipated game of 2015. It doesn't take too long to complete if you have a backlog, and will definitely get you hyped for the Witcher 3.

Not a great game, but not bad game for sure.  Not reccomended for those that aren't fans of The Witcher or 3rd person action rpgs specifically.
Story:  The story is somewhat standard for the post 90s dark fantasy genre.  Everyone and their grandmother is scheming to betray everyone else and rule over their little corner of the world...And it's done reasonably well.  I feel like fans of the books will understand more of what's going on between this empire and that empire, and why xyz side-character is important.  As someone who only played the first witcher but didn't read the books, a lot of the finer points of the intrigue were lost on me, but I was able to follow.
Performance:  Passable.  The game crashed on me several time, and for whatever reason any time I access the in-game menu the mouse has a weird negative acceleration.  As you can imagine, for an RPG that can be pretty annoying.  Lots of minor non game breaking bugs, but that's to be expected in a game of this type.  Pretty good array of options in the menus, and more available in the config files if you feel like messing around.
Gameplay:  Here is where the majority of my complaints lie.  In my experience, about 35-40% of the game is combat.  I never really felt fully in control of my character.  Is Geralt going to do a leaping stab?  Is he going to do a quick slash?  Will he roll across the battlefield and come up into a thrust or flail impotently at the open air?  You just don't know.  When you die, most of the time it's basically because you're just stunlocked to death (and that's how you kill the enemies as well).  The controls feel a little sluggish, which often makes any of the more nuanced aproaches to combat a liability.  All that said, the combat is 'fine'.  But being such a big part of the game, it falls a little flat.
Another 35-40% of the game is moving from point a to point b.  Now, I'm not a fast-travel evangelist, and while I think moving around the actual world is a great way to experience it, the map/radar in game is pretty bad.  Most of the time you'll need to stop,  open the full map, and actually plan out your route.  Although, even on the full map, you're never quite sure what is an actual legitimate route, and what just looks like a route, but is actually impassable.
There are a number of mini-game elements sprinkled around.  The stealth sections are notably bad.  There's  a sort of poorly implemented cover mechanic which you can't count on working, and you're never really sure what an enemy's visual range is.  In some sections getting spotted is an instant fail (either a guard shows up and escorts you out of the area, or a cutscene plays where you're shot to death by arrows).  The other mini-games are fine, and they mix up the gameplay a little.  The dice game annoyed me a little in that you can accidentally roll the dice off of the board, and then lose them!  The dice game from the witcher 1 is just better.  Easier to play, easier to read the dice, faster, etc.  Why mess with it?
The character progression is good, but never really wows.  Potion brewing, crafting, and gaining information on the various creatures you fight is also a lot more streamlined than the previous entry.  The ability to meditate (and save) mostly freely is greatly appreciated.  But then why make drinking potions limited to places where you can meditate?  Especially when the places where you'd need it the most won't allow you to?
Also, why does the game feel the need to unequip your swords all the time?
Visuals:  The game really shines here.  Several years later, on a technical level, it still holds up pretty well.  Where I feel the visuals are the strongest though, is in the art direction itself, especially the costume and creature design.  Particularly in some of the early sections of the game, the feeling of 'presence' is very strong.  A very minor complaint is Geralt himself.  In the first game, Geralt felt distinctly inhuman.  Here in the Witcher 2, he feels more like a tough guy who happens to have glowing eyes and pale skin.  And while the maps are frusterating to traverse, the do feel convincingly organic and interesting.  Overall, really excellent visuals, and art direction.  This almost overcomes the other problems I have with the game.
Audio:  Not really a section where I'm all that picky, but the audio seems to be pretty good.  Good music, and generally good voice acting across the board.
Overall, I'd give the game a 7/10  Certainly not bad, it it does excel in certain areas, but it trips over it's own feet too often to really be enjoyable for me.  You can find the game on sale fairly often for a good price, so if you have the free time, and not a huge budget for games, it might be worth checking out anyway.  For myself, the time investment vs. enjoyment is the more relevant consideration, and there it doesn't quite make reccomendation territory for me.

rF2 is a great Simulator. It has a ton of content in the steam workshop and more can be found online. The graphics are not flashy and bright like other racing games. It has a more "actual vision" look. This means that it shows you what your eye would see instead of what a camera would see (Lens flares, overly saturated colors. Etc)
Game uses DX9 but will be gettign it's DX 11 update in Q1 of 2017. This will usher in VR compatability as well as significant increases in graphical overhead resulting in better FPS and room for more graphical eyecandy to be added.
Studio 397, who now owns rF2, is a much larger studio and has quite a large number of developers working on rF2 development. They will eb releasing content and updartes significantly faster than ISI ever could. EVen if Studio 397 never made any further content or physics improvements the game would still be worth every penny spent on it.
Online mode is now free with game purchase and the serves are begining to fill with new rF2 racers.
For me, I have rF2 and Assetto Corsa. I prefer rF2 and it is my Goto sim racer. For me AC does not have nearly the same feel as rF2. Breaking, FFB, Sense of speed, real road, physics in general. It all feels better to me. Your mileage may vary.
Remember that rF2 has both its fanboys and haters. Both groups do their part to try and make rF2 look good and bad. The real deal is that the game is still in development and I think the furure is bright for rF2. It is worth having in your game list.

If you've read (and loved) the Witcher books, this is a must have. If you haven't read the books, buy them read them, they're awesome. But even without knowing the books, this game is the definition of Action RPG. No DIablo-esque clickfest, no party balancing, just one character under your control. If you want to play a greatsword-wielding sneaky healr-mage and fine-tune everuthing about you character from race and gender to underwear color, look elswhere. Here, you play Geralt of Rivia - a human turned by magic and mutation into a monster-slayer.
You can still shape you developement and focus on swordplay, signs {simple magins spells) or alchemy (potions to drink, oils to coat your blade, bombs to throw around). You will need a bit of all of them and common sense, if want to survive most battles - flailing your sword around won't get you far. Also, forget drinking a healing potion in the middle of a battle: drinking potion is something you do as preparation, when no enemies are around. But most of the potions will last 10 minutes, which is enough to clear a cave of necrophages and go back to town.
The battle-system is very straightforward - a fast, weaker attack, a stronger, slower attack, block and dodge. You can direct every attack at a different opponent just by aiming at them with your mouse and Geralt's moves actually look natural - like a quick stab behind you or a running lunge at a distant foe. Add a bit of magic (signs), throwing daggers or bombs and setting traps and you have enough options to survive in this world. Just a hint - avoid playing on Easy. Boss fights are cut short and their QTEs a removed, which makes them a lot less satisfying.
The world is... complicated. There is no Evil Overlord, just monsters that attack because humans are yummy and a lot of politics. Everybody has their own agenda and can't be split into "good" and "evil". Including you. This also gives you the choice in some quests - will you lie for an elven girl to save her from the gallows? The evidence you have point at her, but you have the choice in the dialog, with different rewards for different outcomes. Will you simply kill the troll, or find out what his problem is a help him? There is no right or wrong answer, it your choice. And at the end of chapter one, you have to choose sides, which will result in a completely different chapter two. Talk about replay value...
Finally, if you want a change from the monster killing, go to town. Dice poker, arm-wrestling, QTE fist-fighting and side quests (not necessarily about killing) await. Not even mentioning the brothels and soft-core sex scenes. Took me about 30 hours on medium and I know I'll be back, just to try the other version of chapter two.

FMV's.

Surprisingly funny in between all of the dark moments, again, making the atmosphere strangely appealing.

Cons:
Graphics - Look, let's face it, they take a bit getting used to, but at the end of the day any RPG die-hard really won't care. Anyone nostalgic enough can turn on classic graphics mode, getting rid of the mouths, which look stupid on some characters, (Sephiroth looks like he's in perpetual shock any time his character model is on-screen), though sacrifices the sharper detail and making it a little harder on the eyes.
Gold Chocobo side quest - Only way to make it quick and painless is by doing this:
Story can be a little too vague at times and may lose some
Easy with materia, but two of the optional bosses are the hardest in the game, and I mean HARD, another thing common in FF games. Playing with no Materia presents a real challenge though, so use Yuffie for this.
Level Grinding - This is a sin commited by most old FF titles, which has long been accepted in the gaming community.

This game is like junk food. You know it's not the best quality, you know that you have over a hundred better ways of spending your time, and that's excluding your vast library of games, but you...
just...
keep...
.
What is this game about? It's exactly what it looks like. You are going to shoot that raptor
. You are going to get in a big stompy mech and force-feed a T-Rex a rocket sandwich slathered with molten lead. You are going to pistol whip a pterodactyl that's been annoying you for half the wave.
All of this, for less than it costs you to buy a soda.
----
Now, onto the useful bits of this review:
This game is geared towards five and ten-player matches. While the game offers a wealth of game mode options, you are primarily going to be concerned with PvE content, or Conquest and Survival, both of which are co-op.
Straight out of the door, you are equipped with a pistol, and absolutely nothing else. There is a minute of downtime each round in Survival/Conquest, in which you can buy weapons and augmentations for your character. Pistols will never run out of ammunition. Secondary weapons consist of SMGs and shotguns. Primary weapons are automatic rifles, sniper rifles, and burstfire rifles, all usually with some form of scope for ranged shooting.
Augmentations are permanent upgrades for your character that you buy with credits from killing dinos. Three augmentations are specific to your class, while the rest beef you up as the going gets rough.
There are three classes in this game: Assault, Support, and Recon. Assault players have access to a jetpack with a generous amount of energy to use to get in hard-to-reach spots. Support players are equipped with a Medigun, with the ability to heal (and, with an augmentation, repair) other players and vehicles, as well as the ability to self-heal with right-click. Recon players have access to cloaking devices, allowing you to shed off your attackers as you
slink away into the darkness.
Adrenaline weapons are power weapons, supposedly unique to each class. It is worth saving up the credits to get one, trust me.
Progression. This game has progression for yourself, as well as your three classes. The more you play, the more permanent upgrades you get for them. Things like 10% higher jumps, available weapons on spawn in PvE modes, and so on.
Now, here's the thing. This game is, for better and for worse, a tad wonky at times. The menus aren't snappy, the third-person animations are offensive (and, in the case of certain taunt packs, deliberately so), and the game isn't exactly Crysis 3. The game also has cosmetic microtransactions (gun skin, armor color/skin, silly hat, cape, and taunt pack), but the vast majority of the items available are as cheap as $1. You know, like an actual microtransaction. This would normally be a huge turn-off for me, but the game's price allows it some wiggle room.
TL;DR: for the money spent, this game serves as a good distraction, especially if you're not fussed about a sci-fi shooter in which you reenact the meteor that extinct-ified everything.

Magical Diary is a video game created by indie developer Hanako Games who specialise in RPGs and visual novels staring female leading characters. Set in a school where magic users learn the art of spell casting, it is pretty clear to see that the title gets its inspiration from the popular Harry Potter books. Players simulate the life of a freshman going through their first year at the prestigious Iris Academy where you’ll have to contend with strict teachers, managing your studies and attracting a date for the end of year prom. As a macho man, I’m clearly not the target audience for this game, but I decided to give it a go after enjoying Hanako Games’ 2012 offering Long Live the Queen. If you are interested in trying out either title they can be purchased from Valve’s Steam service or directly from Hanako’s website.
Gameplay wise Magical Diary feels like the adventure books some of you may have played during your youth. You’ll read some story until something noteworthy occurs. When a key event happens you’ll be asked to choose what to do from a list of multiple-choice answers. What response you select has an impact on the plot making it branch off in a different narrative path, which certainly adds replay value for anyone curious enough to explore all of the game’s content. Will you be a model student and ace your exams or will you skive classes and potentially risk expulsion? When it comes to dating will you try to court one of the school’s bachelors or do as I did and break the heart of a blue skinned senior by pursuing a lesbian relationship with my bookish roommate instead?
As a student of Iris Academy you’ll be expected to complete various exams, but these are nothing like the coursework or written tests you would find in a regular school. Examinations in Magical Diary consist of being teleported into a dungeon and using your spell-casting prowess to find a way out. In order to succeed you’ll be expected to solve brainteasers using the enchantments you learn in class. In one dungeon for example you can escape by destroying a wall that is obstructing the exit with a well-placed fireball. Whether you know how to cast a fireball or not however depends on if you have completed enough lessons in red magic (I wonder if Ryu from Street Fighter attended those classes.)
This all means that planning out your curriculum plays a big part in Magical Diary. At the start of each week you have to decide what types of magic you wish to learn. Blue magic focuses on transformations, green magic allows users to manipulate nature, white magic is used for communicating with spirits whilst pink magic makes you appreciate musicals and say the word fabulous in a camp voice (okay I made that last one up.) Don’t go overboard with the cramming though as stress can have a detrimental effect on your character. Thankfully it is possible to combat the effects of mental fatigue by unwinding at the mall on weekends.
Much like an examiner grading a student’s homework, the time has come for me to rate this game. My final score is four stars out of five as I enjoyed Magical Diary a little more than Long Live the Queen (which I awarded a three.) Visually speaking Long Live the Queen is the more polished of the two, but I enjoyed replaying Magical Diary more as it has a more fleshed out cast of characters. I also liked how your decisions have a greater impact on the plot as opposed to Long Live the Queen’s more linear storytelling. As far as visual novels go Magical Diary isn’t top of the class, but it’s a solid B student all the same. Strong writing, light romance elements and a story told through a girl’s perspective make this an ideal purchase for female players who may be frustrated that there aren’t enough games on the market catering to their tastes.

This is a re-release of the original PC port from 1998.
Nothing has really been changed here, glitches and exploits included. It's plays exactly like the PlayStation version only with slightly better visuals and faster loading times. The only major difference in gameplay is how control prompts/instructions are displayed in-game.
- Cannot use dpad or triggers (bumpers work, but not triggers.)
- Original game did not have rumble support, nor does this.
- Very playable.
- No mouse.
- Majority of keys are rebindable.
- Very playable.
- Can be played in a higher res compared to PlayStation version.
- Models do not look as jagged and blurry compared to PlayStation.
- FMVs (while compressed) have aged pretty well.
- Game battles are locked in at 30FPS, menus included making Tifa or Cait Sith's limit breaks a bit harder to use.
- Framerate is not consistent across world map and has major pop in of objects.
- Pre-rendered backgrounds while upscaled are very pixelated.
- Would recommend playing on a TV or a Window for those that do not like pixels.
While the game has a "widescreen option" I would highly recommend playing the game in its original 4:3 aspect ratio with your regular screen resolution, playing this game in widescreen will only stretch the image and make it look worse.
With a patch from Sqaure-Enix the game has all of it's original PlayStation music tracks, I have noticed some sounds are missing however. Not a major distraction.
Yes! I played through the game through it's full story and some side quests and had no major problems or technical issues. It's not a perfect port but I support the Final Fantasy series being ported to PC and hope to see more in the future.

If you were a fan of Galactic Civlizations II, you will love Galactic Civilizations III.
It seems to have everything the other game had, with all the annoying bits taken out.
Starbase management no longer feels like a chore and the alien creator is much better, allowing you to create your own races of aliens and give guidelines for their personalities.
The strong RPG element of the game is still there, with a very complex system of diplomacy. The computer opponents don't simply try to defeat you and each other; they can be assigned general personalities. The many paths to victory also allows the player much flexibility in style.
Also, I give credit to Stardock for always abiding by strong standards and providing beautiful finished products. The battle simulator is extremely fun to watch, especially with large fleets. Play is intuitive, but complex.
In short, I found it to be a beautiful, fun product that no fan of the genre will want to be without.

TL;DR - If this game is on sale and you've played and enjoyed the first Danganronpa (Trigger Happy Havoc), this game is 100% worth the money.  An instant buy if on sale, and still completely worth it at full price.
Long version below.
-----<< Non-Spoiler Review >>-----
For those interested in buying, I'm going to try to keep this as SPOILER FREE as possible.
First of all, this game can be played without any prior Danganronpa knowledge but it is HIGHLY recommended you play the first Danganronpa entry before purchasing/playing DR2.
--<< WHAT IS IT >>--
The gameplay and premise in Danganronpa 2: Goodbye Despair is the similar it it's predecessor, Danganronpa: Trigger Happy Havoc.  If this is the first Danganronpa entry that you're going to play, then Danganronpa plays like a regular visual novel, but with mini-games and collectibles.  If you don't know what a visual novel is well it's technically like a book.
What makes Dangonronpa 2: Goodbye Despair different than any other visual novel?  Well it's not about finding your favourite waifu and giving them presents (okay there is some of it, but it's not the main point!) but rather it is a darker toned, muder-mystery type visual novel.  Sort of like a weird, zany, mix of Phoenix Wright and Zero Escape.
--<< PREMISE >>--
As I said above the premise is similar to the first game.  You play as a rather normal looking male highschooler hoping to attend one of the worlds most prestigious school, the inspiring and incredible Hope's Peak Academy.  But before you long, you realize you've actually been thrown into some sick, battle royale-esque, life or death game with other extremely talented and goofy students.
The only way to escape this terrifying game is to MURDER another student and get away with it.  After a certain amount of time after a bodies discovery, a class trial will be held.  At this point you and the other students must discover the 'Blackened' (in other words the killer) and vote him/her as the culprit.  If you're wrong, well then.. everyone get's executed and the Blackened will escape the game!
P.S - There is a lot of death in this game.
--<< GAMEPLAY >>--
Now that you get a gist of the premise and what type of game it is, now let's go over the general gameplay.
For the most part, the game is a regular visual novel.  There are lots of text and lots to read.  The game is usually broken into segments of:
Free Time
Investigations
Class Trials
Free Time is when you're allowed to do, well, whatever you want.  You can travel around and speak with the other students and learn more about them and you know, give your waifus presents and good stuff like that.
Investigations are moments in the story where you are given an amount of time to go around investigate and gather clues before the Class Trials begin.
Last but not least, the Class Trials are where your wits will be put to the test.  A lot of the minigames require you to logically point out/agree with mistakes in your classmates testimonies, and this part of the game is rather intense.   There are a lot of mini-games and they're rather difficult to explain so I'm not going to, but they vary from intense jeopardy type games to slicing words across the screen with a blade and then countering to rythmn mini-games.
There are also up to 3 different difficulty settings if you just want to casually enjoy the game or want to challenge yourself (and the game is challenging).
There is a sort of world map like hub where you get to walk around and travel to where you want to go.  After entering you can move a first-person camera around to click and investigate on certain objects.  There are also some first person dungeon-like maps where you can physically walk around and look at stuff but these are a bit more rare.
If we compare the game to Danganronpa 1, it improves on this point in almost every aspect (I'm looking at you Hangman's Gambit mini-game.. -shudders-).
--<< MUSIC >>--
It's good.  Certain themes are quite memorable.
DUAL AUDIO ! (Yayy!  JP VOICES!)
--<< CHARACTERS >>--
If not for the f**king insane story and cases you're going to have to solve, pick it up for the incredible and lovable cast of characters.
Danganronpa is a type of game where, well, you're never going to be sure who's going to survive to the end.  But because of the Dating Sim-like Free Time segments, there are some characters that you're going to really grow attached to.  Which is a good thing in most games.  But in this game, where you're never sure who's going to get the axe next.. It's a pretty scary feeling.
It's also what makes Danganronpa games so fun in general.  There's something about picking out your favourite characters at the very beginning, getting to know them, and praying to god that they make it through this ordeal with you.
It's nothing like watching the cast of characters dwindle down, only to see a handful remain, growing to trust them, only to tragically realize another body has been found.
It's rather heartbreaking.
I also enjoyed these characters more than the ones in the first game, but that's probably preference.  By the end of the first game I was probably only attached to 2 of the suvivors, but by the end of DR2 I was heartbroken, and attached to everyone that made it through.
--<< STORY >>--
Don't want to go into detail here.  There are a huge amount of references to the first game which make this game much better to play.  But you can definitely jump into DR2 without playing the first one.
But to sum it up, the story is amazing.
--<< CONCLUSION >>--
If you're a fan of Phoenix Wright, Zero Escape, or Visual Novels and are looking for something new, buy DR1 THEN buy this game.   It's challenging, decently long from 20-30 hours depending on how you pace yourself, with an INCREDIBLE story that only builds upon everything that was great from DR1 and makes it even better in DR2.
It's completely worth the cash.  Every cent of it.  Easilly one of the best games I've played in the last few years and I cannot wait for Danganronpa V3 to come out on the PS4/VITA.

So I completed Dangan Ronpa 2 a few days ago. I also played through Island Mode as well. I have a lot I wanna say, but it'll take some time to gather my thoughts.
==WARNING FULL GAME SPOILERS==
Dangan Ronpa 2 is a good game. I liked it a lot. I really got into the story, the characters among other things. Though I think I'll start off with some issues I had with the games.
Case 3 - The murder weapon that was used to kill Saionji was never found or even searched for. Having played Ace Attorney before, I know that in the (not exactly) words of Phoenix Wright "Evidence like that would never be overlooked". Apparently the reason why this was the case (according to the DR Wiki) is because the developers had originally intended for Kuzuryu to be killed during Case 3 rather than Saionji, however they decided to repeal this decision because "Peko's sacrifice would have been for nothing"... Honestly, wouldn't her sacrifice being all for nothing have been the more despairing? It ended up causing an issue with Case 3 that bothered me a lot besides Mikan being the killer :/ A friend of mine were discussing Case 3, and he believed that Case 3 would have been better if it was just Ibuki getting killed.
The Island Mode... I wish there was more attention to detail in it. Their only excuse was "it's an extra mode anyway", comon now, you could have the extra mode have more... extra in it. At least the endings in Island Mode were very satisfying for me. Island Mode is a fun mode at first, but I can see it getting a bit boring after you gained everyone's hope fragments and are just trying to get everyone's ending. After getting everyone's ending in Island, I can say confidently that I felt very happy.
Monomi mode is pretty interesting. The keyboard controls suck, and I'm only able to use my controller by using JoytoKey.
Every murder in this game was very tragic. Either because of the murdered or the murderer. Teruteru was trying to kill Nagito to protect (Faker) Byakuya, but ended up killing him instead. Peko was trying her best to protect Kuzuryu and ended up being sacrificed in the end and with her loved one nearly dying too. Mikan is the one person you would have ever expected to commit murder. However, some stupid despair disease made her do it... I'll speak on this later. Nekomaru and Gundham fought it out, a "mutual killing" for the sake of their friends. Nagito, as twisted as he was, was trying to get rid of all despair, and he was inadvertently helping AI Junko.
Speaking of which, finding out that every classmate in DR2 was an Ultimate Despair was really surprising... Can you really imagine Nekomaru being an ultimate despair? I know I sure can't.
This ending isn't "as" despairing as DR1 in a way, but thinking about DR1 makes it more despairing. It makes you realize that everyone who died in DR1, is actually dead. No hope of ever coming back. This wasn't a dream. Celes, Ogami, Chihiro, Ishimaru, Mondo, Yamada, and everyone else is just dead. At least DR2 is kind of a dream. At least your friends are comatose. However, you could also say that's worse than death. Also, according to the wiki, because Mikan and Nagito had died knowing that the world they were in was all just a game, they have a higher chance of waking up than everyone else. DR2's ending really left me in between hope and despair.
Picking up where I left off about Case 3, I really felt cheated about that one. Despair Disease? Really? Why didn't AI Junko ever use that again huh? Had everyone killed off. Despair Disease just felt like a crappy plot point to get an unlikely character to be a murderer. (My favorite DR character from each game just so happened to be the murderer in CASE 3). However, thinking on it I can also see its purpose. To give you a taste of how everyone once was. Everyone in this class except Chiaki was an ultimate despair. Even the most unlikely like Mikan had an evil and despicable personality in their past. This is why they're using the Neo World Program to restore hope. So they could change.
However, after some thinking on it, I realize that the despair disease itself wasn't bad, it was how it was executed. Using despair disease to "force" a motive on someone is just really bad. It was nice with Akane, Ibuki, and Nagito just having the despair disease. If the Case 3 murder were just left off with Ibuki being killed, it would have been an even more interesting case, but no, they needed an extra person to die to parallel to DR1 case 3.
As for characters, I don't feel like going into it. My favorites were Mikan, Chiaki, Nekomaru, and Gundham. I will admit that Nagito is very well written, but he's a golden turd, ya know. Kuzuryu was also pretty good, and knowing that Kuzuryu was originally intended to die in Case 3 makes me kinda wish, or well, want to see how things would have went if it went the way it was originally intended to be. With Saionji being a survivor instead of Kuzuryu. (Pick your Loli Shota). Saionji is an annoying foulmouthed brat but... she grew on me. I kinda like her. Frankly, I don't feel any guilt in it.
Other than that, the story was fantastic. I had many feels. "The Day Before the Future" made me cry. Soundtrack in general is pretty good. Kill Command was a great track during case 5.
But yeah, good game.

The Witcher 2: Assassins of King is an action roleplaying game which serves as a sequel to the original Witcher game and was made by the same Polish videogame studio, CD Projekt RED. The story follows the Geralt of Rivia, a mutant who was especially designed to hunt down monsters, as he tries to survive a dangerous plot to kill all the kings of the Northen Kingdoms in a chain of events destined to change the game's setting forever.
As far as gameplay goes, and keep in mind this is my personal opinion on the matter, Assassins of Kings improve basically every aspect of the original game. The feature that has been changed the most is without a doubt the combat system: while the first game was about chaining your sword swings carefully with your mouse and use your magic (signs) to help you out, the sequel adopts a far more traditional action RPG combat fare, with controls to attack, dodge and guard in real time. There are also certain unlocked abilities that alter the flow of battle drastically, like the ability to counter enemies' hits, increased chances to instantly kill your foes and others. Assassins of Kings also introduce a deathcam function, which is triggered on instant kills and blows on stunned foes. Another original addition of the sequel are traps and bombs: they can be crafted via alchemy and can be used to better manage big groups of enemies, humans or monsters. There is also an unlockable ability that allows you to throw daggers.
As mentioned above, the other features of the Witcher have been severely tweaked: the quests that actually require you to switch to a precise moment of the day have been cut down a big deal; signs in general have become much more entertaining to use and the new balanced vigor system allows you to cast them with a better rhythm; the talents' tiers (bronze, silver and gold) have been dropped in favor of a more traditional talent system (with some talents being "mutable" by some mutagens in the game to add even more passive effects); enemies are now more varied and behave differently from one another; ... It'd be extremely hard to point out all the improvements from the original game. Particularly noteworthy is the much better interface, much more streamlined and easy to navigate, with the only issue being the inventory having been divided in slot depending on the kind of item collected, which is a bit annoying to navigate in full all the time to reach a specific item.
It's worth mentioning however (and this is a well known fact) that The Witcher 2: Assassins of Kings is also a serious difficulty spike compared to the first game: Geralt could be best described as a very fragile glass cannon at every stage of the game, and the enemy AI is incredibly relentless to boot, always trying to flank you and taking advantage of every opening you can give it. This remains true at every level of difficulty, from Easy to Insane, and is especially noticeable during the prologue and the first act, where you have yet to unlock vital abilities (counter-attack above all of them). The increased difficulty is also due to the severe lack of basic information to the player on the game's part: while the Enhanced Edition finally added a tutorial mission, said tutorial passes several advices you should really know before going into the game proper (like the whole backstab mechanic or the importance of oils and equipment upgrades).
The main story of Assassins of Kings is divided in three acts, plus a prologue, an epilogue and a good number of side quests (a couple of them also spawning across different acts). What's really unique about the sequel is that at the end of the first act of the story you'll be tasked to take a decision which will determine the story path you'll experience in the second and third sequence: choosing an option over the other opens interactions with different characters in different locations with different missions. The differences between the two paths are such that only by playing both of them is possible to gain a complete understanding of what's really going on in The Witcher II. That aside, the sequel continues the series' tradition of hard story choices on the player, which will affect the ultimate outcome of the plot and change the world around you forever, often in ways very hard to predict.
Aside from the tutorial mode, the Enhanced Edition added an intro cinematic to the main game and some DLC side quests, as well as a bonus post-credits scene.
In short, The Witcher 2: Assassin's of Kings is one of the greatest jump in quality for a videogame's sequel I've ever seen and totally able to deliver a stunning low fantasy, incredibly realistic and mature tale where your choices actually matter and you'll seriously starting to think about their consequences

The graphics of this game remind me of old days when CPU clock speed was measured in MHz. Even back then there were 3D shooter games like DOOM or Wolfenstein 3D where you could look around by moving your mouse or fancy pointing device, and there were 2D shooter games which were more like arcade games, I think.
JETBROS clearly is a 2D shooter game, a good 2D shooter game.
Oriented towards the graphics style of above games' era, JETBROS uses hand-drawn textures for all possible things that you see on your screen when playing the game.
There are options available to change graphics quality for weaker computer systems like mine, and there is a setting for gamma correction. You might need it because on good graphics the game has a kinda dark theme.
The music that plays in JETBROS is specially composed to fit each level and gets more advanced towards the end (currently level 2). The style of the music generally fits to the retro style of the game, mostly using the "instruments" available at that past time, but without the restriction of music chip's polyphony.
JETBROS's music also fits the term "background music" as it doesn't get too backgroundy so that you miss it but it also does not get too annoying by being too loud or intrusive.
Of course there are options available to change the volume of the music seperately from the sound effects.
To play the game you also need something to take control of the protagonist.
You can play the game either with your keyboard or a controller.
The dafault keyboard controls are kinda unusual but you get used to it. JETBROS detects most controllers connected to USB, Xbox 360, Xbox One, third party NES and SNES USB controllers, and even original NES and SNES controllers connected through a adapter. But be aware that the game is designed to be played with Xbox controllers, so other controllers might not work as expected.
When playing the game with a controller, you have the choice of play using the D-Pad or the control stick, both are working.
In the settings you can also rebind any key to another to make the controls more suitable for you.
The game's difficulty is pretty hard for beginners, but as you get used to the controls, you also learn how to dodge the drones' shots and how to kill the drones with skill.
Generally the learning curve is pretty steep in the very beginning but becomes more flat during the levels and as you learn to play, enemies are "introduced" to you and will return later in higher quantities or in more difficult locations.
The most notable thing is that you don't need to refill your ammo, every weapon you have has infinite ammo. But if you get hit while having some weapon active, you'll lose it. If you lose your weapon, you have to collect it from the next box that contains it; the normal pistol will always be there as a fallback.
There is a variety of weapons for you to explore, each one with a different ability.
But the game does not consist of only shooting drones and office worker. There is also some platforming. You need to jump over lava seas, bottomless pits and make your way through some kind of facility with different rooms and obstacles. To help with jumping over things you are provided with a jetpack which can lift you up to some enemies or in different locations, and of course over obstacles.
It's said pretty simple: Shoot enemies, jump over obstacles and repeat. If you die you'll respawn at the checkpoint you passed by last.
If you need help you can ask someone to play the game with you in co-op mode. There you have two characters running through the level. The second player can also use a game controller to play, but it is also possible to have one player use the keyboard and the other a controller. I should mention that the co-op mode is local co-op, not online play.
+ Retro graphics
+ Nice background music
+ Control settings
+ Easy to learn
+ Infinite ammo, infinite lives
+ Low graphics mode for bad PC's
+ Multiple weapons
+ Jetpack
+ Controller Support
+ 2 player co-op
- Steep learning curve in the very beginning
- Strange default keyboard key bindings
- Only local co-op (Online play impossible due to latency)

After removing the online season pass, and making this a one time only purchase, this simulator is a must buy.
I have already improved my braking technique by using this sim (2 seconds gained!), the physics simulation and FF is the best in the market and even if the number of good mods is quite small now, after integration with steam workshop it can only grow.
Pros:
- The physics are (probably) the best among all the simulators.
- Online subscription permanently removed.
- The hardware requirements are not extreme, I can run the software with good frame rates in a machine that's 5 years old.
- Driving the cars in this simulator is a delightful and rewarding experience.
- Mods can be managed with Steam Workshop, I like to manage everything with Steam. New mods will be added here, and it supports paid content (good bye rfactorcentral).
Cons:
- VR is still not supported (December 2016).
- The online servers are either empty or private. iRacing is still the best for competitive multiplayer.
- The AI drivers are not good. (The other simulator I drive has no AI drivers, which is the logical option.)
- The amount of good mods is small compared to the first rFactor.
- The graphics are not as good as the graphics in non-simulator driving games. This is not important for me, but may be it is for the person reading this review.
Therefore this simulator can be recommended to anyone wanting to practice their driving, to improve their technique, to shorten their lap times and to master the nuances of the difficult cars like the Brabham, in practice mode or racing against the AI. Disable all driving aids for a good wheel experience.
I can only recommend this simulator for multiplayer if you already are member of a league and they want to use rFactor2. Otherwise stick with iRacing.

Dark, Retro, Surprisingly Addictive, Hardcore, Hack & Slash.
Upon initially playing this game I am warmed by the Dark 'Tron'esque graphics & audio and the grim prespective your character takes. From what I gather, your some sort of Warrior trying to liberate a Temple full of Monsters. Why? Well who knows, the game makes little attempt to explain the why, but quite frankly who the hell cares!? Its the revelry in the challenge which drives you on! The challenge to complete the game, gain Internet Fame and become an Internet Hero! err.. yea..
To describe the game briefly, its a single or 4 player game, where you raid levels in a dungeon, you get diamonds (money) to buy recipes for crafting, or potions or healing or stat boosts. Your character is differentiated by the weapons you use, albiet a larger slow weapon with a powerful special or a smaller quicker weapon. You defend yourself by using a shield or dodging resulting in mastery of the game being a combination of perfectly time attack and defense. This is a strongly skill based game as you have to work out how to defeat individuals or groups of monsters using the correct tactics and potions.
The game IS hard at first, mainly down to the fact the controls cannot be rebound. They have swapped run from shift to V. Block is control and direction. Which feels very uncomfortable at first. However, after 4-5 deaths, I can confidently say, i can see why they did it this way.
In combat you can free hit, which leaves you vulnerable as its hard to control direction. Or you can Tab to lock onto a target, you automatically face it, then use ctrl + dir to dodge accordingly. This does in actual fact make a very efficient way of avoiding attacks which becomes second nature surprisingly quickly. However some do regard the fact you can rebind keys a major downfall. But you never know, devs could change this under abundant pressure.
The weapons and armour you find are set items, which I do find disapointing, random item stats would have added an element of surprise when an item drops not the "oh its that ♥♥♥♥♥♥ thing" after the 10th play through. Items dont show stats, you have to use it and work out what it does and how powerful it is, the only grading feature they have is Tiers.
The game is fun in Singleplayer, but VERY unnerving, if you die even once, thats it game over start again, whilst in multiplayer your team mates can ress you if they get to your body quick enough. If they dont you respawn having lost all your gear and It affects your game final score. This does make survivability alot higher, but in the case of pick up groups it generally makes everyone just race in without any tactics. Voice is a definate requirement, as you get to higher areas (7+) you will need to coordinate your specials and attacks. Unfortunately its not built in, this needs to be addressed. The only issue ive found with multiplayer is there is no matchmaking system, leaving you to rely on your friends list. This also needs to be addressed!
Graphically the game is very pleasing, it reminds me heavily of Tron especially with the sound effects and music. Animation is very fluid and feels perfect. This for me is a very important part of any game, poor animation pisses me the ♥♥♥♥ off!
Lastly, whether or not I recommend game depends on how many hours I get out of it. This game has me addicted so far, and I imagine will keep me playing into the longterm. However, I imagine if I do complete the game, its replayability will be voided.
A good game, is it worth £22? Hm, possibly alittle steep, but fair to say its just released. Buy if your bored you will enjoy it! Otherwise wait until it drops to £15.
Conclusion: Good Game!

I wrote a review for the game near abouts when it was released back in 2015.
Back then it was a good 4X that had a lot of potential. Fast forward to today, GalCiv 3 has been the beneficiary of a tonne of developer support, which is ongoing. The CEO of the company himself has been more recently involved in the improvement of the game, particularly with the AI which has significantly improved. My experience with Stardock themselves has been great, where they have even been prepared to help me out with issues that are not strictly their concern.
Right now GalCiv 3 is one of the best classic style 4X games you caan currently play. It's relatively easy to learn, and has plenty of depth in its systems to make a new sandbox game feel different pretty much everytime. Recently for the 2.0 updates, we have been seeing lots of improvement to the overall balance of the game, as I mentioned above, the improvements in how the AI manages fleets and planets have been much appreciated.
The grahpics and sound stand up very well, and is definitely among the more impressive 4X games currently on the market. Alongside the game, there are a number of expansions (Mercenaries and Crusade) and some extra content packs to help spice up the game.
I definitely recommend the Crusade expansion. Mercenaries is a nice addition that complements both the base game and Crusade, and for the smaller conent, I personally recommend Precursor Planets. Generally speaking, the other stuff is optional. On its own, the base game holds up quite well and should provide a nmew player with plenty of stuff to play around with. You can always come back and pick and choose the the extra conent that appeals to you most and it is not uncommon to see great deals on the steam store.
If you like 4X, this game is easy to recommend. It has, over time, become a great game that scratches the 'one more turn' itch. We also have more content to look forward to in the future. Buying the game also means you get to support a very hard working team of people at Stardock who put a lot of passion into this game.

I have always been a huge fan of Uplink, which is what got me looking at Exosyphen's hacker games so many years back.  The old ones are good, but this next version is a huge step forward in making hacking into an actual "game."
The current version is very unfinished (maybe 10 minutes of total gameplay), but Robert is updating often with huge new features and gameeplay changes.  For example, just today he added a world editor, allowing you to create your own levels!
Like other reviews have stated, he is very interested in feedback from the community as he develops this game.  This is not like so many early access games that will never be finished.  I trust Robert to make this into the next big hacker game.  Support him and his studio; they will not let you down.
Gameplay - Finally!  A hacker game where there is more to do than just click or type a command and wait!  With sliders to control your CPU (overclocking), Download and Upload Bandwidth, and task priority, there is constantly a mini-game keeping you engaged.
Again - in it's current state, it's nothing more than a tech-demo, but this studio is no joke and will move fast to fully flesh out this idea.
As a final note - I bought a couple of Robert's old hacker games.  A few times over the years I have lost access to my account and had to email support.  Robert himself answered promptly, with an immediate fix.  He is personable and cares about his customers in a way I don't see from many other developers (I'd put him with the likes of introversion).

Made by the same people as Long Live the Queen, Magical Diary involves you making a character (name and appearance) who goes to a hidden magic school and ends up in a variety of adventures and crazy situations. Like LLTQ, there is a skill system where you have to choose what to level each week, and those stats will determine your success later on. However, this game is considerably more forgiving and it is much easier to complete the game. There is some replay value in that there are multiple mini-routes, often romantic, you can follow depending upon what conversation choices you make. Sadly, like LLTQ, once you have played through it once or twice having to go through the same dialogues early on just to get to the later ones that get you on different routes gets a little tiring. Unless of course you don't care about such things and are perfectly fine with one or two playthroughs.
In short, it is an easier Long Live the Queen that trades the brutal violence and murderous intrigue for a (mostly) benign school life experience with some romance possibilities. If that sounds interesting to you, there's a demo you can poke at, though it only gives you the first month or so of gameplay. I had fun with it and you might too. :3

In general, Necropolis is a very fun game. Exploring a mysterious dungeon with your friends and uncovering its secrets with your friends is a great experience.
However, I would not recommend purchasing the game at this time. While the core of the game is good, albeit lacking much polish, there is just not enough content to justify its current $30.00 pricetag.
I completed the entire nine floor dungeon in around three hours, on my second run with a friend. Necropolis is much more challenging single player, of course, with multiplayer adding the ability to revive (and mistakenly kill) your friends. Single player just isn't as fun.
The combat is fairly good, and heavily inspired by the 3D Legend of Zelda games and Dark Souls - almost a 1:1 mapping of Dark Souls when using a controller. One of my complaints is that the animations are somewhat floaty and enemies will sometimes only flinch at the heaviest of attacks, giving no feedback or indication of how much damage you've done until they finally die.
Necropolis' simplistic art style is stellar, but can fall flat in some of the longer, maze-like floors of the dungeon, where every wall appears the same. If you can complete the first few levels, you will be rewarded with much more varied and visually impressive environments.
Enemy behaviors are very simplistic - enemies simply charge forwards to you, often running into walls and other obstacles. In multiplayer, enemies frequently focus attacks on one player and ignore the others, rarely switching focus, even if other players deal significantly more damage. Occasionally, enemies will spawn behind the players (or directly in the view of players) with no indication or warning.
Weapon and enemy variety is also lacking. You will often encounter the same enemies repeatedly, and most of the weapons you will find (even the rarer ones) are identical. Simple modifiers randomly applied to weapons and enemies could be beneficial (large enemies/weapons, fast enemies/weapons, fire enemies, etc.)
The humor is very hit or miss (read: if you don't like it in the beginning, you probably won't like it at all), and can often be charming and quirky, but occasionally leans towards being completely random and overshadowing any sense of plot. Additionally, flavor texts for weapons, items, and codices (permanently unlockable character modifiers) will often merely be a funny line or two and tell you very little about what the item is supposed to do, though that may be part of the appeal of discovery.
Despite my complaints I had a lot of fun and would recommend it, except for the lack of replayability and content. Once you've beaten the game, there isn't a lot left to do. You can play through again to unlock more codices to... make it easier to beat the game again(?) There are only 9 floors in the entirety of Necropolis, and a single boss.
MINOR SPOILERS: The ending of the game is very underwhelming. My initial impression of the final floor was "Wow this is really cool! There's a mini-boss before the final boss". I was really disappointed to find out what I thought was the mini-boss
the final boss, and there was no 10th floor.
The final boss was a larger variant of the clockwork soldiers encountered with additional attacks, including a fireball grenade. The boss fight was enjoyable at first, but there was no real challenge, as the boss was very sluggish, though its fireball attack and the size of the boss gave a sense of a truly epic fight. The final boss also had an overly large amount of health, as once we discovered his attack patterns, we proceeded to wail away for 5-10 minutes with no resistance until he died. Faster attacks and lesser health could be a potential improvement on the boss, and it would be refreshing to see smaller bosses throughout the dungeon.
The only permanent unlocks are the codices (as previously mentioned) and different skins for your character. More unlocks, or some kind of hub area with unlockables could really improve the replayability.
And that was the end of the game.
I can't really recommend spending $30.00 on the game as it is, but I would love to see the devs listen to community feedback and make improvements, as well as adding additionally content, because, despite its flaws, I think Necropolis has the potential for a really great game at its core.
tl;dr
The game is fun if you play with friends, but the enemies and weapons lack variety. Combat is fun but sluggish at times, and the enemy AI is very simplistic. Limited unlocks, occasionally repetitive environments, and a short dungeon really limit the replayability. Good game at the core, but I would not recommend for the current price.

This is a very unique game that was a joy to play through. I wasn't sure what to expect when I bought it, but I do enjoy burning things so I went for it. What I found was a clever little game centered around burning things in a fireplace while receiving messages from the outside world. There is a steady progression as you burn things in combos to unlock more catalogues with more things to burn, and there is an engaging story happening at the same time via letters you receive. There are goals you can achieve such as unlocking all the combos, earning stars on all the catalogues and reaching the end of the story. However, I spent a lot of time just burning things. Most of the objects have animations that are activated when they are set on fire. Here's a tip - burn the edge of the object rather than just setting fire to the middle so you don't miss out on the clever animations. For example, there is a boat that will simply explode if you burn the middle. If you burn an outer edge, you get to watch it spurt oil and then fire before blowing up. The burning is great - oil paintings melt, fragile things are quickly reduced to ash, metal things leave charred skeletons. The only feature I would have liked to have seen would be a way to make up your own combos and share them with others. If you're looking for something different that you can enjoy at a leisurely pace, this game is an excellent choice.

Unlike most of the reviewers that reviewed FFVII, I didn't grow up with this. So, I expected the worse from this based on the majority of reviews, which were unfortunately negative. I've got to say, Final Fantasy VII blew my mind.
The story, well, WOW. I loved every second of it. The game wasn't too linear and clear on where to go, and I'm thankful for that. I had to use my intuition and memory to decipher where to go in order to progress through to the next cutscene.
Having played the more fantasy-like (I, II, III, IV, etc.) games of the series, I was a bit thrown back by the mechanical stuff. Of course, airships are no huge surprise. However, I wasn't expecting guns and such in a Final Fantasy game. The result was a brilliant mix of modern(ish) technology along with the fantasy we are used to.
Nobuo Uematsu, being a major part of the soundtrack in the Final Fantasy series, delivered an amazing soundtrack. And this is almost 2 decades prior to his modern pieces. They just fit into the game so well.
As for characters, they're pretty memorable. Then again, hello, Final Fantasy. At times, you'll dislike the characters, but you'll find yourself loving them again. It's just a matter of seeing how and why they say their lines at points in the game.
I believe that Square Enix should've updated the game, or at least more of the graphics, but an hour or two of scrounging for a high-definition mod and installing it easily remedied my complaints. At least the fanbase cares. However, the only downside is the lack of achievements. Again, easily remedied. Just play with the high-def mod, and then load up the official Steam version with the save from the modded game. I was able to retain my achievements and progress.
All in all, I do highly recommend this game. It's a classic, and it will always remain one. Final Fantasy VII shouldn't be missed out on, despite the lack of any new content with the re-release almost 2 decades after the original. 8/10.

With the addition of the Magic System, this studio has managed something truly astounding:
This game is at the same time insultingly simple, and yet an absolute mess of trial and error gameplay.
In General, Dating Sims of any kind get measured by an different standard compared to most games. At its best the Genre is Character Development/Discovery condensed. Saddly most studios use that excuse to release sub-par titles with little to no imagination and even less effort, and while Magical Diary may not lack the latter, it definetly lacks imagination.
The Characters: Copy Paste. You've seen it before, you'll see it again. A forgettable parade of cliches.
The Choices: Linear in all but appearance. Choose in whoose pants you want to get and stick with it. This would be less of a problem if not for....
Gameplay and Story integration:  The Holy Grail of all dating sims.    Does it feel like you are playing the game, or like you are gaming the system?  Magical Diary takes the sledgehammer approach to subtlety and even those unafiliated with the Genre will see any character twist coming for miles.
Except for the magic system, which I had alluded to earlier. Along with the usual fair of stats, as the game progresses you  get to learn a selection of different colour coded magics. In theory you get to use these to influence the events arround you. In practice, the rather ethereal description, limited application of every spell, and utter lack of audio-visual cues, I often felt thrown back into the era of Adventure games, where every puzzle was solved by liberaly rubbing anything in your inventory on anything in the environment.
That's where the game steps in, and limits just what you can try via an MP-Gauge, or simply time constraint.
I'm sure after a second or third playthrough I could have gotten the results I wanted, but the entirely predictable characters, and obvious right/wrong choice system left me with little desire to play again.
All in all Magical Diary is rather tragic: A novel idea that lacks any kind of substance to back it up.

Well, its been a while to wait, but developing a new engine and new features takes a lot of time, and testing, and people complain about lack of content.. Well I guess they don't get the concept of 'early access' - that being, you get to see the development of the game (bugs and all) , you get the chance to offer suggestions, improvements, ideas and so on, which are actually listened (and replied) to by the developer.
While content was small to begin with, I spent a good 40+ minutes trying to figure out how to solve the first mission, which involved some really fine balancing of components in your 'system', maxing the download rate when downloading, increasing the cpu power while decrypting (and keeping a fine eye on it so the system doesn't become toast).. but now there's at least 1 patch per day released, so you can really get a feel for what is going on in Roberts mind while he's in dev mode.
Early access is indeed a gamble, some succeed, others fail, and i have been burned by some, however, unlike the ones i was burned by, i know that the dev will actually strive to satisfy the fans of the game genre, so this tile, i don't really consider a gamble, rather its a rare glimpse at what is actually involved in designing, and launching a game successfully.

The game is really fun and I really like the art style, even down to the polygonal character models. The combat is slow and thoughtful with swings from your weapons being lightning quick and weak for small weapons, and slow but powerful for the larger ones. You have a dodge, sprint and block with a shield as well as a shield bash to knock enemies down. I find it flows really well and the animations look really nice.
Between each level is a little rest area which lets you pay to gain more health and power (Power as in a mana-esque feature), the closest you get to an actual 'leveling up' system, and can spend Tokens which you earn by completing little tasks given to you which lets you buy various codexes; you can only have one active at a time but grants various bonuses, which are left up to you to discover or just assume. The codexes and tokens remain through deaths, while everything else is lost.
However, there's just not enough content right now; you roam around a floor without a map and very rarely do you get any helpful landmarks, though you can craft chalk to mark the areas you have been, if you want to waste the material. There aren't even any bosses, at least that I have discovered. I'd honestly say hold off on buying the game for now, until more content is added; $30 is a lot for what amounts to a rather bare-bones experience. I want to give it a thumbs-up, I really do, but I just can't justify it for the amount of content-to-price ratio.
What I would love to see:
Various bonuses that last for only that run that affect your health, movement speed, jump height, and maybe even some that drastically affect how you play the game.
Bosses! Giant enemies that do not have other fodder enemies around; specifically a one-on-one fight with a tough guy, but you get really good rewards for winning. They wouldn't even need to be required; have a door which requires you to spend tokens to open. High risk, high reward.
Larger variety in enemies. Enemy types did differ a bit from level to level, but I see a lot of what just amounts to recolors. I would love to see a larger variety in enemies and their tactics.
Unlocking system somewhat similar to how Binding of Isaac tackled it; defeat a certain boss and a new item is added, though in this case it could be defeating enough of a specific enemy, completing enough tasks or some sort of challenge such as "Complete a floor without being hit", "Do not heal" or "Use only primary attacks". Just some ideas, but they wouldn't need to be so cut-and-paste.
