Danganronpa 2: Goodbye Despair is the official sequel to 2010's hit release of Danganronpa: Trigger Happy Havoc, available at long last on PC. Its premise is the same as the first - a large group of quirky characters find themselves robbed of their memories and stranded in a closed environment, with the only possibility of escape coming as a reward should they manage to commit a murder and escape identification as the culprit by their peers in the subsequent class trial. When this happens, they are allowed to go free while everyone else is executed, while if they fail, they themselves will be executed while everyone else gets to keep on living.
It is no exaggeration to say that I absolutely adore nearly everything about this game. The story is composed of (as you'd expect) a series of murder mysteries that take place within a greater overarching narrative wherein the protagonists try to plumb the mysteries of why they're being confined and forced to murder each other, as well as the events that lead them to their current circumstances. The characters are a good mix of anime tropes and actual development, and for the most part come off as very sympathetic and believable in their motivations, given the context and genre. Unlike other VNs, there's no branching routes or choices to be made in the main game, for the most part, and the story is entirely linear. There's a few parts that I felt were
too fanservicey (and I don't mean the ones where the resident whimpering dojikko keeps tripping herself into ever more compromising and risque positions) but overall, the writing is excellent, hitting all the emotional beats and following a logical progression even when it appears to be devolving into complete and utter nonsense. Unfortunately, DangitRonpaul 2 continues the tradition started by 1, in that the best girl dies far too early on, but thankfully so does the worst, so I guess I can't really complain in the long run.
The actual gameplay consists of two parts - exploration, which consists of a looping side-scrolling section you use to navigate the game's islands, static scenes that resemble pop-up books where you interact with things and people using your cursor, and first person sections that you use to explore certain specific environments. The other major part is the investigation and trial section, where all of the actual meat of the gameplay is - you examine locations and talk to people in order to gather clues, and then deploy these clues in a trial setting in order to determine the culprit. Sometimes this takes the form of straight-up questions, sometimes you're asked to pick a relevant piece of evidence for a particular problem from your entire big list, and sometimes you have to play an infuriating minigame in order to accomplish the same thing as the latter two options, but most often you'll be going around a circle listening to everyone make propositions about what happened, and either calling out inconsistencies by shooting their words with the damning piece of evidence or backing them up using the same process. At other times, your peers will call you out themselves, prompting a verbal duel where you use the analog stick to slice apart their arguments in preparation for a final devastating rejoinder. I played on mean difficulty for both logic and action for all but the final chapter (where I set the action difficulty down a notch to kind) and I found the trials fair and for the most part fun. The order of events makes sense, and there's only a few instances which required significant leaps of logic in order to figure out the proper way to proceed, but there's enough twists and surprises in the mysteries to keep you guessing and doubting yourself even when you're pretty sure you've solved it.
You can't actually fail in either the evidence collection or the trials, of course - trying to leave a scene before you've got all the pertinent clues results in your character refusing to do so, and running out of influence (which is like HP) during a trial only reduces the reward you get at the end, and so should be entirely appropriate for products of the modern Western education system. My biggest complaint against the gameplay would be two minigames that seem entirely out of step with the theme of the game and completely unfun, and whose removal would have only served to make the game much better. The hangman's gambit game is just a very slow and often frustrating way of spelling out an obvious thing, and the snowboarding minigame is out-of-place and tacked-on, where its only relation to the events it's representing is that you sometimes answer multiple-choice questions. I honestly would have preferred just getting the multiple-choice questions alone without the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t snowboarding.
In terms of presentation - which is to say art, music and voice acting, I have nothing but good things to say. I played with Japanese voices, and you can tell that they really shelled out for an A-list cast. My only complaint in that regard is that when you get KanaHana to voice your character I only hear KanaHana and not the character. The art, meanwhile, is characteristically great, and even the lo-fi lo-res pop-up book look of the game's various environments has a distinct charm to it. Some of the CGs are a little spotty in parts, great in others, but are somewhat rare overall, and, most importantly, the character sprites you'll be looking at for most of the game look great.
One aspect which I felt could definitely be improved was in the localization - some of the translations felt more than a little awkward, and the script is riddled with minor but noticeable grammatical errors. Not enough to ruin the experience by any stretch of the imagination, but nonetheless enough to bug you if you're the same sort of friendless pedant as me.
Beyond that, I'd say that the game is absolutely exceptional. Not only that, but it comes with a good amount of goodies, including a whole alternate route where the killing never started, which plays a bit more like a conventional school life VN, and a bonus LN by Narita Ryougo of Baccano and Durarara fame. If you were a fan of the first game, I would absolutely recommend you check this out. If you like VNs, anime, murder mysteries or good stories, I highly suggest you check out the first installment if you think it'd interest you even the slightest little bit. You're highly unlikely to be disappointed.

In the game's current state, I can't recommend buying it at full price, as it's severely lacking in content and polish.
Combat is floaty, imprecise, bare bones and not that satisfying.  They took the controls from Dark Souls, but they didn't capture the depth, precision, weight or complexity.  There are fast weapons, medium weapons and slow weapons in 4 different tiers of damage.  The movesets aren't different enough between weapons to be noticeable.  Some weapons appear to be different only cosmetically.
The crafting is uninspired and not particularly fun.  Ranged combat is lacking.  Magic is near-nonexistent.  You're locked into a one-handed melee weapon and a shield or crossbow.
The only permanent unlocks are color schemes for your character and codexes.  Color schemes don't affect gameplay at all, and the codexes don't change gameplay enough to make grinding tokens appealing.
There's very little enemy variety, and between enemies you don't really need to change your strategy or adapt.  Either dodge behind the big bulky guys, get a hit in and back off, or shield bash the lightweight guys to the ground and finish them there.
In the second half of the game, enemies have insane amounts of health.  Fights drag on and on, which would be great if the AI was good enough to keep you on your toes, but most enemies just switch between 2-3 moves, and they get stuck easily.  Combine that with the fact that in later levels, enemies just won't stop respawning, and the game feels like a slog.  Long, drawn out fights versus the same damn enemy spamming the same damn move ad nauseam isn't fun or challenging, it just feels like a chore, something to pad the length of this bare bones game.
There are 10 floors, and only one boss, and he's not much to speak of.
The procedurally generated levels are neat, but they don't vary enough to make a second playthrough feel like a new game.  There are only a handful of rooms, and there's not much variation within a particular room, so exploration tends to get monotonous.
The story of the game is told through writing on walls and the cryptic babbling of a snarky robotic head, but none of it seems related to what's actually happening in the game.  I've beaten the game, and unless I missed something huge, the central figure in the story never actually makes an appearance.  The game begins without giving your character a backstory or a reason to be in the Necropolis, and ends without any real development or revelations.  It's all vague and disjointed, and not particularly interesting.
TLDR:  If you're looking for a roguelike version of Dark Souls, you'll be disappointed with this one.  Skip it unless it's on sale, or unless they refine the combat and add tons of content.  This game needs an overhaul to be worth its current price.

I am really enjoying Stellaris. It is described as a blend of a 4X and grand strategy game (GSG); however, I think it is much more of a 4X. Many people, including reviewers, have tried to liken it to Crusader Kings II or Europa Universalis. Personally, I think it is more similar to Hearts of Iron as the game, at its heart, it is a war game. If you go into it with that expectation than it is excellent. If you are expecting a political similuation like EU or CK2 you may be disappointed.
Pros:
+ Galaxy exploration / colonization best in any game of this genre
+ Very little micromanagement
+ Great graphics (for a 4X)
+ A galaxy that feels alive (but not to the degree of EU or CK2)
+ Music (A+++)
+ The AI is respectable.
+ Wars are fun with a caveat (see cons below)
+ Great decision tempo. You constantly have to make hard choices.
+ Great tech tree design.
Cons:
- Early Bugs (this is a Paradox product after all, and so similarly they will be fixed quickly)
- More 4X, Less GSG (this doesn't bother me but it is worth noting)
- Wars can have a long mopping period. Basically, often wars come down to a couple of skirmishes and then one major battle. If you win, the enemy will generally just fold up because it is very hard to recover enough fleet strength quickly. If you lose, similarly, expecting to take a beating as it takes a long time to build your fleet back up. HOWEVER, I find the wars to none-the-less be a lot of fun because the positioning of fleets and getting yourself into that key position is challenging.
- Sometimes hard to track what is happening in your empire due to a lack of immediate information

An incredibly clever twist on the rougelite and rhythm genres, mixed in a really unique way that's very satisfying to learn and master. The soundtrack is incredible thanks to Danny B being at the top of his usual game let alone the excellent bonus remixed soundtracks that are also playable. There's lots of little unlockables and secrets to keep you coming back and feeling consistently rewarded and there's even an active modding scene adding more to the game every day. It's a great all-around package.
It's not perfect though. The game is hard. VERY hard. Bordering on frustrating due to how quickly you can die and how unfair it can seem a lot of the time. This is a game that requires practice, dedication, and constant repetition to win even as the default character, let alone any of the optional extra characters.
There's also a serious lack of consistency in tone. The game works off this really fun and playful concept and this crazy high energy soundtrack but between major areas you're given one of the least self-aware and least fun stories I've seen in a game. It's not even a particularly interesting story and it really feels out of place. It's a minor thing but it definitely drags down what is otherwise a great experience.
I like the game a lot, but it's definitely not for everyone. Casual players are going to get burned by it hard.

First, to address the bad reviews: If you're expecting a full story mode and a full campaign within the first week of an Early Access launch, I don't know what to tell you...  Wait until full release and you'll have a better time.  (Hopefully)
If you've played earlier titles in the Hacker Evolution series, especially the first two, you'll feel right at home here.  You've got a console, you've got a map with some servers on it, and you've got some status information about your machine.  It already feels quite polished, with a nice looking UI, non-invasive animations, and exactly the type of soundtrack a game like this deserves.  As stated above, there's not a whole lot of content here, (5, maybe 10 minutes) but without a need for expensive models and textures, animations, etc I don't expect any reason why that won't change significantly before release.
New to the series (Unless I forgot them in Duality, but I think they're new) are the dials in the bottom right corner. These control hacking/firewall balance, upload/download balance, and CPU clockspeed. (And therefore temperature)  Turning up your upload speed and CPU clockspeed will speed up the time it takes to break through a firewall, but at the cost of higher temperatures.  Sadly I didn't try actually overheating, but it seems like a mechanic that could add a bit more manual risk/reward to a series which is otherwise reasonably repeatable.  A good first step, time will tell how the mechanic shapes up in future.
The most glaring ommision right now for me is the lack of cursor key controls.  Up will navigate command history, but left and right didn't do anything for me, more frustrating because I had first attempted control + left to go back a word at a time.
EDIT: Within a week of this review going up tab complete and cursor keys are now supported.
Right now this Early Access release seems to be about getting community feedback and making sure they're developing a game that people want to play.  Hacker Evolution Duality wasn't my style, and it's nice to see even a short playable game that says "This series is going back to its roots."

There is huge potential here, and I should point our that I only played single player. Ok, have been hyped about this for a while now. Watched the livestreams, consumed pre-release info and felt I knew what I would be getting. Finally get it installed (am a bit miffed that the soundtrack I was supposed to get didn't land, but hey ho, these things happen), plug in my controller (the keyboard and mouse keys are made for people without finger joints and you CANNOT REBIND KEYS) and go...
...I understand its meant to be hard. I also play a lot of "rogue like" games, and get the concept. I never got past the second room, because each time I would be overwhelmed by groups of 5-8 enemies at once. I never got near to enough gems to unlock even one codex, and eventually just thought "I'm not having fun", and "I'm done". I don't mind dying because I mess up. I love having to learn from my mistakes in a game. However, this always felt arbitrary and often beyond my control. I learned only that this game was not for me.
It's quite buggy - there are a lot of strange pauses that get you murdered in combat, and the camera is....on drugs or something. Nothing worse that trying to dodge attacks you can't see because the camera is floating at some strange angle, and you are trying to find the fingers to move it and your dude at once.
Those playing in the streams I watched commented on the lovely feel to the combat. Maybe this just wasn'y the game I thought it was, but I found it clumsy, sluggish and actually, quite unresponsive.
In truth the whole game feels half done. The procedurally generated levels look samey, and despite its "dark" (allegedly" feel, it felt silly. In play, the art style is ok, but not dark.
So yeah, I only played less than an hour. As a general rule, if a game irritates me this much so quickly, I'm not giving it any more time.
Multiplayer I suspect is better, but cannot comment.
Anyway, requested a refund. I'm not pleased.
I'll keep my eye on it. I really want to like it, but at this time, I have other games I want to play, and could use the money for this elsewhere.
If Necropolis was only £7.99, I'd cut it some slack. It's not, it's damn pricey especially for what it is at the moment. My advice - wait and see how it goes.

This game is shapping up well, and may end up being the best improved game of 2016 if they keep going at the rate they are.
In the last couple months:
A new character class, new tiles sets, and new enemies.
There have been changes to how the enemies spawn so there is a lot less getting blindsided by mobs coming out of cleared areas (it still happens from time to time, but it feels, for lack of a better word more "fair" than it did.)
Enemy AI is also a little better, although still not particularly bright.
Crafting has seen a bit of rebalancing, overall making healing a bit harder to abuse.
I'm still not sure I would call this a great game, but it is a pretty decent one.
There are still virtually no ranged combat options (although this is will suposedly changing soon), and no spells outside of scrolls and only a few spell-like craftables (i.e. bombs). Weapons are largely interchangeable outside of size (heavy, light, and large) and appearance. Higher tier weapons do more damage, but two weapons of the same tier can vary quite a lot. You need to just bash some stuff with them and note the amount of damage they do rather than expect a plain "+4 damage" in the description.
The game tells you nothing. For example, there are elemental enchantments and damage types, but it is left to you to figure out what, if any difference they make. Most glowing weapons, have special elemental burst attacks that can be done by charging the attack, or doing a jumping strike, but often what the AOE actually does is hard to tell. This will delight some people who enjoy figuring out systems, and annoy those that want a little more guidance. The developers have stated in the past that they plan on revising the item descriptions to make it a bit more obvious what does what.

I've never been a huge fan of the series but i do like 4x space strategy games so i bought a founder's edition and waited till i got new pc to play and review it.
While the game doesn't look half bad its unfortunately ridden with bugs some of which are game breaking. In fact i could not complete the campaign because AI put the planet (there are abilities which create planets) on the hexagon i needed to end the game. So i had to delete the planet using console. This sort of a bug should not exist in a final patched version of the game.
There are text bugs, there are crashes (especially when loading saves), buttons appear to be unresponsive at times and AI sometimes goes "derp" and just stacks all of its fleets at one spot without moving them (on normal at least).
I suppose i can say that the music is good, the ship designer is pretty neat though time consuming. There are quite a few buildings but unfortunately not enough planet variety or resources. There are no automatic governing options either (promised in the next patch) and more disturbingly - you can't even end the turn unless you move or set all your ships to guard mode, select research, select something to build on planet. Its even more disgusting considering that each time you build a ship you have to move it and each time you add another ship to a fleet it unsets the guard mode. So you are constantly forced to micromanage everything... and im not talking about making decisions, rather you are forced to make a lot of unnecessary clicks all of which could've been fixed with forced end turn button.
Overall i've remained unimpressed, bored and slightly annoyed by this game. I suppose i should be happy i've got founders edition and should be getting every dlc's they release for free but id prefer fixed, complete and polished main game first.

This game was great fun, and totally worth the money, though it could have been much better. In general I don't like the anime look or wacky sense of humor but the progressiveness and impossible strangeness made this a very interesting experience.
The world is clearly based off of Harry Potter, with a sham Severus Snape and students group into houses (On a side note, I named my character Serpentina Hissmark and I laughed when she was glad not to be in the Snake house. But on one playthrough she was transferred- yay!). However, it's not a rip-off and has it's own unique feel.
I would say the strict gameplay element is limited- there aren't enough chances to use magic, especially outside of exams. The exams, composed of using spells learned in class to escape dungeons, are great fun. There are five fields of magic based on colors, and the game would have been far more interesting if the outcomes were more based on which fields the player specialized in.
Instead, the real interest in the came comes from the visual novel element, a feature that I usually enjoy less. It seems that this game focused less on the fantasy fulfilment of the perfect lover, or one of a 'type' of perfect lover, and actually made realistic characters with interesting storylines.  However while a few of the paths were fairly standard (oddly enough, these included the lesbian paths! I think a few of the non-human ladies would have made better romantic interests) two of the male characters offered very unique and at times surprisingly touching romance options. I was genuinely rooting for one of my couples during a play-through, though the relationship was far from traditional. All I need to say is that a possible sham marriage with your Severus Snape stand-in professor is NOT the most WTF relationship option. I appreciated the fluid sexualities of the characters, the character of Professor Potsdam and her very enlightened views on teen sexuality and transgenderism, and the presentation of a friend's realistic abusive relationship. The game allows you to enter an worse-than-Edward-Cullen manner abusive relationship yourself, but it's up to you to interpret whether it's a good or bad thing.
I do find it slighty annoying how you were pushed so quickly into a relationship with the demon, and the others were more difficult. I had to look online to find most of the paths, and I think there should be more hints and opportunities to pursue characters. In some cases, you need to be taking a certain class on a certain day, which I find too random.

On to the actual review...
I have played many hacking games before, starting with Uplink in 2001 and most recently HackNet. I have not played any previous Hacker Evolution games.
More detailed review below:
This game has literally five minutes of gameplay -- one minute if you know what to do -- and
of it is shown in the 1:18 minutes long video and screenshots on the Steam store page. The game seems to be level based, and the game currently has
level. When you complete the level, you are taken back to the main menu and your only option is to start a new game.
The options menu is completely empty, and there is no saving or loading. During my five minutes of gameplay, I also experienced a CTD.
The developers even say so themselves in the Early Access description:
The game has a fairly standard setup with a CLI (command-line interface) where you type commands. When you start the game, you are prompted to type 'help' to see available commands, of which there aren't that many available. Your objective is to retrieve a file, even though you are not told from where or why you should retrieve the file. The game seems to be 'roguelike', in that failure means you start over. There is no saving or loading.
In order to download the file, you must gain access to one of two available servers. This is done using a balancing minigame, where you must balance your CPU, firewall and network resources using dials in the lower-right corner. These resources seem to deplete your firewall depending on how they are set up. They don't add any real depth to the game, however, as there is a single setup that works best at all times, making any tweaking pointless. The same minigame-ish setup is used both for gaining access and to download the file.
And that's pretty much all there is to it at this time.
- Good music
- The interface looks nice
- Virtually no content(!!!)
- Unstable
- Empty options menu
- No story, no purpose, no nothing
- Unsure about balancing mechanic
- Bad GUI / UX (no tab completion, no mouse click adjustment of balance wheels)
If it actually had any content, a decent story and great gameplay, this game could be good. As it currently stands, it is barely an empty shell (no pun intended) with virtually no content.

First section for people who have played Danganronpa 1
Danganronpa 2: Goodbye Dispair is an amazing detective game, though certain contradictions on mean mode are a bit unusual but what can you expect with a detective game that involves a mechanical bear. Characters, at least to me, are more relatable than the first with less crazy attributes. The class trials have different game modes and the old ones have been polished.  Murder schemes are highly detailed with a lot of surprises as the debate goes along. There's now a Tomadachi like gameplay aspect with feeding it and the more you walk from place to place it levels it up. Now the story, another mechanical animal, a bunny take you and others on a "school trip". The concept of ultimates are the same but you are the one who can't remember their ultimate. The ultimates consist of athelete, breeder, luckster (again), mechanic, photographer, traditional dancer, swordswoman, team manager, chef, mafia leader (weird but ok i guess?), gamer, princess, nurse, and heir (I guess I could call it that). Don't question where the others from the first game are but I will say just to clairify it's after the first.
Second section for people who are missing out on the first game.
Story:
Danganronpa 2: Goodbye Despair is a detective game with a very interesting plot involving 15 high school students on an island known as Jabberwock Island with no memory of how they got there. The main game revolves around a stuffed bear named "Monokuma" taking over Monomi's school trip then starting a death game in which 15 high school students have to escape an island through murdering other students. Once a murder occurs the remaining students need to figure out the murderer and how they commited it or the innocent will all be "punished" (excecuted). The "Blackened" A.K.A the murderer will then be executed. You need to interact with items and other students to find clues to "who dunnit" as Monokuma frases it.
Main gameplay:
Once all clues have been found you are taken to a "class trial" where Non-stop debates, Hamgman's Gambits, Logic Dives, PTAs, and Final arguments take place, in the nonstop debates you go through multiple characters talking back and forth and you need to use the facts that are chosen to poke a hole in someones testimony, or agree with a person on what they said. Hangman's Gambit is a game in which letters fly across the screen and  you need to spell a word or collection of words based on a question. Think of it as "Hangman" but with clues to the word and more chances to miss (depending on the amount of influence you have). Then your Final argument is where you place comic panels in a collection of pages refering to the events and order of events that took place. One on one debates require tactical slicing through a person's statements then you look for the correct weak point and contradiction. Also the PTA where you play a rhythm game then select the correct order of phrases poking a whole in their argument. Those are the main Class Trial game modes but there are more that are revealed. I recommend you play on "mean" difficulty or you will lose some gameplay and dialogue. These class trials on mean mode for me at least lasted about 2-3 hours each and provide great entertainment.
Side gameplay:
The mode described as "Free Time" develops relationships with certain characters and once you interact with one enough you get a perk for  class trials. During class trials characters reveal many hidden sides to each of them and will develop them each time they're forced to execute their friend. There's a Tomadachi like gameplay aspect where when walking it will slowly level up this virtual pet. You can also gift this pet to bring up its "hope meter" the higher the meter, well you'll see what happens. Side events that are mandatory (I call them side because of it not being the promised gameplay) will catch you off-guard and others will help you to figure out what's oing on. Just a nice distraction from the trials.
Critisism:
1.Certain gameplay aspects can get annoying such as bullet lag in Non-Stop Debates and impossible to react Hangman's Gambits.
Positives:
1. Characters provide unique and interesting dialouge.
2. Class trials are very exhilerating and have unique mechanics.
3. The story progression is very nicely paced and many unsolved problems keep you wondering.
4. Class trials have great gradual difficulty increase (for the most part.)
5. Motives are very interesting and you normally end up interacting with them and provide more gameplay in completely different ways.
6. Class Trials develop characters showing you who they really are.
7.Class trials are perfectly crafted with the motives, weapon findings, and convincing others to who's the killer.
8. Many unique points with side problems are a good distraction from all of the class trials.
9. Transitioning is HIGHLY improved from the last game with side-scrolling sections.
Personal note:
Danganronpa 2: Goodbye Despair is the best game I have played this year combining a game genre I have never tampered with, along with familiar elements. You will surely grow to love the unique characters. the main gameplay is akin to many different genres keeping it fresh. After this spoilers for the rest of "personal notes" section. Introduction:
I am a huge fan of the metroidvania genre, and Dust: AET is probably one of the most top-quality platformers out there, and the fact that this masterpiece was crafted by a single person makes me amazed, since this has one of the greatest art styles of any metroidvania game.  This review may contain spoilers, but I'll make sure that I won't include a lot.
The Pros:
+ The artstyle.
+ The easy-to-understand mechanics.
+ An interesting plotline.
+ You have a sidekick that can get new abilities, just like you.
+ The music adds drama to every moment in the game.
+ The difficulty is challenging, but not impossible.
+ An interesting set of characters.
The Cons:
- There are some moments in the game that makes you want to throw your controller across the room.
- There are some spots early on that you cannot pass unless you get a certain ability that appears later on.
Neutral Ground:
Nothing.
Rating: ★★★★★ 5/5
Explanation:
I really like the fact that they added RPG elements into a metroidvania-styled game, yet they still kept the zing of the genre.  The cons are only minor complaints, but there can be a difficulty spike in some levels, in it requires a lot of backtracking.  None the less, this game is a masterpiece, and should be enjoyed by all platforming fans.  If you can't get this version, there's an Xbox version of it, so it's a win-win for PC and Console gamers.

So where do I start? There is so much good to say about this game.
Let's start with the realism: Cars handle very nicely and realisticly. The handling kinda reminds me off iRacing, which in my mind is a good thing as iRacing's physics is 10/10. I would actually say that rFactor 2 has slightly better physics, no doubt. They pushed it to 11/10, and how? Well one example that blew my mind happened in a 3 hour race I did in a GT2 Corvette. I was battling with the AI (we will look at the AI later) and in the exciting battle I got a small hit, went sideways and stood on the brakes while the cars was going sideways on asphalt or concrete. When I continued everything was fine until I reached higher speed or high speed corners and experienced lots of vibrations in my FFB wheel. Why? Because the game simulates flat spots really well. You might say that Assetto Corsa also simulates this, but not as well as rFactor 2.
Then we have the AI. Let me first talk quickly about Assetto Corsa. Assetto Corsa is, at least for me, a game where you do hotlapping, often around the Nurburgring. It is a very fun game, but the level of simulation, the way the cars feel, its not really a racing game, more like a hotlapping game where you drive different cars around different tracks either online of offline for fun. The AI isn't that enjoyable to race with in Assetto Corsa, but when it comes to rFactor 2 they AI is just amazing! If you are close to them they will, not always but often, move to the inside line and give up the ideal racing line to defend their position. They will also dive bomb you if you are going slow into a corner. The AI can also do things wrong, just like a normal person, like get one wheel on the grass and spinout. The AI is also extremely fun to battle with in rFactor 2. I did a 3 hour race in GT2 Corvettes mixed with LMP2 cars. I was in a Corvette. The faster LMP2 AI cars would respect you and find a safe way past you, but they could also cut somewhat close in front of you once they pass you, it just feels so realistic.
There are lots of leagues for this game and race series for the fast and good sim racers out there. Like VEC, Virtual Endurance Championship. It really is a game for racing unlike Assetto Corsa, and obviously you have day night cycles, rain, etc. Not that many cars or tracks included, some cars and tracks are also fictional, but as this is a game for league racing you will find LOTS of HIGH QUALITY cars and tracks. I downloaded a Sebring 12hour track with a league configuration. It is just so good, with the bumps, etc. This is a MUST have game if you're into sim racing. It is kinda like iRacing but with singleplayer and extremely good AI. Obviously you have online racing as there is league racing, but this costs money. You can buy lifetime online service or a subscription.

rFactor 2 is the best Sim I have played to date, sure, if you're looking for a visual experience, go to Project Cars, however they have said that visual improvements and a move to DX11 is in the works, giving more FPS and better graphics.
The AI are fantastic and the most realistic I've seen, they are competitive and know how to defend a position.
Now I've never driven a GT3 at Silverstone, or a NASCAR Chevy round Daytona in real life, but it feels like I am, I feel like I'm taming a beast that could escape from my hands at any moment.
Of course, the game does rely heavily on mods, I will admit, the game does suffer from many poor conversions of cars and tracks from other lower quality games, but there is a big selection of fantastic reworks of some great tracks, you just need to have an extensive look, once you find the golden mods, you'll love the experience.
People need to understand rFactor 2 IS A SIM, it does not have a career mode, it is not marketed to the casual gamer, it's focus is on competitive driving, and race fans.
If you're a race fan go and buy, if you're looking for a mario kart fix, wrong platform m8.
EDIT (90 Hours): Welp I'm at 90, I'm chucked many hours into this title since my last review of the game, and since then, many great things have happened to the title, Studio 397 have taken over, and development of the game is flying, with better graphics on the way, as well as VR support, and tracks and cars coming to the game. The AI are unbelievably real, can't wrap my head around it, turn 1 they're 3 wide fighting for position, when a car gets a blue flag they will hold their line so the faster car can pass. I've had many fun hours in this amazing title, and i plan to have many more, who knows what the game will be like when I've invested another 90 hours :)

I liked parts of this game and disliked other parts.
Pros:
- Different & unique romance options! I loved that I could go for one of my female roommates. :)
- You get to customize your characters hair, eyes, and body type. This makes the protagonist feel more "yours."
- The characters get put in absolutely hilarious situations.
- Your choices in the plot certainly have a big impact and can lead you to many different routes, so replay value is deifnitely there.
- The "magical school" setting is unique compared to some other dating sims.
Cons:
- I felt like the personality traits were worthless. I saw no point in getting points in the "cute/weird/smart" categories because they don't seem to affect anything.
- The magical tests never seem to get interesting/complex.
- Art was subpar. The characters all look similar in the face and their appearance doesn't change a whole lot. It starts to feel monotonous.
- There are huuuuge chunks of dialogue/description with no pictures sometimes, which gets annoying. With such a cool, magical setting, I would expect to actually see some of the magic going on. Unfortunately, you never do. This is what makes this dating sim way less enjoyable than ones like Dandelion, which go above and beyond with scenery and drawing out pivotal scenes. The only time Magical Diary shows you a picture to go with a scene is if you kiss somebody, which for me, was only twice.

Pros:
+ Gameplay is similar to Danganronpa for all the right reasons, and to make matters even better, they improved upon the original formula and added additional minigames that can get pretty challenging.
+ Runtime is even longer than the first game, with several new bonus modes as well. I beat the game on the hardest difficulty within 26-30 hours, with some bonus time sprinkled in.
+ Character development, music, and art are still fantastic. They also put a lot more effort into this title, with cutscenes and environments having a bit more "oomph" to them.
+ The story is very interesting despite being seemingly "obvious" from the beginning. A lot of twists and turns that, just like the last game, have you on the edge of your seat. It also resolves a LOT of the issues the first game left unfinished, and without a cliffhanger!
Cons:
- PTA is... confusing. Not only does the timing feel off, they changed the system to where you have to hold it and let go according to the beat, which I admittedly must have missed completely in the explanation. What's funny about this is there is no system to correct this misunderstanding: you can freely spam the buttons without consequence, so that's what I ended up doing. A punishment system (especially on the hardest difficulty) to correct this mistake would have helped teach the mechanic.
- The usage of a certain element as one of the motives felt like a cop-out. Some of the motives in this game in particular were pretty weak compared to the first one.
- Even on hard mode, the experience was pretty easy to overcome, despite some ridiculous minigame sections.
Overall:
Danganronpa 2 is a solid follow-up to the first game. Again, not HUGELY into anime visual novels, but I would recommend the series to anyone with a love for investigative games.

Okay, time I updated this.  I originally gave GalCiv 3 a scathing review because it was in pretty poor shape on release IMO.  However, Stardock has consistently released patches for the game, improved manyof the issues I had with the original release and promise more down the road.
I plan on updating this review later with some more detailed thoughts but overall the game is good with ONE caveat:  I'm playing with ALL of the DLC and that makes a huge difference in my opinion.  Especially the Precursor Worlds and Lost Treasures.  Those two spice up the game with new and interesting things.
The strongest part of the game:  Planetary management.  The adjacency bonus is sheer genius and if you top that off with the unique Precusor worls' expansion it makes for some interesting strategies.  The improvments that they've made with starbase management have made things much easier
Weakest part of the game: Combat; plain and simple, just sucks.  Stardock opted for hands-off combat mode so outside of ship design you have no influence over combat.  Now, I consider myself more of a MOO guy than a CIV guy so not having tactical combat is a big downer to me but I understand why they opted for a hands off approach.  That being said, it would be nice to have SOME limited options in battle or outside of battle to better direct my ships.  Ships just charge at one another until they get into point blank range and slug it out.  Also, the weapons are simply incremental improvments to each other.  "Laser does 10 damage, Plasma fart gun does 30" etc.  There's no unique abilties or characteristics of weapons that gives it any flavor.  Come on guys...you're the studio that gave us FE:LH and Ashes.  Surely you guys can do better than this for combat.
Those aren't the only strengths and weaknesses of the game, but those are the main two for me.  Overall, its a good game now but still a big uneven in places.  However, Stardock has made greate strides since release and they plan to do so for several years to come.

Before I rag on this game, I'd like to say that I did enjoy it. I had fun getting spooked, I got excited with my first T4 weapon, and the story writing was enjoyable. If you like the Souls series, I'd say you'd probably enjoy this, as the combat is pretty similar.
The only reason I can't recommend this game is the price. It claims to be a rogue-like, which it holds some aspects, but a big one it lacks: replayability. Now you're probably thinking "But what about the codexes, and the colors pallets you can get, not to mention the dungeon generation!" Let me cover that.
My first problem is the documentation. Yes, I understand finding things out in a game is fun, and a lot of rogue-likes don't have good in game documentation because of that, but when it's so bad that you can't tell what most of the codexes do, then we have a problem. Why should I grind tokens just to get a codex that I might not even be able to tell what it does? Also, the color pallets you can get. Being able to change how you look each run is cool, but is that all it does? My first few runs, I noticed that as I swapped what color or "Son/Daughter of *" I picked, the dungeons felt harder, or the gen was different, but since I only did 4 runs before beating the game, was it just a fluke, or is there something to be said about it?
The second Thing is the enemies. They're cool, don't get me wrong, but that's it. Once you've gotten to level 4 or 5, you don't find new ones, it's just different varients of them, sometimes mixing in an ability or aspect from another archtype to spice things up. The boss on level 9 was interesting, but using a long sword, I could stagger it with two quick attacks, making damaging it rather easy if you could dodge his first attack.
I actually kind of liked the weapons, and I felt like what I used actively changed my play style. For main hand weapons, you had Dagger, Short Sword, Long Sword/Great Sword, Warhammer, Spear, and Staff. For off hand, you had Shield, Wand, and Crossbow, which I didn't even find until a shop on level 8.
Once you finish the game, that's it. Done. Finished. Wanna run again? go ahead, but there's not much that changes aside from dungeon gen, which is actually kind of upsetting since each floor has a specific tile set that it pulls from.
TL;DR
It's a good game, but not worth the $30, and not enough documentation to tell what half the long term items do.
Also, I felt like I should mention this, but even though steam says I have 17.1 hours of play time, I have more like 8 or 9. I went to bed last night while still alive, and I was on floor 7, so I just left it open, so steam says I've played longer than I actually have.
I'll be requesting a refund, though I don't know if it'll pass, but there's no harm in trying. I think this game needs to either be cheaper, or it needs more replayability to backup the asking price.

Rfactor 2 is a whole lot harder than Gran Turismo 6.  The learning curve is steep.  Quake 3/Live was that way.  The feeling of accomplishment keeps me going.  When I make a mistake in Rfactor 2, I understand what it is.  The physics engine feels intuitive.
3rd party content is scattered across a dozen fan sites.  Fan-made tracks are decent to good quality.  Some are rough around the edges.  All are harder to find than they should be.  I've managed to download all of the real world circuits found in Forza 6.  I have several friends who run a weekly Forza racing league.  We'll see if practicing in Rfactor 2 translates to better skill in Forza, or Gran Turismo for that matter.  I picked Rfactor 2 because it's cheaper than buying an Xbox One, game and compatible wheel.  $650 total, minimum.
In terms of fun factor, Gran Turismo/Forza wins.  In terms of feelings of accomplishment, Rfactor 2 is better.  I think it's easier for me to learn tracks in Gran Turismo; however, learning racing lines is easier to do in Rfactor 2...because it's a requirement to avoid spinning.
I recommend this game if you want to learn to handle a car better and are patient.

The reviews that came out for the game are mostly worthless, taking umbrage with the deliberate obscurity of the item descriptions, and calling the game repetitive (which all roguelikes are), but the truth is that the combat and the meat of the game are quite polished.
What really makes the game worth buying is the multiplayer. I was able to run with 3-4 person party, and the game quickly descends into an absolute cluster♥♥♥♥ because friendly fire is always on (Protip: Don't stand near the guy with the huge broadsword!).
In addition, there are persistent items that you can buy, such as codexes and color palettes for your character. Codexes give you certain buffs, such as reduced rate of fatigue or vampirism, which siphons health from the enemy on hit (I just got vampirism last night). I really like it when there are persistent items and something to work toward during the long slog to the game's end, so that repeated deaths are less discouraging.
The game, however, is not perfect. The game does stutter on infrequent occasion, and there are bugs when playing a multiplayer game (random disconnects), which caused us to restart a very successful run. At one point, we all had to reconnect, and I lost a fantastic weapon.
I'm confident these issues will be fixed, and only slightly mar what is shaping up to be my favorite roguelike since Dungeon of the Endless.
I'm not sure the game is worth $30, though. I got it as a birthday present, but I feel that $20 would be a more appropriate asking price, particularly because there are things still missing from the game (like classes, for example). Some may want to wait for it to go on sale.

An incredibly fun, Zelda-like, dungeon crawler with art by the always amazing Edmund McMillen, and programming by Florian Himsl. You play as Isaac, a young boy who is being hunted by his mother, who is on a mission from "God" to sacrifice Isaac. You travel through a series of randomly-generated basements and caves, collecting a huge variety of power-ups on your way. The religious themes in Binding are a breath of fresh air, providing some provoking, yet subtle storytelling as you play. The soundtrack as composed by Danny Baranowsky, who had collaborated previously with Edmund McMillen on the critically-acclaimed platformer, Super Meat Boy. Baranowsky created an amazing, metal soundtrack with a few ambient tracks as well. All the music fits the gameplay perfectly. With a huge replay-value and quirky yet creepy environment, there's no way I can't recommend this game, especially at the low price of $4.99.

I just wish the game was just a little more interactive, especially with the creation of your character (you can choose appearance, but no other characteristics). I'd definitely recommend this game, but I'd also recommend waiting to get it on sale. Even considering the replay value, it's a very short game.

-Megaman-style scroll feel with incredible graphics >> background, foreground, ability/fighting animation.
-Decent music, although I was far too engrossed with the game play to even hear it.  Good, but not overwhelming.
-I really like having the "no rush" sense of the game-creator(s) gave with the dialog.  They could have edited a lot of the "flavor text" out of the dialog with other characters, but they didn't.  Not only does a NPC thank you for saving them, but it's not a rushed "thanks", they'll tell you why they were in danger in the first place, opening up another quest, a little about their personal lives and a reward an a little info on it.  All this in full speech so you can here the different dialog, accents and slang of the different parts of the map.  I'm usually not much on dialog, but this really struck me as different and refreshing.
-Full speech (as stated above).  Love the fact that they took time to do that instead of just reading dialog boxes.
-Good storyline.
-Responsive movement controls.  No problems w/ platforming.  Quick reaction time >> no delay in movement.
-Large crafting system.
-Merchant stock-system.  Sell any item to the merchant and he'll get more in stock later.  Good for rare materials so you dont have to grind.  Rarer items do cost more money though obviously so the merchant isn't just a duplication machine.
-Lots of side quests.
-4 difficulty levels.
-Problem-solving, hack'n'slash, and battle-tactics game play.
-Hearing-impared, visually-impared (HUD size is adjustable), and color-blind aid options from the start.
Cons:
-Attack controls are quick until you try to pull off a specific combo.  Bit of a lag in trying to string the combo-clicks. This isn't that big of an issue as you have your normal attacks, Fidget-attacks, and dual-power attacks to really own the enemies.  That, and if you mouse-mash you're bound to pull off a few combos.
-Most levels only have two ways out to get to the map.  This makes for some tedious side-scrolling to get out of a level.  But again, there are several ways the creator(s) help alleviate the problem; When you enter a level you can start from any save point in the level >> makes getting to a specific point much easier.  You can use a teleporter gem (forgot the real name) to get out of the level to the map from any save point in that level.  And last (and my favorite) using the whirlwind-dive attack, you can sweep through most sections of a level very quickly.
All this said:
Love this game.
Well worth the buy.
Needs a prequel, sequel, and a show.

I'm not a huge fan of turn-based games, the careful calculation isn't my cup of tea outside a bit of casual play. I like action roguelikes, which give me a challenge I can quickly work through, but by nature there'll always be a glut of deaths that seem more random chance than my fault.
This game solves both problems. By making it technically turn-based but setting each turn to a less-than-half-second timer, every move is forseeable in advance; but you have to keep moving. So it beats me up but every time it does I realize I "obviously" could have just used that bomb, or staggered one more turn.
Beating the final story is simply one of the most satisfying thing I've done because I felt like I had legitimately EARNED that victory through-and-through. Quick-thinking, experience, and timing got me there, not just lucky drops. That feeling is what makes this easily one of my favorite games I've ever played. But getting your face stomped in repeatedly in hopes of one day achieving the goal isn't for everyone. I'm just in the right place for this game.
Also, good job on making the music bearable even after hearing it for 28+ hours

Just beat the game, my expectations were met since I first started playing.
I`ve seen a ton of negative reviews, which is what prompted me to write this review.
I think this game is great fun.
In this review I'm going to adress some of the things I saw other people complaining about. I'm sorry for my♥♥♥♥♥♥formatting, but I just wanted to spew out the highlights and mechanics of the game.
It`s definitely got a lot of classic "rogue like" elements. Such as needing to use an item (potion/scroll) before knowing its effects. Although there are also identify scrolls (if you don't want to risk it), another classic item in the genre. There's also permadeath, and procedural levels (which aren't as repetitive as people are claiming).
You start the game as either a male or female, and the colour (family) you choose changes what kind of potion recepie you start out with (I assume some give you other recepies than potions, but I haven't tried that many yet).
You can purchase skins or tomes (they will give you various helpful modifiers) with favours, which you earn by generally defeating monsters or completing tasks for the Brazen Head. The tomes can be switched out at any elevator-library.
You pay money to the gods (mainly what you spend cash on) to get a permanent health increase. You can also activate shrines found in the necropolis to heal or gain stamina, or water wells that will replenish you.
The game has outdoor as well as indoor "rooms", most levels have two different kinds of "environments". There are about 4 different indoor "environments", and about 4 outdoor ones.
The enemies vary a lot more than some reviews have been implying. Yes, some are just reskins of the same model, but they have different armor/colour/details/attacks than the other models.
They're not all just a recolour (although I think two of the viking fellows just have different coloured armour).
The combat is challenging and fun, although I've also seen a lot of people bashing it.
The stamina system is perfect in my opinion, and it's no issue to replenish between challenging fights.
If you have a weaker weapon and/or are fighting a more armoured unit, they will stagger a lot less, or not at all.
Some people really hate this, but I think it seems fair if your pathetic starter sword doesn't stagger an armour-clad skeleton. Although power attack or shield bash will usually do the trick, unless your weapon really sucks.
You are able to block, dodge, and sprint to avoid damage. Although staggering, potions, and scrolls also helps a lot.
Don't be reserved with your potions and scrolls later on, it makes a hell of a difference. On the last few floors I usually had potions/scrolls on for just about every fight.
I've also seen a few people complain about the spawning. A handful of enemies respawn if you leave an area long enough, but it's not usually more than a couple (I've found out on later levels that enemies simply won't respawn, as I was trying to gather more supplies while backtracking). Sometimes enemies spawn infront of you, but it's hard to get caught offguard because they usually make quite a bit of noise. Although often chests or certian rooms will be trapped, and as soon as you enter enemies will spawn. That's intentional (such as sevral laser-beam things spawning as you walk near a chest) there are also things like piles of bones which will spawn 4 skeletons.
I did a lot of back-tracking, and there are often no enemies to speak of in most of the rooms you've already cleared. Although spiderbots and pixie-things will spawn and bumble around for you to get some extra supplies.
You should always look over your shoulder before you decide to craft something or grab a bite to eat, if you're complaining about getting lasered "out of nowhere" while trying to heal up, it's almost definitely your fault.
There are 9 floors, and 4 teirs of armor/weapons. There are also various "enchantments", so far I've only noticed fire, lightning, frost, death, pink stuff, and... ooze?
Enemies have weaknesses to these effects (and perhaps even resistance, but it's hard to tell). I'm not going to say which ones are which, but some are obvious (death damage doesn't do a whole lot more to undead).
You carry a weapon in one hand (there are slow, medium, and fast ones) and a shield or ranged in the offhand. So far, the unique offhands I've come across are:
a wrist that blocks like a shield and also fires your bombs, wands, crowssbows, fire shooty hand-things.
As far as I'm aware there are only two "secret" vendors. One sells potions and recepies, the other sells armour and weapons. A few of the rarer teir 4 gear looks especially badasss, but there are more plain ones too.
I experienced no frame-rate issues, but I've heard other people are having this problem.
Also if you fall off the edge, the Brazen Head saves you. Thank god.
The main concerns I've had were that sometimes an enemy will spawn inside of a wall/block. Although in the end it's just 1 less enemy to fight. I've heard bad things about the AI in multiplayer (tunnel vision), although I think it's pretty decent in single player. There seems to be a bug currently where enemies will sometimes stand still while you use ranged weapons on them (if they don't detect you).
Finally, the humor. I don't know who wouldn't find this game hilarious, I definitely got a few chuckles out of it.
TL;DR: I love this game. I think the combat is satisfying, the levels are pretty, there is a lot of different gear/monsters/enchants/supplies/environments. I've beat the game, and I continue to play it.
If you don't like it, that's fine. Different people, different tastes I suppose.

Despite the hours played on Steam I've owned this game for a couple of years already (transferred the license to a steam key) and it has come leaps and bounds since it's initial release.
If you want the very best simulator it comes at a price. That price is time. If you can invest the time to get the most out of rFactor 2 it is an unmatched driving experience. Don't bother with this title unless you have a wheel + pedals. Until recently I was using a 10+ year old Logitech Momo and it was fine.
rFactor 2 isn't very gamey at all. No career mode. Very little hand holding. Not much in the way of fancy trinkets to appeal to the masses, but if you want the best approximation of how a car performs on a track this is it. So much so that real racing teams (including F1) use this software to train drivers and test car setups.
It should be noted that it has the best racing AI of any game. With a few exceptions on some modded tracks, they will challenge each other and you to the point where you might think they are human.
I am not a petrol-head. In the grand scheme of things I understand very little when it comes to car setups. For those that do you have a lot to work with. For those like myself that don't, this is still a hugely fun and rewarding experience.
Okay, for those getting this, there are a couple of things that will make a huge difference that you should take the time to do (20 mins?).
1. Grab the TrackMap plugin from here:
This basically adds an extra HUD with a ton of useful information. It's fully customizable in game - just press ALT + SPACE to get the menu then use arrow keys and Enter to navigate. With an object selected move your mouse to reposition it. Simple.
2. Set up your force feedback (FFB) correctly using the guide found here:
This guide is not particularly well written, in that he makes corrections at the end of the text but doesn't fix some of the main body with those corrections. Basically each step you do just check the edits at the end to make sure it's the most up to date information. For example you don't have to edit any files, the FFB torque parameter is available in game.
Those two are what I would consider pretty essential improvements to the game, particularly the second. By default there can be a lot of software clipping going on. Imagine listening to your favourite classical music with a heavily distorting pre-amp, then hearing it with correct levels in all it's dynamic glory. Note that this is set on a per car basis, and not all cars will be the same. The process is very quick after you've done it once. I found that a great track to use was Spa*, as going up the hill at full speed after you exit the pits will clip the FFB if it's going to clip. Makes tuning it very fast.
3. If you're FOV challenged, or just want the extra help in avoiding collisions, there is a great radar plug-in that will keep you aware of what's going on around you. Available here:
.
Be aware that much of the content you may end up playing will be mods. So don't think you're limited to the selection of cars and tracks ISI have developed.

After playing through The Witcher, and reading Andrzej Sapkowsk's books, Blood of the Elves and The Last Wish, I didn't think CDProject RED could pull off anything better.
I couldn't have been more wrong.  With the new engine and graphics, the gameplay goes perfectly in telling the story.  The ability to skip cutscenes (whether you've seen them or not) is great, especially on multiple play throughs.   This option is, more often than not,  unavailable in many games as they rely heavily upon them to tell the story.
The game play and interactions will tell the story with cutscenes adding a break from the fray with in engine rendering.
You do need a pretty good machine to play on ultra high settings, but it's worth all the eye candy.
Get the game, but be prepared to play many many hours.
This is not a game you compare to the likes of The Elder Scrolls, simply because it's really not intended to be.  The battles are brutal and bloody, the scenery gorgeous, and the voice acting right on the money.
GET IT NOW if you love a great action RPG, with a completely different way of character progression and leveling.

It's bad, oh it's absolutely a bad game in many, many ways but it's so bad that it's good! It's short, stupid, colourful and fun! It definitely feels like a game from the PS1 era from the mechanics, the story, the visual style and just about everything else and I find a certain charm in that and that really brings my inner kid out when I was playing this. You can beat it in under an hour with it's five levels where you go from arena to arena, battle horde after horde of cartoonish enemies until you reach the end of the level and it's silly and fun - I'll give you a quick list of pros and cons just to save you some time:
Pros:
- Short but sweet, doesn't outstay it's welcome

- Colourful, childish and cartoonish, you can run it on a potato
- Funny but somewhat racist dialogue
- Very cheap
- It has an arena mode if you ever want to just smash cartoon baddies
- Supports controller (With so few buttons being used, you could use a USB SNES pad)

Cons:
- It definitely looks like a PS1 game for those who want fancy graphics
- Pickups are almost non-existant, only coins in two levels as well as life pickups
- It's really just an arena brawler
- Fighting mechanics are dodgy, normal attack is literally useless
- For some people, it's way too short
- Might be offended by the voice acting
That's really all I have to say about the game, I got it in a bundle and I decided to play the game and found myself enjoying the badness and stupidity of the game that I played it to completion in less than an hour and I don't regret my time with it, it's dumb fun and reminds me of my kiddy days playing on the PS1 and for £1.59 (Or your regional equivalent) which I might add is a LOT less than what most people charge for a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ game (I'm looking at you Citadels), so I'd say it's worth it if you want to sit down for an hour and play something dumb for a change. Like I said before, it's so bad that it's good!

so i saw a recent review and wanted to clear things up for some people since i am an expert in duck history
some people say its the great duck game war but that is false
This game is a metaphor for the early years of World War I
It tells the tale of how many countries (or ducks) went to war because they created alliances meant to keep them safe (which is ironic considering this was the most deadly war by this point). They sent out troops one after another to face certain death. Much like how you can respawn in duck game and are sent out into an arena like battlefield where only one of them can survive, honestly the mortality rate is HIGHER than that of world war one, where around 75% of the participants face a gruesome death at the hands of fellow ducks.

much like in World War one the ducks used any weapons available like flamethrowers and pistols and giga laser rifles from the planet xenon. these weapons often leave the victim completely disfigured just like in the real war, some weapons completely cook the victim turning them into a delicious thanksgiving meal, just like in the real war. often times the ducks will use any means available to end their lives, whether it be a grenade or just throwing a box up and breaking their neck.
and just like how the real war seemed it never ended, in an infinite stalemate killing eachother over and over, even when it seemed their was a victor another battle would begin making the victory very short lived. honestly, in my opinion from the evidence i have seen, i would much rather be in World War I than be a duck in duck game. The makers have really brought to life the horrors of war in a disturbing way. some ducks even pretend to be dead so the other bloodthirsty ducks would leave them alone. But then the ducks would just pick them up, and jump off the infinite void ending both of their lives, just like in the real war.
so yeah that was a quick history lesson and appreciation of the game makers impressive attention to detail.

I'm not a huge fan of turn-based games, the careful calculation isn't my cup of tea outside a bit of casual play. I like action roguelikes, which give me a challenge I can quickly work through, but by nature there'll always be a glut of deaths that seem more random chance than my fault.
This game solves both problems. By making it technically turn-based but setting each turn to a less-than-half-second timer, every move is forseeable in advance; but you have to keep moving. So it beats me up but every time it does I realize I "obviously" could have just used that bomb, or staggered one more turn.
Beating the final story is simply one of the most satisfying thing I've done because I felt like I had legitimately EARNED that victory through-and-through. Quick-thinking, experience, and timing got me there, not just lucky drops. That feeling is what makes this easily one of my favorite games I've ever played. But getting your face stomped in repeatedly in hopes of one day achieving the goal isn't for everyone. I'm just in the right place for this game.
Also, good job on making the music bearable even after hearing it for 28+ hours

Wind Waker-looking graphics, dark souls gameplay, procedural dungeon generation... rogue-like with crafting elements.  That's what you're getting, served with an eclectic sense of humor.
Coupled with hot join/drop co-op, and character progress that lasts until you die, I'm reminded of Realm of the Mad God, but without world persistence.  You get one character at a time, and you keep said character until you die, or presumably, escape the necropolis.  I've not yet managed to escape.
The game doesn't offer you lots of data, but I like it. There's a rough concept of "leveling up", but your character doesn't really have a level in the RPG sense.  You just boost your max health and stamina, and they're not presented numerically. Weapons are nicely varied, no they don't have stats.  The armors I've seen thus far looks fantastic, though their effect is obscure.  It's a bit reminiscent of robes in Magicka.
With a few hours played, Codexes represent the only persistent progress you make in the game.  You earn tokens, which persist across characters.  Tokens unlock Codexes, Codexes provide passive benefits.  You can equip one at a time, and have the chance to change on each floor.  Examples include food never making you sick, increased damage, better shield efficiency, double gem collection, and super high jump.
I've really enjoyed my few hours spent, though I do wonder what the  longevity of the game would be.  $30 was fine for me, but when/if it goes on sale, don't pass it up.  Even by yourself, the game is worth a look.  I've primarily played with 1 friend, but playing solo could be viewed like building up a character to co-op with later.  Or to just unlock codexes.

Okay, so this will be a tough one for me to write.
No. I do not like this game. I'd give this game around a 5/10 (if we were doing numbers). It functions, quite well actually. But it's aggravatingly so much weaker than its predecessor. If you'll permit me, I'd like to explain why.
I've gone through about 35 hours of the first game. I thought it was a great game, despite its flaws. I disliked the ending and it ultimately left me at a low point. but I preordered this one midway through the first game and figured "what the hell. I'll give this a fair shot." and try it out.I'll be mostly trying to use comparisons from Trigger Happy Havoc, as that's really the best point to bounce off of. I've gone through the prologue and all of chapter one, ensuring I didn't miss anything in conversations.
For those of you looking at the meat of this, thank you!  To summarize for those who have never played these kinds of games before: You will play what seems like a dating sim for a good potion of the game. you get to know these students, develop a rapport, and generally A student will be murdered and you have to investigate a crime scene. collect enough evidence and a trial starts. This is where the game picks up. You'll go through rapid discussions about the case, and find contradictions that you shoot with 'truth bullets'. It's exciting, and a lot of it is left generally intact from the first game.  Now, for the sake of fairness. There are new ideas here I absolutely love. The game has this new feature where, during trials, students will contradict you, and you have to go toe to toe with them, literally cutting through their statements with (sigh) "truth swords" until you guide them to the statement you can contradict. It's a refreshing take on the whole idea and adds a dynamic that makes characters more present and gives that 'debate' feel to the whole experience. Not only that, but there are moments where you can

rFactor 2 is one of the most realistic racing simulators currently available on the market. Where most racing games allow you to plunk yourself down into a race car of your choosing and then just gives you the option to drive in automatic or in manual, rFactor 2 takes it much further.  It takes it so far that it is actually a little overwhelming when you first start playing as there is the need or at least the option to customize your car to suit the track you are taking it out on!
When you first start rFactor2 you can be a little overwhelmed with all the options that are available to you while at the same time being a little underwhelmed at how few cars or courses there are. The reason for the latter is the fact that Developer has opted to integrate Steam Workshop into the game in such a way that they actually release pretty much all new cars and tracks to the Workshop itself.  This leaves it up to you to decide which cars and tracks you want. It is a good design as it allows you to personalize your experience by only installing the elements you want. Due to the large download required just to install the base game, those of us with data capped Internet can still play the base game and then just cherry pick the add on Workshop content we actually want right away. This leaves us free to download the rest at some point later on.
Where this game really shines is how realistic the simulation is. Before the rubber even hits the road, there are quite a few settings for you to play with that go well beyond the standard options. Almost every car can be tuned to suit your desires and the track you will be driving it on. It isn’t simply a copy pasted feature either; each type of car has its own unique tuning options that make each car type feel completely different in game.  There are number of different kinds of cars for you to choose from, ranging from vintage and modern day racers to junior go-karts and everything in between.
Once you manage to make your way to the racetrack, the simulation gets even more immersive. With realistically working headlights to pierce the darkness, daylight slowly transitions into night and back again. Most games nowadays have rain which will reduce visibility and that is about that, when it stops raining everything reverts to normal. In rFactor 2, rain actually makes the road more slippery which impacts your ability to maintain traction and control of your vehicle. Even once it stops raining, the roads remain slick until the water on them evaporates much like it does in real life.
Another bit of realism is something you might not even notice right away. As vehicles speed around on the road surfaces, their tires wear down and take damage. This rubber doesn’t magically just vanish, it actually gets embedded into the road itself, meaning that as the race goes on, your traction will actually improve. Even the outside temperature impacts your car’s behaviour, so you will want to pay attention to the expected weather conditions and outfit your car accordingly.
Damage in this game also affects performance. In some games, damage is all cosmetic until you destroy your engine completely. In rFactor 2, the damage you take accumulates over time, which in turn impacts your overall car performance. For example, tires (or tyres) depending on where you live, take damage  just by being used. They wear down, they blister, vibrate, flex, overheat, and take damage from your careless driving. Same with the engine, gearbox, suspension, steering column, aerodynamics, etc. all can take damage. The more damaged your car becomes, the worse it will perform. Taking trips to the Pit are necessary to ensure your car operates at peak efficiency. When in the Pit, you can even control what gets done to your car, so even that isn’t just automatically done for you. Do you find yourself overheating? Adjust your radiator grill! Tires not performing that well? Adjust the air pressure or just change them entirely! So many things to do!
Visually the game is a bit mixed. Most of the game looks great, but it does look quite dated in some areas.  Things like the tires themselves are visually stunning. The attention to detail is fantastic. Even the cars themselves look great. The roadways and general tracks look fine as well. The people not so much, but really that doesn’t matter all that much. The sound effects in the game are great and immersive; it gives the feeling like you are actually there racing the car. Some of the vehicles have an odd clicking sound, as if a certain sound effect is supposed to be playing but isn’t, but I am willing to chock that up to not having a dedicated sound card.
The game has its faults, as many games do, and I feel compelled to point them out. The first one I have to mention is the settings. When first starting out you will likely find that it is quite overwhelming. I know for a fact that I really messed up my settings because the very first thing it did was automatically drive my car out of the Pit (like it was supposed to) then it proceeded to do a U-turn and crashed into the garage it came out of. It did that every single time. Even turning off my input device caused it to happen. Turning off Auto-pit fixed that, but it meant I had to drive it myself (which was fine!). I did a few practice laps, finding it difficult to turn regardless of the settings or controls I used. Spinning the wheel as hard as I could, even at lower speeds, often had me careening in a straight line off the track and into a wall. Worse yet, after fixing that issue, it had me spinning out completely on a straight stretch while attempting to center myself in the lane. Playing with the settings some more made it easier to turn. Unfortunately, turning steering assist to full caused the go-kart I was driving at the time to drive out of the pit and blow past the flagman telling me to stop. It then proceeded to drive like crazy nowhere near the track, basically simulating what it would be like to be very drunk while go-karting, mowing down any pedestrians that happened to be in the fields. Stepping on the brakes even lightly seemed to make the car want to lock the brakes, meaning you had to press lightly unless you felt like drifting around a corner backwards. It would have been nice if when you pushed the pedal all the way down , it locked the wheels rather than locking it at anything after the half way point. Again, this could be a configuration issue on my part, or an incompatibility issue.
If you are looking for a casual racing sim that can give you hours of enjoyment, look elsewhere. If you want an extremely realistic simulator that is very immersive, then look no further than rFactor 2!

Ninja Guy for Steam is hilariously random! You really can’t expect a game featuring a “Holy Cow Sensei” to be taking itself seriously! lol
The game is priced pretty much the same as Ninja Guy HD on iOS - except now it has huge waves of enemies, support for joypads and really cool effects that weren’t in the original (of which I was also a fan).
The game mechanics revolve around managing your “Ninja Focus”. When you use your ninja stars, jump attacks, whirlwind or torpedo moves this all uses up Ninja Guy’s blue bar. Even though it regenerates slowly on its own, the idea is that killing enemies boosts your Ninja Focus allowing you to potentially chain an unlimited supply of special moves one after the other. If you simply hack and slash without much thought (without killing enemies), you’ll run out of Ninja Focus and be left with simple melee moves - and that leaves you vulnerable to ambushes. There is definitely an element of tactics required to succeed in this game.
All things considered, for this price the game is great fun!
