The Binding of Isaac... An action RPG shooter with heavy Rogue-like elements. Do not be fooled by the cute cover image of Isaac. Being one of the most simple, yet morbid games I've ever played, I found myself strangely enjoying the disturbing feel of  illustration. This isnt exactly one of those games where you can call the scenery "beautiful".
Upon first gameplay, you will either love the game or hate the game; however, for most people... For a flash based game being only $4.99, this is a game where you will feel your money was well spent. You play as Isaac, one of the six unlockable characters, braving your way through randomly generated levels using very simple contrls. Each floor of the basement dungeon has monsters you must clear through before you can advance to the next room. Along the way, you collect money to purchase items from a shopkeeper and find weapons and power-ups to boost your stats and chances against enemies. Each floor of a dungeon includes a boss you must fight to move on to the next level dungeon. Though the controls are very easy to play with, this does not change the fact that you will certainly be provided with challenges; expect to die... a lot.
I was lucky to catch this game on sale for 0.99, and I was very satisfied with what I got, including the DLC and soundtrack. If you have any friends seeking an exotic experience, definitely introduce this game to them.
+ Randomly generated levels = endless replay value
+ Wide variety of items to seek and collect, adding to replay value
+ Morbid illustration keeps you strangely interested
+ Simple controls
- Since levels are randomly generated, difficulty can occasionally spike. Practice, practice, practice!

so i saw a recent review and wanted to clear things up for some people since i am an expert in duck history
some people say its the great duck game war but that is false
This game is a metaphor for the early years of World War I
It tells the tale of how many countries (or ducks) went to war because they created alliances meant to keep them safe (which is ironic considering this was the most deadly war by this point). They sent out troops one after another to face certain death. Much like how you can respawn in duck game and are sent out into an arena like battlefield where only one of them can survive, honestly the mortality rate is HIGHER than that of world war one, where around 75% of the participants face a gruesome death at the hands of fellow ducks.

much like in World War one the ducks used any weapons available like flamethrowers and pistols and giga laser rifles from the planet xenon. these weapons often leave the victim completely disfigured just like in the real war, some weapons completely cook the victim turning them into a delicious thanksgiving meal, just like in the real war. often times the ducks will use any means available to end their lives, whether it be a grenade or just throwing a box up and breaking their neck.
and just like how the real war seemed it never ended, in an infinite stalemate killing eachother over and over, even when it seemed their was a victor another battle would begin making the victory very short lived. honestly, in my opinion from the evidence i have seen, i would much rather be in World War I than be a duck in duck game. The makers have really brought to life the horrors of war in a disturbing way. some ducks even pretend to be dead so the other bloodthirsty ducks would leave them alone. But then the ducks would just pick them up, and jump off the infinite void ending both of their lives, just like in the real war.
so yeah that was a quick history lesson and appreciation of the game makers impressive attention to detail.

Just to get straight into this: I fell completely for the unique charms of this game. During summer 2014 I've played a lot of
, and I enjoyed every single minute of i. It's basically a 2D sidescroller hack and slash game, with some lightweight RPG elements. You play as Dust, a strange character who doesn't know where he is, who he is or what he has to do. There a two friends on your journey: a magical sword, and one of the most cute characters EVER in a game: Fidget, who has to look after the sword. It took me only minutes to fall in love with Fidget, especially thanks to the exceptional voice-acting. The story may look bland at first sight, but actually is very good and cleverly conceived: there is one main storyline throughout the game which unfolds in an often unexpected but still easy-to-follow way.
As far as the actual gameplay is concerned,
mainly focuses on swift attacting combo's (which are ideally suited for an Xbox 360 gamepad, the game actually being an Xbox-port) and some jumping and puzzle-solving action. None of these are really difficult, but there are some hidden places which need skill to be found, and six arena's that offer a good challenge to anyone. Combat combo's are limited, and once one gets up to strength by levelling up, things get a bit too easy. During the last third or so of the game, I felt like incincible strong, almost invincible, only to realise at the very end I needed all my strenght for the final boss fight. I strongly suggest playing the game on the "hard" difficulty setting - it will be difficult during the first hour or so, but then the extra challenge really pays of.
Visually,
is stunning. The combines a gorgeous 2D sidescrolling scenery with a handpainted look with very distinctive figures of all characters, used during the dialogues. Some of these are so cute that I'd like to have them printed out and hung above my bedside. The visual style gives the game an unique artistic look: it feels like having a soul of its own, just like a good comics book or a series of drawings. Soundwise,
is a blast as well, with very well suited music, and absolutely fantastic sound-effects, not to mention the exceptional voice-acting.
All in all, this is a gem of a game, a non-pretentious masterwork with a touch very much of its own. I can't think of any other game using the same visual style, nor the adorable cuteness of Fidget.
Overall score: 8.5/10
Go and get it, and enjoy it to the full.

Hello Gentleman and Ladies just want to tell you of this game called Stellaris.   In my opinion this is easiest to learn and less obtuse of all Paradox games I have ever played.  I am referring to Europa Universalis and Crusader kings, which I still don't understand the whole mechanics of both them.  With Stellaris I jumped right in and with the Help of the in-game tutorial I was off to a running start exploring my Galaxy.
The interface is really slick, polished and easy to learn compared to the previous games I mentioned from Paradox.  Events where not all coming at once and you can soak each one in and make decisions pretty easily without getting logged jam.
I might have not logged a ton of hours yet on the game but what I have accomplished in the game like design multiple different races and ships already for first hour of game speaks alot of the depth this games has.  I also started 3 single player games and even chatted on the multiplayer server which had people ready to jump into some multi player fun.
Everything about this game yells quality.   The soundtrack, user interface and attention to details of the planets is astounding while zooming into them.  I don't play alot of 4x games because it gets kinda gets that same ole feeling after awhile, but this game is random and so deep in strategy I can't begin to tell you where to start on what they put in this game.  One example is how you choose your ruler.  I choose Democracy and they have election every 5 years.  I noticed one of the 3 nomiees was favored by the people, even without me endorsing the delegate {which you can at the cost of some influence points}.  I noticed he had a special ability called the peoples champion, just like the ROCK {you know Dwayne Johnson},  which I thought was nice touch.  Of course he won even without my endorsement.
As I saying this game is deep for my brief play thoughs so far.  You can go as deep in the Rabbit hole as you feel comfortable.  Heck you can stay on the main universe map and let the computer micro everything for you, but you would only be scratching the surface on what this game has to offer.  To be honest it wasn't that hard to learn either and I am kinda surprised for Paradox game.
Well this game is going to only get better as people start modding it and future DLC from Paradox {especially the diplomatic portion is there, but lacking alot of option we expect from a Paradox game}.  I am looking forward to the day someone Mods the Star Trek Universe!
Buy this game if you are s Science fiction fan or into any Grand Strategy games {even Civilization games}.  This game has it all.  Let your imaginiation go crazy.  This game has so much potential even though it already is a enormous game from the get go.  Just go buy it, you won't regret it, your going to have memoriable memories in this game.  Its that good.

I started it off not really knowing what to expect, and thought that it didn't give you enough choices. After classes start up though, the game gets really fun. Learning new spells and finding applications for them is fun. Mostly you will use them to get out of dungeons, which function as exams, but you will also be able to use many of them to unlock unique options in random events, which is an awesome touch. Speaking of random events, there are enough things that happen each week to make the game interesting, and a surprising amount of variety in the situations you can find yourself in. I didn't do a second playthrough for a long time, but it's worth it for some different endings. None of the endings are really "the good ending". They're all a bit open-ended, and all have something about them that you'll have to leave behind. The story is enjoyable; definitely interesting and unique enough to keep you engaged. I like to think that this takes place in some female-oriented alternate dimension of harry potter, what with the whole magical wizard school and professor Grabineer*cough*snape*cough*. But it has enough of its own story elements to set it apart from the universe that it drew much of its inspiration from. The main character is a little bit generic, but you're given enough of your own choices to project your own character onto her. My only real gripe is that you're character alludes to parents and a backstory at several points, but her parents are mostly left blank. Although I do have this theory that the school directors hypnotized them with magic to think that you just went off to boarding school... I mean, it really makes sense, and feels like it's hinted at a couple of times. I digress. The game is great to play with a friend for ♥♥♥♥♥ and giggles, as well as for a couple of serious playthroughs alone. I think all of my friends have played at least halfway through this game when we got bored, and I've played it multiple times, so I feel I definitely got my money's worth.
In short, best game ever 10/10. Buy it or yur a ♥♥♥♥♥.

I've owned Rfactor 2 since the very first beta release, long before steam. For me at least it's a strange title to place, I find the level of realism and quality of simulation with Rfactor is only as good as the current car and track that you're in, with a very wildly varying experience, the player also really needs to have at least a basic knowledge of car setup and a good understanding of wheel peripheral setup to get the right experience, it's not a fantastic "plug and play" experience.
At it's best Rfactor 2 is perhaps the best driving simulator out there, or at the very least it's on a par, but at it's worst it's let down by less than fantastic content quality that isn't helped by the equally inconsistent default setups.
The graphics were already dated when it came out back in 2012, but a bit of artistic flair and some quality lighting can make them hold up even today. The same can be said about the sounds, they range from really great to hopelessly dated and weak sounding. The UI really doesn't hold up, it's neither functionally well designed nor is it good to look at, it's about as basic barebones minimal effort as can be. Tracks take an unreasonably long time to load, so if you're running on a traditional hard drive you might wanna put your favourite trilogy on while you wait.
It sounds like a negative review but it's not given what Rfactor 2 is. Rfactor 2 is a simulator for serious driving simulator fans, for people who want a tool for driver training. If you put enough effort into Rfactor 2 to source the best quality content, to optimise your control setup, to work with the car setups and to maximise your experience then you will have a must have driving sim. But if you're looking for an out of the box driving sim experience there are better options out there.

The game is incredibly short, there is no real depth, and the combat doesn't even offer the same meagre variety of Dark Souls.
"...NOT WITHOUT PERKS. Each new dungeon is littered with powerful weapons, armor, and upgrades to wield against your foes. (And there’s crafting, too!)"
Crafting consists of making potions. Armor is a pointless skin and offers no variety of gameplay. As you advance in the game, you don't really get any form of a real upgrade. In Dark Souls you might eventually obtain a cool boss/unique weapon with a unique moveset, in Necropolis you eventually get a version of whatever you're using that deals slightly more damage! Yippee! Enchanted weapons are mildly more powerful than their unenchanted breathren, but the crazy cool looking particle effects don't have any relationship with the hitbox. You just did some cool frost nova? Awesome, nothing's frozen, it barely even got knocked back, and suddenly you're hungry and you need to eat so you can swing as many times as you did before you got into this fight.
Weapon variety is meagre. A large portion of the weapons are reskins of each other, but don't have any variety in stats. That hammer is the same as the sickle is the same as a greatsword. Weapons like longswords feel absolutely pointless when the option for either much faster shortswords exist and significantly more powerful but not noticeably slower greatswords also simultaneously exist.
I played six hours with a friend and beat the majority of the game without losing any progression. I haven't touched a Codex yet. Yet at the same time, when I played through, I really enjoyed the game's pacing as something similar to Dark Souls, but not. I liked being able to plow through multiple enemies - but I didn't much like how I did it: is charging up a single attack to mow down a group of enemies interesting? Not that much to me.
In a way, I suppose I like the game, but it wasn't worth 30$ and it didn't do much. I think it's got potential, but that potential is poorly misused and the game goes nowhere. It looks cool, but if you're really this desperate for a Souls fix, or still haven't gotten enough out of Dark Souls 3, your money is probably better spent buying that game's season pass.

If you are looking for a TL:DR review, this is not it.
This is the good, the bad, and the ugly.
The Good
Graphics - The Graphics of this game are 10x better than those of GalCiv 2.  I am rather impressed by the communications screens between races as those you are speaking to look much more like a true, living thing looking back at you.  The improved graphics also includes the cut-scenes, and fleet warfare.  An all-round improvement.
Ship Design - Much more comprehensive than before, and it seems to me more meaningful.  If you enjoy tweaking your ship designs as I do you'll spend a crap ton of time doing that and feeling that the effort has been rewarded.
Technology - The Technology Trees have been redesigned and make more sense now.  Tech is divided into 3 (really 4) ages.  Certain techs can only be researched if you have reached the minimum age.  So no more having Nightmare Torpedoes before your society can even build a life-support system.  This makes perfect sense to me.  Now every technology you research counts toward elevating the age of your society.  At 180 techs you can push for things such as research victory, and the ability to duplicate precursor-level technology which will make your ships...well woe to the poor ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s who have to fight them.
Enemy Surrender - When an opponent surrenders to you now, you don't just get his planets you get everything he has left.  Any remaining ships, starbases...everything.  This can often make it worthwhile to beat an enemy into submission rather than just conqueror every world he has outright, and also saves you the trouble of fighting a new armada of pirates as in previous games.  The AI will no longer surrender to an uninvolved 3rd party just to spite you.  (But if your opponent is at war with more civs than just your own, there is still a risk the surrender will be given to one of them instead of you.)
ADDENDUM - After writing this review I did have an enemy Civ surrender to an uninvolved 3rd party, but I am unsure of the nature of the relationship between the two.  In any case it has only happened to me once in 100 hours of gameplay, versus every damn time in the previous game.
ADDENDUM II - From what I can tell, the risk of 3rd Party surrender exists if the two parties have a friendly or alliance relationship with each other.  While it makes sense, it is still profoundly frustrating, and and really feels that it cheapens your victory.
Diplomacy - Is more comprehensive, I actually have races try to pay me to attack those they don't like now.  That never happened to me in previous games.
The Bad
Some features have been removed that I am not happy about.  There is no longer an auto-kill command that you can issue a ship or fleet.  Every attack action for every ship/fleet must be manually given by you.  If you like to play on larger maps as I do this can become a real pain in the♥♥♥♥♥and make each turn take a very long time simply because of how many enemies are on the map.  It is especially bothersome if you have an enormous tech advantage over your foe.  You feel like you've walked into a swarm of gnats and are having to individually slap each one of them.
It is much harder to negotiate favorable surrender terms.  Most of the time when I offer to let an opponent surrender, he won't take the offer no matter how badly I out-match him.  Meanwhile when he contacts me begging to surrender I have only the option to accept or reject, no option to force him to cough up some reparations for peace.
The Ugly
No Super Weapons - No Terror Stars, and no planet killers....at least one of the two should be present in a game like this.
The Ship Designer
Yes I know I already lauded this in the positive points, however I do have one big gripe.  By the end game, you are still reduced to building glass-cannon ships with all offense, and no defense.  That is a dynamic I wish had changed, but which sadly has not.
There are some serious cases of Artificial Stupidity here.  I can be so technologically advanced that the rest of the races are bacteria by comparison, have a fleet three times the power of all opponents combined, and STILL have both major and MINOR races ring me up and demand tribute.....I'm going to call this a bug since it is a pretty big damn oversight otherwise.
The galactic resources such as antimatter, elerium, etc can make a huge difference due to what they will allow you to build.  Problem is its possible to have a map spawn that lacks one or more of these resources entirely!  I'm guessing this is a bug as well, but I cannot say for certain.
The Campaign Mode - Stardock couldn't even spring for some no-name voice actors to spice things up a bit.  Meanwhile your reward cinematic for beating the campaign is all of 15 seconds and has no dialogue.  Granted I certainly didnt buy this game for the campiagn so this is a minor issue to me.
The AI's awareness alternates between brilliant and stupid.  If you have a ship trespassing in another civ's territory, they'll actually deploy ships to keep an eye on yours which I thought was great.  But then I noticed that I was able to build an enormous armada right on another nation's border (which I did in fact use to invade him) and that nation never said a thing.  (In GalCiv 2 on any difficulty above normal the AI would see that and preemptively declare war on you.)  They will still declare war on you if you move a huge assault fleet through their territory.
I am not really sure if the AI is no longer capable of realizing a huge armada massing on their borders is bad news, or if this behavior was intentionally pruned.  (I did have civs declare war on me in previous games, when the armada I was building was actually meant for an adjacent 3rd party).  In some ways its an improvement over GalCiv2, other ways its not.  In any case its easier to prepare to invade a neighbor than it was, but he WILL declare war on you as soon as you bring planetary assault ships into his territory.
An annoyance - other powers become agitated if you have ships in their territory, and it will harm your diplomatic standing with them unless you negotiate an "Open-Borders" treaty.  The AI however has no problem whatsoever happily flouting your territory with its own ships.  It will even occasionally mock you over it, sending you messages about how you should negotiate an OB-Treaty since they obviously don't respect your borders anyway.
Carriers are SEVERELY bugged.  While they spice up fleet warfare and can add some punch to a fleet, the game doesn't know how to treat them.  More than once I have watched the fleet battle and seen my carriers curb-stomp enemy ships....only for the carriers to then lose and be destroyed in the quickbattle that follows the full battle....WTF.  Does not seem to be a problem if carriers are not operating alone, without the escort of non-carrier ships.
There are some open questions about the live-action fleet battles.  More than once (fairly often in fact) ships will continue fighting after reaching 0hp. I don't know but it needs to be addressed.
I would say that whoever was in charge of proof-reading deserves to be fired, but that would imply there was a person tasked with that responsibility, and I'm just not convinced that's the case.
Overall I give this game an 7/10

Nostradamus: The Last Prophecy was made by a group of french developers who were related to Cryo the company that created Atlantis The lost Tales in 1997. This game was made in 2007 ~ so it was a welcome back to some great puzzles and game things that were missing at that time. The game doesn't have high production values and that shows especially today after 10 years, but still what keeps my interest in this game now and kept it long time ago when i played it for the first time was the game mechanics. This game has a story of course (it is not only puzzles) there are many dialogs and there is story development to be found, suspense and murder along the way, but the main thing about this game was its puzzles (most of them, not all) wich are, interestingly @fun@ (who would knew!) something that other adventure games lack some times (many times).
Of course, that depends largely on what you consider fun as a puzzle, but if you are interested in playing as madeleine, daughter of nostradamus, in the XVI century france, making potions , food and weird concotions at the laboratory and then drawing astrological charts, writing predictions based on natal charts and looking at constellations to find hidden clues to a murder(s) then i think you will like it. The game, as a said, gives you in several parts of the game receipts to prepare all sorts of things ranging from making bread (!) preapring tea, to preparing aphrodisiac and then making a mold key or even make up. All is fun and well done and you have many of the ingredients in you lab, but some of them you will have to go and look for them.  In other parts of the game you go to Nostradamus observatory and look to the stars or use one of his contraptions to make predictions and birth charts. Some of them are intuitive and some of them are not (there are a few obscure puzzles there) but you always have the option to use a walkthrough if you are stuck) The game has many environmental and action puzzles, meaning doing things related to a scene. Of course you investigate crime scene(s) and you have your hour glass thingy, and you scalpel, and tweezer and all the renaissance detectives tools you could wish for (and you will use them, each one of them)
The third and most interesting thing about this game was the role played by madeleine (the main character in this game)
She is a woman from the XVI century and as such she is not given the same allowance to do things as his brother, cesar, so, when a murder is comitted in the royal court and nostradamus is called to investigate but he is not able to go because of his deteriorating health, he sends his daughter dress as man (madeleine's brother) so as to allow her to investigate and do all necesary things to solve the mistery. And far from being a gender thing (wich it is of course) the character uses her disguise as a man to investigate and meet some characters, but also changes to be dressed as a woman (as herlself) to take advantage of that in certain situations. So, instead of taking a solemn approach and making it a gender thing only, and showing up as a victim herself, on the contrary the main character, madeleine, plays around its limitations that society puts on her because of being a woman in the XVI century and instead she takes advantage of that and plays around it and takes advantage of all the characters around her, as a woman and as a man, making it a true androgynous character, wich is refreshing in a way, and also takes courage to do so in a game. But, anyway, thats not the main point of the game (allthough you are crossdressing from beginning to almost the end, when you cover is off) but the main story is the murder of someone in the court of the queen wich is related to an old prophecy nostradamus wrote , and off you go to investigate that and work with nostradamus across several days.
The end of the story, its a little rushed and could have been a little more developed, but it serves the story right and all is completed, one way or the other. The expression of all the characters in this game, its a little lacking...especially for that few moments where important things happens, but again, its a game from 2007, and a low budget one at that, so you can't ask for a fully developed graphical experience here. What you will get instead its a game full of things to do, obects and ingredients to get , many potions to prepare, a lot of crossdressing to take advantage of and a good amount of astrological drawings and birth charts to make along the way.

Nostradamus: The Last Prophecy is a length point-and-click game that ultimately disappoints.
Pros:
- Voice acting throughout. I appreciate games that do that. I don't want to be reading the entire time!
- Long length. I like to see any game in this genre that is longer than 5 hours. I want my money's worth.
Cons:
- Sometimes the subtitles at the bottom of the screen didn't match what the character was speaking. That bothers me.
- There wasn't any kind of tutorial in the beginning to explain how the game mechanics work. The inventory system and the tools on the side of the screen (scissors, scalpel, etc) are more complicated than they seem.
- No achievements! Lame.
- Some of the puzzles in this game were way too cryptic or ambiguous. There is no way I would be able to finish this game without a walkthrough. For example, there is a moment in the game where you need the key to a locked door, and you are able to make an imprint of the key shape when a certain character isn't looking. You are only able to do this when you are speaking to that character though. If I recall correctly, that is the only point in the game where something is interactable while a conversation is going on.
- Maybe I wasn't pressing the right buttons, but the dialogue wasn't skippable! One of the most annoying things a game can do. I don't want to sit through the same lines multiple times.
- The whole last section of the game was terrible. There is a time limit to finding the solutions. A time limit to finding the solutions to an already diffficult game! What an awful idea. Also, the ending to the game was extremely lackluster.
I didn't have high expectations going into this game, and I'm glad I didn't. I was very disappointed in how the game played out, and I don't think I can recommend this game to anyone who doesn't have loads of free time on their hands.
There were no jump scares exactly, but sometimes you turn the corner or into a new room and someone is just standing there staring at you. That could get a little unsettling.

I'm actually a little bit on the fence with rFactor 2. I respect the incredible technical achievements and amazing features that ISI have packed into the sim and I support them as licensing the rFactor 1 engine has given birth to other sims that I love, but rFactor 2 largely feels a bit lifeless and clinical - like it takes itself too seriously to be much fun. The free content that ISI offers on Steam Workshop is a nice addition because otherwise the game comes with very little in the way of stock content. The problem is that older content "feels" old and newer content gets the physics and graphics updates, but they never go back to update all of the rest of the existing content.
The AI are decent and the sounds and graphics are okay. The FFB is detailed but there are way too many canned effects added with spring and damper and the only way to adjust it is to close the sim, edit the files, and then start it up again to see if you like the new settings... it's a bit of a chore, honestly. They do provide some ability to tune FFB and control inputs from the settings within the game, but there are a few things missing here and there.
Also, you have to buy the online subscription services if you want access to multiplayer, the Steam version doesn't come with the complimentary 12-month subscription like the non-Steam version did. It's a silly and archaic model held over from their attempts to stop the rampant piracy of rFactor from the pre-Steam era and they should really just do away with it now. I only got the base game so I haven't tried the multiplayer.
Final notes: make sure you set the track to have at least light rubber, if not medium rubber, on the surface. A pristine "green" track surface will drive like ice and is no fun at all. Also, the modding community isn't super active but there are some worthwhile third party mods and tracks. I would recommend you try out the demo from ISI's website before deciding to purchase. It's not my everyday "go-to" sim, but rFactor 2 has day/night cycle and rain/weather combined with "real road" technology, so it's worth booting up every now and then.

If I would have to summarise Magical Diary in one word I'd choose: Magical.
Glad I don't have to use just one word. Magical Diary is a mix between a Visual Novel, a Role-Playing, a Dating and a Puzzle game. You play (or are) a female student in a Magic School. You can customise your player character pretty well, especially considering it is a Visual Novel, mostly. You can choose a general body type, hair type, hair colour, eye colour, skin colour, etcetera.
Your days are partly spend studying a type of Magic (or activity) which you choose at the start of each week and specific events (influenced by choices and responses). On the weekend you have a variation of activities to pick from. This cycle basically repeats through out the game. Every few weeks there'll be a test, which consist of a first person puzzle you'll have to get through with the Magic (or skills) you've learned. In other words you're living through a normal school life... well, normal, except for the Magic, Demons, etcetera. This of course... includes dating! There's a few different candidates, both male and female to choose from: each with their own story and choices within that story. So there's replay value there if that's high on the priority list.
It took me roughly six hours to finish my first play-through. Second lasted about four. All in all an enjoyable experience.

I really liked this game. Its my first graphic novel type game at least from what I can remember and I have not played any others yet although I do want to in the future. What I am getting at here is that I really have nothing to compare this game to so my review may seem a bit to positive but oh well I think it deserves it. So this game is about a girl that was told that she was a witch and that she could, if she chose to, go to a magical school. She then goes to class meets people and lives her one year at the school in which the game ends with here dating someone or the other multiple endings.. or you might just screw up and get expelled before school finishes. The game did really well opening up the magical world to you without hammering you down with uneeded explanation at the start. You basically learn about the world as you go along. The relationships for the most part felt real and were not to over the top romantic which allows you to get much more involved with the characters I find. The game had a lot of story lines and a lot of your choices effected how that storyline would go. I have replayed this game many times and still havn't uncovered every storyline part. I know this because I still have not unlocked all the achievements yet. So the game can easily be replayed many times. The game is also pretty short so that also makes it easier to replay.
Umm there not really any huge issues with the game, i guess after replaying the game a few times you will get a lot of scenes that you have seen before, especially at the start, but you can quickly skip over those if you want to. I remember reading some one elses review saying that the game was to short and that it was only one year of school. I dont know if this is an issue for me really because if the game was longer than I think the replay value would probably lower so good job developers with making the game short. Maybe the developers can make a second game. Thats always a possibility I guess.

Abzu is an amazing, hidden gem of a game, but is a little short for the price. (I bought it on sale for $9.99, and am satisfied with the experience I had for the money, but I'm not sure I can reccomend paying $19.99 for a game I completed in 3 hours.)
The experience is beautiful, dreamlike, and surreal. Gameplay mainly consists of diving through, and exploring a vibrant, underwater world filled with colorful plants and marine life, that you can interact with to a various extent. The fun of the game mainly lies in exploring your enviornment, the small discoveries and gameplay mechanics, and those "Hmm, I wonder if I can do this..." moments, so I won't go in to too much detail on what you can expect to find.
(
)
If the premise of a relaxing dive through an ever changing marine world, that may have something more sinister hidden among the beautiful surface, then I can reccomend you pick this title up (on sale) and you won't be sorry.
Pros:
+ Stunningly beautiful world to explore at your own pace. (not "open world")
+ Wide variety of plant and animal life, many of which can be interacted with or unlocked.
+ Low stress, simple puzzles and gameplay mechanics add some variety to the exploration.
Cons:
- As much as I enjoyed this game, I expect more than 3 hours out of a game Steam is charging $19.99 for.
- Low replay value. I'll probably pick it up from time to time, when I want a relaxing distraction, or time waster, but it's a fairly linear game.
- Controller is essentially required, and even then the controlls take some getting used to. I got a little motion sick at a couple points.
Overall verdict:
I very much enjoyed this game, and think you will too. Give it a try!
I give it a solid 8 Starfish out of 10.

I'm actually a little bit on the fence with rFactor 2. I respect the incredible technical achievements and amazing features that ISI have packed into the sim and I support them as licensing the rFactor 1 engine has given birth to other sims that I love, but rFactor 2 largely feels a bit lifeless and clinical - like it takes itself too seriously to be much fun. The free content that ISI offers on Steam Workshop is a nice addition because otherwise the game comes with very little in the way of stock content. The problem is that older content "feels" old and newer content gets the physics and graphics updates, but they never go back to update all of the rest of the existing content.
The AI are decent and the sounds and graphics are okay. The FFB is detailed but there are way too many canned effects added with spring and damper and the only way to adjust it is to close the sim, edit the files, and then start it up again to see if you like the new settings... it's a bit of a chore, honestly. They do provide some ability to tune FFB and control inputs from the settings within the game, but there are a few things missing here and there.
Also, you have to buy the online subscription services if you want access to multiplayer, the Steam version doesn't come with the complimentary 12-month subscription like the non-Steam version did. It's a silly and archaic model held over from their attempts to stop the rampant piracy of rFactor from the pre-Steam era and they should really just do away with it now. I only got the base game so I haven't tried the multiplayer.
Final notes: make sure you set the track to have at least light rubber, if not medium rubber, on the surface. A pristine "green" track surface will drive like ice and is no fun at all. Also, the modding community isn't super active but there are some worthwhile third party mods and tracks. I would recommend you try out the demo from ISI's website before deciding to purchase. It's not my everyday "go-to" sim, but rFactor 2 has day/night cycle and rain/weather combined with "real road" technology, so it's worth booting up every now and then.

The game starts nicely enough, and I must commend the artists who have done an excellent job. The renaissance Italy, full of colors and rich in details, provides an excellent and atmospheric setting for the upcoming adventure. Nostradamus, horoscopes (strangely called "charts" in the game), historical figures, sinister plot threatening the ruling family, all that is very promising and fresh. You can even pose as man or woman according to your wish, and the dialogues play slightly differently, which I found impressive.
However, as the game unveils, its quality starts to deteriorate. The translation is not very good, sometimes you wrestle with an odd expression of unclear meaning. There is absolutely minimal amount if animation in the game - a guard extends his arm, woman throws dice, Nostradamus nods and smiles. At one occasion, you talk to a person over a closed door, which no doubt saved the dev team some time and effort.  The late game puzzles become infuriating, especially a particular substitution cipher where you must decipher.. a French text, probably because translating the cipher would take too much effort. The characters are barely legible and sometimes similar, for example the character "-" (hyphen) means three different letters.
The game also suffers from a split personality disorder. One moment you discover a dead body in a room, and are getting ready to open his personal chest to shed light on his murder, but your character refuses - Nah, probably nothing in there. Just another corpse. Without reporting your find, you are suddenly teleported to your home. Nostradamus listens to your  report about the murder and then gives you a very important task - to brew a herbal tea, so that you can sleep better. I run back to the castle in the middle of the night, but the drawbridge was closed. Nobody cares. Another dead body? Old news.
The game ends, I imagine, in a moment when the dev team run out of finances, their creditors probably stormed their offices, and started confiscating computer equipment. A duo of a artists have decided to quickly conclude the game with a 20 seconds long cutscene that makes absolutely no sense whatsoever, and that's it, end of story.
"You have finished the game with %d points".
"%d" is a symbol for numeric value in formatted print. The programmer was probably dragged away by then, so there was nobody to correct the error.
What a pity.

rFactor 2 may very well be the sim title with the most potential. But the best thing I can say about it is it feels incomplete.
The things that rfactor 2 does, it does best. It has fantastic FFB & driving dynamics. Ever changing track conditions, tires, temps, to my eyes one of the most natural & realistic visuals, great A.I, and on and on. But it somehow feels unfinished. It is a little short on content, but does have a decent modding community which is now a part of Steam's workshop.
rFactor 2 is an ever evolving title, and if you can stick with it, it will reward you from time to time. It is beautifully immersive with great sounds, 24hr day cycles (hello night racing!) full weather cycles, full car systems such as tire temps, brake temps, water, and oil, etc.
I recommend this game for driving purists. It is a demanding title, and will require you to work on your driving technique & style, car set up, constantly aware of track conditions, line racing, and fighting for position.  If this sounds overwhelming to you, perhaps check out other titles such as Assetto Corsa. If not, you cannot go wrong with rFactor 2, and similarly Automobilista.
Over all 7.5/10.
PS: Keep in mind that online racing is paid via subscription. However, it is one of the best titles for offline racing.

The cast is way better this time around - there's only one character that annoyed me and that's only because that character was intentionally designed to be annoying and the voice acting is also vastly improved in my opinion.

First off let me say I am very disappointed by this title due to the fact that it had such potential to be a great genre-defining game. A genre I will gladly embrace if another developer spearheads the project. I was excited to play this title from the moment I found out about it. It lacks features/content/direction in so many different areas it's almost laughable.
Let me also say I do not have a bias against HBS. I loved all three Shadowrun games and would recommend them gladly. I may do a review for each game just to prove this.
Combat:
The combat controls are a blander, less intricate, clunkier version of all the Souls games. On its own, considering the fact that the studio is an indie studio, this is forgivable. Less resources typically equals less polish. Where this game loses me in the combat aspect of things is the difficulty. The game is flat out easy -- to the point of being boring. With a friend I was able to clear the nine levels of this game in under seven hours dying only once due to a lag related issue. My friend did not die at all. The developers make so many comparisons to Dark Souls you would think the overall hardcore feel of Dark Souls would carry into this as well. Your thinking would be flawed in this respect. Difficulty aside, the basics work fairly well as a nod to the Dark Souls series. The core concept is there, but the meat of what makes Dark Souls so enjoyable is not. The variety of weaponry/move sets/enemy attack patterns etc. are all severely underwhelming. And using "DLC WILL FIX ALL PROBLEMS WITH THE GAMEEEEEE!!!!!" as a crutch is just a lazy and dishonest argument that should be seen as placation. Please remember that these DLCs will not be free in the future and that, in my opinion, are required to make this game feel finished.
Environments/Overall Atmosphere:
The environments are bland and same-sy. My friend and I both noticed a few variations on stock rooms we'd encountered early in the game. We also noticed that late into the game the dungeons become a mash-up of all the previously explored biomes rather than new, interesting biomes. Save for the last stage of the game. I liked the minimalistic art style meshed in with the bleak surroundings as have most people I've spoken to that played this game. On the flip side of that coin is the dialogue. The comical nature of whatever the narrator is supposed to be is jarring and feels completely out of place. It, simply put, contrasted powerfully against the overall tone/setting of the game. I am a fan of the Dark Souls style of storytelling wherein you're mostly left to piece together the lore and whatnot but in this game the terrible comedy removed any interest I had in learning more about the lore. The lack of variety in the enemies faced was also a fairly serious letdown. Floor after floor, room after room of differently coloured enemies with a differently coloured attack became boring very quickly.
Music:
Don't nobody give a♥♥♥♥♥♥ Kind of boring I guess.
Price:
29.99 USD (or 32.99 in real dollars) is far too steep for a game that lasts seven hours and that promises paid DLC to add content that should have been in the base game to begin with.
Summary:
Combat is easy/lacks variety. Differently coloured mobs. The game is laughably short. Nine levels short. The atmosphere of the game is drained by the comical nature of the lore. An ambitious attempt at genre-meshing, but a failed attempt at best. HBS can do/has done much better than this. Paid DLCs to finish off a game that is half complete is a joke. 4/10.

This is a good game. In order to make this a helpful review I'll review different points below.
Good stuff:
------------
- The game has interesting races to choose from and in addition has excellent functions for you to make your very own custom race including; racial traits, different leader/race pictures, starting system planetary setup and so on.
- Excellent automation options. You can set rally points and many other parameters for ALL shipyards, and so on, via a very simple and fast menu, no hassle at all to manage a sprawling empire.
- Very good ship customization. This isn't something I use as I lack the patience for it, but if you like to decide how your ships should look then you can spend a LOT of time in the ship builder!
- Nice cutscenes and pictures when you colonize and gain resources. I'd like more of them though since they set the tone and atmosphere in the game.
- Not all planets are equal. Some planets will have more/less building space than others. You CAN develope them so they can house more imprevements, but only to a degree. I like this, this makes planets different and you would do well to protect your more precious planets.
- Space battles. I actually like that you have no direct control over battles. I'm the leader of the nation, not the admiral in the fleet.
- Bad stuff: (Some of this stuff is more about my own personal preferance rather than objectively negative things)
------------
- The game could have used more immersion than it currently has. Perhaps more specific and different UI:s or so.
- For me personally the mid game turns much into a click fest where I just press "next turn". I suspect that this has to do with me playing too passively and too peacefully.
- I'm also not a fan of how planets are developed. Buildings of the same type give proxomity bonii to buildings of the same type. This is a true and tried mechanic but, without being able to give an example of a  "better" system, I would have liked a different logistics systems.
- Space battles. This is my first GC game so I have no idea how battles were modelled before. But battles look a little silly. Ships bump into each other and circle/wobble around each other in a drunken fashion making the ships look like little rubber toys rather than advanced warships engaging in deadly space battles.

Challenging and interesting mechanics for a 2D sidescroller where you can't even jump or turn around! I see it in the same light as "Receiver." Like Receiver, it's got a set of unique controls that you really have to get down if you want to win, and rhythms/timing you have to get just right, too. Simple, fairly straight-forward premise, with in depth mechanics to make it really shine.
There's a real satisfaction once you start to figure stuff out and nail your attacks. I sure had a smile on my face once I started plowing through enemies on the first level! I'm about half-way through the game at the time of writing this, and I guess there's only 20 different enemies spread over 5 levels, meaning it's a fairly short game, but thus far the variation in enemies has kept the game challenging and fun. At least up to this point, it doesn't feel like the kind of game where you  learn everything over a short period and then just breeze through the rest of it; it doesn't really get easier as you progress.
Oh yeah, and the graphics, too, are really nice. What initially pulled me in while I was browsing through titles on the steam store was the black background with that font that reminds me of an old fantasy strategy or point-and-click game or something (and the name, too, I gotta say).
It looked like they were going for retro, but not effortless modern indie retro where its just like "everything is pixelated but the animations are probably bad or the character designs are probably bad/minimally thought out". Here, the environments and characters are detailed and very nice looking while sticking to color palettes and traditional sprite animation; no rotating pixels for swords/arms or anything like that, everything is done frame by frame to look consistently good.
The designs of characters actually look like they make the most out of what they can be, as well. They don't look overly stylized or minimal or generically indie, they look like they were the best efforts made to represent detailed and readable enemies using more traditional means. No black outlines, no noodle limbs, no oversized heads!
I think this game is well worth the fairly small price, and during a sale, certainly worth picking up for just a couple bucks!
-----NEGATIVE REVIEWS-----
Someone complained that the game is stacked against you. I mean, I guess if you're looking for an easy nothing game to just annihilate and be done with, this isn't the game for you. Yes, the game is stacked against you. You die. A lot. That's kind of the point of it, to be a challenge. And as for arguing about "unfairness" in the difficulty of a game that's supposed to be difficult... well, this is a single player game. I don't remember reading a promise anywhere that said "this game is going to treat you nicely and let you win" and it's not like you're playing against people online. The AI isn't going to back off and be like "ok, I smacked you too much, here have a swing." You bought the game as advertised, they didn't say "here's a game that you can play if you don't want to lose or struggle ever."
I also saw somebody complain about the controls being sluggish, which might play into that "unfair" thing. You move slowly in this game (while moving forward) but the controls are pretty responsive. The attacks have a delay to them (in that there's a swing animation before you strike, not that they just pause for no reason and then swing), but the blocks are instantaneous, and you can quickly dodge if you need to. I never felt like I was dying from the controls being poor or unresponsive, personally; what it comes down to is having good reflexes and observing your enemies to figure out how to close distance properly.

Little Inferno is a lovely little game that, on the surface, seems like the strangest game premise ever:  order stuff from catalogs and burn everything.  And, on the surface, that is what you do.  Your time is spent staring into a fireplace creating flames and burning everything you get your hands on.  The act of burning various ordered items that produce a wide array of effects when sent up in flames as well as finding each of the 99 unique combinations of burned items quickly sucks you in.  It is a visually beautiful game with an intriguing and poignant ending that takes a turn you don't see coming.  Being that it is quite short (100% completion in less than 6 hours) I would recommend picking it up when it is on sale rather than full price but it is definitely worth a play through.

Part of the problem is that there are no walls to hold you in the level, so you fall to your death easily, due to the fact that the floor has many gaps, and the actual walking space is rather narrow. In addition, mobility is extremely hampered, either by invisible barriers, or zombies that hold you in place when hitting you. It really seemed like i simply couldn't jump or run to other areas, leading me to believe there are invisible barriers. However, if it's indeed zombies that can immobilize you, well that's just silly, given that it assures you will die, since it only takes about 2 hits to do so.
Just not fun, poorly designed, and not something I could ever recommend, especially not at $5. I was "lucky" enough to get it in a bundle, but I would be absolutely outraged if I bought it for full price.

Recently, I've been on a point-and-click spree. While most games disappointed, Nostradamus: The Last Prophecy actually won me over, and over, and over again.
What is so good about this game?
First of all, it's the graphics - they are old, sure. But they are accordingly old. It's not like you're supposedly playing a game set in 2044 while it looks like it's actually 1999. Then, you have an immersive OST and a lovely background music choice in most locations.
The puzzles are something that I would like to compliment extensively. You have puzzles that are actually involved in the story line. This, you won't see often even in puzzle-based quests. They are different; you cannot solve two in the same way or even with the same type of analogy. You have different types of puzzles: from reflectory to balancing to runes. On top of this, they really do seem important.
Something else I love about it is that they never really killed the good old guy, although many characters did meet their end.
I particularly enjoyed the cross-dressing part. A nice twist on the old gender definitions. And yet, even this was realised through puzzles. You need to arrange voice manneurisms in order to achieve complete consistency.
If anyone is wondering if they want to try this game, I wholeheartedly recommend it to them. If you think the puzzles are too hard, it just means you need more experience - they are one of the most pleasurable parts of point-and-click adventure games.

GalCiv 3 is a turn-based strategy game where you start off with three ships and a single planet and go on to explore and strive to prosper in a galaxy as immense and interesting as you choose to make it. It plays similar to Sid Meier's Civilization, but with so many controllable variables that you literally can set the features to only include what you enjoy and turn off whatever annoys you. Unless you just don't like turned based 4x games at all, it's pretty much impossible not to love this one.
If you are a fan of the series, you will enjoy GC3 for the same reasons as its predecessors. It's very much the same game with a few new wrinkles and augmentations that fit comfortably into the formula and leave the core look and feel intact. In fact my one complaint about GalCiv 3 is that I was expecting, and hoping for, a more dramatic improvement in the production values. Apparently, most of the new features that made 64 bit processing a requirement for this game have to do with things like unbelievably large maps and not so much with making the experience seem more realistic and immersive in the course of normal play. It must be said that you get absolutely gorgeous detail (and excellent sound effects) when you zoom in tight on a ship, or a world, or even a star or junk planet. But you can't actually PLAY up close like that, and at the zoom level you'll have to use for everything but combat, GC3 still looks and feels like a 2D board game with 1990s graphics, with ships, planets, and resources reduced to crude icons and the overlay destroying the sense of being in outer space. That's heartbreaking when the components look so 3D, realistic, and beautiful close up.
Speaking of combat -- as in previous GalCivs and even more so in this edition, the space battle graphics and sound are near motion picture quality, and in that sense aesthetically satisfying. I was disappointed however to find no improvement at all from GalCiv 2 in terms of the visual perspective you are provided from which to see this eye candy. If you choose the "Cinematic" setting, you'll see slick, wonderful pans, cuts, and strafing views similar to watching a movie, but as often as not they don't show the action you're interested in -- for instance, you might get a shot that revolves around the starbase you're attacking without showing any of your ships. The Top Down view is better from a tactical perspective, but it's not particularly immersive and if like me you design your spacecraft to look best in profile, as they are shown in every sci-fi movie, TV show, book cover, and derivative art form, watching them from straight overhead is unsatisfying. You'd think the "Free" view would provide whatever perspective you want to see, and it can -- but it's so cumbersome to adjust that by the time you line up the ship(s) you want to focus on at the angle that's most pleasing to look at, the fight is over. It should also be pointed out, if you don't already know, that GalCiv battles are spectate-only -- you design and deploy your ships with meticilous control, but during an actual battle you have no input whatsoever -- none. It would be nice to have some options such as focusing fire on a particular enemy ship or turning one of your damaged shields away from the line of fire, or even an option to attempt retreat if a fight is going badly. This is not as frustrating as it probably sounds, and probably some future GC rendition will experiment with limited battle control. For now though, it's completely hands-off.
But these observations are offered for clarity only and in no way diminish my enthusiastic endorsement of this game. The GalCiv games are true classics -- a joy to play for any strategy gamer, and particularly if you're into the space setting. And, happily, GC3 doesn't do anything to screw that up. It's the best installment yet in terms of customization, and you can easily make it into a Star Trek game, or Star Wars, or Farscape, or Firefly, or any other Sci-Fi mythos you're into. Custom ships are fun and easy to create with the huge assortment of parts and the best design tools of any game ever, and putting Captain Picard or Han Solo at the helm in place of the game's stock characters is just a download away. I would like to see the series evolve into state of the art presentation at some point -- but in the mean time, I'll keep on playing GalCiv as one of my everpresent sandbox games just because it is so damned fun. It's got that 4x "just one more turn" appeal in spades, and its replayability is essentially without limit. If you're considering this game at all -- get it. You won't be sorry. :)

"NECROPOLIS combines third-person action with Rogue-lite dungeon-delving for a game that’s fast-paced and addictive, yet diabolically hardcore. You play as a nameless adventurer attempting to escape a living, magical dungeon that reconstructs itself each time you play"
In other words, your playthroughs are completely going to rely on three things:
-The dungeons
-The combat mechanics
-The enemies
Im going to explain why Necropolis fails when it comes to combat and the enemies themselves while also giving you my thought about some things regarding the dungeons but first lets talk about the combat.
The controle scheem is pretty much equal to dark souls (with some exceptions like beeing able to craft by pressing "R")
which means that the controles themselves are quite nice for controllers and acceptable for pc players (some attacks require you to press multiple buttons at once while the controller has simply one button for the same thing, you also cant rebind any keys).
Each player starts of with one right and left handed item, you are able to carry two right and left handed items.
Everyone is starting with a shield on your left and a longsword on your right, there are weapons with their own tiers which you can find (from short/longswords, spears and axes to b.astardswords and culls), these however only differ in two out of four of their attacks, all heavy and mid jump attacks are always the same, no matter what weapon you use, what matters however is the effect on the weapon, for example using pyramid weapons electrifies enemies.
All weapons have a tier, besides increasing overall damage for weapons of either hand it will also change the amount of stamina required to either use or block a powerful attack, all weapons dont have any description to them which could explain in any way what they are good /weak against, they are just as useful as this discription (not an actual quote) "looks liek a sword f.gt, Y u askin me bithc?", this wouldnt be an actual problem if there would be a way to identify weapons by simply using scrolls (there is a mechanic with random potions, you can find out what these do by  either drinking them, using a codex which is comparable to "perks" in other games or using scrolls which explain to you what they do) sadly there is none of that.
Now to the enemies themselves,
the AI is so r.etarded that they cant cross 10 cm stairs, once you jump on a table you are literally using godmode, the enemies are either going to fall back to their designated area or look at you until you either kill them or you jump down, even if you decide to not use exploits enemies get stuck most of the time, not that this really matters since you can kill most of the enemies without getting hit once by doing an heavy attack, dodge, heavy attack or just spam  the jump attack even though you are going to drain stamina you can simply walk backwards and you will regain the amount of stamina you lost before the enemies can even walk properly towards you again.
But oh dear god if you really decide to play by the games rules then prepare to die an extremely unsatisfying and frustrating death which wasnt your fault, thats right, the devs of Necropolis had the great idea of spawning enemies randomly into your room, maybe even next to you, this especially triggers during a fight with other mobs, when im dying during my playthrough i want to be the problem, i want to  be able to say "alright i should have used a different tactic when it came to engaging this enemy" and not "oh the game spawned in eight soldiers next to me while i was fighting three giants which kill me in four hits anyways, well time to restart all over again and pray to the RNG gods that that doesnt happen again".
Now to the dungeons,
ATTENTION, ALL OF THE THINGS IM GOING TO SAY ABOUT THE DUNGEONS IS SOLELY BASED ON MY OPINION/EXPERIENCE AND THINGS IN ENCOUNTERED DURING MY PLAYTHROUGH AND MIGHT NOT REPRESENT WHAT OTHER PLAYERS EXPERIENCED.
While you "maybe" noticed that the game has a "unique" artstyle going for it, which is mostly unique because of its flat design regarding characters and overall environments i hoped that the dungeons would still look as unique as shows in previous gameplay footage from the devs (mostly the E3 2016 footage),
While all of the footage was about handcrafted levels unlike the dungeons currently in the game, the developers said that the scenary and dungeons themselves are going to be as impressive and full of such opportunities (some enemies fight each other so you could lure them into each other by kiting), sadly that was a complete lie (according to what i experienced, i reached level 8 and there is a maximum of 9 levels per walkthrough), the dungeons themselves are often wide open but completely empty areas always looking alike (dont understand me wrong there still is some epic scenary, for example you are walking through a building with giant skeletons in them) and because the enemies return to their designated zone you cant use such knowledge effectively.
Overall this game lacks polish and content for the asking price, my recommendation is to wait for a sale.

Little Inferno is a game about gaming.   More specifically, a game about gaming too much.  It achieves its goals with humor, screaming marshmellows and achievements that really mean nothing.  There are no points.  Currency is easy to earn.   And yet the mood is somewhat foreboding with the intrusions of mail messages from your half-literate neighbor and reports from the enthusiastic weatherman delivered right to your Little Inferno fireplace to be read and easily discarded in a puff of smoke.  Even checking the achievement list changes the music to one that includes a distant phone ringing, reminding the player that there is something or someone out there that they are missing out on.  I felt like I emerged from being underwater after playing through this game in one sitting.  The art, quite similar to the previous game (World of Goo) by these developers manages to be cartoony but also provides environments that illustrate themes of isolation and numbness.  We never really see much beyond the fireplace and the snowy town you reside in, but multiple characters allude to great things beyond your bleak but small comforting world.

Necropolis is a rogue like game with combat comparable to Dark Souls/Bloodborne (your stamine is used for attacking, dashing out of the way, sprinting, weapon arting, though using a weapon art will drain the max amount of stamina you can have-which is recovered by eating food or drinking potions.).The game will take you through 9 floors of randomly generated dungeons to the end, each one having the same types of weaponry each time. While this is disappointing it's understandable and this could be easily added onto through updates. In the game currently are hand axes, sickles, wands, a fire shooter you attach to your wrist, greatswords and staves that behave like greathammers. While I did see at least one spear in the game it too behaved the same as the staves do; just like greathammers. The farther you go down the enemies get stronger, of course, while still having the older ones show up rarely to mob you. Do not come into the game expecting an adventure game with content equal to that of an open world game like Skyrim, many reviews I see complain about the lack of it but, there's enough for what the game is at the current moment in time, though the biggest issue I have with this game is the price. Until they add more content they should cut in in half, what you get feels like a $14.99 game-not a $29.99 game. If you want to look for something to do there are color schemes for your player character you can unlock for Tokens of Favor-the currency you are rewarded for completing objectives that are generated for you. They can range from smashing 43 pieces of pottery to becoming invisible using a potion, or defeating a certain number of one enemy. At the end of your run you're presented with a score screen, showing you how long you've played, how many things you've killed, how many things you crafted, etc. At the end your gems (the currency you find on corpses and in pots, used to buy from vendors) are converted into an XP-ish thing that fills up a meter. You can use these tokens to open a golden chest at the beginning of a level for good loot or you can  buy a perk in the form of a book. After buying one you can equip it at any one of the small bookstands you'll find throughout the game without having to earn it again. The perks are things like being able to craft a larger variety of things, or being able to drain enemies HP and use it yourself on each hit. Is the game bad? No, not at all. While it's a little buggy at the moment a quick patch should remedy it. at the time of review you cannot access the achievements through steam and the game also will not pop up with a picture if you receive it as a gift, nor will it give you records of what you've most recently played on your profile. Is the game bad? No, not at all. It's great but more weapon variety would be great and I request the deveopers to please make the spears work like spears, add a bow class, more variety for the charged up attacks. While they're great looking I feel like some weapons deserve to have different looking ones. Not all greatswords should have the exact same one should they? My final verdict is that the game is good yes, but not worth the $30 pricetag. If you're itching to buy it pick it up on sale or if they cut the price down, pick it up then.
EDIT: There are crystals that you can activate in dungeons that seemingly do NOTHING but what they do is unlock enemies and biomes for the game to generate. If you're hating fighting "the same" enemies over and over, look for these crystals. You have to find the content simply put. Also, there are illusionary walls to find scattered throughout. Happy hunting

I've spent all day playing this game. It's addictive.
There's a civilization creator that allows you to create your own civ, to a degree. You can be space faring monkey xenophobes who praise Cthulu (not really but you can be spiritual!) whom have no regard for anyone else, or a reptilian anthropod that lives in a desert climate... or an arctic or even a tropical. The choice is yours.
The game is simple enough to learn, but in depth enough to hold ones attention. Its combat is simple, point and click. No need to micromanage abilities. All you have to do is ensure your fleet is well armed and that they can take a punch.
The diplomacy is pretty simple, similar to that of civilzation but less "I'LL MURDER YOUR FACE FOR NO REASON!" It's been handled well enough for what the game is.
Graphically the game is simple, but beautiful. Zooming in up close to ships and planets reveals a lack of high quality graphics, but what were we to expect? When viewed from afar it is beautiful.
Multiplayer is well handeled. I've tested it with 3 friends. We chose to play in a clustered start... Me and one friend ended up right next to eachother in a spiral 4 armed galaxy. The other ended up on the other side getting juked by all the aliens.
The game is a real time strategy, there's no turns. You can slow down, pause, or speed up the game. It works great in single player, and from the limited experience I've had in multiplayer it works just as well. Though I can see the hassle of dealing with people who pause the game every 30 seconds. In multiplayer getting a pop-up doesn't pause the game.
The inability to alter the control scheme is a bit unfortunate, but it is simple enough that you don't really need to. The only thing I found that I wanted to do was change the pause button from space to my mouse.
Research is quite unique in the way it has been presented. There are 3 types of research, each with a large amount of tech trees. However being able to research a specific tech tree all comes down to chance. Each researcher is presented between 3-whatever choices. Typically three. Each choice is randomized after a tech is researched. This requires the player to pick and choose which tech is more important to them. Do they go for the research that allows them to build destroyer sized ships? Or do they instead get defense stations?
10/10 would pre-order again. I don't see myself playing anything else for awhile. As I paly the game I may change my recommendation, but as is it's a thumbs up. Get it, the price is worth it.

I was very apprehensive about this game because I didn't enjoy the other game this company put out and because I already enjoyed Overwatch. I really only even tried it because my brother practically made me. However, I couldn't have misjudged this game more. I almost immediately fell in love with it. Now, about a month later, I have clocked more than 100 hours into it and I still love it.
All the characters feel playable and enjoyable save a minute few, unlike Overwatch which had several bad picks for me. Also, this game is F2P whle Overwatch it B2P. If this game cost a full $60, I would buy it, assuming the community somehow didn't shrink due to that. Speaking of the community, I rarely have issues finding a match. Most queues are within 10 seconds, many even faster. The longest I ever waited was like 4 minutes. I have never quit the game because I could not find a match.
On the development side, this game is very active. They output fixes and new content all the time. Normally, F2P games are either low quality or are heavily P2W or at least P2E (Play to Enjoy). I have never once felt pressured to pay with this game. You cannot pay to become stronger. At best you can pay to unlock things faster, but primarily, paying is just for skins. It should also be noted that the pay currency is obtainable without paying through completion of rare quests and inviting people to the game who become active. Every functional thing in the game can be obtained through a very reasonable amount of play time. To give you an idea, I have all characters unlocked and a large surplus of gold after a month of play. I could have had them all unlocked in two weeks had I wished, but I'm a gold hoarder. Non-functional things are a little harder to get without paying, but still very possible with a bit of effort and dedication.
To finalize my thoughts, this game is stellar. 10/10. Please play this game. I will be partaking in purchasing some pay currency for skins soon. It is not because I feel like I need to, but rather because I don't. Thank you for your time.

Very enjoyable, and also at later stages very difficult. It is what it looks like: a rhythm-based almost-roguelike game - an unusual combination of genres which works surprisingly well. The game does not have a vast number of areas, but the  levels are procedurally generated so it is not too predictable and the challenge is great enough that the game will not be over too fast. There are also various unlockable characters with different playstyles and varying levels of difficulty, which helps to extend the life of the game. The soundtrack is good, which is crucial for this type of game, although it is occasionally difficult to pick out the beat which the game expects you to move to. The only major complaint I would have is the aforementioned limited level variety which does become frustrating when replaying the same sorts of levels over and over with any one of the several ludicrously difficult-to-play characters in the game. Overall, however, the game is still well worth buying if fast-paced 2D games hold any appeal for you at all.

While there are similarities to Japanese-style visual novels, this one is basically a Harry Potter knock-off.  That said, I really enjoy it.  There are a lot of different storylines to follow, depending on the choices you make in the game.  If you aren't interested in reading (because it IS a visual novel) and don't like choose-your-own-adventure style games, you won't enjoy this.
For those who do, it's an entertaining story about your character, a 16 year old girl who discovers she is magical and goes off to magic boarding school.  Yes, it's Harry Potter-esque, but it has a pretty rich history.  Five colors of magic, lots of rules and oaths...  I was really interested in the storyline.  There are multiple endings, depending on whether you make certain choices.  You can romance several characters, both male and female, or befriend them - each offering more pieces of the entire story.  You'll have to play through several times to find out what truly happens with various situations in the game.
It's not as deep as Hanako's other game (Long Live the Queen - which I also enjoy), but I loved the characters.  My breath caught in my throat on a few scenes.  I only wish I could get more backstory on the world that is created within the game!

I can see the shine on Cloud's sword, I can actually make out the words on some of the small signs in the background, which blows me away.
The only complaint I have is kinda the same one that I had with the origonal game, and that's that the default controlls are counter-intuitive, especially if you're playing on a keyboard and not a USB controller. But that's a small issue, since you can go into the game's options in-game and set them up however you like. First thing I did, Move the "D-pad" controlls to WASD, and the confirm/cancel/menu buttons to my Number Pad. Much more confortable.
If you're a fan of the orgional game, go ahead and pick it up, marvel at how clear and crisp the game is, compared to the origonal. If you're a new player, hey, you're in for a treat beyond the graphics overhaul.

This visual novel has an interesting and at times gripping storyline, has many interesting and relatable characters. But hardly has any time to develop on themas the campaign is so brutally short. Your first run through will last about 4 hours in real time. Which is far too little, regardless of the somewhat limited replayability. I would expect a minimum of 20+ hours and even then I might have een disappointed.
The game has multiple endings but after your first there's very little drive to go back and replay every ending unless you saved periodically after every somewhat major choice in the game. Otherwise you'll be forced to drudge through the first 30 minutes of gameplay you've completed already. That's not fun at all.
Another complaint would be that the game has no 'real ' endings. Every ending leaves you expecting something else to happen and you're left with little resolution. Which isn't a satisfying end for me. I would have een much happier if the game ran through the full 4 years, instead of the first year, which was mostly spent building relationships with characters and finding your click.
In conculsion, the game has an interesting and grippign storyline with many relatable, interesting characters. But falls flat because of the brutally short campaign, no sense of resolution in any ending and relatively high price point. If the game is on a 50% off or more sale I would recommend picking it up for a short but sweet story. Other than that, I see no reason to pick this game up for £10.99, when there are much longer and more gripping visual novels available.
