For me, a good point and click lives and dies on two things: plot and immersion. Myst, for all it's strange and convoluted puzzles, was utterly engrossing, and still is. Conversely, point and clicks made by Telltale and Wadjet Eye are always worth it for their plot and characters, making use of the formula to deliver narrative heavy experiences with some fun puzzles interspersed in between. Even more occasionally, the puzzles can be the main draw with the plot and immersion mixed in perfectly, a la Monkey Island and the majority of LucasArts' work.
Nostadamus has none of these things to keep it interesting. Graphically, it's pretty but uninspired, indistinguishable from any other ye old setting in an attempt to be grounded in realism. The plot is mind-numbingly contrived, going right past charming to a dead serious boredom. Cross dressing is an important concept fascinatingly enough, and is even a key feature listed on the store page. The idea is that as the daughter of the titular character (You don't play as Nostradamus by the way), you're supposed to disguise yourself as your own brother because reasons so you can help Queen Elizabeth solve a curse. I think. There's not much reason for it, outside of the obtuse patriarchal aspect of the olden days, further rendered moot by the fact you're helping a queen and not a king, but whatever.
The puzzles are mundane, but nothing ever had me stumped for too long up to where I stopped. Often times, the solution was obvious,  but finding the right item to finish it is often hidden in plain sight. Washing my main character's face took far more effort than it should've though, believe me.
It's not that NTLP is a bad game. I've played worse, much worse. However, where some games can still have something redeeming about it in some odd aspect, even ironically, The Lost Prophecy is just unabashedly boring, with little to keep one engaged. As an over all experience, there are far better things to spend time on than an excersize in mediocrity.
Worth it if you want to cross-dress as a famous prophet's semi-fictional daughter.

That said, it blows every other sim out of the water when it comes to Force Feedback and Physics. Seriously, I can spen more time in one car, on one track, then I can in most sims. The tire wear, damage model, weather system and real road are some of he most incredible features, and make every single lap a different experience. When I hop in the GT2 Corvette, I am immediately transported to the track, so much so, that I am having trouble going back to other sims. And the historics...you will NOT find any better anywhere. Where I would regularly get 115 FPS on high (NOT ULTRA), I am lucky to get 60 fps in RF2, and that is with certain settings (such as road reflections) turned to low. Bare in mind that the ASUS ROG in question has 12 GB of Ram and a GTX 965m, which while not the most powerful, is certainly no slouch. Coming from other platforms, the extremely detailed FFB and physics do feel odd at first, they quickly become incredible desireable, and I now depend on them. The Mod community is okay, but nothing compared to it's predeccessor, and even Assetto Corsa, though there are a few very high quality mods. They aren't as good as newer ISI content, but they still are much better than most of what you find elsewhere. Overall, I would recommend this sim for anybody with a decent wheel and a powerful enough computer, especially if they are looking for the best and most realistic SIMULATION out there. If you just want a pick up and play racing game, where you can set decent laps after your first 5 minutes though, you should probably look elsewhere. UPDATE: After spending another 250+ hours in RFACTOR 2, I can safely say that it is my favorite sim. The historics are incredible, and the open wheelers are insanely accurate. I have recently tried a professional F1 training simulator, (and had some more on track experience) and ignoring the fact that I have obviously inferior hardware, nothing else comes as close to the real deal. Rfactor 2 on the other hand is getting real close, and at times indistinguishable from what the pros use. There is a reason the Pro simulators use RFACTOR PRO. 10/10 from me and the strongest recommendation I can give....IF you think you can handle it

Early Issues: With many games on Steam once you’ve downloaded the game it’s easy to log in and get going. Unfortunately, that’s not the case with rFactor 2. You’ll download the game which includes the game’s launch program. From here the game wanted to – and needed to – download modifications from the Steam Workshop. This wasn’t a big problem. However, it then also wanted to set things up which took a small amount of time. From here I went into the game. I tried to select my controller from the load options. The game has no load option for the XBox One Controller. However, it does have a presetting for the 360 controller so that is what I selected. It never recognized my controller. I searched the Internet for a solution hoping that someone else would have experienced this issue. No luck. I did, however, find someone making a complaint about them not recognizing an entirely different controller and someone telling them to exit the game entirely and to reload. This was the solution I needed. However, I then noticed that the default settings were set to controller 2. The work through here was easy because all I needed to do from here was to set my controller settings. You’re going to want to persevere with this as the representative that I spoke with at Image Space Incorporated, Tim Whately advised that driving with keys while doable is ‘hard as hell.’
Uber realism: Hard as hell describing the keyboards makes it sound nightmarish. Driving with an Xbox One controller wasn’t much easier.It’s definitely playable but you can see with the amount of hard work and effort that the dev team have put into the game that uber realism has been the absolute premium. You’re not going to be playing this because it’s some arcade racer. Oh, no, it’s a fully fledged entry into the uber-realistic simulation games that have become very popular over the past couple of years. That means that the game is hard as hell and will punish you for the tiniest mistake you make on the road just as a driver’s error in professional racing would. If this sounds like the type of game that’s not for you then I don’t believe Image Space Incorporated would be apologetic – they understand that they are filling a niche and they’re doing the best job possible of being the most significant ‘game’ in that niche.
A technical marvel: rFactor 2 is a technical marvel. There may be other racing games with fancier graphics. There may be other racing games with better sound. There may be other racing games that may argue that their physics system is better. However, no racing game puts all three components to a better combined quality than rFactor 2. The only area that I genuinely believe the title is let down is in a decidedly average pre-racing presentation. The menu system and other design choices before you’re out on the track could do with a complete makeover. Further, the launch program could do with a little bit of clarification. It’s more than a little confusing for your first time players let alone the casual gamers who are passionate racing fans. It doesn’t have to be anything fancy but just something a little more user friendly.
All substance: What you will find most of all in rFactor 2 is that the game is all substance. The game does not make outrageous boasts that it cannot live up to. Everything in the game is substance. It is as deep a racing experience as what you could possibly hope to find on any gaming platform. Where other games waste their budget adding unnecessary features Image Space Corporation have put in the effort on maximizing what they do have. Quite frankly, it’s one of the best racing games – of any sort – ever developed and I hope it receives the attention it deserves from the Steam universe.
Finally on Steam: The game was originally released back in 2013 but only made its way onto Steam in late-2015. This gave the developers an opportunity to work on the game with their core user base without the pressure of it being classified as an Early Access title or being rushed into release before it was ready. I believe that this is a smart decision for some games and it certainly was in the case of rFactor 2.
rFactor 2 is unapologetically not for everyone. The majority of those who speak out against the game are the crowd who Image Space Corporation did not make the game for. If you’re a part of the target audience, however, you’ll likely not find a better racing experience on Steam.

I can tell you the sole reason for why I bought this game: Mclaren MP4/6. Yep. That's it.
I have several other racing sim games that all are good, but when I heard that car's screaming V12 I just had to drive it.
So, how does it stand against the other sims?
First thing, it's DX9 only. For better or for worse. Now, I don't really care that much about graphics in these kind of games since it's way more about the physics that is important. With that said, yes, it does look like it's older cousins (GTR2, Race07 e t c) so it's definitely not ugly but don't expect all that fancy stuff that PCars, Assetto and the others bring to the table. In all honesty, with DX9 being the base, I would actually expect a bit higher FPS.
Graphics: 6/10 (maybe a 7/10 if you consider it's DX9)
Now to the important stuff, the physics.
It's well on par with all the rest of them. I had 0 issues getting the FF and everything else to work with my G27.
It delivers what you expect a sim racer to deliver and it feels very dynamic. You will have to spend time tinkering with your car to get it to suit your driving style but that's why we play these kind of games. Like I said, if you have another sim game you will get what you expect. I have one critisism though and that is that track edges and curbs are a bit exaggerated in the handling. I don't know if it's the cars or if it's the engine itself, but YES, you can drive the curbs without losing traction completely in real life.
Physics 9/10. (That's actually what I would give all the sim racers I have including the new ones).
Connecting back to the reason for why I bought the game, content. It's actually kind of slim out of the box both with cars and tracks. I myself am in no way whatsoever interested in 10 different oval tracks. But.. here is where modding comes in. The game supports Steam Workshop and I don't think I've ever had a racing game where it's easier to add more stuff. Browse the Steam WS, click subscribe and the next time you fire up the launcher the stuff is there. It will, of course, also keep track of any updates to what you have subscribed to. But wait, it doesn't end there (I know, that sounds like TV shopping). There are tons of tracks, cars and entire leagues you can download and it's almost as easy as Steam WS.
Download and extract if necessary to a folder somewhere, point the launcher to include that folder, refresh and it shows up and you can install. Brilliant. I simply love racing from the 80's (F1 or Group C or 5 doesn't matter). I love the pureness and raw feeling without ESC, ABS and TC. The downside is that from what I've seen, rFactor had more enthusiasts that made stuff than to rFactor 2. But, with one install I got all the teams from F1 1992. You can't go wrong with that.
Content and modding support: 10/10
Last but not least, Online racing (yes ladies and germs, that is what you eventually have to do if you want to prove that you can handle 800bhp on a track). Of course racing against your brothers and sisters is way more fun than the AI. And here is where I think they messed up. They chose a subscription model similar to iRacing and even if I can see that it keeps the riff-raff out of the lobbies, it also limits the population. Remember, PCars and the others have no extra fees for online racing. They even support dedicated servers that you can rent. So, yes, this is a mistake since I think that the user base is the most important thing for keeping it alive and, in this case, the mods to keep coming. And with this subscription model you simply will only get the die hard fans (likely the same guys that race rFactor) to pay up. I don't agree to this model since I can't see what added value it would give me. It feels like a pay wall.
Online: 0/10
With all this said, do I recommend it? Yep, I do. Without a doubt. And I think if they get rid of that silly online subscription model, this game will have many more years going for it.

rFactor 2 is one of the most complete racing simulator out there currently. The AI, the racing, the singleplayer features, the game engine - all of it unmatched by any other sim that I have.
The physics feel pretty demanding in rFactor 2. In pCARS, Raceroom and even Assetto Corsa, it's very easy to just jump in a car and drive around. In rFactor 2, you need to have finesse if you want to drive fast. It's easy to overdrive your car, causing you to overheat your tires and lose grip. You can also flatspot your tires if you lockup your brakes or lose control at a high speed, causing heavy vibrations in your wheel. I usually have similar driving styles for all the sims I have, but I have to be extra careful when I step in to rFactor 2. Bear in mind that I'm no race driver in real life. I do race karts but all I've said was based from experience in all those sims.
The AI is probably the best feature of this sim. Where else can you find AI that actively tries to defend its line when you're coming from behind? When you get behind an AI's draft, the closer you get, the more they move to the inside line to try and defend their position. You're both coming in side by side for the braking point. The AI won't give up that position so easily. He will try to outbrake you, either forcing you to go wide or go for the undercut.
When you're ahead and the AI is behind, don't expect them to just let you be in the front in peace either. They will pressure you into mistakes. They will take advantage of the mistakes you make and they're really good at it too. They will stick their nose in the inside if they're close enough. They go 3 wide in some corners if there's enough room.
The best part is that no contact is made by the AI, usually. They still make mistakes but nothing you wouldm't expect.
I've had many enjoyable races in rFactor 2 with the AI. I would even go as far and say that I've had the same level of excitement racing real people on iRacing.
$85 for a lifetime subscription though? Not gonna buy that.

Having read a few reviews and watched many youtube videos on the progress that rFactor 2 has made since it's initial release in 2013, I decided to take the plunge and buy myself the Steam version (Dec 2015) ,  I had previously downloaded a demo in 2014 which to be honest was not a very good experience (A complete nightmare even to get it running)
So here are some of the things you can expect to see in rFactor 2.
1. Some of the best driving physics found on any racing sim to date, especially the tyre model which is extremely realistic.
2. Based on realism the graphics in rFactor 2 are in my opinion outstanding , the draw distance, colour pallette and hdr textures, especially on the road surface are pretty much as good as it gets.
3 The UI is pretty basic at first glance but does offer indepth configuration for every aspect of the game.
4. Force Feedback , easily one of the best Force feedback systems you will find in any game, this is due to the fact that is directly linked to the tyre model, which means you can accurately detect loss of traction/grip at any speed,unlike many force feedback systems which feel predictable.
5.Dedicated server support and online multiplayer are available to those who subscribe. (optional)
6. Customisation and mod support has always been a big part of rFactor , rFactor 2 is no different , however being a newer game and the jump in technical ability requirments, this has led to less quantity and less quality mods being released. (give it some more time)
7. The AI in rFactor 2 are configurable which allows you to set skill/speed and aggression, definitely the least frustrating AI I have played against in all modern sims.
8. Superb performance , I run rFactor 2 in surround mode (triple screens 5760x1080) with everything maxed out , the game looks amazong and framerates are consistantly 100+ depending on track, always above 75fps though.
What not to expect from rFactor 2
1. The main thing most newcomers will notice is the lack of branding or licensing. ( for me this is not a problem)
2. A mainstream game which has a limited life expectancy,
3. A game that holds your hand.
4..DLC
rFactor 2 accurately simulates a speeding race car (really well) , be it a formula or stock car, as well as any simulator I have ever used , there are many other well known great sims on the market, rFactor 2 deserves to sit at the top table of racing sims and imo is an absolute must buy sim for anyone who loves motorsport or racing sims.

The Binding of Isaac Game Review
The binding of Isaac is a indie rogue-like platformer game about a child called Isaac and his crazy religious mother. It is a game filled with secrets and unlockable characters and items with 2 DLC packs. After playing The Binding of Isaac for a few hours I realised there was a reason so many people described the game as “Unforgiving” and “disturbing”, It’s because its filled with satanic references, blood and gore. Not only that but The Binding of Isaac is incredibly difficult, only after my first 10 tries was I able to kill mom once. My favourite thing about The Binding of Isaac would have to be the game breaking aspect. By game breaking I mean there are some incompatible items in the game which cause you to have infinite health or can help you to get every item in the game. There is actually a massive part of the community that has dedicated itself to finding game breaking glitches that can make them extremely overpowered; some of these people have broken the game to the extent that a single attack on any boss will kill them instantly.
Controls and Gameplay
The controls to The Binding of Isaac are basic. WASD to move and your arrow keys to direct your attack. You move around the basement from room to room, each room containing something different. There are normal rooms which contain enemies, gold rooms which contain power up items that will impact your speed, damage, health and can sometimes impact you negatively.
You first meet Isaac and his mother in the loading screen for the game which describes their lives as being happy until she hears a voice from above. The voice of god tells her to kill Isaac and Isaac, hearing this, flees into the houses basement to get away from his homicidal mother which is when the games main menu loads.  The game is about Isaac making his way through the basement to eventually reach and kill the boss, Mom. As you make your way through the basement you will encounter multiple different types of enemies (foetuses, pinworms, embryos, flaming headless monsters and lots of bugs) which will all try to kill you.
Graphics and Sound
The graphics for The Binding of Isaac were made to have a retro feel to them. They have options for the in game detail which affects the rooms you enter. High detail means there will be cobwebs and blood on the walls while low detail will give you none of that. The detail setting also affects the pixels in game so setting it to low will give you a very fuzzy effect while high makes it look HD in comparison.
The music in The Binding of Isaac is very varied. The music changes depending on the floor and room you are on/in. The music keeps you focused while playing and can help you to know what type of room or floor you are on.  The sounds in The Binding of Isaac are very eerie to say the least. The squishing noises when you kill monsters and the screaming from bosses I found to be very unsettling when I was playing and actually impacted on my performance when I was playing.
Replayability and Multiplayer
The Binding of Isaac is literally the most replayable game I have ever played; this is because of how unforgiving the game and how interesting the storyline is. With over 341 items and 178 secrets in the game you must replay constantly to finish the game with everything unlocked.
There has never been a official multiplayer feature for The Binding of Isaac however the great community surrounding it has created a few multiplayer mods for people to use. This let you play 2 players with you and another person on the same keyboard and you can both move around and shoot and fight enemies. Although the multiplayer mod is good, I think it ruins the game as there is no balancing aspect to the mod meaning there is now2 players but the same amount of bosses and enemies.
To Conclude
I found The Binding of Isaac to be a ridiculously good indie game. The complexity of the story line and the references to religion surprised me and definitely made me enjoy the game a lot more. At only £4.00 this game is definitely one I would pick up off the steam store, especially as it is now one of my most played games and it’s one of the cheapest I own, this game practically pays for itself in minutes. The games DLC is also worth getting as it doubles the amount of content that is already inside this jam packed game, it adds characters, items, floors, monsters and more difficult bosses.  So to give this game a rating I would have to give it a:
•	Easy to learn controls ✓
•	Gameplay ✓
•	Graphics ✓
•	Sound/Music ✓
•	Replayable ✓
•	Multiplayer  X

I cant help myself but give this game the thimbs up - and I am going to list the good about it immediately. 2.5 hours in and over 60 more watching youtubers like Arumba, Quill, AngryJoe and of course, Paradox, I do not see much bad about the game apart from a number of bugs, more customization options and the start of the game - someone can get a way more favorable one than the rest. I know I restarted 3 times and 1 of those was WAY better than the other two.
So this is what I really liked about the game so far:
- I LOVE the initial exploration phase. Sending multiple science and war ships to unlock systems and thoroughly scan them for habitable planets and resources is extremely fun and totally scratches my itch for discovery and going where no man has gone before.
- I LOVE how easy it is to get into the game. Granted, I might have had help by watching the youtubers, but I could totally get into the gameplay without any hiccups, unlike Paradox's other Grand Strategies EU4 or CK2, where I was totally overwhelmed, even to the point of leaving them back for a long time.
- I LOVE the freedom the game gives you. You can play with a pre-made civilizazion, or make your own the way you feel like, which is what I did. I totally recommend people do that - it is so much fun mixing and matching stuff and testing them out. You can be a warmonger, pacifist, mercantilist, mogul, expansionist, whatnot!
- I LOVE how the playthroughs can differ from one another. In my 3 starts, I had 3 totally different experiences, based on resources, events, encounters, galaxy composition, star composition, etc. JUST AWESOME!
- I LOVE how everything you do feels IMPORTANT and not even remotely boring.
- I LOVE how choices have meaningful continuations - not like Civilization Beyond Earth for example, where everything resulted in similar outcome. Here you can either continue a quest line, stop a quest line, drive it to a conclusion that gives you various rewards, and so on.
- I like how you get to customize everything after you start. You can let the game guide your hand or go completely wild with your own ship designs, options, and whatnot.
- I like the new research system. Stellaris breaks the mold by allowing you multiple research topics at once, which amounts to crazy amounts of research options, based on anything you find through events, dead alien bodies, destryoned alien ships, and so on.
- I like how everything in your empire can level up and improve - your admirals, planetary governors, scientists, everything but the little settlers levels up and gets more and more useful as the game goes on.
- I like how you are NOT put into a level playing field. Every race has it forte's, and some have been in space way longer than you, which makes them way too overpowered. Like Q in Star Trek.
- I like how you can just play the game and have fun.
- I like how you can easily make friends and enemies.
- I like how the game both holds your hand through quests and missions, but at the same time, does not impose itself on you and lets you do it your way.
- I like how the tutorial helps you as you go, not with simple tips, pre-made missions, or pre-made scenarios that have nothing to do with a real game.
Conclusion: Paradox did it again - they proved themselves as a developer that carefully chooses its games and drives them to perfection. This games does it all for me - it scratches every itch I may have: exploration, development, diversity, diplomacy, variety, engaging play, everything. I expect dumping hundreds of hours into this game, and pray I have the time for that...

I was very apprehensive about this game because I didn't enjoy the other game this company put out and because I already enjoyed Overwatch. I really only even tried it because my brother practically made me. However, I couldn't have misjudged this game more. I almost immediately fell in love with it. Now, about a month later, I have clocked more than 100 hours into it and I still love it.
All the characters feel playable and enjoyable save a minute few, unlike Overwatch which had several bad picks for me. Also, this game is F2P whle Overwatch it B2P. If this game cost a full $60, I would buy it, assuming the community somehow didn't shrink due to that. Speaking of the community, I rarely have issues finding a match. Most queues are within 10 seconds, many even faster. The longest I ever waited was like 4 minutes. I have never quit the game because I could not find a match.
On the development side, this game is very active. They output fixes and new content all the time. Normally, F2P games are either low quality or are heavily P2W or at least P2E (Play to Enjoy). I have never once felt pressured to pay with this game. You cannot pay to become stronger. At best you can pay to unlock things faster, but primarily, paying is just for skins. It should also be noted that the pay currency is obtainable without paying through completion of rare quests and inviting people to the game who become active. Every functional thing in the game can be obtained through a very reasonable amount of play time. To give you an idea, I have all characters unlocked and a large surplus of gold after a month of play. I could have had them all unlocked in two weeks had I wished, but I'm a gold hoarder. Non-functional things are a little harder to get without paying, but still very possible with a bit of effort and dedication.
To finalize my thoughts, this game is stellar. 10/10. Please play this game. I will be partaking in purchasing some pay currency for skins soon. It is not because I feel like I need to, but rather because I don't. Thank you for your time.

Dust is a fine game, but it doesn't resonate with me. It is very much an "art" game: if you like the art and story it will keep you playing. If you don't, there isn't enough gameplay to sink your teeth into.
The good: The story and animation feel like they are strait out of an anime from yesteryear. The cutscenes remind me of the "complete" versions of the Lunar games, except more of them with more polish. The art is really very good for this style and the level of detail is fantastic. Combat moves look interesting as do special powers.
The bad: The story and animation feel like they are strait out of an anime from yesteryear. It's cheesy, full of anime cliches (spunky sidekick, amnesiatic protagonist) and generally felt complete but immature. I don't know why I bothered to give this game another try. I saw that it had a higher review average now, but nothing's changed.
This is a classic example of a game design concept that sounds awesome on paper, but in practice it's a cluster♥♥♥♥. It's a fighting/blocking system focused around directional inputs in a 2D game. With such small sprites, it's impossible to gauge depth with the enemy's attacks, which is pivotal if you're blocking or attacking anything other than overhead slashes. But of course, the enemies don't have this problem, and attack literally relentlessly. When I first started the game, I blocked/attempted to block the enemy until they stopped attacking, waiting for an opening where it would be wise to strike.
But enemies in this game don't stop attacking. There isn't really any rhyme or reason to it, no real patterns other than 'oh these enemies rush at you and you need to hit them before they hit you', or 'you need to knock this enemy's spear out of the way to stun them and prevent their attack, but the only frames in which you can actually HIT their spear are A. When you're far enough away that you won't even be able to reach the enemy with your slowass walking speed before they get up or B. When they're about to hit you. If you hit the vulnerable part of their spear with your sword during any other frame of their animation? Passes through harmlessly.
Avoid this game. Get it for free if you can, get the cards, uninstall, then hide it.

This game really scratched my Harry Potter itch, I got it on a humble bundle sale, I forgot how long time ago, I never played it because lets be honest... Magical Diary? Female protagonist? Visual novel? When am I gonna get time in my busy schedule of playing hardcore action rpgs to try this game out?
Well one day I told myself to give every game in my library a shot for 10 mins. So I play the game. Why not make a cute girl while I'm at it? There is decent amount of character customization. I'm happy with my character and I start the game. Bleah,  this is a lot like Harry Potter, unoriginal much?...  - 10 min later - This game is a lot like Harry Potter, this is amazing!
You got your unique characters, magical holidays and traditions, spells to learn and use in challenges, secrets to unlock, you can follow your own path, the people you befriend help you later on, and the people you cross will remember you for it, balance your magical school work with occasions to make trouble. The story was amazing, cliche? Maybe. Fun and involving? Definitely. You can avoid interactions you do not want, of course there are unskipable events in the game, but I never felt I was being forced on a specific path at any point while playing. There are funny moments, romantic moments and tragic ones, my first ending was... unhappy to put it mildly, it made me stop playing so I can curl up on the bed and be drenched in sadness (I am a 24 year old male).
My only problems with this game are:
- the lack of teachers in Iris Academy, there are 2 people... that's it! No nurse, no janitor, no groundskeeper, no porter, no lunch lady, no coach, just 2 teachers. One of them apparently is the headmistress/ janitor/ doctor/ night watchman/ school councilor AND teaches 3 classes, as far as I can tell said 3 classes happen at the same time.
- the game is kinda pricey for it's length, buy it on a sale
- because of the multiple endings there can be no direct sequel to this title, but there will be a another game with a parallel story in the same setting.
TL;DR Great fantasy visual novel, its few problems don't get in the way of enjoying the game.

An absolute gem of a find. Though many may be turned away by the chunky graphics, this is a game that has really captured the true experience of a well made and thoughtful point-and-click adventure game. The voice acting is well done, the graphics (though blocky) are still pleasing to the eye, and the storyline is top notch.
The puzzles range from simple recipies to weight distribution to complex translation of old celtic to french. Though you may find yourself doing many crafting puzzles, they are balanced thoughout the game and not used as a crutch, but as a way of transitioning the player from one objective to the next.
The only issue I had with the game was that several timed puzzles and one particular quick-time event left me frustrated. It is important to save and save often.
Other than that, this game was one of the most thought provoking and inviting point-and-click games I have ever played. Being a history buff, I would love to see more games like this, perhaps with characters from William Shakespeare plays. I would recommend anyone who wants a true adventuring experience like Myst to check this out.

Ok... I am going to write a full-fledged "feature" review of this.
Take note I played through all 9 tests (in 1.3 hours), and I got it from a bundle.
Let's start with the good parts of the game, because this is going to be so much easier to list.
-Awesome soundtrack; the dubstep fits the the game and the action well enough.
-Environment variation for the most part; you will either be in forest, ice lands, hell, space and whatever going around doing various things, the level layout while pretty much linear is under no circumstance a corridor shooter for the most part.
-The mini-games in test 7 and 8 give a welcomed change of pace.
Aand now for the underwater part of the glacier. I'll start with three arguments that will pretty much nullify the three ones above.
-The soundtrack is repetitive; the same dubstep you will pretty much hear in all of the environments. There's barely any variation for the soundtrack whatsoever, which is dissapointing since what's there is nice.
-The UFO level (test 8); it only throws hordes and hordes of enemies that you seen already at you, making everything just boring as tedious as you will just circle around the arena keeping your left mouse button pressed and hoping you hit anything.
-Barely any hit confirmation; I have a hard time figuring out wether or not I hit a enemy, I can see that their health decreases in a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ almost unreadable font (especially on hordes) but that's it, enemies never stutter, get knockback or anything. Knockback on the shotgun would've made sense would it not?
-Level design; just like another guy said, Falling Simulator 2014. You will find out that you can easily fall of the maps. Even worse, die from blocks you didn't know that kill you (I had that issue from test 7 and up).
-Extremely tedious and bad platforming; platforming in 3D has generally been a issue, but not always, it could be acceptable in arena shooters (would this be an arena shooter?) like this one, BUT it was screwed over completely by physically no mid-air control (why?) and the view lock to I suspect 80 degrees up and down. While looking up is mostly not necessary and it's just enough, looking down is a problem as you can't attack enemies straight underneath you (which would be a great tactic for those little zombies) BUT this also creates the issue that you can never know properly your exact position on the blocks. You need to go through intuition, which is bad enough already.
-Extremely poor weapon design and functionality; there are a total of 4 weapons in the whole game. A UZI with a weird♥♥♥♥♥useless scope on-top, a shotgun (sniper) that looks like some paintball gun, a bat that I mistook as a machete due to the shader for half of the game and tests 7 and up, a plasma gun which is annoying as hell for reasons explained below. The weapon models are awkward in quality compared to the whole rest of the game, while being bad, they are still argruably better. Which is actually still bad since it creates inconsistency in general design.
-Destroyed blocks have collision; and it's not minor, you can barely go through killed enemies or destroyable blocks and you just need to shoot them away or else, that is even more annoying when they just block your bullets, making the hordes of enemies a ton more annoying than they be. Additionally, the plasma gun creates blocks when it shoots anything, and since bullets can shoot blocks for collission and create more blocks, you essentially are able to give enemies a temporary shield wherever you hit them with the plasma gun, I had tons of instances in the last levels where I simply hit enemies with the plasma guns for about 2 seconds and they physically received no damage because I was simply hitting the blocks instead. That is plain dumb. Oh and enemies can go through destroyed blocks JUST fine.
-Completely useleess zoom and crosshair; the crosshair is a spread crosshair, and by default definition and use in other games, it's supposed to define the accuracy (or non-accuracy) your gun will have. Well the weapons have physically no recoil, which is actually perfectly fine since it's sort of an arena shooter and recoil for something like this would actually be worse. BUT the weapons also have 100% accuracy. In fact you can give the same damage with the shotgun at a insane range as you give to a enemy next to you, making it more of a sniper with (somehow) some spread. Then there's the UZI which in fact NEVER has any spreads and will always hit perfectly in the center of the crosshair. This can barely be called a feature since those are things game developers avoided ever since I bloody know of. Don't put in useless features that can't even link properly together. Even worse, the range on the bat is so misguiding that you can barely tell which is that sweet spot range. Not to mention that you would never use the bat when you have another weapon as getting close to an enemy is a bad idea to begin with.
-Inconsistency in level design; this is a minor aestethic issue, but, the game primarily seems to do a mix between voxel and 2000 3D level design by having both voxel cubes as a excuse for lazyness AND some rectangles rotated on every possible axis for whatever reason that just makes everything look bad.
-Useless scoring system; you need to kill every enemy in order to advance to the next level, since that is the only way to get score, the scoring system is completely useless and serves no rewards, not even a high score table or self-gratification as the sole completion of a test will always yield the same score. At least for the most part, there was like one single test which allowed me to not kill one guy in order to advance, which would just essentially make my score like 100 less for the whole game. Oh no.
-Space level is nauseous; playing on the space levels, alternative tests 7 and up has personally made me want to vomit.
-No FoV slider; on a game like this the thing you'd want to do is cram that FoV slider up to max for a Quake-like experience so you don't feel nauseous. Do you have that? Nope.
-Useless graphical settings; the game looks pretty horrible already, there's no texture or effects or particles that can redeem that fact in the current state, yet you have 4 graphical presets for whatever reason that do not explain or seem to do anything.
-No checkpoints of any sort; test 9 manages to do 3 checkpoints by arena changing and that is completely fine and proves that the game had capability of doing so. This only seems ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ as you can just finish a whole level then die from falling off the map thanks to ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ level design.
-No death variation; you get killed by zombies, the death screen shows you being eaten by zombies. Ok, cool, makes sense. You fall down the platform, you get eaten by zombies... what? You burn yourself in laval, you get eaten by zombies. You get smashed by a huge ball, you get eaten by zombies. This is pure laziness.
-You are sent to the menu instantly on death; you don't receive option to restart or go back to the menu (or exit, uninstall the game and burn it), you are only sent to the menu and forced to wait about 5 seconds being eaten by zombies, 5 seconds till you can get in the level then 5 seconds to fall down in the most dull spawnpoint I ever seen.
-Poor "end boss fight"; the game has a extremely dissapointing boss fight which barely explains anything (It took me 3 deaths even if I completed because I didn't know I also had to do one more thing to advance) which is just giving you the same enemy 3 times in a row each time just more powerful. Additionally it ends with what would look a choice for multiple endings but nope, the game chooses for you, which ends up with the game resulting being as linear as it can possible be, with no exploration benefits whatsoever and with no divergence in what you can do. It's always kill everything you see.

Having owned all the current gen of sims (apart from iRacing) & past generations, rF2 has been my favourite by far, purely for the feel of the race.  By that I mean the physics, the FFB, the dynamic changes as the race happens (tyres, weather, lighting), & the AI.  The races have a sense of speed to them, a thrill, not stale as I find with AC, the FFB is the best I've experienced through my CSWv2 and the selection of cars and tracks available by ISI, 3rd part associates or independent modders covers pretty much all aspects of motorsports on 4 wheels.
The cons of rF2 for me are that it does not have a structured career mode or even a simple championship allowing you to create and compete with the AI over a series of tracks with leaderboards.  This is a real shame as the AI is one of the best you will see in any current sim.  Also, I'm sure you have all heard about how outdated the dx9 graphics are, and at times you will agree but other times the game does look very good.  It's not bad but it does not have the polish of pCARS or the post processing of AC.  But what the graphics do achieve, is a real sense of speed which for me AC fails to do.
In summary:
Pros:
+ Physics & FFB very convincing and make the 'feel' of the game superior
+ Dynamic tracks, lighting & weather
+ Moddable platform with some excellent free mods
+ Very convincing AI makes single player races challenging & enjoyable, with a sense of speed and thrill that R3E achieves too.
Cons:
- Graphical quality lacks polish
- No career or championships, especially upsetting after you have such good AI
- Sounds are not as good as R3E, AC or PCars.
- The weather effects are incomplete
- UI is not as polished as AC

CD Project RED have sold their souls in exchange for creating perfect digital art.
I remember back then, when the first Witcher came out it was something refreshing, captivating, even good, but still it wasn’t spectacular, despite some people calling it a new best RPG. Among its great strengths in story, quests, art and music it definitely had glaring issues: most notably, some annoying (to the point of being silly) combat moves and the fact that a good two thirds of it is spent in some sort of swamps, sewers and similar-looking dungeons.
There was no hint of something
coming ahead.
But suddenly and unexpectedly,
is upon us. And here I am, trying to review it with my jaw dropped and dangling somewhere around my knees.
You are Geralt, a witcher — a professional monster slayer caught in a midst of political conflict, intrigue and soon after that, on a long quest to clear your good name and discover more pieces in attempt to solve a puzzle of Wild Hunt and your dark past.
Now
is something like ubelievable upgrade over previous installement, unmatched by anything in recent history. Everything you can possibly think of have been drastically improved, expanded and taken to breathtaking levels of visuals, music and sound. All environments are unique and are extremely rich in details: there’s no copy-paste ever.
The characters, even NPCs, are
, deep and interesting. There’s no other RPG where you would stop just to listen to NPC talk and smile at some story they tell each other. Every place, every spot, be it in town or outside, has an event connected to it and some amazing quest you can take on: escape from prison (be a master of stealth, or you can make it a little rough), participate in an assault on rebellious town alongisde king and teach his stupid son some good lesson, prevent military abuse of innocent civillians by beating an officer in a one-on-one swordfight, and get away with it because your king favors you so much; visit abandoned and haunted asylum to calm down the spirits of its victims and learn about its grim past, uncover treason and crime, take a taste of dirty medieval town life by participating in brawls, dice poker and arm wrestling games — and earn some additional coin with that!
Meet mages, trolls (friendly and not so much), fight a giant Cthulhu with a sorceress by your side, join elves in their guerilla struggle against humans, assist dwarves and visit their mysterious town hidden somewhere deep in the mountains or, if you rather prefer that, stay in a dirty human military camp and become a new star of its colloseum-like fighting arena. The choice is always yours: so be prepared to take it and face the consequences (or enjoy them :-).
And did I even mention how
fights can be? Devise your tactics, approach and hunt monsters: all different, inhabiting their own areas and requiring unique means to successfully kill; pursue finest gear upgrades to assist yourself in your dirty job. Harvest for ingredients during your trips outside to brew and drink awesome poisions (of a witcher sort) and acquire inhuman powers for a short amount time. Buy materials, schematics and construct deadly traps, bombs and daggers to leave your enemies no chance. Approach several knights that dared to threaten you and perform a powerful finisher move, killing them all at once. Redirect arrows back at your enemies, use powerful witcher magic tricks to trap or stun your foes: block, riposte, perform a quick roll away, then jump and cut your unfortunate foe through while he recovers from a good blast of your yrden (not a typo). You have to fight dirty: you have to fight like a witcher.
And all that above is just barely one third of what is in store for you.
I have no idea how CDPR were able to pull that all off.

— Some professional you are!

With a wonderful art style that belies it's simplicity, fast paced yet straight forward combat, diverse enemies, labyrinthine, procedurally generated level design, and compelling loot, Necropolis has everything a great game should have. It's unassuming at first, but it slowly sucks you in with it's occasional breathtaking vistas, and constant suprises. The game's tongue in cheek, subtle humour only adds to it's charm.
The locally hosted multiplayer doesn't hurt it either. In fact, it's not only a joy to play this game with friends because of the ease of creating or joining a game, the netcode is so amazing that it seemlessly hands over hosting to another party if the original game host leaves the game.
Pros:
- Great design, both artistically and with regards to levels.
- Diverse enemies and loot.
- Crafting.
- Super easy multiplayer, possibly the best I've seen in a locally hosted game.

The idea behind this game is a neat one and the pros of this game is:
-You attack using three sides, so to speak: Overhead attack, left attack and right attack which is pretty creative.
-In addition, you also block the same way so you have to coordinate to block enemy's attacks.
-Love the detailed pixelated graphics.
-It's stupidly hard but like Dark Souls and other hard games, you'll overcome them eventually. Emphasis on eventually.
Now you might think, "Wow, this game might be pretty neat!". However, like everything, with light comes dark, with fire comes water, with bread comes butter, with KFC comes fries, you get what I mean. With pros comes the cons:
-There's no way to tell where the enemy will attack unless you have REALLY quick reaction time, you'll overcome enemies eventually like the intellegent human being you are. Again, emphasis on eventually.
-The combat, although creative and sometimes fun, is quite repetitive and lackluster.
-Hitting something feels really weak, especially for a guy with a greatsword and full steel armor.
-It's not a fair game by any means, like the first point mentioned, you'll have no idea how the enemy attack untill after they kill you and in addition, there's no counter-attack or anything other than the repetitive combat.
-The stages feel really lazy since it seems like just a moving picture and no interaction with the environment whatsoever.
-I get it that it's a medieval game and there's only knights and peasants and other soldiers but the enemies' concepts aren't exactly creative or interesting to look at and sooner or later, you'll be bored.
Overall, it's a neat game for 5 bucks but it needs polishing and some more creativity put into it before I can actually recommend it to anyone. It's NOT a chill and casual game if you are thinking that. I hope the devs implement more features, more interactions, more weapons, more items, more variety way of fighting into the game and more combat options to keep the game interesting.

One doesn't need to spend intimate hours with A ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥'s Tale to know what it has in store.  Traipse through the first level and you'll understand that it only gets harder from there (and does it ever).  And by traipse, I mean die horrifically many times before you get the proverbial "aha" moment and meander on through, only to be killed right off the bat in the next level.
You play as an armored footman (or a horseless knight).  There may be a story, but it's irrelevant; the whole point of the game is to go from left to right and defeat the level boss.  This is something we've all been doing for years.  Pretty simple, right?  Wrong.  Despite the clanky armor our nameless hero wears, he's a bit on the fragile side and you'll need to defend yourself from incoming attacks.  Just as you can swing your sword overhead, left, or right, you must also block overhead, left, or right.
You'll quickly learn that the game is not about to hold your hand.  In most games with this kind of gimmick, the enemies properly telegraph their attacks in order to give the player a chance to react.  In
game, however, the moment you encounter your first enemy, you'll find that these peasants are
cheesed at you for some reason and will attack in a flurry.  The telegraphing is still there, mind you, but like the ceaselessly-talking gossip girl in the hallway, you just can't get a word in edgewise.  You'll be so busy trying to block an endless series of attacks that you might forget to switch it up a bit and get a hit in yourself.
It looks pretty great, too.  The pixel art is variable (peasants look kinda wonky), but generally consistent and nothing will seem truly out of place.  The best art is reserved for your own knight and the knights that you will inevitably meet who want to cut your face off.  Each clunky walk animation expertly describes the character's weight and attacks get a boost in frames to really make it feel like combat is lightning-quick.
This is a game for the old-school arcade-goer.  It's a title that would have been perfectly at home munching quarters in a dingy 80s arcade cabinet, only to be mastered by those who refuse to let a game beat them.  Pattern recognition and quick twitchy reflexes will win the day here, not methodical fancy moves and ultra combos.  No superpowers, no special items, no enhanced weapons.  Just you and your fingers navigating a game that is definitely out to kill you, get under your skin, and perhaps haunt your dreams.  The only reason I don't have a lot of time in it is because the second level makes me cry like a b***h.

Play your cards right, and a character that you ignored on your first playthrough might reveal the reasons for their weirdness. First off, a bit of a disclaimer, I love the Gal Civ series of games.  I've played all of them for days and days, except for Gal Civ III.  This game is incomplete, and mostly unworthy of its pedigree.
There are dozens of missing features like a stealth system, espionage system, more diversification of technology trees, a fully fleshed out diplomacy system, as well as things like superweapons, pirates that aren't trash0, battle control, and AI that doesn't cheat, or just screw around until you get around to killing them.
This whole game seems feature incomplete, like it should still be in early access for at least another six months.  All the soul of the past two games is entirely gone in favor of a technically more advanced, but practically stripped title.  Gameplay is leagues more repetitive than past titles, whilst simultaneously being more time-consuming in terms of planet and ship management.
In my experience with this and the past two games, Stardock seems to have scooped out all the planned and improved features of the game we were all expecting years ago, and carefully stitched them into packs of $4.99 DLC, on top of the full priced base game.

Necropolis is a fun game. Especially if you have friends.
The game claims to be very hard, telling you that 'you'll probably die trying' as you adventure. However, the game isn't actually that hard. I beat it on my 4th? solo run. I surprisingly found the game more difficult when I played with friends, but it was more fun that way anyway.
The combat in this game IS pretty similar to Dark Souls', in my experience. Swing, dodge, shield, whatever. It's pretty much the same thing and I think some people are whining when they shouldn't be. It's fun to fight monsters and it's fun to use your different weapon abilites. The combat is not as in depth as Dark Souls (no parry, backstab, etc.) but it is its own game and doesn't need to copy those things. I personally don't even think those mechanics would work very well in this game, considering the large numbers of mobs you'll be fighting at once. It's not very easy to only hit on thing at a time. Thankfully, your special attacks are useful there.
There are plenty of sweet armor sets you can find in the game and a few cool weapons as well. Eventually, you run into the same things a bunch of times, like the same weapons and enemies, which is kind of expected in a roguelike, but it does get a little tiring. The variations of enemies are basically just recolors of different classes, but it at least looks cool. The armor sets themselves look pretty awesome, my favorite one being the one with the antlers. Some armor sets change your speed or how much health you have. I also like the samurai-type one, because of how fast it makes you go. It also just looks pretty cool.
There's a lot of clever writing seen in this game. It's got a cheery personality because of the pyramid dude who talks to you the whole time, the Brazen Head. There's writing on the walls that you can find which tell you lore (which you basically have no idea about because none of it is ever presented to you very well) but the wall inscribings are usually pretty funny. I found one that literally just said "Toilet."
10 levels in total can be found in this game. Some feel really long, seem feel short, and some feel repetitive. I'm not sure if I've experienced every environment type in this game, but there are some pretty cool areas to explore. The final level was kind of a 'wow' from me because I simply didn't expect it to end in that way. The final boss (who, spoilers, is not an important character at all. It's just a big dude) was actually pretty fun to fight. He's basically a Destiny boss, though: he just has a♥♥♥♥♥♥TON of health. It took a solid 10 minutes of whacking at him to kill him. He wasn't hard, but meeting him for the first time was pretty sweet. After killing him, it felt pretty gratifying because of a cool item you get. Sadly, the item isn't used for much other than opening something.
I only ran in to a few bugs during my playtime. One time, an enemy was stuck in a wall. He could hit me, but I couldn't hit him. I died because of it, which was pretty damn annoying. I think the animations could use some improvement, because of how your character snaps from 'I'm running' to 'I am not running' in an instant. It just looks weird, seeing your body teleport to a different position in an instant. If this game had smoother animations, it'd look so much better.
I'd say that if the developers plan on making new content for this game, it's worth it. It's only $30 anyway, which isn't horrible, but you probably won't be coming back to it much after you beat it, unless you have friends. Two new classes and new maps are planned, which is exciting. I'll definitely be coming back for another runthrough when (and if) those are added. Overall, the game is pretty fun, but surprisingly doesn't have too much replay value despite the procedural generation. The game has style and character that made me a smile a lot during it, and it's something I'd love to come back to. Please, devs, keep working on and updating the game!

CD Project RED have sold their souls in exchange for creating perfect digital art.
I remember back then, when the first Witcher came out it was something refreshing, captivating, even good, but still it wasn’t spectacular, despite some people calling it a new best RPG. Among its great strengths in story, quests, art and music it definitely had glaring issues: most notably, some annoying (to the point of being silly) combat moves and the fact that a good two thirds of it is spent in some sort of swamps, sewers and similar-looking dungeons.
There was no hint of something
coming ahead.
But suddenly and unexpectedly,
is upon us. And here I am, trying to review it with my jaw dropped and dangling somewhere around my knees.
You are Geralt, a witcher — a professional monster slayer caught in a midst of political conflict, intrigue and soon after that, on a long quest to clear your good name and discover more pieces in attempt to solve a puzzle of Wild Hunt and your dark past.
Now
is something like ubelievable upgrade over previous installement, unmatched by anything in recent history. Everything you can possibly think of have been drastically improved, expanded and taken to breathtaking levels of visuals, music and sound. All environments are unique and are extremely rich in details: there’s no copy-paste ever.
The characters, even NPCs, are
, deep and interesting. There’s no other RPG where you would stop just to listen to NPC talk and smile at some story they tell each other. Every place, every spot, be it in town or outside, has an event connected to it and some amazing quest you can take on: escape from prison (be a master of stealth, or you can make it a little rough), participate in an assault on rebellious town alongisde king and teach his stupid son some good lesson, prevent military abuse of innocent civillians by beating an officer in a one-on-one swordfight, and get away with it because your king favors you so much; visit abandoned and haunted asylum to calm down the spirits of its victims and learn about its grim past, uncover treason and crime, take a taste of dirty medieval town life by participating in brawls, dice poker and arm wrestling games — and earn some additional coin with that!
Meet mages, trolls (friendly and not so much), fight a giant Cthulhu with a sorceress by your side, join elves in their guerilla struggle against humans, assist dwarves and visit their mysterious town hidden somewhere deep in the mountains or, if you rather prefer that, stay in a dirty human military camp and become a new star of its colloseum-like fighting arena. The choice is always yours: so be prepared to take it and face the consequences (or enjoy them :-).
And did I even mention how
fights can be? Devise your tactics, approach and hunt monsters: all different, inhabiting their own areas and requiring unique means to successfully kill; pursue finest gear upgrades to assist yourself in your dirty job. Harvest for ingredients during your trips outside to brew and drink awesome poisions (of a witcher sort) and acquire inhuman powers for a short amount time. Buy materials, schematics and construct deadly traps, bombs and daggers to leave your enemies no chance. Approach several knights that dared to threaten you and perform a powerful finisher move, killing them all at once. Redirect arrows back at your enemies, use powerful witcher magic tricks to trap or stun your foes: block, riposte, perform a quick roll away, then jump and cut your unfortunate foe through while he recovers from a good blast of your yrden (not a typo). You have to fight dirty: you have to fight like a witcher.
And all that above is just barely one third of what is in store for you.
I have no idea how CDPR were able to pull that all off.

TL;DR: The rest of the review is mostly the launch version of the game, but to give a short blurb the new content and balance changes have really helped the game. I can officially recomend it now for the price.
"A Year in Review":
Once again I've heard some news of the game and the jig is up. Harebrained Schemes have, to my knowledge, ceased all development on Necropolis in favor of working on Batttletech. While it's a good idea to work on things that actually make money, as it stands Necropolis is a unfinshed mess with 2/3 of the characters that should be in the game, only enough content for 1 solid run to the bottom (even repeating in that same playthrough enough to irritate me), and a number of strange bugs and other sequence breaks that can render a run incompletable. I gave them praise when I saw a game get a serious roadmap for success, but now that they just give up on this game in favor of working on something else. It shows their true colors that when a game is not a 'success' they will not make it right, DO NOT TRUST HAREBRAINED SCHEMES WITH YOUR MONEY.
BRUTAL UPDATE!:
I have changed my opinion of the game, they've added a lot. Made it so you can actually die. Even added a new playable class (and there is also another on the horizon, I'm looking at you Arcanist). Hairbrained had me worried with the radio silence, but they have shown they really do care about their games. I can now recomend this game, while I still have small problems with pacing of combat and how 'sticky' things feel. I enjoy it once again.
UPDATE!:
Big list of improvements on their way!
Update:
I'm played through now 3 whole times only dying once (gave up after a shoft lock). I like this game, I'm still playing it, but I can understand if you feel I'm hypocritical for not following my own advice.
Preface: I've always enjoyed Harebrained Scheme's Shadowrun titles and wanted to give them a fair shake for their new Rogue-like title. I was interested in their trailers and promotional material and started to follow it. Two weeks before release looking at reviews and other early content I had became conviced that the game was ultimately going to be a stinker. Against my better judgement I still wanted to see for myself to prove that it was indeed not the game I wanted, and well, I proved it.
Pros:
(+++) Play with your friends!
(++) Discovery in the most lethal way possible!
(++) Fully realized aethetic
(+) Intersting and humorous world
Cons:
(---) Little to NO customization in terms of cosmetics (Colors and Gender)
(---) Terrible variety of items (Weapons, Armor, Potions, and Scrolls)
(---) Overall weak replayability
(--) Price Point
(--) Non-rebindable keys
(--) Low difficulty especially after you reach T4 items
(--) Awkward damage scaling making some enemies trivially easy and others damage sponges
(--) Terrible feedback for how much damage you are actually doing
(-) Repeating voice/text lines within one playthrough
(-) Not a real ending (From what I've seen, could be wrong)
(-?) Not a whole lot of death
(-?) Obfuscation of stats on EVERYTHING
So I bet you're wondering why I don't hate this game given my list of complaints. I might be crazy, but I enjoyed my time with the game, it was a fun and enjoyable game. BUT and a big BUT here, the game is shallow. This game CANNOT stand as a Rouge-like, it simply can't. After one solid run to the end you will have seen it all. Baring some of the T4 equipment you will have seen it all. Every scroll, every potion, every recipe, every enemy. Nothing new will greet you on your second go around and that is crimminally sad for a game with such potential.
I WANT to love this game (You can say it is Choice-supportive bias I guess), but it is NOT worth the $30 entry fee. This game would be at the sweet spot at maybe $15-20 in my personal opinion, but when you are competing with the genre defining titles like FTL, Risk of Rain, or many others it can't match. If this game gets workshop support and we see a really fervent community pop up it will be worth it. If we see many new enemies, items, and tile sets get added as free content patches it will be worth it. If we see a meaningful price drop it will be worth it, but right now the game suffers for lack of content and it shows quickly. I hope I'm proven wrong, that I missed the deep and amazing gameplay I crave, but right now I don't see it.
In my limited experience (A once through with a friend to the end) we were unstoppable. We were able to craft entire inventory's full of powerful potions and armed to the teeth with magical swords that immolated our foes or turned their blood to gems. The final boss boiled down to a timer in till we obtained our final reward. Not to mention that the ending was barebones to the point of anger. This coupled with the 2 times we got so thouroughly lost in a particuarly large Level 6 and 8 it took a combined 1 to 2 hours of back tracking.
The game is so close to being good it hurts, it harkens back to memories of Castle Crashers and plays like it too. You play through with a group of guys unlock some goodies and go again, each time around 5 hours. But the Codicies are not enough to carry me to another game. I played once through without any codecies and found it to be easy enough, I feel like they would only exacerbate the problem.
In conclusion it's a title that one day could be one of my personal favorites and likely will in time, but right now no. I can't recomend it, I can't stand by it, and I'm struggling to find the will to play it another time. Please Harebrained Scheme's I plead for you to commit the unthinkable and perform necromancy and save this game.

This is an adventure game, pretty much like all others, but with some annoyances that makes it impossible to recommend it.
First, the settings. Which really aren't there... The game uses quite a low resolution, which cannot be changed at all. Low res on a 24" monitor, plus low fps (I'm guessing it's locked at 30 or so) - almost immediately after starting playing, it feels very straining on the eyes.

The game has voice acting - obviously they didn't hire professionals for it, because it's horrible.
Small changes could have made this one an excellent game, but as it currently is, I wouldn't recommend this game at all.

I ws actually surprised how much fun this game really is. If you like big trucks and/or technical off-roading then you'll probably enjoy this sim. The base premise of this game is simple, you are a logger in what appears to be the Russian wilderness and you have to get loads of logs from point A to B. The path in between usually involves muddy, rocky, and flooded trails on wide open sandbox maps. You will also need to consider fuel consumption and vehicle damage so fuel depot and garage stops will need to be planned into your route. All vehicles are modular and can be adapted for load hauling, repair parts hauling, or fuel delivery also. It will probably be the slowest driving sim anyone has every played, but that is due in part to the ground physics that simulates the terrain changes. If logging isn't your thing, there is always Workshop vehicles for trail rigs and mod maps for more technical off-roading adventures. This game was so entertaining and the environment quality was so good I had to get the sequal "Mudrunner" to see the improvements.

Stolen from your home, Dead Bits plops you into a voxel world of deadly testing in a retro inspired circle strafing hell. The rules are simple: grab a gun, kill anything that moves, and try to stay alive amid the hordes running your way and the deadly traps in your path. So what's the catch? Well, pretty much everything after the first level..
Dead Bits is a simple game, which I'm perfectly fine with, but it does so very little with everything that it attempts that it's just plain boring. Enemy AI is entirely nonexistent, running toward you with the fever of a teenage girl who caught a glimpse of her favorite pop idol walking buy. This more or less devolves the game into running backwards while holding down the trigger, having to fear more about falling off the edge of the map than anything the enemies might do. The guns are dull and lack any sense of power or recoil, which makes mowing down waves of bullet sponge enemies even less interesting.
The most egregious thing about Dead Bits however is how bloody frustrating it can be, by way or deliberately inflating the difficulty for no reason but to make you angry. Instant kill obstacles that you're never made aware of abound, making for numerous deaths which feel not at all your own fault, and a complete lack of checkpoints turns the lengthier levels into absolute chores to complete. The extended death animation is particularly annoying, itself taking too long to finish and then proceeding to boot you to the level select screen so you can wait for levels to reload before trying them again. I completed the games brief 9 levels in just under 2 hours, but it only took me that long because I died at least a dozen times for cheap reasons every level.
Though it's rather simplistic, I actually did like the cel-shaded art style developer Microblast was going for with most of the game, though for whatever reason they weren't content to stick with it and instead chose to go with a completely different style for the guns and character models. The end result is a complete mess of conflicting styles and really puts to waste the great foundation they had before they added the odd pseudo realistic elements.
Dead Bits is the sort of game I'd expect to see a student or modder put out as a first step toward something more ambitious and polished. If that were the case it might be a commendable, if heavily flawed, first attempt at making a game, but as a finished retail product there is no way I could advise anyone to pick it up, which is to say nothing of wasting your time and sanity playing it. I feel there was potential here at some point, but in the end it's about as enjoyable as banging your head against a brick wall, and could very well do you just as much harm.

Belladonna is a good game with really beautiful art, almost like playing a modern-day cartoon; however, the story itself, is certainly not for kids.  The game is not overly dark or gruesome but story-wise, meant to be played for mature audiences only.
The biggest knock on the game is the price tag based on the length to complete the game.  This game can be completed within a 1 hour and 30 minutes.  Other than that, the game itself is really nicely done even in its simplicity.
There are a couple of gameplay elements in this game that may be considered a negative but should be considered as a positive.
First, this game is a point-and-click game and the player interacts with objects and items like any point-and-click game.  Things you pick up aren’t many so it’s more limited and simple compared to other games.  This is a good thing.  In other point-and-click games, sometimes picking up objects are non-sensical and applying them doesn’t relate to the story.  It’s just a means to an end in progressing the game.  Also, collecting, combining and applying random items can be a common frustration in a point-and-click game.  In Belladonna, the items collected are far and few and sometimes they make sense.  This gets rid of frustration and allows the player to stay focused on the story while being engaged with a bit of gameplay.
Secondly, constant reading can feel boring and tedious.  If you play Belladonna, there will be a lot of reading; thankfully, the reading of journals not only bring context to the story but also purpose.  The journal entries bring light to what happened and the more you read, the more you are invested to collect all entries to see how it ends.
It’s a good game and worth a try for those who enjoy point-and-click adventure games

Been playing rFactor 2 since early 2013 and just migrated my copy over to Steam.  To cut to the chase, rFactor2 is a brilliant racing simulator.  It offers a very robust and detailed physics engine, coupled with an excellent tyre model, which will punish bad driving and reward good driving, in a way I have yet to see in other games/sims .  As well as employing some very cool features, such as proper tyre deformation, both physical and visual, this includes the ability to flatspot a tyre(s) and also tyre curing (hardening of the tyre from overheating).
rFactor2 also features full 24 hour day/night cycles and dynamic weather.  Although the latter is still, to a certain degree, a work in progress.  rFactor2 also features a dynamic track surface, aka real road, which means a track will "rubber in", based on where and how cars drive on the track.   This also applies to a wet track which is drying out too, so you will see a dry line start to form.
The force feedback is, in my honest opinion, the best there is at the moment, however results may vary based on the type of wheel you are using, but this is the case for any racing game, in my experience.  I currently use a Thrustmaster T500rs, and it pretty much works perfectly on default settings, although you will most likely want to tweak settings here and there to suit your own personal preferences.
rFactor2 is a "constantly evolving product" which means new updates to the game itself, as well as the content, are released on a regualr basis (generally every 6-8 weeks there will be something new/updated, although there is no official timescale for releases/updates).  Because of this constantly evolving nature, there are, some areas of rFactor2, where it is a little rough round the edges.  A good example of this is the weather system, at least from a visual standpoint, needs to be finished at this present time, however it will no doubt be addressed in the near future.
The game can seem quite daunting to someone who has never played any of ISI's earlier titles i.e. rFactor (1) and indeed there is a huge amount of settings/customisation that can be done, either via the in-game UI or through fiddling with settings in the JSON game files.
Online multiplayer is good, but don't expect the same as something like iRacing, unless you join a organised league.
To sum up, here are my PRO's and CON's for rF2.
PROS:
1.)  Excellent physics engine.
2.)  State of the art tyre model.
3.)  Very detailed force feedback.
4.)  Dynamic track surface.
5.)  Dynamic weather
6.)  Full 24 hour cycle
7.)  Continually evolving product, meaning new features and content are reguarly added, as well as exisiting content and features updated too.
8.)  All ISI released content and updates are FREE and always will be.  Even if you let your online subscription run out.
9.)  Lots of 3rd party content available.
10.)  Excellent AI for some truly epic offline races.
CONS:
1.)  Some aspects/features are a bit unfinshed at the time of writing this review.
2.)  As with many racing games/sims, rFactor 2 is quite resource hungry and requires a reasonably good PC to run it with all the graphics turned up and lots of cars on track.
3.)  Online multiplayer can be hit and miss sometimes, unless you sign up to an organised league.
4.)  rFactor 2 can be quite complicated to use and setup, to someone new.
In short, if you like racing games and you like them hyper realistic and packed with features, get rFactor 2, you won't regret it!

is a point&click adventure that has decent visuals, story, and music. However, it also has some of the most generic puzzles in the genre. Length of the game is usually subjective criticism but in case of Belladonna, we literally talking about 30 to 60 minutes ( and half of it was reading ). I think it is fair to expect 2 to 4 hours from a point&click adventure in this price range. Personally, I found the theme of the story a lot more intriguing  than the actual gameplay and I was mildly satisfied after beating it. It's just that game is a little pricey for what it is.
Our character is a female corpse that wakes up on the operating table and has to uncover the mystery behind her resurrection. Let's be honest, this isn't the most original plot and I knew exactly where the game was going. Voice acting was not a perfect match for the character but I would still prefer it over silent text. I assume the same person voiced 2 different females and the second one was a lot more distracting. Most of the story is provided through letters that are a little hard to read (where are subtitles?) I got to say that I felt like I read more text than I played the game. Saying that if you skip reading you will probably get 20 minutes of gameplay with no attachment to the characters (that would be one awful experience).
Considering that artwork seems to be made by one person it looks good. Well, he has been cutting corners in few places, you can clearly tell when something has less detail than the environment around it. To me that really ruins immersion. I like when games stay consistent with visuals. The main character is very cute for a corpse and she has some decent animation. Backgrounds, for the most part, are very nice, Overall there are some consistency issues even though I like how game looks.
If anything the game mechanics are very intuitive. Picking up objects from the background is easy and you get a text describing what you looking at. Some other games make these basic functions harder than it should be so I do appreciate nice and clean interface. The weakest part of the game are the puzzles themselves. Everything was a straight forward solution and I never had to use my brain. Maybe some prefer easy puzzles but I played enough of these games to where I expect something more creative.

Definitely one of my most favorite games of all time and the best RPG EVER. In The Witcher 2: Assassins of Kings you play as Geralt of Rivia, a legendary Witcher, based on the novels of Andrzej Sapkowski. Witchers are monster slayers for hire, with their mutated bodies and skills they wipe out monsters for a pay. But in this saga Geralt tries to regain his memory which he lost when fighting the Wild Hunt. (Read novels or play TW1/2 to know more about the story) on his way he has to deal with choices that have influence on your progess in the game.
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
+ Beautiful breathtaking graphics
+ Epic long and interesting story
+ Non-linear gameplay
+ EXTREMELY immersive atmosphere
+ Choices are important, in the game you always have the possibility to make choices you like and they all have their different consequences.
+ Awesome soundtrack
+ Interesting sidequests, unlike other RPGs or games these sidequests will totally not get you bored.
+ Great and original characters
+ Possibility to lay traps and hunt
+ Different Monsters are spread throughout every location
