Galactic Civilizations 3 was a solid game, but it was also dull and lifeless, and its map felt so "gamey" that I had a lot of trouble getting invested in the story. Endless Space, too, is solid as a game but lacking nearly all of the wonder I think good space strategy games should inspire. We all know what happened with Legends of Pegasus... Until Stellaris, I'd been reduced to finding my space strategy fix by playing Sins of a Solar Empire while weeping nerd tears onto my keyboard. "Why?" I shriek forlornly at my wife and my kids and my cats. "Why can't anyone seem to figure out how to make an amazing space strategy game?"
Then Stellaris came out. I've only played about three hours so far, but I feel pretty good saying that this may well be the game we've all been waiting for. I started my first game on a "medium map," which is so immense that I nearly wet myself the first time I zoomed out. And, unlike GalCiv 3, it actually looks like an organic galaxy. Different types of stars dot the map, and nearly all of them are surrounded by planets arranged in a way that looks, again unlike GalCiv 3, like real, organic, God-created space. It all looks absolutely stunning, and the music really sells you the whole "You're exploring space" feeling.
The game backs that feeling of exploration up, too. I found a primitive species of aliens on one planet several jumps away that were busy killing each other with pointy stuff and starting to play with gunpowder. Naturally, I built a pair of orbital platforms to spy on and interfere with their progress while pillaging their moon for resources. Sucks to be the little guys in the galaxy. I also found some floating squids that eat space gas but never attack, and some enormous space "amoebas" that are the size of small moons and look like venus fly traps with sexually transmitted diseases. These creatures fly by Earth every now and then with their nasty tentacles trailing behind them for what is probably about 100,000 miles in the game's scale. When I branched a little further afield, I found some enormous (and enormously terrifying) space crystals that hate my guts despite not having brains. I attempted to take them on to steal their system, and they utterly annihilated my little fleet. The next time I returned, they had tripled their fleets' strength. They will likely kill everyone. On top of all this, I'm fighting a bitter war with some cultists and a bunch of rogue space pirates.
Meanwhile, I'm investigating some strange story about long-dead organic things and the robots that hated them, shuffling population around on planetary titles to avoid bankrupting myself, plopping down frontier and mining stations everywhere I can afford them. I just encountered my first major factions, both of whom look different than me and must therefore be eradicated in the near future--right after I figure out how to build better ships. All along, my faithful robot guide offers me advice (which I nearly always ignore). I've colonized two planets, built some new ships, assigned some governors, hired some scientists, and am now beginning to reach out into the darker places in my little corner of the huge galaxy.
Through all of this, I feel like I am actually exploring our galaxy for the first time. I compulsively read every story-based text box, research every random unidentified ship that pops into my territory, and skitter away from new species in terror while hanging up the galactic equivalent of signs saying, "Nope, don't go that way."
It's all fantastically organic and believable and pretty. It captures the feeling of exploration and discovery I need from a space strategy game, brings a huge amount of depth to the table, and has already hooked me so badly that my marriage may well be jeopardy. In short, it's fantastic, and I absolutely love it. Maybe that feeling will wear off many dozens of hours from now. If it does, I'll adjust my review accordingly.
For now, any self-respecting sci-fi nerd or strategy guru should buy this game right now. It is already the best new strategy game I've played for years, and I think it has the potential to become the best space strategy game every made.

In the game's current state, it lacks a lot of content. For being an indie game, it showed a lot of promise. The art style is nice, the mechanics are good, but there's way too much repetitiveness for a roguelike. A lot of assets are recolors and remodels of others, with minute and superficial variations.
All of the big weapons feel the same, all of the mid weapons feel the same, and all of the smaller weapons feel the same. There's so drastically little difference between any of the weapons that it really boils down to preference. The tech demo for the game I saw nearly 5 months ago showed a lot more thought put into each weapon, but now it feels like each weapon is essentially a skin for the size category. And while I did notice some of the elemental weapons killed certain enemies faster than others, I don't feel that contributed to the gameplay at all. I could pick up a fire weapon and 1-shot Grine, but what does it matter if most of the time there are 3 other races of enemy that are indifferent or resistant to that weapon? Almost every fight is going to be a mix of the different races, so elemental types don't contribute enough to make them valuable. The last balance problem I see is that the big weapon stagger/knockdown is way too good. It works like a form of pseudo-CC that can be used to chainstun huge crowds of enemies, basically removing any challenge from any fight. It made the whole thing unfun.
The enemies suffer from the same problems as the weapons. While superficially they look and act different, they really don't. Sure, there are a few enemies that might use a heavy attack or run faster, but they all just bumrush and mindlessly thwack away at you. It could be a lot more intriguing to have enemies that move around and behind the player, only taking quick potshots from behind while the player is distracted with other enemies. Or having enemies that do more than just block until they attack. It would be nice to have enemies that do more than just go full zombie hoarde. While the enemies don't have to be incredibly smart, having them follow some basic patterns might give us reason to pay attention to whether a particular enemy is the one with or without a particular look.
In addition to the weapon balance, there's a balance issue with things like potions. While I have no issue with there being a short animation for drinking a potion or activating a scroll, they are basically worthless unless used premeditatively for combat due to the sheer number of enemies that are constantly running at the players's face.
If the devs have put out the game as more of a jumping off point for a large number of updates and add-ons, then I have high hopes for the game. Otherwise, I am going to watch where it goes and see if I bother keeping the game installed on my computer. As of now, it was fun for the two hours I played it, but I don't know that I want to do it again without something added to make it worth the price I paid.
And now that I've said what I dislike, I will say what I loved.
The game has excellent ambient music and atmosphere. While I was moving through the first couple levels, I felt very in tune with the idea of being in a Necropolis. The undertones the music had, picking up at unexpected times, made the dark hallways surreal and daunting to explore.
The art style, especially in the end-of-level sections, is gorgeous and adds to the feel of playing a dungeon delver in a (somewhat) abandoned necropolis. Additionally, the models are great. I love how the PC looks between male and female, how the color palate for the skins isn't overtly flashy, and the look of all of the weapons. They all seem to just work well in a cohesive way that makes me sure a lot of time went into the visual designs of the relatively simple looking weapon models.
The engine looks as though it would actually be amazing for utilization of modding. Some games work on expanding a rather average gameplay experience by allowing for the expansion of gameplay through mods. The framework in the game, with the weapons, map, and enemy spawns, presents an opportunity to fix the weaknesses of the game by removing them entirely. Since Steam already has the workshop, and due to the relatively simple design of much of the game, a lot of life could come from the community in the forms of improvements and expansion should the devs decide to go that way.
TL;DR Weapons feel the same, enemies feel the same, combat styles are non-existent, but the game's music and atmosphere is beautiful, core mechanical concepts are solid, and moddability looks high if implemented.
Until there are some updates that fix what's wrong with the game, I'll leave a negative recommendation in spirit, but because I want the devs to know I support them, I'm going to recommend the game with the caveat that it is still in need of some work.

This game is infuriating. Full of cheap tricks, with enemies who can attack just out of range of you and hard to read moves due to the pixelated nature of the graphics. However, it's also pretty fun and you can't help but yell out in joy when you finally bring down an opponent who has defeated you 15 times. The purpose of the game is you are a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Knight who walks from one end of a map to the other. You'll be faced with enemies that must be blocked, dodged and parried if you wish to make it to the end. You'll start with peasants with pitchforks and cattle and by level 2 you'll be fighting pikemen and horse-mounted lancers. The only way to defeat these enemies is to figure it out, step by step. There are no hints, no guides, no tutorials and no power-ups that will give you an edge in combat. It's just you, your dodge, your block and your sword. The difficulty is pretty high and potions that heal are far and few between, generally one per level. Oddly enough, it makes me think of a side-scrolling Dark Souls due to the unforgiving nature and the expectation that you will die... a lot... until you figure out how to defeat your enemies.
Essentially, I found this game to be frustratingly hard but every little victory felt like I had overcome all the odds and I could see I was getting better at the game. For the low price and the relatively simple concept, I would definitely recommend this one to masochists.

A very good member of the uncommon sub-genre of RPG platformers, Dust: An Elysian Tail puts you in the robes of Dust, a mysterious warrior both because of his shady looks and his amnesia. You are accompanied by Fidget, a flying weasel-creature, and the blade of Ahrah, a sentient sword of typically quirky appearance.
Sending you on your way, the game amazingly avoids the "stupid tutorial", instead making the learning of all your skills part of the story. That in turn is delivered through dialogue between Dust and his new friends and any non-player characters (i.e. peasants) that give oddjob quests to keep you busy. Quests are pretty basic: "bring me my stuff from over there", "save my friend from monsters", "bring 5 goblin hides", but some are special or significant, along lines like "you are totally cursed" and "save video game characters", to mention a few trying to avoid spoilers. I'd like to emphasize that ALL of that is delivered through a spoken, animated dialogue. Especially I found it funny how Fidget lampshades your accomplishments and troubles by bragging and whining about them in many a dialogue.
While strong in story, the gameplay and especially combat is the second important part of the game. You hack, slash and sweep through the air and enemy alike through all of the levels. Basic enemies, like goblins and zombies, are weak and at the mercy of the Dust Storm, my attack of choice that makes the enemies (and Dust himself) fly high in the air. Special enemies have special defenses and attacks, like having invulnerability frames, requiring parrying or using Fidget to make them vulnerable to attacks. Also, there are bosses every few hours. Combat doesn't even get boring after a while because despite repetitive it's always pretty awesome and there's that risk of getting hit and losing "chain".
That is at least the case on Hardcore difficulty level. Combat isn't that hard: if you know how to play and like to challenge yourself, I'd advice to pick the hardest difficulty level because then you actually have to avoid getting hit and combat becomes ruthless at times. I tried it on Casual level as well and I can pretty much guarantee it's easy enough for those of you who like to only experience the story.
Cartoony looks, the graphics are nice and well fleshed out. I especially liked how e.g. the map screen (level selection) has got several different scenes. E.g. sometimes Fidget is sleeping but she could also be eating marshmallows looking dreamy. I would also declare the game's various musical pieces to be spot on - there are no annoying ones either to my knowledge/preference.
On Hardcore difficulty getting all the achievements (well, except for one choice-based one) the game got me some 20 hours of adventuring, constant combats, puzzle solving and treasure hunting. It would be hard to be disappointed with this one. Get it, play it and love it!

I really wanted to enjoy this game and through the first level I did. The first level teaches you the basics with no exposition leaving you to fend for yourself and learn how to overcome simple enemies though use of parry and dodge. This is good game design and I rather enjoyed it.
Then came the second level and you're fighting a professional looking soldier type with barely any telegraph on his attacks due to using a one handed sword and his body being in the way of his sword arm. Annoying but not inhumanly fast or anything (later I found out you could literally just spam attacks at him and win) I came to the next enemy, simple timed swing on his lance kills him instantly, and the next which was a fun bit of puzzle solving as how to dispatch him followed by a quick middle finger as he dies in the form of throwing his spear into the air. You then fight sword guy and rider guy again and then come up against your clone more or less.
This knight does not really telegraph his attacks and the only way to damage him is to (I think at least as the visual design never made it explicitly clear) parry him at the last possible second and whack him with an overhead. This is the part where the game goes down hill, as the knight is more or less a palette swap of you and thus I'm not sure his sprite was designed with the intention of the player being able to read his attacks in mind. If he was designed with that in mind then I can't say the dev succeeded.
To eventually learn his move set isn't impossible and to be honest I was getting closer by the time I decided the game was no longer fun to play. The main issues are that once you've bested the stage enemies once or twice they're both easy and very boring to fight, your character moves like a moss covered sloth, and you are most likely not beating a boss without grinding through goons to learn his move to muscle memory because you likely won't be able to by eyesight alone.
If you're either super MLG pro and think I'm just being a weenie babby, or simply ok with a bit of grind and drudgery then  go for it, you'll likely enjoy this more than I did. For others, you'll probably not enjoy this too much, though at 1$ you might be able to justify it for the pretty art.

Dust: An Elysian Tail is a hack-and-slash RPG with some light platforming. It is both artistic and extremely fun to play. Although it employs the standard hit-one-button-over-and-over mechanic found in any hack-and-slash, the combat system doesn't get boring. The Dust Storm and Fidget mechanics add variety to the way you attack enemies, and combined with the air combos, ground combos, and countering, you have a huge amount of control over the way you combat enemies.
As far as the RPG elements go, there are two main things: items and leveling. You can equip items from your inventory to increase attack, defense, etc. and these items can be either found, crafted, or bought from a merchant. The leveling system is very simple; with each level, you gain a skill point that can be used to upgrade health, attack, defense, of FIdget damage. Also, all skills must be within 4 levels of each other before they can be upgraded again. (If attack is 5 and defense is 1, you can't upgrade attack until defense is also upgraded.)
The story is pretty decent (if you don't mind that all the characters are animal people) and is told mostly through dialogue with NPCs. The final showdown is pretty epic, and the ending is satisfying enough.
Played on normal difficulty, it really isn't that hard to beat. If you grind a lot (enemies do respawn if you return to areas) you'll be very sufficiently leveled by endgame and the final area and boss will be no problem. If you prefer not to grind, enemies can be fairly easily skipped by running past and using Dust Storm in the air.
Overall, it played very smoothly. No glitches in gameplay at all. The only issue I ran into was an audio desync during a cutscene (the audio started playing several seconds after the cutscene started, so the voices didn't match up with the visuals.)
I'd say it has some replay value, but works perfectly fine as a one-time playthrough. There are several "choices" you can make during the game, but I don't think they actually affect anything. Collecting all the chests and such doesn't have a huge amount of impact on the game either, besides the occasional find of a good piece of armor or something.
WIth Dust, you get what you payed for and then some. Solid fighting mechanics, artistic graphics, and a relatively good sense of humor throughout. A refreshing and semi-casual-feeling take on the hack-and-slash genre.

So what is Dust: An Elysian Tail? Well, it's a side scrolling 2D Action RPG. And it's great, I couldn't put it down. Basically you unravel the story of who you are throughout the game while helping people fight against and evil general sweeping the land. The game looks beautifully hand drawn, the animations are smooth and fairly precise to your actions on the controller.
This game plays out much like a Devil May Cry or God of War type game. At least that's how I felt the action was, it was quick and fast paced with a few different combos to perform. As you gain EXP you gain levels, when you gain levels you can increase different abilities that help make your character more powerful. This mechanic was ok, but I didn't like how they limited you keep all your abilities within 4 points of each other at any one time. Makes your character grow pretty evenly as you level, but I would have preferred being able to max one out if I wanted to.
The entire game is voice acted, while the voices aren't the best in the ever, they serviced the game well and kept me from having to read everything. Definitely brought life to the characters. The entire could probably be beaten in around 10 hours or so if you did nothing extra, but in the end I played it on Normal and basically did every side quest there was and it took me about 17 hours to complete. Not much in the way or replay value if you do everything other than play it on a harder difficulty level.
I would definitely recommend this game. It was a real surprise to me how much I liked it. Also, I should note I played it with a  PS4 controller. I would probably recommend a controller for this game. If you can get it on sale, great, but this one is worth full price as well. Definitely an A grade from me!

The review above was done in 2015.  Since that time, a new studio has taken over development of rF2 (Studio 397).  Many things are changing, and there's big promises for the future of the game.  My review may not accurately reflect the current state of the game in the future.

The Binding of Isaac is a remarkably enjoyable game, and deserving of much of the praise it receives. While implementing tougher Roguelike elements, it manages to retain the fundamental accessibility and shallow learning curve that hallmark the most well-received indie titles. This is a commendable achievement, and is probably what makes it a foregone conclusion that this game will be remembered as one of the best indie games of all time. But the game does have a very glaring flaw that is too rarely pointed out. The game is short and the dungeons are small, which has the effect of making progression and completion nearly impossible unless you have a lucky start. This is really the worst that can be said of The Binding of Isaac, though, and the game is fun and rewarding at least as often as it is frustrating and unfair. Make sure that you have a very solid handle on the base game before you even consider getting the Wrath of the Lamb expansion, as it ramps up difficulty considerably.

I've spent about 60 hours together playing through both Danganronpa 1 + 2's story. I'm not a guy who usually likes to read a whole lot. Books are hard for me to pay attention to, as is reading in general. But these two games have made me push through that for a story that has left me constantly on the edge of my seat.
Danganronpa 2: Goodbye Despair, (I still hate how they alternated that title from "Farewell Despair Academy", but what can you do...), has taken what made Danganronpa: Trigger Happy Havoc, and somehow amplified it even more. During the final class trial, I felt myself constantly leaned forward, paying attention to every detail I could. Even after having originally read summaries of the games, (at the time it was released only on PSP/Vita and I didn't want to pirate it), I still felt absolutely overwhelmed (in a good sense!) about how well this game manages to pull story off.
I honestly cannot begin to think of anything bad on this game other than it's odd sense of perversion as compared to the first one... I mean, I'm not
about it, but I felt like there was a lot more perverted humour in 2 as compared to 1. I mean, for god's sake, you get the girls' panties when you max your free time interaction with them! Though I only know this from Chiaki's perspective. Chiaki best girl.
Admittedly, though, the final chapter's... 'asthetic', shall we put it, put me off and put a heavier strain than usual on my eyes. Other than that, I have absolutely zero complaints about the game(s).
Please, for the love of god, and for the sake of Hope, please, play the Danganronpa series. I can see why it got so popular a while back now.

I DO actually have to complain about the difficulty settings.
Even when playing under the easiest settings, during things like nonstop debates you find yourself loaded with 3-5+ truth bullets. This was not at all the case in Danganronpa: THH. Even under the standard difficulty, you often only got 1 bullet, maybe 3 on some of the debates.

Final Fantasy VII is a dated yet wonderfully crafted console style RPG. The game is fun, creative and well put together and includes an interesting bunch of characters, locations and scenes.  Also it has a weird mix of light and dark moments.
When compared to the original console release this new PC release has its own pros and cons.
GRAPHICS
Town map graphics in this game are prerendered at an outdated resolution, so it may not be the prettiest game but this is the prettiest version. Battles are drawn in polygons so the battles scenes scale much better than the original version of the game. Animations in battle are still done at a maximum 24fps  so it can still be a little weird looking if your not used to it, this doesnt effect gameplay thankfully as it is a turn based game.
MUSIC.
Gone are the original PSOne sound files used on the official OST and original console release. This is a major downpoint with the new MIDI just not making enough of a change to warrent its existence. To long time fans this can make the music come off poor.There was a Fan patch when I played, but if you have never played this game you may not have to bother at all, as all the music is well writen and still catchy.

OVERALL
Still a good game and worth experiencing for new generations of gamers. A timeless classic to me. An almost perfect version of the game but the music thing is huge to me.

I will recommend this game to anyone who loves Visual Novels in general. This along with Zero Escape are the pinnacle of Visual Novels for me. This series, along with Zero Escape, does one thing that few VNs do; it keeps me interested until the end.
The problem with VNs for me is that the pacing is horrible. Since the pacing is so bad, I get bored really fast. I know a lot of VNs are about the fan service payoff. But I get bored before that point is even reached. So what does Danganronpa and Zero Escape have that those games lack? Intrigue.
Both Danganronpa and Zero Escape have the same issues as a standard VN. Slow pace, exposition dumps (especially in the final two hours of gameplay), and all that good stuff. But what these two games do is keep me interested throughout because of the fact that they're mysteries and pretty decent puzzle games. The slow pace can be fixed because I'm interested in knowing about how these people got in such bizarre situations. Because of that, I don't notice how slow things move, or the exposition, plus most of the characters are super interesting.
A slight aside, I prefer this series over something like Phoenix Wright (the inspiration for Danganronpa more or less) because it's mystery encompasses the entire game. This makes the game feel complete. As if everything up to that point was leading to something larger than the sum of its parts. A lot of Phoenix Wright cases feel contained, which makes sense for the game, but I just enjoy larger mysteries.
All and all, excellent game. My only gripe is that final class trial execution wasn't as awesome as the original game.

"12.4 hrs on record"
It's currently 13 hours after release.
Draw your own conclusions.
Since many of you wanted something of substance, Here's a little thing I threw together.
The game itself shows kinship to 4x games, you’re a new civ on the block with one planet and big dreams. To expand your people to the stars. You’ll soon meet some other races, and realize your destiny to is befriend/ trade with / ignore/ exploit/ exterminate these new creatures. As you expand through use of colonies and strategically placed flags (also called frontier outposts by the humorless), you will work towards your goals for (insert goals here). This expansion will not go unnoticed, and you’re sure to make enemies and friends among the other races you’ve encountered, whose visual appearance has almost no bearing on their preferred world. (Personally my closest ally is a bunch of Sea-warthogs, and I’m also trading partners with a race of desert penguins)
Combat is interesting. The number below your fleet tells you an idea of it’s strength, but not the whole story. You’d be tempted to think like CK2 or EU, where if you have the larger force and a good general you’re generally come out on top. But that’s not the case here. Just ask the 1st fleet of the United Nations of Earth. Armed to the teeth with anti-matter missiles, and assisted by several dozen ships of our fungi allies, up against a force less than 70% of their size.
You actually can’t ask them. They’re all pretty dead. Point defenses turned out to be pretty good at point defense. So remember to not put all your eggs in one basket. Or Spores in one pouch, as the fungi say. Some missiles, some laser, spread the wealth.
Diplomacy is fairly straight forward. You get along better with races that have similar morals to your own, and especially xenophiles in general, but through enough effort you can even getting along with xenophobes. (Those desert penguins mentioned above are kind of racists, but we get along alright). Embassies are a big help. Alliances can be pretty easily formed with those you get along with, and are a great way to both protect yourself and to make offensive wars easier. When declaring war as part of an alliance everyone has to approve it. This is made easier by distributing the war goals amongst the members. Basically a planet to the sea hogs, a liberation to the fungi, etc. Thankfully defensive wars are automatic. You can’t leave them hanging.
The science and tech tree is a bit different from most because it’s not really a tree. It’s a set of cards you draw that you ‘draw’ three from and then decide which to work on. But my favorite part is definitely the science ships. You’re essentially playing as the Enterprise, boldly going where no one has gone before(star trek theme plays here). You’ll run into all sorts of anomalies that require investigation. Sometimes it’s a whole story line about precursors, sometimes it’s just an old cruiser stuck on a planet. Sometimes you run into a system full of million year old mining drones and have to book it. It keeps things interesting.
The random events are very much what we’ve come to expect from paradox. A perfect mix of good writing and humor. Even the ol’ comet event comes around in it’s orbit.
TLDR: It’s a really interesting take on 4x that is everything you should expect from Paradox, and sure to get better with time, and DLCs. A little difficult to learn at first but better than their other games.
TLDR-2: Just play it.

Unfortunately, the biggest flaw of this game is the one it touts in the opening paragraph; procedural dungeon delving. For those kiddies at home new to roguelikes, it means randomised within programmed constraints.
Now, the enviornments look great (despite being skinned similar) when you're fighting your way through it, it feels cool. But the nature of procedural generation is that the clever placement of enemies is impossible in a game like this. I'm going to resort to the "Dark Souls comparison" thing here, Dark Souls enemies are placed in a genius fashion; they make you take risks and assess your situation. This game just feels like someone had a big box of vikings, giant spiders and robots and went "WOOPS I dropped them all over my maze, eh, some adventurer will clean them up". You'll never feel like the enemies are using the environment against you, you'll never look at a group of enemies and think of a way to get past them. The way to get past them is always the same; run at them and mash attack til they die (Optional: Heal afterwards, but you are invincible anyway (more on that below!))
Even in a game like Destiny, you're forced to think about what enemy you're fighting, and adjust your tactic. But in Necropolis the tactic for every type of enemy is exactly the same; hit a bunch, dodge to the side, or special attack in groups. There is both not enough enemy types and very little change in how you fight them. Even when there's vikings, wizards, robots, and skeletons all at once, all you do is hit them til they fall down. The only time they ever change is by health amount (to pretty ridiculous levels of grindy health) and minor reskins. Oh yeah, enemies also never ever block or stop you from attacking, SO GO NUTS.
It also bugs me to no end that one of the only things you use currency, which is gems, for in this game is to level up (AKA, get more health), but by level 6 (of 9) you are already max level. So what do you spend the rest of your gems on? You don't. You can buy crafting recipes or potions and that's it. You will very soon have 8,000 gems in one playthrough that you literally can't do anything with.
For a game with 'difficult' on the tags, I expected this to take more than 3 tries playing solo (in my second try, the game just never gave me an armour drop 'just cuz', so I lost). You have infinite healing items because you can just craft meat to eat, I had somewhere around 50 pieces of meat I could use to craft more healing at the end of the game. And for a game with 'rogue-like' in the title, I expected there to be more randomized RPG elements. There are four tiers of items; the higher the tier, the better the item, no exceptions. The fact that there's so many armour types, but only 4 actual armour classes wastes the potential of all the different sets they hand out. Why not a passive for each armour set? Why, because of the obvious reason; you wouldn't be able to figure out what the passive does without reading the wiki because of the "I'm a smartass" goofy text that makes almost every item wholly confusing. I get it; the weapons and armour have been kept intentionally simple so you don't sit reading inventory screens for years, but the lack of item variety also effects my willingness to replay it again.
The most insulting part about calling it a roguelike is that you are practically invincible! You get a resurrection potion. Yes. A potion where you can keep going when you died. Oh I'm sorry, did I say A potion, I meant the ability to craft infinite resurrection potions. Which, again, would be less of a big deal if you didn't have infinite crafting ingredients on you at all times because every enemy spews out craft confetti so you'll never be short on anything but inventory space.
I sound a bit salty, because I am. I was really looking forward to this, it had a lot of potential. Do I ever think I'll play it again? No, probably not, unless all my buddies end up with it in a humble or something. For $30, you're half way to the 40 hour long Dark Souls 3, not to mention all the other roguelikes that you can get for half that price, which offer a lot more content. Sorry guys; it was a good attempt but fell short of what it could've been.

The Binding of Isaac is a remarkably enjoyable game, and deserving of much of the praise it receives. While implementing tougher Roguelike elements, it manages to retain the fundamental accessibility and shallow learning curve that hallmark the most well-received indie titles. This is a commendable achievement, and is probably what makes it a foregone conclusion that this game will be remembered as one of the best indie games of all time. But the game does have a very glaring flaw that is too rarely pointed out. The game is short and the dungeons are small, which has the effect of making progression and completion nearly impossible unless you have a lucky start. This is really the worst that can be said of The Binding of Isaac, though, and the game is fun and rewarding at least as often as it is frustrating and unfair. Make sure that you have a very solid handle on the base game before you even consider getting the Wrath of the Lamb expansion, as it ramps up difficulty considerably.

Oh dear, oh dear.
This is one of those games that really needs a "meh" button. I did decide to recommend it in the end, but if I were you I'd wait for the next sale. It's not a bad game, but it's pretty expensive for what it is - namely more of a slightly interactive short story.
-Technical Stuffs-
Runs fine. No crashes, no bugs.
-Visuals-
The art style is interesting and appealing, but also pretty rough in places. It's a visually pretty well designed game, though, and everything fits together quite nicely. There's a nice sort of coherence to the entire thing, also regarding the color choices. I like 2D games with a bit of character, so I'm willing to let it slide if the style occasionally went from "stylized and painterly" to "pretty sketch-y, if you know what I mean".
-Audio-
The soundtrack was pretty decent and matched the game well, but it's not completely mindblowing or anything, either. The main character was pretty well voiced (in a characteristically rough-around-the-edges kinda way), the rest of the voice acting was... okay? I guess?
-Gameplay-
You click on stuff, which pretty much works as well as you'd expect it to - namely pretty well, if you're fond of clicking on stuff. On the downside, there's really not much to do except for clicking on stuff. The game is extremely linear, and extremely easy. There are some very, very minor puzzles, but I never even had to stop and think.
-Story 'n Stuff-
There are two big plot twists, one I (and pretty much everyone else) knew about and one I saw coming from a mile off. There were some small things I didn't see coming, too, which was neat. Not quite sure what to think about that ending, though - IMO it was either five minutes too long, or a few hours too short, but the game ending where it does feels a bit odd.
-Conclusion-
I enjoyed the game quite a bit, it was half cute and half pretty thought-provoking and it's certainly quite different. Alas, once you've played through it, you've pretty much seen it all, which leaves you with... oh, around an hour or so of playtime and no reason to go back and play it again. As I mentioned, the full price is fairly expensive for an hour of playtime. Not egregiously so, not by any means, but still. Then again, this is a tiny, tiny indie game made by a tiny, tiny team, so I'm willing to cut the creator(s)* some slack.
I do recommend this game on sale. If you can get it for cheap, get it. If it's worth the money at full price depends on your disposable income - if those seven bucks are a decent chunk of money for you, you should probably pass and go for something with more replay value, but if you've got money to spend... Belladonna is not a bad game by any means.

What this title may lack in complexity compared to a more "traditional" roguelike such as Nethack or ADOM, it more than makes up for with the fresh take on roguelike gameplay that it brings to the table by limiting each turn to the length of a quarter note in the accompanying music.
I highly recommend a controller/gamepad for this game. The control scheme is very general, should adapt well to any pad, and using my thumbs felt more natural and ergonomic than using the keyboard.

Can't really recommed this one. The graphics are ok, but nothing to write home about considering it is supposedly an 'enhanced edition'. Story and lore seem to be dense from what I can tell after roughly two hours.
Unfortunately, combat and interaction are breaking this game for me. Combat is extremely clumsy, it basically boils down to button-mashing, where at no point you have real control over your character, but rather mash buttons as fast as humanly possible and see what the game decides to do.
Combat animations are basic, very basic, you'll sometimes stun an enemy wielding a shield, and when you strike him see a cut-scene like animation where your character delivers a killing blow to an enemy that does not have a shield.
I started the game on 'hard' difficulty, and it took me about 10 minutes to discover how to exploit weaknesses in the AI to a point where I basically go through the fights either with no health loss, the other possible outcome being dying a rather cheesy death due to the no-control combat system.
If I had to describe the combat system with one word, I'm sorry to say that word would be 'garbage', it pretty much ruins an otherwise decent game.
Interaction is similary painful, there is one interaction key (left mouse), which is also one of your main fighting keys, leading to all sorts of unintentional interactions during combat, especially since the 'hot zones' for interactions are placed badly. This also inhibits game flow, you'll sometimes run towards a ledge, and then have to move around trying to find the interaction zone to actually climb it, there is no fluid 'run up to the ledge and climb it' like you'd expect.

An immersive 4X / Grand Strategy crossover, Stellaris is essentially a stripped down version of Master of Orion (or similar) crossed with a stripped down version of Crusader Kings II (or similar), set in space.
9 / 10 (multiplayer)
7 / 10 (single player)
-----------------
I've played this game enough now to have formed a good opinion of the early, middle and late game.  This includes being a 5 hour MP game that started an hour after release, which was impressively stable.  So let me break it down for you:
Survey systems with your science ships for really immersive and well-written events, not dissimilar to side-quests.  Some have unexpected twists, similar genre references and other results that will have you pumping your fist - equally in excitement or frustration.
Colonise nearby planets or earmark future exploits with fronteir stations, allowing you to "blob" despite a drought of colonisable planets.
Meet new races and, once you research their communications (or they, yours), engage in low level diplomacy, establishing embassies and rivals for the near future.
As your corner of the galaxy becomes constrained, you start to realise that the key to winning isn't just expansion.  In-fact due to some very sensible and iconic diplomacy features of the Clausewitz engine, over-expansion will cause others to view you in a bad light (for the most part) founding the way for you to be surrounded by an alliance of people who hate you.
Trust me, this happened to me, and I couldn't even complain about it because I was a warmongering tyrant.
The rivals and embassies you set earlier in the game now bear fruition as threats lead to wars and wards make you consider your potential allies, and your rival's potential allies.  Now is the time to lay the foundations of the wars to come in 50 or 100 years time.
Towards the end of gameplay, I feel that you're pushed into two types of games (or perhaps, playstyles).  You're going to either want to try and conquer the galaxy, and sure you can do that by beating everyone into submission or colonising 40% of the colonisable planets.
To me, that seems very dull, if not boring when the entire galaxy forms a federation to resist your final push to victory.
I'd much rather role play my race's concept right from the start.  Playing my governmental type as I should.  The scientific event chains are futhrered either by your expanding treaties, or expanding borders.  Your research starts stacking up and you constantly nurture and oversee your relations to make sure that one distant ally doesn't drag you into a war that exposes your own border to enemies.
Does it lack features such as more in-depth diplomacy and espionage?  Yes.
Will the above be added later as expansions?  It's Paradox, so of course yes.
Is this the be all and end all of 4X games?  No.
Does it try to go somewhere no one has gone before?  Yes.
Does this game deliver on it's promises?  Yes.
If you still have your doubts about the game single-player, I suggest you find a group, join a voice chat and a game, and lament your failures and celebrate your successes together, for it's the multi-player that really makes this game shine.

I took the risk of purchasing this on release day, with no prior Dark-Souls experience, and when there was only one review written on here. Let me tell you, it was worth every cent. (As I mentioned before, I'm writing this without having played any of the DS titles before, so take that in consideration).
This game is a Rogue-like dungeon crawler, with many similitudes to Dark-Souls (From what I've heard). You advance through a pretty lengthy dungeon, through randomly-generated levels, fighting enemies and getting loot from them. If you die, you have to restart from the beginning, with only a couple benefits gained from your previous runs.
What drew me over to buy this game in the first place, was the art. The scenarios are beautiful and very well done, although maybe a bit repetitive after you play it for a while. The gameplay and controls are really smooth. I really like the "Hunger" system where you have to eat food to have more energy to perform actions.
The game doesn't spoon-feed you information, texts can be vague at times (But still sometimes intuitive), which is good, because it leads you to experiment with what each item does. Since you will be starting over many times (It is really hard not to die), it is understandable that people think this game is repetitive, but once you progress through the levels, it feels nice to find new weapons and shields, unlock codexes (They grant you benefits, but you can only wear one at a time, which makes it interesting), recipes, etc.
It can be addictive if you have the "One more try" mentality. You will die a lot, and you have to start over each time, only keeping the "Favors" (Currency that allows you to purchase Codexes, among other things that provide benefits to your character) you managed to get, which will allow you to get different benefits and bonuses to get farther in the dungeon.
I only got to level 3 during my first game session today, so I don't know if these levels are limited, or what is the total content there is, but then again, it is a new game. I'm sure more cool stuff is to come, this is just the beginning and I already love it.

Update: I stand by my initial review, which has remained unchanged below. However, while I don't recommend the game in it's current state as something for the starting user, if you love racing I highly recommend you buy it anyways! The game offers one of the best physics engines, if not the best, in the industry, and supporting ISI will only make the entire game better in the future. It gets updated often and already has an amazing feature set. The issues I have with the game can only be improved with time and support!
I've also updated my thoughts on Force Feedback and explained what I ment by "faked effects", as I do not believe other users realized I was speaking about the vibration effects that cannot be done realistically by most current hardware. I also am cleaning up the pros and cons to give a much more concise list of positives and negatives. Again, please support ISI and buy this game if you love racing, but please do your research if you haven't played many racing sims and your experience is limited to Need for Speed and Project Cars.
Pros:
Amazing physics
Mod support
Custom Rule plugins
Day/Night Cycles
Rain
AI is uncomparable to any other game. (I swear one stayed stopped on the side of the road until after a set of cars passed after it spun out!)
Cons:
Physics are not 100% perfect despite anyone's comments. Rubber buildup isn't perfect, and the damage model is lacking (heavily lacking. Some cars don't even get damaged visually)
Sounds are strange
Unoptimized graphics system
Rain does not appear on car/windshield
Not all the cars are kept up to date
Poor mulitplayer system (great for leagues, sucks for public racing)
rFactor 2 is a fantastic sim for a cost-saving consumer, offering more in physics compared to Assetto Corsa or Project Cars. Rubber builds up pretty realistically, tracks made directly by ISI are gorgeous, and many of the mods are fantastic.
It's great in league settings and playing against AI, but unfortunately that's where my excitement about the game ends. While many users may disagree with me, I feel it's physics are a bit half-baked in some areas. While it's real-road system is pretty cool, it's no longer unique and does not offer the temp-based system that a competitor, iRacing, offers. The other issue comes with the accuracy of the tracks. While it's true that, often times, a surveyed track can compare to a scanned track in terms of looks, it does not matter if it doesn't feel right. This is often commented on the mod version of Nurburgring, where the rFactor 2 version is often not accurate in terms of the bumps found on the track when compared to other games, such as assetto corsa, that uses a laser scan copy of the track.
Other issues I find with the game is it's confusing UI, the outdated engine that is struggling to keep up, and the community. I gave this game plenty of chance. I played it for over 2 years and nearly exclusivly for almost 4 months this past summer [I didn't have internet], letting my iRacing sub lapse and really trying to give it a go for my money's worth...
It left me bored. Without an online ranking system, there isn't a point. I don't have the time or energy to join a league, and the AI is great but still doesn't compare to the thrill of racing a human driver. While the tire physics are quite out of this world, the FFB has obvious faked effects to try to make it easier to tell what's going on, but it disrupts my driving. This is mostly noticable when it tries to make "vibration" effects, something that cannot be done by 90% of hardware on the market, and is ineffectivly done by the Fanatec BMW racing wheel, as most racing wheels only contain rotational FFB hardware.
The only other major thing it had going for it, the real road effect, has been brought to other games in some effect, whether it's the lap-by-lap system done by AC or the real-time dynamic track brought in by iRacing.
In terms of the buy-and-drive games without a subscription, the lifetime version of rFactor 2 is the best simulation out there. Unfortunately, it's plagued by multiple issues that have yet to be fixed after a near 6 years in development. I hope the release on Steam creates enough income to let them proceed faster with their development, but at this current time I cannot recommend this game to anyone but true racing enthusiasts, if only to try it out to see what's in the current competition or to those who want an EXCELLENT offline experience.
As of their latest updates, iRacing and rFactor 2 feel quite similar. rFactor 2 no longer suffers from it's wonky tire physics,  and iRacing hasn't felt like ice in over a year. I can drive the stock cars almost identically between the two games. Other cars are harder to test due to differences in tracks and the cars available.
It's the package itself that bothers me. rFactor 2 could do great things, but it feels their development team does not put enough effort into providing content and rely on third party creations, which lowers the overal value of the game to me.
Creating a world that is consistant, that is how racing thrives. iRacing has accomplished this. Assetto Corsa is good about this too. rFactor 2 suffers solely on this issue, which is in truth, it's only major flaw.
I will update my review when rFactor 2 shows the world that it is truly capable of being a place for sim racers.
(Please note that I bought the life time upgrade after paying for 2 yearly subscriptions over the past 3-4 years. I want the developers to improve this game, so I gave them support in terms of my wallet. I also bought this game for 3 of my friends, because I wanted them to try it out and, again, to give ISI some support. I do not hate this game, nor do I feel that iRacing is 100% the answer either. Everyone will have their own opinion, but I hope that people do not feel blinded by passion. [Although I will admit I am a bit of a David K fanboy, but even I admit that the NTMv1-4 was garbage]

Belladonna is an odd game. Things start off well enough, with a mystery and an appealing art style. However, as the play continues, it soon becomes obvious that the scenic designer has forgotten to finish the sets, the screenwriter left the script to be written by his curious teenage daughter, and the director is shouting out spoilers from behind the curtain. The gothic castle consists of a couple tiny rooms, the initially dark story soon throws all of that out the window and ends in a puzzlingly cheery end-title screen reminiscent of the game covers from the 90's (think Commander Keen) that looks extremely out of place, and the point-and-click adventure boils down to the game telling the player exactly what and where to use. The entire ordeal is over in an hour, with 3 more hours of idling for cards, and quite frankly you'd be far better off going to the library and checking out a copy of Mary Shelley's Frankenstein instead.

Magical Diary is a Visual Novel with RPG elements.  You play as a new girl at a magical school, and must balance your academic, social and romantic lives as best you can!  There are exams you must pass, which are one of my favourite parts of the game.  You can use the spells you have learnt in class to solve the puzzles set to you in various ways.  I wish there were more of these chances to use magic, really!
There are several possibilities for romance.  I've only followed one through so far, but it was very emotional and moving.  I think I am in love with him XD  There appear to be female options as well as male, so I will probably go this way on my second playthrough.  It is always nice when a game caters to different tastes in this way.
It's shorter than many visual novels; I was a little surprised at how suddenly it ended.  It took me about 4 hours to play through once.  This is easy to forgive though - the game features far more choices and branches than most visual novels.  That means it has a lot of replay value, and if you're anything like me you'll definitely want to play again!
The doesn't have the difficulty of Long Live the Queen, which allows you to sit back and enjoy the story without worrying too much, unless you are striving for all the achievements!  The exams offer a fun challenge which you can take at your own pace.  It is fun to find many different ways to solve the same puzzle.

The game allows you to create a female main character, with few anime style options. It proceeds to drops you into a one year stint as a freshman student in a magical academy. During this time, you interact with various characters, almost all of which can become love interests (male and female alike). The characters are interesting and the romances are endearing.You learn spells and use them in highly limited capacity for very specific events. The most important events would be the exams. You can pass the exams with various spell combinations or simply decide to surrender and fail.

Belladonna is a point-and-click adventure game with a gothic twist. Scratch that; Belladonna is a point-and-click adventure game that echoes M. W. Shelley and tells a dark but fun story without descending into Adventure Game Logic.
Belladonna isn't difficult. There's maybe an hour an a half of content here, give or take, and the puzzles are straighforward and perfectly logical. So, as an Adventure Game, it's unremarkable and not at all frustrating.
Where it really shines, though, is in the voice acting and the art. It is beautiful and charming in its Gothic-Horror appeal. It never even comes close to being scary, but then much classic Gothic horror just isn't. Neither of the gothic horror stories it seems to draw most strongly from (Carmilla and Frankenstein) are especially scary - but they deal in unsettling concepts.
That's something that makes Belladonna special. It's a horror story and a gothic romance, beautifully put together into a package that will occupy you about as long as a movie would. It's frankly just a great game.

You are a female Frankenstein creation, born into an adult body with full language skills and articulation but no memories of your previous life as a human. There are some notes scattered throughout that tell pieces of the story of your creator, which was far from a happy one. With some effort, you eventually can escape your "birth chamber"...and that's when things really get interesting. Such is the basic setup of Belladonna and to reveal too many more specifics would be a disservice.
Okay, let's get a few things out of the way first. One, this is not a long game to play. It took me a little over an hour to make my way though the whole story, there are no side activities and the overall area you're playing in is very contained. Two, the puzzle-solving is logical but extremely basic. I would be very surprised if a player who has made it through the likes of the classic Sierra or Lucasarts series of adventure games didn't have an idea what to do just through careful examination and deductive reasoning (to say nothing of your player character's own observations in the rare event that you are stuck). Indeed, had I not purchased this for an extreme discount during the Winter Sale this past year, I would feel extremely cheated by such features.
So why am I giving this game a thumbs up? Because, as little as it does overall, it does those few things so right as to make the experience memorable. I realize how many modern players object to reading letters as opposed to hearing them given a voiceover but the story the letters you find weave a tale that's worth the VERY few minutes you need to spend reading them. While there are plenty of playful references to Poe and Young Frankenstein as well as surprisingly insightful observations from your player character that emphasizes her innocence, the overall story is the real winner. It is nothing less than the most subversive take on Frankenstein that I have ever seen (and I am a hardcore fan of all things Frankenstein) with a feminist slant that makes me wish the game had lasted a little longer.
If you are willing to overlook the flaws I've already noted, I can promise that this video-game-as-short-story is VERY worth your time.

Since many of you wanted something of substance, Here's a little thing I threw together.
The game itself shows kinship to 4x games, you’re a new civ on the block with one planet and big dreams. To expand your people to the stars. You’ll soon meet some other races, and realize your destiny to is befriend/ trade with / ignore/ exploit/ exterminate these new creatures. As you expand through use of colonies and strategically placed flags (also called frontier outposts by the humorless), you will work towards your goals for (insert goals here). This expansion will not go unnoticed, and you’re sure to make enemies and friends among the other races you’ve encountered, whose visual appearance has almost no bearing on their preferred world. (Personally my closest ally is a bunch of Sea-warthogs, and I’m also trading partners with a race of desert penguins)
Combat is interesting. The number below your fleet tells you an idea of it’s strength, but not the whole story. You’d be tempted to think like CK2 or EU, where if you have the larger force and a good general you’re generally come out on top. But that’s not the case here. Just ask the 1st fleet of the United Nations of Earth. Armed to the teeth with anti-matter missiles, and assisted by several dozen ships of our fungi allies, up against a force less than 70% of their size.
You actually can’t ask them. They’re all pretty dead. Point defenses turned out to be pretty good at point defense. So remember to not put all your eggs in one basket. Or Spores in one pouch, as the fungi say. Some missiles, some laser, spread the wealth.
Diplomacy is fairly straight forward. You get along better with races that have similar morals to your own, and especially xenophiles in general, but through enough effort you can even getting along with xenophobes. (Those desert penguins mentioned above are kind of racists, but we get along alright). Embassies are a big help. Alliances can be pretty easily formed with those you get along with, and are a great way to both protect yourself and to make offensive wars easier. When declaring war as part of an alliance everyone has to approve it. This is made easier by distributing the war goals amongst the members. Basically a planet to the sea hogs, a liberation to the fungi, etc. Thankfully defensive wars are automatic. You can’t leave them hanging.
The science and tech tree is a bit different from most because it’s not really a tree. It’s a set of cards you draw that you ‘draw’ three from and then decide which to work on. But my favorite part is definitely the science ships. You’re essentially playing as the Enterprise, boldly going where no one has gone before(star trek theme plays here). You’ll run into all sorts of anomalies that require investigation. Sometimes it’s a whole story line about precursors, sometimes it’s just an old cruiser stuck on a planet. Sometimes you run into a system full of million year old mining drones and have to book it. It keeps things interesting.
The random events are very much what we’ve come to expect from paradox. A perfect mix of good writing and humor. Even the ol’ comet event comes around in it’s orbit.
TLDR: It’s a really interesting take on 4x that is everything you should expect from Paradox, and sure to get better with time, and DLCs. A little difficult to learn at first but better than their other games.
TLDR-2: Just play it.

Finished this in a few hours with a friend, and I can say for sure, it feels incomplete, but okay. I'll break down the pros and cons that I can remember.
Pros: Great lighting
Great artstyle
Fantastic music
Occassional memes (despite the fact that they are kind of outdated and ruin the lore)
Although I didn't pay attention to the narration most of the time, it made a serious effort to make a world around it that worked great in it's fantasty genre.
Fluid combat (aside from dodging)
Having only played on the release date, I hope to come back in a week, month or two months to a very different experience. And having said that, I greatly enjoyed playing this with my friend, and since we had such a great time, I would love to play more on another date.
Cons: Limited weapons, and weapon variety. There are many weapons, but often are reskins of others, with the same attack patterns, but more damage. I only ever came across three unique weapons. Two of which were small hand crossbow that did almost no damage, and a wand, which did even less. Both were found very early on. The last was an endgame sword, which generated money when hitting enemies. Other than the wand and mini-crossbow, there are no ranged weapons, or magic weapons. This punishes people that play in groups of four, as they will all end up using melee weapons, and since there is friendly fire having four people attack one larger enemy would lead to disaster.
Dodging is pretty much useless, because unlike dark souls, there are no i(invincibility)-frames, so you will be hit anyway. This forces you to spam the use of whatever shield you have.
Multiplayer is fun, with the teamwork, but there is no pvp, and I believe that in the future, it could easily be added.
Multiplayer is overpowered, also. I can't imagne anyone soloing all eight levels. However, I and a friend, managed to get through relatively easily. The only problem we faced was having enemy agro while one of us is downed. If a group of three or four were to play this, I can't imagine them losing.
You lose everything upon death if you are in multiplayer. Your armor, weapons, shields, consumables, money, blessing(s) (levels) and ever crafting components. There is no way to get them back. You can't go to where you died and retrieve them. They are just gone.
The enemies never switch agro. You could be slicing a zombies back, and it will still hobble towards an ally that's run twenty meters away.
There are many "nothing spots" as my friend and I referred to them as, where it would SEEM like there could be hidden treasure to reward you for finding a secret, or going off the beaten path. Many times we thought to venture off the beaten path only to find absolutely nothing.
The camera has a certain threshhold that makes it move. Meaning that if you move your mouse slowly, it will sort of tick to the direction you intend. Instead of moving one degree, it will move five degrees, basically.
STICKY KEYS!!! When one of us were to be knocked down, we would often be fighting, spamming left click to attack, when being knocked down. thirty seconds later when we are being revived, we would attack our savior, because there are sticky keys.
Combat was really sticky. For example, you click three times quickly to attack, and you will swing three times slowly. The attacks are very disjointed from when you click.

I've played this game enough now to have formed a good opinion of the early, middle and late game.  This includes being a 5 hour MP game that started an hour after release, which was impressively stable.  So let me break it down for you:
Survey systems with your science ships for really immersive and well-written events, not dissimilar to side-quests.  Some have unexpected twists, similar genre references and other results that will have you pumping your fist - equally in excitement or frustration.
Colonise nearby planets or earmark future exploits with fronteir stations, allowing you to "blob" despite a drought of colonisable planets.
Meet new races and, once you research their communications (or they, yours), engage in low level diplomacy, establishing embassies and rivals for the near future.
As your corner of the galaxy becomes constrained, you start to realise that the key to winning isn't just expansion.  In-fact due to some very sensible and iconic diplomacy features of the Clausewitz engine, over-expansion will cause others to view you in a bad light (for the most part) founding the way for you to be surrounded by an alliance of people who hate you.
Trust me, this happened to me, and I couldn't even complain about it because I was a warmongering tyrant.
The rivals and embassies you set earlier in the game now bear fruition as threats lead to wars and wards make you consider your potential allies, and your rival's potential allies.  Now is the time to lay the foundations of the wars to come in 50 or 100 years time.
Towards the end of gameplay, I feel that you're pushed into two types of games (or perhaps, playstyles).  You're going to either want to try and conquer the galaxy, and sure you can do that by beating everyone into submission or colonising 40% of the colonisable planets.
To me, that seems very dull, if not boring when the entire galaxy forms a federation to resist your final push to victory.
I'd much rather role play my race's concept right from the start.  Playing my governmental type as I should.  The scientific event chains are futhrered either by your expanding treaties, or expanding borders.  Your research starts stacking up and you constantly nurture and oversee your relations to make sure that one distant ally doesn't drag you into a war that exposes your own border to enemies.
Does it lack features such as more in-depth diplomacy and espionage?  Yes.
Will the above be added later as expansions?  It's Paradox, so of course yes.
Is this the be all and end all of 4X games?  No.
Does it try to go somewhere no one has gone before?  Yes.
Does this game deliver on it's promises?  Yes.
If you still have your doubts about the game single-player, I suggest you find a group, join a voice chat and a game, and lament your failures and celebrate your successes together, for it's the multi-player that really makes this game shine.

Long races is where all the features of rF2 come to life. If you are here just for a 10 lap quickies, rF2 is not going to shine as much as on realistic race lenghs.
Combining the fact that rF2 is the most pure and raw hardcore experience available with the fact that Image Space Inc are not bunch of profit seeking leeches, rF2 is a nobrainer.

I got this game from one of those "vote for our game and get a free keys when it's greenlit" events and it has trading cards, so basically I'm paid to play this game and therefor gave it a try. However after playing, judging from a buyer's perspective, $5 is too much to ask for this game. Even at 75% off I'd still steer away.
Why? Because it's really bad. First of all the story doesn't exist and you suddenly got thrown into some crappy maps for no reason. Crappy because if it's an outdoor map, there will be so many holes on the ground that kill you more often than the enemies ( and every time you die you're forced to watch an un-skipable long scene of your character being banged by the enemies before being taken back to level selection menu. A quick restart button is not included ). If it's an indoor map it'll be a straight tunnel or similar, sometimes there are turns that serves no purpose because they're all dead ends without collectibles. Next up is the combat. For a game in which everything is made from cubes including the enemies, you'd expect to see features like crippling your enemies or tearing them block by block, but no. All enemies are solid, no cubes falling apart until they die. Also there's no different in damage dealt to different body parts including the head. Weapons are poorly designed, for example the shotgun's damage stays the same regardless of how far are you from your target ( there's damage spread so that's no slug rounds ).
Overall this is a badly designed game. Kudos for making the game bug-free with colorful environment but it doesn't help with the mood. I went through the 9 short levels of the game without getting any excitement. For anyone who's interested in buying, I suggest waiting for a huge discount or a bundle to get it, for collecting purpose only. There are far better games at $5. I should also think twice before participating in any "vote for free keys" events from now on.

I was overjoyed when I saw that Spike Chunsoft was porting over Danganronpa 2: Goodbye Despair so soon after their release of Danganronpa: Trigger Happy Havoc.  I obsessively played the first, totally enthralled by the intricate story, the fantastic writing, and the neon-edged psychopunk visuals... then nearly bought a Vita just so I could play the sequel.  I had to know what happened next!
Positives:
-  The writing.  Oh God, the writing is totally spot on.  Full of strangely translated Japanese-isms, chock full of memorable characters, and truly intricate mysteries, what else do you really need?
-  The art style is insane.  Anime/Manga stylings crossbred with 80s retrowave neon, topped off with a heady froth of island beauty.  Never has such an idyllic setting been host to such nefarious deeds.
-  Voice Acting.  Not all of the dialogue is spoken, but the stuff that is is brilliant.  Even the random punctuating exclamations are pretty funny in their own right.
-  Nekomaru.  Big muscle dude wearing his coach's whistle on a big♥♥♥♥♥chain around his neck, willing to give anyone deep tissue massages?  Pinch me.
-  The adult-oriented nature of it all.  Going from Phoenix Wright to this was like jumping in the deep end of a freezing swimming pool.  Here's to hoping there's more Nekomaru oriented fanservice.  }:D
Negatives:
-  If you minimize the game for any length of time, it freezes up.
-  No autosave, so you have to remember to make periodic save stops... lest a minimized freeze-up eats up 2 hours of gameplay.  (Speaking from personal experience, in both games.)
-  The next Danganronpa game isn't due out in the US for quite some time.  I may have to take up a hobby, like shuttlecock.

Minimum system requirements for Linux must be reassessed.
I exclusively run Linux systems and am sick of being sold games that are released as stable for Linux and are far from meeting any standard of even similarity to their counterparts on windows or console simply due to lack of care by the developers.
This particular game looked very good, with great reviews, so i decided to buy it. After the very long download i was quite excited to play! at which point i launched the game, turned graphics to the minimum, and proceeded. My hardware specs are higher than the minimum recommended, but not much higher.
It took EXTREMELY long to load a new game (5 MIN+). at which point the game play saw such a low frame rate and even major input lag.
At this point i considered i may be missing some kind of Linux dependency and started researching the problem. i followed all the help i could find online with no luck, and came across the real reason the game does not run in any acceptable capacity.
THIS GAMES LINUX PORT IS JUST THE WINDOWS VERSION THROWN ON TOP OF A COMPATIBILITY LAYER.
Thats not even the worst part, many games are very playable through WINE on Linux, this game is single threaded only. this means you only get to use one core of your processor.
As i do not recommend the use of windows, i cannot recommend this game. i hope the developers learn from this mistake and Witcher 3 will be real port with opengl and all.

A true marvel, I will go as far as to call this game an masterpiece and a real work of art. For a game that's made by a one man team it really is something great and is more than enough to put every AAA developer to shame.
Dust: An Elysian Tale is a game that has everything in spade, gameplay, humour, gripping story, great graphics, lovely aesthetic, you name it - it's got it. A fantastic port to the PC with a tight framerate and can run on just about any system. Works wonderfully on both keyboard and gamepad. It has tons of weird and wonderful enemies to battle and it will take you across many different places in the game world through it's enthralling story and insanely fun yet simple gameplay.
There's really nothing to complain about with this game, the only thing that will put people of with this game is the art style of anthropomorphic animals which will remind people of the "furry" culture but honestly you won't find anything like that here, it's very well-drawn and animated. I guess if I was to criticize the game in some way, I would say that normal difficulty is extremely easy, I never died once in my playthrough (Sure I struggled with certain areas but never died) and also there isn't enough combos in the melee combat BUT it does make up for it with the awesome Fidget spells and Dust Storm attacks that are immensely fun in mid-air when you can stay in mid-flight for about five minutes straight.
Overall, I would recommend this absolutely. The main campaign will take you around 8-9 hours and doing all the side missions and quests will take it up to 12-14 hours or perhaps even beyond that so there is a ton of content to be had here that's both quality and quantity and with plenty of funny moments with fourth wall breaking, retro game references and much more. And the price is just right, £12 or your regional equivalent is a damn good price for this wondrous game. What are you waiting for? Buy it you damn fools!!

Galactic Civilizations 3 is certainly a good game in its current stage; however, I don't feel like it's currently worth its hefty price tag.
If you're someone who strives to stay ahead in Technology, expect an uneventful start. I didn't get pulled into a war until ~400 turns in, which means I was just improving buildings for about two hours straight. Going to war early doesn't feel worth it since it costs so many credits to upgrade your ships to the latest version. AIs seem to have a static personality for now, which means every game they'll act exactly the same way (Krynn always seem to hate me no matter what). Unlike Civilization, where you can own a single city and still manage to win on even the hardest difficulty, expanion is a must here. But, to combat this, colonizing new planets does NOT affect your overall happiness as it does in Civ.
The combat system is just beautiful. Cinematic views of battles are amazing, and feel very rewarding if you're on the winning side. Likewise, the cinematics throughout the game feel polished and rewarding; whether it's colonizing your first planet or building your first starbase, the game makes it feel like an actual accomplishment.
If you have money to blow, get this game. If not, wait for a sale. Though the game is lacking a bit right now, as most 4X games do when they're new, I trust that it will continue to expand, and eventually justify its price tag.

Hero Academy is an amazing strategic multiplayer game. I played it for two years and truly enjoyed it thoroughly!!! (WOW, 179 hours!? I noticed only now!)
In a sense, it feels like chess, with fantasy characters and many many many more units. You choose one among the 6 available teams and are paired against a random opponent (or a friend) in a random arena. Your objective is to destroy all opponent's crystals or kill all of their units.
All teams are very different between each other and all units are useful in their own way (except you Windblade, you just suck). This opens up nearly endless strategies, depending on the units you get at start - the only RNG part of the game - the team you are facing, the map chosen, and so many other factors.
Since it's turn-based and you have to wait for your opponents to respond, it's perfect to play in short burst; I often played it on my phone during breaks at work and then on my PC when I got home. I usually had 10-20 games open, so I there was always at least one ready.
Pro:
- Cute character design
- Extremely tactical, with very little RNG
- Tons of replayability (I played it 179+ hours, no jokes)
- Great to play on your phone when you have only 5-10 minutes free
- Teams are unique and have very different units and strategies
- Teams are very very balanced
- You have all the time you want to
Cons:
- You typically can't play it for long sessions
- I'm not sure how many people still play this game. Still, I bet you can still find opponents!
- You get only two teams with the basic game, so you'll have to buy the rest. But they are worth it! (I think they are much cheaper on mobile shops, so better to buy them there)
- In high level games, you may have to resort to some basic math pretty often
- In high level games, "standstill" situations may happen, where the board is very balanced. They often take some time to break... like chess.
Hero Academy is easily the best turn-based strategy game I ever player, and one of the best games in my list overall! I wholeheartedly recommend it! 9/10

Stellaris is the game that keeps on giving. You want to be space Jesus and represent peace and prosperity throughout the galaxy? The devs have been releasing steady updates which improve on what is already an amazing game. I am a fan of Paradox's DLC; While none of it is required, it will enhance your gameplay by adding space dragons, megastructures, and more variety. My biggest thing is that you can choose from a few hundred planets to 1000 planets to explore, servey, colonize, scan, research, and mine. You can also choose how the galaxy is shaped. Alone with all of this, you can have up to 17 enemies and choose from over 30 alien life forms to conquor the known universe.
You can also choose from the pre-designed leader, or design your own and choose from a set of traits, skills, and even choose from pictures you would like your alien to look like, your planet to look like, even choose and design your own flag.
Combat is pretty straight forward, aim your ships to the target and the combat is automatic, although you can choose how you want your fleets to attack. This is also true for ground combat. The only downside is that you need to have a combat leader before you can setup a squad.
The only real issue you have to deal with (Although I like the idea) is that your leaders can age and grow old and finally die. This is something that is real and yet gives the game more additional strategy, so you can't just make a character and then hope for the best, you got to watch your characters as they progress through the game.
Overall a great strategy game where you have to watch everything and keep up with everything that is going on. Many really cool options to choose from and plenty of action going on even in the background.
