I played through Blood on Lightly Broiled, Episodes 1 t/m 4, which was the first official release.
I am aware that I might be the odd one out that actually writes a 'not recommended' here, while it seems to have a bit of a fanbase. I actually beat the original game, and I honestly think it's not recommended for the vast majority of the people.
Let's start positive. Yes, there is enough content for quite a few hours of gameplay.
There are a lot of diverse levels, so you wouldn't really get bored if you get into this game.
I also take note of some very well-designed levels, especially in Episode 3. E3M1 & E3M2 are taking place in some town that seems to be a battlefield, and big bombs are deforming the level into different states, opening lots of places during gameplay. The game also takes you to a hospital, a big sluice in which letting the water level actually gives you access to some places, and lots of other distinctive and cool places.
For a 2.5D Build Engine game, it looks quite good, and you can see the amount of work that has gone into animating the enemies, drawing the textures, etcetera. The voice acting is good, the horror is good, there are tons of references towards horror culture, the music is good (although the sound balance is quite a bit off), making good atmosphere. However, I would like to remind everyone that this game came out in 1997, a year later(!) than the full 3D polygonal Quake 1. So yes, it has the best graphics for a 2.5 sprite-based FPS, but the standards were already a lot higher back then.
So what is the problem, you might ask? Basically, the gameplay. The control scheme is horrible, and I had to download some mods (thanks pcgamingwiki) to fix a lot of the stuff I encountered. But that's not the only thing that was annoying.
Moral of the story: The balance in this game is just COMPLETELY GONE. The start of the first episode is idiotically hard because you don't get enough resources. Some levels, later on, are just waay too generous with ammo, which makes it idiotically easy to blast through. The enemies ok, but they have 0ms reaction time, which sometimes means that you will die within 2 seconds from 100hp just from some random (relatively weak) dude around the corner that had a few lucky shots.
Then, you have the flying enemies, the Gargoyles and the stone Gargoyles, which are so glitchy that you don't even take fighting them seriously anymore. Mother Spiders are just plain boring (and have way too much HP), and the second boss was stuck and easily killable without doing any damage.
Also the weapons are completely off. Although having two fire modes on each weapon is pretty unique and fun, they are so unbalanced that the use of some weapons just feels like cheating, while others just don't seem to work at all mostly. I'm ok with the game challenging me to figure out what weapon to use where, but man, just having to take minutes to fight a hellhound with a shotgun and literally taking 0.3 seconds to kill him with a tesla gun, that's just not fun anymore. It's also not like you have to take care of ammo management because once you have a tesla gun, ammo is everywhere. Also, the random traps are fun once or twice, but come on, do I really have to suffer so many random traps where it is impossible to react properly?
This game is so unbalanced that it simply restricts gameplay. Some guns make it too easy, and the enemies are too glitchy and random to have fun fighting, and instead encourage you to save before every corner because they sometimes randomly kill you and sometimes randomly leave you completely unharmed. The supplies are very randomly placed, and I feel like the developers have just designed levels without play-testing them at all. Although the game has good atmosphere, it was graphically and technically way behind.
So should you play this game? Only if you are both a dedicated old-school FPS-fan and a fan of the horror-genre. Generally, there is much better out there, but I have to give it a few kudos for its uniqueness.
TLDR: Probably the most detailed and animated 2.5D sprite-based FPS, good horror, cool references, good soundtrack, but the core gameplay is ill-balanced and makes the game frustrating and non-rewarding to play. Would not recommend unless you are a dedicated FPS-fan ánd horror fan.

One of my personal all time favourite games.
The gameplay:
Fast-paced, top-down mayhem that at first seems like mindless spraying and praying, but as you get deeper into the levels, you will find that strategy as well as quick thinking and reflexes are required.
The art direction:
If you are into the drug fueled aesthetic of the 70s and 80s, then you will find the art direction to be spot on, with just enough modern touches added (for example to the soundtrack) to make it relevant.
The story:
While the story does have its high points, for the most part it feels like a good excuse to transport the player from one slaughter to the next, without much of a deeper impact. On the other hand, the story does deal with some interesting psychological themes, which I won't spoil here.
All in all, I highly recommend the game if you are looking for fast-paced fun in an awesome setting.

After finishing the first witcher a few months ago, I was pleasantly surprised. A different RPG with an interesting if grim story , interesting characters and amazing universe that for once wasn't the usual default RPG universe you usually find in those games. The games had flaws to be sure but since it was the first in a serie, I was looking forward to the announced witcher 2 with excitement.
I didn't exactly disliked Witcher 2 , it's still a good game, but I don't think it a gift to the world of RPGs, if anything I preferred the first witcher. Let's be honest at first I was really impressed , but as I played some annoyances and flaws started to become more and more annoying. Yes the graphics are amazing , you can literally take screenshots of the scenes and use them as your desktop backgrounds, the sound and music is at least as good. great script and voicing. The game has a rich and detailed world  So what did I find wrong with the game?
Well I simply wished they had used more resources on the actual gameplay , which is a strange thing for me to say. Among my friends I am the  most vocal about a good storyline in a game with interesting characters. Witcher2 provides some of the most interesting storylines a game could give , in fact you can get several depending on how you play. Strangely this fact is annoying me to no end, while many appreciate that in Witcher 2.
Simply said Witcher 2 kind of feel like a rather disconnected set of cutscenes, great cutscenes with amazing dialogues and character development, but outside of those cutscenes, the game gives me little to feel connected to this world. I wander around in the detailed but rather small world hoping to not miss an opportunity for a sidequest. It's not that the gameplay is very bad, it could just be a lot better if they had put a little more effort into it.
The fighting is ok, but they departed from the mouse based fighting of the first game to something that feel very much like the fighting in Assassin Creed or dozens other console action games. If the fighting in the first game wasn't perfect , at least it was a bit out of the ordinary, but here Project Red decided to make sure it was console friendly, strangely they omitted the vibration function in the gamepad altogether. The use of potion which is a trademark of the witcher games have also been nerfed, now you can only drink your potion before a fight occurs. If some enemy attacks you and you haven't taken any , well it's too bad, cause you can't while you fight which I find rather ridiculous...I could go on, but let's just say that the fighting in Witcher 2 isn't really what I think a game of that stature deserve, it's not totally bad, it's just "meh!" and honnestly I prefered the fighting in Witcher 1.
There are also many other features in Witcher 2 that annoy me, the heavy use of "invisible walls" everywhere , the klunky (to say the least) savegame system , the button sequence events in many bossfights , the menu which is annoying for both PC and console users, the "same body, different heads" sex scenes... Those things could have been improved, but it seems to me they didn't prioritize that, betting people would be impressed enough by the amazing story and graphics to overlook the rather shaby gameplay.
Another thing that really annoyed me was the system of choice in the game, your decisions can affect the game in very real way. It sounds great on paper, but those choices are rather distinct paths you have to take during the gameplay. So if I take path A I will miss all the content in path B and vice versa. I'm aware that many people love this feature which enhance it replayibility greatly. But for me I rather play a whole game once and move on, rather than bits of it , and then replaying to see what I have been missing. Especially since the adventure in itself isn't that long to begin with, I feel that this "choose your path" system restrict the game more than anything.
I don't regret playing this game, I just think it could have been done better. I wish steam had a "meh" button between the "yes" and "no".

I am amazed by this game. I've only just finished the Prologue + Tutorial and stepping into Chapter 1 and I want to play more. There's so many interesting things about this game and it's just the beginning. I am taking note of Polish game developers because of Witcher. Getting it for $4.00 on sale was a super bargain for me, since this is the first time with the Witcher series for me.
Note: Game always crashed when I exit
1. Decisions
Everything you choose to do in the Witcher 2 affects how the game progresses. It's amazing. E.g. Sparing Baron Aryan La Valette gives you additional quests and story. If you don't spare him, no more interaction. Saving Newboy with the plate armour.
If you make a mistake, you can fail a quest very easily. E.g. Mavrick "Crapper"
2. Tutorial
Wow. They incorporated the tutorial into the game and it's a whole stage to decide your skill level in the game. Teaches you almost everything from alchemy, meditating, potions, swordfighting, traps, spells, using items, toxicity, etc. Much better than games that only teach you basic things such as the WASD keys and looking.
3. Combat
Simple to understand. Press E to block, parry or riposte. Left Click for quick slash, Right Click for heavy slash. Space to Dodge. Love it a lot. I would love using a bow as well, just like the archer who shot the pots. I think there's room for more impressive combat but I'm quite happy with easy-to-learn.
4. Story
It's so interesting and well-done. The way the developers put it into an action scene instead of a bland dialogue appeals to me so much. I want to watch and listen to what goes on. This is in sharp contrast to other games where 2 characters just stand opposite each other and talk. They even put in fan service in the beginning. E.g. Trish, the "royal advisor"
5. Medallion
Very good way to pick up loot and items. Could have made easily made everything you can interact with shiny but I guess it helps for secrets. Actually, I kind of enjoy how the herbs don't stand out and blend into the environment. Shows traps and doors too.
6. Cat Vision
So cool. I love the X-ray vision and the view of the enemies' veins.
7. Interactive Mini-games/Cut-scenes
Loved most of it. The punching game with the guards, outrunning a dragon, aiming a catapult with a spyglass. I did not enjoy the Left Click Fest events though.
8. Cinematics
Loved the assasination on the boat. So beautiful. I thought it was some old crusty scribe sitting next to the king, until he did his flame shield.
9. Paying Attention
There's a quest to collect the Dun Banner where a wraith will test your in-game knowledge. It helps knowing that paying attention to lore helps to answer the questions.
10. Questing
I love how the quests intertwine with one another. Not completing one side quest may affect another quest. E.g. Dice games to get a Troll Head.
11. AI
There are very few "lamp posts" (AI that just stand still and only function like a lamp post) in the game. Particularly noteworthy were the children of Flotsam. If you interact with the children, the children will chase you and say things like "Can girls become a witcher?". These things help to increase the immersion in the game.
12. Battle Arena
Very cool. You can even go to the lower floors to look at the pens where they keep the Nekkers and the Werewolf. You can even toss people off the combat arena onto the spikes at the base of the waterfall. This is an amazing arena and I hope they continue to work on it. They even provide background story for your NPCs, compared to some games where it's just Spearman No 5, Archer No 8.
1. Bugs
There's a stupid bug called a "Script Compilation Error" that occurs when I tried to start a New Game. It's a critical bug since you can't even start the game without solving it. Luckily, some kind soul on the forum solved it. Very upset with Project Red for not patching that and leaving it to the forums. You have to replace a file in the Witcher 2 folder by downloading a file from a web link.
2. Spells
I can't remember what Igni, Aard and so on do individually. I'm literally guessing and hoping to remember what they do by trial and error. Some tiny hints would go a long way. I can guess Igni is fire but the rest is "Number-X-does-what-again?"
3. AI
In the siege on the castle where you need to use the ballista, some of the AI just spawn in the corner and stand there. You actually have to look for them to continue the game.
In the prison, if you alert one guard, all of them magically teleport into existence. They don't run in.
4. "Corridorring"
You can't really move freely to explore. The area you are meant to be in, it's set for you.
5. Item Interaction
Very clunky. If a torch and a door are next to each other, you can easily mis-click on the door if you were aiming for the torch.
6. Backtracking
With a Teleport spell in the story, it's quite tedious to walk back and forth to hand in a quest.
7. Potions
It's very rare to use potions as you have to anticipate them before battles and there's toxicity. Toxicity is fine but not being able to use them in combat really takes away a lot of usage of potions.
8. New Game Plus
No new game plus. You are only able to port Witcher 1 saves to affect Witcher 2. This is most silly as the reward for replaying again should not be bogged down by the tediousness of repetition. While I wanted to play again, I was quite turned off by the idea of having to do everything from scratch again.
Please note: When I completed the game, I think I had only advanced a lot in the Swordman Advancement Path + Witcher Path. It is near impossible to get all the paths in one playthrough. The amount of grinding would be phenomenal.
Having a NGP would allow players to redo their options while being able to complete the alchemy potions, diagrams and skill tree. It would prevent the silly option of playing the same game twice.
I would want to complete the 2nd time round much faster, skipping some parts like rolling poker dice over and over again.
If story consistency is the issue e.g. Replay Witcher has a sword named Caerme, a super sword in the last chapter at Loc Muine, you can just force a resell of some "quest" items into gold / experience points, so players don't have to get a feeling of redoing everything from scratch.
1. Sneaking
I am unsure if it exists. You can't crouch or stick to walls and the lighting isn't exactly pitch black when you put the fires out. Sneaking happens during midnight but only for certain quests. E.g. Loredo's courtyard.
2. Archery
Throughout the game, I was expecting to use a range weapon since every NPC has a cross-bow.
3. Poker Dice
Easy to understand and easy to play. I think the game is rigged. The difficulty does scale up accordingly, with early Chapters losing pretty easily and later Chapters being able to win a Full House by re-rolling 4 dice. There is also very little poker involved as you can see the AI's hand and you do probability calculation.
You may want to include some more elements of skill. Lookup "Perudo" for a type of poker dice game that involves bluffing.
4. Battle Arena
No save games? I have to play all 30 levels at once? This is quite ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. I have to allocate a whole hour just to see if I can complete them. Really dumb.

Do I like Spintires? Be precisly sure of it. Do I recommend it? NO! Absolutely negative.

And the developer isn't really trying to do something about it. Instead, he is revamping textures (and breaking some things instead of adding new) for the last 2-3 years, and now selling a little update as the "new" game, Mudrunner. Which in reality is pretty much the same title, with all the same features as before... except maybe a free camera view. So, I downvote the Spintires and I'm not gonna buy the Mudrunner any time soon, since it's the same thing from the same greedy developer, who can't do something above his current level and prefer to create a drama behind the curtains instead of doing better coding or hiring some more coders... I like indie, unless it's mutating to something like you, Pavel.
I like Spintires, since some real off-road trips I've witnessed with my own eyes and buttocks. Yeah, especially buttocks. Here, I can do even more of the extremely stupid dirt-swimming with some KAMAZ or URAL, without the need to clean myself afterwards. And even my back is safe now. Fantastic as it is. It's looking not so bright at the first look, yes, but after some time behind the wheel you'll get the complexity of the environment. And especially the dirt. All kinds of it. From a technical standpoint, I feel like the launch was smoother than with the first game - Linux version available day one, and unlike the first release of DR1's Linux port I haven't had issues with fullscreen crashes, nor have I had to disable Steam integration to get sound working. Even on Intel HD5500 graphics (which, admittedly, are capable enough for MGSV and Tales of Zestiria at 720p/30fps on Windows) work without major hiccups at 1080p.
From a plot and gameplay standpoint, Danganronpa 2 is also an improvement, perhaps because it has such a solid base with the first game. The twists are satisfying even when the major ones are telegraphed practically from the start, and while it may not be enough to satisfy super-sleuths, many of the murder scenes have more depth than the first game's. If you weren't a fan of the rhythm-game stylings of the trials, you probably won't enjoy this a whole lot better, although some of the minigames have been improved upon.
The game's not flawless - by design or otherwise, Monomi is still one of the most annoying characters of the last half-decade, and the handbook's virtual pet system serves only as an annoyance - a necessary one to get 100% completion, unfortunately. Some of the new students are certainly less endearing or memorable than those of the first game, but there's never going to be a writer who nails every new character they create.
Overall it's certainly a good game and an improvement on the original in many ways, and if you're on the fence I'd recommend buying just to show support for Spike Chunsoft (and the larger Japanese gaming industry) bringing their games to an accessible platform overseas.

As an off-and-on fan of rogue-lites/likes, I am always torn determining the amount of skill and the amount of luck you will find in these games. Unseen probabilities within games are something I always am wary of complaining about when I could've had some really bad luck.
However, Crypt of the NecroDancer is a game where I blamed myself more so when I made errors than blame the odds against me. This is the first rogue-LIKE where I could tell I was improving myself, and it's the first one in the genre where the demands on the player's skill were mandatory.
Because with each failure through the familiarity of the controls and the coodrination of my fingers to the bass-line of the music I was reading the enemy telegraphed moves. Or adjusting myself to a new tempo-change. Or finding myself becoming at ease with the bizarre control-scheme. (Minus the DDR pad.)
The novelty of this game is that it takes the game of Rogue and gives it a beat. Literally.
The musical theme is not solely an aesthetic. The gameplay is interwoven into the music itself. From the way you move around/attack to the amount of time you have to explore the dungeons. Once the song ends, you are dropped to the next stage. (There are red-bars to show that the song is nearing its end.)
Every movement/action you make is managed by moving in-time of the music. You and every enemy move according to that rule, which gives the game a charming tactical feel while sometimes relying on you thinking on the fly. Enemies attack in a specific manner which usually results in them having an "off-beat" to strike them. If you simply attack head-on with no regard, you'll die a lot.
If that sounds too convulted about how the combat works, let me rephrase it like this: You are the metronome; the music is what you need to match (as the tempo can increase and decrease); and the enemies are the other instruments in play. The game plays more like reading a music sheet than another rogue-like game.
The controls are the first major obstacle to get over, which you can play this game legitimately with either a controller or keyboard (or a DDR pad, which has an easier difficulty just for itself). To get the best experience, I would suggest you map your directional keys separate from your combo keys. There are too many moments towards Zone 2 and onwards that rely on twichy relfexes in-time with the music to coordinate your fingers in combinations.
Thankfully, the game isn't too demanding on you maintaining a constant rhythm. If you're like me, I struggle to keep a rhythm going longer than a few seconds without going faster or slower than expected. The game is leniant on being perfect, but you cannot spam your movements. The game simply won't let you, and you won't be able to obtain the modifiers to your gold (and modified items) if you don't keep the beat.
I was able to get past the first zone on my KB alone, but the second stage's music tripped me up when I had to make those split-second motions to drop a bomb or use an item. Switching out the combos to other keys fixed it for me, and I would strongly suggest that if you play the game with a controller you get the directional pad some love.
Many rogue-lites rely too much on probabilites of which you can and cannot control (FTL). Others rely on attention to details of your item and the levels to spot those small benefits to get you to the end (Binding of Isaac). Crypt of the NecroDancer is a part of the trend where they provide permanent progression across chunks of the game.
(There is a story mode for purists who want to play a more traditional rogue-like experience. However, I chose the permanent item/stat increases as I am not the best at these type of games.)
There are stat increases and new loot to give your next playthrough something to change it up as well as possibly improving your odds. None of which are mandatory--I wouldn't think of going without them--if you are good enough at the game to read your enemies' movements.
Outside of the item/stat increases, you also have another means to improve your next game: Practice rooms.
You have a training room for enemies and minibosses that unlocks with a certain amount of kills for every enemy, a boss pratice room (unlocked via currency you accumulate in every run, diamonds), and a weapon-training selection screen to practice in either room. These rooms are unlocked by finding trapped tradders within Zone 1 and 2 and unlocking them with the Golden Master Key.
Having a story-mode option and a perma-progression system as choices is the best compromise as both the purists who prefer to learn the game on their own and everyone else has the means to finish the game. But it ain't so easy, nor free.
The bosses cost in-game currency to unlock. And you can't simply practice on all the enemies from the get-go--you have to kill each enemy type several times to unlock them. Simply, you can't cheat yourself out of a challenge without investing first.
(And if you don't like some items, you can discard them for diamonds with the Janitor).
Perhaps the game's own lacking feature is the infamous difficulty of its genre. The game doesn't feel that hard.
Make no mistake; the game is difficult for all the right reasons, and you will die a lot. But there are plenty of items to circumnavigate the game's difficulty, and some enemies that make me wonder how fair the game truly is.
For example, blood items let you regain your health, slowly, with enough kills chained together. There are also magic spells that might stun enemies, blast horrizontally, or give you some buffs to become overpowered in some situations. I would chalk these up to limitations of making a novel game without all its polish.
Some enemies also break the rules. There are some enemies that move in diagonal movements, which you are never allowed to do. The red-dragons also seem unfair without a "ranged" weapon (weapons that extend beyond one-tile, such as long-swords or broad-swords) to get around taking damage.
Zone 2 seems to have a sharp difficulty spike because you start off with nothing (even if you finish Zone 1). So expect that you may still have some bad runs when you begin new zones.
The only feature of this game I hadn't tried is adding your music into the game. This game's music was tailored for the game, and I am sure slow songs will break it while Megalovania will result in a very bad time.
This is one of few rogue-likes I'll always come back to because it's a fun experience. It's not a brutal old-schooling, nor is it coddling to the new players. The game's sense of challenge makes an otherwirse creative deviation into a worthwhile game of its own.
And how can you not have fun dancing on a plastic pad like an idiot?
(Kudos to the devs who put this through Early Access and finished the game. As well as for adding new content to the game itself with no DLCs. If they have another product through Early Access, be sure to give them a second glance.)

One of my personal all time favourite games.
The gameplay:
Fast-paced, top-down mayhem that at first seems like mindless spraying and praying, but as you get deeper into the levels, you will find that strategy as well as quick thinking and reflexes are required.
The art direction:
If you are into the drug fueled aesthetic of the 70s and 80s, then you will find the art direction to be spot on, with just enough modern touches added (for example to the soundtrack) to make it relevant.
The story:
While the story does have its high points, for the most part it feels like a good excuse to transport the player from one slaughter to the next, without much of a deeper impact. On the other hand, the story does deal with some interesting psychological themes, which I won't spoil here.
All in all, I highly recommend the game if you are looking for fast-paced fun in an awesome setting.

Dead Bits is an arcade FPS where you are apparently trying to gain your freedom by shooting things while walking backwards in between bouts of pointless platforming.
The intro level seems fine enough.  Here's a gun, shoot those guys, watch them explode in a mess of cubes.  Ok, this could be fun to mess around with.  That feeling quickly fades once you start going through the monotony of the following levels.  Enemies essentially consist of kamikaze monsters that run straight at you with reckless abandon.  They swing wildly and miss as you circle strafe around them, but the game throws a red puff on your screen indicating you've been hit anyway.  That leaves the strategy to walking backwards and killing the enemies as they filter toward you.  But wait just one second, because some levels make the ground behind you magically disappear causing you to back into your death.
And death is so much fun.  There are no checkpoints and every death kicks you back to the level select screen, because who doesn't want to reselect and reload the same level constantly?  Of course, if you like reselecting and reloading the same level you are going to love this...platforming!  Very few games do first person platforming well, and this is clearly not one of them.  One section has you jump from disorienting spinning cube to disorienting spinning cube.  Fun times.  There are also moving platforms that for some reason, even when you are standing on them, don't move you.  So you have to actually walk with the platform as it moves toward your destination.
The gunplay in this is also rather poor.  The weapons are bland and boring and pack no punch.  The smg sounds more like a typewriter than a firearm.  Occasionally a kill will trigger a slo-mo moment.  Unforunately, it's not the kind like Killing Floor that allows you to pull off a couple quick headshots, but the kind where everything just slows down around you for a couple seconds and then you carry on.  The melee weapon is a frustrating tool you are forced to use due in part to poor hit detection using it, and the aforementioned poor hit detection when enemies swipe at you.  Your best bet is to creep toward enemies slowly and stopping as soon as you pull one, since enemies only start their kamikaze attack once you reach a certain distance threshold.  But by creep I don't mean use the crouch button.  It's there and entirely pointless.
The concept of the game seems decent on the cover, but the execution leaves much to be desired and I wouldn't recommend it.  If you want to walk backwards and shoot things play Serious Sam.

This review is mainly just so the developers can see.
This game is great. I love the concept, the execution is good, despite being a bit slow-paced during certain songs, and it's got a nice difficulty, as well. It's fun to try to make it through a zone, and it's very satisfying to complete one. There were a few things that seemed like game breaking at first. As it turns out, they're not. With the exception of the Bard (who is extremely fun to play as), all characters that I've unlocked so far will drop to the next floor once the song is over. So no worries about being stuck.
If I happen to find anything that should probably be fixed, I'll post it here right away. For now, here are some tips:
1. The Crown of Teleportation is a potentially extremely useful item that will warp you to the shop (if one is available) upon being hit, but only once. If this item sends you to a shop that requires a bomb to access, and you don't have any bombs, no enemies can hit you anymore. This is great for all characters except for the Bard, due to the automatic drop to the next floor when a song ends.
2. The Boots of Leaping cause you to move two tiles per beat instead of one. This is rarely useful, but wait! There's more! Turns out you can toggle these! This turns a run-breaking, bad item into an amazing item that can potentially allow you to escape nearly any battle in just a few beats. I didn't know this until recently because I wasn't paying attention to the HUD. Note to self: Always check th e HUD.
Easy 9/10 for me.
Oh, and did I mention that the local co-op is amazing?
And the best part: THE DEVS ACTUALLY READ ALL OF THEIR REVIEWS AND COMMENTS!
Such precious few dev teams actually take the time to read their reviews and respond in turn, so it's really nice that Brace Yourself Games is willing to do so. I respect that.

To me, Dust: An Elysian Tail is a very weird game. It has art and characters that look like they belong in a reject Saturday morning cartoon or some Newgrounds browser game. However, it doesn't stop the game from looking somewhat pretty in motion, with all kinds of impressive weather and flashy particle effects. The story -- to start at least -- is about as cliché as it gets. Main character wakes up, suffering from amnesia. Doesn’t remember his name or the horrible things he’s done. He comes across characters in the world who know him, or who were at least affected by his actions, and he slowly regains his memories of the past. Yeah, ok. The subpar voice acting and writing doesn’t help things, either. It does have a few interesting twists and turns, but ultimately I feel like it didn’t go anywhere. The game’s saving grace is its gameplay, which of course is THE most important thing. The combat is satisfying and fast paced, giving me enough tools to dispose of enemies to keep me engaged throughout the game. Including massive elemental attacks that take up the entire screen, allowing me to wreak havoc upon any would be foes. However, the game still ended up feeling like a bit of a grind for me at times, as dungeons frequently dragged on and enemies continually respawned, forcing you to kill them before you can move on to the next area.
It’s a flawed gem, but still worthy of a recommendation. Especially if you’re big on action games.

Ooooh, I totally forgot to write a review on this one and now I'm obviously not right there anymore, but let me at least say a few words:
I actually got this game kiiiinda for free at first, played through it, bought it and played through it again twice (it's not very long) because I absolutely loved it!

I enjoyed every minute in this lovingly crafted place. The orchestral soundtrack fits perfectly and some scenes (although sometimes a tidbit corny) will give you goosebumps and an elevated feeling that very few games ever achieve to convey.
However, I'm sure not everyone will 'feel' this. Since I've always had a certain fascination for marine life I was especially susceptible to this :)
This game might have felt absolutely ♥♥♥♥♥♥ if they didn't get the animals right, but that's where you see the developers love for the theme most: The animations (for hundreds of different species!) are breathtakingly realistic and the swarm algorithm must stem from a genious' mind. [Just think about how ♥♥♥♥♥♥ fish (and birds) are animated in other games (so I'm guessing it's just very difficult and/or a ton of work)]. That shoal of Jack Fish and the last (very satisfying) part of the game made my jaw drop!
The background story seems to be much more complex than it seems... there's some interesting speculations to be found online about Babylonian gods and stuff, but in the end you don't really need all that. This game is really more about the abstract experience I'd say.
If you are not the kind of gamer that said about Dear Esther: "What's this?? This ain't no game! What's the point?" I would suggest you try this game; it's not very expensive after all and for me it became one of my personal favorites.

From a technical standpoint, I feel like the launch was smoother than with the first game - Linux version available day one, and unlike the first release of DR1's Linux port I haven't had issues with fullscreen crashes, nor have I had to disable Steam integration to get sound working. Even on Intel HD5500 graphics (which, admittedly, are capable enough for MGSV and Tales of Zestiria at 720p/30fps on Windows) work without major hiccups at 1080p.
From a plot and gameplay standpoint, Danganronpa 2 is also an improvement, perhaps because it has such a solid base with the first game. The twists are satisfying even when the major ones are telegraphed practically from the start, and while it may not be enough to satisfy super-sleuths, many of the murder scenes have more depth than the first game's. If you weren't a fan of the rhythm-game stylings of the trials, you probably won't enjoy this a whole lot better, although some of the minigames have been improved upon.
The game's not flawless - by design or otherwise, Monomi is still one of the most annoying characters of the last half-decade, and the handbook's virtual pet system serves only as an annoyance - a necessary one to get 100% completion, unfortunately. Some of the new students are certainly less endearing or memorable than those of the first game, but there's never going to be a writer who nails every new character they create.
Overall it's certainly a good game and an improvement on the original in many ways, and if you're on the fence I'd recommend buying just to show support for Spike Chunsoft (and the larger Japanese gaming industry) bringing their games to an accessible platform overseas.

This game is wonderful!  Firstly, creating your own custom race and empire is one of the best parts of the game.  You choose everything from what type of species you are, what sort of planet you came from, your ethics and government, visuals, and starting weapon systems (guns, missles, or lasers), and even method of FTL travel.
There are 3 options.  Standard warp, slow but non-restrictive, hyperspace, fast but dependent on naturally occuring hyperspace "lanes" or Wormhole gates, instant travel to or from a system within range of a warpgate. One of the more unique choices i've seen in a space 4x game.  The game even reacts quite well to your choices when it comes to your empire's ethics and government types.  Dialogue boxes will change to reflect your empires outlook on alien lifeforms and the cosmos in general.
You start off just after your first FTL capable ships are created and the whole galaxy is a mystery, your first task is scanning all the objects in your home system that until now your species as only gazed at through telescopes.  You'll find strange anomolies that spawn research projects and discover wonderous new worlds.  The early game perfectly captures the feeling of curiosity and exploration.  As you progress you may encounter primitive civilizations that you can subjagate or silently observe in the hopes of one day uplifting them.  You'll obviously also encounter other empires with which you must either befriend or make your foe.
The war system on this game is also quite unique, at the start of a war you declare what you want to get out of it.  If you are scary enough you might be able to get them to just give you a planet to avoid a war.  If a war does start the game keeps track of battles won and lost and give you a war score that will affect how much you can demand at the peace talks should you choose to negotiate an end to the hostilities.  The better your score the more likely you are to get a favorably lopsided peace deal.
Being that the game only released today i have not gotten much father than my first real war with another empire, which I won and I forced him to become my vassal.  But it is amazing how many options you have to deal with other empires.   You can create an embassy which will slowly make them like you over time or declare them a rival which makes them dislike you greatly but you gain influence points which you spend on things like frontier outposts to expand your borders or on Edicts (essentially passive bonuses to your empire that cost continual influence upkeep).
Graphically the game is gorgeous.  I often find myself just roaming my systems staring at the strange or beatiful worlds I encounter.
All in all if you are a Sci-fi fan, or a fan of 4x games your gonna wanna check this out.  If you like Sci-fi AND 4X games this game is a MUST HAVE.
If your new to the 4X genre the game might be a bit overwhelming as there can be a lot of micromanaging.  However the game has a great tutorial system that explains the game as you go without getting in the way too much.  Also there are a few ways to automate management on certain things if you hate micromanagement.
I'm not sure if I've played it enough to give it a X/10 number yet but I played it non-stop since release today and never felt bored or frustrated.  It has excellent pacing and is the most enjoyable 4x game i've played in a while.  It does a great job of making the galaxy feel vibrant and alive.  Honestly I can't recommend this game enough.  Buy it, Play it, you'll have a great time!

great game, played it 7 hours straight and still came only to the 6th floor.
the areas are huge and reward exploration with many different weapons, armors, shields, wands, bomb throwers, flamethrowers, crossbows ... you name it...most of it is in the game albeit still medieval / steampunk esque.
necropolis has also TONS of crafting elements, most of the recipees you have to find though which improves replayability and changes your runs sometimes quite drastically.
the combat is quite fluent yet needs some proper timing and learning the attack patterns of certain enemies which get mixed up during the runs. i have already found over 20 different kinds of enemies and still discovering new ones (like i said, i only came to floor 6th).
the game is described as a mix between dark souls and roguelikes, well this is true in the sense that the combat of this game works SIMILIAR to dark souls but it DOES NOT have the indepth character stats of dark souls. there is some dodging but this game is focused more on blocking due to the nature of the character being mostly one shield + weapon or weapon + sidearm (like crossbow or flamethrower). the combat is similiar yet different  to dark souls, but its fun enough that kept me till 5 am (time of w riting) in the morning playing. at the end i have to say though that necropolis is more a mix between dark souls (similiar combat s tyle), roguelikes (randomly generated levels and permadeath) as well as games like enter the gungeon where you have permanent unlocks and temp stat boosts.
you can unlock a bunch of codexes, around 20 which seemed all "tier0", i am not far enough in the game but this tier0 would indicate i think that you can unlock higher tiered ones. the codexes are somewhat mysterious in terms of their advantages and i can't wait for the wiki to fill up. these non-descriptive codex, potion and item description in general can be a bit off-putting but are one of the classic roguelike elements which reward experimentation.
take the codex "survival guide" (or something similiar), the description said something like "if you beat it, you can eat it"...now i thought that this means if i kill an enemy they will drop a ration or have at least a higher chance of dropping once. well i don't have observed this but what i have found out quite quickly is that i had 18 (!!!) recipees of potions in my crafting menue now. this low cost codex (4 token) gives you a ton of potion recipees, one of the strongest being a tier4 potion which lets you cheat death by automatically reviving you with 50% hp after you die. now in coop this means that if you die you won't be lying on the ground but reviving instantly. in singleplayer this will most certainly save your run! some other potions like enabling you to jump huge heights, being invisible, super fast running etc. give some nice tactical or just plain fun elements to the gameplay.
bottom line is that there is tons of stuff to explore and unlock, people who just play for 1-2 hours will most certainly not even scratch the surface of the game.
level 5 and onwards become increasingly harder but i still hope for an option from the devs (in a patch not dlc / expansion pack) to change some of the difficulties in the run like enemy hp, damage, spawnrate or attack speed (or simply just difficulty levels). this would increase the replayability once you have beaten the game and might provide some further entertainment until the first expansion pack arrives which i hope will be in the cards, game is pure fun!

The game feels very inspired by Phoenix Wright. Lots of comedic moments, and a handful of despair inducing ones. The gratuitous amount of "peptol bismol" blood, language, and setting give it a somewhat more mature feeling intended for an older young-adult audience.
You've got a murder happening, an investigation, and then a class trial. In the class trial, characters will discuss ideas like the murder weapon, setting, how it was done, etc. When a contradiction occurs, you fire evidence in the form of "truth bullets" and break them down in order to progress/unravel the story. One prominent feature added is the ability to consent, or agree with someone. Instead of firing truth bullets to break a contradiction, you can actually support someone's idea.
It's all very linear, keep that in mind. But it's set up very well that the entire trial feels tense and revelations feel rewarding. Game difficulty isn't terribly hard. There are three difficulties in game but they don't really impact the gameplay. Just like in Phoenix Wright, if you run out of "health", you start over from a checkpoint and resume the trial.

At the moment I just cleared the first trial, so I might slip-up and accidentally reveal some self-fulfilling spoilers but I'll try my best not to.
DR2 is a direct sequel to DR1 and while I highly recommend DR1 in its own right, the opening to DR2 spoils some bits of the end of DR1, and some of the more subtle character moments are going to be lost on you if have never played or seen anything of DR1; and I suspect playing this first is going to ruin part of the mystery of the first game, as DR2 is more self-aware of its crazier twists than DR1 was right out of the gate.
Hangman's Gambit. Bullet-Time Battles, and the Closing Argument have been partially to totally reworked from the original and I would say it is a bit disorienting so far to see all of the changes (but that may be because I'm playing on the hardest difficulty) but there is nothing I found to be so different that I didn't understand what was going on.
Hangman's Gambit and BTB (now called Panic Talk Attack, or PTA) are both significantly harder and are more proper challenges than the jokes they were in DR1.
tl;dr Play DR1 first. If you like it, you'll like this. If not, you won't.  I do NOT recommend playing this game first, but I do recommend this game.

One of my personal all time favourite games.
The gameplay:
Fast-paced, top-down mayhem that at first seems like mindless spraying and praying, but as you get deeper into the levels, you will find that strategy as well as quick thinking and reflexes are required.
The art direction:
If you are into the drug fueled aesthetic of the 70s and 80s, then you will find the art direction to be spot on, with just enough modern touches added (for example to the soundtrack) to make it relevant.
The story:
While the story does have its high points, for the most part it feels like a good excuse to transport the player from one slaughter to the next, without much of a deeper impact. On the other hand, the story does deal with some interesting psychological themes, which I won't spoil here.
All in all, I highly recommend the game if you are looking for fast-paced fun in an awesome setting.

A decent dungeon crawler.  The developer adds an element to turn-based combat which I've never seen in a dungeon crawler: the ability to change which characters are in the melee.  The usual dungeon crawler places the first two, three or four into melee range, with the rest safely in the back.  It's completely random in this game.  A random battle could start out with the first two characters in melee range, but it could also mean all six characters in melee range.  Each individual character can then take a turn to drop out of or enter melee, or the lead character can order everyone to back off or press forward.  There's also a Lv. 2 sorcery spell that backs all of the enemies off.  I think this is ingenious, adding more tactical options.  It works especially well when dealing with monsters that hit hard at close range.
Some have complained about the difficulty.  My first party was a failure after a few levels, but I started a second party and learned to beat the system by raising Endurance hard and fast with everyone (luck as well with gnomes) and making sure the RNG didn't shaft me too badly on the level-ups with luck-raising items and clover stew.  It makes the first several levels a slow grind, but then I could practically cruise through the rest of the game. I never once rested outside of an inn or messed with the bestiary.  The one time I got the crap beaten out of me was at the goblin hideout... but that was a dum-dum move on my part.  However, then I picked up
So my wishlist for the remake...
Keep the combat system as is.  It rocks.  Except...
Don't go all Might and Magic on us and cause the encounters to go crazy upon level-up.  Hated that so much about early M&M games... individual random fights taking an hour apiece on level stupid.
What about a hybrid sorceror class?   I didn't make a paladin, but would have likely made a warrior-mage hybrid instead of a second knight.
I liked the inclusion of a riddle...  but dumbasses like me wouldn't have been able to come up with the answer given even two more hints.  Funny thing is, by the time I surrendered and looked up the answer (which I could just barely piece together the logic of), my knights were dual-wielding greatswords and the thing was worthless. Ha.
More NPCs, possibly, and with more relevance?  I love NPC interaction in dungeon crawlers.
A couple more forms to the last boss would have given me a greater sense of satisfaction upon completion of the game.
A fan of Wizardry and M&M will get his money's worth.

While most visual novels intended for females hit you over the head with romance and pretty boys, this game actually takes this idea and almost puts it as a side note. Don't get me wrong, your relationships will be a major plot point however you also need to manage your friendship with your two roommates as well as the role you play in school. You might be treasurer and have to help plan events, or be part of a club designed to seek revenge on others.
Of course, your love interest still does play a point in the game. You can date either a male or female or even a Professor if you go down the right path. What makes this game great is how it developes the relationships. Your character is not swept off her feet instantly but the first cute face. Each relationship feels realistic and is built on many layers. You even get quite a bit of back story to each character you date (save for one bonus Steam added relationship which is a secret bonus one added to the Steam version of the game). But don't think you can't get dumped at any time by your SO. Pick the wrong options and it's back to the single life.
Of course since there's magic in the game and you're going to school, you do take exams where you use a few spells and common sense to solve the problems in a dungeon that is a screen by screen styled place (aka it's not a free roaming thing but you move from one screen to the next like a hidden object game without the hidden objects).
It's really nice to have your own PC (playable character) have internal conflict as well with her family so you get some character developement as well.
Overall, I've put over 10 hours into a graphic novel game and I read fast. There are so many paths to go down and things to do differently in each run through that the replay value is super high. It's a very interesting game which incorporates a lot of different aspects into one wonderful game.

Even though this game has some good characters and the gameplay is quite fun, the fact that it is so abusive towards women makes me unable to recommend it.
Good:
+ You get to chose how your character wants to respond in the story and it allows you to avoid certain situations.
+ Fastforward option that speeds through any previous dialog you have read.
+ There is some customization to your character, with name and appearence.
+ Ability to save and quit the game at any time.
+ Soundtrack is good, I enjoyed the tune that played when people were mischivious.
Bad:
~ Dungeon Exams ~
Every now and then, the girl you play gets an exam where she is put in the same generic looking dungeon and has to use her magic and smarts to find a way out of it. And there are so many problems with these exams that they are unenjoyable to play through.
- You have to have certain magical skills or you can't complete them. This is not told by the game or what skills you need.
- 98% of your spells are useless. This leads to the same problem I had with ”Cthulu saves the world”, where you have to constantly scroll through useless spells to find the ones you need. It also leads to a lot of frustration as the spells really give you no idea what to use instead.
- Your magical points are extremely limited. I failed one of the dungeons because I missclicked where I wanted to place an object. Ugh.
- Some dungeons I have quite frankly never been able to figure out what to do. They look too samey and there really isn't any indication of what they expect you to do. If you fail, the professor yells at you to study what the solution is. But you are never given the option to actually study it.
If it wasn't for these dungeons, I may have recommended the game, because the fastfoward option let's you play around with the story as much as you want. But instead you get stuck in these tedious dungeons.
~ Abusive relationships ~
I am not sure which age group this game is for, but this has a huge red warning flag about what message it sends to women and young girls. Any male-female romance you can persue in the game is always aimed towards ”If I love him enough, then I can change him and he will love me back.” and some of them are emotionally and psysically abusive. I see these kinds of stories a lot when the girl is forced into being ”saved” by the ”bad boy”, which should make her eternally grateful to him, while he continues abusing her until her love makes him ”kind”.
To give some examples of what kind of abuse the 16 year old girl has to take, some of them includes murder attempt (I am not kidding), being pushed and held against a wall, yelled at, blamed for things she didn't do, threatened, lied to, strung along, forced to give up her friends for him... the list goes on. 2 of the 3 possible male-female relationships are 90% abusive. What were they thinking?
One of these relationships you get forced into based on bizarre circumstances, where then the character literally owns you and will continously abuse you as he is unhappy with you.
There are also some girl-girl relationships, but the only reason I haven't tried them out is simply because I didn't find the female characters interesting. Maybe I will when I can force myself through the tedious dungeons again.

The amazing thing that separates PC gaming from console gaming is what I term the "gaming underground", indie developers who do it purely for the love or to create a game they would enjoy playing. Also, the ability to connect with developers of indie games is something that was never able to be done with consoles, it makes the player feel much more involved in the game world. Swords and Socery-Underworld is a perfect example of an "underground" role playing game. Big game studios do not make their money developing games highly inspired from antiquated RPG's of the past like "A Bard's Tale" and "Might and Magic IV". Some newer titles have done well such as the Grimrock series, but those will never ascend to the likes of what the big developers are doing. For those of us who still enjoy the old style of gaming, who don't care about flashy graphics and sound, and just wan't an atmospheric, immersive story and all the fantasy trademarks of yesteryear will do well to check out this game. It's refreshing to download a 256 mb game and be able to fire it up within seconds instead of waiting for hours for a download to finish. A lot of the gaming elements are familiar to aforementioned games in this review, but there is still a learning curve, even for us older games. I truly enjoy the map layout and how the world map is connected more like puzzle pieces, instead of just being able to see your entire map at once. You want to keep exploring the grid based world until every square is uncovered, in hopes you'll come across an elusive rare item or challening foe. I'm about 10 hours into the game and have uncovered the first four segments of the map. I have no idea how big the world is, and that's the beauty of it...to keep exploring and see where it leads next. I highly recommend this game, but only to people with patience and who can appreciate the old days of gaming through and through. This IS your dad's computer RPG!

Yeah. This is a game called Magical Diary.
Is there a diary in the game? Yes. Is there magic? Yes. Is the diary a Magical Diary? ...no, actually. I guess the author needed a title and Magical Diary was just as generic as they could get.
I mean, you can read the diary. Maybe it writes itself or something, but it doesn't do anything special aside from that, if it is the case. It just tells you what you already know. It's useful to see what happened if you haven't played the game in a while, for sure.
But yeah, despite the incredibly generic title, the also somewhat generic art style (you know, the type of art that middle-school girls and boys draw when they want to draw manga characters (actually, the settings aren't bad, just the character portraits, but there's like 10 settings in total...)) the story is actually pretty unique.
It doesn't really pander, it isn't light, there are routes that simply don't have a good end, no matter how hard you try, just because that's how they SHOULD be. It doesn't indulge a teenage girl's fantasy of going to a magical school (well, to some extent. It isn't a perfect world.)
You would expect "Magical Diary" to be some wet fantasy like Twilight, but it has its moments where little choices have a bigger impact.
Also, this isn't just a straight up visual novel. It IS a game, it DOES have puzzles, and while short, it can be a challenge.
You CAN lose. Heck, I survived, but I didn't feel like I had a "good" route, aside from being a fairly adept sorceress by the end.
Get this game. If you like visual novels, get this game. If you like those old interactive stories that you rarely see anymore, get this game.
If you don't wanna spend 15 bucks or whatever it costs in your country, wait for a sale. I doubt you'll be disappointed if you've liked a VN before.

Ooooh, I totally forgot to write a review on this one and now I'm obviously not right there anymore, but let me at least say a few words:
I actually got this game kiiiinda for free at first, played through it, bought it and played through it again twice (it's not very long) because I absolutely loved it!
Now, that's not even saying I would recommend this to everyone (although I would love to), and that's because if you look at it soberly there's not much of actual gameplay there. You dive through places, find some spots to interact with to get through to the next area, and... wow, that's actually pretty much it (apart from some optional collecting). I'm actually baffled about the lack of actual gameplay myself. So that's why I'm sure some people will be thinking "this is dull and pointless".
However, those people probably don't have a heart :)
I enjoyed every minute in this lovingly crafted place. The orchestral soundtrack fits perfectly and some scenes (although sometimes a tidbit corny) will give you goosebumps and an elevated feeling that very few games ever achieve to convey.
However, I'm sure not everyone will 'feel' this. Since I've always had a certain fascination for marine life I was especially susceptible to this :)
This game might have felt absolutely ♥♥♥♥♥♥ if they didn't get the animals right, but that's where you see the developers love for the theme most: The animations (for hundreds of different species!) are breathtakingly realistic and the swarm algorithm must stem from a genious' mind. [Just think about how ♥♥♥♥♥♥ fish (and birds) are animated in other games (so I'm guessing it's just very difficult and/or a ton of work)]. That shoal of Jack Fish and the last (very satisfying) part of the game made my jaw drop!
The background story seems to be much more complex than it seems... there's some interesting speculations to be found online about Babylonian gods and stuff, but in the end you don't really need all that. This game is really more about the abstract experience I'd say.
If you are not the kind of gamer that said about Dear Esther: "What's this?? This ain't no game! What's the point?" I would suggest you try this game; it's not very expensive after all and for me it became one of my personal favorites.

TLDR version: Really fun, lighthearted story/characters, great metroid-vania gameplay and combat, beautiful hand drawn graphics, 8-9 hours for a fair price. 8,5/10 - solid purchase
Graphics: the furry artstyle can bother some people but if you look past that you will see that the game is a gorgeous,hand drawn piece,everything is colorful and pleasing to the eye, character design is nice (enemies tend to be pretty dull though) but where the game shines graphically is the beautiful scenery with very detailed and well made stages with changes in weather and light effects, one interesting thing is that everytime you use the dust storm (the whirlwind move) plants,rocks,droplets of water and itens will fly towards you (besides the itens it has no effect on the gameplay but its pretty neat), the animation itself is really smooth and fluid and goes really well with the rest of the game.
Sound: the game has an incredible voice acting crew that brings the characters to life pretty well, the music and sound effects fill their roles nicely and are fun to hear during all the game (but you most likely wont get any tune stuck in your head afterwards).
Gameplay: pretty easy to pick up and play, like most games in this genre it has a light and strong attack (your dust storm) that can be combined to create combos both in the ground or mid-air, plus a projectile attack that can be used to extend them, you can also do quick dodges and parry enemies to leave them open, the combat itself can be really spammy sometimes but it doesnt take away any of the fun, the world and places to explore are diverse, interresting and overall a great example of the "metroid-vania" formula executed right, there is also a little bit of crafting and rpg elements that allows you to fit Dust more to your play style (but keep in mind that its a pretty simple system).
-but here is my main problem with this game, its way too easy, and i really mean it, the hardest difficulty is not a great challenge at all, Dust is pretty OP, mowing down a whole screen full of enemies in matter of seconds plus the ton of recovery itens that you recieve and revival stones means that you are not gonna die so soon (or at all).
characters and story: I wont go into detail here (and end up spoilling something by mistake) but the cast of characters can be described pretty accurately as very likable with a few funny moments here and there, storywise is a really simple one, which goes well with the light hearted nature and tone of the game but nothing exeptional.
Overall this game is pretty solid purchase for its price, that can keep you entertained for a good 8 - 9 hours, 10 - 11 if you are going for completion.

This is a game that knows exactly what it wants to be and delivers it in style. A straightforward, side-scrolling platformer with simple button-mashing combo-style hack n' slash combat, pretty graphics, and a relatively interesting storyline. It's got a very stereotypical anime-esque appearance, but there's beauty in the simplicity of the game. It's extremely well developed, easy to pick up and play, and nicely eyecatching. The animation is wonderfully smooth, with very subtle background effects, and a wide variety of environments to move through as you open up more of the wider map.
I tend to think of this game as being a bit simple, but it's a work of art and it's hard to believe that it was entirely the product of one person. It must have been a labour of love, and that effort shows through. Dust is an interesting character and, almost despite myself, I became engrossed in his story and the way in which it unfolded. I was expecting something very basic and repetitive as this is a 2D platformer I bought during the sale, mainly because I'm a sucker for pretty artwork in games. I didn't expect much beyond a couple of hours of simple gameplay and levelling up a few times before polishing off a boss and ending the game all in time for tea.
A week later, after running through the game twice (I upped the difficulty level the second time around) and earning all of the achievements, proved me totally wrong. At first I was skeptical; I found the characters to be a little bit twee and stereotypical, but as they and the story line developed I got hooked. It's suitable for all ages so don't expect any gore or adult themes, but there's a certain appeal in the innocence of the game; it's certainly not boring, and there are enough challenges and changes to keep you interested despite the fairly repetitive nature of platform gaming. It may appear cartoonish but there are some serious moral themes discussed and life lessons to be learnt. Picking up new abilities throughout the game gets you returning to previous maps to complete things you couldn't do earlier in the game, which nicely prevents it from being a linear run-through from one level to the next.
It's hard to criticise this game because it doesn't promise any more than it delivers. You don't feel short-changed by the simplicity of the game play or the slightly "cutesy" characters. It's easy to play through, which might be disappointing if you're looking for more of a challenge. It is fairly repetitive but the enemies do get tougher as the game develops, matching your character's development. The challenge arenas are the only places where you can really push your skills to try to get that elusive four-star rating.
The other downside is the boss fights - it's a button-masher so just keep hitting the combos for long enough and the boss goes down, it's as simple as that. But again, it's hard to criticise because the game delivers exactly what it promises. It's enjoyable but not astonishing. I recommend it as a pleasant and pretty game to play, a nice bit of simple escapism that isn't going to challenge or frustrate you.

<This review won't contain major spoilers but will talk about the concept which you might not want. Be careful if you want to go into this game completely blind.>
INTRO:
Danganronpa 2:Goodbye Despair is the first game but majorly improved and polished. I'm sure that much is obvious since it's a sequel. The game is about some highschool students attending this amazing school called Hope's Peak Academy. Only the best of the best can attend it and those who do go are called "Ultimates". 2 is about these Ultimates going on a trip to a lovely island called Jabberwock Island. But... then some bad stuff happens with some talking teddy bears.
The game features a great soundtrack and the visuals are quite nice too. It's practically a visual novel but with a lot of action in the way of "Class Trials". If you're a big anime fan then this game is also for you. It features jokes and cliches from manga/anime.
MUSIC: The soundtrack is really nice. It can make you feel tense, happy, excited, pumped and a bunch of other positive/negative emotions. I really enjoy the fact the music can instill the right emotions at the right times. Though... some of the tracks are memorable some just get left in the dust. The tracks are usually displayed at the top right with the name.
CHARACTERS:
The characters are all unique so you can't confuse them with each holding an ultimate talent and filling in some type of trope. Not all of them are likeable in my opinion but I didn't mind going through there conversations and jokes. There's a lot of humour in this game and no matter your sense of humour, you'll probably get a chuckle out of it at some point. Oh yeah, there's a mechanic called "Free Time". When the story isn't advancing you can spend time with the people on the island. This stregthens your bonds and results in some funny/pleasant/weird/deep conversations. You can also gift them a present to make the bond even stronger. You gain hope shards from doing this and then you can use those to buy skills. You gain a small little thing added to the person you interacted with's report card. Each person can have there report card filled in 6 times. After this interacting with them doesn't do much. If you're a completionist you can try to max everyone's report card. Thought this will take beating the game and doing Island mode OR doing multiple playthroughs of the regular game.
CRAP I CAN'T BE BOTHERED TO CATEGORIZE:
Danganronpa 2 revolves around hope and despair. You can feel these two emotions through out with other emotions mixed in too. I have yet to get bored of a mechanic BUT I can see some which may annoy/get boring. You can level up with a cap of 99. You gain xp by walking around, examining and talking to people. Walking around can be insanely slow so there's a sprint button but while sprinting you take less steps and therefore get less exp. There's a weird pet mechanic which is like a Tomogatchi and as you walk it grows. You can give it presents and it will gain hope or you can leave it and it'll gain despair. If it reaches max despair it dies. It has a little pop-up in the bottom left when you should really check-up on your pet. Island mode is unlocked after beating the game and is a little sim which allows you to date all the characters. It'll take at least.. 4 playthroughs to get every characters ending. Though I haven't beaten the game I have read about how Island mode exists and I'm guessing it's 2's version of School mode. It's probably improved. Not sure.
tl;dr:
Buy this game, it's great. :^)

Do you like Brigador? Would you like Brigador with more grind, crashes galor, no support, a paid DLC monster with abilities that crash the game? Congrats, here you go!
Concept wise, this game is cool. In fact I like it a bit more than other games by the company. The RPG aspects, while grindy are pretty neat. The monsters are diverse and each play's very differently. As you conquer cities, you start to feel like a serious threat, as you gain abilities that destroy whole city blocks, the kaiju defense force employs more and more desperate attempts to stop you, and you start to need to worry about defending your secret lair. However a few pretty major problems hold this game back.
Later on, even on good computer's the game has performance issues when attacking some of the bigger cities. These range from slowdowns, to even just outright crashing.
This game is also filled with bugs that never seem to get fixed. Some of the bugs are pretty major. The paid DLC monster is largely non-funtional as it's abilities cause the game to crash to desktop. These are issues that should have been noticed and fixed before launch. It shouldn't even be in the store in that state. There's also a bug where if you delete the first training facility you make after making the next tier of training facility, you literally can't train any skills or build a new training facility until you get rid of all tiers of training facilities you already built and then rebuild them sequentially. I reported that bug months before support for this game dropped, and it is still there, despite being a pretty major bug that can ruin a playthrough.
Finally, this is a pretty minor nitpick but the game just feels like it was intended to be a lot more. Some ingame text seems to indicate that the mad scientists are all trying to conquer the world at the same time, but you never run into any competition. The only opposition you face, is the city defense, and some easily crushed KDF patrols. This causes the game to get really repetitive fast. The game also has the same type of geoscape map as XCOM, but the only thing you ever deal with is moving your kaiju around. You never get another kaiju, or the ability to get a second evil lair. There is no KDF construction facilities or anything to find. It's just more of the same, and leaves the player feeling like some major feature was cut from the final product that was supposed to be in there.
Unforunately, a very similar game called Brigador is now out, which largely has the same gameplay as this, but with continuing support and no game breaking bugs. If the devs came back and fixed the crash issues, then I think this game could compete, but for now, it falls short.

Having read other reviews on here, I expected this to be buggy and crash a lot, but I don't think I experienced a single crash in all my time playing so far. (13.6 hrs at present - I just finished conquering the world for the first time.)
The only bug I came across in the whole time I was playing, was when upon returning to a city I had attempted to conquer before, it was showing the graphics for buildings which I'd previously destroyed, when they weren't actually there. (They can  rebuild them with time)  As a result, my monster was stomping around, shooting missiles at areas and such, and was doing no damage. It wasn't til I moved to a different side of the map that I realized what was happening.
Considering that's the only bug I've come across though, I'm fine with that.
Over all the game has been a great casual romp that I can play for 10 mins here and there, and the tech tree of skills for your monster is huge!
I'm not sure that I would recommend it at the price of $14, but if you can get it for $5 or less, don't hesitate! It's a very odd game, yet so strangely satisfying once you get the gist of what you're supposed to do :)
I was surprised to see that it supported 3840x2160 resolution too! A lot of these sort of games don't support resolutions that high unless you hack it in yourself via an ini file or something, so that was a real bonus for me too!
I finished it with Ginormasaurus, and I think I will actually go back and play it as the default plant creature now as well, partly just due to the fun, and partly to see what abilities await within its tech tree!

Not recommended, but let's be clear here: Kaiji-A-GoGo isn't a bad game. You could indeed have some fun with it, and if you got it in some sort of game bundle I'd encourage you to give it a crack. I did not play far enough to see all the game's content; the game holds promises of kaiju-on-kaiju fights and repelling of base invasions but I kept hitting a wall in my development before I could see them.
Let's back up for a moment. Kaiju-A-GoGo is a game where you are a cartoonish supervillain with a giant monster. You build a villainous hideout to upgrade your monster and go around terrorizing the world. Depending on your base upgrades there can be some strategy involved in conquering the world, but for the most part it all comes down to stompy-stompy-buildings-go-bye-bye. If you're using a controller, you do this by awkwardly moving into buildings whereupon your kaiju smashes them. The better way is to just click where you want to go and watching your adorable giant creature smash everything unfortunate enough to be between A and B without you needing to hold its hand. There are special abilities which can destroy a lot of buildings, or destroy things that would rather you didn't destroy buildings. Some of these are fun to use (Ginormasaurus' tail slap, Armagordon's rad ray). Most aren't (Ginorm's laser eyes, which have a tendancy to hit everything other than what you were aiming at; which is impressive considering it's just Armagordon's rad ray without the unit restrictions), but at least the attack abilities tend to be effective.
The game starts out easy and giant-monstery, with the first city you smash up barely able to put up any sort of fight. You go "awesome!" and go to enact King Kong in New York only to get stomped so flat the only thing you can do about it is roll a d20 to see how many bits of you are left to fit into a matchbox. Cities start out easy to conquer but as you figure out the city tier system and start climbing the ranks invasions quickly devolve into incomprehensible cluster♥♥♥♥s. The worst enemies are flamethrower soldiers, which are so small they can barely be seen and inflict lethal damage-over-time effects on you that can do hundreds of points of damage in seconds, with nothing you can do about it. This pretty much forces you to use Ginormasaurus, since it seems to have an unlisted immunity to fire.
And this is what lets the game down. By city tier 3 you spent most of your time
just in case they happen to be carrying the magic "♥♥♥♥ you, you're dead" flamethrower, waiting for your long-range attack specials to recharge so you can kill them from outside their range, all the while helicopters and fighter jets are pecking away at your non-replenishable HP. Depleting the morale of high-tier cities takes
and the longer you take the more odds are you will get hit by a flamethrower and the more absurdly-long-range missile launchers begin to spawn -- usually in whatever direction you happen to be running at the time.
Kaiju-A-GoGo does not make me feel like the all-powerful city-topping kaiju I wanted to play as. It makes me feel like the bully that all the little kids at the playground eventually realize they can gang up on, and then get the snot kicked out of them. And then one of the kids brings a mother♥♥♥♥ing flamethrower to the school playground, with predictable results.
The flamethrowers are a serious problem, have you gathered that yet?

There is way more than meets the eyes about this game.
While it IS a visual novel greatly inspired by the Japanese games of the same category, it is not "only" a dating sim. You can shape your own path, your own life. On my first playthrough I decided to let things unfold without really trying. I decided to trust my instincts and I thought the game was shallow, empty, predictive...
Oh how WRONG I was. I though for sure this game was "pretty little lady perfect love story" and I found myself in a pretty dire and serious situation. Just "being good girl" and "Acting with kindness and love" will actually kill you.
On my second playthough, I changed only one answer... and got a whole new story. As soon as you make a choice, including which classes to take or not to take, you unlock new possibilities... and lose some. In this game's world, a witch's word is taken literaly, seriously. If you ask something you will be forever bound by those words. I was unsure at first about this facet of the game. It was on my fourth playthrough that I finally realised the actual depth of the game.
Not only can we shape our story, but we can also change the way the game plays. We can change the way every character sees us. We can change the game's world to its very core. And that is something I love. If you think this game is Linear, you simply did not try the other answers. Just so you know, there is 4 ways to unlock the "Soul nibble" (5 if you count the rescue scene) and over a dozen to remove it completly from the game. You have many choice, use them wisely... or do like me and mess everything up just for the giggles.
Last word? I am the worst wife in existence.
