Ok, for some reason while I was writing everything got deleted with no way of retrieving it - it's been a day in which my internet connection goes off and on - and well, I'm gonna take a shorter view here so sorry if this review won't be long as usual!
Anyways, I was telling that this game belongs to a category that I've always kinda enjoyed on Flash websites, in which you have a catapult, an arrow, an arbalest or any kind of weapon with some aiming necessity and you have to 1. kill everything or throw down everything 2. save everyone.
This game falls in the second category; as the in-game story wants to tells us, you'll be presented with 45 levels filled with "football players strung-up by angry fans". They will all be hanging on a gallows pole at different spots and heights and, of course, you will have to cut the rope with your arrow.
So, why I am voting negatively this game?
Well, many reasons. The first one is the price: this doesn't even come for the lowest Steam price, 0,99€, but for 2€.. which is definitely too much, even if it has trading cards and achievements.
But the most important reasons regard the gameplay.
Apart from the childish music and the badly drawn graphics, over pre-rendered Paint background, here you'll only have one weapon and you aren't even a character - you're the weapon. You're a bow, always the same bow, positioned in some part of the screen.
And to add more frustration, there's only a "standard" arrow you can shoot. No poisonous balls, no multiple stones, no fire balls, nothing.. just a single arrow. Sure, on the upper left side you've got plenty of them above the score marker, but they're all the same!
I don't wanna to delve deep into the righteous descriptions that other players pointed out - that this game is a mobile rip-off and so on. I don't know if on mobile it's better to play - at least they say it's free.
What I know is that physics are completely crappy. You have to cut every rope and you'll often have little space, and by dragging the mouse you'll have to make a perfect curve and power in order not to hit (and kill after few shots) your hanging man. Plus, contrarily to the standard of these kind of games, you aren't even given the previous shot/trajectory your arrow took, so that you will start virtually from scratch every time and you won't remember how much power you gave to the arrow or how much curve.
The game itself anyways is easy, I'm not complaining about that, but it's not entertaining at all.
Only some minor things are added throughout the game, like arrows in the sky to hit in order to arrive at an upper location (and this is even easier since they will shoot automatically!) or windmills that block your shots, but really this lacks of almost everything these kind of archery games need - from a wide range of arrows/bullets/whatever to a serious, well-made aiming and shooting mechanism.
As I said, you can replay the levels as long as you want and they're pretty short so there's not a lot of frustration and difficulty overall but there isn't even the sense of playing a funny, different and entertaining game since you will get to the final levels basically in the same way you had faced the first ones.
I love these games, but this one is clearly one of them which had little to no work, reviewing and polishing at all and it seems to have been programmed in few days, given also the childish loop music and the graphics that stays almost the same for the whole game.
And this comes out in small details too: for example, you can notice that if you win with only one arrow left you'll see both the "out of arrows" screen and the victory screen, or other bugs in the hitboxes of the hanging targets.
If you're into these archery/aiming games, there's lots of Flash free ones everywhere on the Internet and really 2€ for this one are too much in my opinion.
Plus, if this game is really copied, ported without permission or freely present on the mobile market well, it's another reason not to buy it. Even if I can't check personally, here on Steam it's really not worth to be played.

I grew up playing these sorts of game, obsessively graphing every square on graph paper in Wizardry, Bard's Tale, Might & Magic.    Each of those games were finely honed to be exasperatingly difficult but achievable.
This game pits your party of 2-6 hp adventures against monsters who do 74 damage per hit in the tutorial room that you first appear in.   Party Creation to Party wipe in four mouse clicks courtesy of a single Vigilante and then back to the Party Creation screen.
In my opinion, the developer(s) have taken the idea of a critical path far, far too literally.   I was supposed to walk two squares forward instead of one forward and one to the right.   Note:  there's no prompting or visual cues that one of the seven doors you're presented with is the "right" way.   There are no clues even to what kind of building you are in to let you know that maybe some of the identical doors are instant death.    This is literally the first split second of the game after it's told you the controls.   You are in a room.   There are seven doors.   Here are the movement controls.   Oops you're dead.
Talk about worst foot forward!
EDIT: Read the comments for this review to see the developer responding to constructive criticism.   Also, please note that this review was for the initial launch version and not the version currently being offered.

Here are some old comments, slightly modified to make more sense here, that I made on the game in the previous engine when I first played it a few years ago. Overall, I would recommend the game if you like old school, grid based, movement type RPGs that were similar to the original Might & Magic games with good pacing, class and spell design, balanced with some challenging, but fair game play. OLD COMMENTS:
I had time to download and play the demo for a bit yesterday and was able to pick it up pretty quickly even without looking at the manual at all. It was familiar enough to the old classics that I was able to jump right in. There are a few mechanics and tactics I didn't try yet, but the basics of fighting, buying/selling, and equipping the party were pretty straightforward so far. It probably helped me a lot that I played the old classic Might & Magic 1 last year as much of the original interface was very similar. I must say that I liked the option to inspect an item and it would show you which class could use the item and damage stats, etc. Also, when I tried to equip a shield while already wielding a 2h weapon, it popped a yellow message up explaining to me that I already had a 2h weapon equipped. I wasn't expecting that level of feedback.
I got my party up to level 7 and unlocked the 4th tier of spells. At first I was a little bummed there would only be 5 tiers of spells, but all the spells are pretty useful even though there are only 4 priest and sorc spells per level. The total spell count may be lower, but the actual usefulness of them seems to be very high compared to similar games.
At first I didn't like the way water/holy water was handled and the sorc runes that you needed to loot to cast the more powerful spells. However, now that I have been playing a while, it just feels right and I can tell there was a lot of thought put into how it would affect game-play and strategy. It is a nice twist on a familiar mechanic.
I was concerned a few times whether I was progressing in the proper manner/order in game, but never ended up being frustrated. By just exploring each map systematically, I was stumbling into all relevant and important events (I think). A few times the monsters seemed to be a bit over-tuned, but then I would soon uncover an item or spell that made them a lot easier to deal with, so I would say personally the game flows very well and the difficulty is just right.
So far the game hasn't grown stale at all, which I am pleasantly surprised with. The pace that new enemies show up with new tactics and the pace that you grow in power through new items and/or spells seems to be just right. I am quite impressed you did this alone. Your efforts at polish in game-play show. Granted, this is ignoring some of the graphics and re-usable sound effects, etc, but concentrating on the core tactics and game-play, I am getting a good experience.
Now I am genuinely interested in finishing the game, or at least progressing further. If there are 15-20 areas/maps? I guess I am only about a third of the way through and easily have over 10 hours into it already I would say. The encounters are already getting pretty tough so I can only imagine what you have in store as I get into the end game.
END OF OLDER COMMENTS
I now recall that I never did finish the game to get to the end game content, but it was more due to my lack of focus and ability to stick with one game (any game) than this game specifically.  Perhaps I will give it another shot in this new engine/interface and make it a bit further!
Watch the available video clips and screenshots and if you can get by the interface and older style graphics, there is some very elegant old school RPG goodness in here.

Belladonna is a decent point-and-click adventure, and it's low price tag makes it easier to recommend.
The story is not exactly inspired, somewhat of a generic "Frankenstein's Monster" story, but it is passable. About halfway through the game you will likely have guessed the rest of the plot.
The game itself is only about 75-90 minutes long, depending on how fast you read and how much backtracking you have to do to grab items you didn't see the first time. Luckily, the game levels are not very large, so backtracking isn't much of a pain. The puzzles themselves are not too bad, I had an easier time with this game than some other point-and-click's where what you have to do next is very obscure.
The writing and voice acting are somewhat amateurish, though for the most part the journals you will read throughout the game were not too badly written. The main character's voice just sounded off to me, more like a young boy than a young woman's.
The graphics and aesthetics in the game are likely the best part of the game, and I thought everything was beautifully done. The only issue graphics-wise would be the walking animation. I didn't notice it too much until I was almost finished with the game, but the characters legs look strange when she walks, it does not work smoothly.
The biggest issue with the game would have to  be the ending. I knew that I was nearing the end, but instead of finishing the storyline, it basically was one last click and then I was brought to a big "game over" screen. The game was mostly wrapped up, but it needed a few more lines of dialogue and/or another cutscene to properly bring the game to an end. It was rather jarring.
Overall, for the asking price, especially if you can get it on sale, I would recommend this game if you are a point-and-click adventure fan.

I had been looking forward to this game for a while, and I was so disappointed in what I experienced. I can say two good things about the game, and if my refund request goes through, that will be three.
Pros:
1) Unique art direction
2) Good soundtrack.
Cons:
1) Poor keyboard control implementation. The game was clearly designed to be played with a console controller, and that's fine. But the inability to re-map the keyboard keyes is a poor design decision. The WASD keys are used for movement, and you have to curl your fiinger under to hit ctrl in order to dodge, a quite vital movement effect.
2) Enemies spawn in previously cleared and empty rooms. If you're running away from a huge mob of enemies that you can't quite take on because your health is low, good luck. You might run into some newly spawned enemies in the room you just cleared. Or they might walk up behind you while you're trying to kill the enemies in the new room.
3) Absolutely no information is given on the codexes beyond a 'humorous' title and 'funny' flavor text entry. Seeing as these codexes cost the sum of what could be hours of play time, you could waste all that time to purchase something that is completely useless. If you didn't know what the codex did before you bought it, that would be almost excusable, but there's no definite feedback on what it does even when you do own it.
I'd write more, but it's just a litany of poor design decisions and poor implementation. Maybe they'll fix it in the next few months with patches. Maybe they won't. I hope they do, honestly.
Edit: The game also detected my flight stick as an XBOX1 controller intermittently, so I had to physically unplug it in order to play the game. I really don't understand how that happened.

This game does a lot right. It's aesthetically interesting, the monster designs are pretty cool, it's got a great sense of humour, it's extremely well optimized, it's replayable to some extent, and it's fairly challenging.
But there's a bit of a problem. It takes four hours to beat after three unsuccessful runs. Others may take longer to beat it, but as a Souls game fan that didn't find the combat too terribly challenging until the ending boss, I feel a bit cheated. I had been very excited for this game, ready to easily dump fifty hours into it on my first week, but then the first day it's out I manage to beat it... That's just disappointing.
As I said, it randomly generates a new dungeon every run, it times your runs so there's a potential for speedrunning, and the roguelite elements make each consecutive run more interesting to the last with the Codex system. But I doubt that's going to give me the 50 hours of content I really wanted. Hell, it probably won't give half. I can't really recommend this game entirely because of the short run time. If you want to spend your money on this, if you really think you can get your money's worth from this game, then go for it. The four hours I spent on my successful run were definitely fun, and I can only imagine it becoming more fun with friends. But you have to go into it knowing that there's not too much to do in this game at the moment. Hopefully more will be added as time goes on, but for now, I'd say you should ask yourself if it's worth it.

By far, my favorite game of all time, as such this is a biased review, but I'll try to be as honest and forthcoming as possible.
Ultimately it is a game which has definitely stood the test of time. This is a result of it's deep and compelling story and characters above all else, each with their own deeply rooted story in the game's world.
Final Fantasy VII's general fighting, inventory and world-traveling mechanics are generic for a Final Fantasy game nowadays, however in the original release on the PlayStation in 1997, it was a dramatic and comendable jump from the previous games on Nintendo's cartridge consoles by adding to each feature with new and improved quality and graphics.
A stunningly visual world, the steampunk-esq setting consists of a huge variety of locals in a huge, fully explorable world with a multitude of towns and villiages. The central city Midgar is the first thing you see in the game and it's clear that Square wanted to stun the player in the first few seconds by changing to a more modern world, and stepping away from the previous game's medieval fantasy settings.
For so many reasons, this game was and still is groundbreaking, one of the best RPGs of all time, and one of the biggest tear-jerkers.
Play it for yourself.

Alright, after reading some of the reviews, I failed to find one that adaquetly represented my point of view. I think the Art, Music, Animations, Optimization, Textures and all that nonesense are polished. I have a decent PC, and it runs at 60 FPS with a few stutters when loading new areas, which is to be expected. Also, the in game video settings are maxed as far as I know.
In regards to gameplay, I would say like 8/10. The combat is very Dark Souls / Salt and Sanctuary -esk. There's a large penatly for getting hit, in other words the enemies do quite a bit of damage, but you CAN string together shield bashes, block, and dodges to go through the game without getting hit at all.
As far the charge attack goes, I think that the permenant stamina decrease is a perfect insentive to only use it when you decide that it's needed. Food gives you back plenty of stamina, and i personally found myself using whenever confronted with about 3 or more enemies. I really enjoyed the game, now here's my cons:
The game feels to me more than anything that it lacks the content of other rougelikes, such as binding of isaac, or risk of rain. I only encountered about 10 different weapons, granted I did only reach level 3. I found about 5 different shields. I did not find any armor ever. I like the potions are crafting mechanics, although I do wish things were a little less implied, and more stated. I can be difficult to decifier what exactly an item or potion does. Although that isn't necassarily unique to this game, it's more of a genre thing.

The level desgin seemed great, and I surprised that the 2nd time I reached level 3, it was completely different. That part of the random generation works excellently. Mostly I would just like to see slightly more enemy and item variation, and more implicit explanations of items and other related things.
I absolutely think it's worth it's $30 price point. If you can justify a completly online game like Overwatch for $60, then this game qualifies for half of that. It's a pretty unique experience.

I wanted so much to enjoy this game, because I love this golden age of video games, plus the setting and premise are peculiar and somewhat Lovecraftian.  However, several hours of playthrough (including hours prior to owning this Steam version), I cannot give this one a passing grade.  Weapons are monotonous and unwieldy, monsters are rock-stupid and unvaried, and map designs look and feel like rough drafts.  The maps, although bearing a lot of creative, new themes for the time, seemed to have been haphazardly rushed to production, are aesthetically very dull, and not very play-tested (during my few hours of play, e.g, I was repeatedly killed by auto-closing swinging doors and cabinetry).  Powerups are useless (reflective shots...?), and the different 'elemental' armors, even though they're provided, seem to serve no purpose whatsoever, at least during the first campaign.  And killer rats?  Not even monster rats, just regular rats... seriously...
There was an astonishing lack of attention to detail throughout this game, yet no opportunity was missed to insert cheesy movie references, demonstrating a lack of dev priorities.
This game is based on the Shadow Warrior engine, itself a modified Duke Nukem 3D 'Build' engine, both of which are vastly more playable -- attentively polished, funny, and thoughtfully-designed gameplay.  Try either of those over this.

It's a strange feeling to pay 57p for a game yet feel oddly cheated after completing it.
In short, my main issues were:
-Makes tons of literary references (to the point of becoming annoying), yet does nothing to build upon said works to present something new or different.
-One of the most interesting premises and moral issues of the game is brought up at the very end, yet rather than starting this game from this point (which could have set the stage for an even  darker but truly deep game that made use of its literary references) or at least continuing on for another chapter, one of the characters immediately dismisses the concern and leaves us with well-drawn, but uttering disappointing end screen.
-Voice acting does not fit the setting or characters at all. The actors really do give it their all, but the acting did not fit the gothic setting.
The game is very short, which isn't necessarily a bad thing as long as that's the amount of time the game needs to say and achieve what it wants to. Belladonna, though interesting enough to hang on through minimal puzzle-solving/ item finding, only begins to come alive (pun intended) at its very end, which is a shame.
Despite all of this, I truly hope the developers continue to make games,  Belladonna is not a bad game, in fact, if it was, then I simply would have dismissed it entirely and not bothered writing this review.
What makes Belladonna so frustrating is that is has so much potential- interesting subject matter, good artwork, ethical issues, etc- but doesn't fully execute on those elements and ends before it truly begins. I will, however, keep an eye out for future games from this company. They have the ideas, they just have to take that final step.

The Witcher 2 is, to me, a very nearly perfect game. There is more than enough here to keep someone occupied for hours and the replay value is immense. There are numerous endings, conversation outcomes and relationship developments that are all impacted by your actions throughout the game. The world of The Witcher achieves a very distinct reality through a complex story that is driven by a large cast of characters, multi-layered political intrigue/alliances and controversial social issues that do not come off as being too transparently modern (e.g. racism, drug abuse,♥♥♥♥♥♥ etc...) On the outside the game is stunning to behold, the world is vibrant and inviting and feels very real the moment you begin playing. While being graphically impressive, this is one area where The Witcher had some issues. Textures did pop and character models would shift awkwardly from time to time. In one instance I did experience a full-on crash to desktop, but this was early in the game and didn't happen again afterwards. Also, in a game where everything is so polished and full of substance the combat did at times feel lacking, though it was still fun. In many instances I found myself simply hitting spacebar to dodge while only having to decide whether to click the left mouse button or the right one. True enough there are some aspects of combat that exist outside of merely swinging your swords but I never felt that I needed to utilize those aspects to progress. Simply put, magic, traps and throwable items don't have the place I feel they should- you can win this game just by swinging your swords. The graphics and combat are my only two gripes with the game, and I would consider them very minor and personal complaints. The Witcher 2 is a game I would highly recommend to anyone who enjoys mature story-driven RPGs.

After playing Super meat boy, I started looking out for new games by the same developer. Edmund Mcmillen’s wonderfully strange imagination is an interesting thing to explore through his games, that’s for sure.
This game was not a disappointment. At first, I had no idea what to expect, the trailer was very strange but a tad intriguing. When I came across it there was next to no information about the game and the mechanics of it on the store page and back then there was no costumer reviews to go off of. Admittedly I never actually brought it to give it a go off of the information I was given, I ended up with it from a bundle and it’s the only reason I really played it. Although I wish I had taken the leap to try it because it is well worth it.
Binding of Isaac is a randomly generated dungeon crawler, one I have heard to be described as “Zelda-like” (I would have no idea about that, never played a Zelda game) you’re a young boy running from his demented mother. Who has been blinded by her hard-core Christianity and believes that the voice of god has spoken to her and told her to murder her son to prove her loyalty. So a very interesting concept, indeed.
A short cut scene plays on start-up, which expands on what I just described, you find yourself wandering through randomly generated dungeon floors, fighting monsters, picking up loot and items as you go along that changes how you fight, gives you different abilities and drastically changes Isaac’s image. At the end of each floor, you fight a boss, and move on down to the next floor. It being harder than before, with a bigger space to explore and more enemies to defeat.
There’s a large range of items to collect that when found for the first time is added to the “things I found” section in the main menu, so a lovely bit of collecting there to entice those OCD minded like myself, There’s new characters to unlock which vary in stats, challenges to complete and even some DLC that can extend your gameplay.
You are given one life and one life only. You can find hearts to heal, but once you are dead, that’s it, you start all over again. So throughout the whole game and especially when nearing the end, it starts to put a little pressure on and gets that heart rate going. I’m not one to be good under pressure so it gets me every time. I FINALLY managed to complete the game a few times over, again, admittedly, only after I gained some “top tips” from my way-to-good-at-games brother. There have been people that have completed the game 10 times over and still not gotten bored. I think that the randomly generated dungeon element to it keeps its replay ability intact. If it were to replay the same levels over and over when you died, the game would be a lot different and no doubt a lot less popular.
I have heard from friends that it is quite hard to complete without “doing your research” on the wiki or seeking tips from those nerdy minded like my brother who managed to figure all of it out themselves. I on the other hand find that kind of thing enjoyable, because it beats you every time and you work and research and try to understand the game more to finally get to that ending. I can quite honestly say that the first time I reached the end, my heart has never beaten that loud or that fast in a long time. And that sense of accomplishment you get from finishing a game, is a on a much higher scale when you work to complete this one.
The music is great, it fits the setting perfectly and is great to listen to. Rarely have I actually wanted to download a game’s soundtrack, I can give most soundtracks a thumbs up but not often do I actually want to listen to game music outside of gaming.
The art, as per usual in Edmunds games, is amazing. And I hear they are also looking to remake the game to have a more “retro” look, with possible multiplayer features. Which should be very interesting. For those interested you can look up “Binding of Isaac: Rebirth”.
All in all, it is a great indie game, which is both fun and challenging. Definitely worth trying, I am not usually the dungeon crawler type, but this game is a lot of fun. The only fault that I had with this game, which has bothered me quite a few times now, is that I have lost my save for no reason. The game is listed as having ‘Steam Cloud’ features, but it definitely doesn't work. I haven't uninstalled the game, I haven't touched it. But recently I hopped on and seen all the progress that I had made was gone. And for a game that has no real save points or ongoing plot to keep up with, your stats, unlocked characters and collection of things you have found is pretty much all you have. I was pretty upset to see it had vanished and it’s something I felt I needed to warn people about.
TL;DR : Awesome music, fun and engaging game with a slightly 'twisted' side to it. It's a challenge to reach the end and you can definitely end up putting a lot of hours into this. Addictive and awesome all around.

Magical Diary is a visual novel style strategy game akin to Long Live the Queen that is heavily inspired by Harry Potter fanfiction. You play as 'Mary Sue', a young wildseed (read: mudblood) witch who has entered a boarding school for magical folk to learn the craft.
My initial impression of Magical Diary is not favourable. On the upside the anime-style character is very customizable, some of the background artwork is nice, and there seem to be a number of different narrative paths that you may take through the game with hints at mysteries to uncover, making for good replay value. On the downside much of the character art is amateurish, and the game does little to hide its fanfiction roots. Because of this you wind up with a narrative that is chock-full of cliches, making the story very predictable. The strategic gameplay also feels overwhelmed at times by the sheer amount of narrative exposition there is to read. It took me almost 30 minutes to get through 2 weeks' worth of decisions, when it should have taken 5 minutes at most.
Bottom Line? This game will not appeal to everyone. If you enjoy reading Harry Potter fanfiction and love visual novel style games you may enjoy playing Magical Diary. Otherwise stay away.

I'll assume everyone has already played this game on PlayStation, so I won't be going into the game itself much besides the changes made to the PC version (I understand the game was also ported to Windows in 1997/8, but I never played it).
That aside, let's do a little rundown:
While no assets in the game were upgraded (besides the party's menu portraits), the increased resolution definitely adds clarity to most of the in-game models. Mouths are now rendered on the field models which were previously obscured in the PSX release. However, because the field backgrounds were not re-rendered, they look like a horrible mess no matter if point or bilinear filtering is selected (try sretching out a 320x240 pixel CG to 1920x1080 and observe the results). The most heinous mistake made in this version was the handling of the FMV sequences. Ripping and transcoding the PSX videos to a PC compatible format is bad enough, but then SquareEnix had the
idea of "upscaling" the movies to 720p. Interpolating low quality footage is a dirty industry (and amateur) trick to create something out of nothing -- all it did in this case was make the sequences more muddy and pad the download size.
This release originally shipped with a bunch of .OGG files rendered from out-of-house MIDI sequences. They used the default software synthesizer to render these and they sounded terrible. Most noteworthy, the live chorus from
was missing; in its place was a lousy clap track. The game was updated recently to include the proper PSX quality music using the original sound library. As for the sound effects, a few of them are off-key, but nothing too terrible.
Aside from the nitpicks I have above, some improvements include much faster loading times: and by fast, I mean virtually none. The roaming profiles (cloud saves) are a nice touch for those who play the game on multiple machines. The new "character booster" is nearly useless as VII is already very easy.
While some may call
the defining title of the entire RPG genre, or even gaming in general, I have to disagree. The sixth game (a.k.a. 3 or III in North America) on Super NES and eight/VIII (also available on Steam) are leaps and bounds ahead of VII in terms of gameplay, plot, character development, etc. I also recommend playing
and
(also on Super NES) before having a crack at this if you haven't played it before.

The Danganronpa series is the Phoenix Wright series on steroids. And it's one of the best experiences that I've had in the past 10 years. Danganronpa 2 received the highest score of games I've formally reviewed on the Youtube channel: and that's for good reason: it's fantastic from all sides of the spectrum. A good murder mystery needs to have a couple of basic elements to be successful, and Danganronpa 2 knocks each of them out of the park. An interesting set of characters with great backstories that make you connect with them almost immediately: which makes the pain of possibly losing/being betrayed by them that much better. The game does misdirection better then any other murder mystery out there, in particular with those who played the first game. This game knows how to get into your head, and knows how to play off what you may be thinking to twist it around on you. The game hooks you and doesn't let you go, and any minor problems I had with the game were knocked out by its sheer strengths of writing and drama.
If you're looking for traditional gameplay, Danganronpa isn't that, but it's able to keep you interested with drama. If you haven't played the first, I'd recommend playing that first. It's great. Then play Danganronpa 2. Not only would you be glad that you did, but you'll remember the experience for a long, long time.

Excitedly picked this up to jump in with friends, I'm reluctantly giving this a negative review, hopefully more is added to the game but currently the Tomb is just too shallow to warrant crazy amounts of playtime. I feel as though my one playthrough left me and my group wanting more where there seems to be none.
The game has hack-and-slash style combat that, while for many who seek Dark Souls inspired combat will seem clunky, is easily mastered. Hitboxes are tight to the characters and weapons, which makes swordplay very fun and large enemies interesting to face. Difference in weapons seems to be weight, attack type and speed, and effect type. Coupled with gear and shield, this makes for semi-versatile loadoats based on speed or tankiness.
However, my group only encountered a single ranged skillshot weapon (which took the second shield slot) which was nigh impossible to aim without lock-on and quickly became useless.  All weapon charge attacks are AOE, and certain pickups (like shields, staves, and certain Pyramid gear) don't have the effects or attacks they do when wielded by enemies. Resistance to damage types seems to be irrelevant in the face of constant blocking, which negates all damage.
Spoilers ahead as it discusses progression in the game, TL;DR is the game is extremely short even if painstakingly combed through. Heed the game's warnings about the amulet's triviality.
In short, the game is fun. It has promise. The base mechanics are here and quite solid. But it doesn't have enough to keep me playing. I got the upgrades I wanted on my first playthough. Playing again, even solo, felt extremely easy. The breadth of enemies and level design wasn't nearly what I expected. Minor bugs prevented smaller parts of the experience, but the largest blocker was the ending. Just when it feels like the difficulty is about to ramp up, it doesn't. Ok, let me put it plainly. This isnt looking like a complete game. The whole game can be played under less than a couple hours with no speeding WHATSOEVER. It really is made with little content at all!
I would have wanted to start with the pro's, rather than con's, but...there are very little pro's to it:
- the concept: it is sort of interesting, sadly it remained what it was, a concept;
- SOME, and i mean SOME of the visuals are truly keeping up with the graphic style entirely;
- voice acting: Klara is rather nicely acted, a nice voice to listen to actually;
CON'S
- game content and inherently its length: are you kidding me??? The game is made out of maybe not even 10 rooms! And some of them are only used as passage from an area to the other, while other contains just a note and nothing else!
- story: the plot is almost entirely unfold through handwritten notes over and over AND over again. If that wasnt enough, they're just an image and therefore the font can't even scale up to proportion, and stays awfully small.
- puzzles: all of the puzzles are just a joke. They take seriously no time at all to figure out, and often you're even told plainly what to do. They're not even puzzles!
- some drawings: i chuckled as i saw Doctor's Wolf body. It has so many issues...and Belladonna isnt truly well drawn either.
- animations: oh my freaking god. Klara literally fluctuates and has no interaction whatsoever with the surroundings.
- overall lack of polish and care: room transitions carrying the description "exit" or "to the next room", truly short soundtrack looping over and over, lack of basic interaction.
- the ABRUPT ending. There's not even a cinematic at the end. Just a colorful screen with an "END" sign so you get it, at least....
In conclusion: this game was either not completely taken care of or maybe it was completed in a rush. As the story stands, it's pretty much uncompleted and feels more of a demo rather than a complete game.

The Witcher 2 is, to me, a very nearly perfect game. There is more than enough here to keep someone occupied for hours and the replay value is immense. There are numerous endings, conversation outcomes and relationship developments that are all impacted by your actions throughout the game. The world of The Witcher achieves a very distinct reality through a complex story that is driven by a large cast of characters, multi-layered political intrigue/alliances and controversial social issues that do not come off as being too transparently modern (e.g. racism, drug abuse,♥♥♥♥♥♥ etc...) On the outside the game is stunning to behold, the world is vibrant and inviting and feels very real the moment you begin playing. While being graphically impressive, this is one area where The Witcher had some issues. Textures did pop and character models would shift awkwardly from time to time. In one instance I did experience a full-on crash to desktop, but this was early in the game and didn't happen again afterwards. Also, in a game where everything is so polished and full of substance the combat did at times feel lacking, though it was still fun. In many instances I found myself simply hitting spacebar to dodge while only having to decide whether to click the left mouse button or the right one. True enough there are some aspects of combat that exist outside of merely swinging your swords but I never felt that I needed to utilize those aspects to progress. Simply put, magic, traps and throwable items don't have the place I feel they should- you can win this game just by swinging your swords. The graphics and combat are my only two gripes with the game, and I would consider them very minor and personal complaints. The Witcher 2 is a game I would highly recommend to anyone who enjoys mature story-driven RPGs.

Mixing the themes of Mary Shelley’s Frankenstein with a grotesque tale of love, Belladonna is an adventure game for those who like their stories a bit weird, even if it lasts barely an hour.
Belladonna is a name of conflicts: an Italian phrase that means ‘beautiful woman’, but also the name given to a somewhat bland-looking flower – a very poisonous flower. This game, named after both, carries that strange duality: it is beautiful, but it is a game about death.
Death and reanimation, death and unlife, death and what could be considered unnatural even by the less religious people too. In short, Belladonna is a game that starts with a re-enactment of Mary Shelley’s ‘Frankenstein; or, the Modern Prometheus’– or, more precisely, the underlying theme of brining the dead back to life.
After this ghoulish start, the game follows the steps of the newly-resurrected girl who slowly discovers the reasons and events that led to her current state: a story about a marriage gone sour and a man getting obsessed with his work about creating life. A story which also has a few small twists in it, even if most are telegraphed in very obvious ways long before their big reveal.
Although this game is a point ‘n’ click adventure in theory, in practise few things will ever stand in the player’s way to discover the story it wants to tell. Only a handful of objects are used and most of the time the game tells how to accomplish the required objective, so the roughly one-hour game time– the only obviously sore spot about Belladonna– is spent by fully immersing ourselves in this weird, somewhat bittersweet, and maybe mildly disturbing tale.

After playing Super meat boy, I started looking out for new games by the same developer. Edmund Mcmillen’s wonderfully strange imagination is an interesting thing to explore through his games, that’s for sure.
This game was not a disappointment. At first, I had no idea what to expect, the trailer was very strange but a tad intriguing. When I came across it there was next to no information about the game and the mechanics of it on the store page and back then there was no costumer reviews to go off of. Admittedly I never actually brought it to give it a go off of the information I was given, I ended up with it from a bundle and it’s the only reason I really played it. Although I wish I had taken the leap to try it because it is well worth it.
Binding of Isaac is a randomly generated dungeon crawler, one I have heard to be described as “Zelda-like” (I would have no idea about that, never played a Zelda game) you’re a young boy running from his demented mother. Who has been blinded by her hard-core Christianity and believes that the voice of god has spoken to her and told her to murder her son to prove her loyalty. So a very interesting concept, indeed.
A short cut scene plays on start-up, which expands on what I just described, you find yourself wandering through randomly generated dungeon floors, fighting monsters, picking up loot and items as you go along that changes how you fight, gives you different abilities and drastically changes Isaac’s image. At the end of each floor, you fight a boss, and move on down to the next floor. It being harder than before, with a bigger space to explore and more enemies to defeat.
There’s a large range of items to collect that when found for the first time is added to the “things I found” section in the main menu, so a lovely bit of collecting there to entice those OCD minded like myself, There’s new characters to unlock which vary in stats, challenges to complete and even some DLC that can extend your gameplay.
You are given one life and one life only. You can find hearts to heal, but once you are dead, that’s it, you start all over again. So throughout the whole game and especially when nearing the end, it starts to put a little pressure on and gets that heart rate going. I’m not one to be good under pressure so it gets me every time. I FINALLY managed to complete the game a few times over, again, admittedly, only after I gained some “top tips” from my way-to-good-at-games brother. There have been people that have completed the game 10 times over and still not gotten bored. I think that the randomly generated dungeon element to it keeps its replay ability intact. If it were to replay the same levels over and over when you died, the game would be a lot different and no doubt a lot less popular.
I have heard from friends that it is quite hard to complete without “doing your research” on the wiki or seeking tips from those nerdy minded like my brother who managed to figure all of it out themselves. I on the other hand find that kind of thing enjoyable, because it beats you every time and you work and research and try to understand the game more to finally get to that ending. I can quite honestly say that the first time I reached the end, my heart has never beaten that loud or that fast in a long time. And that sense of accomplishment you get from finishing a game, is a on a much higher scale when you work to complete this one.
The music is great, it fits the setting perfectly and is great to listen to. Rarely have I actually wanted to download a game’s soundtrack, I can give most soundtracks a thumbs up but not often do I actually want to listen to game music outside of gaming.
The art, as per usual in Edmunds games, is amazing. And I hear they are also looking to remake the game to have a more “retro” look, with possible multiplayer features. Which should be very interesting. For those interested you can look up “Binding of Isaac: Rebirth”.
All in all, it is a great indie game, which is both fun and challenging. Definitely worth trying, I am not usually the dungeon crawler type, but this game is a lot of fun. The only fault that I had with this game, which has bothered me quite a few times now, is that I have lost my save for no reason. The game is listed as having ‘Steam Cloud’ features, but it definitely doesn't work. I haven't uninstalled the game, I haven't touched it. But recently I hopped on and seen all the progress that I had made was gone. And for a game that has no real save points or ongoing plot to keep up with, your stats, unlocked characters and collection of things you have found is pretty much all you have. I was pretty upset to see it had vanished and it’s something I felt I needed to warn people about.
TL;DR : Awesome music, fun and engaging game with a slightly 'twisted' side to it. It's a challenge to reach the end and you can definitely end up putting a lot of hours into this. Addictive and awesome all around.

So far, very interesting. Fans of GC2 should enjoy GC3; much of the gameplay is similar.
The good:
Shipbuilding is MUCH easer now that you can offset parts, so you never have to worry about attachment points being in the wrong spot. Adjacency bonuses make planet upgrade placement much more interesting. The ideology system is a lot more intricate (and useful) than GC2's. The tech tree has a less annoyingly-long succession of weapons and defenses; you no longer have to go through seven different iterations of phasors to get the next weapon. Trade goods can now be traded on a non-permanent basis, and you can sometimes find multiple instances of the same trade good for additional bonuses. Custom races have a vast array of configuration options, far exceeding GC2's. In the combat viewer, projectiles no longer fly absurdly slowly. The game is just as easy to mod as GC2; the .xml's are editable in notepad.
The mediocre:
Upgrading starbases is just as tedious as it was in GC2, but at least you can put multiple starbase construction modules on one ship. Combat is now fast-paced, and defenses deplete as they are shot at, so don't expect a ship with 15 shields and one weapon to slowly cut down an enemy fleet full of lasers. The combat is improved over GC2's, but it still is not very interactive; you cannot give orders to your ships in the combat window. After combat, ships still repair absurdly slowly.
The bad:
The game seems slightly unfinished. The tech tree has a few spelling errors, as do a few of the mouseover-tooltips. Weapon balance is questionable, but technically tolerable. The combat viewer sometimes calculates damage and HP inaccurately; in a few extreme cases, it is possible for you to lose a fight in the combat viewer, but your ship will still be alive and the enemy will be destroyed on the map. The game is also fairly unclear in regard to the mathematical workings of interceptors, interceptor drones, assault fighters, and guardian drones. When making a custom race, you are limited to just a few dozen preset color combinations for your ships.

Not even 15 minutes before I started writing this did I beat the game a second time, finish with 100%, and earn all but one achievement.  Despite the fact that this says I love this game, I will acknowledge that it isn't perfect.  Let's get started, shall we?
First things first, for those of you who are uneasy about the furry tag this game has, I can personally assure you that the characters in here are safe for all ages.  The worst you'll notice is some language, yet even this is used rather lightly –almost not at all.
The way the story is executed leaves me little to say in here without giving spoilers.  You play as Dust who has woken up in glade with no memory of who he is.  A talking sword called The Blade of Ahrah as well as the sword's little guardian, Fidget, accompany him on his journey of self-discovery.  Because of this kind of story, there is a lot of dialogue to go through.  Whether you can enjoy that or not I cannot determine.  Personally, I loved it.  All of the characters had personality, and it was well brought out with the voice actors hired.  The only exception to this, and this depends on your own perspective, would be Fidget.  Her squeaky voice and quirky personality will either be a hit or miss.  On a separated note, the only technical flaw was that the voice actors didn't use the same equipment.
So, on to the gameplay.  The majority of your attacks will be with the use of your sword.  Even though Fidget provides some ranged combat, it will end up feeling like a brawler.  The controls are very responsive.  The actually difficulty of this game may feel a bit low, and this is something I had to find out for myself during my second playthrough.  A wide variety of items are dropped by slayed enemies, some more common than others, but all have their uses for crafting augments (for Ahrah), armor, pendants, and rings –of which the last you can wear two.  These items can enhance, or in a few cases weaken, your attack, defense, luck (chance of a critical hit), and Fidget's power.  Overall, very solid.
The artistic side of this game is probably what can put this game above many others.  The artwork in here is stunning to say the least.  You might find yourself staring at anything and everything in this game.  It has all been hand-drawn by the one and only member of developer Humble Hearts, Dean Dodrill.  The soundtrack is likewise stellar.  Most tracks were created by the Northern Ireland duo Hyperduck Soundworks with a few others done by Funky Rustic, a.k.a. Alex Brandon.  The only times I felt the soundtrack was lacking was during the majority of boss fights, though even this is more so of my expectations.  I still listen to this game's soundtrack very often when I'm doing my weekly chores.  Challenging for me to find something I enjoy as much as this.
Thanks for reading.  If you have any questions/comments/critiques on this “review” of mine, feel free to share.  I will appreciate it.

It's nice for those reasons. It's nice for a lot of reasons, but it seems like the target audience is what will most likely get this game unfair negative attention (in addition to the really cheap-looking production values, even by visual novel standards).
Something this game does very well is CHOICE: The schedule of events and how differently the game can go based on what you do on certain days is mind-boggling. Dust is a game that shows it is made by a veteran gamer, and both it's gameplay and it's writing reflect that.  Those who are familiar with the action RPG style of Castlevania should recognize some of the familiar exploration mechanics.  However, Dust is wise enough not to alienate new players either, and it's intelligent writing helps create moments that train new players while having enough life and humor to avoid being obnoxious for experienced players.
Presentation is easily where Dust shines brightest, and it's gorgeous cartoon art and animation are wonderfully realized.  Despite drawing upon a number of story tropes to establish it's setting, it always keeps itself interesting with it's stunning visual style and it's often wonderfully-delivered dialogue.  It's not perfect, and there are moments when characters are unnecessarily verbose.  These lines seem well-intended, attempting to instill a sense of reality and hint at the greater history of the game world, but can still feel like they linger on a bit too long.
The fighting action in this game has a very fluid feel, as every action responds immediately to input.  At times, this can make the game feel rather easy, but the satisfaction of pulling off large combos easily makes up for it.
Dust may not be the most perfectly realized game, but it does so many things superbly that it shouldn't be missed.

A quick paced, fast-thinking strategic board game, Hero Academy can be a bit of a mixed bag due to poor marketing/DLC practices, but because of its unique nature and cheap price, it's still a diamond in the rough.
Deep strategy and competitive leaderboards are available, but it's also very accessible to casual players. It's very solid and concise on the whole.
* Options to Start games with your Steam friends, Twitter Friends/Followers and more are very useful and notifications of your game progress work well
* Great looking assets and themes, though marketing these as DLC is going too far
* Good Tutorial
There's a real problem with the time it can take to play a match, since the fast pace is sometimes half of the fun in Hero Academy. It plays like chess via traditional mail, in that you can wait hours or even days for your opponent to return a move (there's even an achievement to take 24 hours+ to take a turn), which isn't in itself a bad thing because it helps keep it casual enough that you can have 10+ games open at the same time and not have to worry about committing to each, but it would've been so simple to add options to set time-limits and game-closing options to enforce quicker games, which many people want from a game like this.
The DLC offers extra teams with avatars, and some include items for TF2 and while the extra content is fairly good, it's still a jarring way to use DLC for most people, especially when it affects people who are not willing to buy the DLC negatively, essentially creating a pay-to-win feel, albeit not entirely in your face.
* Selling cosmetics and styling as DLC is fine, but selling teams which affect global gameplay leaves a sour taste for most
* No options to play only faster paced games
* Annoying Robot Entertainment DRM
Priced at between £5.59/7.99€/$7.99 and £12.99/16.99€/$16.99 at the time of review. The nature of this game makes it one of the most replayable games around, and you'll likely continually find yourself coming back to old games.
However, it's also available on iOS, and feels a lot more casual on there due to the more immediate nature of PC gamers. It's also much cheaper on mobile and so is probably the better option for many.
The DLC offers extra teams with avatars, and some include items for TF2. While the extra content is fairly good and adds a lot if you know your playstyle, it's still a jarring way to use DLC for most people, especially when it affects people who are not willing to buy the DLC negatively, essentially creating a pay-to-win feel.
You will probably never use some of the Teams, so if you've never played before, buy the base game only and find out which paid teams you like, if any.

After a few initial teething problems, I am starting to enjoy the game. Said problems involved:
- missing OST (fixed by Devs in recent patch)
- choppy performance (it's still not great. Getting 50 fps. ON A GTX 1070. But it's better and the slowdowns are gone)
- inconsistent controls on Shield Controller (switched to kb+m)
There's a lot to like about the game. The art style is beautiful, if a little repetitive. I love the aesthetic, but it would have been nice to see more variation in the environments and set-pieces. The game has a sense of humor. It's not always a *good* sense of humor, but sometimes it made me chuckle. I guess if you throw enough things at the wall, some things will stick.
On to the downsides. Combat can be a little boring, once you've gotten the hang of it (and before you get the hang of it, it's simply frustrating). The enemy types are quite limited. The dungeon design is quite repetitive. The game is purportedly short, although I haven't come close to finishing it as of this review.
The developers have fixed a few things that were broken at release (pre-order customer here) in recent patches, but there is still room for improvement. More varied enemy types, more interesting level designs, and basic niceties like remapping keys would be appreciated. But most of all, the game needs a price reduction. $30 is simply too much to ask for the content at hand. At that price, it should really be a 4-pack, since the game really calls to be played with some friends.
This has gone from a 'Do Not Buy' rating from me at release to a 'Tentative' in its current state (7/16/2016). If the game is improved and its value prospects similarly increased, it would earn a recommendation from me.

Blood is without a doubt a timeless classic, and one of the best and most challenging FPS games of all time, but sadly hasn't had the support it deserves, with this Steam version being a good example of this, just being a stock standard DosBox upload.
You take on the role of Caleb, a great shot, fast runner and strong swimmer. He's also the now ex leader of an evil cult known as the Cabal. After the dark god (who you worshiped) Tchernabog kills all of your friends, and you, you awaken from your grave seeking revenge. Revenge that can only be paid in blood! Caleb is the definition of an anti hero. He's a bad guy only out for revenge, not to save anyone.
If you've ever Shadowed some Warriors, Duked some Nukems or Doomed some twos you'll know what to expect. This is a product of it's time, so expect to get lost in vast sprawling levels, collecting keys, finding secrets and gettinggunned down by surprise monster closets. The locations you'll visit are some of the most varied you'll find in an FPS game, with detailed textures, sprites and interactive items, many being unique to each level. The locations feel believable in a strange way. You've never been to any place like them, but you just know places like it exist. Most of the levels are heavily inspired by of era horror movies, and the tone often aligned with Evil Dead. You'll visit abandoned towns, train stations, carnivals, cathedrals, hotels, forrests, it really would take too long to list them all. Each level feels more or less connected, with you starting off where the previous level left off, adding to the continuous feel of your journey.
This game is hard, and I mean get out hard. If you think you're an FPS expert, play Blood on well done, then we'll talk. Quicksaving is your best friend here, the levels are long, and if you don't know what you're doing you'll die, a lot. Is the challenge legitimate? Yes. If you know how to manage your resources and know how the enemies behave, you can get through this game start to finish on Lightly Broiled, which I STRONGLY suggest for a first playthrough. Once that's down, you have Well Done, and boy am I thankfull for that setting. It's like the middle ground between normal and get out hard, like right in the middle of Doom's Ultra Violence and Nightmare. If it weren't for Well Done, the game would be much less fun casually for multiple playthroughs.
Blood packs some of the best weapons I've ever had the pleasure of using in an FPS game, and that's saying something. From tommy guns, to vodoo dolls all the way up to a napalm launcher, this game has weapons you won't forget. Each weapon serves a purpose, and that's killing whatever abomination in your way. The enemy roster in this game gives Doom two a run for its money. The sprite work is absolutely phenomenal, and breaths life into each enemy you face, not to mention the fantastic voice work by Stephan Weyte, who gives Caleb a real presence with his likeable attitude and off colour humer. The music is also a treat, with a full 13 track midi soundtrack. Each song fits each level accordingly, with chants, wispers and catchy tunes midi tunes.
TLDR, the game is fast, fun, challenging, great to look at and listen to, and oozing with creativity. You should buy it, it's FIVE DOLLARS which is highway robbery, even when it's not on a sale. Just a little bit of set up will be needed to get the game running properly, and if you need any help with that just comment and i'll try to lead you in the right direction. Truely a timeless classic.

Kaiju-A-GoGo is a game of staying above the difficulty curve. Controlling a handful of different evil scientists, all with unique giant monsters, the bulk of the game is raiding, and eventually control cities around the world, for their resources. However, as your kaiju causes terror, the global military will respond in kind, beefing up their city's defences and attacking your secret lair back with the hopes of toppling it. When this happens: game over.
As mentioned, keeping your Kaiju strong enough to weather the storm is a game of upkeep. Training your monster will give it a better advantage, necissary for much strong cities like Tokyo and Paris. The rest of your time will be spent in your secret base. Gathering supplies and constructing the right buildings in the right order will be learned through trial and error. This can be tedious, and frustrating at times. As each new month brings an upkeep value, you will find yourself in the red, certain buildings that generate power, or food for your kaiju will turn off, and everything will quickly spiral out of control. On top of that, your when your kaiju is slightly behind the curve, attacking cities can be a struggle. This has turned a lot of people off.
If it doesn't, and like me, you're a massive fan of giant monsters having grown up on Godzilla, then the style will outweigh the substance and you'll feel like a towering GOD wrecking havoc on those poor suckers around the world. Bonus points: attacking cities you know the streets of intimately (Sydney and Vancouver represent). I was giddy razing famous buildings I've been inside of.

'Blood' is absolutely one of my all-time favorite games.
While it is essentially a 'Doom' clone, 'Blood' carries it's own twisted charms in that the story makes little to no sense (unless you know your Horror films/fiction) and because of the sheer volume and variety in it's content. Yes. I see you all rolling your eyes and telling me that it is mostly running around shooting anything that moves, and that is true. However, there truly is SO much to love about this game.
Lacking the misogyny of 'Duke Nukem 3D' and the veiled racial stereotyping of 'Shadow Warrior', 'Blood' instead plays firmly up to it's cliched B-Movie roots. Players find themselves thrust into a Lovecraftian dystopia, choc-full of homicidal cultists, ghouls and mimes (yes, I said
They're annoying...at least in this game) as the game's maniacal undead protagonist Caleb sates his veracious lust for revenge against those who've wronged him. Another great aspect of 'Blood' is the choice of weapons on offer which range from the relatively mundane to the downright cruel. Personal favorites include Caleb's starting weapon - a rather nasty pitch fork that he most likely brought back with him from Hell - and a voodoo poppet capable of reducing even the most resilient foe to dust.
If there are any down sides to 'Blood' it's that while the game has some considerable length to it, it is recommended that the game not be played in a single sitting. The game's soundtrack is suitably apt for the subject matter but 6+ hours of listening to foreboding synths and children chanting pseudo-Satanic mantras does tend to prove detrimental to one's overall mood - and I've been a Metalhead for 17 years so I'm used to this sort of thing. Also worth noting is that like it's biggest inspiration, Sam Raimi's 'The Evil Dead', 'Blood' is NOT child friendly. Like many games from the irreverent 1990s, developer Monolith designed 'Blood' as a game for adults and as such the young-uns need to be kept clear of this title. You wouldn't let your kids play 'Doom' or 'Carmageddon' would you? Well, the same goes for this game as well.
In summary, if you're a conservative you'll hate 'Blood'. If you're a fan of revisionist post-modern Horror gaming, you'll love it.

This game is similar to Overwatch in some ways, but that's fine.
Some things that are different and I like:
-It's F2P. You can just jump right in. And best of all, it's not really pay to win. Maybe look up some balance guides considering the ability cards (see below), but otherwise considering that you can just get those card with in-game currency that is easy to earn, it's no problem.
-Interesting Capture mode. Most of the maps take place in symetrical arenas that consist of a path from each spawn to a central capture point. Capping the central capture point summons a payload that you must then guide into the enemy's spawn. Capping/delivering the payload/defending your spawn from a payload each give you a score-point, you need 4 score-points to win. HOWEVER, if you have 3 score-points you HAVE to capture the central caputre point to get the last score-point, defending your spawn can only lead to up to 3 points. This leads to INTENSE situations where each team has a score of 3 leading to an intense final battle in the middle of the map.
-Longer time to kill. It takes longer to kill enemies which is a bit nicer for newer players PLUS it forces you to prioritize healers and focus on specific enemies with your team.
-MOBA-style counter-picking and item buying. At the start of a competitive game you take turns picking heros. IMPORTANT because once you choose a hero at the start of each game, you're locked into that hero for the rest of the game. And because some heros directly counter others, you have to consider your team composition. During the game you also gain credits which you spend on items that can be used to FURTHER counter the enemy team, like making your shots reduce the amount of healing targets get, give your shots armor penetration to better kill tank characters, etc. This adds depth which I appreciate.
-Faster play-style. I don't know if it's just me, but Overwatch has some issues where it takes a LONG time to run to the objective. In Paladins, you spawn on a horse! This ensures you get to where you need to go quickly so that you're spending more time shooting stuff.
-Supports/Healers are more fun to play. If there is one thing I hear as a gripe against some games, it's that playing as the support/healer is boring. Be it Medic in TF2 or Mercy in Overwatch, you're not doing a lot of shooting in those first-person shooting games. In PALADINS though, healing is often done passively or very actively. Ex. Ying is a healer that summons clones who stand in one spot and heal around them, Pip's heal is a grenade that he throws at his teammates, Grover's heal is basically a first aid kit that he deploys instantly healer anyone standing around him PLUS he passively heals people near him. What this means is that by playing as any of these healing characters you are helping your team stay alive while also doing more than passively standing near them, you get to shoot stuff, too! PLUS all supports are viable as main healers. It's not like Overwatch/TF2 where you NEED an Anna/Mercy/Medic, as long as you have ANY support, you stand a good chance at winning.
-More hero customization. In Overwatch you pretty much have an entire hero's kit from the get-go. HERE, you can augment that kit using various ability cards that can modify hero abilities in various ways. Again, more complexity.
-Ultimates don't always decide games. In Overwatch I think the Ultimate Abilities are much more powerful. This game has a bigger neutral where, granted, Ults help, but they don't mow people down in insane numbers as they would in Overwatch. This is great when playing less co-ordinated pub matches. PLUS, you save your Ultimate between rounds! So you have to ask yourself, "Should I pop my ult NOW or save it for the next round?
-More diverse looking characters. In addition to normal-looking human and elf characters, Paladins has a giant turtle, a non-humanoid fairy, a dragon, a small furry Ewok (basically), an ent, a goblin in a robot suit, a dwarf, a stone lady, an orc, and I sh-t you not, THE KING OF BOMBS (a living bomb-man who is the literal fuedal lord of explosives!). This means you get to shoot at a lot more different stuff, which I appreciate.
tldr, Paladins is a game like Overwatch in that it is a character-based shooter, but I think it is a bit more complex when you really get into it.

It might be the game I will be playing a lot in a couple of years. It's not there yet.  You might want to read the reviews on the expansion to understand the current state of the game, bellow is my impression some months after release.
[Review from the game's 3rd major update]
The game is far from what it should have been. I've backed the game in the alpha stage, but after reading into what they were planning to do, have avoided playing it too much prior to its release as I didn't wanted to spoil my experience after that point. Now, in perspective, I should have waited even more for the game to be completed... but here we are.
As with the previous Gal Civ, I've spent most of my time playing this game in the designer mode. In this new iteration, the designer is even better, if you can believe it. If you like Sci-Fi, you'll really like designing your own space faring armada. And with the changes they've made, ships will look more smooth and you'll have more options in terms of angles and shapes. With mods, this can only get better in time. If the developer adds more artefacts, it would really be awesome.
However, this great feature isn't, yet, backed up by a balanced and immersive game. There are tons of little misgivings that ruin immersion and I won't go into details to avoid spoilers. Game balance is a big issue though. For me the experience started on the wrong foot, the map didn't spawned the resources required once I've changed the defaults of a new game. Think how it feels finding this out 50h into a savegame. Once you learn how to workaround all these issues and spend several hours to epxand, you'll run into the AI issues. In my case, the AI was passive in many playthroughs. I was the only player on the map with fighting capable ships for 1/3 of the duration of the playthrough in some of my games. I've tried changing my playstyle to see if anything changes. Nope. The AI does an aggressive job at some of the Xs out of the 4x. Exploration and expansion are performed gregariously by the AI, they don't know how to exterminate once they reach another player's borders, human or AI. Also, it's not clear to me how does the AI have the resources to spawn as many ships as it does (it might have been fixed with the latest patches, but it's really hard to playtest this, players don't have enough time for it and it should be counted as a negative for the developers for letting this slip by to begin with).
Improvements from the previous Gal Civ 2, like the hex pattern and adjancency bonuses, are nice and all, but they add too little to the gameplay to compensate. They're great ideas, but it's not enough and considering that the game feels poorly balanced, they don't really compensate for the shortcomings.
Other nitpicks. The UI looks nice, but it's not well thought through. Elements that are required are barely visible, while non-functional elements take most of the screen (in the designer or shipyard for example).
Diplomacy is rather childish and the text options are repetitive. Game length is too high considering what it has to offer. Customisation exists, but you'll be more likely to run into gamedesign limitations and functional issues if you attempt such a thing (for me it's a plus that a developer even attempts such a level of customisation, even if they fail, because it's a dying art in the game industry and I would hate losing it - still, people should know what they get into).
In conclusion: I will try to complete a game from time to time, but I'll be returning to GC3 because of the designer, unless it improves considerably.

I'll start by saying this is more of a first impressions than a complete review.
Necropolis is exactly what it is advertised as, a dungeon crawler rogue-like, I myself am a fan of rogue-like's and dungeon crawlers, and am very familliar with the Bloodborne and Souls series so this review was formed because of my interests, I bought this game under the pretense that it was going to be fun, re-playable and difficult to be honest.
I've seen a lot of reviewers giving a bad rap on both the art and the combat mechanics, if you're not a fan of the art style, you're not a fan, it harcons to a very LOZ : Windwaker theme, cartoony, approachable and light.
Combat is completely based on how well you can perform, meaning you have to know what your current weapon is capable of, despite what some reviewers seem to believe not every weapon is the same. The game emphazises on it's weapons, if you're familliar with dark souls every different weapon has a different move-set, a 2h greatsword is going to be different than a dagger or short-sword. This is especially true for the two charge-attacks that every weapon gets, some might have a more linear heavy charge attack whilst others might be focused on AOE or a combination of both.
Offhand tools other than shields ARE in the game, Examples I've encountered are Hand-crossbows ( Like some of the Grime you see use ) and a basically Bobba Fett's wrist flamethrower, Granted I've only gotten to around level 6-7? on my first playthrough these were around levels 4-7 which is understandable given how excellent they preform.
The levels change increasingly more as you get further in, the nastier the enemies ect, although this is a rogue-like you will actually benefit from getting far and dieing, the game rewards you with points used to purchase skill-books which GREATLY increase your odds of passing the levels as the buffs from them can be very powerful and the optional purchase of additional cosmetics for when you restart.
A few cons is that the procedural dungeons although varied do tend to mess up mob-wise, I've seen a few mobs within walls and above the actual map ( whilst transitioning levels ) another big one is that you are unable to rebind your keys.
Personally I like this game very much, the Dev's seem like they want to keep working on it too, adding more classes in later updates and such. There are many things I didn't mention here but these are just a few of the disputed concepts I thought worth mentioning for anyone wanting to purchase this game.

Great potential but the difficulty kills it.  For perspective, I beat Xcom Terror from the Deep and that is a challenging, but fun game.  I found this game difficulty to be unfair.  Examples of this include spawning in cities surrounded by enemies that force me to run immediately or when in the process of running have numerous enemies spawn around me that drop my health to zero quickly.  I get that enemies need to spawn in the city but having over a dozen laser tanks suddenly appear in my vicinity when I'm trying to exit the map (which can be hard enough, I'll get to that later) is just waste of time when they suddenly kill me.  The controls can be clunky.  I understand this isn't an action game but part of the strategy seems to be clearing lanes and staying near the edge of cities.  I can click on buildings near the edge to destroy and I constantly get prompts to "Leave city?".  That's frustrating enough but when I try to run out of the city and click off the map the monster goes wandering parallel to the edge indefinitely (and dies when the spawns appear out of nowhere).
I am confident I could beat this game, but don't intend to because the randomness/difficulty makes it a grind where I have to return to each city many times to take them. It's not rewarding when I feel like my success/failure is a result of random factors and not skill/strategy.   Plus I'm not on the biggest/final tier cities yet so I'm throwing in the towel and not wasting my time.  For reference, I lowered the difficulty from "Normal" to "Easy" and using the default Ginormasarus with Tier 5 skills.  I guess this game needs a very easy choice  or some balance thrown in.  It seems that some people like it the way it is, but this review is from someone that put in a lot of time and tried to like it.  I would consider changing the review if the difficulty is adjusted but I can't see the average buyer enjoying it in the current state.

Do not believe the amount of hours played on this game. Trust me, I've played this back when it first released long ago, and I still remember where most of the secrets, though I forgot how excrutiating and difficult this game can be, and the death count can rise higher than even Dark Souls or Super Meat Boy.
How can a more-than-a-decade-old game compare in difficulty to modern games like Dark Souls? Let me explain.
This game's challenge comes with the selection of difficulty mode, but the maps and monster dynamics as well as numbers change. Consider the 'easiest' difficulty to be the first time you play through Dark Souls, and conside the hardest difficulty (Extra Crispy) to be New Game +4. Monsters are more numerous, more dangerous, and come with more surprises that are worse than the last. Only difference is there's not RPG gear elements here; only your wits, your guns, and the strange menegerie of cult artifacts you use to destroy the minions of The One That Binds.
You play as Caleb, a ressurrected foul mouth cowboy ex-cultist hellbent on avenging the betrayal done to you by the Dreaming God. Each episode introduces new sets of monsters, weapons, and challenges, each level designed rather meticulously and advanced for it's time, much like the memorable maps of Doom 2.
The weapons are some of my favorite and memorable ones from any game (from the simple sawed off shotgun and dynamite bundle to the more cult saavy Voodoo Dolls and the all-powerful Life Leech staff). Nothing satisfied me more than the Napalm Launcher and even the Can of Hairspray. Each weapon has an alternate attack mode, with the Sawed Off merely firing both barrels of the gun at once while the Can of Hairspray changes from a simple homemade flamethrower (lighter included) into a molotov cocktail that can clear a whole room.
The maps are loaded with all sorts of traps, ambushes, close calls, and unfairness. You'll find out quickly which maps you like and loathe, but each of them always have a good bit of dark humor mixed in with the fear of every corner hiding Tommy-gun wielding, dynamite-hurling cultists ready to put you back in the dirt from where you came.
For the things I glorify, the game engine itself is clunky and sometimes rage inducing, much like Dark Souls. It takes time to figure out how the dynamite bundles toss and mouse-aiming has not been improved too thoroughly. Some of the weapons like the Flaregun have issues with connecting properly when firing at steeper angles other than horizontal (the game relies more on the autoaim and assumes you are using keyboard only). The amount of times I've killed myself due to tossing a bundle of dynamite into an invisible wall thinking it would make it over or it strikes a panicking human that runs in front of my toss and sends both of us back to hell. All I can say is Save. Save. Save.
I have quite a bit of nostalgia for this game, along with Doom and Duke Nukem 3d, and while I wish the core engine and mechanics where implemented better (the Cursed Doll alternate fire works like a giant room clear but seems broken and uses the ammo while only killing 1 enemy), the maps and the atmosphere are memorable as well as the gravelly sarcastic one liners the MC dolls out while setting zombies and cultists on fire brings out the sadistic glee from wiping evil from the face of the earth, and I don't just mean the mimes.
Addendum: If ever you see a hand creature crawling towards you, KILL IT FAST OR RUN. If it touches you, it will choke you to death. Mashing USE key can pull it off (may not in some cases), but you'll probably die before you do. This game is harsh, unforgiving, and these ♥♥♥♥ers literally choke you to death at the WORST POSSIBLE ♥♥♥♥ING MOMENT. Worst handjob ever.
"I hate mimes." - Caleb
