When I was younger. I played a game with my brother. It was called Rampage. I have fond memories of that game, smashing buildings and general chaos. Alas I grew up and those games seemingly have been forgotten by time. This genre needs to make a come back and Kaiju-A-GoGo may be the start of it. The goal is simple, world domination. Is it easy? No. Is it fun? Yes. Is it repetitious? Sadly, yes.
Kaiju-A-GoGo is a sound video game on paper. Kaiju attacks city, gets resources, takes said resources back to base for upgrades and base expansion. However there is certain things that just hold the game back from being amazing. Controls are abysmal. Base management is more  a chore then actually fun. The long grind to getting your Kaiju up and running with powers. Despite this though, Kaiju-A-GoGo is still a really fun game. The moments you find yourself blasting lasers, fire, or god knows what. Watching everything explode around you is blissfully giddy and captures that giant monster magic. With more Kaiju monsters coming and PLENTY of abilities and upgrades. You have plenty of bang for your buck. The graphics and music are just fine as well. I want this genre to come back and Kaiju-A-GoGo can make it happen. With some patches and changes.

There is a lot to say about Stellaris. Whether you think this is the best 4x Space Strategy game of all time or you cannot get the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ to start, there is plenty to talk about. Yet, I will keep this review simple, as I plan on writing one hell of a monster very soon.
Gameplay from an Ork:
Jokes aside, for those who have played about 30 minutes and are ready to give up: I know the UI is almost impossible at the beginning, it's because Stellaris is unlike many 4x Space Strategy games in the same genre. Take your time, learn how to play it and what makes it unique compared to the other 4x's games out there. You won't regret it, you'll be glad you learned this new take on the genre.
For those who are having a buggy launch: Give it time, don't refund it yet as this may be a game you end up enjoying if the problems are solved.
For those who think this is the best game ever: After 9.5 hours of straight Stellaris goodness, I can safely say, somethings are being exaggerated. This game is damn good and leaves room for plenty of additional content in the future but it's not the best 4x Strategy game ever. It does a lot good but it mostly does things that have already been done in a new way so it's more of refreshing perspective than it is a genre defining masterpiece.
For those on the fence: Take the plunge, unless you're having a buggy launch, you can't go wrong. Look at the treatment other Paradox games get, there will be more content to go with this already sizeable game.

Lots of people compare Stellaris to games like Alpha Centauri and GalCiv. Personally, I consider Stellaris to be a worthy successor to Distant worlds: streamlined, but with a lot of the complexity intact, and relying on real-time management rather than static turn-based doldrums. Paradox has always excelled at information-rich interfaces, and Stellaris is no exception, solving a major drawback to a lot of 4X games (Distant Worlds in particular) by providing multiple access points to information and screens, and offering the Paradox-standard Outliner that updates in real time to show you what your units are doing.
I have minor quibbles. The resource options are a bit stale (energy, minerals, influence) and lack immersion. More problematic, the research mechanic hearkens back to MOO (and Star Drive 2), where you have to pick from a small set of options each time. Both of these issues make Stellaris play more like a game than a simulation, and I  prefer my 4Xs to be more of the latter than the former.
But hey. It's Stellaris, it's Paradox, and it scratches my Distant Worlds itch for those times when I can't be bothered to fire up my VM and boot into Windows. 10/10, with rice.

I have mixed feelings on this game.
On the one hand, it's all I always dreamed in a game. "Free" swimming and interacting with all the wild life. On the other hand my expectations were a bit too high.

The game feels like the Disney magic that films tried to sell to me as a kid but never managed. Gorgeous music playing while you, basically a sea wildlife whisperer, ride the back of an orca, commanding it to breach the surface with its family, and the nearest schools of fish joining in. I honestly cried the first 2 times i did any of the current riding sections.
However not all of the sea is bright and gorgeous, some of it is dark and majestic, and some parts even feel dead and you have to find the source of the ailment.
I do have a couple complaints that did bug me through the game:
- The area with the big ball of fish, the "open sea feeding" one? Have you tried meditating on it? Ok, don't. As soon as you lock on a fish from that ball, you get stuck on those fish.
In general the issue with meditating is the apparently random way that a fish is picked for you to lock on, when changing fishes.
- The spermwhale area felt underwhelming compared to the rest of the game. The deep sea was what I looked forward the most, and you are given scripted whales on a place so cramped that the other creatures can't help but get clipped through. This really breaks immersion. The volcano chimneys do look cool but they make the area a hell to navigate properly on the back of anything bigger than the swimmer.
-Lastly, area transitions.
Basically when you are in a big cave and change to a smaller corridor, there seems to be a soft wall in between the 2, and despite both you and the animals being able to transverse it, if you go on the back of something or go fast in general, the game acts like you hit a wall in that transition, preventing you from going in the corridor, despite there being no reason for it.
ABZÛ overall is very enjoyable tho. Just keep in mind it isn't for everyone. If you like the ocean and wish for something  that gives some Journey vibes, this is for you.

This is the second adventure of Geralt of Rivia, and it really is a magnificent sequel and a darn good RPG.
What are the biggest changes between this and Witcher 1? Well, first there's the visuals - everything's gorgeous now, and Zoltan no longer has a bizarre unfocused look in his eyes that makes him seem permanently stoned. I spent a ton of time just panning the camera around taking in all the scenery, and I was only playing this on LOW settings.
Control-wise, the combat system has been revamped. It's still occasionally clunky when it comes to switching between Witcher signs/bombs/traps, but this awkwardness eventually goes away after a few hours of play. Overall, everything feels more natural (when played with a controller) and skill-based than the clicky combat of the first game. The different stances are out and now it's action-orientated, and you've got to roll around a lot and dodge blows with precision. The game is tough at first because Geralt starts as a weakling compared to his foes, and the in-game tutorial does a pretty crap job of explaining the combat, so try the game out on Easy or Normal difficulty first until you get the hang of things and level up Geralt to non-weakling status. (Use the Quen sign as much as possible and try specializing in Swordmaster skills like roll and block if you're having trouble in the beginning.) Normal difficult in the Witcher 2 = hard difficulty in a lot of other games, so be aware.
And then there's the story. The plot in Witcher 1 occasionally seemed like it was rehashing the most memorable of Geralt's adventures from the novels with some odd discrepancies; ie: Triss' personality was more like Yennefer's than anything else. Witcher 2 fixes this by making the characters more in line with their book counterparts and crafting a story that is very political and seems like a natural extension of the books rather than a "best of" compilation. The kings of the Northern Kingdoms are being killed by assailants from a forgotten Witcher school, and much of Chapters 2 and 3 focus on the importance of the Pontar Valley, an area that borders the more notable kingdoms in Geralt's world. A lot of names are dropped and places referenced, which can be confusing to newbies that haven't read the books or played the first game, so referring to the in-menu Journal is a must. Lore fanatics will eat this up; impatient players perhaps not as much.
As long as you've got time and patience, the Witcher 2 will eat up many, many hours of your life. Best of all, this is one of the few games I know of that's really worth replaying - a critical decision at the end of Chapter 1 will COMPLETELY change Chapters 2 and 3 for you. Lengthy RPGs are usually low on the replay list for me...but I'm planning on a completely new playthrough on Hard difficulty just to check out Iorveth's path, so that's saying something.

It's a rather delightful pixel platforming puzzle game. For the record I'm absolutely terrible at puzzles, but I actually enjoy the game. The puzzle involve you controlling multiple character where you need to move a to a certain point, activate switches at correct timings, and get to your character icon.
After that, you rewind the tape, select the other character and play in tandem with the recording to match up levels, buttons, and jumping over hurdles to try and make it to the end.
It's extremely well made, and can easily mess up if you had your timings off, even by half a second. Even more so since as the levels progress more and more classic platforming dangers appear. Simple spikes, easily avoided in most games become a difficult obstacle as you need to help create a platform to jump with one character, rewind and then manoeuvre the other across it all.
Neko, did a splendid job on the game, and can appreciate the time and effort they put into it all. I enjoy the game, even though it takes me far far too long to complete what others would solve in possible tens of seconds.
You should get the game? Do you like platforming, and puzzles with an interesting mechanics? If so, yes.

TLDR: If you are serious about photo editing or image creation, try the
It's way more powerful than Pixeluvo, opensource and free. If you just want to do amateur photo editing, or if you have a camera that takes RAW pictures and want to digitally develop them, Pixeluvo might be a good option for you.
Arguably, Adobe's Photoshop is the best image editing software, for a number of reasons, the main one being money: Adobe invest a lot of resources in making it's software powerful and (relatively) easy to use.
However, Adobe's subscription policy is a big problem for me. Not being able to open your editable files unless you pay a rent is just unadmissible, as it makes Adobe virtually the owner of my work. That's why I migrated to GIMP a while back (and also to
as my main OS).
Sadly, GIMP has a number of shortcomings, like it's ugly GUI (fixable via themes) and it's color management. Specifically, GIMP doesn't do a good job managing color for print (CMYK). That's why I decided to try Pixeluvo.
Pixeluvo has a great GUI (that kind off resembles PS), a bunch of filters and RAW support. It's interface is amicable and easy to learn, and all the core tools for photo editing are here (levels, curves, saturation-color-balance, threshold, etc). It has non-destructive editing (which GIMP doesn't) and overall has a pleasant 'feel' to it.
On the bad side, Pixeluvo is more gimped than the GIMP when it comes to color management (pun intended). Simply put, it doesn't. Not RGB nor CMYK, pixeluvo does not manage color profiles, which means that if you are not using your own RAW photos, you won't be seeing the 'right' color, which basically makes it unusable for professional graphic design or photo editing.
Also, Pixeluvo not being open source makes it unable to use opensource third party plugins like the G'MIC project, which can be used in GIMP, Krita, Natron and other opensource software. So pixeluvo is unable to compete with other proprietary software feature wise (COREL, Adobe) and can't benefit from the opensource comunity.
I bought this with a 70% discount. The software is not expensive considering it's features, but I woudn't buy at full price.
Do yourself a favor, and play it. This game shouldn't be missed by anyone.

Why do I think MD is awesome? (Because I do think that.) There are plenty of things I COULD list, from being a fan of the maker, to the cute artwork, to the by turns adorable, dark, intense and thought-provoking stories told in the form of romantic paths, the the simple quality of the game. Oh, wait, I just listed them. Oh well.
My point was, what I really love, even after so many playthroughs, and so much more experience now of RPG and VisNovel games than I had when I first played it, is how it walks the line of complexity. Most VisNovels give you simple text, with choices that affect outcome. Simple, enjoyable, easy to figure out. Other games also incorporate a skill system that affects the outcome just as much, and can be fiendishly difficult to figure out - do you have enough charm to be with this character, and if you don't, do you have enough energy to build on it without your character burning out or starving? The combinations can be endless - or at least so numerous that it takes a true devout to get through them all.
Magical Diary, to me, is a perfect crossover. Because the magic system is complex, but straight-forward and, most importantly, it's in the game as a BONUS. Talk about replayability - when you're done with the romance routes and want to replay them, you can play around with your class shedule and skill levels to unlock some bonus content. And there's even a direct payoff to your skill building with the fun dungeons. The dungeon exam at the end of the terms might not change between playthroughs, but you, like the characters themselves, can have a lot of fun keeping your character from learning the spell for the obvious solution and really trying to think outside the box.
In short, whether you're in this for a cute, fun, deep VN, or a skill-builder with the occasional secret bonus that won't eat up weeks of your life or require a walkthrough, Magical Diary is something you should try out. I loved it when I first bought it and, unlike other VNs, I still love it now.

I try to buy indie games at or close to full price, particularly from first time developers who do something that looks cool or interesting. Sure, I've taken a bath on a couple of games that weren't as good as I'd hoped, but it's never been too punishing.
Until now.
Belladonna is the first game that I truly,
regret buying. Even if I had a time machine and could go back and buy it dirt cheap, knowing what I know now,
. As I write this review, it's currently on sale for sixty-nine cents and my brain is still going, "NOPE." Listen to my brain. It knows what it's talking about. Don't make the same mistakes I did. By all means, laugh at my pain, but save yourselves.
Ostensibly, Belladonna is a point and click adventure game consisting of exploration, a mystery narrative and puzzles. That assessment is...generous, at the very least.
In a game that takes place in what's supposed to be a
, there are about a dozen locations,
Most contain one item--two if you're extremely lucky!--and maybe two or three short bits of flavor text so bland I hesitate to call it flavor text at all. If light vegan mayonnaise were flavor text, it's what you'll find here. I guess if you've never had anything else, it might seem robust, but I can't imagine anyone with half a dozen decent-to-good adventure games under their belts finding it anything but dull.
The narrative isn't much better than the flavor(less) text. The plot hinges on a mystery so transparent it's easily solvable after the first clue or two if you've got a couple of spare braincells lying around to rub together. Halfway through the story, you're likely to get fed up with how it's belaboring the point you've already figured out. “I know something you don't know!” the narrative teases, “Such a mysterious mystery! Oooh!” while you start drinking heavily and praying for the sweet release of death.
The prose is written in a style that I can only adequately describe as “olden time-y,” superficially reminiscent of Gothic literature if you tossed any old novel in a blender and diluted it with heavy doses of pretentious goth kid who swallowed a thesaurus but neglected to get enough dictionary in his diet.  This might not be so bad if the story and characters were stylish or over the top enough to carry the awkwardness—Hammer or Universal horror films are hardly historically accurate, but are cool enough you don't care—but Belladonna has the panache of a worn out shoe.
The story is told primarily through diary entries written by three different characters: the scientist, his socialite wife and the maid. They all sound virtually the same. The only discernible difference between them is that our Frankenstein writes in a slightly more ornate style and throws a few scientific terms around. I repeat: a socialite and a scientist both write the same way a maid does. In the Georgian/Victorian era. (Which is it? Who knows!)
The diary entries also contain only explicitly plot related bits with nothing else to really round out the characters. They're basically props to be moved around at the whim of the developer like little cardboard cutouts. This is not the way to tell a story with any hope of emotional potency. The villain gets what feels like three times as much “screen time” through the diaries as the two main characters we're supposed to care about—and he's dead before the story even starts!
Because the whole thing is written as telling rather than showing, in spite of the fact it's all plot, the relationships between the characters are barely touched on in any meaningful way. The main romance is written about in detail—as in, what actually happened between them during the course of their months long affair—in
; it's given no development beyond that.
Character motives are thin on the ground. The writer tries to convey that the characters are driven by grief, but does so poorly that I'm not sure they've ever met and interacted with a real live human being. Since the story picks up
, their motivations appear for all intents and purposes to consist of such compelling reasons as, “Because science! I guess?” and “Because boredom! I guess?”
The puzzles would be insultingly easy to even the most casual of gamers over the age of nine. And though I may have blocked out the more excruciating aspects of the experience, as far as I can recall with the exception of the final one, they all have the same basic end goal: open a door/container. That's it. Kill a cat to open a door. Rifle through a dead body's pockets to open a box. Get a screwdriver to open a clock. Necessary items for solving these “puzzles” are often just left lying around in plain sight, require no extra steps to acquire them and no critical thinking to make them function. Can you put two and two together and not come up with “cheese”? Congratulations, you too can finish Belladonna!
Worst of all,
. Nothing. Because everything has
happened. This narrative device
work in games (Analogue: A Hate Story managed to pull this off pretty handily) but the writing is so lousy that even the attempt is torture. After forty-five minutes of opening doors, it finally looks like something will happen!...and then the story cuts to black. The end!
If for some reason—masochism, morbid curiosity, a large iron spike in your head tickling the 'lack of common sense' centers of your brain—you're still considering shelling out dough to buy this, let me at least mention that the less story-based aspects suffer too in hopes I might dissuade you from such folly.
First, the voice acting is dismal and one actor portrays both speaking characters: the first in a plain American speaking voice, the second with electronic distortion and a high school play English accent. Never mind that this apparently takes place in Eastern Europe or...Germany? (Much like the time period, who the ♥♥♥♥ knows for sure??)
The diary entries are all written in fonts that border on unreadable to various degrees. They're either too flowery, too tiny, or joy of joys both.
It's bare bones in the extreme. There are no extras. No behind the scenes character art or similar unlockables. No achievements.
Now that's commitment to minimalism!
Replayability is nonexistent.
If after all this you still want the game, well...Godspeed, you beautiful, romantic fool. I envy your optimism, naivete and by the way would you like to buy a bridge in Brooklyn?
In closing, I will say: if Belladonna were updated in the future and whole swaths of it were rewritten, expanded and for the love of all that's holy
, it might be something special, or at least an interesting if noble failure. Currently it is anything but. My playtime will be just long enough to collect all the cards and not a second longer.

This game is cute, in a dark and twisted kind of way. I'd give it 5/10, and I recommend it only because it's 0,69€ now, and for that price it's a total catch.
PROS:
+ I loved the artwork and the general environment.
+ Music wasn't annoying, and voice acting was ok.
+ I liked the Steampunk vibe, the theme, and the story was cool.
+ References to Mary Shelley and Edgar Allan Poe, which made me squeal in delight.
+ Easy and logical, there is no constant backtracking, no pixel hunt, and no nonsensical inventory combinations.
CONS:
- Extremely short. I'm a VERY slow player, and I finished it in 2 hours, and that is including a pause I took for dinner while leaving the game on.
- Too easy. Not one puzzle and not one remotely challenging situation.
- The ending leaves lose ends, almost as if hoping for a sequel.
In short, if on sale, go for it. It's a nice hour and bit of a dark little story. But if you're into really challenging stuff, this one may bore you a bit. I still enjoy it and I'm not sorry I got it (then again, I got it for 0,69€).

A deceptively simple interface (point and click to devastate everything in your path, half a dozen hotkeys to unleash nuclear fires, deathrays or other monstrocities of super-science) hides a steady stream of tactical decisions. Chase down those fleeing civilians to crush your enemies will to resist your power? Crush that annoying APC that's been plinking away at your health all the way through suburban Seattle? Chase down that helicopter that keeps buzzing you and watch it crash into an office block, engulfing it in flames? Turn back to loot the mall that burnt down after you casually set it aflame in passing? Or press on to finally smash the Space Needle that dares to rival the height of your precious creation? Defend your monster by crushing the forces sent against it, but leave the city mostly intact, or recklessly risk having to rebuild your monster and lose a rampage's worth of loot by pressing on to rob that research lab of its secrets, heedless of the armies dogging your heels? Interesting gameplay is usually about making choices, and if you want those choices to involve laying waste to the cities of the Earth because it seemed like a reasonable thing to do at the time, Kaiju-A-GoGo is for you.

Dungeons are fairly bland looking with very little color.  Alof of the graphics look like they are still in alpha.
Each dungeon is different and I feel like that is where most of the dev's effort went into.  Most roguelikes have fairly bad combat systems.  Usually spamming 1 or 2 buttons.  This one literally takes the control scheme from Dark Souls and uses it here.  I mean it.  I didn't really even need to look at the controls as they are exactly like the souls series.
I think the price is a bit much for a game like this though.  20 bucks would've been perfect.  Game needs more polish in a few areas, namely combat and the camera.

Salutations fellow gamers!
I just wanted to write a quick first impressions review of Stellaris so far. I am only 3 hours into it so far but so far its been great! I have a good number of RTS and 4x strategy games. Only a few of them are Paradox Interactive games such as Mount and Blade, War of the Roses, Magicka, King Arthur Strategy Game, and of course now is Stellaris. My class mates have been talking it up for the past few weeks and enticed me to finally get it on release day and I am very pleased with it.
For a strategy game it is very fluid yet methodical. When I say this I am thinking in my mind that this is a slight hybrid of Endless Space and Sins of a Solar Empire: Rebellion (both of which are great). Yet, this game is fluid without turns and you can even adjust the time to even pausing the game. This also is in effect in multiplayer but more on that later.
________________________________________________________________________________
Cost: It varies on what edition you get of the game, I personally got the Nova edition because it comes with a portrait species (literally only cosmetic, no effects on gameplay apart from just an alien spider like Arthropod archetype species) as well as the soundtrack. The soundtrack is definitely worth the extra cost for its great quality and good atmosphere. Though for those who are into the game alone then just get the base game, the upper tiers of editions are really only cosmetic and support of the developers (along with social goodies such as forum badges, though that may I have changed by now). I would say for the quality of game it is in right now, it is worth the $50 I spent for the Nova edition.
Gameplay is rather unique and I do not think I gave it justice by implying it was a hybrid of Endless Space and Sins of a Solar Empire because it is a really interesting and great style of play. Generally speaking it is just like any other RTS where you develop your empire and encounter other species with differing responses. The empire creator by the way is wonderful and very finite, with editing the style of government and its ethics (all very compliced and not going into it with this first impressions, essentially just traits of your empire but could have different styles based on choices. There are a specific trait system that balances out with negatives and positives, much like Zomboid character traits, etc.) All in all the gameplay is typical for anyone who has played an RTS/4x game and I had no problem picking up the mechanics within the first 10-20 minutes.
Multiplayer is very interesting because supposedly it can go beyond 32 players (not recommended for ease of play). It is very simple to play with friends and even random people, though I would sit down prior and create your own empire if you so choose to rather than making everyone wait. The only gripe I have with multiplayer is that the thing I mentioned about controlling time is available to everyone (no clue if there is a host option to limit power or not). So at first people were pausing and slowing/speeding time up for EVERYONE so we had to set up some ground rules. All in all very fluid, my friends experienced minor lag problems but nothing hindering playability (could've been my friend's crappy internet hosting).
For a game that I never heard about until the last few weeks, it is a suprisingly great game that I would recommend to anyone who enjoys a good RTS/4x game much like Endless space/etc. If you have friends than more the merrier because I've been enjoying playing with them quite a bit. This has been my first impressions and I give it a good thumbs up! :)

Before I start this review, I would like to mention the quality of this port, or lack thereof. Blood is confugured to run in Dosbox, and is configured like crap. There is a way to fix it, thanks to
Now on to the main review.
People well versed in the FPS genre will always talk about the Build Engine Trinity games. Those games being Duke Nukem 3D, Shadow Warrior, and Blood. I have completed Duke 3D, and the Life's A Beach expansion pak, while also playing a good chunk of Shadow Warrior's campaign. Even though I like these two games, the both suffer from severe problems which hinders them from being put in a pedestal next to other FPS classics like Doom 2 or Unreal. Based off my experiences with those two games, I expected Blood to follow in a similar vain. I haven't been this pleased to be wrong about prior thoughts to a game since Doom 2016 (which I thought would suck, but is awesome).
Once you configure Blood to your liking, you are then taken to the game's menu screen, where you are able to select the episode, and the difficulty. In Blood you play as Caleb, a guy in a trenchcoat with a fedora, who is seeking vengance after his master betrays him, by burrying him alive. Afterwords you wake up from your grave, to then quote a line from Army of Darkness. Blood stands out from the other Build Engine games for 2 reasons.
1) The atmosphere in Blood is creepy and unsetteling at times, engrosing you in it's world that has been carefully constructed. Notable levels include the Dark Carnaval in Episode 1, a good chunk of Episode 2, and a Forest level in Episode 4. In comparison, Duke 3D and Shadow Warrior lack any sense of atmosphere, as focus was put on other elements.
2) Blood has a unique weapon lineup. Starting with a Pitchfork and Flare Gun, up to more devestating weapons like the Napalm Launcher, and Tesla Rifle. These weapons do an exelent job at dispatching Caleb's foes.
Speaking of which, the enemy design in Blood fits the theme like a glove. From Zombies and Robed Cultists, to Sea Monsters and Hellhounds, Blood's enemy roster is unique in both appearance and functionality. This only slightly let down by the fact that the flying enemy types suffer from poor A.I. at times. Gargoyles in particular have a hard time doing anything usefull in big open areas, and will just ♥♥♥♥ around in the air, being a general nusance. Episode 3 also suffers a bit from mazelike level design, and forgetable backdrops, and is easily the most forgettable episode in the game. Other than those complaints, Blood is an amazing experience. This is without mentioning the hidden secrets, the refrences Caleb makes, the awesome powerups, the extreme usage of blood and gore, and cool but not too challenging boss fights.
Blood also had two expansion packs released for it as well. The Plasma Pak was an official expansion by Monolith, and upgrades the main game to Blood With Plasma. This pack adds a new episode, multiple new enemy types, and a new boss. It's fun, and is a good test of raw skill for those well versed in older FPS games. Later released was the Cryptic Graves expansion pak, released by Wizzard Works, who also released a lot of Duke Nukem 3D expansion Paks. Cryptic Graves is a pretty good expansion pak, with memorable locations, and fun level design, that only falls short of being pretty easy. Both these expansion packs are included with this purchase, so this is the definitive version of the game to get at the moment, only short of a full HD source port. Blood is now one of my favorite FPS games, and is my favorite game of the Build Engine Trinity. I highly reccomend that anyone who is a fan of FPS games pick this one up, as it lives up to its name in every regard. I'll end this review by quoting Caleb quoting Army of Darkness.

Blood is a first person shooter that came out in the busy PC game market of 1997 and runs on a modified BUILD engine, the same engine that powered Duke Nukem 3D a year prior. While Duke3D was developed by 3D Realms Blood was being made by Q Studios, an independent dev funded by 3D Realms and originally by the working title 'Horror 3D'. Scheduled for release in early '97 Q Studios was acquired by Monolith Productions in late '96 and a press release not long after announced all the rights being sold to Monolith so 3D Realms could focus their efforts on Shadow Warrior, another FPS using a more advanced version of the BUILD engine, slated for release the same year. Where Duke3D paid homage to 80's and 90's action films and Shadow Warrior being an Oriental flavor of the same game, Blood would take its inspiration from horror films instead.
The story in Blood is more fleshed out than other BUILD games, beginning with the legendary and ruthless gunslinger known as Caleb, the protagonist and effectively anti-hero of Blood. Born in Texas, he worked up his merciless reputation at the young age of seventeen in the late 1800's. One day Caleb discovered a woman named Ophelia, who had her homestead burnt to the ground by the Cabal after her husband tried to rescind, killing him and her young son in the process. Enraged and heartbroken, not at the Cabal, but blaming her spouse's foolish actions for the death of her child. Caleb being perplexed but intrigued would take the woman in and nurse her back to health. She would later become his lover, and the gateway to the underworld of the Cabal, a cult who worshipped the dark god Tchernobog, The One That Binds, aptly named for his binding of the realities in the known universe.
Tchernobog's true age and origin are unknown, his original body having been destroyed long ago, forcing him to take control of another in order to fulfill his duties, thus the Cabal was born. He is a morally ambiguous entity who underwent numerous incarnations over the course of his existence. The earliest known was that of a Buddhist high priest, converting the Cabal into a religious regiment, practicing docile rituals of penance and self-control. But his latest incarnation was colored by that of a bitter and hateful man, who bent the Cabal towards the dark goal of world domination, acting as Tchernobog's personal army on earth. Tchernobog is now a more active force in the world, discarding the position of the Cabal leader in favor of direct influence over the cult himself, giving orders from his throne in the Hall of Epiphany. He would however select four in his ranks to become The Chosen, with Caleb and Ophelia being part of it, with the others being Ishmael and Gabriel. The Chosen were the Cabal's elite servants, as well as the highest generals in Tchernobog's army. Caleb was designated to be the leader of The Chosen, and to be selected as the next incarnation of Tchernobog himself if the need or opportunity ever arised.
But for reasons unknown Tchernobog had deemed his Chosen as failures, casting them down and leaving their ill-fated destinies to Cheogh, ruler of gargoyles, Shial, mother of spiders, and Cerberus, a massive two-headed dog, who act as generals for Tchernobog's otherworldly army. Whereas the other Chosen were taken away by monsters, Caleb was confined into the tomb of a hallowed grave instead. Not content with staying dead, Caleb would rise again, in a body he no longer knows, and in a world he has grown to despise in the year 1928. Being a sarcastic man with a strong bent towards sadism, and with the love of his life being taken from him, his journey will be a bloody and vengeance-filled war against the Cabal, while hoping to learn the reason for his exile and seeking out the other Chosen, for with their combined power and strength can he hope to take on Tchernobog.
Blood lives up to it's namesake, it's easily the bloodiest FPS in 1997. Enemies die in several violent ways, with zombies being decapitated and the player able to kick around their severed heads, to cultists and other humanoid enemies being set on fire and burning alive while they cry out in pain. Most outcomes result with over-the-top red showers and gibs galore that litter the ground, making Duke3D and even SW look tame by comparison. There's also other unique deaths that can be triggered with specific weapon types. Viscera aside there is also several enemies with their own special resistances and weaknesses to certain damage properties which you will have to learn in order to master combat.
Gameplay is traditional for the era, in which you roam some thirty-odd levels, key-hunting and killing everything that gets in your way, all contained within the game's five episodes (six if you count the add-on Cryptic Passage). But like other BUILD engine titles what seperates Blood from the-then common Doom clone is the level of interactivity, realism and various gags in the game's levels. There is a host of pop culture references and easter eggs of the era that are still delightful to discover to this day and the maps all ooze with atmosphere and small details, with even the horror elements more fun than frightening.
To make your life miserable there is a large and varied bestiary of semi-humans, ghouls and other things that go bump in the night that stay true to the game's themes. From nuisance enemies like rats and spiders, to the common and crazed yapping cultists and axe-wielding zombies, as well as more otherworldly horrors like gargoyles in flesh and stone variants, ghostly phantasms, fire-breathing hellhounds, and oddities like the severed hands that have a personality all on their own while trying to choke the life out of you. They all hit hard, making battles with them deadly, especially the cultists who are the sole hitscanners, capable of lopping dynamite in your direction, definitely making them high priority to dispose of ASAP.
But you too wield a large and powerful arsenal of your own to fight back with. Starting with only a pitchfork, unconventional for the genre, but quickly work up to a flare gun in place of a traditional pea shooter, a double barreled sawed off shotgun, gangster style tommy gun, the explosive and highly flammable napalm launcher in place of a rocket launcher, several types of dynamite, some of which can be remote detonated, improvised flamethrower in the form of an aerosol can, to the almost anachronistic tesla cannon and even the dark arts with the voodoo doll and life leech. All firearms can be dual-wielded with a power-up called Guns Akimbo and most weapons possess an alternate firing mode, revolutionary for the time. Other pickups come in traditional and non-traditional flavors, you can heal via a portable medikit or from the life essence of fallen foes in the form of a still-beating heart, and there is armor types tailored to absorbing specific kinds of damage. Better yet is power-ups to make you completely undetectable or invincible for a short duration.
Visually the game is on par with Duke3D or SW and has faux 3D elements in the engine like room-over-room and voxels for things like weapon pickups and certain decorative objects. While it lacked the true 3D technology of Quake II that year Blood's personality made the game far more charming than its competitors that overshadowed it. Sound design is loud and satisfying, and the soundtrack comes in midi and CD audio form, with both being equally great to listen to.
Criticisms allude to the lack of polish, most notable in Blood compared to other BUILD games, with bizarre enemy behavior, weird hitboxes and collision detection, and some bad exploits like crouch and physics abuse, the bosses are far too easy to kill and the instant-reaction from cultist attacks paired with the high damage output can lead to some unfair moments.
Blood is still bloody good fun however and thus comes as highly recommended to fans of the genre and the BUILD engine in general. Spill some.

I rate the game Blood: One Unit Whole Blood 3.5/5. Pretty good.
Despite the fact that this is now an extremely old FPS (first person shooter) game from the same family of games as Duke Nukem 3D (using the same game engine as the original Shadow Warrior and Duke Nukem 3D), this is still fairly fun to play, despite how ugly looking its graphics are. In fact, as this version is probably far more stable than the original version of the game, being far less prone to crashes and freeze-ups, this version may be even better than the original ever was. There are some drawbacks however, the worst of which is the game's inability to have its resolution increased beyond a lowly 800 by 600 pixels.
+Good and responsive controls for mouse/keyboard though the now antiquated manual method of pressing buttons to look up and down remains clumsy in the extreme. If you remember, this was always clumsy and was not remedied until the advent of the first Quake game and the general adoption of the control style used therein.
+Still an exciting game to play with lots of action.
+This game is extremely inexpensive and gives you at least 10 hours of gameplay on the easiest difficulty level. The gameplay consists mostly of finding keys to unlock doors into yet another area, one level after another but the maze-like level design is well made with lots of intricate puzzles and clever references to movies and books throughout. As an added benefit, this game should work on pretty much any computer which now exists and can run dos box.
+Good, highly atmospheric, interesting and creepy music. This game features the same music which was on the CD (compact disc) version of the game way back when it first game out.
+Not very many bugs (asides from certain non-essential menu options not doing what they claim to do but instead having no effect whatsoever). While it was normal for the original version of Blood to freeze up totally back when it first came out, this version is very, very stable and runs fast.
+/-The sound is often fairly good, the screams of characters (especially when certain ones are set on fire) are pretty detailed. That said, many of the sound effects can seem tinny and as the exact same sound effects are repeated over and over (like they were in the old days) the sound can seem boring. The nifty things your character says to himself (in a fairly Duke Nukem sort of way, but with a very different personality) does help spice things up however.
+/-The blood and gore in this game, or at least its depiction of it, may seem tame by comparison to today's higher resolution, more detailed games. Still, the amount of gore seems fairly realistic thus adding a bit of grittiness to an otherwise cartoon-like atmosphere.
+/-It is very easy to save your game anywhere. However there are NO autosaves and it is also easy to potentially save your game so that you may end up reloading your game into a totally impossible-to-survive situation.
-The graphics have not aged well and the maximum resolution which this game actually let me set it to, a lowly 800x600 seems dismally low and textures and characters alike seem terribly ugly and primitive looking. Games with throwback/retro graphics like Minecraft look better by comparison. The game has options for higher resolutions but the game does not let you actually select these resolutions making for some potentially frustrating menu interactions. The game's animation is, I think, not anymore jerky than it originally was. The graphics for Blood were intended to be played on an CRT (cathode ray tube) monitor which featured extreme contrast versus brightness ratios. This means that the textures and everything else in this game are intended for an entirely different type of computer imaging and lighting technology. A technology where the pixels of the screen themselves glow with their own light (not with any back lighting). The textures, on any newer LCD (liquid crystal display) or other new technology monitors will look too bright, the colors will not be as intense and indeed, the entire game will seem somehow faded like old parchment and the deep blacks will instead merely be gray. There is no way to decrease the game's brightness below a certain point (which is what would be required to make this game look as it was intended). You might try, if you really care more about this game than I do, to further increase your current generation monitor's contrast ratio even further, for on the old CRT screens, pretty much anywhere that was not fairly well lit, was completely dark.

This is a very enjoyable game, and takes the rogue-lite genre the farthest it has come in most aspects.
It awards exploration greatly,  and provides a challenge to explore every corner of a level. The pickups are incredibly creative, as grotesque or terrifying as they can be. The pickups manage to still be interesting, as not every pickup is just a range, speed, or attack upgrades like lesser games in the genre tend to do.
Bosses are all unique and equally terrifying, the issue though is that bosses vary in difficulty, and it is possible to lose to the most difficult boss on the first level, because all you picked up on that level was a fly that follows you around.
It is, of course not without its issues, but they are acceptable ones. The Binding of Isaac has the same issue almost all modern rogue-lite/likes have. A weak combat system. although you can sort of bend you shots by moving, the 4 directional shooting mechanic makes combat much more difficult than it need be. What makes this acceptable, however is that a majority of enemies are bound to this shooting system as well. the reason after this, is that a large portion of enemies attack by touching you. if an enemy comes at you at an angle, it becomes extremely difficult to attack them if your movement is restricted.
Besides these minor issues, The Binding of Isaac is still a very enjoyable game, and can be picked up played, and has an enormous amount of replayability. If you do ever manage to brutally murder your mother, than there are still challenge modes available which are all unique, and provide an increased amount of difficulty or just improve upon the exploration in general.
I highly reccomend this at a 5 dollar price tag, and if youre still unsure, wait for a sale and you could grab this at as little as 2 dollars. This is a great deals, and a very enjoyable game, and is one of the best in its genre.

Read on if you're getting The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt, but trying to decide if you should play the previous games...
I'm a longtime fan of fantasy role-playing games and have come to prefer non-linear open world titles.  I'm a huge fan of the Elder Scrolls series and have put countless hours into Morrowind, Oblivion and Skyrim.  Recently, I have been seeing promotions for The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt and I must say that it looks beautifully crafted and very intriguing.  Having no prior experience in the world of the Witcher, I wondered if my future planned adventure would be hampered by my lack of knowledge of the series lore, the world and its inhabitants.  I set forth on my own quest and began to read about the previous games.  While both were received favorably, it seemed The Witcher 2: Assassins of Kings had a slight edge over the original.  While I'm sure I'd have enjoyed both games, time can be at a premium and choices must be made, whether right or wrong.  In the end, I decided to go with The Witcher 2: Assassins of Kings EE.
Having made the decision, and prior to firing up the game for the first time, I began to wonder if I made the right choice.  Sadly, no special bell rung. No unobtrusive little prompt popped up to let me I made the right call.  No signal, no nothing.  It was just me and my decision.  A little apprehensive I would be lost, I mustered up some courage and began my journey with Geralt of Rivia.   After being thrust into Geralt's world, I began to wonder who these characters were, where they came from and what happened in this world prior to my arrival.  Overwhelmed in the beginning, I thought I had made the wrong decision, but I continued on and ploughed forward.  As time passed, I began to understand the world of the Witcher and its history.  The gameplay itself and the expansive journal helped fill in some of the major details and brought me up to a comfortable speed.  While I'll undoubtedly will miss out on some of the finer details from the original game, and the book series for that matter, I have been immersed in the world of the Witcher.  And I must admit, I don't want to leave anytime soon.
So, if you're reading this and find yourself stuck in the same predicament, let this serve as your bell, your prompt, your signal and get The Witcher 2: Assassins of Kings EE.  You will not regret it.  Be warned however, from hence forth, I will not be here to guide your journey.  The coming decisions are up to you and only time will tell if you made the right one.  As for me, if I find the time and the orens, I'll be making a trip back to the original game and I'll be sure let you know how my journey ends.

A 16-bit, top-down, DDR dungeon crawler? Yes. It's brilliant and a shining example of why Indie games are incredible.
Crypt of the NecroDancer is combination of rhythm-game (think things like DDR, Guitar Hero, or Audio Surf) and a Rogue-like (games that typically have perma-death, randomly generated dungeons and items) with a fantastic retro '16-bit' art style. If you already like Rogue-likes and don't have this game then you're doing it wrong.
I'm a fan of Rogue-likes in general but one of the struggles I have is replayability. The features that define many Rogue-like work for a while but eventually one gets tired of replaying the first stages over and over, then FINALLY making it to "that one level" only to die immediately and repeat the whole process again. For many Rogue-likes the entire game is centered around this cycle, there's really nothing to *do* elsewhere; no open world to explore or shops (outside of shopkeepers inside the dungeon). Where CotND differs is in offering players a way to customize the game's meta. It starts with little things like buying items that will show up in chests, buying permanent character upgrades, and removing undesired items from random drops. You can also take up a daily challange, practice against dungeon foes and bosses, and test your brain/reflexes in additional challenge modes. There are NPCs to unlock, a mode designed to be played on a DDR 'dance pad', and a whole slew of characters to unlock, each of which have their own properties/features/mechanics to master.

But if you like a cool little story, pick this one up on sale.  Not sure its worth full asking price though.  Oh and the game ends as if its just the start to more of the like.  Even the final screen picture suggests that but I dont think any others like it were ever made.  Too bad.  I woulda grabbed them on sale as well.

The videos, the trailers, and even most of these acclaiming Steam reviews simply cannot do this game justice. I will not attempt to achieve what others have not--I know that it is simply impossible to capture the beautiful essence of "Dust: An Elysian Tail" through a medium as unworthy as meager words. This game, while being child-friendly throughout, is anything but juvenile. The dialogue is beautifully written and witty, and the cleanliness of the jokes does not feel contrived. The animation, as many others have said, is something unlike anything I've experienced in any RPG, and I love it. No other game gives off the same vibe as this one. The feel is entirely different, the controls are unique, but not confusing, and the story is incredibly immersive, though it does provide those who either hyperfocus upon or ignore these details with the option to skip or pause most dialogue.
This game is simple to grasp, but from its puzzles to its challenges, its difficulty is well-set. It's simplicistic in its setup (by which I mean it's very easy to keep track of all your goals and abilities. You won't struggle to remember what button does what or which meter represents which of your values.) but complex in its well-paced story. The combat is fun, the music is gorgeous, the expressions and personalities of all the characters shine, and overall, I'd rate this game as a must play to anyone who enjoys fantasy. While cute, Dust is also profound and emotional, and after your first play-session, you'll notice that the desire to play Dust is a craving unlike that which any other game has given you.
As a longtime story-focused gamer who  has consummed most big titles, I had Dust on my wishlist for awhile solely due to the reviews, but when I actually got around to trying it, I was upset that Dust had not been one of my TOP priorities to acquire on Steam. As I said before, reviews and videos CANNOT do this game justice.
Do yourself a favour and purchase this game.
It feels like a crime when it goes on sale for only three-four dollars when I've had more fun playing Dust for seven hours than I have after completing fifty dollar Assassin's Creed games.

There is a lot to say about Stellaris. Whether you think this is the best 4x Space Strategy game of all time or you cannot get the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ to start, there is plenty to talk about. Yet, I will keep this review simple, as I plan on writing one hell of a monster very soon.
Gameplay from an Ork:
Jokes aside, for those who have played about 30 minutes and are ready to give up: I know the UI is almost impossible at the beginning, it's because Stellaris is unlike many 4x Space Strategy games in the same genre. Take your time, learn how to play it and what makes it unique compared to the other 4x's games out there. You won't regret it, you'll be glad you learned this new take on the genre.
For those who are having a buggy launch: Give it time, don't refund it yet as this may be a game you end up enjoying if the problems are solved.
For those who think this is the best game ever: After 9.5 hours of straight Stellaris goodness, I can safely say, somethings are being exaggerated. This game is damn good and leaves room for plenty of additional content in the future but it's not the best 4x Strategy game ever. It does a lot good but it mostly does things that have already been done in a new way so it's more of refreshing perspective than it is a genre defining masterpiece.
For those on the fence: Take the plunge, unless you're having a buggy launch, you can't go wrong. Look at the treatment other Paradox games get, there will be more content to go with this already sizeable game.

Necropolis, for me, manages to tick every box for what makes a game interesting and worth playing. It's a rogue-like dungeon crawler with randomly generated dungeons and
, yet it never becomes repetitive or boring.
The art style is interesting and well-done; do not let the fact that it isn't graphically intensive make you think that it's lazy or poorly done. It gives off a very-much Wind Waker or Journey feel. Music direction, as well, is fantastic. It gives you a bit of a pumping fight-tune, but not so much that it gets annoying or becomes too boring. It is lighthearted and dark at all the right moments.
Despite criticisms, the combat system is pretty fleshed out and has a good feel. There are multiple tiers of weapons, with different categories within those tiers. Some weapons are slow (in particular, the starter weapon), others are fast. Some deal a lot of damage, others... you get the idea. As you get better weapons, the lows and highs become more apparent. But if you never manage to find a weapon other than the starter sword'n'board, you'll definitely think that combat sucks.
My only complaint is that dodging/escaping from a large group of enemies is incredibly difficult. Stay out of corners and you should be fine.
One very Souls-esque bit is that there is
handholding. You're told the controls, you're told when you need to eat, and that's it. You'll find potions and items that have effects you won't know about. Some have positive effects, others don't. The same goes for spells and codexes (buffs that last through your death).
Ultimately, this game is an immense amount of fun (for me, at least). There's nice visuals, good music, a good combat system, crafting, and decent writing all around.
PROS:
CONS:
All-in-all, 9/10.

SUMMARY: Though it has its heart in the right place, Kaiju-A-GoGo is a game that just doesn't offer enough to do it's great idea and design justice.  Repetitive play, clunky design, and a feeling of being unfinished get in the way of the fun.
Kaiju-A-GoGo is a kind of reverse X-Com or reverse Defend The Planet type game.  You're the force of evil that threatens the world, and it's your goal to conquer it while others try and stop you.  They will, of course, fall before your might.
The game itself is a mixture of Kaiju stomper/environment destroyer, RPG, resource gatherer, and evil base management.  You send your Kaiju forth to devestate cities, gather resources while you traumatize the population into submission, and then upgrade your base.  As cities fall before you, they send tribute to further fuel your efforts - which you'll need as forces rally to stop you.
The game comes down to:
1) Send a Kaiju to a city, and use a simple point and click method, plus various powers, to cause havok.  Gather resources as you smash and conquer.
2) Use resource to upgrade your Kaiju.
3) Use resources to upgrade your base (including deciding on geographic layout).
4) Repeat until you conquer the world.
Unfortunately, the game's various pieces don't line up:
1) Combat feels clunky and repetitive - point, crush, lookt, continue.  It moves slow, targeting is iffy, and environments get samey very quickly.
2) Kaiju Upgrading takes time, though there is an extensive upgrade system for those who get deep into the game.
3) Base management has some strange interface issues, but mostly comes down to trying to clear land and build structures with resources.  There's not a lot of guidance or help to determining your path (some simple projections would help)
The game ends up being less fun, more management, rather slow, and not that exciting - and there's not a lot of initial guidance on the gameplay that make a lot of it a case of stabbling in the dark.
Though the game is, simply, very flawed and unpolished, I do have to credit the great art style and the enthusiasm.  There's a kind of cartoony vibe provided to the game, with amusing character designs and a real sense of humor.  It's a game that feels "right" - until you play it.
The designers seem very commited to the game, promising new monsters and updates.  That gives me some hope as it shows promise, but it's not there yet.  It feels very Early Access - and not in a good way.
So I have some hope - but for now, take a pass, unless you truly want to relive the old days of Crush, Crumble, and Chomp or The Creature That Ate Sheboygan.  The game has a way to go, it's a bit of a monster of the wrong kind.

Lots of people compare Stellaris to games like Alpha Centauri and GalCiv. Personally, I consider Stellaris to be a worthy successor to Distant worlds: streamlined, but with a lot of the complexity intact, and relying on real-time management rather than static turn-based doldrums. Paradox has always excelled at information-rich interfaces, and Stellaris is no exception, solving a major drawback to a lot of 4X games (Distant Worlds in particular) by providing multiple access points to information and screens, and offering the Paradox-standard Outliner that updates in real time to show you what your units are doing.
I have minor quibbles. The resource options are a bit stale (energy, minerals, influence) and lack immersion. More problematic, the research mechanic hearkens back to MOO (and Star Drive 2), where you have to pick from a small set of options each time. Both of these issues make Stellaris play more like a game than a simulation, and I  prefer my 4Xs to be more of the latter than the former.
But hey. It's Stellaris, it's Paradox, and it scratches my Distant Worlds itch for those times when I can't be bothered to fire up my VM and boot into Windows. 10/10, with rice.

Just the name of this game has you wondering what it could be about. Abound with curiosity, diving in head first might not always be the best idea. What claims to be an homage to City destroyers of yester year, ends up making us wish this game remained in that time. Kaiju-a-GoGo has a somewhat creative concept but, does having a game with giant city destroying monsters automatically make it worth your time?
With basically zero tutorial you are dropped into the intro of the game. Some characters flash on the screen only long enough to become annoying, and to tell you that you’re about to unleash your monster on Anchorage. This may seem like a fine way to teach you game mechanics, but the only mechanics really to teach are click where to go, and automatically destroy things along the way. Each building you destroy gives out some type of resource that is indicated by a symbol. Batteries, Books, Crystals, Money, and Chicken legs; are the resources dropped when buildings are destroyed. It is not immediately, or eventually apparent what each of these symbols represents. Chicken legs are to represent bio fuel in this game; I guess an oil drum was to confusing.
After returning from your first outing with your loot, It is quickly taken from you in the form of expenses for your secret base. These expenses include operating costs mostly, but you can spend your ill-gotten gains on upgrades for your facility. Your monster needs time to recover from its last endeavour; giving you time to explore your island.
Your mad scientist utopia starts covered in jungle that your need to periodically remove. Using the resources that your monster gathers from the destroyed cities, you can build facilities that will allow you to improve your monsters abilities and better defend your island. Defending your island is essential as armies from vengeance seeking countries will come looking for a fight. For the most part you build facilities that produce resources which you use to build more facilities; making this process somewhat of a grind. Other structures include warehouses that give you a bigger max capacity for specific units. It never feels like you will be hitting your capacity but, players who do a lot of grinding could eventually run into this problem.
Essentially the game is a kind of cycle where you use your monster to destroy cities, use the resources to build up your facilities, which in turn makes your monster better at destroying cities. For some this might be seen as a grind, and it certainly feels like one too. Your monster has a capacity for how many resources it can carry back from a city. This makes the progression incredibly slow paced, and feels like an intentional way to stretch out the game. You’ll increasingly feel the futility every time you come back to your island with such a small amount of loot.
All of these problems resemble something that you would find on Facebook, rather than Steam. In fact the entire game reeks of a freemium online and mobile game. The resources you collect are over simplified, the monsters power ups are few and far between, and the improvements you make to your island take time to be completed. Your monster also needs time to be repaired between destructions. Granted there is an in game clock that you can manipulate to make faster or slower but, this seems like an online flash game with real time waiting periods that has been adapted for a full release. This kind of game design is essentially flawed. Constructing a game that is designed to waste time and make money, isn’t the way to release a full game on Steam. It also feels like that’s how they landed on this rather expensive price tag. The price you pay on steam must factor in what they think the average person online spends on this game over their playtime; but that’s just a theory.
Besides being a cash grab some of the artwork is okay. It resembles the first Plants vs. Zombies, with a colourful hand drawn art style. Although where PvZ was over the top and cartoony, this game sits on the fence between cartoon and reality. Not picking a side in this matter becomes problematic. The art style wants to tell a quirky story while some of the dialogue contradicts it with references to real world cities. I think this game could reach the same kind of audience as PvZ, if they would just play up the wackiness of the concept. For instance, your monster looks like something out of a kids cartoon; thumbs up. But the building you destroy are obviously illustrated with a certain level of realism. The cities you destroy look more out of SimCity then what I would expect a skyline to look like in a kids show; thumbs down. Overall the artwork has potential, but looks cheap and is cheapened by the animations. The monster moving doesn’t look very convincing, in fact it just looks like twinked animation. Not something that most people would really notice while destroying a city, but it’s so bad it’s distracting
On the whole this is a game for kids. I guess it’s not really something to aspire to, selling a game to kids who don’t know that it’s worse than any other game from the 90’s and early 2000’s. Ultimately I would give a child Roller Coaster Tycoon, also available on Steam for less money, before I gave him something as confusing as this mess of menus. That’s not a knock on RCT, it’s legitimately an entertaining game for all age groups. This game just fails on the execution of its gameplay; and if a game isn’t fun to play then whose going to play it. Games that grind are fun when it’s amounting to something, but this just doesn’t ever seem worthwhile. Your money would be much better spent on either game aforementioned in this review. We just wish this monster never reared its ugly head.

But some of the issues that the game has right now are ones that the developers need to fix and not the players. It doesn't take an entire studio to fix some issues and not having the others work on other things is a waste of resources. So the whole "OMG WHY ARE THEY DOING DLC? FIX THE GAME FIRST," thing is silly.
The problem that I have with the game is that after like ~50 hours in you can really tell how rushed out the door and bare bones this game is.Vanilla CK2 and EU4 had way more to offer mechanically than this game does now. That is not to say that Stellaris won't be great down the line but what we got on offer at the beginning I don't think was worth the asking price.
If you are still on the fence right now about buying it, hold off for a little while.

"How could I kill such a beautiful creature? I am a witcher, not a dragon slayer."
I know, my review for The Witcher 1 was bad, and I am honestly sorry about that. But if you want to play The Witcher 2, buy and play through The Witcher 1. I will explain why in the Features-Section.
___________________________________________________
++Story++
A ship is swimming before a coast. On the ship, sitting on his thrown, is King Demawend, and his minions are amusing him. In that moment, a big bulky assassin with the eyes of a cat climbs on the ship, kills all minions and decapitates the King. You can imagine the havoc that is caused by the assassination of a King.
Some time later:
King Foltest is mid in the war against his beloved wife, because he was having too much sex with other woman that gave birth to his ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s. Foltests consultant is no one less but Geralt of Riva. They fight together against the La Valettes. At the end of the battle, Foltest stands infront of his children and their guardian, an old blind monk. As Foltests children come to him and Geralt does not pay attention, the monk ends the masquerade and shows his true self, the killer of King Demawend. He slays Foltest and dissappears without a trace. Geralt is the black sheep and swears that he will find the killer on his own.
You get many many chances to make decisions that will change the story significantly, and that is amazing!
++Gameplay++
The gameplay is sadly the weakest point of the game.
The fights have changed from clicking to an actual action adventure combat system, which is a great step into the right direction, BUT they are horribly unprecise, the recoil from an enemies hit strikes Geralt so hard down that getting up will give the enemies enough time to kill you as if you were more of a helpless puppy but a great white wolf.
The level- and skill system is well made. You do not get enough experience to end up as the ultimate witcher of doom at the end of the game. You can skill into 3 main directions: Alchemy, sword skills and magic. I took the sword tree because I am just a dull brawler, and it worked well, even though the fights are unfair.
The menu is at first confusing as ♥♥♥♥, but eventually you understand it.
Sadly, the programming is so bad that the game simply crashes in random distances, but I managed to get this game working for full 12 hours without one crash.
++Grafics++
The grafics on ultra settings are great, and together with the beautiful design of the game, they will make you gape in amazement.
++Music++
Like in The Witcher 1, the music is wonderful, so beautiful that I want to cry that the Enhanced Edition does not contain the OST. Especially the song "Dwarven Stone on Dwarven Stone", the song that plays in the Credits as well, is unbelievable beautiful.
++Features++
The game has the "import save file" from Mass Effect, so you are technically forced to play through all games to see your ending. I will do it and play The Witcher 1 again, even though I prefer The Witcher 2 by far.
There are handdrawn flash scenes in the game that show you flashbacks of Geralts past, and both the scenes and the art are absolutely stunning and wonderful.
Going into a tavern, talking to the people and listening to their problems shows you how much love was put into this game. Much swearing!

A 16-bit, top-down, DDR dungeon crawler? Yes. It's brilliant and a shining example of why Indie games are incredible.
Crypt of the NecroDancer is combination of rhythm-game (think things like DDR, Guitar Hero, or Audio Surf) and a Rogue-like (games that typically have perma-death, randomly generated dungeons and items) with a fantastic retro '16-bit' art style. If you already like Rogue-likes and don't have this game then you're doing it wrong.
I'm a fan of Rogue-likes in general but one of the struggles I have is replayability. The features that define many Rogue-like work for a while but eventually one gets tired of replaying the first stages over and over, then FINALLY making it to "that one level" only to die immediately and repeat the whole process again. For many Rogue-likes the entire game is centered around this cycle, there's really nothing to *do* elsewhere; no open world to explore or shops (outside of shopkeepers inside the dungeon). Where CotND differs is in offering players a way to customize the game's meta. It starts with little things like buying items that will show up in chests, buying permanent character upgrades, and removing undesired items from random drops. You can also take up a daily challange, practice against dungeon foes and bosses, and test your brain/reflexes in additional challenge modes. There are NPCs to unlock, a mode designed to be played on a DDR 'dance pad', and a whole slew of characters to unlock, each of which have their own properties/features/mechanics to master.

This game manages the feat of being both too short and too long.
How you may ask?
In the first section of the game, if a 90 minute game can be said to have sections, your primary task is gathering journal pages. There are point and click puzzles, but to anyone who plays point and clicks, they pose no real obstacle. Anyway, the journals tell an interesting Frankenstein story that I would pay $1 or so for. I bought the game at $0.50, so at least I feel I got my money's worth.
After you finish reading the romantic horror story depicted in the journal, and wishing there was more story to read, the game takes a hard left turn to making a horrific undead army of mad science. The sudden tone shift is jarring. And then the sequence lasts barely 15 minutes, just long enough to lose the earlier focus, but not long enough to deal with the repercussions of such thinking.
For the most part, I don't recommend the game due to its lack of focus and short run time. But if you're bored and it's on sale, it's not the worst thing you could buy.

This game is a short point-and-click adventuring type of game. There are no "real" puzzles to solve, but there's exploration and commentary from the protagonist. The nods to literary greats like Mary Shelley and Edgar Allan Poe were lovely, especially for bookworms like me! (There's also a character who is extremely reminiscent of the Bride of Frankenstein.)
The history and character information are fleshed out via journal pages/letters that you find while exploring. Each story is intriguing, with maybe one or two unexpected, little twists. While the style of the fonts were pretty, they were sometimes hard to read, but even I -- with glasses several years old -- read them just fine.
The music went well with the art style, and I appreciated some of the more dramatic moments. The voice acting was pretty good, not over-the-top or cheesy at all. Mechanics were easy and intuitive.
Overall, this is a great game for someone interested in a more casual point-and-click experience with a good amount of storyline. A bit short, but more than worth it for a sale price.

This game should be called "Europa Galaxis I". It's a much more appropriate title given that Paradox have merely dressed up a cut-down EU4 as a space game. Most of the mechanics of the base EU4 game are present in Stellaris, and I don't think any mechanics of this game are new or original. I write BASE GAME because, like in EU4 where your allies won't be helpful unless you get the DLC for that, same goes for Stellaris.
If you love EU4 and love space games, you might enjoy this. If you don't know EU4, then I'll describe what I mean in more detail for you... This is a "Grand" strategy game, which means there is (er, "should be") little to no micromanagement. It's all very macro.
For example, you can manage UP TO 5 planets directly, and the rest have to go to sectors, which are AI-managed. But then again "managing" is a strong word, it's more like "overseeing". You can tell the sector AI to focus on minerals, military, science, or energy production, and set a tax rate of 0%, 25%, 50% or 75%. That's it, your job is done. Well, you can assign a governor to a sector, for some bonuses. You can design ships, but only in a very limited way. The automatic, self-updating ship designs are mostly sufficient. And so on.
But for all that "macro-ness", the game is sorely lacking in utility. For example, in a war, you want assault troops. But you have to raise them from each world, tell each of them where to go, and so on. Oh, and once the war is over, you have to do the process in reverse. There are no rally points or any "Land all assault armies on nearest owned planet" button. So you have to spend your time click-clicking like mad to get these guys back on the ground.
Oh, and don't even get me started on the fleets... Sure, you can split a fleet in two, or merge two fleets. You can even transfer individual ships to a new fleet... INDIVIDUALLY. That is, you have to slowly and painfully scroll through your fleet's ship list, which can be hundreds long and is NOT SORTED, and select the individual ship you want to move. Good luck having fun when you are doing that 50 times.
I am confident most of these things will be fixed through patches and DLC. But therein lies the problem: EU4 already has "The Art of War". They already have the code. Except it's not in this game. It will be, mark my words, sold as a DLC for this game as well, while it really should be a core mechanic of the game. Plus it wouldn't even be new content, as it would require only a slight tweak on the EU4 code.
All in all, this game is as empty as the interstellar space it describes. The multiplayer is decent because human players are not as boring as a barebones, content-less game that this is. I am very afraid that Paradox is pulling an Activision on us: release game after game with the same core mechanics and sell you tons of DLC for each. If so, I am very displeased.
TL;DR:
Score: 10
Graphics and sound are great. Performance is OK. Game doesn't crash. Fun factor is highly subjective. However:
-1 for bugs
-1 for core mechanics being absent
-1 for no innovation
-1 for being a space-age rehash of EU4
-2 for lack of content
Final tally 4/10
My recommendation: there are many much better space 4X games out there. This one might be worth half its release price. Maybe.

First off, props to the ambition and vision the developers had for this game. Upon first exploring the combat,design layout, crafting system, various weapons /items, and procedural generation, I certainly received the impression that this game had the potential to achieve endless and addictive replayability. Granted it is an indie-game and I did not venture far to come to my recomendation, but from what little i experienced, this game has fallen short in the most significant of its aspects. Namely the combat.
Pros:
- The art design is polygonic, simple and easy on the eyes, its easy to distinguish enemies and the layout itself. The character models and the particle effects are fantastic, with dyes and elemental weapons simmering with bright colours.
- The music is excellent and certainly brings the right mood for the game.
- Procedural generation keeps things fresh and adds to the excitement of exploring the unknown.
- Weapons possess classes which have their own varied charged attacks (weapon arts) much like dark souls 3 that creates greater diversity in  weapons.
- Unknown potions and scrolls can either have highly beneficial or devastating effects on the player which certainly adds to the excitement.
Cons:
- No options of keybinding, really?
- Poor optimization, sudden lag spikes, stuttering, (I can run pretty much any game on high/max with 60fps)
- The humour in the game feels forced and does not feel natural at all, alot of it isnt very funny, resulting in the overall immersion of the game kinda awkward.
- Combat is very much the biggest issue with the game, the player's attacks and animation doesnt feel fluid but feels very clunky. There arent many variations with attacks on the weapons, there is the light, heavy and charged attack but none of these attacks seem to flow well with each other.The light and heavy weapon swings dont feel like it carries much weight and the animations feel very unpolished and is downright boring.
- Weapons have literally no information other than vague descriptions, it feels very confusing having to choose one weapon or shield between the other due to 0 comparison in their stats. This is lazy and very offputting.
- Lack of progression, and thus lack of fear of death. The only progression one can make between playthroughs are dyes and codexes which are passive effects which of course have no proper description in what any of them do. It seems only one can be equipped at a time which is just isnt enough.
- Character customization is very weak, you can choose between a male, or female model and different colours of their outfit,(there are dyes you can collect to have a larger variety of colours) but thats really it. Although there isnt a class system, having different models to choose from wouldve been great.
- The combat system should have been the most polished aspect of the game, yet it is a disappointment and is the prime factor in my non-recommendation, the devs tried to accomplish many aspects of the game but due to poor focus, most of it feels lacking, especially the combat.

I recomend putting off for awhile till the devs improve the combat and other various details with the game before buying it.
