First and foremost, let it be known this game is exactly as anime as it looks (which is pretty anime). Haters beware.
When I got this game, all I was expecting was a silly magic-themed rpg with schedule-based stat progression (you’ll see what I mean in game). After my first playthrough, it turns out there’s also a solid second half of the game in the form of adventure game-esque dungeon exams.
Basically, you’re thrown into a small dungeon where you need to use the magic you’ve learned so far to solve a puzzle and escape. Each puzzle seems to encourage multiple approaches because of the huge number of utility spells you’ll have access to. Check the screenshot on the store page that has the spell list – the vast majority of them are more along the lines of “detect charm” and “transform stone” rather than fireball or lightning bolt, which usually means you can magical Mcgyver your way through each exam in multiple ways. This ends up being pretty important since how you develop your spell list is entirely up to you, and getting deep into one spell tree requires skimping on the others, so missing a key spell from a spell tree you’ve been neglecting isn’t a completely screwed situation if you can get creative with the other spells.
I’d like to give an example of one of my recent exams for how open-ended it can be, but I’ll post it in the comments instead in case you don’t want any of the dungeon puzzles spoiled.
As for the actual writing and story bits (which honestly make up the majority of the game, I’m definitely always itching for more of the dungeons), while the dialogue isn’t Portal levels of consistently good comedy, the characters are at least fleshed out enough to be memorable and I can safely say at least one event in game made me feel like a piece of♥♥♥♥♥♥for making a poor decision, so I found myself pretty invested in the setting. Turns out giving a schoolfull of teenagers magic might not always be a good idea? Oh, and the default protagonist name is Mary Sue, so the game is fairly self aware about the setting being “Harry Potter, but now I get to go!”

Belladonna has a few things going for it. The setting is well done, a nice old castle with big rooms, and the artwork is pretty good.  The small amounts of music included are decent as well, although the semi-jump scare reveal music tends to play over the other sounds, lessening it's impact. But the game has too many flaws and issues to recommend at full price.
First of all, it's incredibly short. I beat the entire thing in less than an hour and a half, and didn't push myself to go quickly. The extra time is from me letting it run overnight to get trading cards. The primary voice actor for your character is pretty good, but her voice doesn't match the creepy gothic environment. She sounds like a modern, 21st century female, not a recently brought back from the dead monstrosity. But that's not the worst of it. The second voice actor is atrocious, with a faux British accent that is poorly done and not consistently performed. Some of the sound effects are ridiculous. One of them is literally the AIM log on sound for a door opening. The environments feel fairly sterile; except for a few of the more elaborate rooms, most are barren and uninteresting, despite being well rendered.
The story isn't too complicated, and it's revealed mostly through journal pages you find scattered throughout the house you're exploring. There is a bit of mystery, but no major twist or huge intrigue once you figure out who the major players in the story are. It does weirdly go past what would be the natural conclusion, then turns around and ends much too abruptly. And the puzzles are all quite easy, with the protagonist often explaining what needs to be done through her commentary. It's annoying when you think "I knew that!" but don't get the full satisfaction of having figured it out.
Belladona isn't terrible, but it's not all that good. Still, it's frequently in bundles or hugely discounted, and it's worth a look if you can get it for a buck or less, as I did.

Dust: AET is a 2-D platformer that plays a bit like a beat-em-up. Maybe not intentionally, but still like it.  The combat system is similar to that of Muramasa: The Demon Blade, so fans of this game would probably enjoy Dust: AET as well.  Essentially, you have your left and your right mouse buttons, and using different combinations of them (along with Fidget's projectiles) you can perform different moves to beat up your foes!
With that in mind, the game is essentially very easy even if you're spamming buttons. I started my game on casual and because of the lack of issues I ran into, I bumped it up to normal. Found the game to be slightly tougher but not too much.  The gameplay itself wasn't too challenging, save for the timing on parrying though if you test it for a bit you'll get the hang of it.  The puzzles aren't difficult either, and only had real trouble with one or two, though finding some of the hidden secrets can be a challenge but the map tells you in what section they are which helps.
The story is decent, and it's what kept me playing the game (after the addicting combat style in which it felt fun to beat up enemies). The story has it's ups and downs, and while predictable in some elements, it does have some twists that I didn't expect, along with dealing with racism and death.
Overall, I massively enjoyed the game, way more than I expected to, and would have happily paid the full game price if I knew I would have had that much fun with it! If it happens to go on sale and you're contemplating getting the game, I say go for it.  At the very least you can feel like a blade-spinning tornado god with the massive amount of damage and destruction you can do with multiple enemies on the screen.

I'm going to keep on playing this a bit more and edit this as needed, but here's my current feel for the game.  It needs ...more...  They have a good game foundation built (other than some bugs that can be annoying but not game breaking), but I can see it getting old fairly fast.  After a bunch of runs in to destroy cities, usually about 3-4 per city so far to conquer it all the way, it does gets a little old hat doing the same routine each time.  Especially the early game.
Stomping around in the cities is just left click to move and it auto attacks anything in your path.  Your abilites are tied into the same energy pool of pickups that you want to bring back to your island, so for quite awhile you will be conserving your energy as much as possible.  Makes things feel very slow early on, although later it gets better.
I should also add that it is a bit on the grindy side to the point that cutting build/training times in half would really help kill off the facebook game vibe you get while playing sometimes.
All that said, I do enjoy playing it.  It is by no means a terrible game, without Rampage around anymore there really isn't much else like this out there.  The graphics are fine, the cities look good with a fair number of different structures in them, and a city on fire at night is flat out beautiful.  It does a great job with the atmosphere and making you feel like a giant monster running amock.

I have no regrets purchasing it but I am leaving my review negative for now simply because this game is not for everyone.  TLDR - Very slow begining, fairly grindy, has a bit of a facebook game feel to it, but fun concept and great in small doses.  Really wish there was more than a YES/NO system honestly, I'd say 7/10 in it's current state.  Will update as they patch the game.

This game should be called "Europa Galaxis I". It's a much more appropriate title given that Paradox have merely dressed up a cut-down EU4 as a space game. Most of the mechanics of the base EU4 game are present in Stellaris, and I don't think any mechanics of this game are new or original. I write BASE GAME because, like in EU4 where your allies won't be helpful unless you get the DLC for that, same goes for Stellaris.
If you love EU4 and love space games, you might enjoy this. If you don't know EU4, then I'll describe what I mean in more detail for you... This is a "Grand" strategy game, which means there is (er, "should be") little to no micromanagement. It's all very macro.
For example, you can manage UP TO 5 planets directly, and the rest have to go to sectors, which are AI-managed. But then again "managing" is a strong word, it's more like "overseeing". You can tell the sector AI to focus on minerals, military, science, or energy production, and set a tax rate of 0%, 25%, 50% or 75%. That's it, your job is done. Well, you can assign a governor to a sector, for some bonuses. You can design ships, but only in a very limited way. The automatic, self-updating ship designs are mostly sufficient. And so on.
But for all that "macro-ness", the game is sorely lacking in utility. For example, in a war, you want assault troops. But you have to raise them from each world, tell each of them where to go, and so on. Oh, and once the war is over, you have to do the process in reverse. There are no rally points or any "Land all assault armies on nearest owned planet" button. So you have to spend your time click-clicking like mad to get these guys back on the ground.
Oh, and don't even get me started on the fleets... Sure, you can split a fleet in two, or merge two fleets. You can even transfer individual ships to a new fleet... INDIVIDUALLY. That is, you have to slowly and painfully scroll through your fleet's ship list, which can be hundreds long and is NOT SORTED, and select the individual ship you want to move. Good luck having fun when you are doing that 50 times.
I am confident most of these things will be fixed through patches and DLC. But therein lies the problem: EU4 already has "The Art of War". They already have the code. Except it's not in this game. It will be, mark my words, sold as a DLC for this game as well, while it really should be a core mechanic of the game. Plus it wouldn't even be new content, as it would require only a slight tweak on the EU4 code.
All in all, this game is as empty as the interstellar space it describes. The multiplayer is decent because human players are not as boring as a barebones, content-less game that this is. I am very afraid that Paradox is pulling an Activision on us: release game after game with the same core mechanics and sell you tons of DLC for each. If so, I am very displeased.
TL;DR:
Score: 10
Graphics and sound are great. Performance is OK. Game doesn't crash. Fun factor is highly subjective. However:
-1 for bugs
-1 for core mechanics being absent
-1 for no innovation
-1 for being a space-age rehash of EU4
-2 for lack of content
Final tally 4/10
My recommendation: there are many much better space 4X games out there. This one might be worth half its release price. Maybe.

Liked:
+ General presentation of the game is great! Everything is atmospheric and there are many locations where the pieces of art and sound come together so perfectly, it demands a press of the screenshot key.
+ For as detailed of a game as it is, it runs amazingly well even on an older machine.
+ The Combo Chain system introduces an element to combat that flows well and keeps the pace high.
+ The story is simple and easy to follow, but it's presented in a way that holds your attention and imagination.
+ The "metroid-vania" design roots the game in familiar territory.
+ Character Progression: starting off knowing most of the combo attacks that you will be using throughout the game feels powerful, and allows the eventual power ups to be more specialized.
Disliked:
- Occasionally, character designs and animations have jarring differences between dialogue, cinematic sequences, and gameplay.
- Sometimes there is too much happening on-screen, causing you to lose track of characters, which often means getting hit and breaking the Combo Chain.
- There's an arbitrary mechanic that keeps your stats from getting too unbalanced from each other, and so, does not allow you a whole lot of freedom in making custom builds.
Other Notes:
= Recording quality and mixing for vocals is all over the scale and changes throughout the game.
= Combat is very melee focused; there are not as many options for spell and ranged attacks.
In Closing:
Dust: An Elysian Tail is a game that plays with your imagination, and rewards you in turn. While not earth-shattering on any technical or design level, it has a lot of heart and character that it is willing to share with the player from the word "go;" and that's something I think the industry has been losing touch on over the years.
The art, music, sound, writing, effects, and gameplay all perform their roles together to make a very unique experience, and though there may be bumps and hiccups through the adventure, this is an easy recommendation to make.
I actually feel a little guilty buying it at a discount.
Bonus:
* Dean Dodrill is the sole man who designed and programmed Dust: An Elysian Tail. Major props to him on this major accomplishment. I am eager to see more.

Prior to the recent popularity of crowdunded games, this game is what a publisher would call "a loser". Many of us who grew up in the games world of the late 80's and 90's miss the days when a neat concept game would hit the shelves and surprise with something new. For the decade prior, a new game was the latest FPS, RPG or MMO whos distinguishing feature would be how much sharper the graphics are THIS time. Far from perfect, but a lot of fun, Kaiju-A-GoGo is essentially a unique strategy and tactics RPG about destroying cities and conquering the world with a giant robot.
Concept: Rather than state that the game is bad or good because I happen to like it, It would be better to simply describe the product's appeal to me, and let the reader decide if it appeals to him/her as well. The objective is to conquer the world. The game consists of a strategy metagame and of course the tactical destroy-the-city game.
The strategy gameflow is to build up various resources to improve your Kaiju. You only get one. The game has a base building feature to generate resources and train the Kaiju similar to X-com. The Kaiju is improved by adding abilities you research in a tiered structure. Each successive tier features more abilities than the last, causing the player to be more judicious about which abilities he wants to research.
The tactical game consists of ordering the kaiju to move in a certain direction in the city and using the active abilities for certain effects. The objective is to destroy as much as possible, driving the city's morale down and picking up resources to bring back with you. The lower the morale, the higher the chance the city will surrender. Building types will generate certain types of resources and certain cities have more of some resources than others. As the city wears down, the defenders will grow stronger and the player has to consider the endurance of the Kaiju vs. the his ability to escape or cause a surrender. A surrender is the main way to generate the money resource.
I'm a big fan of this type of gameplay, so this is basically my list of pros. The game is a progressive/grind type of metastrategy game, which does not appeal to everyone. Making the Kaiju stronger and destroying a city is great fun for me, and though the mechanics have some problems, the build up is quite satisfying.
Now for the problems:
The Kaiju can be hard to control sometimes and the amount of enemies and congestion makes maneuvering more difficult than it should be. Some common sense changes, such as allowing clicking off map to escape, and scrolling using arrow keys or some alternate method would be helpful. The kaiju also has a tendency to just shoot whatever it wants rather than the intended target. This can be frustrating.
There are some siily bugs, boats on land and at least once, I had an issue where I wouldn't take damage, my shots wouldnt land and the defenders stopped spawning.
Todays gamer needs a much larger amount of handholding than any generation prior, and this game does very little of it. Though the game can be figured out quite easily through trial and error plus deductive reasoning, these players often have youtube accounts with thousands of other easily confused player subscribers. A manual would probably help them enjoy thier game experience better. I don't know, for me the idea that I should look for an escape route for my Kaiju and be prepared to dig through some buildings when I'm at a certain health level...seems common sense to me.
Unfortunately, this small team of developers did not make the game in first person, or use the unreal-whatever engine to generate graphics. If you need these things to enjoy a game
, maybe there will be an action spin-off rail shooter if this game takes off...just for you. The art style won't appeal to everyone, and sprites are a thing of the past, though for some sad reason, creepy not-really-lifelike awkward 3d models of people are not.
Thousands of people that have wasted their entire lives playing an mmo where you grind, have done a good job of telling the world how bad it is to grind. This game has a grind. If you enjoy the game, it's an enjoyable grind.
tldr: All in all a fantastic example of a decent crowdfunded game. It provides a gameplay concept (destroying cities with a giant robot x-com style) that would never see the light of day in the traditional model. Even though there are hits and misses, this is a great time to be a gamer.

I got this game during a sale and didn't expect to like it as much as I did.
First up I should probably mention that I played this game with a controller, and I'd highly recommend playing Dust with one yourself if you can.
As a fan of Action RPGs I find the combat in Dust quite fun, It may come across as button-mashy but there are plenty of times where you really need to think about what you're doing, and the game tries to make sure you can't just button-mash your way through by throwing a new enemy that needs a certain tactic every so often. While the combat isn't exactly what I'd call deep, its surprisingly fun and I don't find myself getting bored of it, and you feel like a boss when you manage to pull off several-hunred-hit-combos.
The leveling up system is pretty standard, every level you can choose to increase your HP, Attack, Defence or "Special Move" stat, but there isn't much more to it then that, it is nice to be able to have some control over how the character grows though. The same goes for the customization, every so often you'll come across a new piece of weapon or armour that outclasses what you currently have equipt, so there isn't much reason not to equip the new piece. You can craft new pieces of equipment if you manage to find a blueprint and have the neccisarary materials (both the blueprints and materials come from killing monsters, or the occasional quest reward).
As far as story goes, its not exactly anything special, but it's managed to keep me interested. All the dialogue being voiced is a nice touch too, although some of the accents from the villagers are painfully stereotypical. The music is quite nice too, especially for an indie game, I found myself noticing how nice the background music was more times then one.
Overall I'm more then happy with this game, I'd be happy to pay the normal price for this game (which is currently $15) knowning what its like, and if you can get it on sale then its an easy recommendation from me!

ABZU is an utterly captivating experience from start to finish. It is one of the most peaceful and relaxing games you can play. Its art style is vibrant yet simple, and its story is vaguely conveyed yet completely relatable. The controls become pretty intuitive especially to those who have played driving games or flight simulators with a controller. If you are a fan of Journey, Flower, or flow this game definitely deserves your attention.
As previously mentioned, the story is not told through any expositive cut scenes but rather through the environment. The whole of the experience takes place in the water, either in the beautiful tropical aquatic setting or an oddly mechanical and dangerous area which appears to be taking over afore mentioned pretty one. There are also the ruins of some ancient underwater civilization adorned with paintings on their tiled walls which help give some context as well. Aside from that it is left up to the player to piece together the specifics of the narrative to the best of their ability. The simple narrative is perfect for this kind of environmental story telling. It is mysterious but gives you just enough to keep you wanting to see more and can be completed in an hour or two. Though it is short it is quite satisfying.
The level design and environments accompanied by the music really complements the game play, the music especially as it changes dynamically according to what is going on currently. This helps to create moments where you can’t help but be completely awestruck or crack a big fat grin. Game play is pretty simple; to swim forward use the right trigger kind of like accelerating in a racing game, analog sticks are used to change direction of turn the camera in order to take in the sights. One very relaxing feature found throughout is the ability to meditate while sitting on certain statues. While meditating the player can observe all the sea creatures in the area and learn their names, which makes for an educational experience. Very simple puzzles are found and used as obstacles to progress to the next area. The gameplay may seem minimalistic but it is just right for this kind of experience.
Performance is solid for the most part but there are a couple serious frame hitches which occur particularly when there are a large amount of particle effects such as after one of the couple less peaceful moments in the game. The performance drop does not occur frequently enough to garner any concern anyhow.
If you want to sit down for an hour or two and dive into one of the most Zen like games you will ever play, look no further than ABZU.

Well no - it's definitely not 6.3 and ♥♥♥♥ you IGN once again.
At it's current state the game is playable albeit very unpolished. It is very similar to Europa Universalis or Hearts of Iron and unfortunately is rife with micromanagement of the latter one. You have to constantly tweak your planets, pay attention to science and construction vessels and negotiate with dozens of empires which sounds interesting at first but quickly turns into a repetitive chore. Allowing faster ways to switch between planets and auto-upgrading of planet tiles should be a priority for Paradox.
The whole vassal system seems to be unfinished as well - AI will never build or upgrade space ports and ships, and you have to manually select every planet in sector from the map to do it yourself.
Other than a lot of unnecessary micro and lack of some UI features the game is actually pretty solid even without 100 inevitable dlc's paradox is going to release. The graphics are decent, the music is good, AI makes "some" effort and it is true that it doesn't actually attack you the moment they become slightly superior like in other 4x games.
The game also restricts your expansion with influence points, borders and lack of habitable planets. Even on a huge map with 1000 planets you won't get that many colonies before you are surrounded by other empires. This means that unless they are really lucky with starting point and resources - everyone is going to be more or less equal mid game. Which can be good or bad depending on how fast you built those frontier bases which extend your borders early on.
I can recommend this game even in it's current state. I have no doubt that paradox is going to release numerous patches and dlc's to address most of those issues. Considering that modding support is also there we can expect a lot of custom races like star wars, star trek, babylon 5, etc that will make this game even better.

Blood has to be one of my favorite games ever, period. It is the one game I always come back to.
So, why am I then not recommending it? Easy: this game did not age well. If you did play the game before, you already know how awesome it is and you don't need this review. But if you are the target audience of this review - someone who hasn't played it yet and whose vision is not clouded by nostalgia - I can imagine you will have a hard time to get into it.
Even at release the graphics were dated, everything being drowned in blurry brown and grey pixels. This release has literally zero Steam-integration and just runs in Dosbox, with a fairly minimal resoluton and pretty disappointing framerate. I know that gameplay triumphs graphics, but this Blood really looks and feels outdated.
The controls are very oldschool and you will have to use external programs if you want decent mouse + keyboard. Again, those who did play it when it came out decades ago will have no problems with only arrow-keys or, if you are a bit younger, wasd-control, but otherwise jumping into this FPS unprepared will be quite disappointing.
You know what, this release literally looks worse than it did at day of release, more than 20 years ago. You were once able to run it in VESA mode (1024 and beyond resolutions), but the Steam version does run any higher than 800x600.
Now, scroll up. Seriously scroll up: one of the top reviews on Steam today is a negative one, questioning how to change controls. Answer me this: do YOU, potential buyer, know how to change the control scheme of a DOS game? Those who payed this in the nineties will know, but does someone who has never touched it before?
If you know of yourself that you are able to appreciate ancient games with ancient looks and ancient controls, then you in for quite a treat. Gameplay is fast and fun. You remember that? Straightforward, undilluted fun? Pure FPS goodness in a 1930-ies horror world, with so many winks to horror movies that it will make your head sping. The weapons feel great, the humour is on the mark, the sounds and music breathe atmosphere and level-layout in general is fantasic.
Oh God the level design, no other game ever came close to it ... just thinking about it makes me want to load up Blood again! Of course the story is rubbish, but if you really expected better from a 1996 FPS then you are probably in the wrong place kid.
So, I repeat: this game is a marvel. But if you don't already know that, the chance that you will ever come to agree with me is small. The barrier for a new player has become just too large to overcome and this will end up being another "classic" game in your steam folder that you simply never come to actually playing.

A complete repackaging of the classic 1997 Build Engine FPS.
If you've already played Blood, you know what to expect.
For those who have never played Blood, it is a run-and-gun shooter in the same vein as Duke Nukem and Doom, but focuses much more on gothic/occult horror more so than sci-fi elements. Out of the three shooters it tends to have the largest and most maze-like levels, although some of them are guilty of padding (there is a lot of 'use Key A to open a room where Key B is literally just sitting on a desk') and lots of backtracking.
All of the weapons feel pretty powerful and the enemies are fun to kill, especially the Cultists. Expect to see a lot of blood, gore and graphic imagery, it lives up to the game title!
I feel it is important to note that this is NOT a modern port - it is literally the original DOS version running in a DOSBox emulator. All of the polish and niceties that come with programs like GZDoom and eDuke32 are absent; you'll have to edit the config files in the game folder for things such as setting your key bindings or mouse sensitivity. The performance and mouse-support is decent, but definitely lacks fluidity.
This is an excellent game but I can't but help want to see it with OpenGL dynamic lighting, modern resolution support, and other doodads that are now standard in Doom and Duke3D; hopefully we will finally see a source port (official or unofficial) someday.

Lots of hoops need to be jumped through in order to make Blood even playable on modern machines, but thankfully there is a very helpful guide by MrEWhite that tells you everything you need to do to get it running. Regardless, it's a shame that this is even necessary. Warner Brothers owns the rights to Blood, and they're unwilling to part with them for fair price - even though it's highly unlikely they'll even -do- something with the license. A source port will probably never happen, and that's a damn shame.
Still, it's a great game that every fan of classic shooters should experience.

There's a reason this is one of the big three.  The game is fantastic.  The level design is some of the best I've seen in a long while, where the level designers utilized as much real estate as they could, having players loop around and cover the same ground a few times.  It leads to levels that can take quite a while to beat, and can sometimes be confusing, and it gets a bit old having these giant winding levels all the time.  But they are incredibly well designed and fun to go through.
The enemies are varied, as are the weapons.  And with that comes a whole lot of weapon swapping.  You'll quickly find that just trying to power through everything with your workhorse is no an efficient, or even effective, method of dealing with the hordes.  Some weapons just work better against some enemies than others.  I really like this.  It wasn't often you had games that made you actually USE the arsenal you collect through the game.
There are a couple downsides.  There's at least one level where you can block yourself off from a key and not be able to complete it without cheating or restarting.  And, as I said, the giant levels CAN cause some fatigue, and get a bit repetitive at times.  This is especially bad in the episode where three levels back to back feature frozen hedge mazes.  The game also has a few areas where they've put too many hitscanning enemies in one area that just leads to large amounts of automatic damage.
But, for the most part, this game is balanced, challenging, and fun.  Absolutely worth a try!
Cryptic Passage: Well, I had some issues with this one on Steam.  Textures were off on the third level, so I ended up playing it from my older CD copy.  Overall, this expansion has a few thematic problems, but the quality is very high.  I was in fact very impressed with it overall.  There really wasn't anything new added to the game, and the story was weak, but it served its purpose.  It's a shame you can't just choose this one natively on Steam, you have to edit the dosbox config file manually to play it, but once you do you're good to go.  I dislike a few things they did, such as using life essences as medkits - yes, the game needs medkits (and it has them via medicine pouches, as this expansion uses later on), but life essences come from the fallen enemies, thematically.  On top of that, Wizard Works didn't really seem to understand how various enemy types needed different weapons to be most effective with, and kinda through groups together than didn't mesh well that way.  in and of itself that's not a huge problem, it actually adds a bit of challenge and diversity to the game, but I think they did so a little too often.  They also kept putting the spider boss, which spawns other spiders, in small areas where she was difficult to fight.
Plasma Pak/Post Mortem: This one gave me issues with both the Steam and CD version.  Level design is still pretty good, the new cultists add some variety.  The other new enemies, however, didn't show up for me.  I mean, they were there on the maps, but there were no graphics for them, and corrupted graphics for the attacks.  And, without graphics, I was unable to actually fight them.  The literally only took damage from AOE attacks.  This made them very annoying, since I couldn't tell where they were, and couldn't fight them off.  That was a very sour note for me and gave me a more negative view of this episode than I probably otherwise would have.  Likewise, the new boss added - which I'm glad they did - I couldn't tell if it was missing attack graphics or not because it just seemed to hurt you based on being close to you.  I had no visible indication of anything else.  They also did the things I criticized Cryptic Passage for, using life essences as med kits and mixing groups of enemies. First things first, for any of you who are Souls-Borne veterans or have played at least a single game from the series, then you will find this game to be very, very easy. For those of you who aren't, you will get a little bit of challenge. If you are playing solo through the entire game, you'll find yourself facing more enemies without any backup but this is not too much of a problem. There are enemy units who seem to kill each other because some are defenders of the Necropolis, while others are inhabitants or invaders to the Necropolis. You can use this to your advantage if you're fortunate or clever enough. The more people you play with, the easier the game gets with no change in enemy numbers. If you have a full party, expect to clean house.

The game's biggest strengths lie in the jolly cooperation, rogue-like elements, and wonderfully unique art style while you descend a ten-floor dungeon with each floor having a different environment and randomly generated loot. Every other aspect though can be considered weak (except for the soundtrack which sounds rather nice). Fighting feels floaty, bloated, and slow at times with you missing your enemies a fair bit even when you are locked on, how delayed your shield feels when you bring it up, and the fact that even your fastest weapons feel slow (the enemies are slow too at least you're on an even playing field). Rolling (or rather dashing like in Bloodborne) is rendered almost completely useless by just moving out of the way of the slow enemies. Also, the control setup is rather terrible especially since you're unable to change your keybindings (at the time of this review). Do you have an idea how awkward it is to us the "v" key to sprint or to use the "control" key to roll?
Controls aside, you'll spend your time roaming through a floor with two main paths that both lead you to one of two exists with no real difference aside from loot you might find in a room; it's ultimately rendered useless since you'll likely find the best equipment and get the most money for buying items and "leveling up" by going through both paths. Enemy AI is functional and competent at best and is typically what you find, but then you have moments when you can cheese it by unloading crossbow bolts into enemies who don't move or react to you until they either die or you get close enough to them. Enemies themselves are easy and simple to take out, the only time things might get difficult is if there's a lot of environmental hazards or if there's a horde of enemies. This is made easy by your ability to craft items from materials you pick up from dead enemies and find lying around to make items like meat to heal you or a potion that could regenerate you HP. Since materials are abundant to the point of ludicrosity where you never ever need to worry about making that next big meat that heals most of your health.
Truthfully, I feel that bosses on each floor would've greatly helped Necropolis. But this is likely because the devs wanted to make sure each experience would be unique without a given setpiece, so a boss on each floor would make things predictable. (I think a random boss from a selection of 10-15 would've eliminated that problem). Here's my reasons for how bosses could've helped.

Long story short, this game is an overpriced, junky flash game, at least at the time of this review.
The game has its humor and it's clearly visible what it wants to be, but it completely falls on its face. I can give it credit for its humor and the nice art and all, but mechanically, this is a complete mess. I've been waiting until I was finished the campaign to write this review, and it was an honest pain. Bugs a-plenty (This isn't Early Access, and is $12.99 as of this post), locked aiming to only cardinal and diagonal directions (I don't care what your♥♥♥♥♥♥poor reasoning behind having it be this way is, it sounds more like an excuse than an actual reason), glitchy as all hell UI (Ammo literally never showed correctly for me what my current magazine was, as well as a bunch of times where dialogue windows would cover the game), and just poor balance (Difficulty is easy in the first world, ramps pretty high in comparison for the second, levels off with an okay ramp-up for the third and fourth, and then just out of nowhere becomes absurd on the fifth). Most of the bosses just seem lazy, especially the Killionaire and Ghoul Squad ones. The champion enemies that drop health and ammo have a crazy-high health multiplier to the point that it takes several mags to destroy one if the wrong enemy happens to get it, and in the case of the last world, if the floating head enemies are a champion, they have health equal to that of a miniboss, and still never actually drop their equipment. Melee is a completely useless function for the most part, the character differences don't really make a noticeable impact until you're forced to change your playstyle because of the level's enemies, guns don't very well describe how they are in comparison to others, despite their being stat windows for each, each weapon requires you to essentially run around in circles and endlessly kill enemies to grind for the money to buy them, instead of just being accomplishment rewards, or having the prices be within check. I haven't tried the multiplayer, but if it's as bad as the singleplayer is with its glitches and problems, I dread to think about it. There's so many issues for a game that's supposed to be finished that it'd be laughable if it wasn't so frustrating and disappointing trying to, in vain, have an enjoyable time with it.
Honestly, for the price, just get Nuclear Throne instead. At its price, this game is most definitely not worth it. I probably wouldn't even recommend it on sale. You could find better browser-based games of the same ilk for free.

I guess it's best described as a cross between a visual novella and a short adventure game. Regardless of how one might best categorise it, I found it somewhat lacking at the end, and it left me thinking, "Now what?"
The plot is interesting, very much like Frankenstein, as you will already have gathered from the Steam game page's description, but isn't followed through to a satisfying resolution. It's almost as if the developers ran out of time and finished it before they'd really got into their stride. Certainly in the short timeframe in which you'll play the game -- it took me 67 minutes to complete the game; the rest of my Steam-reported game time is idling for the remainder of the trading cards -- there's no opportunity for in-depth character development or anything but the most obvious plotline.
The graphics are good: cartoony, with an attractive visual style reminiscent of many point-and-click adventure games. The main character is reasonably well animated and the title screen is particularly attractive. The few still images present in the game are well done as well.
Sound is so-so. Music is good and sets the mood for the game. Voices are not so good. Or rather, they're okay, but don't fit the characters at all well. The main character sounds like a well-spoken, but somewhat pretentious American teen, whereas the other voice (yes, there are only two in the game) is a bit mumbly and not so well spoken. Given the roles they are meant to represent, the voices really don't fit.
So, overall, I was disappointed by Belladonna. I had expected more than what I received, but what was there was, on the whole, pretty good. It's just a shame there wasn't more. It doesn't really offer anything new, but it is quite nice all the same.
I recommend it, but with the caveat that you should take into account the very short play time.

F*** Yeah. This game has a lot going for it. There is something primal and satisfying about laying the smack down on an entire city and watching it react to your engine of destruction.  This game is a great buy as is, but with an active dev tweaking the game on a regular basis, Kaiju-A-GoGo is going well on the path to being an epic standalone in a genre I will coin S.O.S. or strategic overlord simulator.
This is an early access review...yada yada yada, followed by yada.
Interface
Currently fairly simple and barebones. You load the game or start a new one. Aside from the options to turn off sound there are no real options to speak of. You can turn off the tutorial, but there is not enough of one yet to be considered. oh yeah.. be sure to save your game often, as there is not autosave. I repeat SAVE YOUR GAME ON A REGULAR BASIS, less your game crashes and you go back a year in game time...sigh. To dev, please please I beg you implement an autosave.
-Tutorial
see above. The game is simple and forgiving enough that you can find your way, but it would be nice to have something to explain some of the mechanics, units, and world system.
-Graphics
I am going to be totally honest, I am slightly torn on the graphics. On the hardware side of things, it runs on my laptop for the most part, so I'm happy. Definitely not going to tax your turbocooled hyper threaded pc. The characters and monsters have a hand drawn feel. The cities, monster and military units are all isometric, but the units that actually move have about 4-6 frames, covering most angles. I like it, reminds me of the days of Mech Commander.
The stylized look of the kaiju kaiju works, and I like it just fine, but it would be interesting to see if the design was a little realistic, and less comic or cartoon like. The animations are really cool for the attacks, and its really refreshing to see that quality and know that someone put in the time to make them.
Sound
The background music of the game is cute and quirky, while the in game music is of the ominous type. Some variation or options would really enhance the mood of the game. Sound effects for the bang pow stuff, sounds like explosions and gunfire, so that works well. The attacks and abilities also have nice sound effects. In its essence, the game actually sounds like you are watching over a 200 metre behemoth tear apart a city.
Controls
I have a feeling that this is where this game is going to have a lot of attention, as the in game character is controlled via left mouse click while abilities are used with the number keys. Some will cry that more control should be allowed, like a WASD scheme, and while that would be a cool option if that would work with this style game(isometric), I don't know/think that it would translate very well.
Bugs/Issues
- The base development and resource management aspect is fairly solid, although there are a couple issues with menu overlay- like when you are trying to build multiple buildings near each other when zoomed out.
-Crashes. the game has crashed on me a couple of times out of nowhere, leaving me to load from my previous save.
-SAVE SYSTEM- autosave would be a really great tool to prevent minor frustration from when the game crashes.
-In the assigning abilities menu, no info is available when you click on the abilities. To get that info you have to go to the training menu wheel and click on the ability you want info about. Can be a little confusing when you have a large wheel of abilities.
As I write this, only one Kaiju is available, but I think 2 are on the way, with skins I hope/pray. You can tell I lot of thought and creativity went into the upgrading system, the game, the artwork. If I were ever to make a game, this would the game I would want to make. ciao

UPDATE 7/9/2015 (version 1.0.13):
After much consideration I've changed my recommendation from "No" to "Yes".  That doesn't mean the game is perfect, or even fixes all the issues I had at launch, but I think in the last 2.5 months it has improved enough to be more good than bad and feel like a more complete game.
The controls are now more responsive, with the monster not ignoring so many clicks to tell it where to go.  They've added a second monster that plays pretty differently.  I'm not crashing frequently like I used to.  There are now proper sound sliders.  And many other bugs have been fixed alongside small additions and tweaks as you can see in the patch note posts.
I'd still love to see some better handling with a "flee/non-aggressive" mode toggle, as well as improving the base building and defenses part of the game, making it less grindy, improving readability/intuitiveness of the economy readouts and several other things.
But overall I think enough has improved to make this worth a recommendation for the default price if you like giant monsters.
ORIGINAL REVIEW:
I was an Indie GoGo backer so I have been looking forward to this game for a while.  Unfortunately, I can't recommend it at launch.
By many measures this should be an Early Access game and not considered a "full" release.  The game only has one of the three promised kaiju, contains plenty of bugs, and it just does not feel done.
The controls are abysmal, frequently frustrating and responsible for multiple infuriatingly avoidable deaths already.  I have no idea how they thought this was a good control scheme.  Or the fact that you can't tell your monster to not attack things as you are trying to run for your life.  Whether your robot listens to you or not seems like pure luck.  Juck keep clicking and hope that it quits being so stupid.
I'm not personally a fan of the art style and I think the way that the monster is made up of several detached sprites instead of being a single animated sprite looks kind of bad.  The cities don't look bad, though, and when lots of things are burning and exploding it's pretty cool, especially at night.
As mentioned, I have run into several bugs.  I've had the game crash to desktop.  I've had cities where no enemy AI every spawned despite raising several Defcon levels.  There are Patrol Boats that drive right through ground terrain in many areas of cities.  There are no actual volume sliders for Music or Sound Volume.
The game is also very grindy.  You'll have to keep attacking the same beginner cities for ages to build up enough resources to upgrade your island to then upgrade your monster.  But then when you inevitably die because of the poor controls you'll be knocked back a bit and have to build up resources again.  And be ready to spend most of your time speeding up and slowing down the passage of time as you repeatedly wait for basic things to complete, like walking to a city or repairing your monster.
Overall, this is just not ready.  There are some fun concepts here, but the actual gameplay is sorely lacking.  Hopefully in time this will be more fleshed out, better to control, and more polished overall.  Time will tell.

Dust is a fantastic adventure from start to finish.  The story itself isn't long or complex, but it tells exactly as much as it needs to in order to make a satisfying experience and I mean exactly that.  I could throw in some complaint or request wanting to know more about *blank* but the story really told me enough.  I'm satisfied having played this game.  I honestly wish I had a hard copy to display proudly in my personal library.
All that aside, Dust: An Elysian Tail is a quick action packed beat'em up style platformer with RPG elements.  It has a ton of save points allowing you to pick it up and put it down at your leisure.  The animation is fantastic.  The animated scenes are marvelous considering they were hand drawn.  The FPS during the animations is a minor complaint but the actual art frame by frame is beautifully expressive and without flaw.  The music was fantastic during major story moments.  Oh! Did I mention the FULLY VOICE ACTED DIALOGUE?  The cast's performance shows every bit the same quality as the artwork.
Overall, I'd give it a solid 9 out of 10.
-The story and its execution in gameplay is phenominal.
-The art and voice acting are highly memorable and show the considerable amount of love that went into this game.
-The music while good never really stood out while I was playing the game.  I honestly cannot remember any of it 20 minutes after beating the game.  The music during the cutscenes; however, did a fantastic job in setting the mood and brought me close to a weeping mess during one scene.

As Edgar Alan Poe himself once defined "A short story should be read in a single sitting". If there is ever a way to define a "Short Story" in  video game form, a screenshot of this game will be right there, illustrating the definition, since one sitting is all that it takes to finish it. as of this writing, I had logged only 1.4 hours into the game  (probably going to add a bit more, since there is still one item to get).
That, is at the same time its best and worse feature.
If you consider this game a short story, its for the best. Its a small tale of lost love and love beyond death. there is no big developments or big twists. you character is the center of the narrative and uncovering what happened to you makes the story goes foward. small as a short tale should be.
But, specially because of the whole inspiration from Frankenstein, you can't help to wonder what if the developers decided to do a Novel instead of a short story. what if we could see each and every detail of how that final illustration came to be. what if there was more! in that regard, being so short takes from the enjoyment, specially if you consider most playthroughs are supposed to last more than 1 hour.
other than that, the game tells too much instead of showing, but that is a problem even with AAA games out there. being a bit heavy on exposition does makes to comparisson to a short story or novel stronger tough.
on the sound department, its excelent. the soundtrack does convey the right mood at the right time. perfect. nothing much to add.
Graphicswise, its competent. The characters could use a bit more animation, but once you realize what they are supposed to be, the point becomes moot. but even for a abandoned mansion, the place looks rather empty.

This game is everything I've wanted for 20 years, ever since Mail Order Monsters on the C64/128.  I truly hope the developer continues to add more Kaiju after the 2 additional already planned and/or immediately begins taking my money for a sequel.
ETA:  Many many more hours in, I wanted to expand on this.  The game definitely lives up to it's X-com meets Evil Genius vibe.  Plenty of other reviews, and youtube footage explain or show how the game works if you want to get a feel for the actual gameplay.  I just want to say, if you enjoy giant monsters and enjoy strategy games, I can almost guarantee that you'll get at least some fun out of this game.  If you love giant monsters and mad science more than anything, you'll love this game because a decent game that feeds that love only comes along maybe once or twice a decade really.
At this point I feel the game has a very satisfying level of difficulty and rewards smart playing, while not being too punishing in the learning curve to figure out what exactly a smart play is going to be.
The original game balance was a touch easy, and in the first week it's been tweaked up and down a bit in response to player feedback.    While it's easy for some people to say 'Well, it should have been right the first time, why don't they have testers/what are the testers for?' Sometimes it isn't so easy to see the forest for the trees if you've been involved during the process.  Fresh eyes on the subject, and a wider range of play styles brings a lot of new info in and the devs have been HUGELY, AMAZINGLY responsive.  In fact, they've been so on the ball that I'm confident enough in continuing support for the game to want to be sure that they have the opportunity to do so and have bought 2 more copies for friends.  If this turns into a franchise with the legs to last I'll be quite happy, but after the effort the dev team has put in I feel confident that even if there were never another full game released in the series I'll be able to play it years from now and find bugfixes and compatibility updates for Windows 2035 HyperWeb Edition.  Well worth the money I've spent.

A 2D brawler with RGG elements of character progession, loot and quests Dust: An Elysian Tail has no right to be nearly as good as it actually is. It is an excellent metroidvania style game.
The graphics are slick and colourful and the animation is smooth, fast and very energetic. The only times the quality wanes in in some of the few animated cut scenes which look on par with an average flash animation
Gameplay wise the titular character feels very responsive, I've never felt screwed by the game, only myself. the sides quests are nothing much more than kill or fetch quests but the loot system feels effective without being useless or completely overpowered. There is also basic crafting to create your items of power from the 30 or so crafting materials that can drop from varied monsters spread out over several zones.
To do everything in the game is roughly 20 hours gameplay which is not only good value for money but like portal it means the game progress at a rate that feels like your moving forward rather than killing time and you end up finishing the game long before it outstays it's welcome.
The characters and style have been crafted in the same mold as the animated movie 'An American Tail' albeit with an anime twist. An odd yet comfortable creation. Unfortuantely you never get much time with many of the side characters so they can appear very 1 dimensional. the story likewise is fairly simplistic but with some nice twists in the tale to keep things fresh. What really helps though is the excellent voice acting, nothing on par with something like Bioshock or Mass Effect but more like an excellent dub of an anime, which considering the art style works very, very well. You do have a typical anime style sidekick though and it is entirely possible you could hate them, that is up to you to decide.
Speaking of the sound the music track is probably the only part of the game not composed by the creator of the game, Thankfully it is likewise excellent, providing all the right moods at the right time from energetic, daramatic compositions to some tracks providing a sense of unease in a haunted house.
Being a port of an Xbox Live game you will be suprised to know the port is one of the best ever. In anything. Large publishers have been royally put to shame with the amount of options a PC user can change in the settings from basic visuals and FX settings to physically putting the HUD anywhere you like on the screen. Anywhere. As an addition the animations themselves are either the best upscale from 720p I have ever seen or they went back to the original art and took higher resolution images to be used in the PC port.
All in all Dust: An Elysian Tail is one mans labour of love and it really shows. As long as you don't mind the obligatory talking found in RPG's, don't hate anime, and are a fan or even curious about metroidvania games this needs to be in your collection. Don't even bother with a thumbs up or down on this review, just buy the game.

Little Inferno is an oddball. It's funny, it's quirky, it's dark, and it's disconcerting. It's also short. I finished it in just under five hours, and you could probably shave a few hours off of that if you ignored all but the required number of Combo Badges. On top of which, there's very little here to call a proper game, and gameplay mostly just consists of placing things in the fireplace, and then burning them for fun and prizes. "Prizes" in this case referring to more things to burn, money with which to buy more things to burn, and stamps for speeding up the delivery of more things to burn.
It's the ciiiircle of liiiife! And it burns us aaaall!
That said, there's a lot of variety to make it interesting, and you're never really positive how a new item will react when you set it on fire or throw it around. I burnt a floppy disk, which caused my fire to become pixelated, and a coffee cup I set ablaze spontaneously grew a face and began screaming. Which brings me to a point: This game is disturbing when it wants to be. On the whole, though, it's all cartoony enough that I think you won't leave your comfort zone.
The categories of items are interesting. There's a video game category, of course, and it contains little references, like World of Goo goo balls and a tablet which displays a Duck Hunt nod. My favorite category, however, is the one filled with manly things, such as a monster truck, a flamethrowing chainsaw, and a moustache. And I burned them all.
So, what's the point? Well, besides just burning things and seeing what happens (which is kind of its own reward), there are 99 2- or 3-item combos to figure out based on the combo's name alone. These will probably take up the majority of your time. There is also, actually, a plot, told mainly through letters until the endgame, which is... surprisingly different. The ending does what it needs to. It won't answer that feeling you'll get while playing the game that there's something bigger going on here than just people keeping warm, but it gives you a personal conclusion that's a little more than "Try to guess what happened for yourself!" Which, considering the tendencies of indie games these days, is a glorious gift.
There's an underlying message to be picked up on, as well. It's a message which rings true, and while it's one that I've seen in various forms in indie games before, I think this is the best presentation I've seen it given, yet.
Little Inferno's a short game, but it's good entertainment, if pretty basic in the gameplay department. It'll hold your attention until it's over, but if you're worried about the short length over price, well, that's what Steam sales are for.

This isn't the only cross-platform (PC, iOS, Android) asynchronous turn-based tactical game but it great one and continues to both enterain and challenge me after move than 500 hours of play (I've spent more time via Android than via Steam)
The range of arenas, factions, faction units and special powers are more than enough to provide a depth of tactical options and challenges and when this is combined with human opponents - really the only way to play in my opinion - the longevity is indefinite.
I don't pay attention to the online leaderboards or achievements at all, I just find the core game extremely enjoyable. Each turn takes about a minute, less if there is an obvious set of moves to make, more if you have many options to choose from.
Some of the frequent choices (dilemnas!) are -
> Will you focus on winning by killing all opposing units or by killing crystals . . . and will you pursue a crystal damage lead in order to compel your opponent to make an aggressive move that may over-expose them?
> Do you risk applying power-ups to an unit in the early stages of the match, when your opponent still has specials which will enable them to gain a safe-kill?
> Do you hold back on your own specials or make use of them to gain an early game advantage?
> After downing a unit when your opponent has no healers on the board (which can ressurrect) do you stomp the downed unit or take the risk that they will have a healing option in their hand?
> Do you concede balance of power on the board in order to quickly cycle through your deck in order to hopefully draw into your hand a key unit for your intended tactics?
There are many more!
This is a fantastic "easy to learn" and "difficult to master" game,
Nah.
No need to complain about bad or dated controls, just configure the controls to your desire (you can even use mouselook) and you're all set to enjoy one of the best FPS's of all time!

It takes some time to get DOS working, and I had to dig around the files to get the final episode (cyptic passage) running but once it's all up and going, the amount of content you get is pretty solid.
If you're a fan of Duke or Doom I would recommend this game in a heartbeat, it's my favorite first person shooter from the '90s.
Gameplay: The game is run on Ken Silvermen's Build Engine through DOSbox and plays very similar to other games of it's time, namely Duke Nukem 3D. You have your classic shotgun, rocket launcher, and SMG arsenal. With a few stand out weapons, the dynomite and voodoo doll. The over the top dismemberment and gore was pretty crazy for the time, and in my opinion is still pretty badass.
Sound: I had an issue where the ingame music would fail to play the next track, really I think its an issue with the port, nothing a quick google search couldn't fix. The gun sounds pack a lot of punch and the screams/maniacal laughter of the enemies and the player character are crisp and really take you back to 1997.
Graphics: It's a pre Quake '90s shooter, so it was still in the 2.5D style of the era, enemies are rendered as sprites, while ammo boxes and weapons are voxels. Overall it has a nice style and really nails the horror aesthetic it's going for.
Story: You are Caleb, a sort of cowboy/cultist that rises from the dead to seek revenge against a dark god. Pretty basic stuff. It's all pretty tongue and cheek, and is a nice homage to classic horror movies.
Conclusion: I paid five bucks for it and I would've paid twice that much after finishing it, I plan to come back to it one day. Aside from the port itself, namely the trouble with getting it running smoothly on modern operrating systems, it's pretty solid for what you pay. Blood is one of the last great shooters from the era. I would definitly recommend it. 8/10

I am a long-time Adobe Photoshop user, and consider myself an advanced user of it, although the version I had was several years old (I'm a semi-professional photographer). After my motherboard died on my last computer, and I got a new one and upgraded to Windows 10, I found my copy of PS wouldn't work. And, since the lovely folks at Adobe won't give you free upgrades on software you've spent over $600 on, that meant purchasing a new one - for another $600. I said to hell with that, and searched on Steam for an alternative that still had a lot of the same features that PS had, but at a much more reasonable price. And I found...Pixeluvo.
FANTASTIC software. FANTASTIC price. I have admittedly only used it so far for a few hours, but already I have picked up the basics and some advanced functionality of it (layers, layer masks, etc.) and edited a ton of photos using it. I can honestly say that the results are easily as good as I used to get with PS - can't tell the difference at all, and I get the same results I wanted but at a MUCH more reasonable price.
This is very powerful software, that goes way beyond so many of the other photo-editing programs out there on the market that really are just a dime-a-dozen. I highly recommend this for anyone who can't afford (or doesn't want to pay for) the outrageous price that Adobe charges for PS, but still wants most - if not all - of the sophisticated and in-depth features that PS provides, at a fraction of the price. SO glad I found Pixeluvo - will be using it for all of my photo editing - both casual snapshots and my serious photography - from now on.

A fun, well-written visual novel with RPG elements whose cutesy anime artwork and setup as an affectionate parody of self-insert Harry Potter fanfiction disguise its depth. There are 6 possible love interests, and each one has multiple possible endings instead of just the usual good/bad. It's not a very long game, but the sheer amount of ways scenes can play out and events you can trigger encourages multiple playthroughs. The writing is great and likes to play with your expectations of both visual novels and teen fantasy romance, and the main characters and many of the minor characters are all really fleshed out. The weakest part of the game is the RPG elements -gaining skill points in certain schools of magic and using the spells you've learned to solve puzzles, which are pretty open-ended and have multiple different solutions- but the puzzles are interesting enough and offer an occasional change of pace. All-in-all, this is a game that I feel was created by someone loves visual novels and wants to see the genre become more than what it is, and really wants to see more girl-oriented games out there that aren't pieces of crap. If you like visual novels, lighthearted fantasy stories, romance games, or if you're still waiting for that Hogwarts letter, I recommend you look into this game.

How should I describe Paladins? It certainly isn't a B-TEC Overwatch, and the hate it recieves definitely isn't warranted.
I'm going to start this review by comparing it to Overwatch, since that seems needed.
-Paladins obviously contains similar gameplay mechanics to Overwatch, does it copy Overwatch? No. If anything, Overwatch copies Team Fortress 2... What I'm trying to say is, these kind of games take inspiration from eachother, and as a market, isn't that what games do? (and have always done?)
-In some places, this game is better than Overwatch. It has quality of life additions, such as mounts which greatly improve the flow of the game, and of course the pace. The problem with Overwatch is that it is very slow to get back into the game after dying.
-Overwatch certainly looks better than Paladins, but Paladins is a free to play title. That's the best part, it's free.
-Paladins has it's own unique, thought-out characters that all feel different to play.
-The competitive scene is big.
You lose nothing by trying this title, and I assure you if you like team based games you will most probably like this one.

It... uh. Bleh. Guns are really bad at describing what they do before you use them in a level, which is fantastic since they're all terrifically expensive and several of them are an incredible pain to unlock via any method except running around in circles killing easy enemies for an hour, since you need to get hundreds of thousands of points in a single run.
"But points! You get them by doing well!" Well, actually you don't get all that many by doing well, because you get points for killing enemies en masse, and you complete levels by ignoring most of the enemies and destroying the objectives, since enemies infinitely respawn and can be rather tough... especially enemy corporals, who sometimes take almost a full magazine, if not more, of your gun unloaded directly into their face to kill.
Between that and several glaring bugs still present in the launch version (enemies spawning or being knocked on top of walls in the Killionaire missions, a level of Bionic Cop that took me 5 tries arbitrarily deciding it would never end after I beat it) I wasn't really having that much fun with the game. Half of the bosses (Yatcha Queen, Ramishar) are interesting, but the others were just an exercise in running away from them in a straight line while shooting, and Ramishar's HP bar overstayed its welcome for me, a bit.
I unfortunately wasn't able to complete the game yet, having gotten bogged down in the final level set, Bionic Cop, but I don't think it would change my review much even if I manage to get through it next time I try. Ultimately, there's much better twin-stick shooters and better, uh, Broforces. Like Broforce.

That's right. There are no puzzles left for the player to solve. The only ones you encounter are either so simple or outright explained and solved by the protagonist herself as she speaks to herself, leaving you no room to experiment or even ponder what you ought to be doing. I've never played an adventure game this easy in my life unless you count games targeted to toddlers with similar game mechanics. I would argue those games to be even more cerebral experiences than Belladonna.
The staple, the hallmark of a good adventure game to me has always been that they force the player to think outside of the box. A constant effort must be made by the player to figure out what to do. Careful and most importantly thoughtful game design is needed to keep the player entertained in these type of games. That combined with a vivid and interesting story, a deep mystery, or simply a protagonist that is interesting / quirky and full of character are also very important in a genre that only uses the left mouse click to play it. Belladonna has none of that. There is a mystery there but it's not meant to be solved. The game simply makes you read journal pages that explain it and that's it. The only difficulty in the game is finding an item (if you even missed it -- they are very easy to find) or trying to read the journal pages as the font is set to be so small it makes your eyes bleed.
The only positive I can give to the game is the art design. It's hard to explain just how little is in this game though. In the store page there are 7 backgrounds shown. The game only has about 12 of them, so it basically shows you over 50% of the game's scenery right there. There are also no cutscenes. Sometimes the game just fades to black and we get to hear sounds as if they couldn't finish the game or the artist couldn't bother drawing vital scenes in the game. I mean the entire ending has no cutscene at all. It just fades to black, we hear a few corny lines and then we get to see someone's doodle with the words "The End" on it.
The music is good. The very little there is. I mean I can't complain about it so my only memory of it is that it didn't bother me. It sets a tone and keeps it there. The voice acting is ok. You won't be moved by the characters at all since they are devoid of any. I can't blame the voice actors at all as the writing seems very corny. The game sets a good atmosphere at first in the beginning, but immediately breaks it by having joke descriptions when you inspect objects more than once (a staple in adventure games yes -- but very out of place in the games milieu). If you establish that the main character is a "tabula rasa" an empty slate, but then she makes quirky Monkey Island esque remarks, you just destroyed all the character you worked so hard to establish right of the bat.
Belladonna is a game that falls flat I'm afraid, unless all you're after is a short novel length story that's only twist is the protagonist discovering a note that tells her she was a lesbian when she was alive and the lover of the only other character in the game and that's it. That's it! No character arc, no nothing. It's disappointing because it's established early on that she has no memories, no personality and possibly no emotions at all and is basically an empty slate. Yet she reads a note left by her living self and instantly she's now the person she used to be I guess.
It would've been so much more interesting if the game actually played with these concepts rather than just introduce them and then take the short route out. The game could've made strong statements about sexuality and the human persona, what it is to be a human and to exist. But it doesn't. It just says "o-oh... I'm a lesbian? L-lewd!" and then gives you an ending drawing out of a b-movie with the main character in a slave esque pose under another woman like she just accepted it no problems at all. The game begins "tabula rasa" and ends "tabula rasa".
The most disappointing fact is that the game teases with a lot of good philosophical questions and hints at many possible interesting side effects of what it might be like to be a reanimated human being. But then it doesn't even explore them. It's like there's two lines of the main character pondering about possibly being a sociopath after killing a cat and then talking about it with another character and then this is entirely forgotten. The ending of the game is also insanely cheesy and left me even more disappointed.
I can't recommend this game to anyone. Sorry.

While Triss Merigold can make you rate this game before finishing it, let's take a look at this game.
Witcher 2 is a direct sequel to the first game (duh) picking up the story where the other ended.
And as expected the story again has it's turns and twists in the same special manner as expected. The plot while it's not very complicated, is a real gem. The characters are believable, the writing is one of the best in gaming history, and all the little sidequests feel just right as they're not chasing away the charm of the main storyline, but they expand it.
Gameplay wise we can't really talk about a special thing going on here. The battles are basic, the RPG elements are very simple and without much variety.
The visuals are gorgeous, while I was pretty much angered by the fact that they changed Geralt's look ( the wolf face from the first was closer to the witcher personality) pretty much everything is gorgeous. The locations are varied and big, but there are not many different locations, then again it's expected since this is a story driven RPG game, not exactly a completely open world sandbox game. Still the open world elements are there, but it's not the main focus of the game.
Overall it's a MUST have for RPG gamers, and with it's rpg simplicity I can recomend this to even those who are not big fans of RPG games. It doesn't require much planning, thinking, building to shape your character over the course of the game. Have fun!

Interesting and different kind of game.
You start off attacking Alaska with limited abilities and limited resources. This quickly builds as you collect resources from the cities you destroy and take them back with you to your base to construct facilities for production, defense and storage.
Also, one building type in particular gives you ability enhancements. From here, you will purchase and train your Kaiju in skills chosen from a tech tree. All the cities are different and have a variety of difficulty levels. You are attacked by various military units and there is quite a few. You can only pick the one Kaiju for the moment but more are coming in Summer. Here's my pro/con list:
pros:
- Unique & successful idea set into motion.
- Easy to start but yet pretty deep
- Really fun destroying the cities (each city has special buildings or landmarks)
- Can advance your Kaiju and make him stronger and stronger
- The art style is interesting and looks good
- There are many cities to conquer and some simply can not be conquered from the start
cons:
- loading times are a bit long
- controls can be a bit wonky why you are trying to destroy a military unit attacking you
- UI controls for the base are a bit confusing (I didn't realize I had to build a advance facility to get to Tier 2 skills until later that I would have liked)
- the game crashed a couple of times due to a bug when leaving a city (twice but isn't a huge issue)
- some cities regenerate pretty quickly (rebuild and restore morale)
But all in all, it is a fun game that you should try if you like action mixed with base building and an a bit of an RPG element. It is a game for all ages!

Dust: An Elysian Tail is a game that explores the effect of one's choices, both past and present, on the person one is.
I've never really been into action platformers, but I'm glad I was talked into playing this one. The gameplay was fun and occasionally challenging, but not terribly difficult even for someone new to this style of game. At first I was just mashing buttons, but once I got the hang of the controls, it was very satisfying to figure out how to approach different enemies and obstacles. Every time the combat was starting to feel a bit stale, a new ability would come into play just in time to liven things up. Some of the biggest challenges came from navigating through and around environmental hazards, and with save points few and far between, getting through certain areas could get pretty dicey. One of the most rewarding aspects of the game for the completionist in me was going back through previous areas after gaining new abilities to seek out and claim hidden treasures.
The story took a little while to draw me in, but once it did, I was hooked. The further it went on, the more engaging it became. While the revelations that come late in the game were a bit predictable, it was still a well-executed take on a familiar story. I loved the friendship between our hero, Dust, and his nimbat companion, Fidget. At times I found myself identifying more with Fidget than with Dust. It was Dust's story, and I was just following along, watching his character develop, and helping out where I could.
I may have teared up a little at the end. Just a little, I swear.

Another entry into the "90s shooter that kicks your♥♥♥♥♥quot; library of awesome oldschool games.
It's hard. It's satisfying. It has very original weapons (albeit some of them are a bit gimmicky), a voodoo doll, a spray can and lighter, and my favourite, the flare gun. It has a creepy, oldschool horror themed art style and a wonderful soundscape. First time I played this game I thought "I'm blasting black/death metal in the background" but I decided not too, because the sound of the game is so engrossing I'd ruin the atmosphere.
And did I say it's hard? This is one of those games that makes you shiver at the sight of run-of-the-mill mobs, yet alone tougher enemies. You have to stay on your toes, save often, conserve ammo, that stuff.
My only complaint is that the combat is hitscan based and not projectile based (which essentially means you're given less of a fair shot at... not dying), but other than that, big thumbs up.
Also, if you have problems running the game, check out the steam forums, plenty of successful and helpful solutions there.

Ingredients:
1) 2 cups Flour
2) 1/2 cup Sugar
3) 1/4 teaspoon Salt
4) 2 sticks (1 Cup) Salted Butter, Cut Into Small Cubes
5) Filling
6) 1-1/2 cup Sugar
7) 1/4 cup Flour
8) 4 whole Large Eggs
9) Zest And Juice Of 4 Medium-sized Lemons
10) Powdered Sugar, For Sifting
Directions:
1. For the crust: Preheat the oven to 350 degrees F. Grease a 9-by-13-inch pan with butter.
2. Stir together the flour, sugar, and salt. Add the butter to the bowl and use a pastry cutter to cut it all together until the mixture resembles fine crumbs. Press into the prepared pan and bake until golden around the edges, about 20 minutes.
3. For the filling: Stir together the sugar and flour. Crack in the eggs and whisk to combine. Add the lemon zest and juice and mix until combined. Pour over the crust and bake about 20 minutes.
4. Allow to cool in the fridge for a minimum of 2 hours, then sift powdered sugar over the top before cutting into squares.
(Use an 8 x 10 pan if you'd like the layers to be a little thicker.)
