Yes. it's a sidescroller. However, I can't say I felt like I was playing Metroid or Castelvania, Commander Keen or whatever else (for both, positive and negative reasons, those who played this and those know what I am talking about ;) ).
I can't also understand why people who compare this game to either of these old platform games think that the graphics are old-school. You know, there are different styles, and 'modern' is not a synonym for '3d'. The graphics in Dust fit into my concept of 'modern' by all means, and the degree of detail of the background planes makes of it a very nice game, visually speaking. The animations are also nice and fluid.
The sound is another department where it shinnes, it's easy to see that a lot of care have been put in the voices, and the soundtrack in general has good quality and is more than adequate, without being disrruptive at any point. I can't comment on accents cause I am not a native speaker though.
As for the gameplay, there are mixed things here. The combats are easy, even the last one. In fact, they only get easier and easier as you progress. Specially, if you revisit a couple maps to explore them 100%, since even at higher levels the monsters still give you a very high quantity of experience points, not to count that you can kill like 50 of them by traversing a map from one side to the opposite one without even putting your feet on the ground. It's not even difficult, just randomly press the three combat buttons until your hand tears appart. The gear is also overpowered and easy to find all the way, don't want to spoil, but... you don't even have to walk for it.
It requires some degree of hability to explore everything throughly, though for accustommed players it's not really difficult to get by. But the maps are interesting and fun to explore anyway.
The story however, even if it seems unoriginal, makes it shine. While the argument has been revisited a thousand times, I must confess that I have only very rarely seen such consistency in the story line.
And, since no one mentioned it, I think I'll just throw it: besides being a side scroller, and having some reminiscences of those "I lost my memory but I am reborn from an amalgamation between the forces of light and darkness to save the whole planet and who knows if even the universe"-kind-of-game, it also kind of reminds me of some other game series that no one mentioned, namely, Soul Reaver, for one... no two... no, three or four reasons. Just play it, and think about it a bit and you'll see ;)
All in all, it's fun, it's nice, it's a relaxing game to play though, and has an adequate price.
A bit more love in the combat and drop system, and a longer story would make for an incredible second part. But only if it doesn't screw up the story line. I've never been a fan of broken arguments and completelly unrelated side-quests that are blatantly put there just to fill up the gap.

I'm pretty sure if you woke up on a laboratory table, bolted together from corpse bits, you wouldn't be as peppy as your character in Belladonna. The poor dear takes on the role of the monster in this point & click spin on the tale of Frankenstein, and her sunny outlook isn't the only twist in store. Venturing through the castle, you collect notes from the doctor and his wife, revealing a morbid little story between them. There are a handful of inventory items to scrounge up to solve a smaller handful of puzzles, as well as some awkwardly-voiced dialogue to enjoy.
...And that's it. The game is 30 minutes long. I struggled a bit with whether I thought it was worth it, and in the end I decided it was. The animation is not much past Flash level but the art is clean and the look of the castle is a stark modern gothic that I haven't really seen elsewhere. The twists are interesting, and I like where the story ends up, though the conclusion itself is extremely abrupt. You wouldn't lose much watching a let's play of Belladonna, but it's a fine little adventure game to keep you busy between meatier offerings.

I wanted to like this game, but after playing for a while, I would join the chorus of others who are not as satisfied. Here are my main gripes:
1. AI is really bad, even on the highest difficulties. If you resign the game every few turns, just to check what are the top techs the AI was working on, EVERY RACE is focusing on weapons. It's ridiculous. Why wouldn't they invest in techs that would improve their research? I guess the cybernetic race occasionally focuses on techs that increase the population, but that's about it. You can gain a huge technological edge and crush them in the mid to late game.
2. They get upset at you pretty soon, so good luck trying to win a diplomacy victory.
3. They ignore culture and focus on mining and economy starbases
4. Diplomacy is too simplistic

Belladonna is a point & click adventure game, featuring subtle horror/ Frankenstein-esque atmosphere, beautifully painted backdrops and a sweet, likable protagonist. She wakes up in a laboratory, not knowing who she is or what she is, but exhibits joy of discovery & curiosity rather than fear. Her character traits quickly emerge, like the urge to name things (suit of armor? must be Roland the Poet:) making her the more fleshed out.
The story is quite simple, but still graceful & interesting. We learn most of it by reading torn out journal pages, which are well written & well paced out. Some additional information comes from interacting with objects or looking at things. Her commentaries about the surroundings are quite enjoyable, even if they have nothing to do with the plot itself.
I liked it myself, hence the thumbs up, but it has one major flaw - length. This is very short game. If you read everything carefully and listen to the protagonist's every comment on every subject, you still will finish it under an hour. It's is also quite easy, especially if you pay attention to what is said (the main character will often hint herself as what to do next), so you basically breeze through it, which just intensifies the length problem.
Also personal & really minor gripe - card settings. I basically finished game 3 times when I hit 2 hour mark and first card dropped, and then I left it idle, but cards seem to be set do drop every half an hour or more, so I had to idle over 5 hour mark to obtain them all, in a game that takes under 1 hour to complete (and that's only if you try hard to prolong the experience).
Overall I liked the atmosphere, the story and the characters. Belladonna is an enjoyable and definitely memorable, albeit short game :)

This game is an incredible experience that is let down by 2 things, it's length and it's price.
Starting with the pro's of the game you can see from the screen shots that the artstyle of this game is beautiful. The use of lighting and colour makes this one of the best looking games on the market ,and that 10 years down the line this game will still look beautiful, just like The Legend of Zelda: Windwaker. The artstyle looks especially good with the fish because it makes them simple yet colourful, although the blue whales you encounter don't look very good because of there lack of colour or texture. The game takes you through so many different areas that have new colours, new layouts and new fish which you can examine with the meditate mode.The music in this game is nothing short of perfect with it being composed by the man who did all the music for Journey, a very similar game.
[Mild spoilers ahead if you've played Journey] Speaking of Journey, if you have played it before you will know what you are in for with ABZU, but the games are almost too similar. They both follow a similar pace and a lot of the plot seems to be almost the same, except Journey gives you purpose from the start. With Journey you start the game in an empty area with the only visable thing being a light on a mountain that is obviously the goal. With ABZU you start the game in the water and you use basic video game knowledge to go forward because that's where the game pointed you until you see a shark, and then I guess you follow the shark for some reason or maybe the shark is follow you? It isn't clear at all what you're doing except follow the linear path layed out in front of you. The way Journey controlled always felt graceful as well, with your scarf trailing behind you and your small glide ability, and ABZU mostly feels graceful, until it doesn't. The big problem with the controls is that you are nearly always moving on all 3 axis and this can get complicated at times. To move forward whilst underwater in ABZU you hold down the right trigger and use the left stick to chagne your pitch and direction, but I think that this could have been done better by moving forward, backwards, left and right with the left stick and aiming yourself with the right stick. The movement also gets clumsy when you are upside down or are against a wall, as the controls are designed with you being right way up the whole time.
Now the biggest problem that a lot of people have with this game is the cost and the amount of time you get out of this game. This game cost $26 Australian dollars and if you look at the price of Journey that game cost me $15. I would be ok with this if the game was something like 3-4 hours in length but I beat this game in 1 hour and 50 minutes. That is barely more than your average movie and a movie is a more dense and complete experience that costs me $10. I would also like you to keep in mind that I really took my time with this game, I used the mediatate feature a lot just to look at all of the beautiful fish swimming around and I didn't use the boost for most of the game just because I wanted to really take in the world around me.
In conclusion I would highly recommend you play this if you don't have a PS3 or PS4 to play Journey, have played Journey and really want to experience something similar yet differ or you really like the style of ABZU and are willing to pay for it even though it is way too short for the price.

in?  What other game gives you the opportunity to ride on the back of a blue whale as it breaches?  (Don't try this on your next whale-watching trip, kids.  It will
)
That said...  I don't think I have ever played through any other game in which I spent so much of the total game play time wondering what on earth was going on.  Half the time I felt I was just along for the ride.  I went through the game with only a general idea of what I was supposed to be doing, and almost no idea at all why I was doing it.  There is not at any point anywhere in this game any explanation of who you are, where you are, or why you are there.  If you expect purpose and direction, or any option for non-linear gameplay, this might not be the game for you.
Oh, and where it says a controller is "strongly recommended" to play Abzu?  Let me restate this a little more clearly:  Unless you have a very high frustration tolerance, don't even
to play this game with mouse and keyboard.  Let's just say that of all the possible ways that control for this game could have been mapped onto a mouse and keyboard, most of the possible options I can think of are better than Abzu's.  At that, I discovered one move by accident:  press E to do a kind of tuck-roll in place.  I have no idea what other easter-egg movement controls may be hidden somewhere on the keyboard.  I tried several likely guesses after discovering the E roll, and didn't find any others, but I didn't try anywhere near every key.
Overall, on balance, Abzu was worth playing once.  But I don't see it as having a lot of replay value.  It might have more replay value if there was more of a sense of agency in the game, if you felt that anything at all was under your control.  But quite honestly, this game would lose almost no interactivity or immersion if you just watched a video of someone else playing it.  It's mostly a completely linear spectator experience, with just enough depth of interactivity to make you feel that you're playing something instead of purely following a script and reciting your lines on cue.
But it's a heck of a spectacle.  So relax, sit back, and enjoy.

From developer Ran, and publisher Visual Wordplay comes Once Upon an All Hallow’s Eve; a horror, romance otome visual novel. You play as Cara Lee, a twenty year old graduating student who escapes to the mountain rest house with her friends.

She decides to try and take shelter there – but is there more to the mansion and the inhabitants than what first meets the eye?
I first downloaded Once Upon an All Hallow’s Eve, believing it to be like Trick and Treat – Visual Novel by Eternal Night Studios. The characters were all boring, flat characters and hardly any thought seemed to be put into their personalities. After finishing the first route, I just skimmed through the remaining three routes. There seemed to be nothing interesting about the story, and there was nothing to hold my attention, other than completing the game and deleting it from my computer.
Honestly, there was nothing about this game I can think to even say as a pro, other than the fact it is a short story. It took me twelve minutes to complete, after completing a whole route and then skimming through the rest of it. It’s quick, easy to get to 100% and this is really just a game for completionists, rather than anyone else.
If this is a game that’s right up your alley, then go for it! But if you aren’t 90-100% sure this is a game for you, I would definitely skip it. It’s really not worth it.

Blood: One Whole Unit is an FPS game originally released in 1997 and features both expansion packs that were released for it. We play as an anti-hero protagonist called Caleb who has been betrayed by a demigod he once loyally served and has risen from the grave for vengeance. Hearing your motivation and the fact that Caleb dresses like an emo cowboy with glowing red eyes one might assume this to be a rather serious game but boy is that wrong. Nearly every word out of Caleb's mouth is either a reference to pop culture of the 90's or a witty one liner. Freshly risen from the grave your only weapon will be a pitchfork which is mostly a last resort weapon only useful against the lower tier creatures such as undead ax wielders. You'll quickly find your next weapon, a simple flare gun that once fired at an enemy will usually set it on fire within a couple of seconds.
Nearly every weapon has an alt-fire for added diversity and options during combat. Your simple flare gun's alt-fire allows you to shoot an exploding flare that has decent area of effect allowing you to clear out rooms in a rain of fire at the cost of more ammo than normally firing it. You'll eventually run across your run of the mill shotgun and machine gun that are staples of the FPS genre but the rest of your arsenal is much more unique and memorable ranging from holding a lighter in front of a spray can for an improvised flamethrower to a voodoo doll you jam with a needle in order to harm the enemy in front of you. Learning how to use whatever is on hand is a necessity in Blood since there is simply not enough ammo for blasting your way through the game with the normal weapons. Fire and dangerous explosions will be your best friends if you plan to survive this brutal world.
Above all skills learning how to chuck a stick of dynamite thru a window without blasting yourself is a must. Dynamite is common and is devastating to most enemies as well as great at evening the odds when you are greatly outnumbered. There is a great variety of enemies but the most common are also the most dangerous. These enemies are The Cultists and they are packing heavy weaponry like machine guns and shotguns to ruin your day. While you may be undead, getting shot in the face still hurts and will drain your health/armor in no time. The Cultist's aim is superhuman, being able to nail you right in the forehead from a huge distance with robot like reflexes and their placement in the levels further stacks the situation in their favor. If you expect something bad to happen or think that the sudden corner up ahead would be perfect for something to kill you chances are your instincts are right so be ready to fire at a moment’s notice or if you have a decent supply of dynamite chuck one to make sure there isn't a mime waiting in the shadows to strangle you.
In addition to your weapons you will have multiple items at your disposal. These range from a portable medkit to a pair of boots that allows you to jump insanely high. They can be used anytime you wish however they do have very limited use and will be gone quick if you use them excessively. Scattered around the levels are items that will be used upon picking it up such as Akimbo Guns that allows you to dual wield two of the same weapons allowing you to relive the ending to Scarface with twice the manliness. In all seriousness that power-up would have been far better as a portable item instead of an immediate since whenever I usually picked one up I either didn't need it or didn't want to waste that much ammo. The more useful ones are the invisibility that allows you to wail on the clueless enemies in ghost form and a weird floating eye that will supercharge your overall health from the typical 100 to 200. The amount of options and opportunities to annihilate your foes are massive which leads to much more engaging gameplay than just going in blasting with a shotgun.
That's not to say using the shotgun isn't fun as well. As you may imagine with a name like Blood the game is very violent and enemies just fall apart, especially when you use the alt-fire to unleash both rounds from the barrel at once to splatter the room. Sometimes their head comes off and you can kick it around like a soccer ball until it breaks apart which is admittedly yet morbidly great fun. One thing that I love about Blood is that our character just loves what he is doing and will occasionally laugh like amadman whenever he causes carnage which never fails to bring a smile to my face. The voice acting is pretty good too and it really helps Caleb's dark sense of humor. Whoever did the screaming for enemies on fire deserves some kind of acting award and it adds just that much more personality to this title.
Levels in this game are enormous and are brilliantly designed. They feature your key card hunting you'd expect out of the FPS games of yesteryear and require you to pay attention to your surroundings. From a level that has you fighting your way through a moving train, a city being bombarded by planes and your more suspenseful horror themed levels Blood has a ton of levels that will stick with you far after you completed the game. It's not as simple as walking around everywhere to reach the end of a level. Multiple times you will have to go swimming underwater to reach a location which sounds like an easy task until the first time you see a giant shark with legs rapidly approaching towards you. Luckily you can still fire your guns underwater somehow but that won't be much help when you are being attacked from all sides. Fleeing out of the water does you no good as they will jump right out and run on their freakish legs as they will not be denied their feast, lack of lungs be damned.
One semi-serious flaw of the underwater sections is the lack of visual feedback telling you how close you are to being out of breath causing you to start losing health. Your screen does get slightly red but something more noticeable such as an oxygen bar would have been far more preferable. Unfortunately this version of Blood is pretty sub-par. It has many problems running on modern machines like music not looping leaving you with nothing but ambiance noise throughout, tons of screen tearing and slowdown and the final 6th episode isn't even playable in game, instead you must go to the game's directory and drag the “Cryptic.exe” to the Dosbox program. The controls have been slightly modernized and movement is now “WASD” while offering horizontal mouse view meaning you can't look up or down upon starting. Simply pressing the “U” key will allow you to look around freely and pressing the “I” key will add an aiming reticle. People say that the GOG version is better but as I don't own it I can't confirm these statements. Steam's version is not unplayable but the poor performance and screen tearing are a major detractor.
It's a shame really as this was my favorite of the trilogy of Build Engine games, the other two being Duke Nukem 3D and Shadow Warrior. Those two have been brought into the modern age and play great thanks to Devolver Digital's respect for the hit 90's shooters while Atari just plopped “Blood” onto the market, running on Dosbox with just enough tuning to make it playable. Blood is still a fun and unique game that has great level design, tons of weapons and interactive environments like workable light switches, certain walls being destructible and tons of creativity. Having 6 episodes to play through this is one title with a ton of playtime. For those of us that played this game back in the day it is a solid low costing purchase regardless of the flaws but for those looking to get into old school shooters I'd suggest to start off elsewhere.

One of the classic Build Engine games, along with Duke Nukem 3D, Shadow Warrior, Redneck Rampage and some others. Basically, what Duke Nukem 3D did with satire towards action films and Shadow Warrior did with kung fu films and anime tropes, Blood does with horror films; just about everything in the game is a parody or satire of a horror film or horror trope, from the Gothic setting, occult enemies and monsters, individual levels inspired by classic horror films, right down to a lot of secrets containing direct references to those films. The game itself looks as beautiful as a 2.5D game made for resolutions lower than 640x480 can be; texture and sprite art is incredible and the sprites are actually animated using stop-motion figurines, giving the game quite a creepy, old-fashioned feel. On that note, Blood definitely lives up to its name - one of the selling points for the game was that it is violent to the point of it being over-the-top, giving you the ability to blow enemies to pieces, set them ablaze and watch them run around screaming on fire, and even wither them to dust and kibbles with a voodoo doll. The way that every enemy is animated is really something quite special to behold.
Gameplay is typical of games on the Build Engine: tight, frantic and extremely fast-paced. You can kill most enemies in seconds but just about every enemy can do the same to you, so the game outright relies on your quick reflexes and ability to learn how and when to use each weapon. This game comes from a time in the mid-nineties where "innovation" was the keyword when designing FPS games, so the standard "melee, pistol, shotgun, machine gun, rocket launcher, better machine gun, BFG", loadout popularised by Doom (carried through by Quake and Serious Sam) is changed up a bit: the very first gun that you get is a flare gun, which will kill most smaller enemies with one shot but takes a few seconds to start them burning, and that's the closest thing that you'll ever get to a standard pistol; while there is a typical rocket launcher-like weapon, you also get several different types of dynamite that you can throw, light and drop or use to set traps for enemies (and even the rocket launcher that you find is actually a napalm launcher). As you can see from the screenshots, you'll also find a voodoo doll, which actually works a bit more like a hitscan pistol than the flare gun does. Sometimes, these weird weapon designs can seem a little gimmicky or clunky to use, but just about every weapon is balanced, has its place and uses during combat and is extremely fun to use.
Like any other Build Engine game, the level design is beautiful, fun and very creative. As classic 2.5D FPS games tended to do, Blood expects you to explore, remember where doors are for when you find their keys and travel around the levels to open up new areas beyond places you've already been, rather than ushering you down a single corridor. There is (generally) only one intended way to complete a map, but it still feels a heck of a lot more open-ended than the FPS games of recent years. You're also rewarded for exploring - as they should be, secrets are abundant, and it's actually rare for any single level to have less than 6-8 secret areas. Blood also tried (and, sadly, failed) to introduce the concept of "super secrets" to games, which are deliberately ridiculously hard to find on your own and aren't even shown on the end-of-level tally so you won't know if you've missed one, but will reward you in turn with things like receiving a very powerful weapon early or getting every single powerup in the game at once. Just searching for secrets on its own is a huge factor in the fun of Blood.
Sadly, the game was somewhat overshadowed by virtue of it being a DOS game released right at the end of the DOS era and a 2.5D game released after Quake's true 3D environments, but, overall, if you can stomach some hyperviolence (why would you be looking at a game called Blood if you couldn't?), don't mind some slightly clunky early FPS mechanics (why would you be looking at an FPS from the nineties if you did?) and don't mind that the game runs in DOSBox (the source code was never released, sadly, so we'll most likely never see a true Windows-native source port like Doom, Duke3D and Shadow Warrior have), I would
recommend this game to get your frantic FPS action fix.

Magical Diary is a dating simulation where you essentially play as a female Harry Potter, trying to survive a year at a magical school. It's American-made, but very Japanese in style. Most of the gameplay is interacting with characters and building your own story with short dungeon crawl segments to make use of the magic you learn.
I had a lot of fun with this game. It's fairly short (~4hrs) but there are many paths to take, and you won't see most of the content in a single playthrough. The characters are interesting and believable. The game sadly lacks a plot, but you probably won't miss it too much. The dungeon segments are neat, but too short and shallow to add much. You get tons of neat spells; it's a shame that most go unused.
If you think you might like it, there's a lot of fun packed into this game. However, some will be turned off by the anime style and by the girliness of it. Check out the demo online if you're interested; saves carry over.
UPDATE: In hindsight, I've come to realize that I enjoyed this game despite it really being objectively bad. It's a very fun kind of bad, though. For me, the general goofiness, overly dramatic story, and overused tropes and cliches made it enjoyable for me. It's the sort of game that you'd want to riff on, MST3K style. There are many better dating sims out there, but I would still recommend Magical Diary.

When I hear "indie" in a game's genre list I immediately think of something original and quirky. "The Binding of Issac" matches this mold perfectly by fusing the old adventure style seen in the Legend of Zelda and adding a PC gaming component of difficulty and originality. (10/10)
1. Controls +1
Controls in a game can either make of break it for me, as well as optimization for graphics cards. All that aside, Issac has excellent and responsive controls that make blasting baddies fun and rewarding, and deserve to be mentioned in the strong points of this game's arsenal.
2. Replayability +2
For me, no franchise can match with the replayability of a Pokemon game, but this one sure gets close. There are plenty of characters to unlock, different bosses to encounter and lots of dungeons to be generated, leaving this game to be one of the best yet when it comes to playing it again after beating it over and over.
3. Difficulty +4
This game has the perfect balance between ease of playing and difficulty scaling. The game gets harder as you go at a civilized rate, with dungeons that are fun to explore and bosses that require you to think - There are dozens of ways to beat each floor and plenty of collectibles to get (or miss) for a non stop progressive feeling.
4. Story +3
This game's story cracks me up. I was raised very religiously by my parents and was always creeped out by their loyalty to the bible, and this game's story really hit me home when It came to putting a cherry on the sundae. The story is funny, relatable and goes great with the game, something few games seem to have nowadays seeing as most mainstream titles focus on graphics and mulitplayer functionality to make their money.
Overall, the Binding of Issac has received the coveted "10 out of 10 would do again" title and remains one of my favorite games to ever write electrons on my hard drive. Thank you for releasing this masterpiece.

Stellaris is besides Endless Space 2 one of the major X4 hypes 2016 for me.
First of all the absolute fantastic selection for your own starting population paired with ethic and other choices is incredibly detailed. Your aim is to lead your empire from pre-ftl (mod) one-system empire into global galaxy leader...by force but at your choice also by diplomatics, economics or other fields. It is up to your very own idea and imagination how this should be done.
Still impressed by the 'old' Clausewitz-Engine, well known from historic based Europa Universalis and other games from Paradox developer. Anyhow it's still 32bit (so far I know), you are able to play Stellaris with more then 1000 star systems and more then 32 competitors...even in multiplayer. As known from Paradox they constantly patch and upgrade game and content of their great games for free, while offering steady flow of DLC to enhance players experiance and certainly also to fund their efforts.
While Stellaris is out I have seen 4 DLC plus free updates of this great game, anyhow I didn't buy one of those DLC so far as most of them are purely cosmetic so I wait for sale to get them. More impressed I am from full workshop support from day one, so players could alter their game experiance into anything they or the modders might think about.
Back to first line, I want to state that Stellaris is more then a common 4X title for me personally, even when it is real-time while I prefer turn-bases instead. I'd say Stellaris should be named 4X-S, where 'S' is synonyme for simulation, as you form your own starting race and culture and simulate their way throughout the following centurys while you eXplore the universe, eXpand your empire till you reach hard-to-beat neighbours, eXploit your goods to finally eXterminate your competitors.
Base game is great, comes for an absolute effordable price and offers hours of fun, no matter if you prefer single or multiplayer. If you see it on one of the several sales, go grab you a copy, you will be impressed if not overwhelmed by in-depth gameplay.

I wanted to like this game. I played it at a Comic Convention a month ago and was hyped for it. Unfortunately, despite doing many things right, there are a slew of 'soft' problems that prohbit me from recommending the game, and in full disclosure my refund request is currently pending.
Combat feels imprecise and floaty, a concern I voiced on the forums. The developers commented, stating they had tightened it since the beta build I played but this was not the case. For a game that tries to harken back to Dark Souls, the awkward fumbling and stiff, stilted animations make comitting to an attack graceless. Dust: An Elysian Tail looks a little different than your typical action/adventure game, but its similarities should keep you around for a while.
The game begins with you, "Dust" waking up to find yourself in a forest with no memory of your past or how you ended up at your location. As if it wasn't strange enough, a magical sword finds you and speaks to you, followed by a small, annoying creature. They accompany you on a journey to find who you are, why you awoke with no memory, and why you were chosen to wield a magical sword.
Presentation: 8/10
The story isn't groundbreaking but is enough to get anyone to wonder what's in store for a protagonist with amnesia as he travels through the country. Dust is a kind character, who helps those he can (if you complete the quests) until he finds his past. The game adequately tells the tale from start to finish, but you can never really tell how much of an impact you're making by the end.
Graphics: 7.5/10
Cute cartoon artstyle settles well and takes your mind off the fact that Dust: An Elysian Tail was designed and programmed by a single individual.
Sound: 7.5/10
The pleasant music never stuck itself in places unneeded, a good addition overall. The voice acting was good for some characters, but never made Fidget any less annoying.
Gameplay: 8/10
Fluid, fast-paced and with different options to attack your enemies, the combat was well received. There are many items to acquire, along with the secret non-playable characters hidden throughout the game. My only gripe is the hideous transitioning of the camera as you fly through the map.
Overall: 7.8/10
A good purchase if you're looking for some action/adventure. With only limited replayability, the game can keep you busy for several days before you find yourself with not much else to do, but for a well-polished game, its price is definitely worth it.

Welcome to the Necropolis, an ever-shifting labyrinthine superstructure created by Archmage Abraxis. It's the navel of the world, and also the place he did his laundry.
I've had my eye on this one for a long time. It's a witty and humerous adventure game with an interesting concept: there are no checkpoints. Once you die, it's straight back to the beginning. And be warned-- this title certainly doesn't lack in difficulty.
The art style and procedural generation of rooms is incredible, to say the least. Each run feels distinctly different, and to my surprise, I wasn't upset at all when my avatar kicked the bucket.
Over
and over
and over again.
Almost nothing is explained to you except the controls. Different weapons, for example, have different styles. However, it isn't described in the item description weather a sword is faster, or does more damage. It's up to you as the player to discover that for yourself.
However, as much as I seem to be gushing about this game, that doesn't mean that it's without faults, a few of which I'll lay out below :
-The inablility to edit key bindings is surprising for a game that seems as hardcore as this one. One wrong move and hours of progress can potentially be lost. Quick example: As someone who's played a lot of Witcher 2 recently, I keep automatically pressing the spacebar to dodge incoming attacks (It's the jump key in this title). I'd love the ability to rebind dodge to spacebar as it would feel indefinitely less cumbersome.
- While the game's combat system seems solid overall, it mostly seems to consist of baiting small groups of enemies. Once they're after you, run away. Turn around, land a hit or two, and run away again. Rinse and repeat. As such, I found myself rarley using my shield. Even when I did, it seems you've got the point the shield directly at an incoming attack to block it. That option doesn't really seem worth it when you're trying to fight two or more enemies at a time.
-You're still vulnerable while looting chests. While this may seem like a minor gripe, let me explain: I came across some kind of potion merchant stuffed into one of them. While reading the vauge descriptions for his merchandice, I heard the hiss of an enemy behind me. I quickly exeted the merchant's menu, only to be met with the animation of my character gingerly closing the chest while he was attacked from all sides and quickly killed. That just feels cheap.

I do wish steam had an in-between rating system for games such  as these. While it lacks polish in some regards, all in all, this is an awesome base for a game. It's a bit too expensive at it's current listing though, so I'd recommend picking it up when it's on sale, or when it's content can be justified for it's price tag. It's also a lot better with friends.
On that note, I will be giving this game a positive review because of it's undeniable porential. WIth a few updates, I'm sure this game will soar.
One thing that I can be sure of is that you will die.
A lot.

OK, the graphical visualization of this game is very, very cool.  That I cannot deny.  I have also rarely seen so many exotic real creatures accurately portrayed in one game.  What other game have you ever seen
in?  What other game gives you the opportunity to ride on the back of a blue whale as it breaches?  (Don't try this on your next whale-watching trip, kids.  It will
)
That said...  I don't think I have ever played through any other game in which I spent so much of the total game play time wondering what on earth was going on.  Half the time I felt I was just along for the ride.  I went through the game with only a general idea of what I was supposed to be doing, and almost no idea at all why I was doing it.  There is not at any point anywhere in this game any explanation of who you are, where you are, or why you are there.  If you expect purpose and direction, or any option for non-linear gameplay, this might not be the game for you.
Oh, and where it says a controller is "strongly recommended" to play Abzu?  Let me restate this a little more clearly:  Unless you have a very high frustration tolerance, don't even
to play this game with mouse and keyboard.  Let's just say that of all the possible ways that control for this game could have been mapped onto a mouse and keyboard, most of the possible options I can think of are better than Abzu's.  At that, I discovered one move by accident:  press E to do a kind of tuck-roll in place.  I have no idea what other easter-egg movement controls may be hidden somewhere on the keyboard.  I tried several likely guesses after discovering the E roll, and didn't find any others, but I didn't try anywhere near every key.
Overall, on balance, Abzu was worth playing once.  But I don't see it as having a lot of replay value.  It might have more replay value if there was more of a sense of agency in the game, if you felt that anything at all was under your control.  But quite honestly, this game would lose almost no interactivity or immersion if you just watched a video of someone else playing it.  It's mostly a completely linear spectator experience, with just enough depth of interactivity to make you feel that you're playing something instead of purely following a script and reciting your lines on cue.
But it's a heck of a spectacle.  So relax, sit back, and enjoy.

(Note: I got this game for free, so I may have a different view then someone who bought it full price. Also some minor spoilers.)
Belladonna is a game that revolves around 3 characters:
- The Scientist (I can't remember his name, so I'll call him Scientist Dude)
- Belladonna (The Scientist's wife)
- Klara (Belladonna's maid)
The introduction is that Scientist Dude and his wife Belladonna live in this big mansion place, the wife has a son (Lucas) that dies soon after birth. Scientist Dude and his wife start becoming distant, with Scientist Dude always in the basement and his wife always upstairs staring out a window. The mansion starts falling apart, with many of the servants quitting, until only one is left, Klara. Klara and Belladonna have a thing for each other. Scientist Dude has learned the secrets of reanimation (Frankenstein stuff).
What I enjoyed about this game:
- the art style
- the music
- the chilling/spooky parts (even though you can always tell when one of these is about to happen because normally the screen shifts automatically while you move but these parts it doesn't until you get close to the edge and the area obviously has more to it that it isn't showing immediately)
- the idea in the story of same-sex romance (which is rarely featured in games)
- the idea in the story of clockwork reanimated people
- The attention to detail in some parts, (Spoiler here!)

- How you have to figure out the story for yourself, as not much is revealed to you without collecting the journal pages. I also liked how the end of the story is revealed first, then everything leading up to that point.
What I didn't enjoy about this game:
- The majority of the voice acting. It seems forced, usually without emotions. (especially the very first lines. They are really weak and made me want to stop playing in the first 30 seconds). Occasionally there is obvious cuts that don't sound too good.
- The attention to detail in some other parts. (Spoiler here, again!)
- The shortness of the game. I could see why someone who bought this game for full value might be a bit frustrated.
- With the shortness mentioned, I hated the ending. It was abrupt, and I felt like alot more could be said. There is a difference between a suspensful cliffhanger that keeps you guessing but still satisfies (think Inception) and an ending that is so sudden that it literally gives you a picture of what ends up happening, which is what this game did. The last thing happens, and the 'The End' screen shows a single picture that defines the future, no making up stuff allowed!
In the end, I have to say I did enjoy this game, although it should have been longer and not had such a rushed, sudden, and unimaginative ending. The highest I could give this is a 6/10, but I feel like most would settle for less, especially paying full price.

It is a big step up from OG GC2 though, maintaining most of the innovations from the completed effort of both expansion packs. So if you go into it expecting a groundbreaking new game, you will be disappointed. I haven't played a game in a while that made me feel the way ABZU has. Its hard to put a finger on it aswell. Most people mihgt use words such as relaxed, at peace and zen when describing this game, and they'd be right. But for me there's something else aswell.
I think I kinda feld sad while playing ABZU. But not necessarily the bad kind of sadness. The kind of sadness one might feel watching news coverage of a war or a terrorist bombing. Its more the kind of sadness you feel when you're pet passes away of old age. You feel sad when your pet dies, but you also fondly remember all the good times you had, and how much love there was between you. And eventhough your pet is gone, that love still remains, and that means something.
This game, more than any other, made me feel like a human being. And perhaps that's what I needed. Perhaps that's what the world needs. To be reminded of what its like to be a human.
See there's not much of a story to speak of and there isn't any dialogue or character devlopment or plot. But I didn't really need it, because this game leaves it up to you to fill in the blanks. And since its not that long, I completed in in about 6 hours, it suits this game very well.
As I gracefully drifted through the marvellous underwater scenery, I felt sort of lonely, but also at one with the enviroment at the same time.
The visuals are absolutely gorgeous and eventhough the game doesn't boast very detailled graphics I never felt like there wasn't something interesting to look at. The water is filled with thousands of underwater species ranging from small reef species to massive whales and everything in between. They've even thrown in some extinct animals.
If you're looking for an underwater diving simulator, you should look further. However if you're looking for a very well made meditative zen game set in a gorgeous enviroment, ABZU is your best pick.

Released on Halloween 2016 by Visual-Wordplay,
is a visual novel about a girl who goes away with friends on Halloween. On the way, a minor landslide knocks her out and when she wakes up, she finds her way to a mansion and meets three brothers with a secret.
The game contains four characters: a 20 year-old college student, Cara Lee, our female protagonist that gets lost and finds her way to the mansion and the three brothers: eldest Viktor, middle Vonn and youngest Vern.
The background art is clean but nothing more. The characters personalities are plain, though distinctive. The relationship between Ms. Lee and the other characters felt forced and unnatural. This VN had potential to give more and presents a lack of a more-in-depth story and characters.
Much of the gameplay is reading through the story, though there are several decision points to make along the way that decide what route you will take along with different kinds of dialogue. In total, there are four different endings in this game. Another short and predictable Halloween fairytale. A good game just to get 100% achievements (there are four).
A 20-year-old graduating student in college. To celebrate their upcoming graduation next semester, she and her friends go on a hike to a popular mountain. However, it starts storming in the middle of their hike. Along the way, a minor landslide knocks her unconscious, and when she wakes up, she finds herself alone in a dark and scary forest.
Even though he’s only 23 years old, Viktor has made it his responsibility to take care of his two young brothers. He’s very nice and always has a warm smile on his face. Viktor can be sort of a jokester and a prankster at times. He can be pretty stern to his siblings, however.
The second of the brothers at around 22 years of age. He tends to be a grump about everything, but he does have a sweet and funny side to him. He’s rarely a talkative person, but when he does talk, it can be pretty hard to shut him up.
The youngest of the brothers. He’s actually a friendly guy, but he’s too shy to show it at first. Like his oldest brother though, he likes jokes and funny punch lines. A lot. At first he didn’t want Cara Lee’s presence in his home, but he warms up to her, eventually.

Hero Academy is an asymmetrical turn based strategy game featuring colourful cartoon style sprites battling each other for dominance of the board. You select the team you wish you use, each featuring their own characters, spells and synergies and then off you go. Board is selected randomly as is your opponent, though you can select from your friends list.
Once play commences, each round gives you 5 action points with which to either place a unit, move a unit, attack with a unit, or cast a spell. Units and spells are randomly generated at the beginning of each turn to fill up to a selection of 6 items. Then you submit your turn and await the opponents manoeuvres in return.
You can aim to either wipe the board clear of opponents, or try to take out any crystals the opponent has on the board.
You can run more than one game at once which is great, and the game will notify you when a turn is ready to play your next round. so you can play this as a quick distraction game with two games running and login once a day or so, or you can start 20 games at once if you want a non stop session.

I've been following for awhile and super hyped for this game to release. It looked really fun, unique art style, good character/weapon design. I'm a fan of rogue-likes as well Dark Souls. I figured this game would be perfect for me, but I just don't have any drive to play or see more. That right there is a deal-breaker for me.
Pros:
-Unique and aesthetically pleasing art style. (Personal opinion, I like it, and the characters.)
-Crafting system is a good addition, and a great mechanic. It was enjoyable making potions, and unlocking a codex to fully unlock the recipes. I'm a sucker for crafting and gathering so I really liked this idea. Wish more games had on-the-fly crafting like this.
-Stamina management isn't a burden and while there can be times where it'll drop and you'll be left vulnerable, I never had a point where I didn't have a way to regen it. Plus if it regens stam, it probably regens health as well so, bonus.
-Humor is good. If you're into dry, friendly Bill Cipher asking for help as he wishes death on you, then you'll like this. There are some good lines, and got a few chuckles out of me.
-The unlock/token system is pretty fun. It gives you tasks to complete to earn tokens in game, as well as tokens after dying/completing a run. Which can be used to buy new dyes, codexes, open certain chests, and other things. Little goals like that help keep it fresh.
-Unique mechanics and characters, such as a shopkeep alchemist in a chest, and one in a drain. That's pretty cool.
Cons:
-Combat is extremely slow, and clunky. Using a fast weapon alleviates this a but also has 0 knockback or stun so you just end up trading. It's much more efficient to just use a large weapon and kite. I got a boosted fire weapon that did even less than a broken sword I got off the first enemy. Legendary my♥♥♥♥♥
-The shield is worthless and uneccessary, and you can't get rid of it. I would much prefer to drop the shield and two-hand a larger weapon to swing faster. When I did use the shield I got a stam drain when hit, and was stunned momentarily. Why do that when I can just kill and kite? Especially when I take damage when blocking.
-AI is eh at best. The game suffers from a few things Dark Souls did as well with enemies. They're not intelligent, there's just a ton of them in a small area. I think I had about 20-30 enemies in a single area, with about 6-8 trained on me at once. While you don't take THAT much damage, they can wombo you to death easily, especially with the red(elite) variants if you're not careful or get body blocked. That's not really difficult so much as just an annoying amount of enemies swinging at me at once. They're easily wiped out with a large weapon, a power-attack, and/or decent kiting.
-Everything looks the same. Watching a few streams, playing the game, it all just kinda blends together. I love the art style just wish there was more to see, more variety.
-$30 price tag. I figured it'd be worth it seeing as the game appeared to be massive, but I hear people are burning through it in less than an hour, and I got pretty far myself just goofing off. It just doesn't feel $30 worthy, $10-$15 maybe, $20 is pushing it.
I feel like the game has potentional, and adds a lot of new mechanics an ideas that I'd love to see explored in other games. However, after playing a few rounds and trying to avoid the refund timer I just never felt like I wanted to see more or continue. That's my dealbreaker. It started off ok, then I just got bored. Might revisit the title at a later date, or on a sale. Hope for a content update or something. Right now it's just not going to hold my attention sadly.

Point-and-click adventures were a dead genre. And not unlike the protagonist of
, they didn’t stay dead forever. In a sea of modern adventures that eschew traditional puzzles in favor of character development and moral choices, I was interested in tackling a traditional point-and-click adventure game. Especially one with a horror aesthetic.
influences become obvious very early on. We start our game on a slab in a laboratory, suffering from amnesia, of course. We are a reanimated corpse and our goal is to piece together the events that lead to our initial demise. So you can see how Mary Shelley’s
plays a key role in the creation of this game, even before the game clumsily makes a reference to her within the first five minutes.
The laboratory we’re in happens to be housed inside the dungeon of a castle, occupied by Dr. Wolfram von Trauerschloss. Now if that name doesn’t sound silly to you, it’s probably because you don’t speak German, because “Trauerschloss” literally translates to “Mourning Castle”. So you can see why this was one of the early warning signs about this title, for me at least. The good doctor, true to his inspiration, tinkers with the elements of life to bring back recently deceased organisms.
Unfortunately, we don’t really see him do that. You see,
is more of an investigative story than one we’re directly involved with. We’re here to run around the castle, looking for clues and objects to solve puzzles and uncover what actually happened. That means, we’ll be collecting a handful of journal entries that explain to us the events and character motivations. It’s a rather clumsy attempt at delivering a story, mostly relying on exposition instead of actual story development. The problem with this however is, besides being a rather weak writing tool, that a lot of what we’re reading easily foreshadows upcoming revelations. This makes the story seem to be a paint-by-numbers affair, which it actually is, and does little to engage the player.
This is only further exacerbated by the fact that almost every interaction with this world seems to yield a “funny” response from our main character. The game obviously follows the example made by the old LucasArts games, but unfortunately it undermines the gothic horror atmosphere the rest of the game wants to invoke. And the reason I put “funny” in quotation marks is because the humor constantly falls flat. Besides, this isn’t a funny story, none of the elements are amusing at all. This is a story about personal loss, about tragedy, interpersonal relationships, envy and madness. Disconnected, sarcastic humor doesn’t really fit well when contrasted with the serious nature of its themes.
This wouldn’t be a problem in most other games where gameplay is king, but unfortunately, adventure games rarely contain any gameplay outside of inventory management. If I’ve counted correctly, there are maybe 4 or 5 puzzles you have to solve, most of which have solutions that are immediately obvious to anyone playing. Inventory management is very basic, you can combine two objects in order to solve puzzles with the resulting combinations. And if that weren’t enough, the constant vocalizations of our protagonist makes the solutions even more obvious. We’re rarely required to get creative or think outside the box.
The only aspect that registered positively with me was the visual presentation. We find ourselves in a lovingly designed, very detailed environment that manages to give the game some semblance of a gothic horror atmosphere. And the music helps to underline that. But unfortunately, this is largely undone by the aforementioned tonal discrepancies between the world we’re in and the theoretical gravitas of the story, and the lighthearted nature of the simplistically written dialogue.
Now some of you might be perplexed by the low number of puzzles presented to us and ask how long this journey through
actually takes. And to be perfectly blunt, it takes less than an hour and 30 minutes. It’s a very short affair with no secrets, and the fact that the story is entirely linear also means that there’s literally no replay value.
So at this point, the only thing I can say is that, in spite of its beautiful visuals and nice soundtrack, the game unfortunately doesn’t manage to capture the charm of popular point-and-click adventure games. The story would’ve had potential if it would’ve focused more on the more polarizing and grotesque elements in there, but in this state, you’re probably better off watching the Universal version of
. Or if you like a bit more humor in your horror, why not go for
instead? Because in the end, you’re about as passive in
as you are while watching a movie.

You are able to find crafting receips - well so far nothing new - you won´t be able to craft them yourself but a blacksmith will help you about that. Dust: An Elysian Tail is an RPG (Not turn based, thank god), where you move in a sidescroller fashion and fight enemies in real time. It is sort of like a "beat em up" type of game, where you traverse different parts of the world, fighting enemies as you move.
Gameplay (8.5/10) - The fighting in this game deals with you fighting waves of enemies with combos you learn throughout the game. You can upgrade your damage and defence with upgrades along the way (like most RPG's). The combos you can do are very fun to mix up and you can come up with brilliant ways to kill mobs of enemies in a few seconds. There is also a sort of "magic" in this game, that you must combine with your combos to make full use. Absolutly great.
In the game there are also quests you can preform to acheive EXP, money, etc. Some quests are just fun, laughy type of quests, but some delevel deep into the main characters role in the game. Extremely great.
Two problems, one, the boss fights, which were pretty easy (Even if I was on the hardest difficulty). Two, there really is no replayability besides finishing off sidequests. Once I finished the game, I didn't really feel the need to go back and finish it to completion.
Art (10/10) - Beautiful, haven't seen anything like it. More of a cartoonish approach, but well done.
Story (10/10) - A very deep story of the main character trying to find his true self in a war of trying to "cleanse" the land of a certain people. It is so well done, honestly, I was very happy with the ending.
Music (9/10) - The music is great, I love listing to the OST. It's a classical type of tune, which really brings you into the world. It does become quite repetitive later on in the game, but I never had a problem with that, the music was good, what's not to like.
Overal (9.5/10) - Play this game, seriously. You won't regret it at all. Such a fun game that I even got my brother hooked on immediatly. It's definetly a game you can't finish too quickly!

This game is a lot of fun and has plenty of potential if it is updated further.  The basic gameplay mechanics are fun and is very entertaining if you play militarily.
Many of the problems in this game lie in diplomacy.  I found the game nearly impossible to understand playing it from a diplomatic angle.  For example there are diplomacy points that you supposedly gain from researching certain techs and building embassies.  I still have yet to see any effect of these diplomacy points in my interaction with other races, and there is no concrete change to my standing with them.  When I trade with other factions, I often can't propose any treaties without any explanation why.  There are also many minor annoying bugs like the income slider changing rates slightly without using it, and certain technologies not doing what they are supposed to (research treaty is one example I can think of).
A very major (and ridiculous) problem I've encountered with the game is United Planets voting.  The AI is incompetent in this regard.   In one game I played, all of my allies voted for an enemy (who we were ALL at war with) giving the enemy a stat boost.
I like this game and have enjoyed playing it, however, I would recommend holding off on buying it until it is further polished.

I've really been enjoying the game.
There is a very different feel when playing multiplayer versus single player. Multiplayer has friend ressurection, while single player feels like you actually get attacked by more enemies. This could just be a side effect of level generation though.
The only discernable stats are the tier values of an item. In multiplayer, we found that even same tier weapon can do differing amounts of damage.
Permanent upgrades can be found in the codecies, a selection of equipable books that can be found a codex locations. Again, things aren't explained to the player as to the discrete effect these will have.
All in all, I see a lot of games likening this on to Souls; however, it reminds me more of a real-time Nethack.
The game is great if you like some skill-base combat, unknown resource management, and learning through playthroughs. I also feel the gaming community has gone too long without a seriously fun and flexible co-op experience like this in a long while.

I'm sorry to say that I can't really recommend Belladonna. This is a short point and click adventure game about a woman who wakes up reanimated in a dungeon and has to figure out what happened to her. Most of the story is told in journal entries that your character finds throughout the castle. The story in these is interesting (if pretty scary and tragic) and told well, but the fonts chosen for each character are quite small and can be hard to read. It's a bit of a weakness that the player character has amnesia, since her relationship to the other characters is difficult to flesh out because she doesn't remember them. There's one particularly disturbing story thread that kind of ends up going nowhere for this reason.

In some places it's a bit difficult to figure out which objects can be interacted with. The voice acting is decent, and it was nice to hear so many object descriptions.

I have mixed views on Belladonna. On one hand the story is dark and intriguing and has pretty solid voice acting, but on the other it does not explore these themes in enough depth to make a lasting impression. I think this game is worth trying if you already got it on sale or in a bundle. My completion time was 1.5 hours, and the remaining time on my counter was for trading card drops.
Belladonna explores some dark and mature themes, including life, death, murder and other moral issues. The game follows an animated corpse as she tries to find out about her past life and how she came to be in this state between being alive and dead. The dark and macabre nature of the story was interesting to me, and will interest those who are also fans of this type of story. I did enjoy unraveling the mysteries behind Belladonna as the story progresses, and some of the twisted revelations throughout the game I did find satisfying.
There are several shortcomings to this game, however, that prevented me from enjoying it as much as I felt I would. The story simply is too short and doesn't explore enough of the dark themes, and felt like a wasted potential. Play time isn't always the most important thing if there is enough emotional impact, but Belladonna felt very rushed at times, for example as some other reviews have mentioned, notably so near the ending.
Belladonna is certainly a point and click adventure game, but within this genre people do have different expectations. I would describe Belladonna as more as a story-exploration game with adventure game elements, that is the focus is more on the story while the puzzles are not very difficult, and do not take up much time. I personally do not mind this as there are other games I could play if I wanted a challenge, so as long you're not expecting some super difficult brain teasers you shouldn't be disappointed in this aspect.
I enjoyed the story of Belladonna, but felt there could have been much more to the game. If you enjoy dark, macabre stories and don't mind easy point and click puzzles, I think this game is worth picking up on sale or in a bundle, but no need to go out of your way to do so.

In
you play as a 20 year-old college student. (You can choose her first name and she may have ended up with the awkward name of Donald Trump Lee in my play-through, but I digress.) Ms. Lee is taking a hike on a mountain with her friends when a landslide happens that knocks her unconscious. When she wakes up it is raining and she desperately looks for shelter when she comes across a beautiful mansion in the mountains. She heads for it and is given shelter by its residents, a trio of brothers about her age named Vonn, Vern, and Viktor. Ms. Lee tries to figure out what is going on, but also tries to get to know these young men better.
This game is a visual novel, a type of video game that is entirely story-driven. Much of the gameplay is reading through the story, though there are several decision points to make along the way that decide what route you will take along with different kinds of dialogue. In total, there are four different endings in this game.
To start with some aspects that I liked in this game, I would say that the art is good. The background art is really nice and clean. It works well in the game. The character sprites are a little more plain, though distinctive. I thought the music was only okay. It was a nice addition, but it was not long before it started to feel repetitive.
I do have to admit, I was disappointed with the writing in the game. While it never really felt bad to me, it never felt good, either. The establishing premise of the game was quite interesting and I was curious to see where it would go, but it never went very far. The ending was somewhat interesting, even if it was a bit predictable. However, between the beginning and ending, there was not much going on. The relationship between Ms. Lee and the other characters felt forced and unnatural. Too much of it felt like a dopey romance plot without much depth. It is rather disappointing because the premise of the game has such great potential and the writers could have ran with it, but what is in the game was a deeply unsatisfying experience.
Overall, this visual novel left me frustrated. While not terrible, the lack of a more in-depth story and characters in an otherwise interesting premise was a disappointment. This game is available for free and it might be worth a play if you really like visual novels.

This is sort of like chess but with multiple moves per turn, factions that play very differently from one another, and CCG-style luck-based drawing of pieces/items to play.
Ok, so not very much like chess. This is probably quite a bit more fun. The luck factor can be quite frustrating at times, causing you to lose a close match when you draw the wrong "cards" several times in a row; on the other hand, when your luck is bad and your opponent is strong and you *still* manage to win through sneakiness and misdirection, well, that's a victory to savour.
Anyway, been enjoying this a great deal. One of the things this game does right is that your opponent doesn't get to be cheap and refuse to play his turn: you win automatically if the other guy does not play his turn for 7 (or 14) days.
(One minor annoyance: I can't seem to find my win/loss% stats anywhere. There's a leaderboard showing us how many games we have won, but that's about it. A table of our greatest rivals (the people we've lost the most times to and/or played the most number of games against) would be nice too.)
Bottomline: This is a *really* good 1-on-1 turn-based strategy game. Highly recommended!

Blood is a game that is part of the Build engine "Holy Trinity", which also includes Duke Nukem 3D and Shadow Warrior.
Whilst Duke Nukem 3D was the original and is easily considered the King out of the other games, both Blood and Shadow Warrior bring unique features and design compared to Duke Nukem 3D. Duke Nukem was a parody out of 80's action heroes, Shadow Warrior a parody of Kung Fu movies and the ultra-violent Asian movie craze whilst Blood was a parody of Horror movies, especially with the atmosphere, easter eggs and spoken lines by the protagonist which is often a famous Horror movie quote.
Blood was a popular and somewhat successful game at its time, but both Blood and Shadow Warrior were overshadowed by not only Duke Nukem 3D, but the rise of Quake which saw most people rather buy and play Quake instead.
Now onto the game itself, you play as a man named Caleb who comes back alive in his grave at the start of the game. Caleb was once part of the evil cult named Cabal. The leader of the cult, Tchernobog, betrays Caleb and kills him, putting him in a grave, this was done as Tchernobog feared Caleb's power in case he ever turned on the cult.
When the actual game starts itself you rise from your grave ready to strike vengeance against the cult and Tchernobog, as well as save the rest of The Chosen (who Caleb were a part of). There are 4 episodes in the game and the first 3 episodes are about saving 3 of The Chosen who were also betrayed by Tchernobog, whilst the 4th is about destroying Tchernobog himself.
The gameplay is pretty much identical to Duke Nukem 3d, but the differences are the enemies and the weapons as well as the items that Caleb uses. You start the game using a pitchfork to kill the first zombie but then quickly move on to the flaregun. I have played Duke Nukem 3D, Shadow Warrior as well as Blood, but out of the 3, Blood is by far the most difficult. This is because there is less emphasis on weapons that deal direct damage, such as Duke's pistol, shotgun and chaingun etc, whilst in Blood even though you are equipped with a shotgun and tommy gun yourself, a lot of time you are using the flaregun which kills enemies over time and doesn't stop them from shooting you until they catch fire and die, as well as the TNT bundles which explode on impact, unlike Duke's pipebomb which can be detonated at any time.
There are remote detonated TNT and a lot of ammo for the hitscan weapons in later episodes, but on harder difficulties just don't expect too much use for them, as you will be using a lot of it up quickly.
The game prides itself on it's Horror atmosphere, so expect gore (hence the name of the game haha). Unlike the other Build games, using TNT to blow someone into lots of pieces, or kicking a decapitated zombie head like a football or even setting a cultist on fire and watching them panic and melt away is the best feature about this game that stands out above the others. Although there is gore in Duke Nukem 3D, it is not on the level of Blood's. The gore is very satisfying.
There is no freezethrower or shrinker or any weapons like that in Blood, oh no, there is a voodoo doll which allows you to stab it to hurt and destroy enemies, a napalm cannon which uses gasoline as ammo to fire an explosive ball of napalm which sets entire groups of enemies on fire and a tesla cannon which just obliterates enemies. Although some of the weapons in Duke Nukem 3D and Shadow Warrior are funny and unique, Blood just goes all out in painful and nasty weapons which do what you expect them to do, they are all very satisfying to use.
The enemies mainly compromise of zombies which are melee only and rather easy to kill, but can revive themselves if not killed by a flare or pitchfork. There are also the cultists which, along with the zombies, are the most common enemies you see in the game, they can throw bombs at you, shoot you with shotgun or tommy gun and generally destroy you in an open area. These enemies are actually the most difficult in the game, because they are very good with their hitscan weapons and you have to use TNT from cover or maybe tag one of them at a time using the flare gun to kill them without harming yourself too much.
The level design is excellent and has a very spooky atmosphere (2spooky4me), but there are levels ranging from an evil rollercoaster to a moving train, making each level exciting and unique to play, whereas even Duke Nukem 3D had its filler levels a lot of the time.
Each episode has an end boss, the first boss is very easy, as he only fires projectiles and you can just circle strafe and shoot him to death to win, whilst the other bosses bring more to the table and forces you to be more skilled to defeat them.
The weapons, enemies and levels are all fantastic and I find this game to be the most fun to play out of the Build engine games if you enjoy gore, carnage and sadistic pleasures in setting cultists on fire, blowing them up and hearing their screams.
Caleb is a fantastic protagonist who is actually still evil and has awesome voice lines, although not as quippy or as funny as Duke's or Lo Wang's, Caleb is more sinister and constantly makes sarcastic remarks when you blow up enemies or set them on fire, adding to the pleasure you get from killing enemies.
The source code is yet to be released for Blood, therefore there is no modern sourceport that runs this game. This is the worst part about this game on Steam, as you are forced to play it on DOSbox. DOSbox works as it should but even when you freshly install it, it is highly recommended you check out these guides to get it running as best as possible on your system:
Guide for fixing the game up for your system:
Guide for using a launcher to easily launch the game and its expansion pack:
It seems like extra effort spent better actually playing the game, but trust me, it is worth your time as you will enjoy this game.
The game itself is easily a 9/10, but the fact there is no modern sourceport due to the source code being undisclosed is what annoys me, it is all up to Atari who holds the rights for it to release it or not.
But if you enjoy good singleplayer FPS games where it is all about just obliterating everyone, whether you like classic FPS games or not or even if you don't like the Horror atmosphere, this game is very fun and you should play it.

A really good RTS game. It's kind of like a blend of Crusader Kings and Total War, with both sides being simplified, but is better for it.
The CK elements roughly corespond to your royal family and the diplomacy, allying yourself to powers through marriage and spreading your dynasty. The Total War elements are the conquering, governing and the campaigning. The army system is what the current Total War model should be: you can fill a town with a custom garrison *but* in you cannot recruit past a certain number and only marshals can actually take troops and march between towns with them.
The early game is all about setting up the stage for your future: conquering neighbours, making lasting alliances and eternal enemies. At the beginning, no one has walls on most cities, so you'll be giving and receiving very devestating surprise raids and conquests, but you'll be hampered by rebellions. Mid game, you'll have a stronger economy to build walls and units other than peasants, meaning wars become about avoiding the citadels and raiding the unprotected hinterlands. Late game results in giant armies baiting each other onto the open plains to prevent either side starving and losing their gigantic money makers to a siege.
Diplomacy is very good. The AI actually tells you what they will and will not accept as you demand it, for example, by yelling that only your destruction, or just a small ceding of a province, will result in peace.
Overall a great game, though it is recommended you use the HD mods as others have pointed out.

Dust: An Elysian Tail is the best indie game you'll ever play. I guarantee it. The story is phenomenal, with a couple of plot twists that I saw coming, and a few more that caught me off guard! The voice acting is actually great, which is something I don't find in many of the indie games I play. The animation is all handpainted, and sans the soundtrack and voicework, it was all done by ONE GUY. What? That's awesome. Totally worth the $15 you'll pay for it, and definitely worth the $3 I got it for on the Steam Summer Sale. Also, anthropomorphic animals are the entire cast, so if you have a problem with that, you should get over it and play it anyways because this game is awesome. My only complaint is the last stretch before the final boss, which seems like it NEVER ends, but that's a paltry complaint in the face of this absolutely gorgeous game.

Before you leave because this is a negative review, hear me out. This game is great, its got a great art style, has witty dialogue, crafting, souls-esque gameplay and difficulty, and fun dungeon crawling. Now if all of that sold you, go buy this game, but if you're still sceptical, continue on.
What this game lacks is the juice. The FEEL. Attacking doesn't feel smooth at all, it feels like different slashes cut and smashed together to make a jumpy animation (and most of the time you'll be using the same attack animation repeatedly). Moving feels great, but the fact that it abruptly breaks to attack things makes it feel poorly tweened together. Even eating is slow and stops your character entirely so that mid fight nourishing can easily get you killed (maybe thats intentional). Although walking feels decent, jumping and trying to sprint or parry all feel choppy. Even the health and stamina bars refill animation feels choppy instead of satisfying.
Everything just lacks polish.
These devs need to take a note out of the Game Feel book or they need to play Super Mario 64 to see what I'm saying. Movement should feel fast and energetic, I should glide through this dungeon slaying enemies in my path (it should feel like this, Im not saying the game should be easier). Instead it feels choppy and slow, while standing to hit the attack button a couple times before the enemy flashes red and lumps over. Its lacking that polish and juice to make me want to try again after I die. While this is one of the shortest point and click games I've played, this one made me very disappointed it wasn't longer. It was simple, but don't fix what ain't broke.
There is an atmosphere of dread that is captured very well with the music, art, and voice acting. The story, while somewhat predictable after a few diary pages, was still chilling enough that I found myself cringing and being disgusted with every action I took. My character's questioning of her own actions and morals gave me a nice feeling of just how much this was inspired by Mary Shelley's work.
It was an appropriate love letter to Frankenstein. It really was.
Yet there are some things I should add that are huge, glaring downfalls in this game. The big reveal cutscene after dealing with the cat (UH. THANKS FOR THAT, BY THE WAY!) seems a bit awkward. The one character no longer seems to fit in with the artstyle of Belladonna and just looks out of place. We have all of this lovely art
Yet this is easily overlooked. It's not very long and you'll get back to PRETTY! 2D! soon enough.
The largest concern is this game is ENTIRELY TOO SHORT. You will get to the end, not realize it, and reach the THE END screen and start bemoaning how this game deserved much longer. You're expecting the next phase of the game to begin, especially since your character seems to be wanting to voice her concerns, but...nothing! The puzzles, being simple enough as they are, make it feel as if this game needed much more time devoted to it.
Those are my gripes. Was it worth the $6.99 I paid? Probably not. Was it a good experience? Enough to write some cheesy fanfiction because you ripped my heart out.

Obviously the second play results in decision, that you have to play that game at least one more time.
To deeper understanding the story I really recommend to read all Witcher books from Andrzej Sapkowski which are events before Witcher games.
