I bought this game in a bundle with the first one for really cheap.  I played, errr, tried to play the first one.  The gameplay is just not what I am used to and the combat in the first one was horrid.  So I had no intention of playing this one.  But, since I paid money for it I decided to give it a whirl.  Let me just say that this game is my favorite fantasy RPG out there.  Yes, I like it even more than Skyrim!  But let me say this, gameplay wise Skyrim and Witcher 2 are not comparable.  Skyrim is open world and you can go anywhere any time. (For the most part).  Witcher 2 is a more linear RPG so they aim for two different types of gameplay.  Where the Witcher 2 excels and beats Skyrim to a bloody pulp is story and character.  Skyrim, the character you play has no personality and is just there.  The story is very loose and unfocused.  (I do grant Skyrim leniancy on that unfocused story because it is open world and that is a draw back for strong drivin story telling).  Witcher2 you are a character that is already defined and everyone knows him.  He already has a character and you just guide to see how his character grows or changes.  The story for Witcher 2 is very strong too.  With each place you visit there are lots of side quests and while they can deviate from the main story line they don't detract from it but can sometimes give you greater meaning to the main story by uncovering something you wouldn't have otherwise.  You get to see and feel how the world in Witcher 2 works and how its morality unfolds.  Witcher 2 is definitely a darker fantasy story but it is rich in characters and story.

Before dozing off to bed and finally being able to rest after playing this nonstop from 2 am to 5 am, I figured I should write a review while it's still fresh in my mind.
First of all, did I enjoy this? Yes! Is it something everyone can enjoy? No. I'll pass on pointing out the good things for now and look at the bad things throughout, so that I can get started with how to improve it. First of all, it's full of bugs, and some scenes seem a lot like rip-offs from other rpg horror game(ex: in the opening you learn that your mother died and you ask your father to go visit her grave tomorrow). There was a lot of frustrating scenes in it which were really hard to figure out on your own. No clues were given for them what-so-ever. One example is when in the mansion I had no idea I could fill the bottle with holy water, and I had no idea I even needed holy water! The game does not tell you ''go get holy water'', no, it just leaves you alone wandering around trying to find what to do next. It also has a lot of tile and clipping errors. If I had a penny for everything I could walk over in this game, I would be one of the richest men of my country. It also has a lot of spelling and grammar errors. At times sentences aren't started with capital letters, and at one point in the game you see that the word ''orphan'' has been spelled as ''orphin''. The maps are empty and bland, and unnecessarily huge, and there are a lot of tiles error like I mentioned. Why did the bookshelves have additional bookshelves below them? It did not make sense, and there were gaps too. Light effects felt cheap, most of the time they went over walls and they had no blur to them what-so-ever, and that's not how lights work in real life at all. You can also interact with things even when not facing them. Also the final scene with lots of monsters was just, way too hard. It took me like 50 attempts trying to get all endings(atleast I didn't die at all with the true ending X3). The game also teaches you that angel statues save, however later on there are angel statues in the game that don't do anything. If they won't do anything, why did we learn about them? One other thing is, the developer does not know how to remove party members from the looks of it.
Jacob is still in your party, and also, one game breaking bug I found is when you go to the room where you place the dagger after forging it, returning to the big library will cause the flashback to reset.
So why did I like this?
Honestly, no idea myself. It had lots of flaws, and needed a lot of polishing, but something about me just really wants to like this game. Is it my sense of being way too easily impressed? Is it my love for these kinds of games? Something about it really drawed me into it, and I thought it was really bad, but in the same time I thought it was good. Honestly, with a few bug fixes and a little more dialog improvement this could be made into something great. It really has that potential. I did a 3 part let's play on it, and I will share the playlist when all parts are done uploading. It had good scenes, and some parts that were actually pretty good, like the library and the crypt. Although I don't see how
. There were some nice death scenes along the game but also some that are plain lame. For example in the sewers if you enter a room you will be killed by a goblin. No warning was given for this at all, and you did not get to save before it either. I could clearly see that this game follows WilliamTheUnproPro's Let's Make A Rpg Horror Game tutorials on youtube, and one map is just a plain rip-off of it.
Again, I'm saying it. This game isn't for everyone. This isn't a professional rpg maker game that really stands out, it's very amateur. The Forgotten Forest, developed by Dylan Wentz, is one of many RPGMaker games purchasable on Steam… but if you’re looking for a scary and (or) dramatic experience crafted on this engine, I’d say you’re better off looking elsewhere.
You play as Rebecca, a simple girl leading a simple life. With her mother’s death, she finds comfort in her father, who seems more than capable of raising a child. But, as the story quickly unfolds, that’s where things go downhill; not just for our protagonists, but for the game as a whole.
You see, The Forgotten Forest is anything but subtle. Almost instantly, in the midst of a school day, Rebecca’s class is greeted by a strange old woman whom none of the children know. She proceeds to tell the students of a cursed forest nearby… and that’s it. That intro alone sums up the style of this game’s story.
It’s very random.
Plot twists and conflicts will just spring out of nowhere, and before you can blink, something else has already happened. For example, after Rebecca returns from school, she sits down with her father. Only seconds into their meal and there’s a crash at the door. The father explains that he owes some men money, or something.
My reaction: “…… ok…..?”
After escaping the house and running off into the woods, that is where our game begins.
Now, there really isn’t too much to say about gameplay. You collect items, solve puzzles, and that’s about it; pretty standard for most RPGMaker games. But your objective throughout these puzzles is not always clear. It got to the point where I’d collected 10 random puzzle items and I had no idea what to do with any of them.
Oh, but there is one thing that really, really pisses me off: Cheap Deaths. They. Are. Everywhere. I must’ve died at least ten times due to completely random scenarios that were unavoidable.
The game has heart, I know so, but I just don’t think it’s worth your time or money. However, I believe this dev is totally capable of making something great, had there been a little more time and effort put in. But until then, we’ll just have to wait and see.

Everyone must already heard how awesome Final Fantasy VII about one million times so I'll keep it short.
Yes, Final Fantasy VII is awesome and most likely the best in the series. The story is amazing. The soundtrack, just like in every other FF game, wonderful and now actually fixed to sound like the PS1 version instead of the terrible PC MIDIs.
The graphics? Well, sadly, this isn't a remake and only a very small upgrade. The video quality is improved and the game is rendered in 1080p. However the models are still really low-polygonal and the pre-rendered 2D images that make most of the environments look quite pixelated a bigger screen. The framerate is locked at about 30-35 fps in the world and only 15 in the battles. If they're not making a true remake, they could at least adjust the old one a little more.
When it comes to gameplay, it is pretty good. The battle system and the materia features are quite enjoyable. The only minor issue I had with those is that some animations take way too long but at least they look cool. Controls in the world are quite outdated and a little crappy at times but it's nothing that makes the game a worse experience. The only bigger complaint I have about the game is the minigames. While a few work just right, some of them are annoying, especially since the buttons are named [OK], [CANCEL] etc. instead of their actual names and you might get lost.
Still, it's a really great game that everyone should play all the way through. Let's just hope that Square will give us a true remake this game deserves someday... hopefully not smartphone-exclusive.

Please keep in mind I write this after 100%ing the game and getting most achievements: I did not enjoy my time with this game. I didn't enjoy it and it makes me sad. I got the game bundled with Guacamelee so I may compare both games even if they're pretty different.
Since the first time I opened this game I felt like it was a labour of love. Everything about it is so nice. I just couldn't bring myself to like it.
Let's divide this thing because that's what cool people do, I'll keep it spoiler free:
- Story: I read about this game and everyone seems to love the story. I have to admit it has some parts that gave me feels but they felt like simple tear jerkers just for the sake of it. Dust wants to be this interesting character who I can't give a♥♥♥♥♥♥about. I couldn't care about any of the characters, really. The plot wasn't anything unique and I could see every twist coming from a mile away. It's a story good enough for it to give you a sense of purpose but that's as far as it goes. The last episode didn't even achieve that. I didn't know why I was doing what I was doing.
- Graphics: Game looks good, there's no denying that. I don't specially dig the art style but everything looks great. Your abilities are all flashy and will make the entire screen glow with beams of different colours... All the characters have nice portraits and
. The snow was great.
- Gameplay: This is my main problem with the game. Most of the time I don't care about the rest of the game as long as the gameplay is fun. It wasn't. What do you do in this game? You go around exploring, retrieving items, killing hordes of monsters, taking quests and completing them. Pretty standard, right? All of this is ruined by the difficulty levels in the game.
- Exploration:  Exploring is pretty nice, most areas feel different (except caves, endless caves) or, at least, look different. This, however, becomes a problem when you have to walk past the same area for the 3rd time to do some quest or get to some guy. The areas in this game are far too big and don't have enough quick travel spots. The fact that your character moves at snail's pace doesn't help either.  Your only ways of moving fast are limited by energy or whatever limits you from spinning in the air like a madman. This means you can only move quickly for a few seconds before stunning yourself or hearing the annoying no energy sound effect. You know how to fix this? Play in easy difficulty! Unlimited energy! Unlimited rolling around! WRONG - You don't want to play on easy mode.
- Combat: The fighting is far too easy. There are too many enemies and all of them are too weak. You end up feeling like this monster who kills everything in its path with no effort. All of your abilities have a really nice look to them, they're cool - you're cool. But they don't feel right, everything is so flashy yet it gets boring after the 10th time you see the same ability being used, which is the first few minutes of gameplay, considering you have like 4 different attacks. You pretty much have all of your abilities after 10 minutes into the game, after that all you get are boring stats that make you hit harder or have more hp. Yes, you unlock a few new things but they all do exactly the same thing - kill everything on sight. What can you do to make combat more interesting? Play on a higher difficulty. Do I wanna do that? No! This is more of personal preference but I don't want to fight boring monsters with even more damage and hp. There's dozens of enemies at any given time and all of them are just pieces of meat waiting to be whacked. Even the bosses die in seconds to simple attacks, if you ignore all their fancy lights and explosions. There were a few good parts where they introduced interesting enemies that had some mechanic to deal with them, like counter attacking or whatever... But those were really rare or died far too fast anyways. I wish the game had less enemies but more fun to fight.
- Questing: The quests in this game were pretty standard. Pick this up. Kill this monster. Find my dog. Find my brother. Bring me three bird feathers... They all had a little lore in them and made characters evolve in some way. Some quest chains were long and interesting... They move you around the map and tell you where to go next. Standard. The game has a few hidden secrets that I'd count as quests. There are hidden hints around that will lead you to them. Some of these secrets were the best part about the game, in my opinion. I wish the game had more quests about thinking a little bit, like the 2-3 secrets, instead of about bringing your friend some book you borrowed. You'll also find a few challenges hidden around the world. The first one I found I thought it was great, had to draw a little map and everything... But the rest were boring and annoying at times.
- Unfinished stuff?: The game has some things that look like things that seemed like a good idea some time during development and then were left in there. There's a crafting system I used literally once. The economy is ruined because of how materials for crafting are obtained (they drop, you sell them, you don't craft anything, you get money), you have so much gold and nothing to spend it on. The leveling up system is boring and uninspired. There's one enemy that silences your furry companion but past the tutorial for such enemy I didn't get silenced a single time during my entire playthrough, even if I was just running past enemies and taking hits. All of this could be interesting but NOPE.
Looking back, the game wasn't bad. Even during my playthrough I forced myself to finish the game because I knew inside the game was trying to be good. The difficulty, however, ruined the game for me. Not only it made exploring painful and boring, but it also made the combat repetitive and not challenging.
You know what Guacamelee did right (well, it wasn't an original idea either)? The abilities you unlocked both helped you explore and fight. In this game you unlock double jumps and other platforming skills but they don't apply to combat. This means you fight the same way 1 hour into the game or 10 hours in. In Guacamelee the last ability you unlock gives you a much faster way to move around and makes it fun, too (and if you 100% the game you can literally fly anywhere!). ♥♥♥♥ damage boosts, ♥♥♥♥ double jumps. Give me a flying kick or something cool.

When I purchased this game, I was expecting an ordinary sort of game to just kill time. And while it certainly did just that, it was also so much more.
The game is a sort of Metroidvania style beat-em-up RPG. You play as Dust, who has just woken up to find himself confronted by a talking sword and a flying creature named Fidget, as he tries to remember who he is.
The gameplay itself is very simple and becomes slightly more complex as the game progresses. I played using a keyboard on a MacBook Pro and found the game easy to control. Movement is done with the WASD keys and attacking is done with JKL, and SPACE jumps.
To compliment the gameplay, there is also the option for different difficulties, ranging from a casual mode to an extremely difficult one. I played through the casual mode first and it's very good if you just want to enjoy the story and not worry so much about how many hits you're taking.
Aside from the different difficulty modes and controls being well done, the game looks beautiful. The various areas are large, beautiful, and fun to look at. I often found myself revisiting places just to admire the backgrounds and all the little details in them. The characters look wonderful as well, with a very Disney-esque style that is very appealing.
They are also quite well written. A lot of the characters seem very realistic and the main characters are especially so and relateable to boot.
I'm sure there is stuff I'm forgetting, but overall, this is a game that I can't help but recommend.
The only downsides I have to mention would be a few glitches I encountered during cutscenes, but there was nothing really game-breakingly bad, just minor annoyances.

It is a perfect game for those who want to start grasping the adventure genre. Other games of the genre can be too hard (with puzzles), too long or too crazy (with their story), but "Belladonna" is very well written, it has a few logical puzzles, pretty characters and backgrounds. So it's perfect for a taste of what is an adventure game.
On the other hand, for adventure games veterans this game might seem too short (only an hour or so) and like a missed opportunity to make more environments, implement more puzzles, characters and dialogues. But after all this game was made by one person - Niklas Hallin. So that explains the game's length.
Despite the fact that this game is short and a little too easy for those who eat adventure games for breakfast, "Belladonna" has a very unique style, it looks pretty and it's easy to get attached to the main character - she's nor good nor evil and that adds some depth to the overall feeling.
Ah, and one other thing - the developer himself wrote somewhere on his website that his work is highly influenced not only by other video games, but also by literature. I can say that it really feels, especially while reading the pages torn from "Belladonna's" characters diaries.
All in all, i can highly recommend this game for people who value atmosphere, characters and story in each game. And those, who like only long and/or hard puzzle adventures might as well look elsewhere.

In a very basic nutshell Belladonna is a fun, although short point&click adventure experience.
The story, without spoiling too much, takes place in a old seemingly abandoned castle somewhere in Europe.
You wake up in the castles basement surrounded by ghoulish scientific experiments and you soon realize to be one of those experiments. A living corpse basically.
As you suffer from videogame amnesia, not really surprising considering that you have clockwork machine in you're head and being dead, you must explore the castle to find out what took place there.
Gameplay is what you would expect from a point and click. Point. Click.
The game will have you to also combine items you find in the level as one would expect.
Some puzzles are present, but they are not that challenging.
The story is nothing special, but it is enjoyable and I found myself to wanting to know more on what's going on in the castle. Although there's one part of the game which a lot of people on the internet will hate, I know I did :'(
The visuals are very well made and really help to set the mood in to the game.
If you like point and clicks I see no reason on not getting this, well it is a bit short so do keep that in mind.
And if you are uncertain you can view my let's play of the game here if that helps you.

This game is quite wonderful with some small annoyances. I've seen reviews giving it a thumbs down after only 10 or so hours of gameplay saying that it has no depth...they are very mistaken. This is a game that is quite easy to start playing, still quite easy to become rather good at but there are always another level of strategy for you to explore. This is the kind of game where you can't do it all by math and you can't do it all by gut feeling, you have to have a combination of both to be a successful player. Weigh your aggression with your analytic skills and you'll soon be a worthy opponent.
Something that I do feel is annoying is that you have to buy the different teams one by one, but on the other hand you can pick the game up for free for your android or ios pad or phone with one of the teams available and the games constantly comes up for sales. You don't need to have many teams to become a good player or enjoy the game.
The different teams are very different from eachother but still very balanced. There are some combinations where you feel that one of the teams have an advantage but you don't know what team the other guy is going to choose so you can't really plan for that.
All in all, this game is worth your time if you want a relaxing game that require you to think while playing rather than react to what is blinking on the screen.

This has got to be the first game I actually felt like my choices made a difference in the story. Sure, the story must end somewhat the same for all players due to the imminent sequel but the middle of the game, the journey seems to change to players. Talking to others who played it and hearing which missions they have done because of it, I feel like playing it again just so I can go and play to see what I missed out on. I loved the ambiguity of it. I was always left wondering if I was doing the right thing or not and that is important. The world and characters are not black and white.
It is mature, with lots of nudity, swearing and violence but it never felt forced, everything moved at a natural pace and thats very welcome. Even the side mission/quests dont feel like they deviate from the main storyline, something that I always felt lots of games do wrong (Example: Mr. Freeze waiting hours for Batman while he goes♥♥♥♥♥♥around beating up thugs and looking for riddler trophies around Arkham city, for instance).
I ended up reading some of the books while on vacation away from my PC and it was really great getting to know more of the characters and it definitively made me rethink some of my choices.
If there are any complaints to the game, is that the tutorial is its worst enemy. What a chore for someone that had no experience with the game mechanics but after that, it was a delight in game design. Also, playing this game as an intro to the Witcher series, it gave me no idea who some characters where and why I should care for them. Something that the first game might have shown but I got around to it by reading the books, which by the way, are an excellent companion. CDProject Red made an excellent adaptation of the world in the game.
The Witcher series might not have been on my radar but The Witcher 3 is now my most anticipated game in a long while.
If any of this sounds good to you, GO PLAY IT. NOW.

I can't help feeling this game is actually artistically important. It's one of the best little gaming-as-satire-of-gaming meta-commentaries I've seen, which gives it a very great distinction as one of maybe two or three times I've seen it attempted at all. It's not FUN, really--but it's nice to see more games trying to do something other than just having fun.

I like it. Im a big fan of dungeon delves and its even better with co-op. Its weird, its stylish, its got the strange fantasy humor I enjoy. The world has this neat dark fantasy cyberscape vibe which I really dig.
The combat is a little clunky feeling at first, but once you learn the moves its not bad - simple, but not bad. This is also where the bulk, at least from what Ive seen with my 2 hours in the game, of the difficulty lie. Combat. There are traps here and there - and some sudden dangers that show up - but mostly the difficulty comes from properly managing your very small inventory of replenishment items and fighting smart (pretty standard for roguelikes). My only problem was being out of power/stamina/whatever-they-call-it seemingly all the time - now I know the stronger the attacks you use the quicker it depletes, but it seems like relying on normal, weak attacks just takes too long to kill anything and puts you at too much risk.
Overall, my first impression is that the game is very neat and fills a co-op void thats been empty for me for a long time. The combat controls could maybe be tweaked to feel a little more fluid - but it doesnt stand in the way of enjoying the game, least not for me.
Id say if you like dungeon crawlers and you have a few pals to play along with - and you dont mind perma-death - give it a whirl. Its alot like a 3d Magicite/Roguelands, so if you are a fan of those, you cant go wrong here. =)
On a side note: I think alot of the negative reviews are coming from folks who were expecting something else than what this game actually is...

I really wanted to like this game. I even downloaded a blank BIK movie file to replace those stupid, obnoxious, SCREAMING non-skippable (What were you thinking, developers?) movies in the beginning.
But I don't. It's got a lot of very interesting elements to it that could have made for a great game, but then the execution has some stupidity like the thing I listed above that just destroy the game for you. I'll give two more examples:
The tutorial is terribly incomplete. It doesn't tell you how to actually start trade routes, or that you're just going to lose if you don't pick a world power as your starting country the first time through, because you don't know how to check to see which countries make the most, or that you need to tell your merchant to trade with them. Instead you'll just go broke and get irritated with the game.
Hell, the tutorial doesn't even tell you how to make your armies board ships.
After you get past that part, even on normal it was pretty easy.
The problem is after you've invested 6 or more hours into a game only to realize that your king won't necessarily have an heir. Ever. Especially if he became a king too late, because his age is randomly decided when the old king dies. And you can't assign an heir to someone else.
It seems in THAT situation, after you've conquered Ireland, Scotland and half of Europe, your oldest warrior (Who was previous immortal and you've invested a ton of time into building up XP and increasing hsi skills) now becomes King, will age and die, and a bunch of the nobility steals your land.
It specifically said:
"Unfortunately we've lost vast amounts of land."
What it meant was:
"You lost all the land you'd conquered since the game started so the game basically reset from the +30 you had to the single province you started with, only now you can't take it back because you built WTF-walls-of-doom around all of them and manned them with elite longbowman so you might as well quit this stupid game and go play something that won't intentionally ruin itself with something over which you've no control."
Maybe it's got positive reviews cuz some people like that. I do not. Hopefully my warning will help others who don't either.

The main problem with this game is the disconnect between you and your equipment. Your character feels light, you can run and jump around with ease. The weapons seem to be all heavy, which means you risk taking damage while swinging the sword. As a result, it never feels like you are exchanging blows with the enemy. What you are doing is running away from them and then swinging at them, hoping that it will land. Usually when the attacks actually do land, you end up taking a ton of damage.
Like most people my main draw to the game was the fact that it was a Wind Waker looking Dark Souls you could play with friends, but in Dark Souls you are usually able to tell how fast you can attack with a weapon. The starting swords in this game float around and feel super heavy even though they look like they could easily swipe back and forth.
Overall I would recommend this game if there wasn't so much risk involved in just swinging the sword, but right now it just doesn't feel like your character has ever wielded weapons of this caliber before.

I'm beginning to think The Binding of Isaac could sit comfortably as one of my top 10 favorite games of all time. Over the last few weeks, I've played about 35 hours of it, and I plan on playing it at least that much more in the months to come. It's hard to name a roguelike that is better designed than Isaac. Spelunky (of course) comes to mind. It's widely considered the best there is, or ever was, in the genre. I would mostly agree from a macro-level perspective, but in my personal opinion, Isaac is better overall. Both games are really hard, and one could spend hundreds of hours in both, but most people won't, because these games take a slightly masochistic personality to have any fun with.
Starting a new life is always the most exciting moment in The Binding of Isaac. The level layouts, enemy orders, secret rooms and loot are completely unpredictable, and you never know what item combinations you will end up with. In this way, it is similar to how FTL makes me feel in the beginning: Like the possibilities are wide open, and my slate is completely clean; there is nothing but upward potential for me to be better than last time. And then, of course, the adversity starts and I have to react dynamically to greater and greater obstacles with what ever items I find myself with. The game ebbs and flows. Sometimes I think I have no chance of finishing the current level, but I rally and make it 5 layers deeper with a chance to kill Mom. Conversely, I could get overconfident too early, and die because I didn't dodge a fly in the middle of the caves after a great start. Each life is different, and as I said, I plan on playing much more.

This game will keep your fingers close to the WASD keys and the arrow keys for shooting your Tears. It rewards those who know how to exploit the RNG, and punishes those for stupid mistakes. Don't let it's apperance and art style draw you away. Though some items and such may be but crude childhood humor or downright disgusting, ignoring that fact and laughing along and seeing how interperative this game will hook you in.
If you can, buy the base game before hooking yourself in to the DLC. You'll appreciate the change the DLC adds to the base games once a few tens of hours have been plugged away on it.

DISCLAIMER: I understand this was made almost entirely by one man and appreciate that, however I feel like a review should be based on whether or not I liked the game, not whether or not it was impressive considering the development process.
For a game that pushes RPG elements, it's sad to see that the story was so poor. I really wish I was exaggerating when I said that this is easily one of the poorest stories I've ever played through, and it was so hamhanded about trying to force you to care that in the end I lost all interest entirely and finished the game more out of a test of my patience than out of anything else. The voice work and animations are similarly weak, meaning that any time spent outside of the core gameplay was boring and tedious.
This is a shame, because in my eyes the gameplay is quite strong. The boss battles aren't spectacular and there is a bit of balance work required (without any significant work I was able to Dust Lightning Storm every battle quickly and easily), but the core elements of the platforming and combat were really quite engaging. If it weren't for the fact that the story was forced so heavily upon the player which broke the flow of enjoyment so consistently, this would be a recommendation.

I have been playing this game for 13 hours and i feel like ive only started. I don't want it to end!! This game grips you from minute one, with a well told sotry, intense gameplay and, frankly, quite difficult combat that will have parrying and dodging like your life depends on it. Monster encounters are difficult as packs of enemies try and surround you whilst you wait for your spells to be back up. I find everyting about this game excelent. The alchemy and crafting system seem a little complicated at first but give depth to the game, also, i feel this game is one of the only rpgs i've played where potions do actually matter. It's not like skyrim where you can chug 10000 potions to keep yourself alive, in this game you have to prepare for battles either by deciding what potions to consume to give you an edge or where to hit a monster to do the most damage. You need to make some research, and surprisingly this detective style work is one of the elements which make this game so real and immersive. You can't go in killing everything, you must think your strategy and use all the elemnts the devs give you to your advantage. Also, your choices matter... A LOT. I've found myself in situations where I wished I hadn't killed that guy or gone through another path, there are very tough decisions and you must face the consequences, good or bad.
In conclusion, great game from very promising devs. Can't wait for The Witcher 3.

... and there I was thinking "Soccer with super moves? How rediculous! It kills the realism and ruins the game."
Then I saw the game on sale and thought I'd pick it up nevertheless just to try it out -- I was hooked. 5+1 players (of which 1 to 5 human players), 6 + 6 minute matches (by default, can be adjusted), one ball, and no referee. Havoc and slide tackles soon become a norm.
The gameplay is smooth and the AI offers a pretty decent challenge for starters. A grinder like me takes on the challenge and plays only on pro level (until platinum gets unlocked). You will be crushed for a few matches but once you get the gist you'll soon become a pro yourself and winning a game becomes a walk in the park. Challenging and fun at the same time.
These super moves, there aren't that many but they add an element of surprise to the game. Your breakthrough with the ball may be short lived as your opponent just stole the ball using super magnet, and now he's ready to catapult the ball to your goalie's face! Literally, as you watch your goaltender fall back on his butt after getting hit right between the eyes by the ball that is now slowly but surely bouncing accross the goal line. So you retaliate right from the kickoff by swiftly blasting through their defences without losing the ball and launch an extremely swerved shot right past their goalie, and you do this three times in a row withing 30 seconds (realtime) -- and you get rewarded with three achievements by doing so.
The way achievements are incorporated into the game is one of the best ways I've encountered. In the beginning of each match you get a suggestion of what to do in a match to earn fame poins, like "win without using slide tackles" or "score three more goals than your opponent", and each one of these is tied to a steam achievement so gradually you end up getting them all simply by playing the game (and completing the given challenges of course). Play as a pro and you'll get the medium and easy level achievements, too.
Soundscape is good, the intro track is catchy, and the controls are pretty intuitive except that I swapped the left and right swerve buttons. This is one of those games where local co-op supports up to 5 players so you can either team up against the AI or go rogue with elbow tacktics and have fun, yet painful brawl on a virtual soccer field. Wether you win or you lose, it's still fun.
The one thing that annoys me the most in this game is tesla chopper flying sound, but this is just a personal opinion.
All in all, this game is definetly worth checking out if you're even remotely into soccer / football. It is simply fun!

The music in NecroDancer was more than made to compliment the gameplay; it was made to be a key part of gameplay, as well as to simply enjoy - whether that be in-game or on it's own. You can even implement your own music if you so choose, furthering the possibilities.
Now, as for the overall gameplay, I'll make this simple:
- Do you like dungeon crawlers?
- Do you like Rougelikes?
- Do you like pixelated graphics?
- Do you like kick♥♥♥♥♥soundtracks?
- Do you like Metal or EDM?
If you said yes to any of these, I suggest giving NecroDancer a try.
If you said yes to a 2 or more of these, I HIGHLY recommend giving NecroDancer a try.
If you said yes to all of these, why the hell haven't you played it yet?! This game was made for you!

After finished the first Act, I found mysfelf desperate for more and more. Good thing is - I received it. More and even more goodness.
Flaws? Not many. There are some things that I would have liked to be a tad different. For example:
1) Conversations with your pals; sometimes they feel a bit plain. I mean, unlike Mass Effect, for example, where you usually have more possibilities on this matter, here conversations more often fall into some questions regarding the (politic) plot and nothing more. No hanging out or anything like it, for the most part.
2) Final Boss Fight; too damn easy. For real.
3) Animations; very few of them. Maybe it's asking too much, but still.
And that's all I can think about right now. Minor things that don't really♥♥♥♥♥♥all over the experience at all. The Witcher 2 is, overall, a really great, great game. Story is quite good - with twists and all. Characters are easy to like or hate and the end leaves you hanging at the very edge, gasping for another final adventure - The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt. F*ck yeah I am ready for diving into that.

No problems on a win 7 e-350 1.6 GHz laptop with HD 6310, though the game did crash a lot near the end of my game. Sadly you can't bind keys, so the speed up and slow down button didn't work for me.  Used alt+ctrl+left mouse button to slightly fast forward thru the intro. I consider this game Total War with worse graphics or a simple version of Crusader Kings. I got this game for $2.50.
Since everything is random at the start, there is less incentive to play the other nations. Your king and his heir's stats are random, starting resources and initial buildings are random, and who you might be at war with is random. You can restart a new game to get favorable results. Didn't notice any difference between the early, high, and late periods. My army did very well on auto resolve, so I didn't bother playing the tactical battles. There are 168 provinces to take over.
Even though the game looks complicated it really is not. Your hired advisors don't die, as long as they are not related to the king, enemy spies, or Pope. There is no maintenance for your army, so basically you will have your best men available, though your army is capped at 9 units and 4 siege units. My first real game I played as Sweden, so I had 2 armies of 6 to 7 Vikings, and 2 or 3 archers. Looking at the stats, I think Vikings are best bang for the buck with only axe building needed. At the start of my game I had me and my kids be merchant and trade with the most powerful nations. Plundering and capturing prisoners is also a good way to earn money early in the game. Spent money on kingdom power first. Eventually had 2 clerics, 1 spy, 2 merchants, and 4 marshals. Had to use another spot for cleric because my main one always became pope. Builder and landlords aren't worth the space, since you should eventually have too much money and nothing you need to spend it on. Eventually you probably could do without your merchants. I had a run of bad luck where none of my kings would produce an heir. I did get a civil war once, but I just reloaded. I think if you are at peace and your king dies without an heir, then your empire should be fine.
I did like when my princess was married to another country's prince and their king die; I would sometimes be able to get territory out of it. However, being isolated is better than having some sort of dealings with other countries in the long run, because either they will drag you into their wars or if you break them, it reduces kingdom power and might negatively affect relations with other countries.
Annoying to have rebels pop up because of the nostalgia factor. I usually ignored them, but once you are churning out books just have a cleric solve that problem. During the early middle of the game, I got the resources for most of the kingdom advantages and that is when you really get over powerful. There is a long middle to end game where my 2 to 6 armies were going from province to province and having my cleric convert the conquered population.
The enemy AI is average at best. Enemy spies are the only thing the AI is very good at. Annoying when you keep hiring enemy spies, just pray that your master spy isn't an enemy spy. I think it caused my generals to rebel and cause me to lose some provinces, but that was late in the game. However, it can't fight tactically. Your general gain additional skills when they level up. Having Tactics gives you a really big advantage. Since you can tell the enemy's path, you can instantly put up fixed defenses and easily win. Also when you go to the enemy castles, there armies rotate thru the castle, so either you can pick them off and they are dead or they come to your fixed defenses and you bring in your 2nd army, so 2 vs 1 plus fixed defenses equals easy win.

At around 15 provinces I didn't feel like I was going to lose. I was wondering at what point they would consider me a threat. From start to finish, I was mostly able to pick and choose who and when to attack, except when the Pope wanted me to go on a crusade. However on hard, when I had 100 provinces, is when half of the remaining countries declared war on me. Fun, chaotic times, but too little, too late.
This seems like it would be a great multiplayer game or if the AI was close to human levels it would be a lot more of a challenge. If things won't so random at the start, I might have actually went through all the nations. Rate this game 7.5/10. I have high hopes for KOH 2, if that ever comes out.

This game is amazing if you like real time campaign mode, if you are more into RTS battles i'd personally recommend something else. I'd say it would've been a perfect strategy game if not for its imbalance and easy exploits which make the game too easy. It's still incredibly enjoyable but can become easily repetetive because of its lack of depth in some of it's aspects.
The game has a beautiful art-style and an overall enjoyable gameplay experience mostly early-game, when everyone is fighting to establish themselves in the world and you have to constanly pay attention to your economy, relations and the size of your army. I do have some problems with the game, which do not take away from the overall enjoyment but are rather holding the game back from reaching it's full potential.
First and foremost, the morale system is holding back the RTS battle aspect of this game massively in my opinion. Yes, it might bring realism into the game but most of the time its just annoying and boring. Battles would be much more thrilling if you just had to worry about unit counters and tactical unit movement instead of relying on the enemy retreating after 3 seconds of fighting because of your overpowered marshall skills. This forces you into exploiting the morale system and eventually makes you avoid RTS battles.
Secondly, the AI i is just too stupid. Of course i don't blame the game for this because it's just old but it's still holding the game back. When i say AI i mean the way the marshalls and diplomacy are handled. Some examples: Enemy marshalls dive into battles they can't possibly win and ignore obvious ambushes, kingdoms constantly bombard you with ridiculous requests and never want to comply with you unless you bathe them in gold you desperately need and kingdoms never know when they're losing a war and that they might have to make sacrifices to survive.
The last problem i have is with the province management. Its amazing early game trying to figuere out a strategy and at the same time fending off enemy armies but once you have established a economy and are expanding rapidly it becomes pretty much irrelevant. Late-game you only need a couple of places to replenish your army and make sure to keep rebels at a minimum but that's really it.
TL;DR
RTS campaign mode is good.
RTS battle mode is bad.
Art-style is good.
AI is bad.
Early-game is good.
Late-game is not very good.

I'm beginning to think The Binding of Isaac could sit comfortably as one of my top 10 favorite games of all time. Over the last few weeks, I've played about 35 hours of it, and I plan on playing it at least that much more in the months to come. It's hard to name a roguelike that is better designed than Isaac. Spelunky (of course) comes to mind. It's widely considered the best there is, or ever was, in the genre. I would mostly agree from a macro-level perspective, but in my personal opinion, Isaac is better overall. Both games are really hard, and one could spend hundreds of hours in both, but most people won't, because these games take a slightly masochistic personality to have any fun with.
Starting a new life is always the most exciting moment in The Binding of Isaac. The level layouts, enemy orders, secret rooms and loot are completely unpredictable, and you never know what item combinations you will end up with. In this way, it is similar to how FTL makes me feel in the beginning: Like the possibilities are wide open, and my slate is completely clean; there is nothing but upward potential for me to be better than last time. And then, of course, the adversity starts and I have to react dynamically to greater and greater obstacles with what ever items I find myself with. The game ebbs and flows. Sometimes I think I have no chance of finishing the current level, but I rally and make it 5 layers deeper with a chance to kill Mom. Conversely, I could get overconfident too early, and die because I didn't dodge a fly in the middle of the caves after a great start. Each life is different, and as I said, I plan on playing much more.

This game will keep your fingers close to the WASD keys and the arrow keys for shooting your Tears. It rewards those who know how to exploit the RNG, and punishes those for stupid mistakes. Don't let it's apperance and art style draw you away. Though some items and such may be but crude childhood humor or downright disgusting, ignoring that fact and laughing along and seeing how interperative this game will hook you in.
If you can, buy the base game before hooking yourself in to the DLC. You'll appreciate the change the DLC adds to the base games once a few tens of hours have been plugged away on it.

In
we play the role of Helen, a young woman who was staying in a small village in the amazons, until one night, fire arrows covered the skies, and she had to flee. Only to find herself the chosen one in a prophecy to save the world, or face extinction, such as many other civilizations around the globe.
The game plays exactly like your traditional adventure game, using the same mechanics we've seen dozens of times in Hidden Object games, but this time without the "Hidden Objects", which makes it a Point & Click. (I guess?!)
The puzzles are really basic and easy, and this is fantastic for the casual young gamers who just start their journey in these adventures. Those looking for a challenge, don't bother looking. Changing difficulty settings don't help either, as only removes hints and tips, as you would expect!
The player adventures into the deep jungle and the more we advance, the more we enter the underworld. Helen must save the humanity, and as far as the story goes, it's simple and reasonable enjoyable, with some good ideas.
Visually, it matches the basic storyline, it's good, but not great. It's not the best atmospherically, but it does create a really good ambient surrounding the native rituals and puzzles around it.
From deep Amazonian sacred temples, to a city above clouds, and even underwater, we must find clues and special artifacts to defeat the ultimate evil that has been possessing the native villagers. To help, a few NPC's join in nice conversations, to give you some extra hints. Not that you could need any... There are no surprises when comes to the whole game, but it's a nice short adventure for anyone who has a few hours to spend, or enjoys adventures in general.
In technical terms, we don't get ourselfs any treat, but it's nice to see wide resolution games none the less. Although there is no custom resolution, the game runs natively at 720p, but anyone can scale to whatever resolution the player sees fit.
As for design, it's just like your traditional 2D that gives a fantastic impression of 3D, many times using CGI for object movements. With good and vibrant colors, they are nice assets, in which
have been improving in that area. This was one of their first games after all.
Overall
is a nice and simple Point & Click game, that tries to take you into a fantastic journey through South America.

Black Rainbow is a mostly storyless casual adventure game (but not a hidden object game), in which we spend a few hours running around in a beautiful scenery collecting junk with the sole purpose of getting more junk. Despite this, it is quite enjoyable, especially for a lazy afternoon.
While Steam store says Black Rainbow is a hidden object game, it has no hidden object elements whatsoever: this is strictly a casual first-person point ‘n’ click adventure.
The biggest strength of Black Rainbow is that it is an incredibly simplified, but fun scavenger hunt. We spend the entire game looking for random objects either to find more objects or to start some puzzle. While this may sound repetitive and boring, this simple nature and the great puzzle design result in a fun and easy time-waster.
The game, technically, has a story. Only technically, because it has no real start or conclusion, we just know that we need to thwart a generic evil force, after which the game simply stops. This means that you will almost surely forget about its existence fast, but for what it is worth, Black Rainbow is pleasant enough to recommend to any casual gamer.

In a different review, it is said that Kopanito All Star Soccer would be a mixture of "Mario Strikers" and "Sensible Soccer". From own experience, it cannot be accounted for the first one, but for the second. Strictly speaking, what the developers might have done is commuting the x and y axis and put the Sensible Soccer AI up again. In addition, the banana shot style and GFX remind us at least a little bit of "Micro Prose Soccer".
As so often, this impressions may be seen as a strength and also as a weakness of the game. The strength is nostalgy, the weakness lacking complexity, as it refers to 20+ years old titels. In deed, from todays perspective, it looks like an only half complete game:
-  regardless of the four difficulty levels and the teams chosen, the AI reacts always in the same way with a difference set only in attacking aggressivity depending on the difficulty level (reducing the player's time to (re)act).
- There are procedures to invoke goals regardless of difficulty (as in Sensible Soccer) that make the game (as long as the player intends to win) extremely repetitive.
- Some parts just seem to be incomplete and terribly unnecessary, for example the "long shots": There is no chance of passing the ball over long distances, instead there are straight shots invoked in mid-air that almost cannot lead to goals (0,2% propability) as they are harmless, automatically directed towards the middle, but fill the player's skill bar for a special ability... A bit strange, this shots should be more refined such that the player can show his/her skill performing them as this game is praised as "skill based" by the developers. Since this feature is well established in Sensible Soccer, it's even a minus compared to a 22 years old game!
Since this can be, in some way, read as a comparison review to former games, we'd like to conclude it by stating that the special abilities, such as SUPER SHOT, ELECTROSHOCK, FREEZING, WIND MASHINE (behind the goal) and last but not least the BALL MAGNET can clearly be seen as inventions and novelties to improve this kind of arcade genre, but a general recommendation looks different and shall only by given for a 70%+ sale as already stated in other reviews.

I bought Mafia III Digital Deluxe during the Steam Winter Sale. I had finally brought myself to buying the game after seeing multiple reviews, both on steam and other websites. Most reviews I saw were pointing out the negative aspects of the game, but they all basically pointed out the same things. The positive reviews on the contrary, brought up new points in each different review. I gave the game a shot, and after 24 hours, I completed the main Mafia III storyline. The storyline I found to be a strong narrative with even better characters. Lincoln Clay is such a great and dynamic character that actually behaves like a human. Sal Marcano on the other hand, is not such a strong antagonist. While your whole goal is to kill him (as per usual to kill the antagonist in most games), he is hardly developed as a character. Throughout the entirety of the Mafia III storyline, there are about 4 very important moments with Sal. That aside, I'll get to the gameplay. The gameplay is great, with some solid shooting. The stealth takedowns are a beautiful, bloody mess. The downside however is that there is only a handful of takedowns. The missions are extremely repetitive. I had seen an IGN review which said that the missions are fun to do the first 2-3 times but got boring at around the 20th time. While it may seem like an exaggeration, they aren't off by very much. You repeat a lot of missions up to 18 times. Those missions result in the majority of the gameplay. The enemy AI has a lot of speaking involved while you go over to attack them. A lot of them repeat the same lines. Bottom line is, the game is stupidly repetitive. However, do I reccomend Mafia III? Yes, absolutely. I especially reccomend the digital deluxe edition if it is on sale for atleast 60% off. (By the way, the Sign of Times DLC Storyline is a lot like L.A. Noire, for any of you fans of the game out there.)

A fun and addictive turn-based strategy game that is easy to learn, but takes some serious thinking to master. I particularly like that you can have several games going at once, which alleviates some of the tedium of waiting for your opponents to make a move (the challenge DLC also gives you something to do between turns). You should know that the asynchronous nature of the multiplayer means that it could be a full day or even longer before you see the other player's turn (think chess-by-email for comparison), so the actual games could take a while, but the nice thing about the design of the game is that you can play it in short bursts. I also really like that the multiplayer is cross platform against IOS and Android, so the game has a decently sized playerbase. What's even better is that all of your games and DLC transfer over, so a game you've started on PC can be continued on Android, for example. Another great thing is that at least some of the achievements seem to transfer over, as I won a game on android, then when I logged onto Steam, the achievement for winning a game unlocked. Also, the game has an icon in the system tray that alerts you that it is your turn if you leave the game running in the background, which is a fantastic idea. My only gripe is that there is no local multiplayer, as this game seemes like it would be well suited for that.

To paraphrase Hyperbole and a Half: "Burn ALL the things!"
Little Inferno is a curious way to waste a few hours. You have a fireplace. You order toys and other objects from catalogs not to play with, but to burn. Sometimes, the mailman brings letters from the neighbors. You'll burn those, too.
It's a little bit creepy and, yes, entertaining. Is there more to this game? Yes. No. Both, I think.
Fans of Kyle Gabler's earlier work, "World of Goo", will recognize a similar smug poke at the things we take for granted in this always-online age, but I don't mean to suggest that there is somehow more of a game here than "burning stuff." Suffice to say that there are varying levels of interaction going on with the things you burn. I don't think that's a spoiler. It's game enough that there is a beginning, a middle, and an end.
However, the artistic style and soundtrack are the true star of this game. My daughter walked in on me playing, and within 10 seconds she asked "Is that a new game from World of Goo?" Gabler's artwork and music are immediately recognizable.
Just as in "World of Goo", the art of Little Inferno defines a warm and unsettling world, where a fun game with simple mechanics is just the exposed surface of a much larger world gone awry. Or... not! These games can be played by a 5-year-old, but jaded adults will naturally seek deeper meaning.

A tech system that allows you to choose where to spend your precious points on a few different pathways after ever tech tree level up is nice as it allows many different combinations and a slightly different playthrough each time due to the randomness of options provided to you.
While none of us can yet comment on how the game will last versus Paradox's other offerings like Europa Universalis 4, or Crusader Kings 2 - to me this game does feel like a good addition to the realm of their grand strategy offerings. Really looking forward to playing further in to it after work, and especially once all the mods begin running amok.

I wish steam had a "mixed" review, something in the middle. As it stands I'll put "not recommended." Buy with caution, or not. It's entirely up to you and this is simply my thoughts.
This is subject to change depending on whether or not the game gets updated in a meaningful way that addresses some of the negatives it has on offer.
I'll try to avoid any comparisions to Dark Souls as it's unfair and Necropolis is quite unique. My disposition to the Souls series would be unfair to this game, and so I'll try not to let that weigh in too heavily on my review here.
THE COMBAT.
The game has a solid foundation that falls short in a few departments, most notably the combat. The combat is NOT like the methodical and precision timing of Dark Souls combat, with parries and counter attacks as some people have been lead to believe; it's more in line with Legend of Zelda, which is the precursor to Dark Souls combat.
A stripped down version without as much depth; attacks are floaty and unsatisfying to do. There is no commitment to swings, which leaves a lot to be desired. There's no weight, no impact, save for instances where enemies get knocked down or become staggererd,
Magic wands/ ranged weapons are fairly fun to use for a short while, but you will find enemies will rush up to you forcing you into the tedium of melee combat once again. Shields are useful only until enemies start mobbing you, which is a positive. They are strong without being too strong, and if you're not careful you can find yourself guard broken easily, resulting in being whacked in the face a few times.
THE LOOT.
The loot can range from disappointing to interesting, with a large portion of weapons being identical in moveset, damage and what I assume swing speed. The best loot is often found in metal chests or on difficult enemies, which become more and more common the further down into the Necropolis you go. You can find armour sets and powerful weapons in the golden chests that are at the start of a new level. These chests require tokens that you earn while playing the game.
There is also a merchant that stocks a variety of items you can purchase to help you on your run. Food, recipies, clothing dyes, and the occasional weapon or two. These cost gems (dyes are the exception, as they are bought with tokens), which most enemies drop upon death. There are also other merchants. They are found where treasures lie.
In addition to gems, weapons and equipment, enemies can also drop food, which is used to both heal and replenish stamina.
THE CRAFTING.
The crafting system is basic, but intuitive and (mostly, more on that below) hassle-free. To start with, you can craft basic food and
supplies like ground markings, to let you know where you've been; a helpful reminder so you don't get lost. As you progress you can purchase or otherwise obtain recipies for bombs, potions and other goodies. These are utilitarian in nature, and if you're not careful with bombs you can harm yourself and your allies!
Now, there are a couple of issues with crafting that begin to get slightly annoying as you get more resources;
1.) Crafting animation. This happens every time you craft an item. The animation lasts around 2-3 seconds, so try not to use it in combat!
2.) There is no ability to bulk-craft as far as I've noticed, so you will have to go through the crafting animation a lot the more materials you acquire.
THE WORLD/ GRAPHICS.
The world is mysterious, and can leave you curious as to the nature of the Necropolis. Why does it exist? Who made it? The game tells little, and you must figure out most of these things on your own or with very little help. Something I can really appreciate.
The levels are procedurally generated and are quite large in nature, filled with enemies, loot, traps, and pottery for your to smash, maul, and die to. The art-style is low-poly, vibrant and stylish. It looks great without overdoing it. Character models, weapons, and the environment all look stellar, but are marred by often poor looking animations, which again, detracts from the combat as a whole.
Particle effects are excellent, some equipment may have electricity on it, others fire. All of these look great and colourful, just the right amount of flashy. These usually provide light too. which is an added bonus.
CO-OP/ MULTIPLAYER.
The co-op works as you'd except. you and 3 other players, all battling for your share of loot and glory. Players can hop in and out of the session at any time, though your single and multiplayer characters are not shared. They are tied to the host's game. Progress is seperate.
When you are downed in combat, players have 30 seconds to revive you. If they do not manage to get to you in time, you are sent back through the level, without your fancy weapons. If everyone dies before others can respawn, it is game over!
When jolly co-oping, be careful not to hit your friends. Or not, you can kill them if you like. Friendly fire is on and it punishes you for bullying a lonesome enemy all at once. This leads to PvP. You can have impromptu PvP with random players or friends if you like, just don't except them to play fair. They might heal, after all.
OVERALL.
While I didn't touch on every aspect of the game, it's not without its positives, the core mechanics except combat are all fun, interesting and enjoyable. But that's the issue. The combat is the main focus of the game and indeed, you will be doing a lot of it. It just isn't fun and bogs the overall experience down.
Combat: 2/10
Exploration: 8/10
Challenge: 5/10
Level design: 7/10
Graphics: 9/10
With the right changes, combat can be fun, and I'll consider re-buying this game. As it stands, I'll put in for a refund. I will absolutely re-buy this and change my review entirely if said issues are fixed (I don't expect that to hapen. after all, it's simply my opinion on the game!)
Sorry devs. I appreciate the amount of work you put into this game but it's currently not for me.
Thanks for reading.

Blood; Designed in a time where FPS's weren't made to be taken seriously.
: For anyone who is a fan of FPS games, this is a must play. Developed by Monolith Productions and published by GT Interactive(Now known as Atari) and Eidos Interactive in 1998. One Unit Whole Blood is powered by the same engine that ran Duke Nukem 3D and Shadow Warrior.
Blood is still a favourite of many, holding heaps of unique characteristics, even to this day. Before the gaming industry really began taking itself seriously due to a very small scale market, games like this could be released that was more-so what the designer personally wanted; a crazy, fun, senseless violence filled shooter.
: You soul is shredded and palmed off to a dark god whose only reward to you was empty promises, false claims and betrayal, and whoes ultimate goal was to completely eliminate humankind. Now, the only way you can settle the score and have your revenge is blood being spilled. Zombies, gargoyles, demons, hellhounds, cultists or even innocent bystanders, none are spared from your vengeful wrath.
: Wonderful ambiance ties in perfectly with the cheesy one liners and the all round atmosphere of the game.
: As chunky as any classic game running through DOSbox. Not that many options but a decent amount for it's time.
: Running rampent through 4 episodes each filled with 8-9 maps, starting with "The Way of All Flesh" and finishing with "Dead Rockoning" you face up against a vast range of foes(e.g; Zombies, Cultists, Hellhounds etc.) with a charming array of unique weapons(e.g; Pitchfork, Sawed-off shotgun, Voodoo Doll etc.) my personal favourite being the iconic pitchfork. It's senseless gore, non-serious plot, classic FPS horror.
: On par with Doom and Shadow Warrior, it's the classic pixely goodness you've come to know and love. It was amazing for it's time, and honestly, it still is.
: A classic must play for anyone into the FPS genre or just after some difficult gore-filled fun.

If I could give it a neutral review, I would. I think the best way to describe the game is
.
, like there was very little to it. The worst part about the game is the lack of exciting sound design, and in that area, the game is extremely weak. If I recall correctly, there's music in the menu and then there's barely anything to be heard during the game, and the crowd cheers feel unconvincing.
Some other things about the game is that it really doesn't leave a lasting impression, and to me, has a stylized but pretty unattractive character design. It's hard to identify with any of the teams when you can't get into any of their designs. I don't think any of the players even have names, and it makes it even harder to identify with any of the characters or differentiate between them. Even in soccer games, there are specific players I gravitate towards because that specific person has good stats or has done a lot in a match, but I can't even identify them here.
pretty much plays like you would expect it to, but it's nothing to get excited over. It controls solid, it feels pretty responsive, there's not much else to say about it. Other than that though, it painfully lacks variety. If you've played it once, you've played the whole game. To some degree, the gameplay mechanics feel too simplistic, actually. I don't even think different teams have different statistics or player stats.
A thing the game advertises is that there are crazy super powers but none of them feel meaty or anything. You'd think if there are super powers, they'd feel impactful and special with some flair, but instead they feel like they fall short of being spectacular and impressive and end up feeling lackluster and disappointing.
. Far from it, actually. The problem is that they don't
special in any way, and the game doesn't even try to make a big deal about them at all.
There's just a lack of flair in every aspect of the game, and makes the whole game feel lackluster when it feels like it has potential for something really impressive. It's another one of those games that could use some variation, especially in the teams. An example of where balance doesn't mean it's fun. The game lacks identity and just feels really barren, to the point where I could say it completely lacks any atmosphere whatsoever. The lack of music and overall excitement each match makes it hard to play the game for very long sessions, and I tried to play it a lot, I swear- but it was just unenjoyable.
It's just everything else that really kills it for me.
There's a lot of things that could help the game build a stronger identity or sense of replayability. More modes, a cutesy campaign tournament, more powerups, more music, more custom rules, player names, character customisation, individual character stats and specialties- there's a lot that could be (or could have been) done.

There is an evil force threatening to take this world, and it would seem that you are not just an ordinary person but one who is chosen. You will use items around you, and solve puzzles that block your way, the only question is will you be fast enough, and smart enough to survive.
Graphically I have to say that for the most part you are looking at the middle of the road game, there are times where some of the scenes look a bit dated, but it's definitely not going to stop you from playing the game, and the puzzle parts to the game look pristine, and once you figure out what the solution is, you will see that graphically this game will suffice. I think my biggest issue, graphic-wise, is the character models of those you meet, that's when the game looks dated, or perhaps the better way to put it is that all the models look fuzzy/blurry. They just don't seem to actually blend in with the rest of the game.
The music in the game is subtle but definitely feels like a part of the game. There's also the occassional interaction with other characters, which I am glad to see are voiced, and the voices work with the characters.
The controls of the game are really straight forward you are going to be pointing the mouse and clicking to pick up objects, to solve puzzles, and to change locations.
For the most part once you start playing the game the transition and game going along smoothly, there was only one or two times where I could not figure out what I needed to do, or how I was going to get past a certain part. There was also a refreshing variety of puzzles to sink my teeth into. The foundation of the story is something that has been used over and over again, but that did not take away from the enjoyment I had playing. I also did like the fact that if you were in an area that didn't hold any importance at the time and you clicked on the hint button it would simply tell you to leave that area, and you could rinse and repeat that action until you were in an area where you might have missed something. The other BRILLIANT part to this game is the entire time that you are playing you are adding information to your map, so if you know you have to go four screens over, or perhaps into a different part of the game, you could fast-travel. WHAT A CONCEPT!! This definitely made things easier when where I needed to go would have taken several screen changes. You also carry a journal, that for the most part I never used, but it did hold information that could prove useful when in a bind.
As much as I enjoyed my time playing this game, the overall experience was actually kind of short. I believe I spent a total of two and a half-ish hours on this game from start to finish. So in a way you are going to be hungering for me, which isn't necessarily a bad thing, but I do not believe there is a continuation to this story, at least not at the present time. So in the end this game, though short, did do its job of entertaining me, even if it was not for long, and for that I give this game an 8.3 out of 10.

Definitely felt this game deserved more love than it received.  Was buggy (but what AAA release isn't nowadays), and it wasn't the Mafia sequel everyone wanted, but i thought it did a good job of living up to that legacy.
The city is beautiful (and such a nice change to be in New Orleans).  The atmosphere is vivid and perfectly captured.  I loved the fact that it tackled racism in a realistic way, and frankly most of the characters were a lot more true-to-life than i expect out of video games.  The plot and the way it tells its story was marvelous; maybe not quite up to the level of the Illiad, but certainly more compelling than the average Hollywood blockbuster.  It helps that it's willing to tackle more issues than some safe summer blockbuster would ever dare.
Some of the accusations about the gameplay being grindy and repetitie have truth to them.  But a lot of them are optional side missions, and i personally didn't find them to be particularly worse than games from Ubi or Rockstar which basically recyle the same plot from one game to the next as well as bascially just rely on go-somewhere, kill-some-people.
The shooting is good, the driving is better than GTA, and the environment is gorgeous.  Really the only particular complaint i had was they went with a soft-focus look that i don't like.  Still think it's a gorgeous place to cruise around.  Overall, it does things differently than the average open-world game, which probably will annoy you if you stick to cookie-cutter sameness and can't enjoy anything else.  But for me, this was a really nice evolution of the genre, and i want to encourage more developers to take a couple risks like Hangar 13 did with Mafia III

This game fooled me, but in a good way. I was expecting a cute gimmick - a music game disguised as a rogue-like. Instead, I got a solid dungeon crawler with a musical twist.
Crypt of the Necrodancer is the first game to combine two of my favorite things; EDM and The Undead. The style is cute, cohesive and somehow works without jumping the shark, which is hard to do for such an odd mix.
+'s
* Gameplay is solid and difficult, but not because of the musical aspect. "Spinning Plates" and managing many simple enemy patterns together takes awareness, practice and planning.
* The beat is there as a turn-timer of sorts. By forcing the decisions to be quick, there's opportunities for mistakes (and therefore mastery/learning!)
* Several characters with different styles, rogue-like style.
* TLC put into the production value, even considering a more throwback/pixel art style.
* Soundtrack is fantastic.
-'s
* While there's a variety of characters, the game's core gameplay has to eliminate a lot of the dungeon options and items that make the full-run version fun, meaning many of the alternate characters are less interesting than the default.
* It's said before, but Aria is extremely punishing to play. This is where it truely becomes a rhythm game, but it also has the problems listed above. Not a deal-breaker, but a sore spot.
Highly recommend this if you're a fan of strange mash-ups that work, or want a dungeon delver with its own unique feel and flavor. The game holds up without the music, but is greatly enhanced by having it. :)

Commonly said to be one of the best games of all time, and probably for a good reason. Despite being made in the Playstation/Nintendo 64 era, many of the elements of FF7 still remain relevant (in other words it's like it bought one of those anti-aging-wrinkle-remover-things that are overadvertised but actually work for the most part).
In terms of what remains "unaged," the battle system is better than most turn based games in the genre, primarily because of the materia system, which allows the user to customize their character's "loadout," to a better degree than in other RPG's ("What do you mean my Priest can't learn anything other than Heal?"). While on the subject of characters, the game features nine playable characters (including representatives from the animal kingdom
), all with varying backstories and "special abilities." The story is hard to understand at first, like most RPG's, but is fairly interesting and unpredictable with all of its plot twists
(although I may have just been tricked by the wonderful music that "sets the mood").
Unlike the "FarmVille," branch of the gaming industry, this game was clearly made with love by the creators. Instead of repetitive fetch quests and every enemy being a reskinned dragon, different "mini-games" of varying design are offered throughout the plot, and most of the game's monsters have unique models. Secrets (or in other words "fancy," details) are littered everywhere, ranging from beneficial weapons to comedic text, and it's likely that most players will miss 73.12% of said secrets if they are not using a guide.
As for what is outdated (or is considered bad), the graphics are very poor in comparison to most modern games that aren't retro (I spent the first hour critizing the weirdness of Cloud's arms and later ended up trying to use a background object as a bridge). The original translators for this game weren't exactly perfect at their job, but luckily most typos were fixed in this version. As to be expected to a game of this detail, there are quite a few bugs and glitches, which remain unfixed and could be considered game-breaking in some cases, although most of the major ones can be easy to miss (unlike Skyrim without patches). Personally I have a tendancy to get bored of the repetitive random encounters, but one could argue I shouldn't be playing this game in the first place if I knew of said tendancy previously.
Overall this game retains most of it's prided aspects, but was unable to perfect the fountain of youth.
(P.S. If you are wondering, all main Final Fantasy games have independent stories, so there isn't much need to play the previous games before this one).
