Before I start reviewing this game I think it is important to state that I did not play this game when it first came out in 2004, just recently while I was looking through steam I found it was on sale and thought it was worth a shot. So there are no nostalgic feelings attached to the game which concludes that the review is not clouded by overpowered childhood memories. To my own astonishment I was positively surprised that its quiet a good game and still playable even if it is already more than 10 years old.
I think it is also important to state some other games published in this years to be able to make better comparisons and really look at games place in gaming history. Other 2004 releases are: Lords of the Realm 3, Settlers: the Heritages of Kings, Rise of Nations and Rome Total War (of course I only listed other strategy games). Moreover I think it is good to also state some milestone games in the strategy genre and their date of publish: Europa Universalis 3 2007, Crusader Kings 2 2012, Hearts of Iron 2009, anno 1701 2006 (in my opinion some of the most important strategy games for the genres development)
I initial thought that this is a great game taking into consideration that it is that old and I was convinced that the nowadays modern and good strategy games ow a lot of their success to this title. I mean every good strategy element present in modern strategy games is also present in this game. Good diplomacy, I mean it is no different than the diplomacy of Europa Universalis 3 and it also contains the main principles for the diplomacy in crusader kings 2 for example.
The occurrence of unexpected, unanticipated and shocking events that pushes the player to use different tactics and rethink his plans is present. In one of my games where i leaned heavily on my army and did not use any spice (as the game was already won because I owned more than half of Europa) the papal state succeeded in revolting all my marshals and attack in the prefect time with all his allies. İt was a hard bit of work to drive the enemies back with my unexperienced and very few armies. But his situation showed me that the general game design and tactical development worked quiet well and the game mechanic with the marshals, spies, builders, clerics and so on is well thought trought. And that is all a good strategy game needs: one well working game mechanic and in depth tactic giving part and the game is almost set to be a success.
The graphic presentation of the game is not really good taken into consideration the high standard of graphics nowadays and even compared to other games released in the same year (like Rise of Nations or the Settlers) its seen that the graphic is threatened to bee called ugly. But two points need to be considered here. First of all in strategy games often times the graphics are not that crucial for the overall gameplay experience. The best example fir this is Europa Universalis 3 or even King of Dragon Pass (where there is no graphic at all). And the other thing is that in strategy games the menu navigation and design is far more important than the graphics. And in that aspect Knights of Honors can keep up with other strategy games as the menu design is solved in a good way.
Of course the battel system and units movement is in no way as intuitive as in for example the total war series even compared to the 2004 released Rome total war.
The variety of different units, nations to play, buildings to build is present but not phenomenal executed.
Taking everything into consideration I still think this game holds a rather important place in the strategy game development history. If available for a small amount of money it is definitely recommendable.

I've been playing Knights of Honor for many years. A popular comparison would be to say this is a real time version of Medieval 2: Total War. However, there are a lot more nations and quite a bit of options. I was delighted to see this game was on steam ever since I broke the original CD I got back around 2004 or 2005.
This game is very deep with a lot to discover, but not a lot of information about what is available. For instance, if you are in the Early period, you can take control of Normandy and try to recreate the Norman conquest. Once you eliminate all English nations, a popup will appear with an option to change your name to England and get a bonus, or stay as Normandy. Also, in the (I think Late) medieval period, you can control a Spanish nation and attempt to reunite Spain.
One thing to note, there are cheat codes for this game, and there once was a very robust and active community who developed some fantastic mods. There used to be challenges for who could conquer England the fastest, beat the game with Kingdom Advantages, total conquest, etc. It's sad that this community is all but gone now since it added a lot of life and variety of the game.
This game has a huge learning curve, but once you get it, it's fairly straight forward. Develop your own strategies for running your kingdoms, building your castles, raising your armies, and conquering the world. I recommend this to any strategy lover or medieval fan.

Gameplay is straightforward: two teams start at opposite ends of the map and have to secure an objective in the middle. Whoever fills in the capture ticker unlocks a cart—earning a point— which they then escort towards the enemy spawn (à la Team Fortress 2, Overwatch, Chivalry, etc.)—earning another point if they succeed. The first team to earn 4 points wins. So you play round after round until a team can finally boast victory. The deveopers have introduced a few new modes, such as an elimination-type game which is quite interesting.
Thanks to Paladins’ simple map design you’re constantly thrust into fierce brawls for control of the objective. Environments are small: a main hallway with various pathways on either side to promote flanking and sneaky long-range picks; always watch your sides, and swivel to check behind you. Because the name of the game is the objective. You need to work together to make sure your team is capturing the point, otherwise you lose.
Paladins is a solid hero-shooter with enough nuances to differentiate itself and warrant the widespread praise it's received from players. While it suffers in the map diversity department, a fair roster of heroes and a game design that emphasizes constant brawls makes it an attractive addition to any Steam library. And hero customization through cards and items means the same hero on both teams could be fulfilling entirely different roles. By the time it releases from Beta I imagine Paladins will be great.

Necropolis is frustrating. You will die. You will die often, you will die early, and you will die when you least want to. It's all your own fault though - you rushed in, you didn't check your health, you decided eating in combat was a great idea. You zigged when you should have zagged, you thought you could take just one more monster before healing up.
Necropolis doesn't pull its punches - make one mistake, you might live; two, you're back at level 1 with only your Tokens and Codexes to show for all your troubles.
On the flip-side of that, the game allows you to - no, it expects you to - learn by trial and error. If one strategy against a monster fails, try another. Or another weapon. Or, block. Hell, run away; that's always an option.
It's a fantastic game, well recommended, but with this caveat: It is not for the faint of heart, or those who hate dying in games. Because you will die. Repeatedly.
But that's part of the fun of a rogue-like, isn't it?

Wow. This game is beautiful. The soundtrack, visuals & gameplay feed into a really relaxing and immersive experience. It reminds me of Flower or Journey. They really pull off the underwater ecosystem & the controls of the diver are really solid. I've played the first two areas thus far but it impressed me enough to merit a review after the first time playing.
Definatley recommend a controller - mouse/keyboard support through the UI was dodgy and the game feels like it was built with the controller in mind. Some interesting featuers include being able to meditate and spectate any of the wildlife in the near area + see the name of the animal you are following. You can hold onto bigger animals (like dolphins, whales & sharks) to hitch a ride / somewhat control them when holding their fin. Lastly, there are jet streams that seperate areas which reminds me a bit of the bonus levels on Sonic (the 3D levels) where you are moving around a tube trying to touch something - in this case it's pools of fish which will then glow and follow you.
Has other interesting features around ruins, teleporting to otherwordly locations & robots you find that follow you around and help with obstacles. Worth picking up if you want a solid ocean exploration / diving game or just want to relax to some of the best art style I've seen in awhile. Also, the water affects the vegetation perfectly, I know it's a small thing to call out but it really helps pull you in to the world / make it believable.
